sources.title: Robertson & Saad (2019), Spatially referenced models of streamflow and nitrogen, phosphorus, and suspended-sediment loads in streams of the midwestern United States (USGS SIR 2019-5114)
sources.why: PRIMARY source for the single most promising feature in this angle. The 2012 Midwest SPARROW total-nitrogen model covers the Mississippi/Great Lakes/Red River basins — i.e. ALL of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of Iowa's largest basins, which directly fixes the known inner-join under-count problem for multi-state basins. Spatial unit is the NHDPlus v2 catchment/reach (median catchment ~2.5 km2, 1:500K network), keyed by COMID — exactly the join key already stored per basin, and resolvable at an ARBITRARY MAP PIN via NLDI, so it satisfies the deployment target with no local history and no gauge. Output variables include incremental yield, accumulated (total) yield, delivered incremental yield and delivered accumulated yield in kg/km2/yr, source-apportioned (fertilizer, manure, fixation, atmospheric deposition, point source). Represents 2012 source inputs normalized to long-term 1999-2014 hydrology. Companion data release DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9 (ScienceBase item 5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3) holds model inputs and outputs as bulk files; public domain, no auth. CRITICAL CAVEAT to state prominently: this is a MEAN-ANNUAL model. It supplies a static between-site prior — precisely the term where all remaining headroom lives (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24) — and carries ZERO daily information, so it cannot help the 'good timer' half. Also: basin-area-accumulated yield is partially collinear with log_basin_area, which is already a feature; use delivered INCREMENTAL yield and source-share fractions to get information that is genuinely new. Note ScienceBase returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch — download via browser or the mapper export.

sources.title: USGS SPARROW Mapper — 2012 Midwest models (TN, TP, sediment, streamflow): model description and geospatial download
sources.why: The OPERATIONAL access mechanism, verified by direct fetch. Confirms predictions are at NHD catchment scale (~2.5 km2 typical), source inputs ~2012 normalized to 1999-2014 hydrology, and that outputs include incremental yield, accumulated yield, delivered incremental yield and delivered accumulated yield. Results are exportable as Excel, CSV, or geospatial dataset, plus a 'Download Geospatial Data' section carrying the full model input/output package backing SIR 2019-5114. Free, no authentication, USGS public domain. Practical route for this project: pull the CSV export for all Midwest reaches once, index by COMID, then join to each delineated basin's outlet COMID at inference time — a single static lookup, no runtime API dependency, which matters because NLDI is already an inference-time dependency and you do not want a second one. Also documents that the smallest calibration sites have drainage areas of only 10-100 km2, which is the right order of magnitude for the smaller of the ~85 Iowa sites — relevant to whether SPARROW's spatial resolution is fine enough to discriminate between our basins at all, or whether it will be near-constant across nested basin families and therefore useless as a ranking signal.

sources.title: Saad et al. (2019), Estimates of long-term mean daily streamflow and annual nutrient and suspended-sediment loads considered for use in regional SPARROW models of the Conterminous United States, 2012 base year (USGS SIR 2019-5069)
sources.why: THE CIRCULARITY AUDIT, and it must be run before any SPARROW feature is trusted in a LOFO evaluation. This report is the companion that documents the actual monitoring stations and estimated annual loads used to calibrate the 2012 regional SPARROW models, station by station. Iowa is one of the most densely monitored nitrogen states in the country, so there is a substantial prior that some of the 22 USGS sites in this project's ~85 (and the corresponding basin families) are ALSO SPARROW calibration sites. If so, SPARROW's predicted yield at those reaches is partly a fitted value of our own target, and a LOFO fold that holds out that basin family is NOT actually leak-free — the held-out family's information already entered the frozen feature. Concrete required step: cross-reference this report's site list against the 85 site IDs and basin outlet COMIDs, then report LOFO both with all families and with SPARROW-calibration families excluded; if the gap is large, the feature's apparent gain is leakage. Note the sample-size interaction: with only 19 independent basin families, dropping even 3-4 contaminated families leaves ~15 and the between-site estimate becomes very noisy. Free USGS publication, public domain.

sources.title: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy — full science assessment document (Iowa State University / IDALS / Iowa DNR)
sources.why: The authoritative Iowa-specific process-modeling baseline, and the honest answer to 'is there an Iowa NRS gridded product I can download?' — largely NO, and that needs stating plainly. The NRS science assessment reports statewide and major-basin nitrate load baselines and practice-scenario reductions built on EPIC/APEX field-scale simulation and SWAT routing, but the published deliverables are aggregated tables and scenario summaries, not a per-HUC12 or per-COMID raster that can be joined at an arbitrary map pin. The associated HAWQS/SWAT Iowa applications in the literature (e.g. Des Moines River basin subdivided at HUC12, monthly nutrient output 2001-2018) are individual-basin studies whose outputs are not published as a statewide layer. Two consequences for this project: (1) NRS output is NOT directly operational as a feature under the deployment target, unlike SPARROW; (2) the realistic path is an email request to the modeling group at Iowa State CARD or to Iowa DNR for the underlying per-HUC12 EPIC/SWAT baseline nitrate yield grid — permitted under the acquisition constraint, but treat it as a speculative multi-week ask, not a plan. Also note the coverage failure mode: NRS modeling is Iowa-bounded by statute, so it would supply NOTHING for the out-of-state portions of the largest multi-state basins — the exact basins where the existing feature pipeline already under-counts. SPARROW does not have this problem.

sources.title: Read et al. (2019), Process-Guided Deep Learning Predictions of Lake Water Temperature, Water Resources Research 55, doi:10.1029/2019WR024922
sources.why: The foundational empirical result for 'pretrain on process-model output, fine-tune on observations', and the source of the specific condition under which it helps — SPARSE LABELS, which is exactly the between-site situation here. PGDL is an LSTM pretrained on output from a calibrated process-based lake model (GLM), then fine-tuned on observations with an energy-conservation loss penalty. Reported behavior: PGDL retains high accuracy when fine-tuned on only a handful of observation dates, substantially outperforming both the pure process model and an uninformed DL model in the low-data regime, with the paper's own attribution that pretraining (the volume of synthetic pretraining data) — not the physics loss term — is responsible for the majority of the gain. That attribution is the actionable part: it says the cheap half of the method is the half that works, which supports injecting SPARROW output as a feature/prior rather than building a physics-constrained loss. TWO HARD LIMITS to flag. (1) Scope: the paper's own stated limitation is that implementations were confined to one or two WELL-OBSERVED lakes with train and test under similar conditions — this is NOT an ungauged-transfer result, so its numbers are not comparable to our LOFO 0.820. (2) Domain mismatch: lake temperature is governed by a well-closed energy budget and GLM is a genuinely predictive daily simulator; SPARROW is a mean-annual regression with no daily state, so the 'pretrain on simulated time series' recipe has no direct analogue here — only the weaker 'use the process model's static prediction as a prior' version is available.

sources.title: Willard et al. (2021), Predicting Water Temperature Dynamics of Unmonitored Lakes With Meta-Transfer Learning, Water Resources Research 57, doi:10.1029/2021WR029579
sources.why: The closest published analogue to this project's actual problem — transfer to UNMONITORED targets — with an explicit sample-size ledger, and the source that most directly stress-tests the n=19-families constraint. Design: source models built at 145 well-monitored lakes (both calibrated process-based and PGDL variants), then a meta-learning model predicts which source transfers best to each target using lake attributes plus candidates' past performance, evaluated on 305 target lakes TREATED AS UNMONITORED in the Upper Midwest. 'Sparsely monitored' is defined operationally as 1-50 sampling dates. Report the numbers, not the conclusion: the actionable structural finding is that transfer quality is predicted from STATIC ATTRIBUTE SIMILARITY between source and target — which is the same signal this project found to be the only thing that works (geometry and static geography won; every temporal feature failed). FLAG PROMINENTLY: the meta-model is itself fitted on 145 source x 305 target transfer pairs. This project has 19 independent basin families, giving at most a few hundred ordered pairs but with only 19 effective independent units — meta-transfer learning as published is very likely INFEASIBLE here, and any attempt would be fitting a similarity function on ~19 points. The transferable idea is the diagnostic (does static-attribute similarity to the nearest training family predict LOFO error?), not the method.

sources.title: Jia et al. (2021), Physics-Guided Recurrent Graph Model for Predicting Flow and Temperature in River Networks, SIAM International Conference on Data Mining (SDM21), doi:10.1137/1.9781611976700.69 (preprint arXiv:2009.12575)
sources.why: The river-network case of process-model pretraining, and the one that directly addresses the completely unread upstream_uid/downstream_uid topology sitting on disk. Method: a recurrent graph network over river segments, PRETRAINED on output from the PRMS-SNTemp process model to initialize the ML model, plus a loss reweighting across segments. Reported effect sizes under VERY SPARSE training data (0.1% of segment-days labeled): 33% / 14% accuracy improvement over the process-based model and 24% / 14% over LSTM, for temperature / streamflow respectively. That sparse-label regime is the strongest published argument that process-model pretraining buys the most exactly where labels are thin — our between-site regime. FOUR CAVEATS to state. (1) The evaluation is on a single Delaware River Basin subnetwork of tens of segments; the split protocol is temporal/sparse-label rather than a clean leave-one-basin-out, so its numbers are NOT comparable to LOFO 0.820. (2) Targets are temperature and streamflow, which have far better-closed physics than nitrate. (3) It requires a daily process simulator to pretrain against — SPARROW cannot serve this role, and no calibrated daily SWAT/PRMS Iowa nitrate simulator has been identified as publicly downloadable, so the full recipe is not currently executable here. (4) The graph structure requires reliable connectivity; this project has upstream_uid for only 28 of 85 sites and downstream_uid for 40, and at 19 independent families a GNN has essentially no independent units to learn edge behavior from. Read this as motivation to first simply TEST whether network position adds between-site skill, not as a recommendation to build a GNN.

sources.title: Willard, Varadharajan, Jia & Kumar (2025), "Time series predictions in unmonitored sites: a survey of machine learning techniques in water resources", Environmental Data Science 4:e7
sources.kind: peer-reviewed review (the single most decision-relevant source for this angle)
sources.why: This is the authoritative review written by exactly the group that built the river-network GNN literature (Jia, Kumar), and it is scoped to OUR problem: prediction at unmonitored sites, not gap-filling at gauged ones. Key negative evidence it surfaces: in Sun et al.'s comparison of spatiotemporal GNNs for streamflow, 'for the transductive case, both ChebNet-LSTMs and GCN-LSTM performed worse in terms of median performance across basins than the standard LSTM, and GraphWaveNet was the only one that performed better' — i.e. two of three graph architectures LOST to a non-graph baseline. It also makes the argument that kills attribute-similarity graphs for us: building a graph from static site attributes 'introduces no new information ... since the static characteristics would be the same' as simply concatenating those attributes as features. Translated to this project: a graph whose edges encode 'these basins are similar' is provably no better than adding the similarity variables to XGBoost. The survey's own framing is that only PHYSICALLY-CONNECTED river-network graphs show promise, and the GNN studies it cites operate at 531 CAMELS catchments or on dense Delaware River Basin reach networks — one to two orders of magnitude above our 19 independent basin families. Use this source to justify NOT building a GNN and to cite a defensible reason.

sources.title: Zwart et al. (2023), "Evaluating deep learning architecture and data assimilation for improving water temperature forecasts at unmonitored locations", Frontiers in Water
sources.kind: peer-reviewed, held-out-NODE protocol (the correct protocol for our deployment target)
sources.why: The rare paper that actually answers the assignment's decisive question — is the reported GNN gain at UNMONITORED nodes, or only at gauged nodes with missing time periods? Here it is genuinely unmonitored: 70 stream segments in the upper Delaware, 5-fold SPATIAL cross-validation withholding segments as 'ungaged' during a 2019 validation period, then testing on 6 held-out test sites over Apr 2021-Sep 2022. Result: RGCN with data assimilation was roughly TIED with LSTM on overall RMSE at 1-day lead (3.18-3.27 C for both), and only separated on the management-relevant tail (high temperatures >18 C, thermal exceedance detection). Read that honestly: on the headline metric, adding the river graph bought approximately nothing at ungaged locations; the gain was confined to the extreme-value subset. That is a directly transferable warning for us, because our primary target is also a threshold/tail event (nitrate >= 10 mg/L) — it is the one place the graph might help — but the effect size at n=70 segments is small, and our network is 85 nodes with only ~40 known downstream edges and 28 known upstream edges, i.e. a sparse forest rather than a connected tree. Also note the data-assimilation component requires observations AT or near the target, which our arbitrary map pin does not have; the 'DA' half of RGCN-DA is not available to us at deployment.

sources.title: Topp et al. (2023), "Stream Temperature Prediction in a Shifting Environment: Explaining the Influence of Deep Learning Architecture", Water Resources Research
sources.kind: peer-reviewed architecture ablation with explicit out-of-distribution / spatial generalization tests
sources.why: An ablation study across graph architectures under extrapolation, which is our exact failure mode (between-site transfer to an unseen basin). RGCN and Graph WaveNet, both pre-trained on a process-based DRB temperature model, tied on in-distribution test RMSE (1.64 vs 1.65 C) — but Graph WaveNet beat RGCN in four of five experiments where the test partition represented unobserved environmental conditions. The stated cause matters more than the ranking: the recurrent (LSTM) component inside RGCN is unstable under gradient-based optimization, and the XAI analysis showed the better-generalizing architecture had learned spatial relationships with higher fidelity to physical processes. Two takeaways for us: (1) 'GNN' is not one method — architecture choice within the graph family swings generalization more than the presence/absence of the graph, which means we would be tuning an architecture family with 19 independent units of evidence, a hopeless model-selection budget; (2) the papers' own gains lean heavily on PRE-TRAINING against a calibrated process-based model (PRMS-SNTemp). We have no calibrated process model for Iowa nitrate to pretrain against, so we would be attempting the hardest variant of this method with the least support.

sources.title: Jia, Zwart, Sadler, Appling, Oliver, Markstrom, Willard, Xu, Steinbach, Read & Kumar (2021), "Physics-Guided Recurrent Graph Model for Predicting Flow and Temperature in River Networks", SIAM SDM 2021 (arXiv:2009.12575; USGS pub 70247905)
sources.kind: foundational peer-reviewed method paper — read for its SCALE and PROTOCOL, not its headline number
sources.why: The origin paper for river-network RGCN and the one most often mis-cited in favor of GNNs. Headline: 33%/14% improvement over the process-based model and 24%/14% over LSTM for temperature/streamflow, with only 0.1% observation density. Critical caveats to record: the evaluated subnetwork is ~42 river segments feeding the Delaware mainstem at Wilmington, and the sparsity being exploited is TEMPORAL sparsity (few observed days) on a DENSELY CONNECTED, fully-delineated reach network where every node's physical neighbors are known — not spatial holdout of whole basins. The 'physics-guided' half is a mass/energy-conservation loss plus pretraining on PRMS-SNTemp output. So the demonstrated capability is 'propagate information along known channel links to fill in under-observed nodes in a connected tree', which is a different problem from 'predict the absolute level at an arbitrary pin in a basin family the model has never seen'. Cite this when stating plainly that the canonical GNN success does NOT establish transfer to a spatially held-out, disconnected new basin.

sources.title: Moshe, Metzger, Elidan, Kratzert, Nevo & El-Yaniv (2020), "HydroNets: Leveraging River Structure for Hydrologic Modeling", ICLR 2020 AI for Earth Sciences workshop (Google Research)
sources.kind: workshop paper (NOT journal peer-reviewed) — the strongest statement of the sample-complexity argument, and the clearest illustration of the upstream-sensor tension
sources.why: Requested by name in the assignment, and its actual mechanism is the crux of the whole angle. HydroNets embed the river's tree structure into the architecture: each sub-basin is a node, edges carry water from sub-basin to containing basin, all nodes share a GLOBAL model component plus small site-specific modulations. The claimed benefit is precisely what we need — the structural prior 'reduces sample complexity ... allows accurate modeling even with only a few years of data' and enables 'transferability to sub-basins that suffer from scarce historical data'. BUT the signal that produces the gain is upstream GAUGE DYNAMICS propagated downstream: a node's prediction improves because its upstream nodes are observed. That is idea (b) in architectural clothing, and it inherits idea (b)'s fatal deployment limitation — it works only for a node that HAS a monitored upstream neighbor. For an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no gauged ancestor, the upstream messages are empty and HydroNets degrades to its shared global rainfall-runoff model, i.e. to what we already have. Also flag: workshop paper, streamflow not water quality, and the gains are reported at nodes that are themselves gauged.

sources.title: Schwarz, Hoos, Alexander & Smith (2006), "The SPARROW Surface Water-Quality Model: Theory, Application and User Documentation", USGS Techniques and Methods 6-B3
sources.kind: authoritative agency methods documentation — the mass-balance/routing formulation behind idea (b)
sources.why: The primary, citable statement of the incremental-area mass balance our cheap trick would rest on: 'the mass of water entering a reach from upstream at time t, plus the mass discharged at time t into the reach from sources within the reach's incremental watershed, equals the mass of water leaving the reach at time t + d, where d is the time of travel through the reach.' This is the formal justification that for a nested pair, an upstream sensor reading is a causally-ordered, non-leaking predictor — and it also tells us what else the identity requires that we DO NOT HAVE: it is a LOAD balance (concentration x discharge), not a concentration balance, so adding a raw upstream nitrate CONCENTRATION as a feature is not the mass-balance identity and can be badly wrong when the incremental area's discharge differs from the upstream area's. With discharge at only 22 of 85 sites and ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites, we cannot form loads at most nested pairs. Equally important for our CV design: SPARROW's own calibration explicitly exploits 'incremental drainage areas (i.e., areas located between nested monitoring sites)' as extra fine-scale information — the same nesting our leak-safe folds currently spend to DELETE data. There may be a defensible middle path (train an incremental-area model on nested pairs as a separate research artifact) but it must be reported separately and labeled as not deployable at an ungauged pin.

sources.title: US EPA StreamCat: accumulated landscape/catchment attributes for all 2.65 million NHDPlusV2 (v2.1) catchments, CONUS
sources.kind: operational dataset — the recommended alternative to a GNN (topology and catchment attributes as FEATURES)
sources.why: This is the actionable recommendation the angle should land on. StreamCat provides ~567 metrics computed for every local NHDPlusV2 catchment AND accumulated over the full upstream watershed, for all 2.65M CONUS reaches. Coverage is CONUS, so it covers the multi-state portions of our largest basins — directly fixing the documented inner-join under-count where Iowa-only crop/N-surplus layers silently truncate out-of-state area, which is worst for exactly the biggest basins. Access: bulk download and REST API at https://www.epa.gov/national-aquatic-resource-surveys/streamcat-dataset (also programmatic via the R StreamCatTools package and Python pynhd.nhdplus_derived); public domain / no authentication / free. Spatial resolution: NHDPlusV2 catchment (~1-3 km2 median); temporal: mostly static, with some layers by NLCD epoch. Pair it with NHDPlusV2 Value Added Attributes (https://www.epa.gov/waterdata/get-nhdplus-national-hydrography-dataset-plus-data) for StreamOrde (Strahler), TotDASqKM (total upstream drainage area), ArbolateSu, slope, and path/level-path position. The decisive property for our deployment target: EVERY one of these is retrievable at an ARBITRARY ungauged map pin from the pin's NLDI-resolved comid — the same call that already delineates our basin — whereas an upstream-sensor-reading feature is not. Given that our only historical wins came from geometry and static geography (lat, lon, log_basin_area, distance-to-outlet), and every temporal hydrologic feature failed, StreamCat/VAA static attributes attack the between-site term directly with no architecture risk. Caveat to state: with 19 independent basin families we can afford perhaps a handful of new static predictors before overfitting the between-site regression, so select a small preregistered set (Strahler order, TotDASqKM, mean catchment slope, hydrologic soil group / permeability, wetness index, riparian buffer land cover, tile-drainage proxies such as poorly-drained hydric soil fraction) rather than dumping all 567.

sources.title: Hydrologic regimes drive nitrate export behavior in human-impacted watersheds (Van Meter-adjacent; HESS 25:1333, 2021; doi:10.5194/hess-25-1333-2021)
sources.why: THE single most on-point source: 5 nested catchments in the Raccoon River, central Iowa (8,870 km2), 2016-2019, daily Hach Nitratax + USGS/IIHR discharge — same sensor network and same state as this project. Reports actual nitrate C-Q slopes: baseflow annual slopes 0.21 (most tile-drained, USC) to 0.79 (least drained, UPN); stormflow slopes form a narrow distribution around ZERO in all seasons, i.e. near-chemostatic during events. This directly explains the project's dead precip features: if event C-Q slope ~ 0, storm rainfall carries almost no concentration information, which is exactly what precip_in_1d perm-importance ~0.000 shows. Critically for the between-site problem, the paper finds drainage (tile) infrastructure density is the primary control on between-site C-Q slope (R2=0.85, p<0.05 for spring baseflow) and riparian cropped area within 100 m explains summer baseflow behavior (R2=0.94, p<0.01) — quantitative support both for the project's known tile-drainage data gap AND for the riparian-bucket result that already gave +0.039 PR-AUC. CAVEAT: n=5 nested catchments, so these R2 values come from 5 points and are not a defensible transfer estimate; treat as mechanism, not effect size. Protocol: descriptive C-Q regression, not a held-out predictive split — NOT comparable to LOFO 0.820.

sources.title: Basu et al. (2010), Nutrient loads exported from managed catchments reveal emergent biogeochemical stationarity, Geophysical Research Letters (doi:10.1029/2010GL045168)
sources.why: The primary seed source and the theoretical core of this angle. Establishes that in heavily managed agricultural catchments nitrate is chemostatic — C-Q slope near zero, load is essentially linear in discharge, concentration varies far less than discharge — because legacy soil/groundwater N stores act as a large, well-mixed source that damps concentration response. Two direct consequences the project should test: (1) if C ~ constant per site and load = C x Q, then modeling LOAD would be modeling Q, and back-deriving concentration from a predicted load would recover almost nothing beyond the site's mean level — this is an argument AGAINST switching the target to load, not for it; (2) chemostasis means the site-level MEAN concentration is the dominant signal, which is precisely the between-site term the project is failing at, and it means adding modeled discharge Q as a feature should be expected to help WITHIN-site timing far more than BETWEEN-site level. Use this to set a prior before spending effort on NWM ingestion. Flag: the chemostatic-slope literature is descriptive C-Q fitting, not spatial-holdout prediction.

sources.title: Ebeling et al. (2021), Archetypes and Controls of Riverine Nutrient Export Across German Catchments, Water Resources Research 57(4) e2020WR028134 (doi:10.1029/2020WR028134)
sources.why: The best available large-sample test of the exact between-site question: 787 catchments, mean nitrate concentration and C-Q slope regressed on catchment attributes. Headline finding is directly adverse to the naive mass-balance hypothesis: between-catchment nutrient variability is dominantly controlled by the SPATIAL HETEROGENEITY of diffuse sources, NOT by geology, climate, topography, or 'the mere input load of nutrients to the catchment.' That is a documented negative result for the simple C ~ N-surplus / specific-discharge relation this angle proposes — bulk basin-mean N surplus divided by water yield was not the controlling term. Nitrate C-Q is predominantly enriching (positive slope) across these catchments, which contrasts with the near-zero storm slopes in the Iowa Raccoon study and shows the regime is region-dependent. SAMPLE-SIZE FLAG: n=787 catchments versus this project's n=19 independent basin families — a 40x gap. Any attribute-to-level regression that needed 787 units to resolve is very unlikely to be identifiable at n=19; this source should be read as evidence that the between-site problem is genuinely hard, not as a recipe. Companion open dataset QUADICA (essd-14-3715-2022) and QUADICA v2 (essd-18-691-2026) are free and could serve as an external pretraining corpus, but German catchments are not tile-drained Iowa. Note: full text returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; numbers above are from the abstract/search-indexed text and the specific R2 values were NOT retrievable — verify before citing any figure.

sources.title: NOAA National Water Model CONUS Retrospective Dataset — AWS Registry of Open Data (authoritative access page)
sources.why: Fully operational spec for the proposed complete-coverage discharge covariate, verified from the registry page. v3.0 covers Feb 1979 - Jan 2023 (44 years), HOURLY streamflow output, 3-hourly land-surface output, CONUS plus AK/HI/PR. S3 bucket noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds (us-east-1), NetCDF for all fields and Zarr for model output + precipitation forcing. NO AUTHENTICATION required (anonymous AWS CLI / s3fs works), license is explicitly 'Open Data. There are no restrictions on the use of this data.' Older versions: v2.1 (1979-2020, noaa-nwm-retrospective-2-1-pds and -zarr-pds), v2.0, v1.2. Streamflow is indexed by feature_id, which IS the NHDPlusV2 COMID — so it joins directly to the comid already stored per basin in this project, and is available at an arbitrary map pin via NLDI COMID lookup, satisfying the deployment target with zero coverage gap. TWO HARD LIMITATIONS FOR THIS PROJECT: (a) v3.0 ends Jan 2023 but training data runs to 2026, leaving ~3 years uncovered — the operational/short-range NWM archive would be needed to fill that, at different bias characteristics; (b) it is MODELED, not observed, discharge — see the bias evaluation source. Docs: https://github.com/NOAA-Big-Data-Program/bdp-data-docs/blob/main/nwm/README.md; retrieval notebooks incl. NWM_output_variable_retrieval_with_FeatureID.ipynb on HydroShare resource 6ca065138d764339baf3514ba2f2d72f.

sources.title: Assessing the National Water Model's Streamflow Estimates Using a Multi-Decade Retrospective Dataset across the Contiguous United States, Water 15(13):2319, 2023 (doi:10.3390/w15132319)
sources.why: The essential bias check demanded before trusting NWM Q as a feature — CONUS-wide gauge-by-gauge evaluation of the retrospective against USGS observations using NSE, KGE, RSR and PBIAS. Two findings that bear directly on the go/no-go decision: the Upper Mississippi (HUC2 07, which contains Iowa) ranks among the HIGHEST-performing HUC2 regions in the skill-score rankings, which is a favorable signal for this project's domain; but KGE indicates 'pervasive mismatches' between modeled and observed flow generally, and NWM parameters are calibrated at only ~1,378 mostly NATURAL/unimpaired gauges and then regionalized by hydrologic similarity to all other reaches. Iowa's tile-drained, artificially-drained catchments are precisely the impaired, non-natural class excluded from that calibration set, so Iowa reaches receive regionalized rather than fitted parameters — the correct reading is 'regionally acceptable on average, but structurally un-calibrated for the tile-drainage process that HESS 25:1333 identifies as the dominant control.' PRACTICAL MITIGATION available to this project: the 22 USGS-gauged sites already on disk can be used to measure NWM error directly at those COMIDs before any modeling effort is spent. Also relevant: a comparative NWM v2.1 vs v3.0 storm-event analysis (ScienceDirect S2214581825000205) reports v3.0 underestimates streamflow and struggles with peak timing. NOTE: MDPI returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; the region-ranking and calibration-count details are from indexed excerpts and should be confirmed in the PDF.

sources.title: Gorski et al. (2024), Stream Nitrate Dynamics Driven Primarily by Discharge and Watershed Physical and Soil Characteristics at Intensively Monitored Sites: Insights From Deep Learning, Water Resources Research (doi:10.1029/2023WR036591)
sources.why: The closest published analogue to this project and the strongest empirical case that discharge is the missing covariate: 46 predominantly agricultural sites across the midwestern and eastern US — the same order of magnitude as this project's 85 sites and far closer than CAMELS's 531-671 basins, so it is NOT dismissible on the n=19 constraint the way large-sample benchmarks are. Deep-learning (LSTM-family) hindcasts of 7-day-average nitrate concentration driven by daily observed discharge plus meteorology plus static watershed attributes covering anthropogenic hydrologic modification (i.e. drainage), N application, climate, groundwater, land use, physical attributes and soils. The title conclusion is the finding: DISCHARGE and watershed PHYSICAL/SOIL characteristics dominate, not meteorology — mirroring this project's own result that raw weather features are dead last while static geography wins, and identifying the specific covariate this project lacks. THE DECISIVE CAVEAT TO RESOLVE: the paper uses OBSERVED discharge at monitored sites, which does not satisfy the deployment target; whether the authors ran a spatially held-out / ungauged-site split, and what the skill drop was, could NOT be confirmed (Wiley returned HTTP 403). Code and data are free at ScienceBase item 661436d1d34e633466530330 — the site list, attribute set and any held-out results should be pulled from there directly, and this is the highest-value single follow-up in this whole angle.

sources.title: Predicting Dynamic Riverine Nitrogen Export in Unmonitored Watersheds: Leveraging Insights of AI from Data-Rich Regions, Environmental Science & Technology (2022) (doi:10.1021/acs.est.2c02232)
sources.why: The only source found that attacks this project's exact deployment target head-on — dynamic (not mean-annual) riverine nitrogen EXPORT predicted in UNMONITORED watersheds by transferring a model trained where data are dense. This is the paper against which any 'train on 19 families, predict at an arbitrary pin' claim must be benchmarked, and it is also the place to check the load-vs-concentration target question: it models export/load rather than concentration, so its reported skill is the empirical answer to whether the load framing transfers across sites better than concentration does. Read the limitations section specifically for how skill degrades at unmonitored versus monitored sites and how many donor watersheds were required — that donor count is the number to compare against n=19 families. Related and worth pairing: Pandit et al. (2025), Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin, WRR (doi:10.1029/2024WR039207), which covers the same basin this project sits in. CAVEAT: ACS is paywalled/403 to automated fetch; the numeric effect sizes, donor-basin count and split protocol were NOT verified here and must be read from the PDF before being cited as evidence.

sources.title: Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach" — AgTile-US
sources.why: RESOLVES THE TILE-DRAINAGE GAP — this is the single highest-value output of this angle. AgTile-US is a binary 30 m CONUS raster (0 = undrained ag land, 1 = tile-drained ag land), reference year 2017, built by downscaling USDA Census of Agriculture 2017 county tile-drainage acreage onto NLCD-2016 cropland using SSURGO v2.0 soil drainage class + SRTM-derived slope. OPERATIONAL DETAILS: download from Figshare, DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, GeoTIFF and NetCDF, unrestricted public access, CC-BY 4.0; code at github.com/NCAR/AgTile-US. Covers ALL of CONUS, so it covers Iowa AND the multi-state (MN/SD/NE/MO) portions of the large basins — this matters because the project's current CDL/N-surplus inner join silently under-counts exactly those basins. Validation: 86.03% accuracy CONUS-wide on 16,000 ground-truth points; 82.7-93.6% across Midwest states; Iowa specifically 91.1% on 5,253 points. FIT TO DEPLOYMENT TARGET: perfect — it is a static raster, so it is computable for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated basin at an ungauged map pin with no local history, and it drops straight into the existing distance-bucket aggregation as tile_frac per bucket. FIT TO n=19: this is a per-basin static scalar, i.e. exactly the between-site information the model lacks, but it also means it is one more predictor competing over ~19 effective units — recommend adding it as a small number of features (e.g. tile fraction of ag land, and tile fraction x N-surplus interaction), not 3 buckets x several derived forms. STATED LIMITATIONS to carry forward: depends on USDA census accuracy (avg error 19.8%); NLCD-2016 underrepresents cropland by ~18% nationally; omission error 13.97% CONUS. It is a 2017 snapshot, so it is inherently a STATIC attribute — which is the correct use here anyway.

sources.title: David, Drinkwater & McIsaac (2010), "Sources of Nitrate Yields in the Mississippi River Basin", J. Environ. Qual. 39(5):1657-1667
sources.why: THE EFFECT-SIZE ANCHOR for tile drainage as a cross-site attribute, and the best available partial-variance decomposition. n = 153 WATERSHEDS across the Mississippi River Basin — a genuine large-sample cross-site regression, not a paired-catchment study. Target is winter-spring nitrate YIELD (not concentration — note the mismatch with our mg/L target). Total model R2 = 0.83. Partial contributions: river runoff x fertilizer-N input = 76% of the explained spatial variation; TILE DRAINAGE = 17%; human N consumption (sewage effluent) = 7%. Direction: tile drainage extent positively associated with nitrate yield. WHY THIS MATTERS HERE: it says the dominant cross-site term is a MULTIPLICATIVE runoff x N-input term, not either alone — which is a concrete, testable static-x-static feature for this project (basin-mean runoff proxy x basin N surplus), and it is different from the antecedent-moisture x surplus interaction that already failed, because that one was temporal and this one is a static basin-level product. It also puts a ceiling expectation on tile drainage alone: 17% of spatial variance is real but is NOT going to close the between_r2 0.21 gap by itself. CAVEATS TO STATE: split protocol is a cross-sectional multiple regression over watersheds with no spatial hold-out, so the 0.83 is in-sample explanatory R2 and is NOT comparable to our LOFO numbers; tile drainage was represented by coarse county/NRI-derived estimates (pre-AgTile-US), so the 17% is likely an underestimate of what a better tile layer could contribute. n=153 vs our n=19 families: the sign and rank ordering should transfer, the ability to FIT this many partial terms does not.

sources.title: Jones, Drake, Hruby, Schilling & Wolter (2019), "Livestock manure driving stream nitrate", Ambio 48(10):1143-1153
sources.why: THE MOST DIRECTLY TRANSFERABLE RESULT IN THIS SET — Iowa, sensor-based, and at a sample size (n=9 watersheds) comparable to our n=19 families, so it is one of the few cited effect sizes that is NOT infeasible at our scale. Nine western Iowa watersheds draining to the Missouri. 2017 flow-weighted-average NO3-N ranged 4.9 to 16.2 mg/L (Floyd 16.2, Rock 11.5, Boyer 8.7, Soldier 8.5, W. Nishnabotna 8.2, Monona-Harrison 7.2, Little Sioux 7.1, E. Nishnabotna 5.5, W. Nodaway 4.9) — i.e. the between-site spread straddles our 10 mg/L violation threshold, which is precisely the quantity our model cannot rank. KEY EFFECT SIZES: FWA nitrate vs MANURE N, R2 = 0.83; FWA nitrate vs COMMERCIAL fertilizer N, R2 = 0.14 (p > 0.10, not significant); FWA vs N SURPLUS significant at p < 0.01. Floyd and Rock (high livestock density) averaged 155 kg N/ha surplus vs 83 kg/ha for the other seven, with near-identical commercial N (112-116 kg/ha) but 111-117 kg/ha manure vs 24 kg/ha at W. Nodaway. ACTIONABLE IMPLICATION: the MANURE/COMMERCIAL SPLIT is the discriminating variable, not total N — our current 2 nitrogen-surplus features almost certainly blur it. Splitting basin N into manure-N and commercial-N as two static attributes is a cheap, high-prior-probability test. FIT TO DEPLOYMENT: fully static and county-downscalable, so computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin. PROTOCOL CAVEAT: cross-sectional correlation over 9 sites, single year (2017 concentrations, 2012 N inputs), no hold-out — treat R2=0.83 as a prior on direction and rough magnitude, not as achievable predictive skill; with n=9 the confidence interval on R2 is very wide.

sources.title: Schilling & Libra (2000), "The Relationship of Nitrate Concentrations in Streams to Row Crop Land Use in Iowa", J. Environ. Qual. 29(6):1846-1851
sources.why: THE IOWA BASELINE RULE FOR CROSS-SITE MEAN NITRATE, and a direct benchmark our model should be beating. Two Iowa samples: 15 large watersheds (1002-2774 km2) and 10 small watersheds (47-775 km2), 1996-1998. Row-crop fraction spanned 24-87%+ (large) and 28-87% (small); mean annual NO3-N spanned 0.5-10.8 mg/L (large) and 3.0-10.5 mg/L (small). EFFECT SIZE: mean annual NO3-N is directly proportional to row-crop percentage, p < 0.0003, with essentially the SAME slope (0.11 mg/L per percentage point) in both the large and small watershed sets — i.e. mean annual nitrate (mg/L) ~= 0.1 x row-crop %. A 70% row-crop basin predicts ~7 mg/L. IMPORTANT SECOND FINDING: the slope DECREASES with increasing watershed size — so log_basin_area should be interacted with row-crop fraction rather than entered additively, which is a specific, cheap change to an existing feature. WHY THIS IS A HARD TEST OF OUR MODEL: this is a ONE-PARAMETER, n=25-site rule for exactly the quantity our model fails at (site absolute level). If a simple row-crop-fraction regression fitted on our 19 families gets between-site rank correlation comparable to the model's between_r2 0.21, that is diagnostic evidence that the 68-feature model is not extracting the between-site signal that is already sitting in the CDL features. Recommend running it as a baseline before adding anything. PROTOCOL: cross-sectional, no spatial hold-out; also 1996-1998 land use, so re-derive the coefficient on current CDL rather than importing 0.11 literally.

sources.title: Nakagaki, Wieczorek & Qi (2016), "Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for the conterminous United States, early 1990s" (USGS), building on Sugg (2007)
sources.why: THE INDEPENDENT SECOND TILE-DRAINAGE LAYER — use it as a cross-check on AgTile-US, not as a replacement. 30 m national raster of estimated subsurface tile drainage extent, reference period EARLY 1990s, produced by allocating early-1990s county subsurface-drain areas onto cropland-with-poorly-drained-soil. Lineage: 1992 NRI subsurface drainage county areas (NRI Conservation Practice 606) and Sugg (2007), who estimated county subsurface drainage for the 18 leading drainage states from row crops on poorly drained soils. Access: free ScienceBase download, no authentication, USGS public domain. Covers all of CONUS including the multi-state basin portions. WHY BOTH: AgTile-US (2017 census) and Nakagaki (1990s NRI) are built from DIFFERENT county source data but a SIMILAR soil-drainage + cropland downscaling rule, so (a) their AGREEMENT map is a usable uncertainty flag per basin, and (b) their DIFFERENCE is a crude 25-year tile EXPANSION proxy — expansion is a plausible driver of between-site level that is not in any current feature. CAUTION AGAINST OVERREADING: because both products downscale county totals using SSURGO/STATSGO poor-drainage + cropland, tile fraction will be strongly collinear with soil drainage class and with row-crop fraction, which our CDL buckets already carry. At n=19 families that collinearity is a real risk of adding variance without information — test tile as a REPLACEMENT for, or interaction with, existing crop features before adding it alongside them. Also note the deeper issue this exposes: neither product is a measurement of tile, both are models of where tile should be, so no currently public dataset gives true tile density; a request to Iowa DNR or to county drainage districts is the only route to observed tile, and would only cover Iowa, not the multi-state basin portions.

sources.title: Falcone (2021), "Estimates of county-level nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer and manure from 1950 through 2017 in the conterminous United States", USGS OFR 2020-1153 (data release DOI 10.5066/P9VSQN3C)
sources.why: THE OPERATIONAL FIX FOR THE MANURE-VS-COMMERCIAL SPLIT, and half the answer on the 2017 cliff. Provides county-level kg of N and P SEPARATELY FROM COMMERCIAL FERTILIZER AND FROM LIVESTOCK MANURE, CONUS, at ~5-year intervals aligned to Ag Census years, 1950-2017. Farm/nonfarm fertilizer derived from AAPFCO state sales; the 2017 fertilizer estimate is a new model from 11 predictors (county fertilizer expenditures, land use, fertilized acres); manure updated to account for livestock weight changes. Access: free USGS ScienceBase/data.usgs.gov tabular download, no authentication, USGS public domain. Covers all CONUS counties, so it works for the multi-state basin portions where the current Iowa-only join under-counts. WHY IT MATTERS: this is exactly the manure/commercial decomposition that Jones et al. 2019 shows is the discriminating variable in Iowa (manure R2=0.83 vs commercial R2=0.14), and the current feature set has only undifferentiated N surplus. ON THE 2017 CLIFF — BE PRECISE: this product ALSO ends at 2017, so it does NOT restore post-2017 coverage. The defensible move is the one the assignment anticipates: use N inputs as a STATIC BASIN ATTRIBUTE (a basin's percentile rank among Iowa basins, computed from the most recent complete census, held constant for all site-days) rather than as a broadcast time series. The prior failed experiment broadcast 2017 surplus forward AS A TIME-VARYING FEATURE (-0.166), which conflates two different errors: it injected a fake temporal signal AND it created a train/test distribution shift between pre-2017 rows with real values and post-2017 rows with a constant. A static per-basin rank feature has neither property and is NOT ruled out by that result — this distinction should be stated explicitly when the ablation is re-run. Also note the 5-year census cadence means the 'time series' was never daily-resolvable anyway, which is independent support for treating it as static.

sources.title: gTREND-Nitrogen: Long-term nitrogen mass balance data for the contiguous United States (1930-2017), Scientific Data
sources.why: THE DEFINITIVE ANSWER ON WHETHER THE N-SURPLUS PRODUCT HAS A POST-2017 CONTINUATION: IT DOES NOT. This is the current, formally published version of the very gTREND product this project already uses, released 2026, and its coverage is still 1930-2017 at 250 m. That closes the question — there is no newer gTREND vintage to pick up, and the 68%-NaN problem cannot be solved by upgrading this source. What it DOES add over the version on disk: it is a full downscaled MASS BALANCE at 250 m with the component fluxes separated — fertilizer, manure, atmospheric deposition, biological N fixation, crop N uptake, and population-based human waste — rather than a single net surplus. That component separation is independently valuable here for two reasons: (1) it supplies the manure-vs-commercial split at 250 m grid resolution rather than county resolution, letting it be aggregated over the same distance buckets the model already uses, and (2) crop N uptake and BNF let a soybean-heavy vs corn-heavy basin be distinguished on N balance rather than only on CDL area fraction. Access: free, via the Scientific Data article's data-availability section (public repository, no authentication); check the article's stated license before redistribution. Covers all CONUS, so the multi-state basin portions are handled. IMPLICATION FOR THE PROJECT, STATED PLAINLY: combine this source's conclusion with Falcone (2021) and the recommendation is unambiguous — stop trying to make N surplus a time series, adopt it as a static per-basin attribute set (surplus, manure share, commercial share, crop uptake), and re-run the ablation under that framing. At n=19 families, keep this to 3-4 static features maximum.

sources.title: Pandit et al. (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin", Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2024WR039207
sources.why: THE single most important source for calibrating expectations. LSTM trained on high-frequency nitrate SENSOR data across the conterminous US (same data genre as IWQIS/USGS sensors used here) predicting DAILY nitrate concentration. Reports BOTH protocols separately, which is exactly what rule 1 demands: TEMPORAL validation median KGE = 0.60; SPATIAL validation (prediction in unmonitored basins, i.e. our LOFO analogue) median KGE = 0.18, rising to 0.34 when restricted to the Mississippi River Basin where donor density is highest. Effect size: spatial holdout costs ~0.42 KGE versus temporal holdout. This is state-of-the-art deep learning with far more donor basins than 19, and it still lands at KGE 0.18-0.34 for ungauged nitrate. Directly implies our between_r2 = 0.21 is NOT anomalously bad - it is approximately where the published field sits. Also note the paper explicitly frames spatial validation as a tool for 'quantifying the impact of current data gaps', supporting the argument that the deficit is monitoring-network coverage, not model architecture. Deployment-target relevant: this is one of the few papers that actually tests the arbitrary-ungauged-pin case for nitrate. Caveat to check on full read: KGE is not R2 and is not decomposed into between/within, so it is not numerically comparable to our 0.21 - use it as a regime indicator, not a direct benchmark.

sources.title: Gorski et al. (2024), "Stream Nitrate Dynamics Driven Primarily by Discharge and Watershed Physical and Soil Characteristics at Intensively Monitored Sites: Insights From Deep Learning", Water Resources Research 60(9), DOI 10.1029/2023WR036591
sources.why: Closest published analogue to this project's sample size and setting: 46 PREDOMINANTLY AGRICULTURAL sites in the midwestern/eastern US, deep learning, target is 7-day average nitrate concentration, inputs are daily discharge + meteorology + STATIC watershed attributes (anthropogenic hydrologic modification, nitrogen application, climate, groundwater, land use, physiography, soils). n=46 sites is the same order as our 85 sites / 19 families, so unlike CAMELS work (531-671 basins) this is NOT automatically disqualified by the n=19 constraint - it is the strongest available evidence that pooled multi-site nitrate models are trainable at small n. Two things to extract on full read: (1) the paper explicitly 'tested different approaches to POOL DATA ACROSS SITES', i.e. it is a direct empirical comparison of pooling/partial-pooling strategies, which is one of the regionalization families in the research question; (2) the headline attribution result is that DISCHARGE plus watershed SOIL and PHYSIOGRAPHIC attributes dominate model performance. That is a direct hit on two known gaps here: discharge is present at only 22/85 sites and unusable at the deployment pin, while soil/physiographic attributes are static, nationally available, and currently ABSENT from the 68-feature set. Given the project's pattern that only geometry and static geography have ever helped, soils/physiography is the best-evidenced next static feature block. Data and model code are released on USGS ScienceBase (item 661436d1d34e633466530330), so the attribute list is recoverable for free.

sources.title: Oudin et al. (2008), "Spatial proximity, physical similarity, regression and ungaged catchments: A comparison of regionalization approaches based on 913 French catchments", Water Resources Research 44(3), DOI 10.1029/2007WR006240
sources.why: The canonical head-to-head of the three regionalization families, n=913 catchments, and it contains the one quantitative rule in this literature that can be applied to Iowa TODAY. Ranking found: spatial proximity BEST, physical similarity intermediate, REGRESSION ON CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES WORST - the regression approach performed 'very close to' simply applying one median parameter set to the entire country, i.e. attribute regression added almost nothing over a global constant. That is a direct negative result against the naive fix of 'add more static attributes and let the model regress site level on them'. Critically, the paper reports a GAUGE-DENSITY THRESHOLD: proximity and physical similarity converge in efficiency at roughly 60 gauging stations per 100,000 km2, and below that density the two approaches give virtually identical results. Iowa is ~145,700 km2 with ~85 nitrate sites = ~58 stations/100,000 km2, i.e. this project sits essentially EXACTLY ON that threshold - so the literature predicts that switching from proximity to attribute-similarity will buy little or nothing here. This independently explains why lat/lon are already top-3 features: proximity is already doing the regionalization work, and attribute similarity is not expected to beat it in a flat, agriculturally homogeneous state. Also reports that ~5 donor catchments is the efficient number and that 1 donor is harmful. Only 5 physical descriptors were used (area, mean slope, median altitude, drainage density, forest fraction), so the negative regression result is arguably a weak-descriptor result - state that caveat. Protocol is leave-one-out pseudo-ungauged; target is streamflow, not concentration.

sources.title: Oudin et al. (2010), "Are seemingly physically similar catchments truly hydrologically similar?", Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2009WR008887
sources.why: Deliberate negative-result hunt (rule 4). This is the follow-up in which the same group attacks the core premise of attribute-based regionalization head-on and finds that catchments that look physically similar are frequently NOT hydrologically similar - the mapping from static descriptors to response behaviour is weak and noisy. This is the single best citation for the claim that the between-site ceiling is partly IRREDUCIBLE with commonly available static attributes, rather than being a feature-engineering failure specific to this project. It reframes our between_r2 = 0.21 from 'we are doing something wrong' to 'physical-similarity regionalization has a known low ceiling'. Use it to set a prior on how much any new static attribute block (soils, tile drainage, physiography) can realistically add before spending effort acquiring it, and to argue against expensive attribute-acquisition programmes that assume a strong attribute-to-level mapping. Caveat: streamflow target, French catchments, large n - the small-n Iowa situation is if anything worse, since with 19 independent families the attribute-to-level regression is fitting on ~19 effective points and will overfit any rich attribute vector.

sources.title: Willard, Varadharajan, Jia & Kumar (2025), "Time series predictions in unmonitored sites: a survey of machine learning techniques in water resources", Environmental Data Science, DOI 10.1017/eds.2024.14
sources.why: The field-defining survey for EXACTLY this project's problem statement - ML time-series prediction at UNMONITORED sites, i.e. the deployment target - and it is open access. Value is threefold. (1) It establishes the standard evaluation protocol vocabulary (spatial/unmonitored-site holdout vs temporal holdout) that this project's LOFO already conforms to, so it can be cited to defend the protocol. (2) It documents 'data synergy': models benefit from a DIVERSE training set spanning multiple regions more than from a homogeneous but topically closer one - relevant to the option of training on non-Iowa nitrate sites (e.g. NWIS/WQP sites across the Corn Belt) to inflate the effective number of independent basin families beyond 19, which is arguably the highest-leverage response to the n=19 constraint. (3) It is itself a NEGATIVE finding on the literature: on direct reading it does NOT systematically report per-variable skill for held-out water-quality sites, does not report site counts consistently, and presents no analysis of how skill scales with the number of training sites; the authors call out that 'comparisons between different classes of machine learning methods are few and inadequate' and that most work is deep learning built on MANY sites. Report this plainly - the requested 'skill vs number of donor catchments curve' for WATER QUALITY does not appear to exist in the published literature, and the water-quality-PUB corpus is thin relative to streamflow PUB. That absence is a finding, and it means our between_r2 = 0.21 has no tight published benchmark to be judged against.

sources.title: Arsenault, Martel, Brunet, Brissette & Mai (2023), "Continuous streamflow prediction in ungauged basins: long short-term memory neural networks clearly outperform traditional hydrological models", HESS 27, 139-157, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-139-2023
sources.why: The best SMALL-SAMPLE ungauged-basin benchmark found: n=148 catchments (not 531-671), so it is far more transferable to the n=19-families constraint than CAMELS-scale work, and it is fully open access. Protocol is strict leave-one-out cross-validation with each catchment held out as pseudo-ungauged (train on 147, of which 118 train / 29 validate) - structurally the same design as our LOFO. Effect sizes, all spatially held out and therefore comparable to each other: pooled LSTM median NSE 0.78; conceptual models CALIBRATED at the target site (an upper bound unavailable to us) median NSE ~0.67-0.68; regionalized hydrological models median NSE 0.58-0.63 across all 18 model-x-regionalization configurations. The LSTM beat all 18 regionalization configurations in 93-97% of catchments. Two implications: pooled multi-site learning beats donor-transfer regionalization even at n=148, supporting the current pooled-XGBoost architecture over any donor-catchment scheme; and remarkably the ungauged pooled model exceeded LOCALLY CALIBRATED models, evidence that cross-site pooling adds real information. Two negative results worth quoting: removing poorly calibrated donor catchments (NSE < 0.7) did NOT improve regionalization, contrary to prior literature - so do not prune 'bad' sites from our 85; and regularization on bias/kernels/weights failed to improve test skill. Caveats: streamflow not concentration, humid northeast North America not agricultural Iowa, and the paper performs NO systematic analysis of skill vs number of training catchments - it uses all data without ablating training-set size, which again underlines that the requested scaling curve is largely missing.

sources.title: Guo et al. (2021), "Impact of the number of donor catchments and the efficiency threshold on regionalization performance of hydrological models", Journal of Hydrology, DOI 10.1016/j.jhydrol.2021.126753
sources.why: The closest thing found to the explicitly requested 'skill vs number of donors' CURVE, and it is at the largest sample in this set: 3444 catchments in North America, 5 regionalization methods x 2 weighting schemes x 2 averaging options x 5 efficiency thresholds x 4 lumped hydrological models. Reported shape of the curve: performance rises steeply from 1 donor (using a single donor is actively DETRIMENTAL), peaks at approximately FIVE donors for both distance-based and attribute-based regionalization, then decays roughly linearly as more donors are added beyond five. That is a saturating-then-declining curve, not a monotonic 'more basins is better' curve, and it is the key quantitative answer to whether n=19 independent families is crippling: for classical donor-transfer regionalization it is NOT, because the method saturates around 5 donors anyway. This substantially weakens the worry that the 19-family constraint is the binding limit for regionalization-style approaches - the binding limit is more likely the weak attribute-to-level mapping documented by Oudin 2010 and the missing static controls (soils, tile drainage) flagged by Gorski 2024. Second finding: spatial proximity with inverse-distance weighting and output averaging (SPI-out) performs better than or comparable to all other methods across climate regions and hydrological models, independently reproducing the Oudin 2008 ranking and further supporting that lat/lon proximity is already capturing most of the available regionalization signal here. Third: efficiency-threshold choice barely matters (median KGE differences <=0.05 between thresholds of all/0.6/0.7). Caveats: streamflow target, parameter-transfer paradigm rather than pooled ML, and the donor-count result concerns donors per prediction site, not total training-set size - do not conflate the two when applying it to our pooled XGBoost.

sources.title: Kratzert, Klotz, Herrnegger, Sampson, Hochreiter, Nearing (2019), "Toward Improved Predictions in Ungauged Basins: Exploiting the Power of Machine Learning", Water Resources Research 55(12):11344-11354, DOI 10.1029/2019WR026065
sources.why: THE canonical PUB claim, and the one that must be sized against our n=19. PROTOCOL: genuinely spatially held out — 531 CAMELS basins, k=12 k-fold over BASINS, so test basins contributed zero training data; ~30 yr daily rainfall-runoff, basins 4-2000 km2, aridity 0.22-5.20. Result: a single LSTM trained on the other ~487 basins and conditioned on static catchment attributes beat SAC-SMA and the National Water Model *even where those benchmarks were calibrated per-basin*. CRITICAL FOR US: (a) target is STREAMFLOW, not water quality — no nitrate evidence here; (b) the mechanism is explicitly 'learn one shared dynamical process across many basins, then index into it with static attributes'. Our 19 independent families is ~4% of 531, and our failure mode (between-site level, between_r2 0.21) is exactly the static-attribute-indexing term, which an XGBoost already receives as plain columns. There is no experiment in this paper at n<40 basins, so it provides NO evidence that the architecture wins at our sample size. Note also the leave-one-basin-out (random k-fold over basins) protocol is WEAKER than our LOFO: CAMELS folds routinely place hydrologically adjacent donors in training, which our basin-family grouping deliberately forbids. Treat 0.820 AUC vs these NSEs as non-comparable and treat the transfer as unproven. Companion code: github.com/kratzert/lstm_for_pub.

sources.title: Kratzert, Klotz, Shalev, Klambauer, Hochreiter, Nearing (2019), "Towards learning universal, regional, and local hydrological behaviors via machine learning applied to large-sample datasets" (Entity-Aware LSTM), HESS 23:5089-5110, DOI 10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019
sources.why: The EA-LSTM paper the assignment names. Establishes the exact mechanism of the deep-model gain and, read carefully, is the strongest argument for CLOSING this angle. 531 CAMELS basins; the architectural innovation is a static-attribute-gated input layer that learns a catchment-similarity embedding, and the paper's own headline validation is that the learned embedding 'corresponds well with prior hydrological understanding' — i.e. the network is learning a CATCHMENT CLASSIFICATION from static attributes, which is precisely the between-site level term we are missing. But an embedding over catchment types is a representation that must be ESTIMATED, and its effective sample size is the number of independent catchments, not the number of site-days. At 531 basins the embedding is identifiable; at 19 independent families it is a ~19-point regression wearing a neural-network costume and will overfit at least as badly as a tree. Also note the regional/single-basin comparison here shows traditional calibrated hydrological models DEGRADE when regionalized while LSTMs improve — a many-basin phenomenon with no demonstrated small-n analogue. Code: github.com/kratzert/ealstm_regional_modeling.

sources.title: Kratzert, Gauch, Klotz, Nearing (2024), "HESS Opinions: Never train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network on a single basin", HESS 28:4187-4201, DOI 10.5194/hess-28-4187-2024
sources.why: The closest thing in the literature to the performance-vs-NUMBER-OF-TRAINING-BASINS ablation the assignment asks for, and it answers our question in the direction that closes the angle. Figure 6 sweeps k-fold random groupings of the 531 CAMELS basins at varying group size; the authors' stated conclusion is that 'models trained on any subset of the 531 CAMELS basins performed worse, on average, than models trained on all 531'. Two regionalization ablations are directly relevant to us: HUC groupings (18 groups, 2-79 basins each) and k-means attribute clusters (6 clusters, 59-195 basins each) BOTH underperform the full 531-basin model — meaning that even 59-195 basins is not enough to recover full LSTM skill. Our 19 families sit BELOW the smallest of those regional groups. CAVEATS I verified rather than assumed: (1) the paper specifies NO minimum basin count and does NOT identify a regime where LSTMs are beaten by simpler models — it is silent, not supportive, on small-n failure; (2) it contains NO tree-based comparison at all, only mHM/VIC process models. So it cannot be cited as 'XGBoost wins at n=19'; it can only be cited as 'the published LSTM advantage is monotone in basin count and is not demonstrated anywhere near our sample size.' Survey stat worth quoting to stakeholders: of 150 papers reviewed, 122 trained on a single catchment.

sources.title: Pandit et al. (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin", Water Resources Research 61(8), DOI 10.1029/2024WR039207
sources.why: THE most important source for this angle and the closest published analogue to our exact problem: an LSTM trained on HIGH-FREQUENCY NITRATE SENSOR DATA across the conterminous US, predicting DAILY nitrate concentration, in the Mississippi River Basin (which contains Iowa — the IWQIS/USGS sensor network we use is almost certainly part of its training corpus). It reports BOTH protocols separately, which is exactly the discipline rule 1 demands. TEMPORAL validation (held-out time, same sites): median KGE 0.60. SPATIAL validation (prediction in UNMONITORED basins — our deployment target): median KGE 0.18 nationally, improving to median KGE 0.34 when restricted to the MRB. That collapse from 0.60 to 0.18/0.34 is the single most decisive number I found: a well-resourced continental LSTM with far more sites than we have DEGRADES SEVERELY under exactly the ungauged-pin condition our product must satisfy, and the residual MRB skill (KGE 0.34) is not obviously better than our LOFO regression R2 0.328 / AUC 0.820. Note the paper does NOT report an XGBoost/RF head-to-head, so it cannot be used to claim trees win — it establishes that the DEEP model does not solve the ungauged-nitrate problem either, which is the relevant negative result. Also useful downstream: their MRB finding that riverine nitrate export is only 19 +/- 4% of N surplus documents large in-basin retention, i.e. a physical reason our 2017-truncated gTREND surplus features transfer poorly.

sources.title: Zhi, Feng, Tsai, Sterle, Harpold, Shen, Li (2021), "From Hydrometeorology to River Water Quality: Can a Deep Learning Model Predict Dissolved Oxygen at the Continental Scale?", Environmental Science & Technology 55(4):2357-2368, DOI 10.1021/acs.est.0c06783
sources.why: The most-cited 'LSTM works for chemically ungauged basins' claim, included specifically so the project can apply the skeptical treatment the assignment asks for. n = 236 minimally disturbed CAMELS-chem watersheds; target is DISSOLVED OXYGEN from sparse grab samples plus daily hydrometeorology. Read the claim precisely: the paper says the model 'exhibits the POTENTIAL of predicting DO in chemically ungauged basins' and its main validation is that the network recovers the DO-temperature solubility relationship. THREE reasons this does not license an LSTM here: (1) DO is largely a thermodynamic function of water temperature, i.e. a near-deterministic, spatially-transferable physical law — nitrate has no such law, it is set by land management, tile drainage and N application, exactly the between-site static information we are missing; (2) 236 basins, and MINIMALLY DISTURBED ones, versus our 19 families of intensively row-cropped, tile-drained Iowa basins; (3) the baselines beaten are hydrological/statistical, not a tuned XGBoost. Also relevant: CAMELS-chem itself (Sterle et al. 2024, HESS 28:611, hess.copernicus.org/articles/28/611/2024/) carries 22,320 nitrate GRAB samples over 429 catchments 1930-2020 — a possible free external source of between-site nitrate level anchors, though grab-sample sparsity and non-Iowa composition limit it.

sources.title: Willard, Ciulla, Weierbach, Kumar, Varadharajan (2024), "Evaluating Deep Learning Approaches for Predictions in Unmonitored Basins with Continental-scale Stream Temperature Models", arXiv:2410.19865
sources.why: The best explicit NEGATIVE result I found for deep models at unmonitored sites, and the best guidance on which regionalization strategy to spend effort on. Scale: 1,079 TRAINING sites (3,584,951 observations) and 281 held-out TEST sites (906,521 observations). PROTOCOL is stronger than plain leave-one-basin-out and closer to our LOFO: sites were first partitioned into 15 clusters by a network-based unsupervised catchment classification, then ~20% of sites within each cluster were designated 'unmonitored' for testing. TWO findings that directly redirect this project: (1) the LSTM — 'the most popular model currently used in hydrology' — is reported as NOT the best choice for unmonitored-basin stream temperature, an explicitly published deep-model failure of the kind rule 4 asks us to hunt for; (2) TOP-DOWN models trained on ALL sites significantly outperform BOTTOM-UP transfer (fit locally, transfer to target) AND the intermediate GROUPED models that cluster sites by region or catchment similarity. Implication for us: do NOT spend effort on per-cluster or donor-basin regionalization schemes at n=19 — they lose even when you have 1,079 sites. Third finding, cheap and actionable: systematically REMOVING dynamic and static inputs retained acceptable accuracy while enabling prediction at more sites — a direct argument for our simplification-over-elaboration pattern (our seven failed temporal ablations) and for treating precip_in_1d-type dead features as removable. Companion survey by the same group, Willard et al., 'Time series predictions in unmonitored sites: a survey of ML techniques in water resources', Environmental Data Science (arXiv:2308.09766), is the taxonomy to read alongside it.

sources.title: GPBoost: Tree-Boosting combined with Gaussian Process and grouped random-effects models (Sigrist), open-source Python/R library
sources.why: My concrete recommendation for the CHEAPER MIDDLE GROUND the assignment asks about, with an important deployment caveat stated up front. GPBoost models y = F(X) + random effects, where F(X) is a boosted-tree ensemble (drop-in for the existing XGBoost) and the random part is either grouped random intercepts or a Gaussian process. DEPLOYMENT VERDICT, split two ways: (a) PER-SITE RANDOM INTERCEPTS DO NOT WORK for our product — a random effect for an unseen basin shrinks to the grand mean, so at an arbitrary map pin it contributes exactly nothing and you are back to the tree alone. Do not let anyone sell site embeddings or site random effects as a fix for the between-site term; they are estimable only at monitored sites and are a leak risk under LOFO. (b) The GAUSSIAN-PROCESS variant IS deployable: a GP over lat/lon (or over a static-attribute similarity space) fitted to the BOOSTER'S RESIDUALS produces a level correction at a brand-new pin by borrowing strength from nearby monitored basins, requiring zero observations at the target. Given that lat and lon are already our #2 and #3 permutation-importance features, the model is visibly trying to do spatial interpolation with axis-aligned splits, which trees do badly; an explicit GP residual kriging is the natural, cheap, low-parameter fix and attacks precisely the between_r2 0.21 deficit. SAMPLE-SIZE FIT: a GP with 2-3 hyperparameters estimated from 19 independent family-level residuals is on the edge but tractable — vastly more tractable than an LSTM — and it must be validated under the SAME LOFO folds, since spatial CV without adjacency between donor and target is where such methods usually collapse (one search-surfaced study reports R2 falling from 0.79 under random split-sample to 0.13-0.61 under adjacency-free spatial CV). OVERALL ANGLE RECOMMENDATION: close the LSTM/deep-hydrology direction. Every documented deep-model PUB gain requires hundreds of basins (531 CAMELS, 1,079 temperature sites, 236 CAMELS-chem), the gain's mechanism is static-attribute conditioning that our booster already receives directly, the only published daily-nitrate spatial-holdout result degrades to KGE 0.18-0.34, and the one large study that tested regionalized/grouped training found it LOSES to pooled training even at n=1,079. Spend the effort instead on new STATIC between-site information (tile drainage density, the unread upstream/downstream network topology, draining_area, co-located conductivity) plus GP residual kriging.

claims.text: AgTile-US is a 30-m resolution binary raster (0 = undrained cropland, 1 = tile-drained cropland) covering the entire contiguous United States (65°20'W–127°53'W, 22°51'N–51°36'N), reference year 2017. It is a SINGLE STATIC SNAPSHOT — the authors explicitly state it 'does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation.' Falsifiable operational consequence: it can supply a per-basin tile-drainage-fraction as a STATIC basin attribute (one number per basin, exactly the between-site static information the LOFO gap needs), but it cannot supply any time-varying tile signal. Because it is CONUS-wide, it also covers the multi-state portions of Iowa basins, unlike the Iowa-only CDL/N-surplus joins that currently under-count area for the largest basins.
claims.effectSize: 30 m resolution; 22,340,442 ha tile-drained CONUS; Iowa 5,706,831 ha (largest of any state); reference year 2017; binary 0/1

claims.text: AgTile-US validation against 16,000 manually-identified ground-truth points from ESRI multi-resolution aerial imagery (0.3–15 m) gave 86.03% overall CONUS accuracy with 13.97% omission error; over the heavily tile-drained Midwest accuracy ranged 82.7%–93.6%, and IOWA SPECIFICALLY scored 91.1% on 5,253 ground-truth points. This is the highest per-state validation density in the paper, so an Iowa-basin tile fraction derived from this raster carries roughly 9% pixel-level misclassification — a per-basin aggregate would average much of that out, making basin-level tile fraction a low-noise attribute.
claims.effectSize: CONUS accuracy 86.03% (n=16,000 points); Iowa accuracy 91.1% (n=5,253 points); omission error 13.97%; Midwest range 82.7–93.6%
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (validated on 16,000 point samples, not basins)
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (image-interpretation ground truth, not a train/test model split)

claims.text: AgTile-US is not an independent observation of tile drainage: it is a geospatial decision-tree DOWNSCALING of USDA Census of Agriculture 2017 county-level tile acreage, allocated to pixels by SSURGO v2.0 soil drainage class (7 categories, iterated D=7 down to D=1) within an NLCD 2016 cropland mask, subject to a topographic slope threshold (0% to 20% max) from SRTM. Falsifiable consequence for this project: a basin-aggregated AgTile fraction will be strongly collinear with basin-aggregated SSURGO drainage class, mean slope, and county cropland fraction — so adding AgTile fraction AND SSURGO hydrologic-soil-group/drainage-class as separate features is largely redundant, and any measured gain should be attributed to the composite, not to three independent attributes. Aggregate CONUS area matched the census to −0.35% (22.34 vs 22.42 Mha) by construction.
claims.effectSize: Inputs: USDA Ag Census 2017 county tile acreage; SSURGO v2.0 drainage class (7 classes); NLCD 2016 cropland; SRTM slope (0–20% threshold). Aggregate deviation from census: −0.35%

claims.text: AgTile-US is downloadable free with NO authentication: primary data DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742 (Figshare, GeoTIFF and NetCDF-4), production code at https://github.com/NCAR/AgTile-US, and a mirrored Google Earth Engine ImageCollection/Image asset at 'projects/sat-io/open-datasets/agtile/AgTile-US' (awesome-gee-community-catalog, 30 m). License is Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY 4.0) with metadata under CC0 — free for commercial use with attribution, so it is shippable in a deployed product. The GEE asset means a per-basin tile fraction can be computed on the fly for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated map-pin basin via a reduceRegion call, with no local raster storage — directly compatible with the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target.
claims.effectSize: DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742; GEE asset projects/sat-io/open-datasets/agtile/AgTile-US; formats GeoTIFF + NetCDF-4; CC-BY 4.0; no auth required

claims.text: AgTile-US systematically UNDER-predicts tile area because it is masked to NLCD 2016 cropland, which itself underrepresents cropland by −18.15% CONUS-wide relative to the USDA census; state-level underestimates reach New Mexico −79.06%, West Virginia −42.38%, Mississippi −15.90%, Oklahoma −14.06%, Texas −11.53%. Accuracy also degrades specifically in the marginal/moderately-drained SSURGO categories 3–5 (higher false negatives), and the 20% slope cap may exclude tile-drained sloped fields. Falsifiable consequence: basin tile FRACTION is biased low, and the bias is not uniform — it is worst in basins with intermediate soil drainage class, which is precisely the discriminating middle of the range the model would need for site ranking. Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio are NOT among the listed problem states, so the bias should be modest for the core Iowa basins but larger for multi-state basin tails.
claims.effectSize: NLCD 2016 cropland deficit −18.15% CONUS; worst state errors NM −79.06%, WV −42.38%, MS −15.90%, OK −14.06%, TX −11.53%; degraded accuracy in SSURGO drainage categories 3–5; slope cap 20%

claims.text: This paper is a Scientific Data DATA DESCRIPTOR and contains NO water-quality analysis whatsoever — it reports zero nitrate concentrations, zero regressions of stream nitrate on tile fraction, and zero effect sizes for the research question 'which static basin attributes explain cross-site variance in mean nitrate.' It therefore cannot be cited as evidence that tile fraction explains between-site nitrate variance; it only establishes that a defensible, free, basin-aggregatable tile-extent covariate EXISTS at 30 m for all of CONUS. The effect-size evidence must come from separate Corn Belt water-quality literature. Falsifiable test for this project, and the reason the feature is still worth trying at n=19 families: unlike the seven failed temporal ablations, a per-basin tile fraction adds exactly ONE static column, so it is estimable at 19 effective independent units, and the specific prediction is that it raises between_r2 (currently 0.21) and between_rate_r2 (currently 0.24) rather than within_r2 (0.42).
claims.effectSize: Zero nitrate/water-quality effect sizes reported in the source; adds 1 static feature per basin against n=19 independent basin families
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (no basins used; validation is point-based and county-based)

result.sourceQuality: High for what it covers, but OFF-TARGET for the research question. The nature.com URL is behind an IdP redirect (303 to idp.nature.com); I read the full published text via the PubMed Central open-access mirror PMC7406500, so these claims come from the primary peer-reviewed article, not an abstract or metadata record.
