Scientific Data is peer-reviewed and this is the canonical, widely-cited CONUS tile-drainage product (Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz 2020, Sci Data 7:257, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x). CRITICAL CAVEAT: it is a data descriptor, so it fully RESOLVES the "tile drainage dataset exists and is downloadable" half of the assignment (name, 30 m, 2017, CONUS-wide including multi-state basin portions, Figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742 plus a GEE asset, CC-BY 4.0, no auth) but supplies NOTHING on the other half — no partial effect sizes, no cross-site nitrate variance decomposition, no basin counts. It also does not address the N-surplus post-2017 cliff at all. Two secondary sources used only for access mechanics: the GEE community catalog page (gee-community-catalog.org/projects/tile/) for the Earth Engine asset ID, and a web search snippet; the Figshare landing page itself returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher so exact file sizes could not be confirmed. Note that AgTile-US's own reference year is 2017 — the same year the gTREND N-surplus product ends — which is coincidental but means both static attributes share a 2017 vintage.

sources.title: Worland, Steinschneider, Farmer, Asquith & Knight (2019), "Copula Theory as a Generalized Framework for Flow-Duration Curve Based Streamflow Estimates in Ungaged and Partially Gaged Catchments", Water Resources Research 55:9378-9397, DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138
sources.why: THE most directly relevant source to this angle's crux. Formalizes QPPQ as a special case of a copula between donor and target: QPPQ = take donor's nonexceedance probability series, map through the target's regionalized duration curve. This is exactly the proposed reformulation (percentile model x site-level curve). n = 74 USGS streamgages (37 Mobile-Tombigbee, 37 Trinity), daily flow 2000-2009; observed+modeled series archived at ScienceBase (https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/5cae0b6ce4b0c3b006549e61), so the evaluation is reproducible. Reported findings: copula approaches (1) match other methods in the limiting case of perfect information about the rank correlation structure and FDCs across the network, (2) HEDGE AGAINST POOR PERFORMANCE AS DONOR INFORMATION BECOMES SPARSER AND LESS INFORMATIVE, and (3) outperform when the target is PARTIALLY GAGED. NSE decomposition showed copula methods carry less VARIANCE error - i.e. they get the spread/level right, which is precisely our between-site failure mode. CRITICAL CAVEAT FOR OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: the paper's headline advantage is in the PARTIALLY GAGED case (a handful of target-site observations), which we do NOT have at an arbitrary map pin; the fully ungaged case is where all FDC-transfer methods degrade to the quality of the regionalized FDC alone. Sample size note: 74 catchments per region, ~4x our 19 independent families, but far closer to feasible than CAMELS-scale work. Protocol: donor/target cross-validation within a gaged network, spatially held out - comparable in spirit to our LOFO. Full text is paywalled (402 on direct fetch); preprint copy on ResearchGate 336987391.

sources.title: Worland, Steinschneider, Asquith, Knight & Wieczorek (2019), "Prediction and Inference of Flow Duration Curves Using Multioutput Neural Networks", Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2018WR024463
sources.why: This is the OTHER half of the decomposition: how to regionalize a duration curve from static basin attributes alone, with no observations at the target. Predicts 15 streamflow quantiles JOINTLY as a multioutput problem (rather than one regression per quantile, which can produce non-monotonic curves), trained/tested on 688 USGS streamgages in the southeastern US, then applied to 9,203 ungaged locations for six decades 1950-2009. Predictive attributes reported include stream length, average slope, elevation, and baseflow index. Two things make this actionable for us: (a) the multioutput formulation is directly transplantable - replace 'flow quantiles' with 'nitrate concentration quantiles', and the exceedance rate above 10 mg/L falls straight out of the predicted curve, which is exactly our between_rate_r2 = 0.24 target; (b) it establishes that basin attributes CAN carry a duration curve, which is the assumption our whole angle rests on. SAMPLE-SIZE FLAG (rule 5): n = 688 training gages vs our 19 independent basin families - a ~36x gap. A multioutput NEURAL NETWORK at n=19 is almost certainly infeasible; the transplantable idea is the multioutput/monotonicity-constrained TARGET STRUCTURE, not the model class. At n=19 the realistic implementation is a heavily-regularized linear or low-rank multioutput model on 3-5 attributes (log basin area, lat/lon, tile-drainage proxy, row-crop fraction), not a neural net. Also note the paper's own framing is INFERENCE as much as prediction - it discusses which attributes drive which part of the curve, useful for choosing our ~5 static predictors.

sources.title: Castellarin, Botter, Hughes, Liu, Ouarda, Parajka, Post, Sivapalan, Spence, Viglione & Vogel (2013), "Prediction of flow duration curves in ungauged basins", Chapter 7 in Bloschl et al. (eds), Runoff Prediction in Ungauged Basins: Synthesis Across Processes, Places and Scales, Cambridge University Press
sources.why: The canonical synthesis chapter from the IAHS Predictions in Ungauged Basins (PUB) decade - the authoritative taxonomy of HOW a duration curve is regionalized from attributes, which is the piece the assignment specifically asks for. Covers the four families: (1) STATISTICAL/quantile regression - regress each fixed exceedance percentile on catchment attributes independently (simplest, works at small n, but can produce non-monotonic curves); (2) PARAMETRIC - fit a 2-3 parameter distribution (lognormal, Kosugi, Weibull) to each site's curve and regress only those 2-3 PARAMETERS on attributes - THIS IS THE RIGHT CHOICE AT n=19 because it reduces the small-n regression to 2-3 targets instead of 15; (3) GRAPHICAL/index-flow - normalize every site's curve by an index (mean flow), pool the dimensionless curves regionally, and regionalize only the index - directly analogous to predicting a site's MEDIAN nitrate and applying a shared dimensionless shape, which matches our diagnosis exactly (within_r2 0.42 shape is fine, level is not); (4) GEOSTATISTICAL - Top-kriging of quantiles along the river network, which can exploit our unread upstream_uid/downstream_uid topology. Also the source for the QPPQ lineage (Fennessey 1994; Hughes & Smakhtin; Archfield & Vogel donor selection). Read the LIMITATIONS discussion for negative results (rule 4): FDC regionalization is consistently WORST in the low-flow / extreme tail, degrades sharply in heterogeneous regions, and small regional samples force the parametric or index-flow route. Note: fetched as a 1.7 MB PDF that resisted automated text extraction - a human or pdftotext pass is needed to pull the specific per-study skill numbers and catchment counts.

sources.title: US EPA (2007), "An Approach for Using Load Duration Curves in the Development of TMDLs", EPA 841-B-07-006, 74 pp.
sources.why: The authoritative US agency source for LOAD-DURATION CURVES, the under-used literature the assignment flags. LDC practice is a mature, regulator-sanctioned version of exactly our decomposition: plot the water-quality standard (for us, 10 mg/L nitrate) as a LOADING CAPACITY across the continuum of flow percentiles, and plot observed loads against it - so the fraction of time a site exceeds its standard is read off as an AREA UNDER A DURATION CURVE, which is our `violation` base rate reframed. Standard practice bins into five hydrologic regimes (high flow 0-10th, moist 10-40th, mid-range 40-60th, dry 60-90th, low 90-100th percentile), and this binning is the natural target structure for a 5-output small-n regression at n=19. EPA also maintains a nutrient-specific track ('Nutrient TMDLs: Using Duration Curves to Develop Nutrient TMDLs', https://www.epa.gov/tmdl/nutrient-tmdl-workshop). HARD CONSTRAINT AGAINST OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET (rule 8): the LDC method as written REQUIRES a flow record at the site - it is built on the site's own flow duration curve. At an arbitrary map pin we have no discharge, and only 22 of our 85 sites have any streamflow at all (zero of the 61 IWQIS sites). LDCs are therefore usable HERE as (a) a target-construction and diagnostic framework on the 22 gauged sites, and (b) conceptual justification for predicting a CONCENTRATION-duration curve directly from attributes, skipping flow entirely. Free, public domain, no auth.

sources.title: Streamflow duration curve to explain nutrient export in Midwestern USA watersheds: Implication for water quality achievements, Journal of Environmental Management (2023)
sources.why: The closest existing application of duration-curve thinking to MIDWESTERN AGRICULTURAL NITRATE - the same hydroclimate, crop system and tile-drainage regime as Iowa. n = 14 Ohio watersheds (western Lake Erie Basin and Mississippi River Basin), 2000-2020, minimum 3 years per site, daily USGS discharge plus daily water-quality samples from the National Center for Water Quality Research (Heidelberg). Quantitative findings worth building against: the top 10% of flows transported MORE THAN 50% of annual nutrient load in most watersheds; median NO3-N load during high flows was 58% of annual export; the top 40% of flows carried 54-98% of annual NO3-N load. Interpretation for us: nitrate export is concentrated in a narrow, well-defined slice of the duration curve, which is strong support for a percentile-based decomposition - and it also explains why our same-day weather scalars are dead last in permutation importance, since what matters is WHERE ON THE DURATION CURVE the day sits, not the raw rainfall depth. TWO NEGATIVE FLAGS. First, the method explicitly REQUIRES daily discharge to build the curve and bin flows - verified directly from the paper; it cannot be applied at an ungauged map pin as published. Second, n = 14 watersheds, so this is a descriptive/comparative study, NOT evidence that between-site curve position is predictable from attributes - it does not test transfer to a held-out watershed. Useful as motivation and as a source of realistic effect sizes, not as a validated transfer method.

sources.title: "Uncertainty of water-quality predictions in ungauged basins (PUBS)" (water-quality extension of the IAHS Predictions in Ungauged Basins programme)
sources.why: The water-quality counterpart to the hydrological PUB literature, and the best entry point for the (thin) evidence base on transferring CONCENTRATION/LOAD statistics to unmonitored sites - the assignment's question of whether anyone has done duration-curve transfer for water quality. Presents regression models estimating MEAN LOADS at UNMONITORED SITES for total nitrogen, total ammonia plus nitrogen, total and dissolved phosphorus, COD, suspended and dissolved solids, and metals, with explanatory variables limited to drainage area, basin imperviousness, mean annual rainfall, a land-use indicator, and mean minimum January temperature. Two reasons this matters despite being older and urban-focused: (1) it is direct precedent for regressing a SITE-LEVEL WATER-QUALITY STATISTIC on a handful of static basin attributes - the small-n, ~85-target regression our angle proposes, and it uses only ~5 predictors, which is the right order of magnitude for n=19 independent families; (2) its framing is UNCERTAINTY, so the discussion sections are where to hunt for the honest statement of how poorly these transfer (rule 4). ACQUISITION/VERIFICATION CAVEAT: only a ResearchGate copy surfaced in search; the exact venue, year and catchment counts were NOT confirmed from a primary publisher page, so the specific n and skill numbers must be verified from the original before being cited as evidence. Also note it predicts MEAN load, not a duration curve - the mean is a much weaker summary than the exceedance curve we actually need for a 10 mg/L threshold.

sources.title: "Multi-site learning for hydrological uncertainty prediction: the case of quantile random forests", Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 30:3549 (2026)
sources.why: Covers the distributional/quantile-regression leg of the assignment, and specifically the MULTI-SITE pooling question that is our whole constraint. Quantile Regression Forests give the FULL predictive distribution from a single fitted forest without fitting a separate model per quantile - so a QRF (or its GBDT equivalents: LightGBM/XGBoost with pinball loss per quantile, or NGBoost for a full parametric distribution) is a drop-in replacement for our current XGBoost that outputs a per-day predicted CONCENTRATION DISTRIBUTION rather than a point estimate. P(nitrate >= 10) then comes from the predicted distribution directly, and is a strictly better-calibrated route to the violation probability than thresholding a point regression. The multi-site framing is the key contribution: how to pool many sites' residual distributions so a held-out site inherits a sensible spread. HESS is fully open access (Creative Commons), so the protocol and per-site numbers are readable without paywall - VERIFY the split protocol before comparing anything to our LOFO 0.820, since much of the QRF post-processing literature evaluates on random or temporal splits at GAUGED sites, which is not comparable. HONEST GAP TO REPORT UPSTREAM: across these searches I did NOT find a strong primary source doing hierarchical/Bayesian partial pooling with a SITE RANDOM INTERCEPT PREDICTED FROM BASIN ATTRIBUTES for stream nitrate at held-out sites. That specific method - which is arguably the best-matched design for n=19 families, since shrinkage is exactly what protects a 19-unit regression - appears under-published for water quality and searches returned only generic multilevel-modelling tutorials (rstanarm/PyMC vignettes) rather than a hydrological application. That gap is itself a finding: it should be treated as an untested but theoretically well-motivated option, not as an evidence-backed recommendation.

claims.text: Pandit, Golden, Christensen, Lane & Husic (2025, WRR 61(8), e2024WR039207, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207) trained an LSTM on a high-frequency nitrate sensor dataset of n=95 CONUS sites with 158,282 daily-averaged observations spanning 2007-2022. This is a near-exact scale match to the Iowa virtual-sensor project (~85 sites, 160,074 site-days), so its results are the closest published analogue available and its failure modes should be treated as directly transferable rather than as evidence from a large-sample regime.
claims.effectSize: 95 sites; 158,282 daily-averaged nitrate observations; 15 years (2007-2022); ~111 samples/year/catchment

claims.text: In the same study, an LSTM predicting daily nitrate CONCENTRATION scored median KGE = 0.60 under TEMPORAL validation (held-out time period at sites the model had seen) but only median KGE = 0.18 under SPATIAL validation (prediction in unmonitored basins, i.e. the true PUB / ungauged setting), rising to median KGE = 0.34 when the spatial-validation evaluation was restricted to Mississippi River Basin sites. The ~0.42 KGE drop from temporal to spatial holdout at n=95 sites independently reproduces this project's 'good timer, mediocre site-ranker' diagnosis (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21) and indicates the cross-site level deficit is a field-wide limitation of daily nitrate models, not an artifact of XGBoost or of the 19-family CV.
claims.effectSize: median KGE: temporal validation 0.60; spatial validation (unmonitored basins) 0.18 CONUS-wide, 0.34 within MRB. Drop of 0.42 KGE units from temporal to spatial protocol.

claims.text: The study explained long-term MEAN nitrate concentration at its n=95 sensor sites with a random-forest model plus Shapley values, and reported the five most influential predictors ranked largest to smallest magnitude as: (1) TILE DRAINAGE extent, (2) ROADWAY DENSITY, (3) WETLAND COVER, (4) SAND FRACTION, (5) PRECIPITATION. Attributes 1-4 are all static basin attributes and NONE of them are present in the Iowa project's current 68-feature set; the single meteorological variable in the top five (precipitation) is the project's dead-last feature by permutation importance. This is direct evidence that the between-site headroom lies in static attributes of exactly this type.
claims.effectSize: Rank order by Shapley magnitude on long-term mean nitrate concentration: tile drainage > roadway density > wetland cover > sand fraction > precipitation. Numeric Shapley magnitudes not retrievable (article paywalled).

claims.text: Pandit et al. (2025) computed their top-ranked predictor, basin tile-drainage percentage, from the 30-m AgTile-US raster of Valayamkunnath et al. (2020, Scientific Data 7:257, doi:10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x). AgTile-US is a CONUS-wide 30 m binary tile-drained-cropland map with reported 86.03% CONUS-scale validation accuracy, distributed free on figshare (https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742, direct bulk download, no authentication) under CC-BY 4.0, and mirrored in the Google Earth Engine community catalog (https://gee-community-catalog.org/projects/tile/). It is a single static layer (no time dimension), covers ALL of Iowa and every neighboring state, and is directly zonal-averageable over an NLDI-delineated basin, so it satisfies the deployment constraint of an arbitrary ungauged map pin. This resolves the project's open 'no tile drainage data source identified' gap.
claims.effectSize: 30 m resolution, CONUS coverage, static (single epoch), 86.03% validation accuracy, CC-BY 4.0, free figshare bulk download + GEE asset

claims.text: Pandit et al. (2025) used Shapley dependence to identify quantitative NON-LINEAR THRESHOLDS in watershed attributes beyond which they begin to exert considerable influence on river nitrate, and framed the intervention question explicitly as 'given a watershed in Iowa with 60% tile drainage and 5% wetland cover, what would predicted nitrate be if tile drain density were reduced from 60% to 0% or wetland cover doubled from 5% to 10%'. This implies tile-drainage fractions in Iowa basins span a wide enough range (the example basin is at 60%) to carry real cross-site discriminating variance, and that the attribute-to-nitrate response is threshold-shaped rather than linear - favoring a tree model like XGBoost, which can learn the break, over a linear site-level correction. The exact threshold values and effect magnitudes could NOT be extracted because the article is paywalled (HTTP 402 on all Wiley URLs including the PDF).
claims.effectSize: Threshold values not retrievable (paywalled). Illustrative Iowa basin cited at 60% tile drainage, 5% wetland cover.

claims.text: Applying spatially-validated flow and nitrate LSTMs across the Mississippi River Basin for 1980-2022, Pandit et al. (2025) found riverine nitrate export equal to only 19 +/- 4% of N SURPLUS on average, but that this export fraction is strongly wetness-dependent: 42 +/- 24% of surplus in WET years versus 6 +/- 6% in DRY years for Midwestern states - a roughly 7x swing. This is a mechanistic explanation for the Iowa project's failed 'broadcast 2017 N-surplus forward as a time series' experiment (-0.166): surplus does not map to in-stream concentration at a fixed ratio, so a flat broadcast injects a badly mis-scaled signal. It simultaneously supports the alternative use the project has not yet tested - N surplus as a STATIC basin attribute (a basin's surplus RANK, entered once) interacted with a wetness term - since surplus clearly does control export magnitude once hydrologic conditions are conditioned on.
claims.effectSize: MRB nitrate export = 19 +/- 4% of N surplus (1980-2022); Midwestern states: 42 +/- 24% in wet years vs 6 +/- 6% in dry years

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed primary source (Water Resources Research, AGU, 2025) and highly relevant - arguably the single closest published analogue to this project (n=95 sensor sites, 158,282 daily nitrate observations, LSTM, explicit spatial vs temporal validation, Shapley attribution of long-term MEAN concentration to static basin attributes). HOWEVER: the full text is PAYWALLED - every Wiley URL tried (landing page, /full/, /pdf/) returned HTTP 402 Payment Required. All claims above were reconstructed from (a) the OpenAlex record abstract, (b) indexed full-text snippets surfaced through search that quote the paper verbatim (site count, sample counts, KGE values, the ranked top-5 predictor list, the Valayamkunnath citation, the export-fraction percentages), and (c) the independently verified Valayamkunnath et al. 2020 Scientific Data paper and figshare dataset page, which were fully accessible. CONFIDENCE: high for the headline numbers (KGE 0.60/0.18/0.34, n=95, 158,282 obs, top-5 predictor rank order, 19+/-4% / 42+/-24% / 6+/-6% export fractions) since these appear as direct quotations; LOW for anything requiring a table or figure - specifically the numeric Shapley magnitudes, the exact non-linear threshold values for tile drainage and wetland cover, the full list of candidate static attributes considered, per-attribute partial effect sizes in mg/L, and the attribute data sources other than Valayamkunnath. RECOMMENDED FOLLOW-UP: request the PDF from the corresponding author (Admin Husic, Virginia Tech CEE) or check for a US EPA-authored open version, since three co-authors (Golden, Christensen, Lane) are US EPA staff and EPA-authored work is typically deposited in the EPA Science Inventory / NSF PAR. The Shapley threshold values are the single highest-value unextracted item for this project.

sources.title: Baggio & Muzy (2026), "Forecasting threshold exceedance of atmospheric variables at a specific location", arXiv:2605.31079
sources.why: THE most directly relevant methodological source for question (a). Explicit head-to-head of the two paradigms you are weighing: M1 = direct binary classification of exceedance, vs M2 = model the full conditional distribution then integrate above the threshold. Dataset: MeteoNet 2016-2018, southeastern France, 278 ground stations (wind) / 268 (rainfall), ~3.5M train / 400K val / 200K test samples. Finding: M2 (distributional-then-integrate) is consistently equal or better on Brier Skill Score, Peirce Skill Score, log score and AUC, and M1 degrades sharply as the exceedance rate p falls; asymptotic error O(p^2+2p^2) for M2 vs O(p^rho^2) for M1. CRITICAL CAVEAT FOR THIS PROJECT: the M2 advantage is explicitly a rare-event advantage, growing as p -> 0 and becoming decisive only below p ~ 0.01-0.05. At your base rate 0.263 the paper's own PSS ratio M1/M2 approaches 1.0, i.e. the two paradigms are essentially tied. So this source supports the project's prior that exotic imbalance handling is a distraction, and it argues that switching from direct XGBoost classification to regression-then-integrate is NOT where the headroom is at p=0.263. It also does not identify any condition favoring M1, so a distributional variant is a cheap defensible alternative, not a likely win. PROTOCOL WARNING: the split is temporal/station-pooled, not spatially held out, so its absolute skill numbers are NOT comparable to your LOFO 0.820.

sources.title: Bias-corrected exceedance mapping of groundwater nitrate using geostatistical and machine-learning models, Environmental Modelling & Software (2026)
sources.why: The strongest negative result found for the regression-then-threshold pipeline, and it is on NITRATE specifically. Finding: several widely used interpolation and ML models UNDERESTIMATE EXCEEDANCE AREA BY 80-98% when the exceedance map is produced by thresholding the concentration prediction, DESPITE competitive concentration-error metrics (RMSE/R2). Mechanism: any conditional-mean predictor shrinks toward the mean, so thresholding the mean systematically misses exceedances in the tail - exactly the failure your REG R2 0.328 model would inherit if you ever computed violations from predicted mg/L. The paper's remedy is directly portable: frame exceedance as a probabilistic prediction task and CALIBRATE the probability threshold so the predicted total exceedance extent matches an unbiased estimate of it, rather than using the naive 0.5 (or, in your case, beta=2) operating point. It is model-agnostic. RELEVANCE TO YOUR 59% FALSE-DISCOVERY RATE: this reframes that number as a threshold/calibration-target choice, not a model defect - the analogous move for you is to pick the operating point so that predicted violation-days per site matches an unbiased estimate of the site's violation frequency, which is a between-site correction and therefore aimed at precisely the term where all your headroom is. CAVEATS: groundwater, spatial-only (no time dimension), and the validation is target-weighted spatial CV over a national well network (hundreds to thousands of wells), NOT n=19 independent units - the bias-correction step needs an unbiased area/rate estimate that at n=19 families would itself be very noisy. Full-text was 403 to automated fetch; retrieve via institutional access or contact authors.

sources.title: Elahi et al. (2025), "Machine Learning, Generalization, and Transfer Learning for Predicting the Exceedance of Fecal Indicator Bacteria Thresholds at Beaches", Environ. Sci. Technol. 59(42):22386-22396
sources.why: The best available BENCHMARK for putting your LOFO AUC 0.820 in context, and the closest published analogue to your deployment target (predict threshold exceedance at a site using only environmental covariates, then transfer to sites the model has not seen). 33 sites total: 19 Chicago freshwater beaches + 14 San Diego marine beaches. Direct binary classification of exceedance (RF and logistic regression), not regression-then-threshold. Split protocol is stated explicitly: temporal block split (pre-2019 train, 2019 test), 4-fold CV repeated 15x, plus SPATIAL/REGIONAL TRANSFER (Chicago->San Diego and reverse). Numbers: within-region source->target AUC 0.733 (San Diego RF) and 0.607-0.693 (Chicago); cross-region transfer WITHOUT transfer learning collapses to AUC 0.567 (Chicago->SD) and 0.482-0.448 (SD->Chicago, i.e. at or below chance); transfer learning recovers to 0.713 and 0.605-0.610. Transfer learning gave +5.4% AUC and +28.3% weighted-F1. TAKEAWAY FOR THIS PROJECT: your LOFO 0.820 on genuinely held-out basin families is BETTER than every held-out-region number in this paper and better than their within-region numbers too. That is real evidence that the model is not underperforming the field - it also means published virtual-sensor exceedance work has the same between-site transfer deficit you have, and nobody has solved it. Also note the asymmetry finding (transfer works one direction and not the other), a documented negative result about generalization. n CAVEAT: 33 sites, but transfer is evaluated at the level of TWO regions - even weaker effective n than your 19 families, so their transfer-learning gain is not strong evidence it would work for you.

sources.title: Jacobs, Weeser, Rufino & Breuer (2020), "Diurnal Patterns in Solute Concentrations Measured with In Situ UV-Vis Sensors: Natural Fluctuations or Artefacts?", Sensors 20(3):859
sources.why: Directly addresses the target-definition worry: whether a DAILY MAXIMUM extracted from a 5-15 min UV-Vis nitrate record is a physical quantity or partly a sensor artefact. Design: 4 stream sites, 6 fixed sensors plus 1 mobile sensor moved between sites, with sensors deployed in PARALLEL at the same location - the only clean way to separate instrument from environment. Findings: parallel sensors at the same site recorded DIFFERENT sub-daily nitrate patterns, with inter-sensor Pearson r for nitrate of only 0.429 (NF), 0.454 (SHA) and 0.813 (TTP); changing sensor position or shading produced inconsistent pattern changes, implicating solar radiation on the optical path; the authors conclude sub-daily nitrate variation at low concentrations may be artefactual rather than biogeochemical. WHY THIS MATTERS HERE: a daily MAX is the upper order statistic of the within-day record, so it absorbs the full sensor-specific noise/drift amplitude, and it does so ASYMMETRICALLY (noise can only push the max up). Because instrument, deployment geometry, fouling regime and record density are fixed per site, that bias is SITE-CONSTANT - it lands in exactly the between-site term (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24) that you have identified as all your remaining headroom. CHEAP CHECKS THIS MOTIVATES: (1) recompute the target as daily MEDIAN or daily MEAN and re-run LOFO - if between-site skill rises, part of your ceiling was target noise; (2) regress per-site violation rate on per-site record density (obs/day) and on operator (USGS vs IWQIS) - a significant relationship is direct evidence of an artifactual between-site component; (3) check whether the 10 mg/L crossing rate changes when the daily max is computed only on days with full 24h coverage. CAVEATS: tropical headwaters, low nitrate concentrations, small study - Iowa sites run at much higher concentrations where relative sensor error is smaller, so this is a reason to TEST, not a reason to assume your target is broken.

sources.title: 40 CFR 141.23 - Inorganic chemical sampling and analytical requirements (Cornell LII mirror of the eCFR)
sources.why: Settles the framing question (b) on the regulatory side, and the answer VINDICATES the project's choice of an instantaneous threshold rather than an annual average. Unlike the other inorganic contaminants, which are judged on a RUNNING ANNUAL AVERAGE, nitrate/nitrite compliance is determined on a SINGLE SAMPLE: para (i)(3) 'Compliance with the maximum contaminant levels for nitrate and nitrate is determined based on one sample if the levels of these contaminants are below the MCLs.' If the initial sample exceeds, para (f)(2) requires a CONFIRMATION SAMPLE WITHIN 24 HOURS (extendable to two weeks if 24h is infeasible), and para (i)(3) then determines compliance from 'the average of the initial and confirmation samples.' So the acute, no-averaging structure of the nitrate MCL is real - it exists because the endpoint is acute infant methemoglobinemia, not chronic exposure. IMPLICATION: a daily-resolution binary exceedance target is the RIGHT temporal grain for nitrate specifically; do not switch to a running-annual-average target on the theory that that is what regulators use. The one nuance worth reporting in your product copy is the two-sample average on exceedance, which slightly softens a single spike. STANDING CAVEAT: this rule governs FINISHED water at a public water system entry point, not raw stream water - see the Iowa sources below for the stream-side operationalization. Cornell LII is used because ecfr.gov 302-redirects automated fetchers; the authoritative text is 40 CFR 141.23, free, public domain.

sources.title: Iowa DNR, "Methodology for Iowa's 2020 Water Quality Assessment, Listing, and Reporting under Sections 305(b) and 303(d) of the Federal Clean Water Act"
sources.why: The authoritative statement of how the 10 mg/L nitrate number is ACTUALLY operationalized for IOWA STREAMS, as opposed to treated water - and it differs from your target in two ways that matter. (1) SCOPE: the 10 mg/L nitrate criterion is a Class C (drinking water source) designated-use criterion and applies ONLY to waters carrying that designation - 61 reservoirs and 18 river stretches statewide (corroborated by Prairie Rivers of Iowa, https://www.prrcd.org/tag/nitrate/). At an ARBITRARY MAP PIN, which is your deployment target, the 10 mg/L threshold therefore has NO regulatory force; it is a screening proxy. That is defensible, but the product copy must say so - do not let a user infer that p(violation)=0.7 means the reach is legally impaired. (2) EXCEEDANCE DEFINITION: DNR does not list a water on a single exceedance. It uses a BINOMIAL 10% EXCEEDANCE TEST - a segment is assessed as impaired only when the exceedance FREQUENCY is statistically shown to exceed 10% of samples (with a small-sample correction), i.e. the regulatory object for streams is a per-site RATE, not a per-day event. THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST ACTIONABLE FRAMING POINT IN THIS ANGLE: the regulatorily meaningful stream quantity is exactly your weakest metric (between_rate_r2 0.24, per-site violation rate), not your strongest (macro_auc 0.90, within-site timing). If you want a regulator-legible product, the headline output should be a calibrated ANNUAL EXCEEDANCE FREQUENCY with an interval, benchmarked against the 10% binomial rule - and you should report honestly that this is the part the model does worst. Free, public, no auth; note the PDF's text layer resists automated extraction, so read it manually. See also the 2026 draft-list joint comments (https://www.iaenvironment.org/webres/File/2026-03-19_Joint%20comments%20-%202026%20303d%20draft%20list.pdf), which argue DNR's binomial test on sparse grab samples misrepresents true exceedance frequency relative to continuous IIHR/USGS sensor data - i.e. the same sensor-vs-grab discrepancy your dataset sits on top of.

sources.title: Islam et al. (2026), "Trends in nitrate levels in Iowa's community water systems (2000-2022): Characteristics of systems vulnerable to maximum contaminant level exceedances and future regulatory scenarios", Journal of Environmental Quality
sources.why: The Iowa-specific bridge between raw-stream nitrate (what you model) and the exceedance that actually has consequences (what a user cares about), covering 22 years of Iowa community water system compliance data. Useful for this angle in three ways. (1) It documents what fraction of Iowa CWS actually exceed the MCL and which system characteristics predict vulnerability - a base-rate reality check on how often a raw-stream 10 mg/L day translates into a finished-water problem, which is the honest answer to 'is >= 10 mg/L in raw stream water the right target?' (raw-stream exceedance is an UPPER bound on consumer risk; treatment, blending, and alternate sources intervene). (2) Its 'future regulatory scenarios' analysis quantifies what happens if the MCL is tightened - directly relevant to whether you should hard-code 10 mg/L or expose the threshold as a user-settable parameter. A model that outputs a calibrated conditional DISTRIBUTION (per the Baggio & Muzy source above) gets threshold-flexibility for free, and that, rather than rare-event accuracy, is the strongest argument for going distributional at your base rate of 0.263. (3) It is an Iowa dataset with Iowa authors, so it is a plausible collaboration/data-request target consistent with your free/public acquisition constraint. CAVEAT: this is about FINISHED water at treatment systems, not ungauged stream reaches - it cannot be used as a performance benchmark for your model and its exceedance rates are not comparable to your 0.263 base rate.

claims.text: In Jones, Drake, Hruby, Schilling & Wolter (2019), Ambio 48:1143-1153, DOI 10.1007/s13280-018-1137-5, flow-weighted-average (FWA) stream NO3-N concentration across nine western Iowa watersheds correlated significantly with MANURE nitrogen alone (p < 0.01), with surplus N (p < 0.01), and with commercial+manure N (p < 0.01), but showed NO significant relationship with COMMERCIAL fertilizer N alone (p > 0.10). This is a falsifiable directional claim: a basin-aggregated county manure-N attribute should carry cross-site signal that a commercial-fertilizer-N attribute does not. Note the analysis is a 9-point cross-sectional correlation with no multivariate model, no r values printed in text for these pairs, and no held-out validation of any kind.
claims.nBasins: 9 watersheds (Rock 1,748 km2; Floyd 2,295; Monona-Harrison Ditch 2,331; Little Sioux 8,350; Soldier 1,049; Boyer 2,202; West Nishnabotna 3,434; East Nishnabotna 2,862; West Nodaway 1,974), all draining to the Missouri River in western Iowa; single year of nitrate data (2017)
claims.effectSize: manure N vs FWA NO3-N: p < 0.01; commercial N vs FWA NO3-N: p > 0.10 (non-significant, an explicit NEGATIVE result); exact correlation coefficients for these pairs are NOT reported in the text (only shown graphically in Fig. 4)

claims.text: Quoted verbatim from the same paper: 'The surplus N relates much more strongly to generated manure N (R2 = 0.83) than commercial N inputs (R2 = 0.14) among the nine watersheds.' Because surplus N is the quantity that tracked stream nitrate, this decomposition implies that the between-basin variance in surplus N is driven almost entirely by the manure term. Operationally for the sustag project: if the gTREND N-surplus layer is dropped (it dies in 2017), a county-level MANURE-N layer recovers most of its cross-basin discriminating power, whereas a commercial-fertilizer-N layer would not.
claims.effectSize: R2 = 0.83 (surplus N ~ manure N) vs R2 = 0.14 (surplus N ~ commercial N); n = 9 points, so a single high-leverage watershed can move R2 substantially - treat these as suggestive, not precise

claims.text: The magnitude of the between-basin nitrate signal attributable to livestock density in this study is large enough to matter for the sustag 10 mg/L violation threshold: the two watersheds with the highest animal densities, Rock (5.00 Animal Units per hectare) and Floyd (3.53 AU/ha), had 2017 FWA NO3-N of 16.2 and 11.5 mg/L respectively, versus a 7.3 mg/L aggregate average for the other seven watersheds (mean 0.84 AU/ha). Animal density across the nine basins ranged 0.45 to 5.00 AU/ha. Both high-density basins exceed the 10 mg/L violation threshold on an annual-average basis while the seven-basin average does not - i.e. this single static attribute separates chronic-violator basins from non-violators in this sample.
claims.effectSize: 16.2 and 11.5 mg/L (high-density) vs 7.3 mg/L (seven-basin average) = roughly 2x; density contrast 5.00 and 3.53 vs 0.84 AU/ha. NOTE: the paper does NOT report a direct statistical correlation between AU/ha and nitrate - the contrast is descriptive, based on 2 vs 7 basins

claims.text: Corn-soybean area fraction - a variable already present in the sustag feature set as 8 CDL crop classes x 3 distance buckets - was the WEAKEST of the significant predictors of FWA stream nitrate in this study: 'less significantly with area portion in corn and soybean (p < 0.05)' compared to p < 0.01 for manure N, surplus N, and combined N inputs. The supporting evidence is that commercial N application rates were nearly uniform across the nine basins (Rock 116 kg/ha, Floyd 112 kg/ha, nine-watershed average 117 kg/ha) despite vastly different stream nitrate, meaning crop area alone cannot discriminate basins whose N loading differs through the manure term. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION for sustag: adding a county-level manure-N basin attribute should add between-site information that CDL crop fractions structurally cannot supply.
claims.effectSize: corn-soybean fraction p < 0.05 vs manure/surplus N p < 0.01; commercial N rates 112-117 kg/ha across basins spanning 7.3 to 16.2 mg/L FWA nitrate (near-zero between-basin variance in the predictor, large variance in the target)

claims.text: This paper regressed 2017 stream nitrate against 2012 agricultural-census-derived N inputs (commercial fertilizer from USGS NAWQA 2012; county manure N from Gronberg & Arnold 2017 for 2012) and obtained its significant relationships anyway - a direct precedent for using N inputs as a STATIC basin-rank attribute across a 5-year offset rather than as a time-matched series. Surplus N (commercial + manure + prior-year soybean fixation - grain N harvested) ranged 55 kg/ha (West Nodaway) to 161 kg/ha (Floyd), mean 99 kg/ha. This does NOT contradict the sustag negative result on broadcasting 2017 gTREND surplus forward as a time series; it supports the distinct hypothesis that a basin's static RANK in N surplus is stable and informative for the between-site term.
claims.effectSize: surplus N range 55-161 kg/ha (2.9x spread) across basins whose FWA nitrate spanned 7.3-16.2 mg/L; temporal offset between predictor (2012 census) and target (2017 nitrate) = 5 years, with significance retained at p < 0.01

claims.text: OPERATIONAL DATASET, resolved from this paper's methods plus USGS catalog lookup: county-level manure N is available as Gronberg & Arnold (2017), 'County-level estimates of nitrogen and phosphorus from animal manure for the conterminous United States, 2007 and 2012', USGS Open-File Report 2017-1021, DOI 10.3133/ofr20171021 - county polygons (plus a 30 m county grid in the ScienceBase release), kg N per county, years 2007 and 2012, full CONUS coverage (so it covers the out-of-Iowa portions of multi-state basins), text/CSV/spreadsheet bulk download from ScienceBase item 581ced4ee4b08da350d52303, no authentication, USGS public domain. For the post-2017 continuation problem specifically, Falcone (2020), USGS OFR 2020-1153, 'Estimates of county-level nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer and manure from 1950 through 2017', ScienceBase item 5ebad56382ce25b51361806a, extends BOTH fertilizer and manure N to county level at ~5-year census intervals from 1950 through 2017 CONUS-wide, same access terms. CAVEAT for sustag: county resolution is far coarser than the existing 30 m grid-cell feature pipeline; basin-aggregation requires area-weighted county-to-basin intersection, and for small basins one county may dominate.
claims.effectSize: not-applicable; spatial unit = county (Iowa has 99 counties, so a 1,000-2,000 km2 basin typically intersects only 2-5 counties, limiting within-basin spatial detail); temporal unit = USDA Census years (~5 yr)

result.sourceQuality:
Peer-reviewed and fully accessible. Jones CS, Drake CW, Hruby CE, Schilling KE, Wolter CF (2019), "Livestock manure driving stream nitrate", Ambio 48(10):1143-1153, DOI 10.1007/s13280-018-1137-5, open access via PMC6722160; full text retrieved successfully, no paywall. Authors are the Iowa authorities on this exact system (Chris Jones and Keith Schilling, IIHR / University of Iowa, operators of the same IWQIS high-frequency nitrate sensor network that supplies 61 of the sustag project's 85 sites) - so the target variable is measured with the same instrumentation as the project's own data, which is a strong point of external validity.

SEVERE LIMITATIONS that must travel with every number above:
1. n = 9 watersheds, single year (2017), one nitrate value per basin. This is a cross-sectional correlation on nine points. It is NOT a predictive model, has NO train/test split of any kind, and no held-out validation - splitProtocol is "not-applicable" throughout, not "unknown". These numbers cannot be compared to the project's LOFO AUC 0.820 in any way.
2. Nine points is even smaller than the project's n=19 independent basin families. The n=19 constraint therefore does NOT rule this evidence out - it is one of the very few sources whose sample size is in the same regime as the deployment problem rather than the CAMELS 531-671-basin regime. But it also means the reported R2 = 0.83 / R2 = 0.14 contrast rests on ~9 points with two extreme-leverage basins (Rock, Floyd), and could be substantially driven by them.
3. Geographic scope is western Iowa / Missouri River drainage only. This is the LOESS-hills, less intensively tile-drained side of the state; results may not transfer to the Des Moines Lobe tile-drained north-central basins that dominate the project's site list.
4. The paper reports significance levels almost exclusively and does not print r or r2 for the main nitrate-vs-input correlations (only for the surplus-N decomposition). Effect sizes for the primary relationships are therefore not quantifiable from the text.
5. On the assignment's required checklist, this source is SILENT: it analyzes NO tile/artificial drainage extent, NO SSURGO soil drainage class or hydrologic soil group, NO baseflow index, NO depth to water table, NO riparian/wetland fraction, NO drainage density, NO soil organic N. Valayamkunnath et al. 2020, Nakagaki & Wieczorek, Sugg 2007, and NASS tile acreage are not mentioned. Those items must be resolved from other sources; this paper contributes only the manure-vs-fertilizer N split and the livestock-density attribute.

WHAT THIS SOURCE IS ACTUALLY GOOD FOR: it is a strong, on-system argument for adding one specific missing STATIC between-site attribute - basin-aggregated county manure N and/or animal-unit density - which is exactly the category (static geography, not temporal dynamics) where the project's own ablation history says the remaining headroom is. It also supplies a defensible precedent for the static-rank use of N inputs across a multi-year offset.

High — primary authoritative agency source, full text retrieved. USGS Open-File Report 2020-1153 (DOI 10.3133/ofr20201153) PDF downloaded in full (20 p.) after pubs.usgs.gov returned HTTP 403 to the standard fetcher; retrieved via direct HTTP with a browser user-agent from https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2020/1153/ofr20201153.pdf. The companion data release (DOI 10.5066/P9VSQN3C, ScienceBase item 5ebad56382ce25b51361806a) was enumerated via the ScienceBase JSON API and the actual CSV headers and first data rows were inspected directly, so all file names, field names, and units below are verified against the files themselves, not inferred from metadata. IMPORTANT CAVEAT FOR THE RESEARCH ANGLE: this source is a nutrient-INPUT inventory, not a water-quality study. It contains NO stream nitrate observations, NO cross-site regressions of nitrate on basin attributes, and therefore ZERO effect sizes of the form the research question asks for. Its value is purely as a candidate DATASET for the 'manure vs commercial N split' and 'N input' rows of the attribute table, and as evidence about the post-2017 cliff. Any claim of predictive value for nitrate drawn from this source would be fabrication.

claims.text: USGS OFR 2020-1153 (Falcone 2021) does NOT resolve the project's post-2017 N-surplus cliff: its terminal year is 2017 and its time steps are USDA Census of Agriculture years only — 1950, 1954, 1959, 1964, 1969, 1974, 1978, 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997, 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017 (15 time points across 68 years, ~5-year spacing). Verified by direct inspection of the data-release CSV headers, which terminate at the '-2017' column (e.g. 'farmfertN-kg-2017', 'Total_N_kg-2017'). The report states the AAPFCO fertilizer statistics underlying the pre-2017 series 'for 2017, however, have not been completed' and gives no mechanism or commitment for later years. Falsifiable: any column dated after 2017 in the data release would refute this.
claims.effectSize: Coverage 1950-2017; 15 discrete years; 0 years after 2017

claims.text: Because the Falcone product supplies 15 repeated county-level snapshots spanning 1950-2017 rather than a single year, it directly supports the STATIC-RANK use of N input (a basin's long-term mean or rank as a time-invariant attribute), which is a different construct from the project's failed 'broadcast 2017 N-surplus forward in time' experiment (-0.166). The report's own stated use constraint is temporal and scale-based, not rank-based: 'For use as a time series, these data are best suited for use in multicounty or regional analysis', and the FGDC metadata useconst reads verbatim 'Data are best suited for use at multi-county or regional scales'. This is an explicit agency warning that single-county, single-year values are the weakest use — the source discourages fine temporal reading while endorsing aggregation, the opposite polarity from a broadcast time series.
claims.effectSize: 15 time points per county; agency use constraint quoted verbatim: 'Data are best suited for use at multi-county or regional scales'

claims.text: The data release provides an operational manure-vs-commercial-N split as separate files with separate fields, satisfying that row of the requested attribute table. Verified CSV headers: 'fert-farm-1987-2017.txt' has STCOFIPS, fips-int, CountyName, State, then farmfertN-kg-YYYY and farmfertP-kg-YYYY for 1987/1992/1997/2002/2007/2012/2017; 'fert-nonfarm-1987-2017.txt' is the urban/nonfarm equivalent; 'fert-total-1950-1982.txt' the combined pre-1987 series; and per-year manure files 'manure1950.txt' through 'manure2017.txt' carry Cattle_N_kg, Cattle_P_kg, Hogs_N_kg, Hogs_P_kg, Poultry_N_kg, Poultry_P_kg, Other_N_kg, Other_P_kg, Total_N_kg, Total_P_kg PLUS raw animal counts (bcows, mcows, cows, othercows, hogs, chickens, broilers, turkeys, sheep, horses). Units are kilograms of elemental N and P per county (P2O5 converted to P by factor 0.437). Manure is NOT split into recoverable vs unrecoverable fractions in this release. Access: direct unauthenticated HTTP GET from ScienceBase item 5ebad56382ce25b51361806a; plain CSV text files 300-590 KB each, plus two XLSX (1.5 MB fertilizer, 14 MB manure) and model_archive.zip; FGDC accconst is 'None'; USGS product, public domain. Covers all 3,066 CONUS counties, so Iowa AND the multi-state portions of large basins are covered by the same product.
claims.effectSize: Farm/nonfarm split available 1987-2017 only; report states that in 2012, '98 percent of nitrogen from fertilizer was from farm use, and 2 percent was from nonfarm use'
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (3,066 counties, full CONUS incl. Iowa and all neighboring states)

claims.text: The Falcone 2017 farm-fertilizer estimates are themselves random-forest MODEL OUTPUT, not measurements, and the only reported fit statistics are out-of-bag: 'The proportion of variance explained (r2) reported for the nitrogen model with 1,000 trees was 0.948 and for the phosphorus model was 0.921.' The model used 11 predictors and was trained on 2002, 2007 and 2012 records (3,066 counties x 3 years = 9,198 rows), then applied to the 2017 predictor values. The validation is random out-of-bag resampling over counties, NOT a spatial holdout, so r2=0.948 measures interpolation among neighboring counties and is not comparable to any spatially-held-out number. Pre-2017 years (1950-2012) are republished from earlier USGS products and are not model output of this kind, so the 2017 column has a materially different error structure from every other column in the same file.
claims.effectSize: OOB r2 = 0.948 (nitrogen), 0.921 (phosphorus); 1,000 trees; 11 predictors
claims.nBasins: not-applicable — 3,066 counties x 3 training years (2002, 2007, 2012) = 9,198 rows; 0 basins
claims.splitProtocol: random-split (random-forest out-of-bag; explicitly NOT spatially held out)

claims.text: Within the Falcone random forest, county fertilizer EXPENDITURE in dollars dominates all agronomic and climatic predictors, meaning the 2017 values are substantially a re-expression of Census-of-Agriculture dollars rather than an independent agronomic measurement. Reported variable importance (%IncMSE, nitrogen model / phosphorus model): fertdolFPI 73.3 / 67.7; fertacres 34.9 / 28.3; CoApasturepct 24.7 / 26.7; CoAcornpct 23.0 / 22.5; pden 22.4 / 20.4; ET 22.1 / 20.8; PPT 22.1 / 20.8; CoAnitrogenfixpct 20.7 / 27.6; CoAmiscpct 19.3 / 18.7; manureTotalkg 15.9 / 13.9; CoAsmallgrainpct 15.4 / 13.3. Because PPT and ET are among the 11 predictors, and CoAcornpct is derived from the same CDL crop data the project already uses, the 2017 fertilizer field is not statistically independent of the project's existing precipitation and CDL crop features — a direct collinearity risk if added alongside them.
claims.effectSize: fertdolFPI %IncMSE 73.3 (N) and 67.7 (P), roughly 2x the next-ranked predictor fertacres at 34.9 / 28.3

claims.text: Falcone 2021 estimates nutrient INPUTS (mass of N and P applied from commercial fertilizer plus mass excreted as livestock manure) and does NOT subtract crop uptake or removal, so it is not a nitrogen-surplus product and is not a drop-in replacement for the gTREND surplus variable currently used; constructing a surplus from it would require separately obtaining county crop yields/removal from USDA NASS. Stated scope: 'tabular county-level estimates of kilograms of nitrogen and phosphorus generated from two sources: (a) fertilizer from commercial sources and (b) livestock-based manure'. The report also identifies concrete accuracy limitations relevant to basin aggregation: USDA withholds county livestock entries for disclosure reasons and these were imputed (for hogs in 2017, 'data entries for 14 of 515 coun[ties]' in the cited state example were withheld), and county-boundary changes are only partly normalized — Broomfield County, Colorado was omitted from the dataset entirely.
claims.effectSize: 0 crop-removal terms (inputs only); disclosure-withheld county livestock counts imputed; 1 county (Broomfield, CO) dropped from CONUS coverage

claims.text: The 2012 Midwest SPARROW total-nitrogen model (Robertson & Saad 2019, SIR 2019-5114, Table 5) was calibrated on TN loads from 1,334 monitoring sites (1,344 considered, 1,335 in Table 1) and reports R2 = 0.950, Yield R2 = 0.913, conditioned RMSE = 0.487 natural-log units (51.8% in real space) and unconditioned RMSE = 0.555 log units (60.0% in real space). CRITICAL CAVEAT: these are IN-SAMPLE calibration statistics from nonlinear least-squares regression; the report presents no cross-validation, no leave-one-basin-out, and no spatial holdout anywhere. The 'Yield R2 = 0.913' is therefore NOT comparable to our between_r2 = 0.21 under LOFO — it is the in-sample cross-sectional fit of a 16-parameter regression to 1,334 sites, and the honest expectation for a truly unseen basin is materially worse. The 'conditioned' RMSE (0.487) is additionally optimistic because it resets predicted accumulated loads to MEASURED loads at upstream calibration sites — that is a gauged-upstream-neighbor protocol that DOES NOT WORK for our arbitrary-map-pin deployment target. Only the unconditioned RMSE (0.555 log units / 60%) reflects prediction with no upstream measurements, which is our situation.
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites (2,012 for the streamflow model; 1,273 TP; 107 suspended sediment)
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — in-sample calibration fit only; no holdout or cross-validation reported in the entire 60-page report
claims.effectSize: TN model R2 0.950, Yield R2 0.913, conditioned RMSE 0.487 ln-units (51.8%), unconditioned RMSE 0.555 ln-units (60.0%), mean exponentiated weighted error 1.129

claims.text: The SPARROW Midwest 2012 outputs ARE directly, freely joinable to our existing per-basin NHDPlus COMIDs with no authentication. I byte-range-read the actual file: the data release (USGS DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, ScienceBase item 5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3, published 2020-01-07, marked CC0 1.0 Universal public domain, no login) contains 'mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt' (493,183,556 bytes, plain CSV) whose header is exactly: comid,IncAreaKm2,CumAreaKm2,wbm_meanq,al_tn,al_tn_wwtp,al_tn_fert,al_tn_man,al_tn_atm,al_tn_urb,al_tn_nfix,al_tn_can,alse_tn,...,il_tn,il_tn_wwtp,il_tn_fert,il_tn_man,il_tn_atm,il_tn_urb,il_tn_nfix,il_tn_can,ilse_...,DEL_FRAC,SE_DEL_FRAC,res_decay,se_res_decay. So BOTH accumulated/total TN load (al_tn) AND incremental TN load (il_tn) are published per NHDPlusV2 COMID, decomposed into 7 source terms (WWTP, fertilizer, manure, atmospheric, urban, N-fixation, Canada), each WITH a per-reach standard error (alse_/ilse_ columns), plus a delivery fraction. Companion files: mw_cats.zip (599 MB, catchment polygons), mw_reach.zip (802 MB, reach network), mw_sparrow_model_input.txt (740 MB, all predictor variables per COMID). Since this project already stores an NHDPlus comid per delineated basin, computing SPARROW-derived static features (e.g. area-weighted mean incremental TN yield over the basin's COMIDs, and its source decomposition) is a pure table join — no modeling, no API, no rate limit.
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (per-reach product; mean catchment size 2.7 km2 across the Mississippi, Great Lakes and Red River of the North basins, 27 states)
claims.effectSize: TN file 493 MB CSV keyed on comid; 40 columns; incremental + accumulated loads by 7 sources with per-reach standard errors

claims.text: SPARROW TN output is a STRICTLY STATIC, long-term-mean-annual quantity and can only ever address the between-site term, never the timing term. The report states the models describe 'long-term (2000-14) mean-annual' transport with a base year of 2012, and explicitly warns in Model Limitations: 'This feature enables model results to be used to rank areas based on their typical losses of a specific constituent; however, this feature does not allow areas to be ranked during any specific year or season.' For this project this is arguably a FEATURE not a bug — the diagnosis is that essentially all remaining headroom is in the between-site term (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21; macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24), and every temporal feature attempted has failed. A per-basin SPARROW incremental TN yield is exactly a static site-level 'expected absolute level' covariate. It adds ~1-8 static columns (total yield plus source shares), which is affordable at n=19 independent basin families, unlike any method needing many new free parameters. Falsifiable test: add area-weighted SPARROW incremental TN yield (and source fractions) as static features and re-run LOFO; the prediction is a gain concentrated in between_r2 / between_rate_r2 with little or no change in within_r2.
claims.nBasins: n/a — applies to our 19 basin families
claims.effectSize: static per-reach feature; base year 2012, hydrology detrended to long-term average over 2000-2014; the report itself disclaims any year- or season-specific ranking

claims.text: SEVERE CIRCULARITY RISK, and it is close to certain rather than hypothetical: the Midwest SPARROW TN model was calibrated using water-quality data contributed by Iowa agencies that are the same sources as (or overlap) our 85 sensor sites. Appendix Table 3.1 explicitly lists the contributing agencies including 'IA DMWW — Des Moines Water Works, Iowa', 'IA DNR — Iowa Department of Natural Resources', 'IA GSWSP — Iowa Geological Survey Watershed Snapshots', 'IA ISUCOE — Des Moines River Water Quality Network', and 'IA VWMP — Iowa Volunteer Water Monitoring Program', alongside USGS NWIS. Site-inclusion criteria were: paired streamgage with >=10 years of gap-free daily mean streamflow including 2012; water-quality record >=3 years with >=24 samples and >=3 samples in each of four 3-month seasons; period of record within 3 years of 2012; and load standard error/bias <50% of the mean-annual load. Any of our USGS Iowa sites meeting those criteria is very likely among the 1,334. CONSEQUENCE: injecting SPARROW TN yield as a feature partially leaks the held-out basin's own observed nitrate level back into the model under LOFO, because SPARROW saw that basin's measured load during its own calibration. MITIGATION REQUIRED BEFORE BELIEVING ANY GAIN: download the SPARROW calibration-site list (Saad and others, 2019, the companion data release) and spatially match it against our 85 sites; report LOFO both with all sites and with the subset of folds whose basins contain no SPARROW calibration site. Do not report a SPARROW-feature gain without this check.
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites nationwide; number falling inside our 85 Iowa basins is UNKNOWN and must be checked
claims.splitProtocol: unknown — the overlap between SPARROW's calibration sites and our LOFO test folds is undetermined and is the whole risk

claims.text: USGS explicitly warns that SPARROW predictions degrade exactly at the small-catchment scale, which bounds how much a SPARROW feature can help for small ungauged map pins. Model Limitations states: 'most of the sites used to calibrate the SPARROW models were located on medium to large streams and may not represent the smallest streams in the Midwest. For example, for the SPARROW TP model, only 5 percent of the calibration sites were on streams with drainage areas less than about 31 km2; therefore, it is difficult to know how well the model predicted loads in drainages smaller than this. Until fine scale landscape data and monitoring data on small streams are available, caution should be taken when interpreting the finest scale model results (for example, predictions for the individual incremental drainages of the reaches).' The USGS SPARROW Midwest mapper adds that for the TN model 'the drainage areas of the smallest calibration sites are typically in the range of 10 to 100 square kilometers' and 'the uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model.' Also flagged: because mean catchment is ~2 km2 while 'much of the source data and landscape data used to describe variability in land-to-water delivery were derived from county-wide averages or totals' apportioned by land use, per-reach values are downscaled county statistics, not independent fine-scale measurements — so a SPARROW feature partially re-encodes county-level agricultural covariates the model may already have. Practical rule: aggregate SPARROW incremental yield over the whole delineated basin (which for our sites is large), never use a single outlet reach's incremental value, and expect the feature to be least trustworthy for map pins on headwater streams under ~30-100 km2.
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN sites, of which the report only quantifies the small-basin share for TP: 5% below ~31 km2
claims.effectSize: only 5% of TP calibration sites on drainages <31 km2; TN smallest calibration basins typically 10-100 km2; explicit USGS caution against using individual incremental-reach predictions

claims.text: This report also closes the project's stated tile-drainage data gap, and does so twice over. The SPARROW Midwest TN model includes 'Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)' as a statistically significant land-to-water delivery term with coefficient 0.101, 90% CI 0.064 to 0.139, standard error 0.023, p<0.0001, t = 4.5, VIF = 2.3 — i.e. tile drainage independently increases nitrogen delivery to streams after controlling for runoff, air temperature, soil clay, CRP fraction and no-till. The underlying dataset is Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, 'Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012', USGS data release, DOI 10.5066/F7W37TDP: a 30-metre raster built from 2012 Census of Agriculture state-level tiled acreage, NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland, and STATSGO2 poorly/moderately drained soils, covering SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY — which covers Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of essentially all Iowa basins except any extending into North Dakota. Free, public domain, bulk download from ScienceBase, no authentication. EASIER PATH: it is already pre-aggregated to NHDPlusV2 catchments as field 'LTILES13_PERC2' inside mw_sparrow_model_input.txt in the SPARROW data release, so it can be joined on comid with no raster processing at all. IMPORTANT NEGATIVE / CAUTION: the sign flips by constituent — in the companion SPARROW total-PHOSPHORUS model the same tile-drain term has coefficient -0.091 (90% CI -0.156 to -0.026, p = 0.0221), which the report attributes to phosphorus sorbing to soil in tiled areas and bypassing overland flow. So tile density is not a generic 'more nutrients' proxy; the positive effect is specific to nitrogen. Also note the dataset is a downscaled state-level census estimate apportioned by soil and land cover, NOT an observed tile map, so it carries the same county-average smoothing caveat as the rest of the SPARROW inputs.
claims.nBasins: coefficient estimated from the 1,334-site TN calibration; tile dataset covers 12 states at 30 m
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — regression coefficient from in-sample calibration, no holdout reported

result.sourceQuality: HIGH — primary authoritative source obtained in full. The pubs.usgs.gov HTML landing page and the direct PDF URL both returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, but I downloaded the 45.8 MB PDF via curl and extracted the complete 13,723-line text with pdftotext, so every quoted figure above is read directly from the report body, Table 1, Table 5 (TN model), Table 7 (TP model), Appendix Table 3.1, and the Model Limitations section — not from an abstract mirror. The data-release specifics (file names, byte sizes, CC0 license, DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9) come from the ScienceBase catalog JSON API, and the TN output column schema was verified by an HTTP byte-range read of the first 3 KB of the actual 493 MB mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt file, so the comid-keyed join is confirmed empirically rather than inferred. LIMITATION OF THIS SOURCE FOR THE RESEARCH QUESTION: SIR 2019-5114 answers the 'what is downloadable, at what unit, with what known limits' half of the question definitively, but it contains NOTHING on the second half — there is no process-guided ML content here (no Read/Jia/Karpatne-style pretrain-on-process-model-then-fine-tune experiment, no physics-informed loss, no test of SPARROW output as an ML input feature). Those claims must come from other sources; nothing in this report supports or refutes an expected gain from injecting SPARROW output into an ML model. Likewise this report says nothing about the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy, EPIC/APEX Iowa applications (it uses CEAP APEX/SWAT output only as a phosphorus BMP index), or gridded nitrogen-leaching products.

claims.text: The USGS Midwest 2012 SPARROW data release (Saad & Robertson 2020, DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9) publishes model output per NHDPlusV2 stream reach keyed by COMID, in four plain-text CSV files downloadable without authentication or login: mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt (493 MB, total nitrogen), _TP.txt (446 MB), _SS.txt (501 MB), _FLOW.txt (270 MB), plus mw_sparrow_model_input.txt (740 MB) and shapefiles mw_reach.zip (802 MB) and mw_cats.zip (600 MB). I verified the TN output header by HTTP range request; its columns are: comid, IncAreaKm2, CumAreaKm2, wbm_meanq, al_tn (accumulated TN load) and its seven source shares al_tn_wwtp/_fert/_man/_atm/_urb/_nfix/_can, alse_tn* (the same accumulated loads delivered to the Gulf/Great Lakes), il_tn (INCREMENTAL TN load) with the same seven source-share columns, ilse_tn*, DEL_FRAC, SE_DEL_FRAC, res_decay, se_res_decay. Both incremental and accumulated loads, and per-source attribution, are therefore directly available per reach; yield is derivable as il_tn/IncAreaKm2 and a mean flow-weighted TN concentration as al_tn/(annual volume from wbm_meanq). Files are reachable via https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/file/get/5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3?f=<pathOnDisk> (enumerable from the item JSON at https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3?format=json). NOTE: the ScienceBase HTML page returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch; the JSON API and direct file GETs work via curl. FALSIFIABLE: download the TN file and check the header matches.
claims.effectSize: 7 files, ~3.85 GB total; TN output = 1 row per NHDPlusV2 COMID with 40 columns

claims.text: The Midwest 2012 SPARROW total-nitrogen model was calibrated on long-term mean-annual TN loads from 1,334 monitoring sites and reports in-sample fit statistics R2 = 0.950 (on log accumulated load), Yield R2 = 0.913, conditioned RMSE = 0.487 natural-log units (51.8% in real space), and unconditioned RMSE = 0.555 log units (60.0% in real space). These are CALIBRATION-FIT statistics with NO spatial holdout, no leave-one-basin-out, and no independent test set; the R2 of 0.950 is on accumulated load, a quantity dominated by drainage area, so it is not comparable to any ungauged-basin skill metric and specifically is NOT comparable to our LOFO AUC 0.820 / R2 0.328. The unconditioned RMSE of ~60% in real space is the closest thing to a transfer-relevant error and implies roughly a factor-of-1.6 typical error on predicted mean-annual load. Source: Robertson & Saad 2019, USGS SIR 2019-5114, table 5.
claims.effectSize: R2 0.950 (accumulated load, log units); Yield R2 0.913; conditioned RMSE 0.487 log units = 51.8% real space; unconditioned RMSE 0.555 log units = 60.0% real space
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites (Midwest region); 1,346 TN sites considered out of 93,994 water-quality sites screened
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (in-sample calibration fit; no holdout reported)

claims.text: CIRCULARITY WARNING, CONFIRMED: the water-quality data used to compute the calibration loads for the Midwest 2012 SPARROW TN model were drawn from 71 Federal, State, regional, local, Tribal, university and private agencies, and appendix 3 of SIR 2019-5114 explicitly lists FIVE Iowa data providers: 'IA DNR — Iowa Department of Natural Resources', 'IA DMWW — Des Moines Water Works, Iowa', 'IA GSWSP — Iowa Geological Survey Watershed Snapshots', 'IA ISUCOE — Des Moines River Water Quality Network', and 'IA VWMP — Iowa Volunteer Water Monitoring Program'. Calibration sites required >=3 years of record, >=24 samples, >=3 samples per season, a period of record within 3 years of the 2012 base year (i.e. roughly 2009-2015), and a paired streamgage with >=10 years of daily flow. Consequence for this project: any of our ~85 Iowa sites that is a USGS/IA-DNR site with 2009-2015 nitrogen sampling and a paired gauge is likely to BE a SPARROW calibration site, so SPARROW output at that reach partly encodes that site's own observed level. A LOFO evaluation using SPARROW as a feature must therefore be treated as optimistically biased unless the overlap is checked site-by-site against the SPARROW calibration site list. Conversely, IWQIS in-stream nitrate sensors (which mostly postdate 2015 and are not in appendix 3) are less likely to be contaminated.
claims.effectSize: 5 Iowa agencies among 71 contributing agencies; calibration window 1999-10-01 to 2014-09-30 with period-of-record required within 3 years of 2012
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites region-wide; Iowa subset not enumerated in the report

claims.text: The SPARROW TN model's land-to-water delivery term includes 'Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)' with a statistically significant POSITIVE coefficient of 0.101 (90% CI 0.064 to 0.139, SE 0.023, p<0.0001, t=4.5, VIF 2.3), and the underlying per-catchment tile-drainage percentage is published as a column in the downloadable input file mw_sparrow_model_input.txt under the field names 'tiles13_perc2' and 'ltiles13_perc2' (log form), keyed by ComID. The tile layer derives from Nakagaki & Wieczorek (2016) subsurface tile-drainage extent for 12 Midwest States, extrapolated to NHDPlusV2 catchments by the methods of Wieczorek et al. (2019), with ND/SD supplemented from Finocchiaro (2014, 2016) tile-permit polygons. This DIRECTLY CLOSES the project's stated 'no data source identified' gap for tile drainage density, at NHDPlusV2 catchment resolution (mean catchment area 2.7 km2), covering all of Iowa AND the multi-state upstream portions of Iowa basins (the release's place tags include MN, SD, NE, MO, WI, IL and the bounding box spans -114.85 to -72.51 lon, 27.66 to 50.15 lat). I verified the column names by range-fetching the input file header. Limitation: it is a single static circa-2013 snapshot, so it supplies BETWEEN-SITE information only (which is exactly where this project's headroom is), not temporal signal.
claims.effectSize: coefficient 0.101, 90% CI [0.064, 0.139], p<0.0001, t=4.5; NHDPlusV2 catchments averaging 2.7 km2

claims.text: Beyond tile drains, the downloadable mw_sparrow_model_input.txt supplies a ready-made per-NHDPlusV2-catchment static nitrogen-driver feature set that is directly ingestible by an ML model keyed on COMID, verified from the file header: ManN2012 (manure N, 2012), fert_sw_N_kg (farm fertilizer N), cmaq_TN_12_kg (atmospheric N deposition, CMAQ 2012), nfix_km2 (biological fixation), CAT_PFARM1 (CRP acres relative to total farmland), lCAT_notill (log % catchment in no-till), tiles13_perc2 / ltiles13_perc2, CAT_STCLAY / lcat_STCLAY (soil clay), lcat_KFCTUP (soil erodibility K), ldrainden (drainage density), wbm_incq_mm / lwbm_incq_mm (incremental runoff), aridity, lPPT_INT, CAT_ELEV, TAV_AVE and DTtav2012 (detrended air temperature), sum_ptsrc_kgn_wwtp (WWTP N discharge), IncAreaKm2, CumAreaKm2, HUC8, HUC12, STATE. This is a plausible fix for TWO known data problems in this project simultaneously: (a) the nitrogen-surplus product that ends in 2017 and is NaN for 68% of rows can be substituted or supplemented by ManN2012 + fert_sw_N_kg + cmaq_TN_12_kg + nfix_km2, which are complete across the region; and (b) the 16.5%-of-cells inner-join undercount for basins extending outside Iowa is avoided because SPARROW's inputs are populated for all 30+ states in the release including MN, SD, NE, MO, WI, IL. Caveat stated in SIR 2019-5114: 'much of the source data and landscape data used to describe variability in land-to-water delivery were derived from county-wide averages or totals' apportioned to catchments by fine-scale land use, so effective resolution is coarser than the 2.7 km2 catchment implies.
claims.effectSize: ~85 input columns per COMID; catchments mean 2.7 km2 vs 480 km2 in the predecessor 2002 SPARROW models

claims.text: Four SPARROW limitations bear directly on using its output as a feature for an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin. (1) TEMPORAL RESOLUTION MISMATCH: the released TN/TP/SS predictions are LONG-TERM MEAN-ANNUAL loads with base year 2012 (detrended over 2000-2014); there is no daily, seasonal, or event-scale output, so SPARROW can only supply a static per-basin LEVEL term and can contribute nothing to the WHEN question — which matches this project's diagnosis that the deficit is in the between-site term (between_r2 0.21) and not the within-site term (within_r2 0.42). (2) SMALL-BASIN EXTRAPOLATION: the report states 'The uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model', and that 'most of the sites used to calibrate the SPARROW models were located on medium to large streams and may not represent the smallest streams in the Midwest' — for the TP model only 5 percent of calibration sites were on streams draining less than about 31 km2. (3) SPATIALLY CONSTANT COEFFICIENTS: source and land-to-water coefficients are constant across the whole Midwest, and the authors report that 'relatively large residuals were still identified in the western part of the study area', suggesting systematic regional bias that would propagate into any feature built from SPARROW output. (4) The report notes a Bayesian hierarchical regionally-varying-coefficient SPARROW (Alexander 2015; Strickling & Obenour 2018) was NOT used here and 'could improve their predictability'. No published evaluation of SPARROW output used as an INPUT FEATURE to an ML model appears in this data release or its parent report — that experiment is untested here and would have to be run.
claims.effectSize: TP model: only 5% of calibration sites on drainage areas < ~31 km2; 14/15/28% of TN/TP/SS lost in delivery to the Great Lakes and 19/23/52% to the Gulf of Mexico
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN, 1,344 TP, 1,262 SS, 2,057 streamflow sites considered
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (stated limitations, no holdout evaluation reported)

result.sourceQuality: High. Primary authoritative agency source, read directly rather than via summary. The ScienceBase HTML page and pubs.usgs.gov both returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, so I retrieved (a) the full item record via the ScienceBase JSON API (https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3?format=json) with curl, (b) the complete 74-page parent report Robertson & Saad 2019 USGS SIR 2019-5114 (DOI 10.3133/sir20195114) as PDF and converted it to text, and (c) the actual CSV headers of mw_sparrow_model_input.txt and mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt via HTTP range requests, so the field names quoted are verified from the files themselves, not from documentation. Peer-review status: USGS Scientific Investigations Report, agency-reviewed, not journal peer-reviewed; the companion journal treatment is Robertson et al. 2021 JAWRA (DOI 10.1111/1752-1688.12905), which was paywalled (HTTP 402) and I did not read it. Two things I could NOT verify: the explicit license/use-constraints statement (the FGDC XML attachment is 0 bytes on ScienceBase and the ?format=xml endpoint returned HTTP 415) — USGS data releases are public domain by default under USGS policy, but that is inference, not a quote from this record; and whether any specific one of this project's 85 Iowa sites appears in the SPARROW calibration site list, which would require downloading the calibration-site table and matching by COMID/lat-lon. The circularity claim rests on the confirmed presence of five Iowa data-providing agencies in appendix 3, which establishes risk but not site-level overlap.

Authoritative primary agency source (USGS Web Informatics and Mapping application + its live ArcGIS REST service). Structural claims below (layer names, field names, record counts) were verified by direct query against https://gis1.wim.usgs.gov/server/rest/services/Sparrow/SparrowMidwest/MapServer, not inferred from prose. IMPORTANT GAP: the underlying documentation report (Robertson and Saad, SIR 2019-5114, https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/sir20195114) and the ScienceBase data-release item both returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so SPARROW's own calibration fit statistics (R2, RMSE, yield R2) and its stated ungauged-prediction caveats could NOT be extracted and are recorded as unknown. The mapper page publishes NO held-out validation of any kind: every performance figure associated with these models is an in-sample calibration fit over the same 1,334 sites, so nothing here is protocol-comparable to the project's LOFO AUC 0.820. This source contains no ML content, so it bears on none of the process-guided-ML pretraining questions (Read/Jia/Karpatne).

claims.text: The USGS SPARROW Midwest 2012 mapper publishes four calibrated models -- mean daily streamflow, average annual total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and suspended sediment -- resolved to individual NHD catchments with a typical catchment size of about 2.5 km2 (the report's stated mean is 2.7 km2, versus 480 km2 in the predecessor 2002 models). Outputs represent a 2012 base year for source inputs combined with long-term average hydrologic conditions for 1999-2014. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: SPARROW output is a STATIC per-reach mean-annual number, not a time series. It therefore cannot contribute anything to the temporal/WHEN term (already the model's strength, within_r2 0.42) and can only act on the between-site absolute-level term (between_r2 0.21) -- which is precisely where all remaining headroom is. This is the correct shape of feature for the identified deficit.
claims.effectSize: Catchment resolution ~2.5-2.7 km2 mean (vs 480 km2 in 2002 vintage); temporal resolution = single mean-annual value per reach, base year 2012, hydrology averaged 1999-2014

claims.text: The total-nitrogen component of the Midwest 2012 SPARROW model was calibrated using 1,334 monitoring sites (verified: a returnCountOnly query against layer 37, mw_calib_sites_tn, returns exactly 1334). The drainage areas of the smallest calibration sites for the nutrient and sediment models are typically in the range 10-100 km2. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: this directly addresses the n=19-basin-families constraint. SPARROW has already spent 1,334 independent spatial units of statistical effort learning the between-site nitrogen-level surface across the Midwest -- roughly 70x this project's effective independent sample.
