Importing its per-reach output as a feature is a way to inherit that between-site information without estimating it from 19 families. This is the strongest argument in this source for the borrow-a-process-model angle.
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites (verified by REST count query); smallest calibration drainage areas 10-100 km2
claims.effectSize: No fit statistic published on the mapper page. SIR 2019-5114, which would carry the R2/RMSE, returned HTTP 403 and could not be read.

claims.text: The Midwest 2012 SPARROW products are served from a public ArcGIS REST MapServer at https://gis1.wim.usgs.gov/server/rest/services/Sparrow/SparrowMidwest/MapServer/ with 43 layers: 36 polygon layers (9 each for tn, tp, q, ss), 4 calibration-site point layers (IDs 36-39), and 3 line layers. The total-nitrogen catchment polygon layer is layer 9, mw_cats_tn; its verified field list is keyed by COMID (plus COMID_ORIG) and carries INCAREAKM2, CUMAREAKM2, WBM_MEANQ, CONCENTRAT, and the yield/load family INCL, ACCL, INCY, ACCY (incremental/accumulated load and yield) plus delivered variants DINCL, DACCL, DINCY, DACCY and DEL_FRAC (delivery fraction), with per-source decompositions ACCL_S1 through ACCL_S7. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: the join key is COMID, which this project ALREADY STORES PER BASIN. No new delineation or fuzzy spatial matching is required -- the features are a table join away. Candidate between-site features: CONCENTRAT (mean-annual TN concentration, the closest available analogue to the absolute level the model cannot rank), INCY (locally generated incremental TN yield), ACCY (accumulated upstream yield), DEL_FRAC, and the S1-S7 source attribution encoding fertilizer vs manure vs point-source vs atmospheric contributions.
claims.effectSize: 43 layers; TN catchment layer field set verified to include COMID, CONCENTRAT, INCY, ACCY, INCL, ACCL, DINCY, DACCY, DEL_FRAC, ACCL_S1-S7

claims.text: The bulk model inputs and simulated outputs are released as a USGS data release under DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, titled 'SPARROW model inputs and simulated streamflow, nutrient and suspended-sediment loads in streams of the Midwestern United States, 2012 Base Year', explicitly marked CC0 1.0 Universal (public-domain dedication, no license restriction, no attribution requirement), contact Upper Midwest Water Science Center, Madison WI. ACCESS: fully open, no authentication, no registration, no cost, satisfying the free/public acquisition constraint. Two access mechanisms exist: bulk download from the data-release DOI, or per-feature query via the ArcGIS REST endpoint (which supports where=, returnCountOnly=, geometry= and standard ArcGIS query parameters, as demonstrated during this extraction). CAVEAT: the ScienceBase catalog item (5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3) and the USGS pubs page both returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so exact file names, file formats, and per-file field dictionaries in the bulk release were NOT confirmed and must be checked manually in a browser before planning an ingest.
claims.effectSize: DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9; license CC0 1.0 Universal; no authentication required

claims.text: CIRCULARITY WARNING, quantified: a spatial query of the SPARROW total-nitrogen calibration-site layer against an Iowa bounding box (-96.7, 40.3, -90.1, 43.6; envelope includes fringes of neighboring states) returns 110 calibration sites. The layer schema carries STATION_ID and STATION_NM, so overlap with this project's 85 sensor sites is directly checkable. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: SPARROW TN was fit to long-term mean-annual loads at monitoring stations, and the 22 USGS-operated sites in this project's set are exactly the kind of station that would qualify. If SPARROW per-reach output is injected as a feature, any site whose own record contributed to SPARROW's calibration has label information leaking into its own feature -- and the leakage is CONCENTRATED in the LOFO held-out fold, because leave-one-basin-family-out assumes the held-out family contributed nothing to the fitted model, which is false if SPARROW saw it. MANDATORY MITIGATION: join SPARROW STATION_ID against the 85 site identifiers, report the overlap count, and re-run LOFO with SPARROW features on the non-overlapping subset only; a gain that vanishes on the non-overlapping subset is leakage, not skill. The 61 IWQIS nitrate-sensor sites are the LOWEST circularity risk (SPARROW predates and does not typically ingest high-frequency sensor nitrate); the 22 USGS sites are the HIGHEST.
claims.nBasins: 110 TN calibration sites intersecting an Iowa-inclusive bounding box, out of 1,334 Midwest-wide (verified by REST spatial count query)
claims.effectSize: 110 of 1,334 TN calibration sites fall in or near Iowa; exact overlap with the project's 85 sites is unverified and must be computed via STATION_ID

claims.text: The Midwest 2012 SPARROW domain covers the Mississippi River, Great Lakes, and Red River of the North Basins -- the entire Midwest, not just Iowa -- and results can be aggregated to HUC8, state, or arbitrary tributary outlets. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: this specifically repairs a KNOWN DATA DEFECT in the current pipeline, namely that 16.5% of grid cells lack crop/surplus data and an inner join silently UNDER-COUNTS crop area and N surplus for basins extending outside Iowa, worst for the largest multi-state basins. SPARROW attributes are complete across the full multi-state extent of every Iowa basin, so a SPARROW-derived nitrogen-source feature has no Iowa-boundary clipping artifact. Separately, the current nitrogen-surplus feature (gTREND) ENDS IN 2017 and is NaN for 68% of training rows; SPARROW's 2012-base-year source terms (ACCL_S1-S7) are a static, gap-free, fully-covering substitute. CAUTION: broadcasting a static 2012 value across 2008-2026 is structurally identical to the already-failed ablation 'broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time (much worse, -0.166)', so SPARROW terms should be tested strictly as BETWEEN-SITE static covariates (one value per basin, never varying by day) to avoid repeating that exact failure mode.
claims.effectSize: Domain = Mississippi + Great Lakes + Red River of the North basins; full multi-state coverage of all Iowa drainage basins; aggregable to HUC8/state/tributary outlet

claims.text: Gorski et al. (2024) predicted the backward-looking 7-day-average stream nitrate concentration at 46 predominantly agricultural sites in the midwestern/eastern US with LSTM models, and the headline skill number — 'median Kling-Gupta Efficiency = 0.66' — comes from SINGLE-SITE models 'in which models are trained and tested at a single location' (verbatim abstract). No site was spatially held out, so this paper provides NO evidence of transfer to an unmonitored basin and its 0.66 KGE is NOT comparable to our LOFO numbers. Every one of the 46 sites is a USGS gauge and daily discharge (NWIS code 00060) is a required model input, so the entire modeling design is inapplicable to an arbitrary ungauged map pin (we have discharge at only 22 of 85 sites, zero of 61 IWQIS sites).
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (per-site train/validation/test periods set by run config; single-site models trained and tested at the same location; no spatial holdout)
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.66 across 46 single-site models; per-site RMSE, NRMSE, NSE and PBIAS reported for training and validation splits in the data release

claims.text: Gorski et al. (2024) report a direct NEGATIVE result on pooling sites: 'Developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model,' and they add 'While many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' Accuracy at poorly performing sites was instead improved by GROUPING sites with similar characteristics (the data release carries a 'cluster' and a 'hydro_terrane' label per site). This is peer-reviewed evidence that for nitrate specifically, the CAMELS-style 'one big multi-basin model wins' result does not automatically hold — and it argues for similarity-grouped models rather than one global model. Caveat for us: with 19 independent basin families, splitting into similarity clusters leaves ~4-6 families per cluster, which is likely too few to fit separate models; the actionable version is cluster/terrane membership as a FEATURE, not as a model partition.
claims.nBasins: 46 (grouped into clusters and hydro-terranes; number of groups not recoverable from the accessible metadata)
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout within sites; comparison is single-site vs all-site-pooled vs grouped, all evaluated on within-site validation periods
claims.effectSize: single-site median KGE 0.66; all-sites-pooled model 'reduced performance at several locations'; magnitude of the drop not recoverable (full text Cloudflare-blocked)

claims.text: The abstract states 'Across all sites, discharge and watershed soil and physiographic attributes showed a strong influence on model performance,' and 'Analysis of drivers across sites revealed considerable regional differences related to controlling processes such as groundwater contributions.' The attribution was computed two ways, documented in the USGS data release: permutation feature importance defined as 'the difference in RMSE when the feature is randomly permuted vs the baseline RMSE,' averaged over 10 replicates with a standard deviation, plus per-variable expected-gradient attributions. This supports our project's hypothesis that the missing information is SOIL and PHYSIOGRAPHIC (static, between-site), not additional temporal weather engineering — but note their strongest single driver is discharge, a dynamic variable we cannot obtain at the deployment target. The ranked magnitudes for individual soil/physiographic attributes could NOT be verified because the full text is inaccessible.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (importance computed on the same within-site validation splits)
claims.effectSize: direction only ('particularly strong influence' of discharge + soil + physiographic attributes); numeric permutation-importance values NOT recoverable from accessible sources

claims.text: The USGS data release for this paper (ScienceBase item 661436d1d34e633466530330, FGDC metadata) enumerates the exact static attribute set, and it is dominated by NHDPlusV2 'TOT_'-prefixed catchment attributes — i.e. the USGS 'Select Attributes for NHDPlus Version 2.1 Reach Catchments' series (Wieczorek, Jackson & Schwarz), which is distributed as per-COMID tables already accumulated over the full upstream network. Verbatim attribute names and definitions: TILE_DRAIN ('tile drain density'), TOT_CONTACT ('subsurface flow contact time'), UNSAT_TT ('average unsaturated zone travel time'), TRANSM ('transmissivity'), WCON ('average water content for unsaturated zone'), NO3_DOM ('predicted groundwater [NO3] in domestic supply zone'), TOT_HGAD ('hydrologic group AD soil, high infiltration rate when artificially drained, very slow infiltration rates when not drained'), TOT_HGBD (same, moderate when drained), TOT_HGB, TOT_HGC, TOT_STRM_DENS, TOT_STREAM_LENGTH, TOT_ARTIFICIAL ('flowlines coded as artificial paths'), TOT_CANALDITCH, TOT_LAKEPOND, TOT_NDAMS2013, TOT_NID_STORAGE2013, TOT_NPDES_MAJ_DENS, TOT_ET, TOT_RH, TOT_CWD, TOT_WDANN, TOT_BASIN_AREA, NLCD_AG, NLCD_FOR. This is directly operational for us: our basins already store an NHDPlus comid, so these are joinable by key with NO raster processing, they cover the entire CONUS (therefore the multi-state portions of our largest basins, fixing the Iowa-clipped inner-join undercount), and they are USGS public-domain. The metadata table is free at https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/661436d1d34e633466530330 (fgdc_metadata.xml, 84 KB, direct HTTP, no auth); the underlying attribute tables are separate free ScienceBase items.
claims.effectSize: not-applicable (dataset inventory); note TOT_HGAD and TOT_HGBD are SSURGO-derived hydrologic-soil-group fractions whose very definitions are conditioned on artificial drainage, making them a tile-drainage proxy obtainable independently of any tile-drainage map

claims.text: Gorski et al. included tile drainage as an explicit static attribute (TILE_DRAIN, 'tile drain density') among the 46-site attribute set, confirming that a basin-aggregatable tile-drainage density layer exists and is usable in a Corn Belt nitrate ML model — this is the single most important missing feature in our project (tile drainage is the dominant Iowa hydrologic control and is currently absent). The data release does not name the source raster in the recoverable metadata (attrdefs field reads only 'This release'), so the provenance must be confirmed against the paper's data table — the strong candidate is Valayamkunnath et al. (2020) 30 m CONUS agricultural tile drainage map (AgTile-US), which covers all of CONUS including the multi-state portions of Iowa basins. FALSIFIABLE AND CHECKABLE: the raw attribute values per site are inside model_archive.zip (1,998,632,301 bytes) at the same ScienceBase item, downloadable free without authentication; a 2 GB download resolves both the exact tile-drainage source and lets us read the observed cross-site spread of TILE_DRAIN directly. Note ScienceBase did NOT honor an HTTP Range request in testing, so the full 2 GB must be pulled.
claims.effectSize: presence/absence only — the paper's reported per-attribute importance for TILE_DRAIN could not be read (Wiley full text returned HTTP 402/403 and Cloudflare challenge on every route tried, despite the article being gold OA CC-BY)

claims.text: Gorski et al. (2024) represented nitrogen inputs to their 46 basins as STATIC, SINGLE-VINTAGE attributes rather than as a time series: TOT_N97 is defined verbatim as 'estimate of nitrogen from fertilizer and manure in 1997' and fert_uN_mt_sqkm as 'nitrogen fertilizer use'. That is, a peer-reviewed USGS deep-learning nitrate study covering 46 sites used a 1997 nitrogen estimate as a fixed basin attribute in models spanning far later years. This is direct precedent for the defensible use our project needs: treating N surplus as a STATIC basin-rank attribute (one value per basin, no time axis) rather than broadcasting a 2017 value forward as a per-day feature. Our failed broadcast experiment (-0.166) tested the latter and does not falsify the former; the two are different features with different failure modes, and this study is evidence the static form is standard practice. It does NOT, however, provide an effect size for the N-input attributes specifically, so the value of the static form remains untested here and must be validated on our own LOFO folds.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (single-site models); attribute is static so it contributes only between-site information in the pooled/grouped models
claims.effectSize: not reported in accessible sources — TOT_N97 and fert_uN_mt_sqkm appear in the expected-gradient attribution variable list but their attribution magnitudes are in the paywalled figures

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed, gold open access (CC-BY), Water Resources Research 60(9), Sept 2024, DOI 10.1029/2023WR036591, USGS-led (Gorski, Larsen, Wingenroth, Zhang, Bellugi, Appling). HOWEVER: despite being confirmed gold OA CC-BY by Unpaywall, the full text was UNREACHABLE from this environment — agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com and onlinelibrary.wiley.com returned HTTP 402 to WebFetch and HTTP 403 / Cloudflare 'Performing security verification' to curl and to a text-extraction proxy; Unpaywall lists only the Wiley location and no repository copy (has_repository_copy: false); pubs.usgs.gov returned 403. So NO figure values, NO ranked permutation-importance magnitudes, NO per-attribute effect sizes, and NO explicit statement of the train/validation date boundaries were read. What IS verbatim-verified: (a) the full abstract, retrieved independently from OpenAlex and the Semantic Scholar Graph API, which agree word-for-word; (b) the complete USGS ScienceBase data-release FGDC metadata (fgdc_metadata.xml, 84,087 bytes, HTTP 200), which gave the exact static-attribute names, their definitions, the metric set (RMSE/NRMSE/NSE/PBIAS, train and validation), the permutation-importance definition, and the per-site 'Train/Val/Test' labeling that establishes the split protocol as temporal-within-site with no spatial holdout. Claims about the split protocol and attribute inventory are therefore HIGH confidence (agency metadata); claims about which attributes mattered MOST and by how much are LOW confidence / unquantified and are flagged as such in each claim. The 2 GB model_archive.zip at the same ScienceBase item would resolve the open questions (tile-drainage source, per-site attribute values, ranked importances) and is free and unauthenticated; ScienceBase ignored HTTP Range requests, so it requires a full 2 GB pull.

claims.text: A per-NHDPlus-catchment TILE DRAINAGE dataset exists and is publicly downloadable, directly filling the gap the project lists as 'the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet'. Child item 'Select Hydrologic Modification Attributes: Estimates of Subsurface Tile Drainage Extent for the Conterminous United States, Early 1990s' (ScienceBase id 58d9dec6e4b0543bf7fda70e), source Nakagaki (2016), units = percent of catchment area, keyed by NHDPlus COMID, CONUS coverage. Verified column names by reading the parquet footer: COMID, TOT_TILES_Early90s, TOT_TILES_Early90s_NODATA. Delivered in three routings: _cat.parquet (local reach catchment), _acc.parquet (divergence-routed accumulation), _tot.parquet (total cumulative upstream drainage area). Falsifiable: download the file and confirm nonzero tile percentages for Iowa COMIDs.
claims.effectSize: No model-skill number is reported anywhere in this data release; it is a data catalog, not a modeling study. Zero evidence here on whether tile drainage improves ungauged-site nitrate skill.

claims.text: A SECOND, INDEPENDENT tile-drainage estimate is available in the same release, permitting a cross-check rather than reliance on one product: 'Estimated Area of Subsurface Drainage on Agricultural Land, 1992' (id 57067469e4b03f95a075ad3e), derived from 'Subsurface Drains on Agricultural Land in the Conterminous United States, 1992: National Resource Inventory Conservation Practice 606' (Wieczorek, 2004), units = percent, files TILES92_CONUS.zip plus _cat/_acc/_tot parquet. A companion surface-drainage variable also exists: 'Estimated Area of Agricultural Land Drained by Field Ditches, 1992' (id 57067257e4b03f95a075ab0c). Both are keyed by COMID over CONUS. Falsifiable: the two tile products (Nakagaki early-1990s vs NRI-606 1992) should correlate but are not identical; disagreement between them bounds the measurement error of any tile feature.
claims.effectSize: None reported.

claims.text: A per-catchment nitrogen input product is available that is a direct candidate REPLACEMENT for the project's failing gTREND N-surplus feature (which ends in 2017 and is NaN for 68% of training rows): 'Select Chemical Attributes: Nitrogen and Phosphorous Estimates from Fertilizer and Manure, 2012' (id 59038bc8e4b0e862d2311aef), sources Brakebill and others (USGS, 2017) for fertilizer and Gronberg and others (USGS, 2017) for manure, UNITS = KILOGRAMS (loads, not rates), keyed by COMID, CONUS. Separate files for farm N, farm P, and totals (FarmN2012.zip, FarmP2012.zip, TN2012.zip, TP2012.zip, RCFN2012.zip, RCTN2012.zip). Related items in the same release: 'Estimated nitrogen from septic, 2010' (5d2f72f0e4b01d82ce821afa), 'Mean Rate of Nitrogen Application on Agricultural Land from Census of Agriculture, 1997' (57053205e4b0d4e2b756b353), and CMAQ wet/dry/total atmospheric deposition 2002-2012 (58af0da7e4b01ccd54f9ef33). CRITICAL for this project: because coverage is CONUS and accumulation is done along the NHDPlus network, this fixes the documented inner-join bug where basins extending outside Iowa silently UNDER-COUNT crop area and N surplus.
claims.effectSize: None reported. Note the 2012 snapshot is a single static vintage, so it cannot supply within-site temporal variation — it can only act as a between-site static level predictor, which is precisely where this project's remaining headroom is (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42).

claims.text: ACCESS IS FULLY OPERATIONAL AND UNAUTHENTICATED, but NOT via the API route this project might assume. Verified by direct request: anonymous HTTP range-read from the public S3 bucket succeeds — GET https://prod-is-usgs-sb-prod-publish.s3.amazonaws.com/<itemid>/<itemid>_tot.parquet returned HTTP 206 with correct PAR1 parquet magic bytes, no credentials, no API key. Full-file download of the 17.3 MB tile-drainage _tot.parquet succeeded. URL pattern generalizes across all 158 child items as <itemid>/<itemid>_{cat,acc,tot}.parquet. NEGATIVE RESULT, verified by me: the USGS NLDI characteristics endpoints returned HTTP 404 — both https://api.water.usgs.gov/nldi/linked-data/characteristics/tot and https://api.water.usgs.gov/nldi/linked-data/comid/<comid>/tot. So although this project already calls NLDI for on-the-fly basin delineation, it CANNOT pull these attributes from NLDI in the same call; the working pattern is to pre-download the parquet tables once and join locally on the COMID set returned by NLDI delineation. WebFetch against sciencebase.gov is blocked with HTTP 403; plain curl with a browser User-Agent returns HTTP 200.
claims.effectSize: Not a performance claim. Operational verification only: S3 HTTP 206 + PAR1 magic confirmed; NLDI characteristics HTTP 404 confirmed.

claims.text: The release is authoritative and current, and its scale means the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint does NOT bite for this data source. Full citation: Wieczorek, M.E., Jackson, S.E., Schwarz, G.E., Sekellick, A.J., and Staub, L.E., 2018, 'Select Attributes for NHDPlus Version 2.1 Reach Catchments and Modified Network Routed Upstream Watersheds for the Conterminous United States (ver. 5.0, June 2025)', U.S. Geological Survey data release, DOI 10.5066/F7765D7V. Publication date 2018-10-02; revisions 2019-11-12, 2021-01-31, 2023-08-02, last revision 2025-06-25. Data temporal extent spans 1870-12-31 to 2020-12-31. Covers approximately 2.7 MILLION NHDPlusV2 stream segments; 158 child theme items across 13 themes (Best Management Practices, Chemical, Climate and Water Balance Model, Climate, Geology, Hydrologic, Hydrologic Modifications, Landscape, Population Infrastructure, Regions, Soils, Topographic, Water use). Four linked spatial components: individual reach catchments, riparian buffer zones around reaches, catchments accumulated downstream through the network, and riparian buffers accumulated downstream. Joins via COMID (flowline ComID / catchment FEATUREID). Because these are DETERMINISTIC LOOKUPS keyed to COMID rather than statistically fitted relationships, adding them costs no effective degrees of freedom at the between-site level — unlike a method whose evidence base requires 300+ calibration basins. The n=19 constraint still applies to whether XGBoost can LEARN a stable coefficient on the new features, but not to acquiring them. As a USGS data release it is US Government public-domain / unrestricted use.
claims.nBasins: Attributes computed for ~2.7 million NHDPlusV2 stream segments across the conterminous United States; no model calibration basins involved.
claims.effectSize: None — no predictive skill is claimed or evaluated in this release.

claims.text: CIRCULARITY ASSESSMENT, which distinguishes two different kinds of item in this release. MOST items are SPARROW *INPUT* variables (landscape descriptors: tile drainage percent, fertilizer/manure kilograms, base flow index, soils, climate), derived from census/remote-sensing/soil sources and NOT from any nitrate observation — so joining them as ML features carries NO circularity risk with respect to the project's 85 nitrate monitoring sites. BY CONTRAST, one item IS process-model OUTPUT and carries both circularity and downscaling caveats: 'National Resource Conservation Service's Best Management Practice Scenarios for Total Non-Gas Nitrogen, Phosphorous, and Sediment' (id 5cc89237e4b09b8c0b77f247). Its own metadata states losses were simulated with APEX (Agricultural Policy Environmental Extender) per location, extrapolated to watershed scale with SWAT, under three CEAP scenarios (2003-2006 baseline, no-BMP, enhanced nutrient management), and that the index is the difference between baseline and no-implementation. Crucially it states the estimates 'were available at a large watershed (HUC2) scale, but were further processed using geospatial techniques and land characteristics to extend the information to the NHDPlus version 2.1 catchment scale' — i.e. it is HUC2-resolution information spread down to catchments, so its apparent per-catchment detail is largely interpolation artifact, and it explicitly says the index was built 'For use in the SPARROW models'. The release also contains 'Selected Conservation Practices (CPRAC) for 2012' (5d76976ee4b0c4f70d01fdcb) and NRI conservation practices 2000-2012 (5d1ceefce4b0941bde64cdea). Falsifiable: check whether the BMP index varies within a single HUC2 only as a function of land-cover weights, which would confirm it adds no genuine independent between-basin signal in Iowa.
claims.effectSize: None reported. This release contains NO evidence on the research question of whether injecting process-model output as an ML input feature improves ungauged-site skill — that evidence must come from the process-guided ML literature (Read, Jia, Karpatne), not from this catalog.

result.sourceQuality: Authoritative primary source, fully retrieved, but only partially responsive to the research angle. Strengths: this is the official USGS data release (DOI 10.5066/F7765D7V, ver. 5.0, last revised 2025-06-25) underpinning the USGS SPARROW attribute library; I retrieved the complete parent metadata and enumerated all 158 child items, then fetched detailed metadata for the most relevant ones, and I independently VERIFIED the download mechanism end-to-end (anonymous S3 range-read, HTTP 206, PAR1 magic bytes confirmed; 17.3 MB tile-drainage parquet fully downloaded and its schema read). Access caveat: sciencebase.gov returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch, so all retrieval was done via curl with a browser User-Agent — not paywalled, just bot-filtered. Important limitation on scope: this source is the SPARROW *INPUT* attribute library, NOT SPARROW model *output*. It therefore answers the 'what is publicly downloadable per NHDPlus reach' half of the research question very well, and answers the 'does injecting process-model output as an ML input feature improve ungauged-site skill' half NOT AT ALL — the release reports zero performance numbers, zero split protocols, and zero basin counts, which is why every claim above records splitProtocol and nBasins as 'not-applicable' rather than a fabricated figure. Separate sources are required for SPARROW predicted incremental/total TN yields (e.g. Robertson and Saad 2021, 2012 Midwest SPARROW models, DOI 10.1111/1752-1688.12905) and for the process-guided ML pretraining literature. The single highest-value finding for this project is that a per-COMID tile-drainage layer exists and is free — the project's notes assert no such source had been identified.

claims.text: Pandit et al. (2025, WRR 61(8), doi:10.1029/2024WR039207) trained an LSTM on daily stream nitrate across the conterminous US and reported a large drop from temporal to spatial validation: median KGE fell from 0.60 (temporal validation, forecasting unseen periods at sites INCLUDED in training) to 0.18 (spatial validation, prediction at basins NOT in training). This is the closest published analogue to our deployment target and says an LSTM does not solve the ungauged-basin nitrate-concentration problem.
claims.nBasins: 95 sites used for model training/validation (drawn from 148 total monitoring locations, 1980-2022)
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 (temporal) -> 0.18 (spatial holdout); a drop of 0.42 KGE

claims.text: In the same study, the temporal-to-spatial KGE degradation was strongly TARGET-DEPENDENT across all 95 CONUS sites: streamflow 0.78 -> 0.65 (drop 0.13), nitrate YIELD 0.59 -> 0.32 (drop 0.27), nitrate CONCENTRATION 0.60 -> 0.18 (drop 0.42). Concentration - our target - degrades ~3x more than discharge under spatial holdout, i.e. the between-site level of nitrate CONCENTRATION is the hardest quantity to transfer, even for a deep model with continental training data.
claims.effectSize: KGE drops: flow -0.13, nitrate yield -0.27, nitrate concentration -0.42

claims.text: The spatial validation protocol was explicit and leak-safe in the same sense as our LOFO: twelve-fold cross-validation in which ~8.3% of SITES were excluded entirely from training in each fold and their FULL time series used for validation. This is leave-one-group-of-basins-out, not a random site-day split, so its numbers are protocol-comparable to our LOFO AUC 0.820 in kind (though not in metric).
claims.nBasins: 95 sites split into 12 folds (~8 sites held out per fold)
claims.effectSize: 12-fold spatial CV, ~8.3% of sites withheld per fold

claims.text: Restricting spatial validation to the Mississippi River Basin - a climatically and agriculturally homogeneous subregion containing Iowa - raised median spatial-holdout KGE for nitrate concentration from 0.18 (CONUS) to 0.34 (MRB). This is direct evidence that transfer performance to unmonitored basins improves markedly when the training pool is restricted to hydroclimatically SIMILAR basins, supporting a regionally-specialized model over a continental one for an Iowa-only product.
claims.nBasins: unknown (MRB subset of the 95 training sites; exact count not obtainable from open metadata)
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.18 (CONUS spatial) -> 0.34 (MRB spatial), +0.16

claims.text: Pandit et al. used random forests NOT as a competing predictor but as an INTERPRETABILITY tool: they 'developed interpretable random forest models that explain the spatial variation in long-term streamflow, nitrate concentration, and nitrate yield at 95 sites used for model training.' No head-to-head LSTM-vs-RF/XGBoost predictive comparison under spatial holdout is reported in the abstract or open metadata. Therefore this paper provides NO evidence that LSTM beats gradient-boosted trees for ungauged-basin nitrate, and should not be cited as such.
claims.effectSize: no head-to-head deep-vs-tree metric reported in accessible text

claims.text: The paper reports no ablation of performance versus NUMBER OF TRAINING BASINS, and its own evidence base is 95-148 sites - roughly 5-8x our 19 independent basin families. Its site-level performance was explicitly conditional on high-frequency SENSOR data density (EPA record: agricultural Midwest sites reached R2 and KGE > 0.7 while data-sparse western sites fell below 0.3), i.e. the reported skill is driven by data-rich sites rather than by architecture. Any inference that an LSTM would transfer at n=19 families is unsupported by this source.
claims.nBasins: 148 monitoring locations total; 95 used for training/validation
claims.effectSize: median R2 and KGE ~0.5 across all sites; >0.7 in agricultural Midwest, <0.3 in data-sparse West

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed primary source (Water Resources Research, AGU, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207, Aug 2025; authors Pandit, Golden, Christensen, Lane, Husic - US EPA ORD and Virginia Tech). HOWEVER the full text is PAYWALLED: both the HTML and PDF returned HTTP 402. All figures above come from the published abstract/plain-language summary text surfaced via search, plus the US EPA Science Inventory record for the same work (cfpub.epa.gov, dirEntryId 360394). The quoted KGE values (0.60/0.18, 0.78->0.65, 0.59->0.32, MRB 0.34), the site counts (148 total / 95 trained), and the 12-fold ~8.3%-site-holdout spatial CV design are all consistently reported across independent retrievals and should be treated as reliable. Anything NOT listed here - per-fold tables, a deep-vs-tree head-to-head, a training-basin-count ablation, whether spatial folds were geographically CONTIGUOUS (leave-one-REGION-out) versus randomly assigned sites (leave-one-basin-out) - could NOT be verified and is marked unknown. The contiguity question matters: if the 12 folds were random site assignments rather than spatially blocked regions, the reported 0.18 is an OPTIMISTIC bound and true leave-one-region-out transfer would be worse. Recommend obtaining the PDF via an institutional library or emailing the corresponding author (Husic, Virginia Tech) before relying on any number beyond those quoted.

claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2024, HESS 28:4187-4201) is a streamflow-only opinion paper: every experiment predicts daily volumetric DISCHARGE on the 531-basin CAMELS(-US) benchmark set. Full text contains NO water-quality, nutrient, or nitrate application, and NO comparison against gradient-boosted trees, XGBoost, or random forests — the only non-LSTM baselines are the conceptual model mHM and process-based model VIC. Therefore it provides ZERO direct evidence on whether LSTMs beat GBDTs for nitrate concentration in ungauged basins.
claims.effectSize: n/a — no GBDT and no water-quality experiment exists in the paper

claims.text: THE HEADLINE RESULT IS NOT AN UNGAUGED-BASIN RESULT. In Figs. 3 and 6, LSTMs trained regionally are always TESTED ON THE SAME BASINS THEY WERE TRAINED ON, during a different time period. Verbatim from Sect. 4: 'This was done using k-fold cross-validation so that all models were tested on the same basin(s) where they were trained (during different time periods)'; Fig. 6 caption repeats 'All models were tested on the same basins where they were trained (during different time periods).' The paper's conclusion — train on hundreds of basins — is thus established under a TEMPORAL holdout, not a spatial one, and its effect sizes are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820.
claims.effectSize: n/a — protocol claim

claims.text: The 'how many basins are necessary' ablation (Fig. 6, blue line) partitions the 531 CAMELS basins into random disjoint groups of ~6 sizes (roughly 50, 20, 10, 5, 3, 2 groups, i.e. group sizes from single basins up to 531), trains a 10-member LSTM ensemble per group on 1999-2008 and tests on 1989-1999. Median NSE over 531 basins rises MONOTONICALLY with training-set size all the way to 531 basins, with no plateau: 'even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough to train optimal LSTM models for streamflow.' CRITICAL for us: the paper reports these medians ONLY as a figure curve — no numeric median NSE values are given in the text, tables, or appendices, so the effect size cannot be quoted, and no minimum-viable basin count is ever stated.
claims.effectSize: monotonic increase in median NSE with number of training basins; exact values not reported numerically anywhere in the paper (figure-only)

claims.text: The direction of the local-vs-regional effect is OPPOSITE for LSTMs and for traditional hydrologic models. In Fig. 3a, conceptual (mHM) and process-based (VIC) models calibrated PER BASIN outperform the same models calibrated regionally across 489 CAMELS basins; in Fig. 3b, LSTMs trained on all 531 basins outperform 531 separately-trained single-basin LSTMs. The paper asserts the per-basin-beats-regional result for conceptual models is 'a consistent finding across hydrological-modeling studies (e.g., Beck et al., 2016; Mizukami et al., 2017).' This implies the large-n benefit is specific to high-capacity sequence models that must learn shared representation, and does not automatically transfer to a per-site-tuned or low-capacity model class such as a boosted tree.
claims.effectSize: CDF crossover shown in Fig. 3a vs 3b; no numeric medians reported

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON HYDROLOGICALLY-INFORMED SUBSETTING, directly relevant to our n=19 families. Training on hydrologically coherent subsets of CAMELS — 18 USGS HUC regions (2 to 79 basins each) or 6 k-means clusters of 25 static catchment attributes (59 to 195 basins each) — produced models that were BETTER than random basin groups of the same size but STILL WORSE ON AVERAGE than the single model trained on all 531 basins: 'models trained on any subset of the 531 CAMELS basins performed worse, on average, than models trained on all 531 CAMELS basins.' Fig. 7 (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank over 10 repetitions, alpha=0.05): 'All models perform worse than the full regional model in more basins than they perform better in.' The paper also explicitly disclaims relevance to PUB: 'this analysis does not account for the value of hydrologic diversity for prediction in ungauged basins.'
claims.effectSize: every subset-trained model statistically worse in more basins than better (Wilcoxon, alpha=0.05, 10 reps); numeric NSE deltas not reported

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON PREDICTING WHICH MODEL WINS WHERE, and on hybrid/physics-informed models. The authors state they 'tried extensively to construct a separate predictor model that uses catchment attributes and/or hydrological signatures to predict whether one model will perform better or worse than other models in specific basins. We have not been able to construct a model that performs well at this task,' and that training-period or validation-period metrics cannot reliably select the best model for the test period. Separately, on hybrid differentiable models: 'so far, to our knowledge, all attempts to add physics to (properly trained) streamflow LSTM models in hydrology have produced lower-performing models.' Both are unquantified assertions in an opinion paper with no supporting experiment reported, and the physics claim carries the escape hatch 'properly trained'.
claims.effectSize: none reported — qualitative assertions, no supporting numbers or ablation in the paper

result.sourceQuality: Primary source, fully retrieved and read (HTML page plus full PDF text extracted via pdftotext, 965 lines including all appendices) — no paywall, CC-BY 4.0, DOI 10.5194/hess-28-4187-2024. Peer-reviewed HESS "Opinions" piece (Kratzert, Gauch, Klotz, Nearing), so it is a position paper with a supporting experiment set rather than a full benchmarking study. Key limitations for our research question, all verified against the full text: (1) it is 100% streamflow — no water quality, nutrient, or nitrate content whatsoever; (2) it contains NO tree-ensemble baseline (no RF/XGBoost/GBDT), so it cannot adjudicate LSTM-vs-booster; (3) NONE of its experiments are spatially held out — every result, including the number-of-training-basins ablation, tests on basins present in training under a temporal holdout, and the paper explicitly notes its subsetting analysis "does not account for the value of hydrologic diversity for prediction in ungauged basins"; (4) it reports essentially no numeric effect sizes — Figs. 3, 6, 7 are read visually and no median NSE values appear in text, tables, or appendices, so quantitative claims are limited to direction and monotonicity; (5) it cites Kratzert et al. 2019a for PUB capability but reproduces no numbers from it. Bottom line relevance to a 19-basin-family Iowa nitrate classifier: the paper argues large-n is a precondition for LSTM use and would, if taken at face value, argue AGAINST deploying an LSTM at n=19 — but it never tests small-n transfer to unseen basins, so it is evidence about a precondition, not about our deployment setting. Kratzert et al. 2019a (Toward improved predictions in ungauged basins, WRR, doi:10.1029/2019WR026065) should be fetched separately for the actual spatially-held-out PUB numbers and the entity-aware LSTM.

claims.text: SCOPE LIMIT / MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT FOR AN UNGAUGED-PIN PRODUCT: Read et al. (2019) never tests spatial transfer. Every PGDL, DL, and process-based (PB) model in the paper is fitted to observations from the same lake it predicts; the paper states 'Our study limited the predictive challenge to a collection of lakes that were treated as independent model systems (no relationships between lakes were used or explored to improve models)' and names prediction 'in data poor or unmonitored lakes' as future work with 'parallels with predicting streamflow in unmonitored basins.' All splits are TEMPORAL holdouts within a lake. Therefore none of the paper's reported PGDL gains are evidence that process-model pretraining improves prediction at a site with ZERO local observations, which is exactly the Iowa map-pin deployment case. The paper's regime (good within-site temporal skill, per-site labels available) is analogous to the Iowa project's ALREADY-STRONG within_r2=0.42 term, not to its deficient between-site term.
claims.nBasins: 68 lakes (multi-lake experiment) + 2 intensively studied lakes (Mendota, Sparkling); 0 spatially held out
claims.effectSize: Not applicable — no spatial-holdout experiment exists in this paper

claims.text: Pretraining a deep network on UNCALIBRATED process-model output and then fine-tuning on local observations beat the process model that generated the pretraining data, by a large margin. Across 68 lakes in Wisconsin/Upper Midwest (temporal holdout: test = earliest one-third of each lake's record, train = most recent two-thirds, 133 to 1,788 training dates per lake), median test RMSE was 1.65 degC for PGDL, 1.78 degC for DL, 2.03 degC for calibrated PB, and 2.78 degC for the UNCALIBRATED GLM (PB0) whose output was used as the pretraining target. Ranges: PGDL 0.91-2.66, DL 0.97-2.95, PB 1.46-3.63, PB0 1.55-4.95 degC. NEGATIVE DETAIL: PGDL was NOT better everywhere — it failed to beat 5 of 68 calibrated PB models and 5 of 68 DL models, and per-lake PB-minus-PGDL RMSE differences included negative values (as low as -0.23 degC). Relevance: shows a fine-tuned ML model can EXCEED its process-model teacher (median 2.78 -> 1.65 degC, a 1.13 degC / 41% reduction), supporting the 'inject SPARROW/SWAT output then let the ML correct it' strategy — but only where local labels exist for fine-tuning.
claims.effectSize: Median test RMSE: PGDL 1.65 vs DL 1.78 vs calibrated PB 2.03 vs uncalibrated pretrainer PB0 2.78 degC; PGDL lost to PB in 5/68 lakes and to DL in 5/68

claims.text: The advantage of process-guided pretraining grows as local labels get sparser, and there is a measurable crossover below which pure ML loses to the process model. On Lake Mendota (540 held-out test dates, training dates subsampled to 980/500/100/50/10/2, five random iterations), with 980 training profiles mean test RMSE was 0.92 degC (PGDL), 1.07 degC (DL), 1.56 degC (calibrated PB). Pure DL beat PB when trained on 500 profiles (1.28 vs 1.49 degC) or more, but LOST to PB at 100 profiles (1.73 vs 1.64 degC) or fewer. With only 2 training profiles, PGDL scored 1.77 degC vs PB 3.03 degC. The authors conclude 'the greatest gains of PGDL temperature modeling ... were when observations were relatively scarce' and that 'even a small number of water temperature sampling dates (e.g., 2-100)' suffices to beat both baselines. CAUTION FOR THE IOWA PROJECT: the sparse regime tested is 2-to-100 labels AT THE TARGET LAKE, never zero; this supports process-model priors for thinly-monitored sites but does not establish behavior at n=0 local labels.
claims.nBasins: 1 lake (Lake Mendota); parallel experiment on Sparkling Lake
claims.effectSize: At 980 profiles PGDL 0.92 vs DL 1.07 vs PB 1.56 degC; at 2 profiles PGDL 1.77 vs PB 3.03 degC; DL-vs-PB crossover between 100 and 500 profiles

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT — process-model pretraining can make the hybrid model WORSE than the process model alone if the pretraining output does not span the conditions being predicted. Read et al. re-ran Lake Mendota experiments with 'limited pretraining' (synthetic GLM output restricted to the training period only, removing 1980-2008) versus 'extended pretraining' (from April 1980 onward). When models were trained on cold-season data and asked to predict summer (seas500), limited-pretraining PGDL scored 1.98 degC RMSE versus 1.19 degC for extended pretraining — and the 1.98 degC was WORSE than the calibrated process model's 1.91 degC. With only 2 training profiles the gap was 1.77 (extended) versus 2.67 degC (limited). The limited seas500 pretraining set was under 20% the size of the extended set and 'contained no data from any summer period.' Conversely, when training data were plentiful and train/test conditions matched (sim980, sim500), reduced pretraining had 'minimal' impact, and the limited-vs-extended difference 'monotonically decreased as data [increased].' IMPLICATION: a SPARROW/SWAT feature injected into the Iowa model must produce output spanning the target basins' full condition range, or it can actively degrade skill — consistent with this project's seven prior failed temporal-feature ablations.
claims.effectSize: seas500: limited-pretrain PGDL 1.98 vs extended-pretrain 1.19 degC, vs calibrated PB 1.91 degC (limited pretraining LOST to the process model); 2-profile case 2.67 vs 1.77 degC

claims.text: The physics-informed LOSS TERM contributes far less than pretraining — relevant because a physics loss is much harder to construct for nitrate than for lake energy balance. Read et al. did not ablate the two components ('we did not separately test the contributions of energy conservation and pretraining') but state 'it is likely that pretraining is responsible for the majority of predictive gains,' and that the energy-conservation penalty 'likely serves as a regularization term that improves the generalizability of the model, while pretraining acts as a powerful surrogate for real observations when comprehensive training data are limited.' They cite Jia et al. (2019) as having isolated the energy-conservation loss and found 'small but consistent improvements in accuracy when compared to an otherwise identical LSTM (although this finding was not tested for out-of-bound training data), and larger improvements when models added a pretraining step.' IMPLICATION: for the Iowa nitrate model the actionable half of the PGDL recipe is the cheap half — use calibrated process-model output as a FEATURE or pretraining target — not a bespoke physics loss.
claims.nBasins: 68 lakes (Read et al.); Jia et al. 2019 ablation basin count not reported in this paper
claims.effectSize: Not separately quantified in Read et al. 2019; cited Jia et al. 2019 reports 'small but consistent' gain from the energy-conservation loss vs 'larger improvements' from pretraining

claims.text: THE ACTUAL UNGAUGED-SITE TEST IS THE COMPANION PAPER, and its effect size is far smaller than Read 2019's within-lake gains. Willard, Read, Appling, Oliver, Jia & Kumar (2021), 'Predicting Water Temperature Dynamics of Unmonitored Lakes With Meta-Transfer Learning,' WRR 57, DOI 10.1029/2021WR029579 (open access), built source models at 145 well-monitored lakes and predicted 305 target lakes TREATED AS UNMONITORED (true spatial holdout; plus an expansion to 1,882 additional target lakes). Median target-lake RMSE: uncalibrated GLM (PB0) 2.52 degC; PB-MTL 2.43 degC; PGDL-MTL 2.16 degC; ensemble of 9 PGDL sources per target 1.88 degC. So the entire meta-transfer apparatus bought 0.64 degC (25%) over simply running the uncalibrated process model at the ungauged site, versus the 1.13 degC median gain PGDL achieved at MONITORED lakes. Notably 'for sparsely monitored target lakes, PGDL-MTL often outperformed PGDL models trained on the target lakes themselves,' and the single most important transfer predictor was difference in maximum depth between source and target. n=19 CONSTRAINT FLAG: this method requires a metamodel trained on 144x145 = 20,880 source-to-source transfer pairs. With 19 independent basin families Iowa would have at most ~19x18 = 342 pairs, roughly 1.6% of that, and lake 'max depth' has no obvious nitrate analogue of comparable discriminating power — meta-transfer source selection is likely INFEASIBLE at this project's scale, though the simpler finding (uncalibrated process-model output as a baseline/feature at ungauged sites) transfers directly.
claims.nBasins: 145 source lakes, 305 target lakes held out as unmonitored, plus 1,882 expanded targets
claims.effectSize: Median RMSE at ungauged targets: uncalibrated PB0 2.52 -> PB-MTL 2.43 -> PGDL-MTL 2.16 -> 9-source PGDL-MTL ensemble 1.88 degC (0.64 degC / 25% total gain over raw process model)

result.sourceQuality: Primary source (Read et al. 2019, WRR, DOI 10.1029/2019WR024922) was PAYWALLED at the publisher (HTTP 402). Full text was obtained from the open NSF Public Access Repository copy (par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10126158) and all figures above were extracted by me directly from the PDF text (pdftotext), not from an automated summary — every quoted number is verbatim from the article body or abstract. Peer-reviewed, USGS/University of Minnesota authorship, high-authority journal. IMPORTANT RELIABILITY NOTE: the automated page-summarizer's first pass on the companion Willard et al. 2021 paper FABRICATED its key numbers (it reported '378 lakes, 188 source, 190 target, RMSE 1.1/0.9/0.8, plateau after 50-100 source lakes' and a nonexistent quote about 'geographic and morphological dissimilarity'). The true values, verified from the extracted PDF text, are 145 source / 305 target / 1,882 expanded, RMSE 2.52 / 2.43 / 2.16 / 1.88 degC. Any downstream synthesis should use the corrected figures in claim 6 and should not trust unverified auto-summaries of these two papers. LIMITATION OF THIS SOURCE FOR THE RESEARCH QUESTION: this paper is about LAKE TEMPERATURE, not nitrogen. It supplies the methodological template (pretrain on process-model output, fine-tune on observations) and its boundary conditions, but contains NO information about SPARROW, SWAT, EPIC/APEX, the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy, gridded nitrogen-leaching products, NHDPlus-reach-level nitrogen outputs, or the circularity risk from SPARROW being calibrated on the same monitoring sites. Those parts of the research question require separate sources.

claims.text: Jia et al. (2021) use process-model output in TWO distinct ways in the same system, and both are directly transplantable in principle: (a) as direct INPUT FEATURES — 'Other input features (shade fraction, solar radiation, potential evapotranspiration) are difficult to measure frequently, and we use values produced by the PRMS-SNTemp model as its internal variables' (3 of their 10 input dimensions are process-model output, not observations); and (b) as PRETRAINING TARGETS — simulated intermediate physical variables (streamflow, stream temperature, relative humidity, cloud cover, groundwater and shallow subsurface flow, surface runoff) supervise the model's latent 'transferred variables' before fine-tuning on real observations. Crucially, the process model was NOT region-calibrated: 'Since a region-specific calibration PRMS-SNTemp is extremely time-consuming, a version with default values of parameters is widely used in the hydrologic domain. We provide a comparison with this version referred to as the PRMS-SNTemp model.' This falsifies the assumption that a process model must be locally calibrated to be a useful ML input — and it also eliminates circularity, since an uncalibrated model cannot have been fit to the target monitoring sites.
claims.effectSize: 3 of 10 input features are PRMS-SNTemp internal variables; 6 simulated intermediate variables used as pretraining supervision; process model run with DEFAULT (uncalibrated) parameters

claims.text: The headline '33%/14% improvement over the physics-based model and 24%/14% over LSTM' from Jia et al. (2021) is measured under a TEMPORAL holdout, not a spatial one: 'we train each ML model using data from the first 24 years (Oct 01, 1980 to Sep 30, 2004) and then test in the next 12 years (Oct 01, 2004 to Sep 31, 2016)', with all models global and applied to all 42 segments. The '0.1% / 2%' sparsity is achieved by RANDOMLY SUBSAMPLING labeled site-days from the first 24 years — it is sparsity in TIME at already-monitored segments, not sparsity in SITES. This is therefore NOT the ungauged-basin regime and these numbers are not comparable to a leave-one-basin-out AUC of 0.820. Temperature RMSE at 0.1% labels: PRMS-SNTemp 3.661 (fixed), ANN 3.706±0.114, RNN 3.234±0.057, RNN-pretrained 2.818±0.059, RGrN 2.849±0.049, PGRGrN-ptr 2.556±0.045, PGRGrN-ptr+ctr 2.464±0.105.
claims.nBasins: 42 segments; temperature observed on 32 segments (51,103 obs), streamflow on 18 segments (206,920 obs), Oct 1980-Sep 2016 (13,149 dates)
claims.effectSize: Temp RMSE 0.1% labels: RNN 3.234 -> PGRGrN-ptr+ctr 2.464 (-23.8%); PRMS-SNTemp alone 3.661

claims.text: The benefit of pretraining on process-model output in Jia et al. (2021) DECAYS SHARPLY as labeled data increases, and for streamflow it essentially vanishes at full label density. Temperature RMSE, RNN vs RNN-pretrained-on-simulations: 3.234 -> 2.818 at 0.1% labels (-12.9%), 1.908 -> 1.810 at 2% (-5.1%), 1.546 -> 1.444 at 100% (-6.6%). Streamflow RMSE, RNN vs RNN-pretrained: 6.885 -> 6.367 at 0.1% (-7.5%), 5.718 -> 5.529 at 2% (-3.3%), 4.406 -> 4.104 at 100% (-6.9%). Full-model comparison at 100% labels: PGRGrN-ptr+ctr 4.076 vs RNN-pretrained 4.104 — a 0.7% difference, i.e. the entire graph + contrastive-loss apparatus buys almost nothing once labels are dense. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: our regime is 160,074 labeled site-days (dense in time, sparse in SITES), which resembles their 100% column far more than their 0.1% column. The published condition under which process-guided pretraining paid off — extreme temporal label scarcity at monitored locations — is NOT our condition.
claims.nBasins: 42 segments (32 with temp obs, 18 with flow obs)
claims.effectSize: Pretraining gain shrinks from -12.9% (0.1% labels) to -6.6% (100% labels) for temperature; full method beats simple pretrained RNN by only 0.7% at 100% labels for streamflow (4.076 vs 4.104)

claims.text: Jia et al. (2021) DO run a genuine spatially-held-out experiment, but at n=5 segments, one at a time: 'Seg A to Seg E are five river segments which have sufficient observation data... We intentionally remove the temperature or streamflow observations for a specific segment during the training period (Oct 01, 1980 to Sep 30, 2004). Then we report the prediction performance... only on this segment during the testing period.' Temperature RMSE without observations (RNN -> PGRGrN-ptr+ctr): Seg A 3.328±0.132 -> 2.501±0.037, Seg B 1.384±0.065 -> 1.205±0.016, Seg C 1.804±0.041 -> 1.589±0.040, Seg D 1.805±0.038 -> 1.297±0.017, Seg E 1.646±0.075 -> 1.345±0.041 — improvement on all 5 (-12.9% to -28.2%). Streamflow RMSE without observations: Seg A 0.879±0.063 -> 0.785±0.064, Seg B 3.493±0.112 -> 3.043±0.091, Seg C 2.151±0.094 -> 1.895±0.061, Seg D 2.711±0.114 -> 2.343±0.079, Seg E 11.828±0.073 -> 10.803±0.103. This is the closest analogue to our deployment target, and it is evidence at n=5 held-out units — comparable in scale to our n=19 basin families, so the method is NOT ruled out by our sample-size constraint on evidence-base grounds.
claims.nBasins: 5 held-out segments, one at a time, from a 42-segment network
claims.effectSize: Temperature RMSE on unobserved segments improved 12.9%-28.2% vs RNN; streamflow 10.7%-13.6%

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT (from the same paper, Table IV and Section V-B/V-F): the river-network GRAPH component actively HURTS on the segments most like an arbitrary map pin. On held-out streamflow Seg A, RGrN scores RMSE 1.271±0.035 vs plain RNN 0.879±0.063 — the graph model is 45% WORSE. The authors' explanation: 'Seg A is a head water and has no upstream river segments. Hence, the graph convolution is not helpful for modeling Seg A. Besides, the information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' Separately: 'we can see that RGrN has much larger errors than RNN over low-flow river segments. This is because the neighboring river segments tend to have similar embeddings after graph convolution and thus the training of RGrN pays even less attention to low-flow segments.' DIRECT CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: the deployment target has NO guarantee of a monitored upstream neighbor, and our topology data is partial (upstream_uid on only 28 of 85 sites). The graph half of PGRGrN is the half that fails exactly in our deployment condition; the PRETRAINING half (which requires no neighbors at all) is the transferable part.
claims.nBasins: 1 headwater segment (Seg A) out of 5 held-out segments in a 42-segment network
claims.effectSize: Held-out streamflow RMSE: RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 — graph convolution 45% WORSE on a headwater segment with no upstream neighbors

claims.text: Jia et al. (2021) report that pure ML can be WORSE than the uncalibrated process model under label scarcity, and that pretraining is what reverses this. At 0.1% streamflow labels, PRMS-SNTemp RMSE 6.834 beats both ANN 7.116±0.120 and RNN 6.885±0.068; only after pretraining on simulations does the ML model overtake it (RNN-pretrained 6.367, PGRGrN-ptr+ctr 5.895). Additionally the paper's own generalization test — 'we test the model performance on streamflow prediction using training data only from segments with higher average streamflows (>3 m3/s) in the first 24 years... then report the RMSE in the next 12 years for segments with lower average streamflows (<1 m3/s)' — is an explicit out-of-regime spatial transfer test, and the authors note 'the performance of RGrN becomes worse in predicting segments with lower streamflows... the graph convolution makes the extracted hidden representation more similar for neighboring segments and thus RGrN simulate streamflows with similar dynamic patterns as in high-flow segments when it is trained just using observation data from high-flow segments.' This is a documented failure mode of learning the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an out-of-distribution basin — precisely our between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21).
claims.nBasins: 42-segment network split by flow regime (>3 m3/s train, <1 m3/s test); exact counts per regime not stated
claims.effectSize: At 0.1% labels the uncalibrated process model (6.834) beats plain RNN (6.885) and ANN (7.116) on streamflow; graph model degrades on out-of-regime low-flow segments

result.sourceQuality: Full text obtained and read directly (arXiv:2009.12575v2, the preprint of the SDM 2021 paper, DOI 10.1137/1.9781611976700.69). All tables (I-IV) and the experimental protocol section were read from the PDF, so every number quoted here is verbatim from the source rather than from an abstract or a secondary summary. The SIAM page itself is paywalled beyond the abstract, but the arXiv version is complete and matches the published title/authors. Caveat: the arXiv v2 may differ in minor details from the camera-ready SDM version (pp. 612-620). IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMIT for the research question: this paper is about FLOW and TEMPERATURE in the Delaware River Basin, not nitrogen, and the process model is PRMS-SNTemp, not SPARROW/SWAT/EPIC. It contributes only the methodological half of the research question (does injecting process-model output as an input/pretraining signal improve ungauged-site skill) and contains NO information about downloadable SPARROW nitrogen products, the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy, or gridded nitrogen-leaching datasets — those must be sourced separately. Also note the paper reports RMSE only; it contains no classification metrics, so nothing here is directly comparable to our PR-AUC/AUC framing.

claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2019, WRR 10.1029/2019WR026065) trained LSTMs on 531 CAMELS basins with k=12-fold basin holdout so predictions were made in basins supplying no training data. The out-of-sample 'PUB LSTM' 10-member ensemble achieved median NSE 0.69 (mean 0.54, min -13.02, max 0.90) versus 0.64 median for per-basin-calibrated SAC-SMA (mean 0.51) and 0.58 for the NOAA National Water Model reanalysis (mean 0.31). PUB LSTM beat SAC-SMA in 307/531 (58%) catchments and the NWM in 347/531 (66%). CRITICAL LIMITATION for our use: the target is DAILY STREAMFLOW, not any water-quality or nutrient concentration variable, and NO machine-learning baseline was tested — both benchmarks are process-based hydrologic models. The paper therefore provides ZERO evidence that LSTM beats gradient-boosted trees at anything.
claims.effectSize: median NSE: PUB LSTM 0.69 vs SAC-SMA 0.64 vs NWM 0.58; win rate 58% and 66% of 531 basins

claims.text: The spatial holdout in Kratzert et al. (2019) is a RANDOM k=12-fold split of the 531 CAMELS basins, not a leave-one-region-out or leave-one-basin-family-out split. Exact text: 'Out-of-sample testing was done by k-fold validation, which splits the 531 basins randomly into k = 12 groups of approximately equal size.' With ~44 held-out basins per fold drawn randomly from across CONUS, every held-out basin retains many hydro-climatically and geographically similar donor basins in the ~487-basin training set. This is a WEAKER transfer test than our LOFO protocol, which groups nested/temporally-overlapping basins into 19 families. The reported 0.69 NSE therefore does NOT establish that LSTM PUB gains persist under leave-one-REGION-out, and the paper reports no region-level or spatially-blocked variant.
claims.nBasins: 531 basins split into 12 random folds (~44 held out per fold)
claims.effectSize: n/a — protocol characterization

claims.text: In Kratzert et al. (2019), essentially all between-site skill came from STATIC catchment attributes, not from temporal dynamics. The Global LSTM trained on all basins WITHOUT static attributes reached median NSE 0.63 (mean 0.45); adding the CAMELS static attributes (soils, climate, vegetation, topography, geology) raised it to median NSE 0.74 (mean 0.68) — a gain of +0.11 median NSE, statistically significant at p < 0.05 (Wilcoxon). Separately, the cost of going ungauged was small: gauged Global LSTM with statics 0.74 vs ungauged PUB LSTM 0.69, only -0.05 median NSE. This independently corroborates the sustag finding that the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE STATIC information, and implies that on this project static-attribute enrichment (tile drainage, soils, geology) is the higher-value lever than any sequence architecture.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout for the 0.69 PUB number; the 0.63 and 0.74 Global LSTM numbers are temporal-holdout on all 531 in-sample basins (train 1981-1995, test 1996-2010) and are NOT spatially held out
claims.effectSize: +0.11 median NSE from static catchment attributes (0.63 -> 0.74); only -0.05 median NSE penalty for ungauged vs gauged (0.74 -> 0.69)

claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2019) contains NO ablation of performance versus the NUMBER OF TRAINING BASINS. Every LSTM configuration is trained on ~487 basins (11 of 12 folds) or all 531; there is no experiment at reduced basin counts and no statement of a minimum viable basin count. The paper's own causal claim is that success depends on training over 'large, diverse data sets' — its conclusion 3 reads that there is 'sufficient information contained in catchment attribute data to distinguish between different rainfall-runoff relationships in at least most of the US catchments that we tested.' At n=19 independent basin families, the sustag project sits roughly 25x below this paper's basin count, and this paper offers no evidence that the reported PUB advantage survives that reduction.
claims.nBasins: 531 (single training-set size; no basin-count sweep performed)
claims.effectSize: absence of evidence — no basin-count ablation exists in this paper

claims.text: The head-to-head EA-LSTM vs XGBoost basin-count ablation the assignment asks for exists in Gauch et al., 'The Proper Care and Feeding of CAMELS: How Limited Training Data Affects Streamflow Prediction' (arXiv:1911.07249; Env. Modelling & Software, S136481522030983X), same 531 CAMELS basins. Median NSE by (training years, basins): at 3yr/13 basins XGBoost 0.41 vs EA-LSTM 0.43; 3yr/53 0.48 vs 0.56; 3yr/531 0.57 vs 0.68; 9yr/13 0.54 vs 0.63; 9yr/53 0.61 vs 0.68; 9yr/531 0.66 vs 0.74. The authors state that at the small configurations 'three to six years and 13 basins, XGBoost and EA-LSTM result in NSE distributions that do not differ significantly (large p-values)', and that 'the effect size d grows with the number of basins, but has no clear relationship to the number of training years.' The deep model's advantage is therefore driven by BASIN COUNT, not record length — the exact axis on which sustag is starved (19 families) and rich (18 years, 160k site-days).
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout — Gauch et al. explicitly evaluate 'on the respective set of basins that they were trained on (in hydrologic terms, we perform temporal validation)', train from Oct 1999 for 3/6/9 years, test Oct 1989-Sep 1999. These numbers are NOT spatially held out and are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820.
claims.nBasins: random subsets of 13, 26, 53, 265, and 531 basins; five random draws at each size below 531
claims.effectSize: EA-LSTM minus XGBoost median NSE: +0.02 at 13 basins/3yr, +0.08 at 53 basins/3yr, +0.11 at 531 basins/3yr, +0.09 at 13 basins/9yr, +0.08 at 531 basins/9yr. Significance threshold: Kolmogorov-Smirnov p < 0.01/15 (Bonferroni) AND Cohen's d > 0.35; not met at 13 basins with 3-6 years.

claims.text: Two further cautions against a deep-model pivot at small n. (1) Gauch et al. (arXiv:1911.07249) report that a prior study by the same group, Gauch et al. (2019a), 'found the GBRT-framework XGBoost to provide more accurate predictions than LSTMs' — a published negative result for LSTM in a rainfall-runoff setting. (2) Kratzert et al. (2019) document severe seed-level instability in ungauged LSTM prediction: across the 531 basins, 103 basins had at least one of the 10 PUB LSTM ensemble members score NSE < 0; only 9 of those 103 had all 10 members below zero, and 55 of the 103 had at least one member above NSE 0.5. One basin (USGS 01142500) had 9 of 10 members at NSE < 0 and one member above 0.7. The authors conclude 'a substantial portion of the uncertainty in these LSTM models is due to randomness, rather than to systematic model structural error', which is why they ensemble N=10. Any LSTM attempt on sustag must budget for multi-seed ensembling, and with only 19 held-out families the per-fold seed variance would likely swamp the effect being measured.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (the 103/531 ensemble-variance statistic is from the k=12 random-fold PUB LSTM); the Gauch et al. (2019a) XGBoost-beats-LSTM result is unknown protocol from the citing text alone
claims.nBasins: 531 for the ensemble-variance statistic; unknown for Gauch et al. (2019a)
claims.effectSize: 103/531 basins (19.4%) had >=1 of 10 seeds produce NSE < 0; only 9/531 (1.7%) failed on all seeds

result.sourceQuality: High for the primary source, with an access caveat. The Wiley DOI (10.1029/2019WR026065) returned HTTP 402 Payment Required, so all Kratzert et al. (2019) claims were extracted from the full accepted-manuscript text of the EarthArXiv preprint (https://eartharxiv.org/repository/object/713/download/1565/), converted with pdftotext; text saved at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/e3f1f490-6fb8-475d-be0e-c0cebf530519/scratchpad/kratzert2019.txt. Abstract-level numbers (median NSE 0.69 / 0.64 / 0.58, 531 basins, k-fold) were independently confirmed against the published abstract via the authors' neuralhydrology.github.io summary, so the preprint matches the version of record on the headline results. Table 2, the k=12 random-split description, and the ensemble-variance statistics are quoted directly from the manuscript body. The secondary source (Gauch et al., arXiv:1911.07249, peer-reviewed in Environmental Modelling & Software) was likewise read in full from PDF text at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/e3f1f490-6fb8-475d-be0e-c0cebf530519/scratchpad/gauch.txt. IMPORTANT GAP: neither source addresses WATER QUALITY. Both model daily streamflow only. I found no LSTM-vs-XGBoost nitrate/nutrient concentration comparison under spatial holdout in this pass; the water-quality hits surfaced by search (Mar Menor watershed, IOPscience 2515-7620/acabb7) are single-basin or unknown-protocol and do not test spatial transfer. That question remains open and should be assigned to a dedicated source hunt. Also note the assignment conflated two papers: the PUB experiments are in this WRR paper, while the EA-LSTM architecture and 'universal, regional, local behaviors' work is the companion HESS paper (hess.copernicus.org/articles/23/5089/2019/, doi 10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019), which was not fetched here.

claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2019, WRR, doi:10.1029/2019WR026065), the anchor PUB result cited by the Willard et al. survey, trained an entity-aware LSTM on 531 CAMELS catchments (4-2,000 km2, ~30 yr daily data) under k-fold SPATIAL cross-validation so that every prediction basin supplied zero training data. Ungauged-basin median NSE = 0.69, which EXCEEDED the calibrated SAC-SMA (0.64) and the NOAA National Water Model reanalysis (0.58) evaluated in GAUGED mode over a 15-year period. FALSIFIABLE/RELEVANCE CAVEATS: (a) the target is daily STREAMFLOW, not a water-quality concentration; (b) the evidence base is n=531 independent catchments, ~28x our 19 independent basin families, so this result provides no support for a deep-model advantage at n=19; (c) no gradient-boosted-tree baseline was run — the comparison is LSTM vs process-based models, not LSTM vs XGBoost. Predicts nothing about whether an LSTM would beat our booster.
claims.effectSize: median NSE 0.69 (LSTM, ungauged) vs 0.64 (SAC-SMA, gauged) vs 0.58 (NWM, gauged); +0.05 NSE over best benchmark

claims.text: The Willard et al. (2025) survey states explicitly that in the unmonitored-site literature 'comparisons between different classes of machine learning methods are few and inadequate,' and that 'most prior efforts have been focused on deep learning frameworks built on many sites for predictions at daily time scales in the United States.' No systematic head-to-head, spatially-held-out benchmark of LSTM vs XGBoost/random forest for prediction in unmonitored sites is identified anywhere in the survey. FALSIFIABLE CLAIM: as of this 2025 survey there is NO published spatial-holdout study establishing that an LSTM beats a gradient-boosted tree for ungauged-site prediction of a water-quality CONCENTRATION target. Consequence for this project: switching from XGBoost to an LSTM cannot be justified by citing the PUB literature — the required comparison has not been run by anyone.
claims.effectSize: no effect size exists — the survey documents the ABSENCE of the comparison

claims.text: The survey's only cited claim that deep learning beats gradient-boosted trees is scoped narrowly: 'LSTMs have shown to outperform both state-of-the-art process-based models and also classical ML models (e.g., XGBoost, random forests, SVM)' — for LAKE AND STREAM TEMPERATURE, a smoothly-varying, strongly seasonally-forced target, not for nutrient or nitrate concentration. FALSIFIABLE: no metric, split protocol, or site count is attached to this XGBoost comparison in the survey. Relevance to this project: temperature is dominated by the WITHIN-site temporal signal (which our model already does well at, within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90); it is not evidence that an LSTM recovers the BETWEEN-site absolute level, which is where all our remaining headroom lies.
claims.effectSize: asserted qualitatively; no numbers reported in the survey

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON SMALL/REGIONAL TRAINING SETS, directly against the n=19 constraint: the survey reports that 'regional LSTM models of stream temperature in the United States perform worse than the LSTM model built on all sites in the CONUS for 15 out of 17 regions,' and describes a 'data synergy' effect in which 'deep learning models perform better when fed a diverse training dataset spanning multiple regions as opposed to homogeneous dataset on a single region EVEN WHEN the homogeneous data is more relevant to the testing dataset.' FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: deep models' documented advantage is contingent on large, geographically diverse training pools; a single-state, 19-independent-family Iowa dataset is exactly the homogeneous small-n regime where the survey's own evidence shows LSTMs underperform. The survey adds that 'it remains to be seen how selecting a subgroup of entities as opposed to using all available data fairs in different prediction applications because much of this work does not compare the performances of both these cases' — i.e. no ablation of performance vs NUMBER of training basins is reported anywhere in the survey.
claims.nBasins: 17 CONUS regions carved from a CONUS-wide stream-temperature site set (exact site count not given in survey)
claims.effectSize: regional model worse than global in 15/17 regions (88%); magnitude not quantified in survey

claims.text: NEGATIVE TRANSFER-LEARNING RESULT AT SMALL n: the survey cites a study transferring ML streamflow models built on North America (987 catchments), South America (813 catchments), and Western Europe (457 catchments) to data-poor South Africa and Central Asia, finding that 'the local models trained on minimal data outperform the models from data-rich regions.' FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION for this project: pretraining a deep model on a large external basin corpus (e.g. CAMELS, CAMELS-Chem) and fine-tuning to Iowa is NOT reliably better than a model fit directly on the local data — the one large-scale transfer experiment the survey cites found the opposite direction. This weakens the main proposed route by which the n=531-basin deep-learning literature could be imported to an n=19 problem.
claims.nBasins: 987 (N. America) / 813 (S. America) / 457 (W. Europe) source catchments; target region catchment counts not given
claims.effectSize: direction reversed — local minimal-data models beat transferred data-rich models; magnitude not quantified in survey

claims.text: GRAPH NEURAL NETWORKS ARE NOT A SAFE BET AND MOST VARIANTS CANNOT SERVE THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: the survey reports that for river-network modeling 'ChebNet-LSTM and GCN-LSTM performed worse ... than the standard LSTM and GraphWaveNet was the only one that performed better,' i.e. 2 of 3 GNN architectures LOST to a plain LSTM. Critically, the survey distinguishes TRANSDUCTIVE GNNs (require the test node to be present in the graph at training time) from INDUCTIVE GNNs, which 'are built using only training entities and allow for new entity nodes to be integrated during testing.' FALSIFIABLE DEPLOYMENT CONSTRAINT: an arbitrary Iowa map pin is a node that did not exist at training time, so ONLY inductive architectures (GraphWaveNet-class, or an encoder over static attributes) are admissible; any transductive GCN/ChebNet result in the literature is inapplicable to this product regardless of its reported accuracy. The survey's recommended cheap middle ground is entity-aware modeling — either direct concatenation of static site characteristics to dynamic inputs (which 'does not require novel ML architecture and is therefore very accessible', and is what our booster already does) or a learned ENCODING of static characteristics via a separate network, which the survey reports gave only a 'slight improvement over the static and dynamic concatenation approach' (Tayal et al., lake temperature). Predicted effect of adding a site-embedding/encoder layer on top of our existing static features: SMALL, and the survey provides no numeric gain for it.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown (GNN comparison); the inductive/transductive distinction is architectural, not protocol-based
claims.nBasins: unknown — river-network reach count not stated in the survey text retrieved; lake-temperature meta-learning study used 305 target lakes treated as unmonitored in the Upper Midwestern US
claims.effectSize: 2 of 3 GNN variants worse than plain LSTM; encoded static attributes gave 'slight improvement' over concatenation (unquantified)

result.sourceQuality: MIXED — the peer-reviewed source itself is authoritative (Willard, Varadharajan, Jia, Kumar et al., "Time series predictions in unmonitored sites: a survey of machine learning techniques in water resources", Environmental Data Science, Cambridge, published Jan 2025; open preprint arXiv:2308.09766; NSF PAR 10592409). ACCESS CAVEAT: the Cambridge landing page and the arXiv HTML v2 rendering were retrievable and quoted, but the NSF PAR PDF returned unparseable binary, so I could not verify a full experimental table; quotes below come from the Cambridge article page and arXiv HTML v2 as summarized by the fetch tool, and short quoted strings should be re-verified verbatim against the PDF before publication. IMPORTANT CHARACTER OF THE SOURCE: this is a NARRATIVE SURVEY, not a benchmark paper — it synthesizes frameworks and does NOT contain comparative metric tables, per-study basin-count tables, or any ablation of accuracy vs number of training basins. Consequently the single most decision-relevant finding is a NEGATIVE/ABSENCE result: the survey itself states that cross-method-class comparisons are "few and inadequate", and I found NO study in it applying an LSTM to nitrate or nutrient CONCENTRATION under spatial holdout with a tree-ensemble baseline. The only water-quality-in-unmonitored-sites work cited is a feed-forward neural network for MONTHLY NUTRIENT LOAD (not daily concentration, not LSTM, no reported basin count or protocol). The Kratzert 2019 median-NSE figures (0.69 / 0.64 / 0.58, 531 basins, k-fold spatial CV) were corroborated independently from the authors' own neuralhydrology.github.io writeup and the WRR record, so those numbers are high-confidence. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE PROJECT: this source does not support switching from XGBoost to a deep model. Its evidence for deep-model superiority in ungauged prediction comes from 531-987 catchment corpora and from smoothly-forced targets (streamflow, stream/lake temperature); its two most transferable findings for us are both cautionary at small n — regional models lose to global models in 15/17 regions, and local minimal-data models beat models transferred from 457-987-catchment data-rich regions. Neither the deployment-critical question (can a deep model recover an UNSEEN basin's absolute nitrate LEVEL from static attributes alone?) nor the n=19-families question is answered by this survey.

claims.text: Xiong et al. (2022) trained their LSTM on a SINGLE watershed — the North River Watershed (NRW), a subbasin of the Jiulong River, Fujian Province, China — not on a multi-basin corpus. Inputs were hydrometeorological data plus anthropogenic nitrogen sources (fertilizer application and livestock breeding). This means the paper is NOT evidence that LSTMs learn cross-site absolute level from many basins; it is a single-basin model tested for transfer. Falsifiable: if the full text shows the LSTM was trained on multiple gauged watersheds simultaneously, this claim is wrong.
claims.nBasins: 1 training watershed (North River Watershed, Jiulong River, China); 7 additional watersheds used only as transfer targets
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (home-basin calibration/validation split); the 7-watershed test is spatial-holdout by construction but with n=1 training basin
