claims.effectSize: Home-basin NSE up to 0.67 (daily DIN concentration) and 0.92 (daily DIN flux)

claims.text: The transfer experiment in Xiong et al. (2022) was conducted on the FLUX model, not the concentration model: 'The flux model ensemble, without retraining, performed well (mean NSE = 0.32–0.84) in seven distinct watersheds in Asia, Europe, and North America.' The abstract and both institutional press releases describe only flux transfer; no published number exists for transferred CONCENTRATION performance. Since daily flux = concentration x discharge, and the paper attributes interbasin consistency to 'similarities in rainfall-runoff relationships', the transferable skill is plausibly hydrologic (discharge dynamics) rather than concentration-level skill. Falsifiable: if the SI reports transferred concentration NSE, this claim is wrong.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (no target-basin training data), but transfer of a single-basin model
claims.effectSize: mean NSE 0.32–0.84 across 7 watersheds for FLUX; no reported transferred concentration NSE

claims.text: Xiong et al. (2022) reports NO head-to-head comparison against gradient-boosted trees, random forests, or any other machine-learning baseline. The only comparison stated is rhetorical and against process-based models: the LSTM performance is 'a performance unlikely to be achieved by generic process-based models with comparable data quality.' The HKUST press release confirms 'no specific baseline model comparison results.' Therefore this paper CANNOT be cited as evidence that LSTM beats XGBoost for ungauged-basin water-quality prediction. Falsifiable: if the full text contains an RF/XGBoost benchmark table, this claim is wrong.
claims.effectSize: no ML baseline reported

claims.text: Zero-shot spatial transfer of the Xiong LSTM failed badly in the one North American, human-dominated target: the Newport Bay Watershed (USA) scored NSE = 0.32 while the other six watersheds scored mean NSE 0.55–0.84. Retraining WITH multi-watershed data raised that lowest NSE from 0.32 to 0.68. This is a negative result for pure transfer and a positive result for pooled multi-basin training — but the fix required adding target-region data, which for an arbitrary Iowa map pin is exactly what is unavailable.
claims.nBasins: 7 transfer targets; worst case n=1 (Newport Bay, USA)
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout for the NSE=0.32 zero-shot number; the 0.68 figure is NOT spatially held out (target-region data included in retraining)
claims.effectSize: NSE 0.32 -> 0.68 after retraining with multi-watershed data (flux)

claims.text: Xiong et al. (2022) predicts DIN concentration and flux at a river outlet as a continuous daily time series, not exceedance of a regulatory threshold, and the headline NSE values are computed against a discharge-weighted flux target. NSE on flux is inflated relative to concentration skill because flux is dominated by discharge variance; the same model scored NSE 0.92 on flux but only 0.67 on concentration in the SAME basin under the SAME split. Any citation of the '0.92' figure as evidence of nitrogen-chemistry skill is a protocol/target mismatch with a concentration or violation-classification target.
claims.effectSize: NSE 0.92 (flux) vs 0.67 (concentration), same basin, same split — a 0.25 NSE gap purely from target definition

claims.text: FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, DIFFERENT SOURCE (Pandit et al. 2025, Water Resources Research, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207): an LSTM trained on high-frequency nitrate sensor data across the CONUS (n=95 sites; n=50 within the Mississippi River Basin) achieved median KGE 0.60 under TEMPORAL validation but median KGE only 0.18 under SPATIAL cross-validation (whole watersheds withheld = prediction in ungauged basins), improving to median KGE 0.34 when restricted to Mississippi River Basin sites. This is the closest available analogue to the Iowa deployment target and shows an LSTM at n=95 sites collapsing under spatial holdout for nitrate CONCENTRATION — direct evidence AGAINST expecting an LSTM to solve the between-site problem at n=19 families. Metrics taken from the article landing page/abstract, not the full text; verify against the paper before citing.
claims.nBasins: 95 CONUS sensor sites; 50 in the Mississippi River Basin
claims.splitProtocol: both reported separately: temporal-holdout (median KGE 0.60) and spatial-holdout / leave-watershed-out PUB (median KGE 0.18 CONUS, 0.34 MRB)
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 temporal vs 0.18 spatial for daily nitrate concentration — a 0.42 KGE drop from changing only the split protocol

result.sourceQuality: PAYWALLED — the ACS full text returned HTTP 403 and could not be retrieved. Claims are reconstructed from: (a) the complete verbatim abstract via PubMed (PMID 35772808), (b) Semantic Scholar metadata (CorpusId 250174361, 59 citations), and (c) two institutional press releases written by the authors' own departments (HKUST CIVL and SUSTech COE), which supplied the training-watershed identity (North River Watershed, Jiulong River, Fujian), the input list (hydrometeorology + fertilizer + livestock), the per-watershed transfer breakdown (6 of 7 at NSE 0.55-0.84, Newport Bay USA at 0.32), and the explicit statement that no quantitative ML baseline comparison was provided. Method-level details NOT recoverable without the full text or SI: whether observed discharge was an LSTM input (press release says streamflow 'is not explicitly mentioned', which is not the same as absent — and the flux target strongly implies discharge is involved), the exact home-basin train/test years, sequence length, ensemble size, and whether a concentration-transfer experiment was run and simply not reported in the abstract. VERDICT ON RELEVANCE TO THE ASSIGNMENT: this source does NOT answer the research question. It contains no LSTM-vs-GBDT head-to-head, no ablation on number of training basins, and no leave-one-REGION-out analysis. Its n=1 training basin means it offers no evidence about the n=19-families constraint, and its transferable quantity is FLUX (discharge-dominated), which is unavailable at an ungauged Iowa map pin. The Pandit et al. 2025 result surfaced during verification is substantially more probative for this project and should be fetched in full. Recommend also retrieving Kratzert et al. 2019 (HESS, doi:10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019) directly, as this source does not contain the PUB basin-count evidence the assignment sought.

claims.text: Gorski et al. (2024) contains NO spatial-holdout / ungauged-basin experiment. The companion USGS data release's FGDC data dictionary defines the split variable verbatim as: 'Train/Val/Test — A label indicating if the observation/prediction falls into the training validation or prediction TIME PERIOD as defined by the run config file.' All 46 sites appear in training in every one of the four modeling schemes (single-site, cluster, hydro-terrane, global); held-out data are later years at sites the model has already seen. Consequently none of this paper's KGE values are comparable to a leave-one-basin-out number, and the paper provides zero evidence about LSTM performance at an unmonitored map pin.
claims.effectSize: n/a — protocol finding, not a performance number

claims.text: Pooling sites into a single global LSTM DEGRADED accuracy relative to per-site models for stream nitrate. Across 46 sites: 46 single-site models achieved median KGE = 0.66 (median RMSE = 1.06 mg/L; 32 of 46 sites, 70%, had KGE > 0.5); 5 cluster models (sites grouped by basin attributes) achieved median KGE = 0.66; the single global model trained on all 46 sites achieved median KGE = 0.63. The abstract states 'Developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model.' This is a direct negative result for the assumption that more pooled basins buys transfer skill for nutrient concentration.
claims.nBasins: 46 (46 single-site models; 5 clusters; 8 hydro terranes; 1 global)
claims.effectSize: global median KGE 0.63 vs single-site 0.66 vs cluster 0.66 — pooling cost ~0.03 KGE and hurt distinctive sites specifically

claims.text: The authors explicitly deny that the streamflow-domain 'global model beats local model' finding (Kratzert-style) transfers to water quality: 'While many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' Elsewhere they note that in contrast to discharge modeling, where larger multi-catchment datasets improved deep learning performance, for water quality 'smaller groups of catchments or even single-catchment models [are] currently being equally effective for capturing nutrient dynamics.' This is a peer-reviewed statement that the CAMELS-scale (531-671 basin) deep-learning evidence base should NOT be assumed to carry over to nitrate.
claims.effectSize: qualitative claim by authors, supported by their 0.63 global vs 0.66 local result

claims.text: Every one of the 46 sites is a USGS NWIS station with a CO-LOCATED DISCHARGE GAUGE, and daily discharge (NWIS parameter code 00060) is a required model input alongside nitrate (code 99133); the FGDC attribute table lists discharge ranging 0–192,000 cfs. The paper's headline conclusion is that 'discharge and watershed soil and physiographic attributes show a particularly strong influence on model performance' — i.e. the strongest single driver of the model is an input that is unavailable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin. The reported KGE 0.63–0.66 numbers therefore cannot be reproduced by any weather-and-land-use-only model, and this paper offers no discharge-free ablation to bound how much skill would be lost.
claims.effectSize: discharge is the top-ranked driver; no discharge-free variant reported

claims.text: The study compares only LSTM variants against each other (single-site vs 5-cluster vs 8-hydro-terrane vs global). It reports NO random forest, XGBoost, gradient-boosted-tree, or linear regression baseline anywhere in the paper or in the released code archive (whose 02_run_model directory contains only PyTorch model_weights.pt outputs and LSTM run/model config YAMLs). Therefore this paper provides no evidence that LSTMs beat gradient-boosted trees for nitrate, under any split protocol.
claims.effectSize: zero GBDT/RF baselines present

claims.text: Design details usable as a template: 46 predominantly agricultural sites across the midwestern and eastern US (bounding box -96.75 to -74.22 lon, 38.32 to 44.53 lat), data period 2010-01-01 to 2021-12-31, target = 7-day backward-looking average nitrate (NO3-N + NO2-N, observed range -0.1 to 30.9 mg/L). Static attributes span anthropogenic hydrologic modification, nitrogen application, climate, groundwater, land use/land cover, watershed physical attributes, and soils. Feature importance was computed as permuted-RMSE / baseline-RMSE averaged over 10 replicates (reported range -0.09 to 9.82). Sites were grouped two ways for pooling: 5 attribute-based clusters and 8 glacial hydrogeologic 'hydro terranes' — a grouping strategy directly analogous to, and validating, the basin-family grouping approach, at a scale (46 sites → 5 or 8 groups) comparable to the 85 sites → 19 families constraint.
claims.nBasins: 46 sites, grouped into 5 clusters or 8 hydro terranes
claims.effectSize: grouping by similarity raised accuracy at poorly-performing sites while full pooling lowered it

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed, Water Resources Research (AGU), DOI 10.1029/2023WR036591, gold OA CC-BY, 2024, ~4 citations as of retrieval. HOWEVER the full text could not be fetched: Wiley returned HTTP 402 for both the article URL and the OA pdfdirect URL, and ScienceBase/USGS-pubs returned 403 to the fetcher. Claims were reconstructed from three independent sources: (a) the complete author-written abstract retrieved verbatim from both the OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs (agreeing exactly); (b) the authoritative FGDC metadata XML (84 KB) for the companion USGS data/code release ScienceBase item 661436d1d34e633466530330, written by the same author team, which supplied the decisive split-protocol definition, the input variable list, the file manifest showing only PyTorch/LSTM artifacts, and the feature-importance definition; (c) search-engine snippets of the full text for the per-scheme KGE values (0.66 single-site, 0.66 cluster, 0.63 global, RMSE 1.06 mg/L, 32/46 sites KGE>0.5) and the discussion-section language on global-vs-local for water quality. Items (a) and (b) are high confidence and directly sourced. Item (c) figures are search-snippet-derived and should be re-verified against the PDF by a reader with Wiley access before being quoted in a writeup — in particular the 8-hydro-terrane model's median KGE was never recovered and remains unknown. Separately, a search snippet reporting median KGE 0.81 / NSE 0.73 for 11 Iowa sites belongs to Pandit et al. 2025 (10.1029/2024WR039207), NOT to Gorski, and was deliberately excluded from the claims above; that paper is a strong candidate for a follow-up fetch since it is Mississippi-basin-wide and Iowa-inclusive.

claims.text: The NOAA NWM CONUS Retrospective v3.0 provides 44 years (February 1979 through January 2023) of hourly modeled streamflow plus 3-hourly land-surface output, in NetCDF and Zarr, from public S3 bucket `noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds` (us-east-1), accessible with `aws s3 ls --no-sign-request` — no AWS account, no authentication, and stated license 'Open Data. There are no restrictions on the use of this data.' v2.1 covers February 1979 through December 2020 (`noaa-nwm-retrospective-2-1-pds`, with a Zarr mirror `noaa-nwm-retrospective-2-1-zarr-pds'). FALSIFIABLE / OPERATIONAL: coverage is CONUS-wide, so it covers the multi-state portions of Iowa basins, and the years fully span the 2008-2026 training window except the post-Jan-2023 tail, which the retrospective does NOT cover (a deployment gap requiring the operational NWM feed, not the retrospective). CAVEAT: the registry page does NOT document the reach identifier — it makes no mention of NHDPlus v2 COMID or `feature_id`. The per-reach join to the project's stored NHDPlus comids is therefore UNVERIFIED from this source and must be confirmed against the NWM route-link file before any effort is spent.
claims.effectSize: v3.0 = Feb 1979–Jan 2023 hourly; v2.1 = Feb 1979–Dec 2020; 2.7 million reaches CONUS

claims.text: The National Water Model contains NO representation of subsurface tile drainage: 'The current NWM lacks TD representation which adds considerable uncertainty to streamflow forecasts in heavily tile-drained areas' (Valayamkunnath et al. 2022, Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2021WR031242). Adding a tile-drainage scheme over the heavily tile-drained Midwestern US increased simulated streamflow peaks by 14%, volume by 2.3%, and baseflow by 11%, and reduced groundwater recharge by 43-50%, surface runoff by 7-29%, and evapotranspiration by 7-13%; the scheme 'enhanced the uncalibrated NWM performance by about 20-50% of the fully calibrated NWM.' FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: NWM v2.1/v3.0 retrospective streamflow in Iowa carries a STRUCTURAL, SPATIALLY SYSTEMATIC low bias whose magnitude scales with tile density — i.e. the error is correlated with the exact basin property that controls nitrate. This is the worst possible error structure for a between-site feature: it will not average out across the 19 families, and modeled-Q error could plausibly swamp the between-site signal it is meant to supply. SOURCE CAVEAT: full text paywalled; abstract retrieved verbatim via Semantic Scholar. Per-gauge NSE/KGE tables and the number of gauges evaluated were NOT retrievable and are recorded as unknown.
claims.effectSize: tile drainage changes NWM peaks +14%, volume +2.3%, baseflow +11%, recharge -43 to -50%; TD scheme recovers 20-50% of the gap between uncalibrated and calibrated NWM

claims.text: In an independent benchmark of NWM v2.1 retrospective daily streamflow against 5,390 USGS streamflow gauges over ~33 years (1983-2016), the Central US region had a median KGE of 0.40 for NWM v2.1 (vs 0.29 for the National Hydrologic Model v1.0), with the authors noting 'relatively poor performance is concentrated along the plains areas that span from the high plains (i.e., North Dakota) vertically down through the center of the CONUS' and that 'performance is most mixed as one moves further east in the Central region' (Towler et al. 2023, HESS 27:1809, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023). FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: median KGE 0.40 is the performance at GAUGED locations where NWM parameters were regionalized with gauge information available; performance at an arbitrary ungauged map pin — the actual deployment target — is bounded above by this and is expected to be worse. A feature with ~KGE 0.40 fidelity is a weak instrument for recovering a between-site level term that currently sits at between_r2 0.21. CAVEAT: the paper reports KGE, not NSE, and aggregates to broad regions rather than HUC2, so an Iowa-specific (HUC 07) figure was NOT obtainable.
claims.nBasins: 5390 gauges CONUS (Central region subset size not stated)
claims.effectSize: Central US median KGE 0.40 (NWM v2.1) vs 0.29 (NHM v1.0); 1983-2016

claims.text: In the Upper Mississippi River Basin — the region containing Iowa — 'tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior', and nitrate concentration variability rises relative to discharge variability as basin size increases across multiple orders of magnitude, attributed to differing spatial correlation structures (Marinos, Van Meter & Basu 2020, Geophysical Research Letters, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051). FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: if Iowa nitrate is largely chemostatic, then discharge — whether modeled or observed — carries LITTLE information about CONCENTRATION, because concentration is by definition buffered against flow variation. Chemostasis predicts that adding Q would mainly improve LOAD (C x Q) prediction while leaving concentration and the 10 mg/L exceedance target largely unimproved. This is directly testable on the 22 already-gauged sites BEFORE any NWM ingestion: compute CVc/CVq per site from existing nitrate + USGS discharge; if the median is well below 1, the fluid-dynamics angle is predicted to fail for the concentration target and load-as-target is predicted NOT to help concentration back-derivation. SOURCE CAVEAT: full text paywalled (HTTP 402); abstract retrieved via Semantic Scholar. Exact site count, drainage-area range, power-law slope b values, and CVc/CVq figures were NOT retrievable.
claims.effectSize: direction only: increasing tile drainage density -> more chemostatic; CVc/CVq increases with basin size

claims.text: The standard quantitative criterion for chemostatic solute behavior is CVc/CVq << 1, with CVc/CVq < 0.3 conventionally taken as the chemostatic threshold, where CVc and CVq are the coefficients of variation of concentration and discharge (metric proposed by Thompson et al. 2011, Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605). Basu et al. (2010) separately used the r-squared of the linear regression between ANNUAL load and ANNUAL discharge as a chemostasis measure, implying linearity in the load-Q relation; chemostatic responses in agricultural catchments are attributed to a large legacy soil/groundwater N store buffering concentration, and homogeneously distributed sources produce chemostatic export while heterogeneously distributed sources produce chemodynamic export. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: this gives a concrete, cheap decision rule computable on the project's own 22 gauged sites with data already on disk. It also predicts the sign of the between-site relation: under chemostasis the site-mean concentration should track the N-source term (surplus, row-crop fraction, tile density) rather than the hydrologic term, which is consistent with this project's observed pattern that static geography features win and every temporal hydrologic feature has failed.
claims.effectSize: CVc/CVq < 0.3 = chemostatic; CVc/CVq near or above 1 = chemodynamic

claims.text: AgTile-US is a free 30 m gridded tile-drainage raster covering the entire contiguous United States, derived from the USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture county-level tile-drainage statistics combined with NLCD 2016 cropland, SSURGO soil drainage class, and SRTM slope; validation against 16,000 ground-truth points gave '86.03% accuracy at the CONUS-scale, and over the heavily tile-drained midwestern regions of the U.S., the accuracy ranges from 82.7% to 93.6%' (Valayamkunnath et al. 2020, Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x). Download: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742 (figshare, direct HTTP bulk download, no authentication, no cost); also mirrored as a Google Earth Engine community dataset. OPERATIONAL FIT: CONUS-wide coverage means it covers the multi-state portions of the largest basins, which is exactly where the project's existing inner-join under-counting is worst. It is a SINGLE-EPOCH STATIC layer (2017 census basis), so it must be used as a time-invariant per-basin covariate — it CANNOT be broadcast as a time-varying feature, which is the failure mode that produced this project's -0.166 result when 2017 N-surplus was broadcast forward. FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION: basin-mean tile-drained fraction, aggregated per distance bucket, is a static between-site feature of exactly the class that has produced this project's only wins (geometry, lat/lon), and addresses the control the project itself identifies as dominant and missing. n=19 CONSTRAINT: this adds roughly 1-3 static columns to a between-site regression with ~19 effective independent units — a defensible ratio, unlike methods requiring hundreds of catchments.
claims.effectSize: 86.03% classification accuracy CONUS; 82.7-93.6% in the tile-drained Midwest; 30 m resolution; single epoch (2017)

result.sourceQuality: MIXED — the assigned source is authoritative but thin, and the key claims required triangulation. The AWS registry page (registry.opendata.aws/nwm-archive) is a first-party NOAA/AWS catalog entry and is fully reliable for coverage, format, bucket names, access mechanism, and license — but it contains ZERO bias or validation information, and notably does NOT document the reach identifier, so the NHDPlus COMID / feature_id join central to using NWM here is UNVERIFIED and must be confirmed against the NWM route-link file. The two most load-bearing scientific sources (Valayamkunnath et al. 2022 WRR on NWM tile-drainage bias; Marinos et al. 2020 GRL on nitrate C-Q in the Upper Mississippi) were both PAYWALLED (HTTP 402/403 on Wiley); verbatim abstracts were recovered via the Semantic Scholar API, so directional findings and abstract-level percentages are solid but table-level numbers, per-gauge statistics, site counts, drainage-area ranges, and C-Q power-law slope exponents were NOT retrievable and are recorded as unknown rather than guessed. The USGS ScienceBase benchmark data release (DOI 10.5066/P9QT1KV7) returned HTTP 403 and its per-gauge NSE/KGE values were not obtained. The Towler et al. 2023 HESS benchmark is fully open-access and peer-reviewed, and is the strongest quantitative source here, but it reports KGE aggregated to broad regions rather than NSE by HUC2, so no Iowa-specific (HUC 07) figure was obtainable. The AgTile-US Scientific Data paper is open-access and peer-reviewed with a free figshare download, making it the best-sourced and most immediately actionable item — though it was found incidentally rather than being part of the assigned NWM question. NEGATIVE-RESULT HUNTING: the two most useful findings here are negative for the assigned angle (NWM has no tile-drainage physics at all, and chemostasis implies Q carries little concentration information in tile-drained catchments), and both point away from the modeled-discharge recommendation and toward the static tile-density raster. No source was found supporting a published between-site regression of concentration on N-input-yield divided by specific discharge WITH a reported R2 under a spatial-holdout protocol; searches returned only qualitative NANI-export relations (approximately 25% of watershed N surplus exported, with substantial within- and across-region variability), which is too weak to justify the target redefinition to load.

claims.text: AgTile-US is a 30-m binary raster (0 = undrained, 1 = tile-drained cropland) covering the ENTIRE contiguous United States (65°20'46"W–127°53'13"W, 22°51'N–51°36'N), representing a single static snapshot for the year 2017. Because it is CONUS-wide, it covers not only Iowa but the multi-state portions of basins extending into Minnesota, Missouri, South Dakota, Nebraska and Illinois — i.e. it does NOT have the Iowa-only truncation problem that currently causes the inner-join under-count of CDL/N-surplus for the largest basins. Distributed free under CC-BY 4.0 as GeoTIFF and NetCDF-4 from figshare (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, plus 10.6084/m9.figshare.12668234), with model/reader R code at https://github.com/NCAR/AgTile-US, and mirrored as a Google Earth Engine community asset at ee.Image('projects/sat-io/open-datasets/agtile/AgTile-US'). No authentication or payment required for the figshare download; GEE access requires a free GEE account. This directly closes the project's stated gap that 'tile drainage density ... is NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet'.
claims.effectSize: 30 m resolution; binary; single epoch 2017; ~22.34 Mha tile-drained mapped CONUS-wide

claims.text: AgTile-US validation against 16,000 manually photo-interpreted ground-truth tile locations (ESRI multi-resolution aerial imagery, 0.3–15 m, imagery dates 2012-10-02 to 2017-04-23) gives 86.03% overall CONUS accuracy (13.97% omission error), and 91.1% accuracy for IOWA specifically on 5,253 Iowa validation points; the six heavily tile-drained Midwest states span 82.7%–93.6%. Accuracy exceeds 98% over very poorly / poorly drained soils with slope <=1% but 'declines sharply' in intermediate drainage categories (3–5) and on steeper slopes. Kappa is NOT reported, and no R2 against an independent (non-calibration) tile estimate is reported. Note the validation is presence-only: the paper states 'unavailability of tile drainage ground truth points over vegetated croplands' and 'uncertainty in croplands without tile drainage', so the 86.03%/91.1% figures are essentially producer's accuracy on known-drained points and do NOT bound the false-positive rate.
claims.nBasins: 16,000 ground-truth points CONUS; 5,253 in Iowa; 0 basins (point-level, not basin-level, validation)
claims.effectSize: 86.03% CONUS accuracy; 91.1% Iowa; 82.7–93.6% Midwest range; >98% on poorly-drained flat soils
claims.splitProtocol: unknown — point-level photo-interpretation validation; ground-truth points were also used to set the 20% slope upper limit, so partial calibration/validation reuse; not a spatial-holdout of basins

claims.text: AgTile-US is generated by a deterministic GIS decision-tree that is CALIBRATED TO COUNTY TOTALS: for each county it selects grid cells starting from SSURGO v2.0 drainage class D=7 (very poorly drained) with slope S=0, incrementing slope by 1% (capped at 20%) and then stepping down drainage class, until the accumulated area matches the county's 2017 USDA Census of Agriculture tile-drained acreage; the cropland mask is NLCD 2016. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: the reported Iowa total agreement (5,706,831 ha modeled vs 5,708,945 ha census, −0.04% difference) is agreement BY CONSTRUCTION, not independent skill. A basin-aggregated tile fraction feature therefore carries information that is roughly (county census tile fraction) x (within-county soil-drainage/slope downscaling). For basins smaller than or comparable to a county, the signal is dominated by SSURGO drainage class and slope — variables that may be partly redundant with existing static/geographic features (lat, lon, log_basin_area) rather than new information. This is a falsifiable, cheap test: compute basin tile fraction and check its partial correlation with the existing static block before assuming it adds between-site skill.
claims.nBasins: all CONUS counties (exact count not stated in paper)
claims.effectSize: Iowa modeled 5,706,831 ha vs census 5,708,945 ha = −0.04% (calibration target, not validation)

claims.text: The paper quantifies its two dominant error sources: USDA Census of Agriculture tile estimates have an average error of 19.8%, and NLCD 2016 UNDERESTIMATES cropland by −18.15% nationally, and the authors attribute regional underestimation of tile drainage 'mainly ... to underrepresentation of croplands in NLCD land cover 2016'. Worst state-level underestimates are New Mexico (−79.06%), West Virginia (−42.38%), Mississippi (−15.90%), Oklahoma (−14.06%), Texas (−11.53%) — all outside the Corn Belt and totalling <0.11 Mha. Iowa is not listed among the biased states. This means the ~20% census error propagates as a per-county multiplicative noise floor on any basin-aggregated tile-fraction feature: with n=19 independent basin families, a between-site predictor carrying ~20% multiplicative noise has limited power to explain between-site level differences, and this should be treated as an upper bound on achievable gain rather than a reason not to try.
claims.effectSize: USDA census average error 19.8%; NLCD 2016 cropland underestimate −18.15% nationally

claims.text: DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THE NWM QUESTION IN THE RESEARCH ANGLE: this dataset was built at NCAR explicitly because the NOAA National Water Model does NOT represent tile drainage. The paper states the map 'is supporting an effort to improve the prediction of streamflow over the Midwestern U.S. within the NOAA National Water Model', and that tile drainage 'causes significant changes in watershed hydrology' — increased annual runoff volume, reduced peak flows, higher infiltration with lower surface runoff, and decreased groundwater travel times. This is strong evidence that NWM retrospective streamflow (which through v2.1/v3.0 uses Noah-MP without a tile-drainage parameterization) is STRUCTURALLY BIASED in exactly the flat, poorly-drained, heavily tiled Iowa basins that dominate this project's site list. Any plan to use NWM-modeled Q as an ungauged-site discharge covariate must therefore be validated against the project's own 22 USGS-gauged sites BEFORE being trusted at ungauged pins; the paper does not itself quantify the magnitude of the NWM bias, so the size of the error is unknown from this source.
claims.nBasins: unknown — no NWM skill evaluation is reported in this paper
claims.effectSize: qualitative: increased annual runoff volume, reduced peak flows, decreased groundwater travel times; no NWM RMSE/NSE numbers given

claims.text: The paper asserts the tile-drainage/nitrate link qualitatively but provides NO quantitative concentration-discharge or nitrate-yield relation: it states that subsurface drainage 'results in higher infiltration and lower surface runoff' yet 'tends to increase ... instream nitrate concentrations', and lists 'modeling of agriculture nutrient transport to the Mississippi River' as an intended application. It reports NO C-Q slope, NO chemostatic/dilution regime classification, NO between-site regression of concentration on N-input-yield / specific-discharge, and NO R2 for any nitrate prediction. THIS SOURCE THEREFORE DOES NOT ANSWER THE ASSIGNED RESEARCH QUESTION about C-Q behavior or about whether modeled discharge converts into between-site concentration skill; it answers a different question (the missing tile-drainage covariate). The C-Q regime evidence (Godsey/Kirchner power-law, Basu chemostatic behavior, Van Meter & Basu legacy N, Damkohler framing) and the NWM v3 retrospective bias assessment must be sought in other sources.
claims.nBasins: not-applicable — no nitrate observations or catchments analyzed
claims.effectSize: none reported

result.sourceQuality: High for what it is, but OFF-TOPIC for the assigned research angle. Peer-reviewed data descriptor in Scientific Data (Nature Portfolio), DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x, Sci Data 7:257 (2020), authors at NCAR RAL (Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis) plus Kristie Franz (Iowa State). Nature.com full text was paywalled behind an idp.nature.com redirect; the complete open-access full text was retrieved from PubMed Central (PMC7406500), supplemented by the Google Earth Engine community catalog page for the asset ID. All numbers quoted are from the PMC full text. CAVEAT: the paper is a data descriptor about tile-drainage MAPPING — it contains zero concentration-discharge analysis, zero nitrate modeling, and zero NWM skill evaluation, so it cannot support or refute any claim about C-Q regimes, dilution mass balance, or the value of modeled discharge as a between-site predictor. Its real value to this project is operational: it is a free, CC-BY, CONUS-wide, 30-m tile-drainage layer that fills the project's explicitly identified missing dominant hydrologic control, and it is a static geographic/geometric covariate — precisely the feature class that has WORKED on this project (lat, lon, basin geometry) rather than the temporal class that has failed seven times. Its 2017 single-epoch nature is a caution given the prior failure of 'broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time', BUT that failure was for a time-varying quantity forced to be constant; tile drainage infrastructure is genuinely near-static on decadal scales, so the analogy is weak and the feature should be tested as a pure static-between-site variable, never as a time series.

claims.text: The USGS data release (Wieczorek, Jackson, Schwarz, Sekellick & Staub, ver. 5.0, June 2025, DOI 10.5066/F7765D7V) provides 158 separate static/basin attribute tables joined to NHDPlusV2 by a single integer COMID key, in 13 themes (Best Management Practices, Chemical, Climate and Water Balance Model, Climate, Geology, Hydrologic, Hydrologic Modifications, Landscape, Population Infrastructure, Regions, Soils, Topographic, Water Use). Every table supplies three spatial aggregations per COMID — CAT_ (local reach catchment), ACC_ (divergence-routed upstream accumulation), TOT_ (total upstream watershed accumulation) — plus companion CAT_NODATA/ACC_NODATA/TOT_NODATA columns giving the percent of catchment area the source coverage does NOT cover. VERIFIED BY DIRECT DOWNLOAD: the tile-drainage table contains exactly 2,699,864 COMID rows covering CONUS, columns ['COMID','CAT_TILES_Early90s','CAT_NODATA','ACC_TILES_Early90s','ACC_NODATA','TOT_TILES_Early90s','TOT_NODATA'], -9999 as the NODATA sentinel. Access: unauthenticated HTTPS GET of per-item zipped CSV from sciencebase.gov/catalog/file/get/<itemid> (13 MB zipped, 154 MB CSV for the tile table); parquet copies are listed but their sciencebase.usgs.gov/manager/ URLs returned an HTML app shell rather than the file, so the CSV zip is the working access path. License: CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain), no authentication. Coverage is full CONUS, so it covers Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins — directly addressing the project's known inner-join undercount for out-of-state basin area, because the NODATA column reports coverage explicitly instead of silently dropping cells. All attributes are STATIC single-epoch snapshots, so they are usable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin provided the pin's basin can be decomposed into NHDPlusV2 COMIDs.
claims.effectSize: 158 attribute tables; 2,699,864 COMID rows verified; 13 themes; CAT/ACC/TOT + NODATA columns; CC0

claims.text: MEASURED ON THIS PROJECT'S OWN DATA (not a literature claim): the percent-subsurface-drainage attribute CAT_TILES92 (source: Wieczorek 2004, 'Subsurface Drains on Agricultural Land in the Conterminous United States, 1992: National Resource Inventory Conservation Practice 606'; ScienceBase item 57067469e4b03f95a075ad3e) was area-weighted-aggregated over each sensor basin's COMIDs and correlated against site-level nitrate computed from src/data/processed/water/data/*_water.parquet. Across n=46 sites: versus site violation rate (fraction of days with daily-max nitrate >= 10 mg/L) Pearson r=0.516 (p=0.00024, r^2=0.266), Spearman rho=0.605 (p=8.3e-06); versus site mean daily-max nitrate Pearson r=0.466 (p=0.0011, r^2=0.217), Spearman rho=0.485 (p=0.00063). In an OLS with log(basin area) as a covariate, tile percent remains significant: violation-rate model R^2=0.317 with tile coefficient 0.0055 (p=0.00138); mean-nitrate model R^2=0.296 with tile coefficient 0.0672 (p=0.00643). Direction is positive as hydrologically expected. CRITICAL CAVEAT ON PROTOCOL: this is an IN-SAMPLE cross-site correlation over all 46 sites, NOT a spatially held-out prediction, so r^2=0.266 is NOT comparable to the project's LOFO between_rate_r2 of 0.24 and will shrink under leave-one-family-out evaluation. CRITICAL CAVEAT ON SAMPLE SIZE: the 46 sites collapse to substantially fewer than the project's 19 independent basin families, so the effective independent n for this regression is well under 19 and the confidence interval on r is wide despite the small p-value. The claim to test is narrower and falsifiable: adding a single scalar tile-drainage percent as a static feature should raise LOFO between_rate_r2 above 0.24; if it does not, this correlation was driven by shared spatial autocorrelation with lat/lon, which the model already has as its 2nd and 3rd most important features.
claims.effectSize: violation rate: r=0.516, r^2=0.266, Spearman 0.605 (p=8.3e-06); mean nitrate: r=0.466, r^2=0.217; with log-area control, viol model R^2=0.317, tile coef 0.0055 (p=0.00138)
claims.nBasins: 46 sensor basins (fewer than 19 independent basin families)
claims.splitProtocol: random-split (in-sample cross-site correlation, no holdout — NOT comparable to the project's LOFO numbers)

claims.text: OPERATIONAL COVERAGE VERIFIED FOR IOWA: the 1992 NRI CP-606 subsurface-drainage layer (CAT_TILES92) has ZERO missing coverage over this project's sensor basins — area-weighted CAT_NODATA was exactly 0.0% for all 46 basins tested (mean 0.0, std 0.0, max 0.0), and the fraction of basins with NODATA>50% was 0.000. Attribute values span 0.03% to 67.79% of catchment area drained, mean 14.57%, std 19.16%, giving genuine cross-site dynamic range for the between-site term the project is missing. The COMID join itself was exact where COMIDs existed (match rate 1.0000). The binding constraint is NOT the USGS data but this project's own basin storage: only 46 of 85 preferred basins could be joined, because 3 basin parquet files lack a 'comid' column entirely and the remaining ~36 are stored as a single dissolved polygon row with comid=None (verified for WQS0115, USGS-05464475, WQS0010, WQS0081, WQS0083, USGS-05418110 — each is exactly 1 row with a null comid). Those basins therefore need COMID decomposition via spatial intersection against the NHDPlusV2 catchment layer, or via NLDI navigation, before any attribute in this release can be attached. This is a solvable engineering task, not a data gap, and it is the SAME operation the deployment path already performs when delineating an arbitrary map pin through NLDI — meaning the deployment path can attach these attributes at an ungauged pin with no local nitrate history and no gauge.
claims.effectSize: CAT_NODATA = 0.0% on all 46 basins; values 0.03–67.79%, mean 14.57%, std 19.16%; COMID match rate 1.0000; 46/85 basins joinable due to 36 basins stored as dissolved polygons with comid=None

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT — DO NOT USE THE HEADLINE 30 m TILE DRAINAGE LAYER: the Nakagaki (2016) 'Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for the conterminous United States, early 1990s' 30 m raster, as aggregated to NHDPlusV2 in ScienceBase item 58d9dec6e4b0543bf7fda70e (CAT_TILES_Early90s), is largely MISSING over this project's basins. Verified by direct computation: 25.6% of the sensor basins have area-weighted CAT_NODATA of exactly 100% (i.e. no source coverage at all), and 42.7% have CAT_NODATA above 50%; the median area-weighted NODATA across basins is 95.84% and the mean is 74.35%. Nationally, 2,689,897 of 2,699,864 COMIDs carry a value but only 12.1% are greater than zero and the national mean is 2.392%. THE CRITICAL TRAP: this layer reports 0.0 rather than null where the source grid is absent, so every basin at the bottom of the sorted list (USGS-415959091441301, WQS0111, WQS0025, WQS0022, WQS0063) has tile percent 0.0 paired with NODATA 100% — a naive ingest would encode 'no data' as 'no tile drainage' and inject a systematic, spatially structured false signal into exactly the between-site term the project is trying to fix. Where both layers have data the two tile products correlate only r=0.688, so they are not interchangeable. Recommendation: use CAT_TILES92/TOT_TILES92 (complete coverage, see companion claim) and always read the paired NODATA column, masking values where NODATA exceeds a threshold. This is the concrete resolution of the project's open 'tile drainage: no data source identified' item — a source exists, is free and CC0, but the obvious 30 m candidate is the wrong one for Iowa.
claims.effectSize: 25.6% of basins have 100% NODATA; 42.7% have >50% NODATA; median area-weighted NODATA 95.84%; nationally only 12.1% of COMIDs >0, mean 2.392%; correlation with TILES92 only r=0.688

claims.text: THE MANURE-VERSUS-COMMERCIAL NITROGEN SPLIT IS AVAILABLE AT COMID, BUT FOR 2012 ONLY. ScienceBase item 59038bc8e4b0e862d2311aef ('Select Chemical Attributes: Nitrogen and Phosphorous Estimates from Fertilizer and Manure, 2012') ships eight separate zipped CSVs whose field definitions were verified from the FGDC metadata XML: FarmN2012/FarmP2012 = commercial fertilizer applied on agricultural land (source: Brakebill and others, USGS 2017, 'County-Level Estimates of Nitrogen and Phosphorus from Commercial Fertilizer for the Conterminous United States, 1987-2012'); TN2012/TP2012 = nutrients from MANURE on agricultural land (source: Gronberg and others, USGS 2017, 'County-level estimates of nitrogen and phosphorus from animal manure (2007 and 2012)'); RCFN2012/RCFP2012 and RCTN2012/RCTP2012 = the same fertilizer and manure quantities restricted to ROW CROP land specifically. Units are kilograms, with -9999 as NODATA, and each ships CAT_/ACC_/TOT_ plus NODATA columns. This directly supplies the requested manure-vs-commercial decomposition and a row-crop-weighted variant, at basin-aggregatable resolution, CC0, no authentication. HOWEVER IT DOES NOT SOLVE THE POST-2017 CLIFF: this is a single 2012 snapshot, not a time series, and the underlying Brakebill fertilizer series itself ends in 2012 — five years EARLIER than the gTREND surplus product that already ends in 2017. If nitrate concentration in Iowa is closer to chemostatic (C roughly flat in Q), then a +2.3% volume change implies tile density buys almost nothing through a dilution/specific-discharge channel, and its predictive value must instead come from flow-path partitioning (below).

claims.text: Regional water-balance effect of tile drainage in the NWM, verbatim: 'TD significantly reduced surface runoff (-7% to -29%), groundwater recharge (-43% to -50%), evapotranspiration (-7% to -13%), and soil moisture content (-2% to -3%). However, TD significantly increased soil profile lateral flow (27.7%) along with infiltration and soil water storage potential.' THIS IS THE MECHANISTIC ARGUMENT FOR TILE DENSITY AS A BETWEEN-SITE STATIC FEATURE: tile drainage converts a basin from a surface-runoff/recharge regime into a shallow-subsurface lateral-flow regime, and shallow subsurface lateral flow through the root zone is the dominant nitrate delivery pathway in Iowa. A -43% to -50% cut in groundwater recharge plus a +27.7% increase in lateral flow means two basins with IDENTICAL rainfall, identical crop mix and identical N surplus will deliver very different nitrate loads depending on tile density. That is precisely a between-site (level) effect, not a within-site (timing) effect - which matches this project's diagnosis that headroom is in the between-site term (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42) and that seven temporal-feature ablations have failed.

The falsifiable operational consequence: with b near zero and sigma_b = 0.3, discharge explains very little DAILY concentration variance for nitrate-like constituents, and the site-to-site spread in b (sigma_b = 0.3) is as large as the mean signal — so a single global C-Q slope cannot be transferred to an unseen basin.

ANSWER TO THE RESEARCH QUESTION, SCOPED TO THIS SOURCE: this paper does NOT support the proposed use. It provides no between-site model of concentration from N input and specific discharge, no R2 for such a relation, and no evaluation whatsoever of NWM, SPARROW, GAGES-II, or any modeled-streamflow product (the paper predates NWM entirely; it uses OBSERVED gauged discharge at every site). Its per-site constant Cf_bar requires that site's own paired C and Q record, which is exactly what an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin does not have — so the mechanism is unusable at the deployment target without a separate, unvalidated regionalization of Cf_bar. The paper's strongest contribution here is CAUTIONARY: (a) chemostasis is an annual-scale phenomenon and is explicitly denied at the daily/monthly scale that this project's daily-max target operates on; (b) the authors themselves flag the L-Q correlation as potentially spurious because Q is a component of L, which undercuts the proposal to switch the modeling target to load; and (c) the transport-limited/legacy framing predicts weak explanatory power for contemporary N-surplus covariates, independently corroborating this project's existing negative result on the gTREND surplus feature. The n=19-independent-basin-families constraint is not a binding issue for merely READING this paper, but note the evidence base here is 35 very large catchments (10^2-10^6 km2, mostly whole river basins) with 10-30 year records aggregated to annual values — roughly 35 sites x ~20 annual points; nothing about this design demonstrates that a per-site level term can be LEARNED from covariates at n=19, since Basu et al. never attempt that regression. Claims about NWM v3 retrospective coverage/bias in tile-drained basins, SPARROW, GAGES-II, and regionalization from the project's own 22 gauged sites must be sourced elsewhere — this source is silent on all of them.

Accuracy at poorly performing sites 'could be improved by grouping sites with similar characteristics.' This is a falsifiable, directly testable design for our project: group the 19 basin families by static attribute similarity (or by Iowa landform region / glacial terrane — Des Moines Lobe vs Iowan Surface vs Southern Iron Clay vs Loess Hills) and fit per-group models, rather than one pooled model or per-site models. Note the caveat: 5-8 groups over 46 sites is ~6-9 sites per group; at 19 families the equivalent gives ~2-4 families per group, which is likely below the point where a group-specific model can be fit at all.
