claims.effectSize: discharge + soil + physiographic attributes ranked as strongest influences on model performance; per-attribute importance magnitudes not obtainable from paywalled text

claims.text: Gorski et al. (2024) found 'considerable regional differences related to controlling processes such as groundwater contributions' in the cross-site driver analysis — i.e. the drivers of nitrate are not stationary across regions, and the same input carries different information in a groundwater-dominated catchment versus a surface/tile-dominated one. Falsifiable implication for our project: a single global XGBoost fit over all 19 Iowa basin families implicitly assumes driver stationarity that this paper reports is violated even within the agricultural Midwest; per-region (Des Moines Lobe vs driftless/loess) driver contrast is a testable prediction, and groundwater-contribution attributes (e.g. baseflow index, glacial terrane class) are candidate static features.
claims.effectSize: qualitative regional heterogeneity in driver importance; magnitudes not obtainable from paywalled text

claims.text: SECONDARY / UNVERIFIED (from search-engine summaries of citing papers, not read directly — must be confirmed against the source before use): a citing WRR paper (Pandit et al. 2025, 'Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin', doi:10.1029/2024WR039207) reportedly restates Gorski et al. (2024) as median KGE 0.63 at n=46, and reports that restricting to the 11 IOWA sites in Gorski's analysis gives global-model median KGE 0.81 and median NSE 0.73. Two flags: (i) the KGE 0.63 figure conflicts with the 0.66 stated in Gorski's own abstract, so at least one of the two restatements is wrong; (ii) even the Iowa 0.81/0.73 numbers are same-site temporal-holdout skill WITH observed discharge as an input, so they are an upper bound that is NOT achievable at an ungauged map pin and NOT comparable to our LOFO numbers.
claims.effectSize: reported median KGE 0.81 / NSE 0.73 on the 11 Iowa sites (global model); conflicting restatement of overall median KGE as 0.63 vs the abstract's 0.66

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed AGU/Wiley journal article (Water Resources Research 60(9), e2023WR036591, 2024), USGS-coauthored with an accompanying USGS data + code release (ScienceBase item 661436d1d34e633466530330). HOWEVER: full text was NOT retrievable — Wiley returned HTTP 402 Payment Required on the full-text HTML, the pdfdirect link, and the ?af=R variant, and ScienceBase returned 403, despite OpenAlex listing the work as hybrid OA / CC-BY. Claims 1-5 are grounded in the VERBATIM abstract retrieved via the Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs plus the four-model-scheme description surfaced from the data-release/paper metadata; they are reliable as to study design, site count, the headline median KGE = 0.66, and the direction of the global-vs-local negative result, but I could NOT verify per-model KGE/RMSE tables, the exact train/validation/test year boundaries, the expected-gradients importance ranking, or whether any spatial holdout was attempted anywhere in the paper. Claim 6 is second-hand from search summaries of a citing paper and is internally inconsistent (0.63 vs 0.66) — treat as unverified. IMPORTANT GAP FOR THE STATED RESEARCH ANGLE: nothing retrievable from this source addresses concentration-discharge slope regimes (chemostatic vs dilution vs mobilization), the Godsey/Kirchner power-law framing, Basu biogeochemical stationarity, Damkohler-number framing, C ~ N-yield/specific-discharge as a between-site relation, NWM v3 retrospective coverage or its tile-drained-basin bias, SPARROW, GAGES-II, or load (C x Q) as an alternative target. This paper uses observed discharge at gauged sites and does not evaluate a modeled-Q substitute; those sub-questions need separate sources.

claims.text: Kamrath & Yuan (2023, J. Environ. Manage., DOI 10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.117598) partitioned daily loads by flow-duration-curve interval in 14 gauged Ohio watersheds (11 km2 to 16,388 km2, 2000-2020, min 3 years, water-quality sampling >=4 days/week from USGS-gauged sites). Across sites the MEDIAN fraction of annual load carried by the top 10% of flow days (m10%) was 58% for NO3-N, 66% for dissolved reactive phosphorus, 72% for total phosphorus, 77% for TSS; the top 40% of flows carried a median 93% of NO3-N export. This is a descriptive load-duration-curve (LDC) partition, NOT a predictive model, and every site required its own gauged daily discharge record.
claims.effectSize: median m10% = 58% of annual NO3-N load in top 10% of flow days; top 40% of flows = 93% of NO3-N load (median); site range for top-40% NO3-N load = 54-98%
claims.nBasins: 14 gauged watersheds (all Ohio, western Lake Erie + Mississippi basins)

claims.text: The paper's ONLY attempt to regionalize the load-duration curve from watershed attributes is a two-predictor multivariate linear regression: m10% (percent of annual load in the top 10% flow interval) = b0 + b1*log(watershed area km2) + b2*(percent agricultural land), fit on n=13 watersheds (Cuyahoga removed as an agricultural-land outlier), giving adjusted R2 = 0.86, F(2,10) = 37.7, p < 0.001, b1 = -4.24 (p<0.001), b2 = +1.1 (p<0.001). The equivalent model for the 10-40th percentile interval (m10-40) gave adjusted R2 = 0.71, F(2,10) = 15.8, p < 0.001.
claims.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.86 (m10%), adj R2 = 0.71 (m10-40); log-area coefficient -4.24 percentage points per log-unit area, ag-land coefficient +1.1 percentage points per percent ag

claims.text: The adj R2 = 0.86 attribute-to-duration-curve regression in Kamrath & Yuan (2023) was fit and reported IN-SAMPLE with NO cross-validation, no holdout, and no leave-one-watershed-out test, on n=13 basins with 2 predictors plus intercept (10 residual degrees of freedom). Therefore this number is NOT comparable to any spatially held-out skill estimate and provides no direct evidence that duration-curve shape transfers to an unmonitored basin.
claims.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.86 reported in-sample only; 13 observations, 3 fitted parameters

claims.text: Kamrath & Yuan (2023) attempted NO prediction at ungauged or unmonitored sites: the analysis is restricted to watersheds with both a USGS daily-discharge gauge and a high-frequency nutrient-concentration record, and the paper contains no QPPQ-style flow-duration-curve transfer, no discussion of applying the relationships to unmonitored watersheds, and no explicit TMDL-practice application. The method as published cannot be executed at an arbitrary map pin with no discharge gauge.
claims.effectSize: zero ungauged-site predictions; 0 of 14 sites tested without local discharge data

claims.text: The direction of the attribute effect in Kamrath & Yuan (2023) is that LARGER watersheds concentrate LESS of their load in high flows (log-area coefficient -4.24 on m10%) while MORE agricultural watersheds concentrate MORE (coefficient +1.1). This is a falsifiable, transferable hypothesis for a between-site level/shape term: basin area and percent-agriculture predict the SHAPE of a site's load-duration curve, and both attributes are already available in the Iowa feature set (log_basin_area, CDL crop fractions).
claims.effectSize: b1 = -4.24 percentage points of annual load per log10-unit of area; b2 = +1.1 percentage points per 1% agricultural land

claims.text: Mann-Kendall testing in Kamrath & Yuan (2023) found NO significant positive or negative temporal trend in m40% (fraction of annual load carried by the top 40% of flows) at any of the study sites over 2000-2020, i.e. the flow-interval/nutrient-export partition was temporally stationary. This supports treating the duration-curve shape as a STATIC per-site property estimable from attributes rather than a time-varying quantity, but it was established only on gauged sites with 3-20+ years of local record.
claims.effectSize: 0 of 14 sites with a significant Mann-Kendall trend in m40% over 2000-2020

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed, open-access via PMC, full text retrieved successfully (not paywalled). Journal of Environmental Management (Elsevier), 2023, DOI 10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.117598, authors Kamrath B & Yuan Y (US EPA-affiliated). RELEVANCE TO THE ASSIGNED ANGLE IS PARTIAL AND MOSTLY NEGATIVE: this is a descriptive load-duration-curve (LDC) study, not a regionalization or ungauged-basin transfer study. It confirms that LDC-style load partitioning is applied to water quality in the Midwest, and it contains exactly ONE attribute-to-curve-shape regression (adj R2 0.86, n=13, in-sample, no CV) which is directionally useful but statistically fragile at that sample size. It contains NO QPPQ transfer, NO hierarchical/Bayesian partial pooling, NO quantile regression, NO domain adaptation, NO ungauged-site skill number, and NO post-hoc site calibration. Two caveats for the parent agent: (1) the paper's n=13-basin regression is a near-exact analogue of this project's n=19-families constraint and demonstrates that between-site shape CAN be regressed on 2 attributes at that sample size, but only in-sample; (2) the entire method presupposes a local daily discharge record, which the deployment target (arbitrary Iowa map pin, no gauge) does not have. Numbers were extracted via WebFetch summarization of the PMC full text rather than by reading the PDF tables directly; the regression intercept b0 was not reported in the retrieved text and the exact per-site m10% values were not enumerated.

claims.text: Full text could not be retrieved: despite Unpaywall listing this article as CC-BY open access with best-OA URL https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2019WR025138, Wiley returned HTTP 402 to every fetch attempt (landing page, /full, /pdfdirect), and pubs.usgs.gov / Semantic Scholar / ResearchGate returned 403 or empty. All claims below therefore derive from the verbatim publisher abstract (mirrored in the USGS Publications Warehouse metadata) and from the companion USGS data release (Worland, Knight & Asquith 2019, doi:10.5066/P92F1ROU), NOT from the results tables. No NSE, KGE, RMSE or bias figures from this paper could be verified; anyone relying on this angle should obtain the PDF through a library and read Figures/Tables directly.
claims.effectSize: none available — no numeric results extractable

claims.text: The study's entire evidence base is 74 USGS streamgages — 37 in the Mobile-Tombigbee River Basin (HUC4 0316) and 37 in the Trinity River Basin (HUC4 1201-1204) — with a decade of daily streamflow (2000-2009), and it compares 16 distinct streamflow-estimation methods on that network. This is an unusually SMALL donor network for a regionalization paper (contrast CAMELS studies at 531-671 basins), which makes it one of the few QPPQ-family results whose sample size is within an order of magnitude of the Iowa project's 19 independent basin families. It is still ~4x more independent units than n=19, and the two basins are dense, spatially contiguous gauge networks — a condition the Iowa nitrate deployment (arbitrary map pin, no guaranteed monitored neighbor) does not satisfy.
claims.effectSize: n/a — sample-size claim

claims.text: The QPPQ framework as defined by this paper explicitly decomposes the prediction into exactly the two pieces the Iowa project wants separated: (a) a flow-duration curve estimated at the ungaged/partially gaged target — the SITE LEVEL / marginal distribution — and (b) a time series of nonexceedance probabilities transferred from DONOR STREAMGAGE SITES — the TIMING / rank dynamics. The paper's stated contribution is a copula-based mathematical framework showing that prior FDC-based methods are special cases of a joint distribution whose rank-correlation structure across the gaging network is modeled separately from the marginals. DEPLOYMENT WARNING: component (b) requires at least one concurrently-observed donor site with an estimable rank correlation to the target; for the Iowa virtual-sensor product the analogous donor signal is the existing cross-site nitrate lag features (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), which already rank as the single most important feature — this paper is evidence that the correct architecture is to keep those as the timing channel and predict the target's marginal (concentration-duration curve) from static basin attributes as a separate output.
claims.effectSize: structural claim, no number

claims.text: Verbatim abstract finding, ranked qualitatively with no effect sizes given in the abstract: copula approaches (1) 'outperform other methods in the limiting case of perfect information with regard to the rank-based correlation structure and FDCs across the gaging network'; (2) 'provide a hedge against poor performance when donor information becomes sparser and less informative'; (3) 'outperform other methods when used for partially gaged sites with several years of available data'; and (4) 'remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network.' Claim (4) is the falsifiable one that matters here: in the TRULY UNGAGED case with realistic FDC-estimation error, the sophisticated copula machinery is explicitly NOT dominant — it merely ties simpler methods. The authors' own framing therefore predicts that the copula/QPPQ upgrade buys little for a zero-observation target, and that the binding constraint is the accuracy of the regionalized duration curve itself, not the dependence model.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown — abstract does not state whether ungaged skill is leave-one-gage-out; the companion data release documents leave-one-out cross-validated site-to-site correlation kriging, which implies a spatial LOO design for at least the correlation component
claims.effectSize: qualitative only ('outperform', 'competitive albeit nondominating'); no NSE/KGE/RMSE recoverable without the PDF

claims.text: Performance is conditioned on an information-quality axis rather than reported as a single number: the paper distinguishes a 'limiting case of perfect information' about FDCs and rank correlations from the case where 'realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network,' and reports that method ranking REVERSES between those regimes (copulas dominate under perfect information, are merely competitive under realistic error). Falsifiable implication for this project: any measured gain from a level/shape decomposition must be evaluated with the concentration-duration curve ESTIMATED FROM ATTRIBUTES under spatial holdout, never with the target site's observed CDC plugged in — the latter is the 'perfect information' regime and will overstate the gain, in the same way random splits over autocorrelated site-days overstate transfer.
claims.effectSize: direction-of-ranking reversal reported; magnitudes unrecoverable

claims.text: The partially-gaged result — copulas 'outperform other methods when used for partially gaged sites with SEVERAL YEARS of available data' but are only 'competitive' for 'partially gaged sites with LIMITED data' — implies a data threshold on the order of years, not days, before target-site observations pay off. This is a direct negative for post-hoc site-level calibration / quantile mapping in the Iowa deployment: the shipped product has ZERO observations at an arbitrary map pin, which sits below even the 'limited data' regime where this paper already finds no advantage. Quantile mapping and site random-intercept correction are therefore usable only for the ~85 existing sensor sites or for future sites after multi-year monitoring, and must be stated as NOT usable for the arbitrary-pin product; the only estimable path for a zero-observation pin is predicting the duration-curve parameters from static basin attributes, which at n=19 independent families is a ~19-point regression.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown (partially-gaged experiments withhold varying record lengths at target sites)
claims.effectSize: threshold qualitative: advantage appears at 'several years' of target-site record, absent at 'limited data' and at zero record

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed primary source (Water Resources Research 55:9378-9397, doi:10.1029/2019WR025138, USGS-authored, CC-BY per Unpaywall) — but the full text was UNREACHABLE from this environment: Wiley returned HTTP 402 on the landing page, /full, and /pdfdirect; pubs.usgs.gov and ResearchGate returned 403; Semantic Scholar returned an empty body. Extraction is based on (a) the verbatim abstract, retrieved independently from two authoritative mirrors (USGS Publications Warehouse META abstract tag and the OpenAlex record), and (b) the peer-reviewed companion USGS data release doi:10.5066/P92F1ROU, which supplies the exact gage counts, HUC4 codes, period of record, method count (16), and the note that site-to-site correlations were estimated by leave-one-out cross-validated ordinary kriging. NO numeric skill scores (NSE, log-NSE, KGE, RMSE, bias) could be verified, so every performance claim above is qualitative and flagged; the paper's own decomposition figure of log-NSE and NSE into bias/variance components exists (visible in a ResearchGate figure listing) but its values could not be read. Recommend a library retrieval of the PDF before acting on the magnitude of any QPPQ gain. Note also that the paper concerns STREAMFLOW only — no water-quality, concentration-duration-curve, or load-duration-curve application appears in the abstract or data release, so this source supports the QPPQ/level-shape angle structurally but contains zero direct water-quality evidence.

claims.text: In the Level 1 meta-analysis of 13 published studies on predicting flow duration curves at ungauged sites (10 usable, all leave-one-out cross-validated, 27 total method-results), the number of catchments per study ranged from 8 to 1080 with a MEDIAN OF 49, and the back-calculated Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of FDC quantiles had 25% and 75% quantiles of 0.60 and 0.90 respectively. This is the closest thing in the chapter to a headline ungauged-basin skill number for regional duration-curve transfer.
claims.effectSize: NSE of FDC quantiles: 25th pct 0.60, 75th pct 0.90 (interquartile range across 27 method-results)
claims.nBasins: 8 to 1080 per study, median 49; 13 studies, 10 used

claims.text: CRUCIAL NEGATIVE RESULT FOR THE ZERO-OBSERVATION DEPLOYMENT CASE: across the Level 1 assessment, estimating a site's long-term flow duration curve from a SHORT LOCAL RECORD at that site beat every regionalization-from-attributes method. Verbatim: 'predictions of long-term FDCs based upon 1, 2, 5 years of observed runoff all outperform any of the other methods' and 'predictions of long-term FDCs based upon five years of observed runoff largely outperform the best performing regional model, while one or two years of daily runoff are generally sufficient to obtain predictions of FDCs that are as accurate as the ones retrieved through regionalization' (Castellarin et al. 2004a resampling experiment). Implication: as little as ONE YEAR of local observation matches the entire regionalization apparatus, and the chapter explicitly warns 'it is generally not advisable to rely completely on any regional model, which should be used to provide a first order approximation of FDCs.'
claims.effectSize: 1-2 yr local record ~= best regional model; 5 yr local record 'largely outperforms' it; only 3 of 27 results were short-record methods
claims.nBasins: unknown (Castellarin et al. 2004a resampling subset); 3 short-record results within the 10-study Level 1 set

claims.text: REGIONALIZATION SKILL SCALES WITH THE NUMBER OF GAUGED SITES IN THE POOL. Level 1 finding, stated as a main conclusion: 'The performance increases clearly with number of stream gauges in the region', with the trend 'particularly clear for the comparison ... for the intermediate classes of catchment number (from 20 to 250 catchments per study)'. The chapter concludes 'even if one is interested in estimating a FDC for a single catchment it may be worth basing the regionalisation on a large number of catchments.' In the Level 2 assessment the authors attribute the index method's poorer showing in Italy directly to 'the lower stream gauge density' there, versus Austria and France which 'both have a relatively dense stream gauge network'. This bears directly on the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint: the FDC literature's own evidence says n~20 sits at the BOTTOM of the range where performance is measurably degraded by pool size.
claims.effectSize: Monotone improvement across catchment-count strata; degradation clearly visible in the 20-250 catchment band; smallest vs largest strata differ clearly
claims.nBasins: 27 method-results spanning 8 to 1080 catchments (Level 1); 1419 catchments pooled in Level 2

claims.text: THE LEVEL/SHAPE DECOMPOSITION IS EXPLICIT AND ASYMMETRIC IN DIFFICULTY. The index-flow framework models daily runoff as the product of two independent random variables: an index flow (mean or median annual runoff) carrying the site's absolute LEVEL, and a dimensionless duration curve carrying the SHAPE. Level 2 assessment quantifies the two halves separately over 1419 catchments, 4 method families, leave-one-out: 'R2 of the slope of the FDC were calculated for all methods in each study separately which gave a median of 0.26. Also the NSE of the quantiles of the scaled FDC were calculated which gave a median of 0.98.' I.e. the normalized SHAPE transfers almost perfectly (NSE 0.98) while the between-site SLOPE parameter is nearly unpredictable from attributes (R2 0.26) - a direct analogue of this project's within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21 split, and evidence that the between-site term is hard in the source literature too, not just here.
claims.effectSize: median R2 = 0.26 for FDC slope (between-site shape parameter); median NSE = 0.98 for quantiles of the index-scaled FDC; indicative performance range 0.40-0.95 reported to Chapter 12
claims.nBasins: 1419 catchments, 7 contributing author groups, 4 method families

claims.text: METHOD RANKING IS INCONSISTENT BETWEEN THE TWO ASSESSMENT LEVELS, AND THE AUTHORS ATTRIBUTE THE RANKING TO DATA DENSITY RATHER THAN METHOD QUALITY. Level 2 (1419 catchments, leave-one-out, ANE of FDC slope): 'overall, geostatistical methods perform best, followed by the regression methods' - but immediately caveated, 'This may be partly related to the higher stream gauge density of the data sets used for these methods.' Level 1 is contradictory: 'In both comparative studies, the regressions methods perform better than the index method, but when one considers all studies the index method performs better', and one of those head-to-head comparisons 'was only over two catchments'. Geostatistical performance 'strongly increase[s] with catchment area' because larger catchments overlap more with gauged ones. Process-based rainfall-runoff models underestimated FDC slope at both the smallest and largest catchments because they were calibrated on daily-NSE - 'the slope of the FDC was not captured well even in the calibration' - a direct warning that optimizing a timing-style loss does not deliver the distributional/level property you actually want.
claims.effectSize: Ranking: geostatistics > regression > index/process-based on ANE of FDC slope (Level 2); reversed in 2 of the Level 1 head-to-heads, one of which had n=2 catchments
claims.nBasins: 1419 (Level 2); one cited head-to-head comparison used only 2 catchments

claims.text: HOW THE CURVE IS REGIONALIZED FROM ATTRIBUTES - the operational recipe, with named predictors. Three families: (a) QUANTILE REGRESSION on individual percentiles (no distributional assumption, but 'regressing a large number of runoff quantiles means a large number of multi-regression models' and 'may result in inconsistent estimates ... the estimate of Q(D1) may be smaller than the estimate of Q(D2)' - i.e. quantile crossing; Archfield 2009 / Archfield et al. 2010 use recursive regression to prevent this). (b) PARAMETRIC: fit a distribution per gauged site, then regress its parameters on attributes - Castellarin et al. (2007) used a 2-parameter logistic for the index flow and a 3-parameter kappa for dimensionless daily runoff, predicting the logistic position parameter (= mean annual runoff, the LEVEL) from area and mean annual net precipitation, the logistic scale from variability of annual net precipitation, and the kappa position (= within-year variability, the SHAPE) from catchment permeability and elevation range; cross-validation showed this beat parameter-regression models fitted to the long-term FDC alone. (c) RESCALED/POOLED: average the dimensionless FDC within a cluster of similar sites. Chapter summary of which attributes matter: 'Geology or geology/soil related indices and topographic elevation (in mountainous regions) are the most frequently used predictors of the slope/shape of FDCs, in addition to the aridity index, which governs the mean of the FDC.' Li et al. (2010, southeast Australia, lognormal FDC parameters regionalized) found catchment area and geographic location NOT sufficiently explanatory for FDC shape once specific (area-normalized) runoff and other covariates were used - a caution against this project's reliance on lat/lon as top-ranked features.
claims.effectSize: Li et al. (2010) index method beat linear regression, nearest-catchment, and hydrologic-similarity methods on within-catchment NSE of FDC quantiles (categories: NSE>0.75, 0.5-0.75, <0.5); exact per-method NSE values are in a figure, not the text
claims.nBasins: unknown for Li et al. (2010) southeast Australia and Castellarin et al. (2007) northern Italy - counts not stated in chapter text

result.sourceQuality: High. Peer-reviewed book chapter (Chapter 7 of Bloschl, Sivapalan, Wagener, Viglione & Savenije eds., "Runoff Prediction in Ungauged Basins: Synthesis Across Processes, Places and Scales", Cambridge University Press 2013, ISBN 9781107028180) — the authoritative IAHS PUB decade synthesis. Full text retrieved and read locally (public PDF on a Tufts server, not paywalled; extracted with pdftotext). It is a SYNTHESIS, not a primary study: performance is reported as meta-analytic distributions (boxplots) rather than per-study tables, so many individual studies' exact catchment counts and per-method numbers are only in figures/appendix tables A7.1 and A7.2 that did not survive text extraction. Two important gaps for this research angle: (1) QPPQ is NEVER named and the time-series reconstruction step (donor-gauge nonexceedance-probability interpolation) is not described — go to Archfield & Vogel 2010 doi:10.1029/2009WR008481 and Archfield 2009 for that; (2) NO water quality, concentration-duration or load-duration curve results appear. The only water-quality link is a citation to Bonta & Cleland (2003) doi:10.1111/j.1752-1688.2003.tb04433.x for duration-curve-based water quality evaluation, plus the general "compose an FDC with a rating curve to get a constituent duration curve" construction demonstrated for habitat and hydropower. Nothing on hierarchical Bayesian random intercepts, quantile regression forests, or domain adaptation — the chapter predates that literature. Also note the 2013 vintage: no machine-learning regionalization.

claims.text: Worland et al. (2019) trained multioutput neural networks (MNNs) on 688 USGS streamgages in the Southeastern US using 40 basin characteristics as predictors and 15 empirical flow-duration-curve (FDC) quantiles as simultaneous outputs, then applied the fitted model to predict FDCs at 9,203 ungaged HUC12 watershed pour points for six decades (1950-2009). This is a pure attribute-to-distribution regionalization: the entire predicted distribution at an ungaged location is a function of static basin attributes only, with no local observations required — structurally the same setup as predicting a nitrate concentration-duration curve for an arbitrary Iowa map pin from basin attributes. NOTE for our project: the evidence base is 688 gages; our n=19 independent basin families is ~36x smaller, and a 40-predictor -> 15-output neural network is almost certainly infeasible at n=19.
claims.nBasins: 688 USGS streamgages for training/testing; applied to 9,203 ungaged HUC12 pour points
claims.effectSize: No exact error metric (NSE/RMSE/R2) could be retrieved — article is paywalled (HTTP 402). Claim of counts and design is from the publisher abstract and indexed full-text fragments.

claims.text: In Worland et al. (2019), predicting each FDC quantile with an INDEPENDENT single-output neural network (SNN) produced 2,316 monotonicity violations (i.e., predicted quantile crossings where a lower exceedance quantile exceeded a higher one) after 400 training epochs, whereas the multioutput network with a combined loss across all 15 quantiles drove violations to zero for every cross-validation fold by roughly 100 epochs, and the SNN FDCs were 'generally less accurate' than the MNN FDCs. Falsifiable implication for us: fitting separate independent models per nitrate quantile/threshold will produce incoherent, crossing quantile predictions; a joint multioutput loss fixes this AND improves accuracy.
claims.effectSize: 2,316 monotonic violations (SNN, 400 epochs) vs 0 violations (MNN, ~100 epochs); accuracy advantage stated qualitatively only — no numeric RMSE/R2 delta retrievable behind paywall.

claims.text: Worland et al. (2019) report a quantile-dependent information split: static BASIN CHARACTERISTICS are most useful for predicting the SMALLER (low-flow) quantiles of the FDC, whereas the predicted values/bias terms of NEIGHBORING QUANTILES are the most informative predictors for the HIGHER quantiles. This is a direct, testable analogue of our level-vs-shape problem: it implies static attributes carry the anchoring/level information at one end of the distribution while cross-quantile structure carries the rest — i.e., a model should predict one anchor quantile from attributes and the remaining quantiles as offsets from it, rather than predicting every quantile independently from attributes.
claims.effectSize: Directional/interpretive finding from local surrogate models (LIME-style); no numeric importance values retrievable behind paywall.

claims.text: Worland et al. (2019) use neural-network DROPOUT AT PREDICTION TIME to generate posterior-predictive distributions for each ungaged FDC, i.e., they deliver a full uncertainty band on the regionalized duration curve rather than a point estimate. This is directly transferable to our deployment case (arbitrary map pin, zero local observations), where the honest product output is a predicted violation-probability distribution with uncertainty, not a single number — and it requires no target-site data.
claims.effectSize: Method described in abstract; no coverage/calibration statistics (e.g., 90% PI coverage) retrievable behind paywall.

claims.text: The Worland et al. (2019) framing has a hard limitation for our deployment target that must be stated: the paper regionalizes the TIME-AGGREGATED distribution (the flow-duration curve over a decade) at ungaged sites, NOT the daily time series. A duration curve tells you 'how high does this site get, and how often' but says nothing about WHICH DAY. Since our model is already 'a good timer' (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90) and a bad site-ranker (between_r2 0.21), the usable pattern is a two-stage decomposition — regionalize the site's nitrate exceedance-duration curve from static attributes, then use the existing daily model only to rank days within the site — but the source itself provides no evidence that such a coupling works for concentration or for water quality of any kind.
claims.effectSize: Scope limitation inferred from the paper's stated target (decadal FDC quantiles at 9,203 pour points); the paper does not attempt daily-series reconstruction (that is the separate QPPQ/copula line, e.g. Worland et al. 2019 WRR 10.1029/2019WR025138 on partially gaged catchments — which by name requires SOME target-site observations and therefore does NOT satisfy our zero-observation deployment case).

claims.text: A citing open-access source (Yi et al., HESS preprint hess-2024-355, 2025) benchmarks four models for 'ungauged' FDC prediction on 140 Korean streamflow stations and reports DNN beating RF, SVR and ENR by an average +0.90% R2 vs RF, +20.4% R2 vs SVR, +2.80% R2 vs ENR, with reported R2 values as high as 0.965-0.988 for individual quantiles. CAUTION: the train/test protocol is not stated as a spatial (leave-station-out) holdout anywhere in the text I could read, so these R2 values are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and should be treated as possibly interpolation rather than transfer. The same preprint also reports a negative result relevant to us: 'Different precipitation metrics had minimal impact on streamflow predictions' — i.e., varying accumulated-precipitation windows barely moved skill, echoing our own dead-last permutation importance for precip_in_1d and our failed rolling-precip ablation.
claims.effectSize: DNN vs RF: +0.90% R2, -23.9% RMSE; DNN vs SVR: +20.4% R2, -395.5% RMSE (as printed); DNN vs ENR: +2.80% R2, -262.6% RMSE. Per-quantile R2 up to 0.965-0.988. Protocol undetermined — do not compare to LOFO numbers.

result.sourceQuality: Primary source is PAYWALLED — agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com returned HTTP 402 Payment Required for both /doi/full/ and /doi/pdfdirect/; pubs.usgs.gov landing page returned 403. Claims 1-5 are reconstructed from (a) the publisher/Semantic Scholar abstract, (b) indexed full-text fragments surfaced via web search (the 2,316-violations figure and the basin-characteristics-vs-neighboring-quantiles finding), and (c) the paper's own summary language.
