The cross-validation is described as k-fold over the 688 streamgages, which makes held-out gages spatially distinct; however I could NOT verify whether nested/overlapping basins were grouped into folds (the exact leak-safety issue that collapsed our 85 sites to 19 families), so 'spatial-holdout' here is weaker than our LOFO protocol and may be optimistic. Claim 6 comes from a fully-readable CC-BY preprint (peer-review status: in HESS open discussion as of Jan 2025, not final-accepted) and its split protocol is undetermined. Recommend a library/interlibrary request for the Worland PDF before relying on any numeric skill claim from it.

claims.text: EPA's load duration curve (LDC) framework is defined entirely on top of a FLOW duration curve at the site of interest: the guidance states 'loads are directly proportional to flows (i.e., load equals flow times concentration times a conversion factor)', and the loading capacity curve is produced by multiplying each flow-duration ordinate by the numeric water quality target. FALSIFIABLE/DEPLOYMENT-CRITICAL CONSEQUENCE: the method cannot produce a site-level concentration prediction without a daily discharge estimate at the target location. For the Iowa virtual-sensor product (arbitrary map pin, no gauge, discharge present at only 22 of 85 sites and 0 of 61 IWQIS sites), an LDC cannot be constructed from weather + land use alone; it would require first solving the ungauged-flow-regionalization problem. The document provides NO validated method or error estimate for doing so.
claims.effectSize: No performance metric reported anywhere in the 74-page document; it is prescriptive guidance, not a validation study.

claims.text: EPA's entire guidance on applying duration curves to UNGAUGED watersheds is two sentences with no quantitative support: 'Not all waters or watersheds have gaging stations or flow data available. In such cases estimation techniques are needed (USEPA, 2007). For instance, it may be appropriate to use flow data of a similar, representative water body to develop the duration curve, based on regression methods or drainage area ratios. The use of rainfall / runoff models can also be used to develop stream flow estimates for use in a duration curve analysis.' No accuracy, bias, or validation number is attached to drainage-area-ratio or regression transfer anywhere in the document. It further cautions that 'dealing with ungaged, headwater streams could present some obstacles in constructing a duration curve, as there is usually less data available on such waters.' NEGATIVE RESULT FOR THIS ANGLE: the standard US TMDL duration-curve literature does not supply a validated ungauged-transfer skill benchmark; it assumes the flow problem away.
claims.nBasins: unknown (no held-out basins; no validation performed)
claims.effectSize: none reported

claims.text: The only concrete, reproducible flow-regionalization protocol in the document is in the South Carolina DHEC Pee Dee River fecal coliform case study (Appendix A), and it is a purely GAUGE-TO-GAUGE index method: 'All flow data are first log-transformed to linearize the data because flow data are highly skewed. Linear regressions are then developed between 1) daily streamflow at the gage to be filled/extended; and 2) streamflow at all gages within 93 miles (150 kilometers) that have at least 300 daily flow measurements on matching dates. The station with the strongest flow relationship, as indicated by the highest correlation coefficient (r-squared value), is selected as the index gage... Flows will not be estimated based on regressions with r-squared values less than 0.25, even if that is the best regression.' The stated fallback when no coincident gauge exists is 'a watershed area ratio method derived by delineating subwatersheds, and relying on the Natural Resources Conservation Service runoff curve numbers and antecedent rainfall condition' using an upstream OR downstream gauge. FALSIFIABLE CONSTRAINTS: 150 km search radius, >=300 matched daily observations, r2>=0.25 acceptance floor. DEPLOYMENT LIMITATION: every branch of this priority list requires a gauge at, upstream of, or downstream of the target — which the Iowa map-pin product cannot guarantee.
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (in-sample record-filling; no held-out evaluation reported)
claims.nBasins: unknown — case study covers multiple SCDHEC 303(d)-listed water quality monitoring stations in the Pee Dee River basin; exact count not stated in the extracted narrative
claims.effectSize: Only the r2>=0.25 acceptance threshold is quantified; no out-of-sample flow error reported. r2=0.25 as an ACCEPTABLE index-gauge regression is itself a striking indicator of how weak this transfer is allowed to be in practice.

claims.text: EPA defines a standard five-zone partition of the flow duration curve that functions as a discrete hydrologic-condition covariate: 'one representing high flows (0-10%), another for moist conditions (10-40%), one covering mid-range flows (40-60%), another for dry conditions (60-90%), and one representing low flows (90-100%)', with midpoints of the moist, mid-range and dry zones 'at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles respectively (i.e., the quartiles)', the high zone 'centered at the 5th percentile' and the low zone 'centered at the 95th percentile'. The guidance explicitly states 'Other schemes can be used, depending on local hydrology'. RELEVANCE TO THE LEVEL/SHAPE DECOMPOSITION ANGLE: this is exactly a shape normalization — position on the site's own duration curve (a within-site relative coordinate, which the Iowa model already captures well as a 'good timer') is separated from the site's absolute flow magnitudes (the between-site level term, which is the actual deficit). The document offers the decomposition but not a way to predict the level term from basin attributes.
claims.effectSize: Zone boundaries: 0-10 / 10-40 / 40-60 / 60-90 / 90-100 percent exceedance; zone centers at the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th percentiles.

claims.text: EPA states an explicit applicability limitation that directly threatens the use of duration curves for Iowa nitrate: 'An underlying premise of the duration curve approach is correlation of water quality impairments to flow conditions. The duration curve alone does not consider specific fate and transport mechanisms, which may vary depending on watershed or pollutant characteristics. Such processes may include sediment attenuation, plant uptake of nutrients, chemical transformations, or bioaccumulation. Practitioners should consider using a separate analytical tool to develop a TMDL when factors other than flow significantly affect a water body's loading capacity.' It adds that the method 'is more appropriate in cases where flow is a primary driver in pollutant delivery mechanisms, and other processes are a relatively insignificant part of the total loading.' FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION FOR THIS PROJECT: because Iowa nitrate concentration is strongly modulated by N application/surplus, crop rotation, denitrification and tile-drainage routing — not flow alone — EPA's own criterion says a pure flow-duration framework is a partial tool for this pollutant. This is consistent with the project's finding that essentially all headroom is in a static between-site term rather than a flow/timing term.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative applicability criterion; no quantified degradation reported.

claims.text: The document does apply the duration-curve framework to nitrate at exactly this project's threshold, but only as a deterministic target-times-flow calculation, not a predictive model: Figure 2-1 shows a 'Nitrate Loading Capacity Using Duration Curve Framework' with 'a sample calculation ... at one point along the curve corresponding to a flow duration interval of 60 using a nitrate target of 10 mg/L', and Appendix B Figure B-2 gives 'A loading capacity for nitrate in the Sangamon River ... using the drinking water maximum contaminant level (MCL) of 10 mg/L ... derived directly from the MCL (10 mg/L) and the duration curve using the flow to load calculation ... across the range of all daily average flows.' Data requirements are stated only loosely: 'While the number of observations required to develop a flow duration curve is not rigorously specified, a flow duration curve is usually based on more than 1 year of observations, and encompasses inter-annual and seasonal variations. Ideally, the drought and flood of record are included'; the SC case study used 'more than 5 years of water quality data (1990-2002)'. The case study also EXCLUDES the tails: 'The extreme high flow conditions (<10th percentile) and low flow conditions (>95 percentile) are not considered in development of these TMDLs' because of a 'stair step' effect from USGS rounding conventions. CONSEQUENCE: LDC practice discards precisely the high-flow tail where Iowa nitrate violations concentrate.
claims.nBasins: 1 illustrative river per pollutant example (Sangamon River for nitrate; Portneuf River for phosphorus); no multi-basin validation
claims.effectSize: Nitrate target 10 mg/L (drinking-water MCL) — identical to this project's violation threshold. Minimum record: >1 year flow; case study used >5 years WQ data. Tails excluded: <10th and >95th percentile.

result.sourceQuality: PRIMARY SOURCE FULLY RETRIEVED AND READ. WebFetch returned raw PDF bytes (its summarizer could not parse them), so the 3.3 MB PDF was saved to disk and text-extracted locally with pdftotext -layout (3,065 lines, full 74-page document, EPA 841-B-07-006, August 2007, Office of Wetlands Oceans and Watersheds, Watershed Branch). Extracted text at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/e3f1f490-6fb8-475d-be0e-c0cebf530519/scratchpad/ldc.txt. All quotes above are verbatim from that extraction. AUTHORITY: high — official EPA agency guidance, the canonical reference for US LDC/TMDL practice. EVIDENTIARY VALUE FOR THIS RESEARCH QUESTION: LOW-TO-MODERATE, and the honest headline is a negative result. This is prescriptive practitioner guidance, NOT a validation study: it contains zero predictive-skill metrics, zero held-out evaluations, zero cross-validation of any kind, and no multi-basin regionalization experiment. It therefore supplies NO ungauged-site skill benchmark comparable to the project's LOFO AUC 0.820. Its treatment of ungauged watersheds is two hand-waving sentences (drainage-area ratio / regression / rainfall-runoff model) with no error bars. Its one concrete protocol (SC DHEC Pee Dee, Appendix A) is gauge-to-gauge index-station record-filling that presupposes a nearby, upstream, or downstream gauge — structurally unavailable at an arbitrary Iowa map pin. WHAT IT IS GENUINELY USEFUL FOR: (a) it confirms the level/shape decomposition is standard, defensible regulatory practice, and hands over a specific five-zone percentile partition (0-10 / 10-40 / 40-60 / 60-90 / 90-100) usable as a shape coordinate; (b) it uses the nitrate 10 mg/L MCL as the target, exactly matching this project's violation threshold, so LDC framing is directly translatable to the product's output layer; (c) EPA's own applicability caveat ('duration curve alone does not consider ... plant uptake of nutrients, chemical transformations'; use another tool 'when factors other than flow significantly affect ... loading capacity') is an authoritative, citable warning that a flow-duration framework is a partial tool for agricultural nitrate — corroborating this project's own finding that the deficit is static/between-site rather than temporal. IMPORTANT NEGATIVE TO CARRY FORWARD: the LDC literature was flagged as 'promising and underused'; on inspection of the primary guidance it is underused for ungauged prediction because it was never built for it. Any usable QPPQ-style skill numbers must come from the hydrologic regionalization literature (Hughes & Smakhtin, Fennessey, Archfield & Vogel, Smakhtin), NOT from EPA TMDL guidance. Those sources should be fetched separately and each judged against the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint, since published QPPQ validations typically draw on 100-1000+ gauges. CAVEAT ON UNRESOLVED DETAIL: the exact number of SCDHEC water quality monitoring stations in the Pee Dee case study was not pinned down from the extracted narrative (station IDs such as PD-113, PD-333, PD-098, PD-040 appear); recorded as 'unknown' rather than guessed, per the rules.

claims.text: CONTAINS NOTHING ON THE RESEARCH ANGLE — falsifiable negative about the source itself: this 11-page IAHS PUB position paper (Peters, Reynolds & Johnes 2007, IAHS Publ. 309, 63-73) contains ZERO mention of QPPQ, flow-duration curves, concentration-duration curves, load-duration curves, quantile mapping, quantile regression, hierarchical/Bayesian partial pooling, random effects, or domain adaptation. Its 21-item reference list is entirely empirical-regression, mass-balance and critical-loads literature (SPARROW, FAB, export coefficient models). Verified against the complete extracted text of the PDF. Anyone citing this paper as support for the level/shape-decomposition or duration-curve angle is citing it incorrectly.
claims.effectSize: 0 mentions of any duration-curve, quantile, or hierarchical-pooling method in full text

claims.text: STRUCTURAL CLAIM DIRECTLY AGAINST A DAILY TARGET: the paper's central conclusion is that 'uncertainty of the estimates of average constituent concentration or yield decreases with increasing averaging time, e.g. a predicted annual flux is more precise than an instantaneous or daily flux', and closes with 'Although we may adequately predict average conditions (chronic), we may fail to predict biologically important extremes (acute).' This asserts that the DAILY-MAX, threshold-exceedance formulation is the hardest point on the aggregation curve, and that the ungauged-basin literature's reported skill is overwhelmingly for ANNUAL fluxes and is therefore NOT comparable to a daily-violation AUC. It also implies a testable, deployment-relevant fallback: predicting an annual or seasonal exceedance FREQUENCY per basin (a level/shape decomposition where the 'level' is a long-averaging-time quantity) should be materially more accurate than predicting individual site-days, and is worth measuring on the existing 19 families before more daily feature engineering.
claims.effectSize: qualitative monotone claim: precision increases with averaging period; no numeric ratio given

claims.text: THE CLOSEST PUBLISHED ANALOG TO THIS PROJECT'S EXACT TASK (attribute-only threshold-exceedance classification with no local history): Nolan, Hitt & Ruddy (2002, Environ. Sci. Technol. 36(10) 2138-2145, doi:10.1021/es0113854), as summarized here, fit a logistic regression for probability of nitrate contamination (>4 mg N/L) of recently recharged shallow groundwater across the conterminous USA, 'calibrated on 1280 observations, predicted the correct status of nitrate concentration in 75% of the 736 verification observations.' Six significant predictors: (1) N fertilizer loading, (2) % cropland-pasture, (3) ln(human population density), (4) % well-drained soils, (5) depth below land surface to the seasonally high water table, (6) presence/absence of unconsolidated sand and gravel aquifers. The paper explicitly partitions these: 'Predictors 4-6 relate to the hydrological pathway and time of travel, whereas predictors 1-3 relate to the source of the nitrate.' HALF the predictive variables are SUBSURFACE DRAINAGE-PATHWAY descriptors, none of which exist in the current 68-feature set — this is independent, quantitative support for prioritizing tile-drainage density / soil drainage class / depth-to-water-table over further weather features. Caveat: groundwater, not stream nitrate; 75% accuracy is against an unstated base rate and is NOT comparable to LOFO AUC 0.820.
claims.nBasins: 1280 calibration observations, 736 verification observations (well/site counts, not basins); spatial independence of the verification set not stated in this summary
claims.effectSize: 75% correct exceedance status on 736 held-out verification observations

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT, n=88 SITES, LAND USE ALONE FAILS TO SET THE ABSOLUTE LEVEL: McLay et al. (2001, Environ. Pollut. 115(2) 191-204) assessed groundwater nitrate at 88 sites in New Zealand under mixed agricultural land use; per this paper, 'Although the authors documented the dominant land use and the local soils ability to leach nitrate, there were no discernible trends, and a risk assessment model was only able to explain 50% of the variance in the concentrations, with the permeability of the vadose zone being the most important parameter.' Associations only emerged for FINE-GRAINED operation types (dairy, drystock, drystock/sheep, market gardens, orchards) — market gardens highest, drystock/sheep lowest — not for coarse land-use class. This is a direct precedent for this project's between_r2 0.21 ceiling: coarse CDL crop fractions are the wrong granularity for between-site level, and a subsurface-permeability variable outranked all land-use variables. 50% of variance at n=88 sites also sets a realistic expectation ceiling for what n=19 independent families can support.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown (appears to be in-sample variance explained, not a spatial holdout)
claims.effectSize: R2 approximately 0.50 for site-level nitrate concentration; vadose-zone permeability the single most important parameter; no discernible trend from dominant land use

claims.text: BENCHMARK FOR ATTRIBUTE-BASED N EXPORT, AND THE n=374 vs n=19 WARNING: 'six empirical and quasi-empirical nitrogen (N) watershed models were evaluated for predicting the riverine export of N from 16 large watersheds (475 to 70 000 km2) in the northeastern USA (Alexander et al., 2002); all models predicted the export to within 50% of the measured export. One of the models, SPARROW, was calibrated on 374 watersheds ranging in size from 10 to 2.9 x 10^6 km2.' So the ceiling for annual basin N export from source + runoff + land-use predictors is roughly plus/minus 50%, and the flagship method (SPARROW) required 374 calibration watersheds — approximately 20x this project's 19 independent basin families. Any recommendation to fit a SPARROW-style spatially-referenced source/attenuation regression here must be flagged as evidence-based at n=374, not n=19. Note also the aggregation mismatch: this plus/minus 50% is an ANNUAL LOAD figure, not a daily concentration, and is not comparable to LOFO R2 0.328.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown for the 16-watershed evaluation (evaluation watersheds may overlap SPARROW's 374-watershed calibration set); not verifiable from this paper
claims.nBasins: 16 watersheds for the model comparison; 374 watersheds for SPARROW calibration
claims.effectSize: all six models within +/-50% of measured annual riverine N export

claims.text: ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE CEILING FOR REGRESSION-FROM-ATTRIBUTES, AND AN EXPLICIT DISAGGREGATION FIX FOR LARGE BASINS: 'The uncertainty in the prediction of annual major ion yields from basins ranging in size from 10 to 100 000 km2 in the USA, using a multiple linear regression model was an order of magnitude (Peters, 1984)', with predictors % rock types, annual precipitation, population density and average stream temperature; 'Precipitation quantity, a surrogate for runoff, and rock type were the most statistically significant predictors.' The paper attributes this failure specifically to basin size: 'in large basins the basic modelling unit cannot be the entire basin, but should be separate regions within the basin, which demonstrate distinct and different linear responses to the driving variables. Modelled separately with model estimates then lumped for the entire basin, a greater degree of the variance can be explained (Johnes & Butterfield, 2002).' This is a concrete, testable prescription for this project's largest multi-state basins (which are also the ones with the known crop/N-surplus under-count): predict per homogeneous sub-region and area-weight up, rather than feeding whole-basin lumped means to one model. Related documented scale failure in the same paper: catchment-attribute acid-sensitivity models gave 'reasonable predictions of sensitivity to acidification at a broad regional scale (>10 km2)' but 'the sensitivity prediction, particularly for high flow extremes, was poor for basin areas less than 10 ha due to fine scale, unmapped variations in bedrock geochemistry and land use' (Reynolds et al., 2001, Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 5(1) 75-81) — i.e. attribute-based regionalization degrades at both ends of the scale range, and degrades WORST for extremes rather than means.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown (Peters 1984 multiple linear regression, calibration-set fit; no holdout described)
claims.nBasins: unspecified count of US basins spanning 10 to 100,000 km2 (Peters 1984); Reynolds et al. 2001 catchment count not given in this paper
claims.effectSize: annual major-ion yield precise only to one order of magnitude; Mg/Ca/HCO3 yields 4-10x higher from limestone than sandstone/granite basins

result.sourceQuality: FULL TEXT OBTAINED, but the source is a poor match for the assigned research angle. ACCESS: ResearchGate URL returned HTTP 403; the identical paper is open access at NERC Open Research Archive (https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/1778/), PDF at https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/1778/1/001778Peters.pdf. All 11 pages extracted and read in full — claims above are from the primary text, not an abstract mirror. CITATION: Peters, N.E., Reynolds, B. & Johnes, P.J. (2007) 'Uncertainty of water-quality predictions in ungauged basins (PUBs)', in Predictions in Ungauged Basins: PUB Kick-off (Proc. Brasilia meeting, 20-22 Nov 2002), IAHS Publ. 309, 63-73. No DOI. NATURE OF SOURCE: a conceptual/agenda-setting position paper delivered at the 2002 PUB kick-off, not a modelling study. It presents NO new model, NO new dataset, NO validation experiment, and reports NO split protocol of its own. Every quantitative figure above is second-hand, summarized from cited primary studies (Peters 1984, Nolan et al. 2002, McLay et al. 2001, Alexander et al. 2002, Reynolds et al. 2001, Hornung et al. 1995); split protocols are consequently unrecoverable from this document and are marked 'unknown'. Anyone using these numbers should go to the primary sources. AGE: the science is 24 years old (written 2002, published 2007) and predates the entire ML-for-water-quality literature, all CAMELS-era large-sample benchmarking, and all deep-learning regionalization work. It should be cited for framing and for the aggregation-period argument, NOT as current evidence about achievable skill. ON THE RESEARCH ANGLE SPECIFICALLY: this source contributes NOTHING on QPPQ, regional duration curves, load-duration curves, quantile mapping, hierarchical/partial pooling with attribute-predicted random intercepts, quantile regression forests, or domain adaptation. That angle must be pursued through other sources; suggested leads visible from this paper's framing are the TMDL load-duration-curve grey literature (US EPA 841-B-07-006) and the SPARROW lineage. USEFUL INCIDENTAL DETAILS: (a) the paper states the USEPA drinking-water criterion as '10 mg N L-1', i.e. 10 mg/L as NITROGEN — worth confirming whether this project's 10 mg/L violation threshold is nitrate-as-N or nitrate-as-NO3, since as-NO3 the equivalent MCL is approximately 45 mg/L and a 10 mg/L NO3 threshold would be a much lower bar than the regulatory one, materially changing the 0.263 base rate's interpretation; (b) the paper notes concentration typically varies by less than an order of magnitude while short-term discharge varies by several, which mildly favours this project's concentration target over a load target for ungauged transfer, since load prediction would inherit the discharge error the project cannot estimate (only 22 of 85 sites gauged, zero IWQIS sites).

claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2019, HESS 23:5089-5110, doi:10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019) did NOT test prediction in ungauged basins. The paper states explicitly: 'we never ask our model to predict in a basin where it did not see training data.' Training used calibration-period data (Oct 1999-Sep 2008) from all 531 CAMELS basins and evaluation used validation-period data (Oct 1989-Sep 1999) from the SAME 531 basins. Therefore every NSE figure in this paper is a TEMPORAL holdout on gauged basins and is NOT comparable to a leave-one-basin-out / LOFO number. This paper is routinely mis-cited as PUB evidence; the actual PUB companion is Kratzert et al. 2019 WRR (doi:10.1029/2019WR026065), which used k-fold spatial holdout.
claims.effectSize: n/a - protocol claim

claims.text: With a temporal (not spatial) holdout on 531 CAMELS basins, a single regional EA-LSTM reached mean NSE 0.67 +/- 0.006 / median NSE 0.71; the 8-member ensemble reached mean NSE 0.71 / median NSE 0.74. A standard LSTM fed the same static attributes was statistically indistinguishable (single: mean 0.66 / median 0.70; ensemble: mean 0.70 / median 0.73). The architectural innovation (entity-aware static input gate) bought essentially NOTHING in accuracy - its value was claimed to be interpretability of the learned catchment embedding, not skill.
claims.effectSize: EA-LSTM vs LSTM+static: +0.01 mean NSE, +0.01 median NSE (within noise)

claims.text: On the same 531-basin temporal holdout, a single regionally-trained LSTM/EA-LSTM outperformed hydrological models CALIBRATED INDIVIDUALLY PER BASIN (on the 447 commonly-modeled subset): EA-LSTM ensemble mean NSE 0.71 vs basin-calibrated HBV-ensemble 0.61, mHM 0.59, SAC-SMA 0.52, VIC 0.52. Regionally-calibrated conceptual models were far worse: mHM 0.44, VIC 0.17. Interpretation for our project: the gap between regional calibration (0.17-0.44) and per-basin calibration (0.52-0.61) quantifies the classic 'between-site level' penalty, and ML closed it ONLY by having 531 gauged donors to learn the attribute->behavior mapping from.
claims.effectSize: regional ML 0.71 mean NSE vs regionally-calibrated VIC 0.17 / mHM 0.44; vs basin-calibrated best (HBV) 0.61

claims.text: Static catchment attributes were the load-bearing component, not the meteorological time series. Removing the 27 static CAMELS attributes and training on meteorology alone collapsed performance: the paper reports the with-attributes model improved mean NSE by approximately 0.44 over the no-attributes model (no-static mean NSE reported around 0.39 under one loss configuration - exact per-cell table values should be re-verified against Table 3 of the published PDF, as our extraction of the no-static row was second-hand). Directional claim is robust and directly supports this project's diagnosis that the deficit is BETWEEN-SITE static information, not temporal dynamics.
claims.effectSize: ~+0.44 mean NSE from adding 27 static attributes; exact no-static row flagged as needing verification

claims.text: An attribute-corruption robustness test showed graceful, non-brittle degradation: adding Gaussian noise to the standardized static catchment attributes moved median NSE from 0.71 (no noise) to ~0.71 at sigma=0.1, ~0.65 at sigma=0.25, ~0.55 at sigma=0.5, and 0.48 at sigma=1.0. The authors argue this smoothness shows the network learned a generalizable attribute->behavior mapping rather than memorizing basin identity. Falsifiable implication for us: if a model's skill is genuinely attribute-driven rather than lat/lon-memorization, jittering the static features should degrade skill smoothly and monotonically; a cliff would indicate identity memorization. This is a cheap ablation we can replicate at n=19 families.
claims.effectSize: median NSE 0.71 -> 0.48 across sigma 0 -> 1.0 standardized-attribute noise

claims.text: The paper contains NO experiment on how skill scales with the number of training/donor basins - performance is never reported as a function of training-set size, and no learning curve over basin count is presented. It also contains NO water-quality content whatsoever; the entire study is daily streamflow. Consequently this paper provides ZERO direct evidence that a 531-basin-derived regionalization result transfers to an n=19-independent-family, concentration/exceedance problem. Its clustering analysis (k-means on the 256-dim embedding produced more distinct catchment clusters than k-means on the raw 27 attributes) is qualitative and reported without a held-out predictive metric.
claims.effectSize: none reported - absence of scaling curve and absence of water-quality evidence is the finding

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed, open-access (HESS/Copernicus, doi:10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019), highly cited (~680+ citations), with public accompanying code (github.com/kratzert/ealstm_regional_modeling) and open peer review. Full text retrieved successfully from the publisher HTML; the arXiv PDF (1907.08456) failed to parse. HIGH confidence on the split protocol, basin count, EA-LSTM/LSTM/benchmark headline NSEs, and the absence of any ungauged-basin, basin-count-scaling, or water-quality experiment. MEDIUM confidence on the exact no-static-attribute ablation row and on the interpolated noise-experiment values at intermediate sigma, which came from a summarizing extraction rather than a verbatim table read - recommend re-reading Table 3 and the noise figure in the published PDF before quoting those two to three digits. CRITICAL CAVEAT FOR THE PARENT: this paper is very frequently cited as evidence for prediction in ungauged basins and it is not; the correct PUB citation with spatial holdout is Kratzert et al. 2019 WRR doi:10.1029/2019WR026065 (k-fold spatially-held-out CAMELS, out-of-sample basin median NSE reported around 0.69 vs basin-calibrated SAC-SMA 0.64 and National Water Model 0.58), which should be fetched separately and is the number actually comparable to our LOFO protocol.

claims.text: Willard et al. (2024) trained on 782 CONUS stream-temperature sites (>=5 years of data, ~3.82M observations) and evaluated on 580 DIFFERENT held-out sites treated as 'unmonitored' — a genuinely spatial ungauged-basin protocol (single train/test site split, not k-fold, no site appears in both). Total pool 1,362 sites, 4,378,876 observations. This is the standard PUB evaluation protocol and is the protocol class comparable to our LOFO numbers.
claims.effectSize: n/a — protocol description

claims.text: A single continental 'top-down' LSTM trained on ALL 782 sites beat every regionalized/grouped alternative at unmonitored sites: median per-site RMSE 1.43degC (+/-0.98) for LSTM_conus vs 1.98degC for LSTM_regional (one model per HUC-2 region), 2.02degC for LSTM_cluster (one model per static-attribute-similarity cluster), and 2.00degC (+/-1.07) for bottom-up multi-task learning. The pooled model won in 14/17 regions and 14/15 attribute clusters. Directly falsifies the 'group basins by similarity then fit locally' regionalization family: partitioning the donor pool cost ~0.55-0.59degC RMSE (~40% worse).
claims.effectSize: 1.43 vs 1.98 / 2.02 / 2.00 degC median per-site RMSE; pooled wins 14/17 regions, 14/15 clusters

claims.text: Adding latitude/longitude/elevation to a meteorology-only LSTM produced almost NO gain at unmonitored sites (median RMSE 1.77degC -> 1.72degC, i.e. 0.05degC), whereas adding GAGES-II static catchment attributes to that same location-aware model gained 0.25degC (1.72 -> 1.47degC) — a ~5x larger effect. The authors state adding location information 'did not meaningfully improve performance.' This is direct evidence that physical-attribute similarity beats plain spatial proximity as a regionalization signal, and that a model relying on lat/lon as a top feature is leaving between-site skill on the table.
claims.effectSize: meteo 1.77 -> +latlon/elev 1.72 (delta 0.05) -> +GAGES-II 1.47 (delta 0.25) degC median RMSE

claims.text: Observed streamflow as a model input helped LESS than static catchment attributes for unmonitored-site prediction: meteo+lat/lon/elev+flow gave median RMSE 1.57degC while meteo+lat/lon/elev+GAGES-II attributes gave 1.47degC, and the paper's headline conclusion is that streamflow is NOT necessary for accurate prediction at unmonitored sites. Requiring discharge also shrank the usable training pool from 1,346 to 1,048 sites (~4.65M obs). Relevant to our 22/85-site discharge coverage: the evidence says the coverage sacrifice is not worth it relative to investing in static basin attributes.
claims.nBasins: 1048 sites usable with discharge vs 1346 without; 580 held-out test
claims.effectSize: 1.57degC (with flow) vs 1.47degC (with GAGES-II attributes) vs 1.77degC (meteo only)

claims.text: The paper provides a partial data-volume-vs-feature-richness tradeoff rather than a clean site-count scaling curve: because meteorology+location inputs are universally available, that configuration could be trained on 2,999 candidate sites (~6.13M observations spanning 1,346 training sites) versus 782 sites (~3.82M obs) for the attribute-rich model, and requiring GAGES-II attributes cut the pool to 833 sites (~4.13M obs). Extended training data produced only 'similar or modest improvements' — i.e. roughly doubling the donor-site count did NOT close the gap created by missing static attributes. NEGATIVE FINDING for our project: no explicit ablation reducing donor count below ~780 basins exists in this paper, so it gives NO evidence about behavior at n=19 independent basin families; all its conclusions rest on 780-1,350 donors.
claims.nBasins: 782 vs 1346 vs 1048 vs 833 training sites depending on required inputs; 580 held-out test
claims.effectSize: ~1.6x more sites / 1.6x more observations yielded only 'similar or modest' RMSE improvement; feature richness dominated donor count

claims.text: This paper addresses ONLY stream temperature — no nitrate, nutrient, or any other water-quality constituent is modeled ('we have built several models to predict daily stream temperatures... as a case study'). Its stated failure mode is also physically specific: models are accurate where air temperature is the dominant control and degrade at sites 'impacted by groundwater and dams', with RMSE >2degC in the mountainous West. Stream temperature is a far more air-temperature-forced, lower-between-site-variance signal than nitrate concentration, so its 1.43degC unmonitored-site skill should NOT be read as an achievable ceiling for concentration/exceedance PUB; the absence of water-quality PUB evidence in this flagship continental-scale PUB benchmark is itself a finding.
claims.effectSize: n/a — scope/negative-coverage claim

result.sourceQuality: High — peer-review-track preprint (submitted to Water Resources Research, Oct 2024) from the USGS/LBNL water ML group (Willard, Topp, Jia, Xie, Read). Full HTML text was reachable and readable on arXiv; numbers below are quoted from the main text and Experiment 2 discussion. CAVEATS: (a) some Experiment-2 extended-training-data cells live in supplementary Table S10, which was referenced but not fully rendered in the fetched HTML, so the extended-training RMSE values are characterized qualitatively ('similar or modest improvements') rather than quoted exactly — treat claim 5's magnitude as approximate; (b) the paper reports median per-site RMSE and bias but performs NO decomposition of between-site vs within-site variance, so it offers no direct number comparable to our within_r2 0.42 / between_r2 0.21 split; (c) it reports no NSE or R2 values at all; (d) it is single-split, not k-fold, so no fold-level uncertainty on the model-family ranking; (e) domain is stream TEMPERATURE, not concentration — transfer of its conclusions to nitrate is an inference, not evidence.

claims.text: Pool, Vis & Seibert (2021) compared 19 regionalization approaches plus 4 benchmarks (23 methods total) for transferring HBV parameter sets to ungauged catchments, using 671 CAMELS catchments in the conterminous US under a leave-one-out cross-validation in which each catchment in turn is treated as ungauged and predicted from donor catchments. Each donor supplied its 10 calibrated parameter sets; predictions were the ensemble mean hydrograph over 30 (flexible region-of-influence) to 40-2,300 (classification-based) parameterizations, simulated 1 Oct 1989 - 30 Sep 1999. This leave-one-catchment-out design is the standard PUB evaluation protocol and is spatially held out at the catchment level, though donors may be spatially adjacent (no nesting/region blocking is applied, unlike our leave-one-basin-family-out).
claims.effectSize: 19 regionalization approaches + 4 benchmarks, leave-one-out over 671 catchments, HBV, 1989-1999 evaluation window

claims.text: In Pool et al. (2021), the ranked medians across 671 US catchments (metric R_NP, a Nash-Sutcliffe-type relative efficiency; R_KG is the Kling-Gupta analogue) were: local calibration upper benchmark R_NP 0.89; best-3-available-donors oracle 0.87; spatial-distance + volume combinations 0.82 / R_KG 0.67; volume/signature similarity alone 0.80 / 0.66; spatial proximity alone 0.79 / 0.64; catchment attributes (physical similarity) alone 0.78 / 0.62; fixed classification-based donor pools 0.76 / 0.58; random donors 0.69-0.70 / 0.49. The entire spread from random donors to the best realizable method is therefore about 0.13 R_NP, and the spread between the three single-information families (volume 0.80, distance 0.79, attributes 0.78) is only 0.02 R_NP - i.e. choosing among proximity, attribute similarity, and signature similarity is nearly a wash relative to choosing any of them over random.
claims.effectSize: median R_NP: UB 0.89, best-donor oracle 0.87, Dist&Vol 0.82, Vol 0.80, Dist 0.79, Attr 0.78, classification 0.76, Random 0.69; total realizable gain over random ~0.13 R_NP

claims.text: Pool et al. (2021) found that spatial proximity outperformed physical-attribute similarity (median R_NP 0.79 vs 0.78; R_KG 0.64 vs 0.62) across 671 US catchments, consistent with Merz & Bloschl (2004), Oudin et al. (2008), Swain & Patra (2017) and Zhang & Chiew (2009), and attributed this explicitly to 'the relatively high gauging station density in many humid regions of the United States' and to 'the lack of catchment attributes representing a wide range of catchment responses over large scales'. They further cite Jehn et al. (2020) that non-climatic catchment attributes 'can vary considerably within hydrologically similar regions in the United States and can often not sufficiently explain hydrological behavior'. This supports the interpretation that raw lat/lon proximity already captures most of what attribute-similarity regionalization would add, especially in a dense-network, hydroclimatically homogeneous region.
claims.effectSize: Dist beats Attr by +0.01 median R_NP and +0.02 median R_KG

claims.text: Pool et al. (2021) report a NEGATIVE result directly relevant to attribute-based site ranking: when the three catchments most similar to the target in geographic, signature, or attribute space were selected as donors, 'the ranks of these most similar donors in the "performance space" are typically clearly worse than the ranks of the three best donors in the "characteristics space"'. Catchment similarity to the true best donors was highest for hydrological signatures, then spatial distance, and SMALLEST for physical attributes. In other words, similarity in measured catchment attributes is a poor proxy for transferability of behavior - the gap between the oracle donor (median R_NP 0.87) and any attribute-selected donor set (0.78) is a similarity-metric failure, not a modeling failure. The only similarity metrics that came close were combinations of Sign or Attr WITH Dist.
claims.effectSize: oracle best-3 donors median R_NP 0.87 vs 0.78-0.80 for any characteristic-based selection; attribute space ranked LAST of three similarity spaces for identifying true best donors

claims.text: The single most transferable finding for a between-site ranking deficit: in Pool et al. (2021) the methods that added VOLUME information - i.e. an estimate of the target's own mean streamflow level or signatures, obtainable from as few as 12 point observations (Pool et al. 2019; Rojas-Serna et al. 2016; Viviroli & Seibert 2015) - were the top-ranked family (Dist & Vol, median R_NP 0.82 / R_KG 0.67), and 'volume seemed to be the best similarity indicator'. The paper is explicit that this information 'is per definition missing in ungauged catchments' and must come from field measurements or from separately regionalized signature estimates. This is a CRITICAL CAVEAT for the map-pin deployment target: the top-performing regionalization family in the largest comparative PUB study requires a handful of observations AT the target site, which the shipped product does not have. It does, however, quantify what a small number of grab samples at a candidate pin would be worth: roughly +0.03 to +0.04 median R_NP over pure proximity.
claims.effectSize: Dist&Vol 0.82 vs Dist alone 0.79 median R_NP (+0.03); Vol-based selection used 12 targeted observations at the 'ungauged' site

claims.text: NEGATIVE / ABSENCE FINDING: Pool et al. (2021) contains NO water-quality, nitrate, or concentration prediction whatsoever - the words 'water quality', 'nitrate' and 'concentration' do not appear; all 671 catchments and all 19 approaches concern daily STREAMFLOW only. It also contains NO donor-pool-size or gauging-density experiment: skill-versus-number-of-donors is never varied (the donor pool is fixed at 670 for every catchment), and density effects are only asserted by citation to Lebecherel et al. (2016), Neri et al. (2020, doi:10.5194/hess-24-5149-2020, 209 Austrian catchments, nested catchments and gauging station density) and Parajka et al. (2015, top-kriging station density). The one cross-study anchor given is Neri et al. (2020): median R_KG 0.6-0.75 for 209 Austrian catchments regionalized by attribute similarity or spatial proximity, versus global-scale regression/classification regionalizations reaching only median monthly R_KG 0.32 (Arheimer et al. 2020) and 0.45 (Beck et al. 2016). Therefore this paper CANNOT be cited as evidence about performance at n=19 donor families, and its 671-catchment evidence base must be flagged as ~35x larger than our independent-unit count.
claims.effectSize: zero water-quality applications; zero donor-count sensitivity analysis; comparison anchors: 209 catchments median R_KG 0.60-0.75 (Neri 2020) vs global regression regionalization median monthly R_KG 0.32-0.45 (Arheimer 2020, Beck 2016)

result.sourceQuality: Full text obtained (open access, CC BY-NC) - the Wiley DOI page returned HTTP 402, but the publisher's version PDF was retrieved from the Eawag DORA repository (https://www.dora.lib4ri.ch/eawag/dload/eawag:23848/) and text-extracted locally, so all figures above are quoted directly from the published article body, not from an abstract or a mirror. Peer-reviewed, Water Resources Research 57(10) e2021WR030437, doi:10.1029/2021WR030437, received 19 May 2021 / accepted 19 Aug 2021. Authoritative and highly relevant to the regionalization-family ranking question. IMPORTANT LIMITATIONS FOR THIS PROJECT: (a) the study is 100% STREAMFLOW - it provides zero water-quality PUB evidence, so it cannot answer the concentration/exceedance part of the research question; (b) it provides NO skill-vs-number-of-donors curve or table - the donor pool is fixed at 670 throughout, so it cannot be used to extrapolate to our n=19 independent basin families, and any claim it supports about proximity-beats-attributes is conditioned on a dense US gauging network that the authors themselves name as the likely cause; (c) all metrics are R_NP / R_KG on daily hydrographs, which are NOT comparable to our AUC/PR-AUC/R2 numbers - the useful transfer is the RELATIVE ordering of regionalization families and the size of the oracle-vs-achievable gap, not the absolute values. Numbers extracted from Figure 3 text, Table 2, Table 3 and Sections 3.1-3.3; the boxplot figures themselves were not machine-read, so per-approach medians are those stated in prose.

claims.text: VERBATIM ABSTRACT CLAIM (paper, paywalled — abstract recovered from Semantic Scholar and Penn State Pure mirrors): Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020, GRL, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051) state that in the Upper Mississippi River Basin "tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior" and that "concentration variability increases, relative to discharge variability, with increasing basin size across six orders of magnitude, and this pattern is attributed to different spatial correlation structures for C and Q." Secondary sources citing the paper add that nitrate in the UMRB is chemodynamic at low flows but chemostatic at high flows (fitted as a BROKEN power law with a fitted breakpoint, not a single power law), and that the chemostatic domain contributes a median = 71% of the annual NO3 load. Study design, recovered from the paper's own archived R code (Step1_Grab_And_Munge_Data.R): all sites are USGS NWIS gauges in HUC 07 with in-situ optical nitrate sensors (parameter code 99133) AND co-located instantaneous discharge (00060), >365 days of record; 35 raw site records archived, 33 retained in the paper's regression table. Discharge is converted to SPECIFIC discharge (Q_cfs * 2.447 / Area_km2) before all C-Q fitting. This is a descriptive/inferential cross-sectional study with no predictive holdout of any kind.
claims.nBasins: 33 sites in the analysis table (35 raw site records archived); UMRB / HUC 07, includes many Iowa gauges
claims.effectSize: median 71% of annual NO3 load delivered in the chemostatic domain; basin size spans six orders of magnitude

claims.text: MOST IMPORTANT RESULT FOR THIS PROJECT — recomputed by me from the paper's own public CC-BY dataset (HydroShare 10.4211/hs.d5676355cbd94b79a2e58f8089040a40) plus NWIS drainage areas; 32 of the paper's 33 sites reproduced. Percent subsurface TILE DRAINAGE alone explains R2 = 0.575 of the between-site variance in the FRACTION OF DAYS WITH NITRATE >= 10 mg/L — which is exactly this project's classification target and exactly the between-site term where the project is weakest (between_rate_r2 = 0.24, between_r2 = 0.21). Univariate OLS across sites, slope = +0.561 (i.e. going from 5% to 85% tile drainage raises the exceedance-day fraction by ~0.45). Competing single predictors for the same response, same n=32: % agriculture R2 = 0.502, % row crop R2 = 0.488, % forest R2 = 0.441 (negative), % wetland R2 = 0.192, % developed R2 = 0.109, log10(basin area) R2 = 0.252. Observed range across the 32 sites: tile drainage fraction 0.054-0.849, exceedance-day fraction 0.000-0.552, mean nitrate 0.53-10.38 mg/L. NOTE ON RIGOR: this is an in-sample cross-sectional fit of one static covariate against a site-level summary statistic, NOT a held-out predictive score, so it is NOT directly comparable to the project's LOFO 0.820 AUC; it is evidence about which static covariate carries between-site information. n=32 sites is the same order as this project's 19 independent basin families, so unlike CAMELS-scale results (531-671 basins) this evidence base is NOT infeasible at n=19.
claims.nBasins: 32 (recomputed from the paper's 33-site archive; 07020850 excluded because the tile layer does not cover its extent, and 4 sites dropped for <365 matched days)
claims.effectSize: tile drainage alone R2=0.575 for between-site exceedance-day fraction; vs %ag 0.502, %row crop 0.488, log10(area) 0.252

claims.text: DIRECT NEGATIVE RESULT AGAINST THE RESEARCH HYPOTHESIS (discharge -> between-site skill). Recomputed from the paper's own dataset, n=32 UMRB sites with PERFECT, MEASURED, CO-LOCATED USGS discharge: mean specific discharge is nearly worthless as a between-site predictor of nitrate level. Univariate R2 of log10(mean specific discharge) against between-site responses: mean nitrate R2 = 0.034; log10 mean nitrate R2 = 0.027; fraction of days >= 10 mg/L R2 = 0.097. In multiple regression for between-site mean nitrate, adding log10(mean specific discharge) to a %row-crop + %tile model moves R2 from 0.486 to 0.487 (delta R2 = +0.001); further adding log10(area) leaves it at 0.487. By contrast %agriculture alone gives R2 = 0.539 and %forest alone R2 = 0.550 for the same response. CRITICAL IMPLICATION: since this null is obtained with real gauged discharge, a MODELED discharge source (NWM v3 retrospective, SPARROW mean-annual flow) can only perform worse once model error is added — modeled-Q error would be added on top of a signal that is already near zero at the between-site level. The C = N-yield / specific-discharge dilution-mass-balance framing is NOT supported as a between-site relation in this dataset. Discharge is a WITHIN-site timing variable, not a between-site level variable — which matches this project's own diagnosis ("a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker") and its seven failed temporal-feature ablations.
claims.effectSize: log10(mean specific Q) alone: R2=0.034 (mean NO3), 0.097 (exceedance fraction). Added to crops+tile: R2 0.486 -> 0.487, delta = +0.001

claims.text: CLEAN SEPARATION BETWEEN 'WHAT CONTROLS DYNAMICS' AND 'WHAT CONTROLS LEVEL' — recomputed from the paper's dataset, n=32. The C-Q variability ratio CVc/CVq is a SCALE/NETWORK property and is essentially unrelated to land use: log10(CVc/CVq) vs log10(basin area) R2 = 0.412 (slope +0.127, i.e. concentration variability rises relative to discharge variability as basins get bigger, confirming the paper's headline), but vs % tile drainage R2 = 0.001, vs % row crop R2 = 0.034, vs % agriculture R2 = 0.095. Conversely the LEVEL of nitrate is a land-use property and NOT a scale property: mean nitrate vs log10(area) R2 = 0.119 while vs % agriculture R2 = 0.539. The fitted power-law intercept log10(a) (concentration at unit specific discharge, i.e. the site's absolute level after removing flow) is likewise land-use controlled: vs %agriculture R2 = 0.585, vs %forest R2 = 0.649, vs %row crop R2 = 0.513, vs %tile R2 = 0.251, but vs log10(area) only R2 = 0.179. ACTIONABLE READ FOR THIS PROJECT: the between-site deficit should be attacked with STATIC LAND-USE / TILE covariates, not with basin size, not with discharge, and not with more temporal features — which is consistent with the project's finding that only geometry and static geography have ever produced wins.
claims.effectSize: log10(CVc/CVq): area R2=0.412 vs tile R2=0.001. Power-law intercept log10(a): %ag R2=0.585, %forest R2=0.649 vs area R2=0.179

claims.text: OPERATIONAL DATASET — this closes the project's stated gap that 'tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet'. Marinos et al. (2020) source their tile layer from Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, 'Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012', U.S. Geological Survey data release (confirmed in the paper's archived Step3_Compile_LULC.R: 'This data was extracted from Nakagaki et al., cited in paper using QGIS and the basin shapefiles'). SPECIFICATION: 30 m raster; each cell stores estimated tile-drained area in SQUARE METRES, so the fraction of a cell that is tile-drained = value/900 (this is exactly the conversion in the paper's code: Tiled = Tiledmean/900). Static single-epoch product (2012 Census of Agriculture), no time dimension. Built from 2012 Census of Agriculture state-level tile acreage + NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland + STATSGO2 poorly/moderately drained soils. COVERAGE: 12 Midwest states — SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY — which covers ALL of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of Iowa's multi-state basins (MN, SD, NE, MO, IL headwaters), i.e. it does NOT suffer the Iowa-only clipping problem that currently under-counts CDL crop area and N surplus. DOI 10.5066/F7W37TDP. Access: free public bulk download, no authentication, from https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/55f6e42ae4b0477df11bff10 (mirror: https://data.usgs.gov/datacatalog/data/USGS:55f6e42ae4b0477df11bff10). USGS data release — public domain / no license restriction. CAVEAT: the paper had to set tile = NA for its one Mississippi-mainstem site (07020850) because the basin extended beyond the 12-state layer, so any basin reaching outside the 12 states needs an explicit NaN/partial-coverage flag rather than a silent inner join. A newer alternative if higher fidelity is wanted: Valayamkunnath et al. 2020, 'Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach', Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x.
claims.effectSize: 30 m raster, m2 tile-drained per 900 m2 cell; 12 Midwest states; single epoch 2012; DOI 10.5066/F7W37TDP

claims.text: C-Q REGIME FOR NITRATE IN THIS REGION IS MOBILIZATION/ENRICHMENT, NOT DILUTION — and discharge explains less than half of within-site daily nitrate variance even where it is measured. Recomputed from the paper's dataset (OLS log10(C) ~ log10(specific Q) on daily values, n=32 sites): the C-Q exponent b is POSITIVE at 32 of 32 sites, range +0.090 to +1.095, median +0.440. Not a single site dilutes on the daily-mean timescale. The within-site coefficient of determination of that log-log C-Q fit ranges R2 = 0.026 to 0.869 with MEDIAN R2 = 0.417 — so at the median site, perfectly measured co-located discharge explains only ~42% of daily log-nitrate variance. The C-Q exponent b is itself weakly land-use controlled (vs %row crop R2 = 0.345, vs %agriculture R2 = 0.310, vs %tile R2 = 0.209, vs log10(area) R2 = 0.147), meaning b is not reliably transferable to an ungauged pin from static attributes either. IMPLICATION FOR TARGET DEFINITION: because b > 0 everywhere, LOAD (C x Q) scales roughly as Q^(1+b) with 1+b in the range 1.09-2.10, so a load target is even more dominated by discharge than a concentration target; back-deriving concentration from a modeled load would divide by a modeled Q and propagate NWM discharge error directly into the concentration estimate. Given that measured Q already fails as a between-site predictor (R2 = 0.034), switching the target to load is NOT supported by this dataset as a route to between-site skill. CAVEAT ON MY NUMBERS: the paper fits a broken power law by maximum likelihood on flow-weighted daily concentrations; I fit a single OLS log-log line on unweighted daily means, so my b values are comparable in sign and order but are not the paper's published estimates.
claims.effectSize: C-Q exponent b positive at 32/32 sites, range +0.090 to +1.095, median +0.440; within-site log-log C-Q R2 median 0.417 (range 0.026-0.869)

result.sourceQuality: MIXED — high confidence, but with an important provenance split that the parent agent must preserve. (1) The primary source is HARD PAYWALLED: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com returned HTTP 402 Payment Required on both the /doi/ and /doi/full/ routes, and Unpaywall reports oa_status='closed', is_oa=false, has_repository_copy=false, oa_locations=[] — there is no legal open copy, no preprint, and no institutional-repository version. I therefore could NOT read the paper's Results section, so I do NOT have the paper's own published regression table, its published C-Q exponents, or its published R2 values. (2) The verbatim ABSTRACT is high confidence — recovered identically from two independent mirrors (Semantic Scholar Graph API for DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051, and Penn State Pure). Peer-reviewed GRL paper, 39 citations, authors Marinos (Waterloo/SUNY Buffalo), Van Meter (UIC), Basu (Waterloo) — Basu is the primary author of the chemostasis literature the research angle names as a seed. (3) The QUANTITATIVE CLAIMS ARE MY OWN RECOMPUTATION, not the paper's numbers. The paper's complete input data and R analysis pipeline are archived openly under CC-BY 4.0 at HydroShare DOI 10.4211/hs.d5676355cbd94b79a2e58f8089040a40 (104 files, 651.8 MB). I downloaded all 35 site nitrate+discharge records (669 MB), the NLCD land-use table, and the Nakagaki tile-drainage table, pulled drainage areas from the USGS NWIS site service, reproduced the paper's specific-discharge conversion exactly as written in its Step1 script, and ran the between-site regressions using the same predictor set as the paper's own Step4_AnalyzeMetrics.R generate_table() function. I recovered 32 of the paper's 33 analysis sites (4 archived sites had <365 matched days after my QC; 07020850 has no NWIS drainage area and no tile coverage). WHERE MY METHOD DIFFERS FROM THE PAPER: the paper computes flow-weighted daily concentrations and fits broken power laws by maximum likelihood with per-site optimizer tuning; I used unweighted daily means and a single OLS log-log fit. My C-Q exponents are therefore directionally reliable but are not the paper's published estimates, and any claim quoting a 'b' value should be attributed to me, not to Marinos et al. The land-use and tile-drainage regressions are much less sensitive to this difference since they operate on site-level summary statistics. (4) IMPORTANT PROTOCOL CAVEAT applying to every number I computed: these are IN-SAMPLE CROSS-SECTIONAL regressions of static covariates against site-level summary statistics across 32 sites. They are NOT held-out predictive scores and must NOT be compared to this project's LOFO AUC 0.820 / R2 0.328. They are evidence about WHICH COVARIATE CARRIES BETWEEN-SITE INFORMATION, which is the specific question asked. With n=32 and a single predictor, the R2=0.575 tile-drainage result is reasonably robust, but a 6-predictor model at n=32 would already be overfitting — and at this project's n=19 families, any between-site model should be held to roughly 1-3 static predictors. (5) The Nakagaki tile-drainage dataset specification was verified independently against the USGS ScienceBase catalog record and USGS data catalog, not taken from the paper. (6) OVERALL BOTTOM LINE ON THE RESEARCH QUESTION: this source answers it NEGATIVELY and the negative is well-supported — measured discharge does not convert into between-site skill (delta R2 = +0.001 over a land-use model), so a modeled discharge source such as NWM v3 retrospective cannot either, since it inherits that null plus its own error. The genuinely valuable finding from this source is not about discharge at all: it is that percent tile drainage is a single static, publicly available, Iowa-plus-neighboring-states covariate that alone explains R2=0.575 of between-site exceedance rate, and it is currently absent from this project's feature set.

claims.text: An LSTM trained on high-frequency nitrate sensor observations across the continental US achieved median KGE = 0.60 under temporal validation but only median KGE = 0.18 under spatial validation in unmonitored watersheds — a drop of 0.42 KGE units (~70% relative). This is a water-quality (not streamflow) PUB result and reproduces the 'good timer, mediocre site-ranker' failure mode at continental scale with a deep-learning architecture.
claims.nBasins: unknown — abstract does not state the number of sensor sites; full text paywalled (HTTP 402) despite Gold OA listing
claims.effectSize: temporal median KGE 0.60 vs spatial/ungauged median KGE 0.18; delta = 0.42 KGE

claims.text: The temporal-holdout figure (median KGE 0.60) and the spatial-holdout figure (median KGE 0.18) come from the SAME model and dataset in Pandit et al. (2025), making this one of the few published head-to-head measurements of the transfer penalty for daily nitrate CONCENTRATION prediction; the ungauged-basin number is the only one comparable to a leave-one-basin-out protocol.
claims.effectSize: KGE 0.18 is the published ungauged-basin ceiling for daily nitrate concentration from a CONUS LSTM

claims.text: Shapley (SHAP) analysis identified tile drainage, roadway density, and wetland coverage as the key static drivers of riverine nitrate concentration across the Mississippi River Basin, with the paper reporting quantitative thresholds for management intervention. Tile drainage is currently absent from this project's feature set and has no identified data source; this paper must have used an MRB-wide tile-drainage layer, making its data section the highest-value unread target.
claims.effectSize: three named top SHAP drivers: tile drainage, road density, wetland cover; threshold values not recoverable from abstract

claims.text: Over 1980-2022 the Mississippi River Basin exported only 19 ± 4% of nitrogen surplus as riverine nitrate, implying most surplus N is retained within basins — i.e. a static N-surplus input maps to export with a highly variable, non-constant transfer coefficient, which is a mechanistic reason why broadcasting a static surplus layer forward in time (already a failed ablation on this project, -0.166) should not be expected to work.
claims.effectSize: 19 ± 4% of surplus exported, 1980-2022

claims.text: In Midwestern regions including Iowa, the nitrate export fraction was 42 ± 24% in wet years versus 6 ± 6% in dry years — a ~7x swing attributed to increased hydrologic connectivity and remobilization of legacy nitrogen. The surplus-to-export relationship is therefore strongly wetness-conditional, suggesting an annual or seasonal basin wetness state variable (not a same-day or short-rolling precip term, both of which already failed here) is the mechanistically indicated interaction.
claims.nBasins: unknown (Iowa/Midwest subset size not stated in abstract)
claims.effectSize: wet-year export 42 ± 24% vs dry-year 6 ± 6%

claims.text: NEGATIVE-RESULT / CEILING claim: despite using an LSTM (which dominates streamflow PUB benchmarks), high-frequency sensor data, and continental-scale training with far more donor catchments than 19, spatial prediction at unmonitored watersheds remained at median KGE 0.18 — the authors themselves characterize spatial predictions as 'lower accuracy'. This is evidence that the between-site ceiling for nitrate is low as a property of the problem, and that adding donor catchments alone is not sufficient to close it.
claims.nBasins: unknown, but CONUS-wide high-frequency nitrate sensor network — certainly >>19 families
claims.effectSize: spatial median KGE 0.18 vs temporal 0.60 for the same model

claims.text: Brenning, Frank & Suesse (2026, Environmental Modelling & Software 204:107097, DOI 10.1016/j.envsoft.2026.107097) report that when spatial models of groundwater nitrate concentration are used for exceedance mapping by thresholding the point predictions, standard interpolation and machine-learning techniques UNDERESTIMATE the total polluted (threshold-exceeding) area by 80%-98%, even though the same models show 'strong concentration-prediction metrics'. This is a direct, quantified argument against the regression-then-threshold pipeline: good R2/RMSE on concentration does not imply unbiased exceedance delineation, because conditional-mean (or kriged) predictions shrink toward the mean and systematically fail to cross the threshold. NOTE: extracted from abstract only - full text was unreachable (Elsevier 403 on both the HTML article and the CC-BY PDF).
claims.effectSize: 80%-98% underestimation of exceedance area by thresholding point predictions
claims.nBasins: unknown (groundwater wells, national-scale dataset; count not recoverable from abstract; authors are at Friedrich Schiller University Jena so the dataset is most likely German national groundwater monitoring, unverified)

claims.text: The same paper argues the correct framing is to treat exceedance mapping 'as probabilistic prediction rather than thresholding point estimates' - i.e. predict P(concentration >= threshold) directly (or integrate a predictive distribution above the threshold) instead of predicting a concentration and comparing it to the threshold. This is peer-reviewed support for the sustag project's choice to make the binary `violation` classifier the PRIMARY model rather than deriving violations from the R2=0.328 regression. It also implies the regression model should NOT be repurposed as a violation detector by thresholding its output at 10 mg/L without recalibration.
claims.effectSize: qualitative methodological claim; supported by the 80-98% area-underestimation result above

claims.text: The paper's core proposed correction is AREA CALIBRATION: 'a calibrated probability threshold that ensures an unbiased delineation of the polluted area', where the total exceedance area is first estimated from the data and the operating probability threshold is then chosen so the predicted positive area matches that estimate. The authors report this 'effectively eliminates this bias and balances omission versus commission errors', and state the method is model-agnostic and applicable to threshold-based environmental decisions generally. For sustag this is a concrete, cheap, testable alternative to the current beta=2 F-beta operating point (recall 0.864 / 59% false alarms): instead of maximizing F-beta, pick the threshold so the predicted violation rate on held-out folds equals the estimated true base rate 0.263, and report omission/commission balance.
claims.effectSize: bias 'effectively eliminated'; no numeric residual bias recoverable from abstract

claims.text: The paper introduces 'target-weighted cross-validation' as its evaluation protocol for exceedance mapping - i.e. cross-validation whose error weighting is aligned to the decision target (exceedance area / classification) rather than to squared error on concentration. Whether this CV is SPATIALLY blocked cannot be determined from the abstract; the abstract does not state a spatial-holdout design, so its performance numbers are NOT directly comparable to sustag's LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634. (Caveat for the reader: Alexander Brenning is the author of the `sperrorest` R package and a long-standing advocate of spatial cross-validation, so a spatial design is likely but is NOT established by the retrievable metadata.)
claims.effectSize: n/a - protocol description

claims.text: The modeling stack in the paper is trans-Gaussian regression-kriging combined with QUANTILE REGRESSION FORESTS, with 'structured non-stationarity across hydrogeological districts' - i.e. district-level (region-level) model structure rather than one global model. Reported ancillary figures: per-district linear model R2 ranges 0.15-0.62 and semivariogram practical ranges 0.3-22.3 km. The quantile-regression-forest component is the 'distributional-then-integrate' route to exceedance probability (fit the full conditional distribution, integrate above the threshold), which is the third of the three candidate approaches and is here used in production alongside geostatistics. Relevance/limit for sustag: the spatial-correlation ranges are 0.3-22.3 km for groundwater wells, far shorter than typical Iowa inter-sensor distances, and the kriging half of the method requires a spatially dense observation network - it will NOT transfer to an arbitrary Iowa map pin whose nearest nitrate sensor may be tens of km away. Only the QRF + area-calibration half is deployable for sustag.
claims.effectSize: linear-model R2 0.15-0.62 across districts; semivariogram practical ranges 0.3-22.3 km

claims.text: NEGATIVE / SCOPE FINDING about this source relative to the assignment: this paper does NOT address (a) peaks-over-threshold or extreme-value theory for water quality, (b) the regulatory definition or averaging period of the 10 mg/L nitrate-N MCL, (c) TMDL or stream-monitoring operationalization of exceedance as distinct from treated drinking water, (d) sensor-derived daily statistics or sampling-frequency bias, or (e) published virtual-sensor AUC/PR-AUC benchmarks for spatially held-out exceedance prediction. It is a purely SPATIAL, static-snapshot GROUNDWATER mapping paper with no time-series component, so it supplies no comparator for sustag's 0.820 AUC / 2.41x lift and no guidance on whether 'daily maximum >= 10 mg/L in raw stream water' is the right target. Its transferable content is confined to the estimator-bias and area-calibration argument. Those other questions must be answered from other sources.
claims.effectSize: n/a - scope limitation

claims.text: Oudin et al. (2008) compared three regionalization families for transferring lumped rainfall-runoff model parameters to ungauged catchments across 913 French catchments using two models (TOPMO and GR4J), and found a stable rank order: spatial proximity best, physical similarity intermediate, regression on catchment attributes worst. Parajka et al. (2013), which tabulates this study in its PUB meta-analysis (Table 1), records Oudin's ungauged-mode Nash-Sutcliffe efficiencies as 0.69, 0.71, 0.55, 0.71, 0.74, 0.68 for the model-averaging / proximity / regression combinations across the two models — i.e. proximity around NSE 0.71-0.74 versus regression around NSE 0.55-0.68. FALSIFIABLE: if the Wiley full text shows similarity outranking proximity, or shows regression within 0.02 NSE of proximity, this claim is wrong. CAVEAT: the mapping of the six numbers to specific (method, model) pairs is inferred from Parajka's method-code ordering 'MA, P, R' and should be verified against the original Tables.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — each gauged catchment treated in turn as ungauged (leave-one-out / pseudo-ungauged), donors drawn from the remaining catchments; Parajka et al. 2013 explicitly describe the cross-validation for this class of study as 'a leave-one-out strategy, where each gauged catchment was in turn considered as ungauged'
claims.effectSize: Proximity NSE ~0.71-0.74 vs regression NSE ~0.55-0.68 across two models; gap of roughly 0.03-0.16 NSE depending on model. Consistent sign across both model structures.

claims.text: MOST DIRECTLY RELEVANT NEGATIVE RESULT FOR THIS PROJECT: Oudin et al. (2008) report verbatim in their abstract that 'The regression approach is the least satisfactory, with results very close to those obtained using one median parameter set for the whole country.' That is, regressing model behaviour on catchment physical attributes over 913 catchments recovered essentially NO between-catchment information beyond a single global constant. This is the exact functional analogue of our between-site problem: learning a site's absolute level from static basin attributes. With n=913 donor catchments — 48x our 19 independent basin families — attribute regression still failed to beat a constant. This is strong prior evidence that adding more static basin attributes (tile drainage, soils, additional land-use aggregates) to predict the ABSOLUTE LEVEL at an unseen Iowa basin will underperform expectations, and it argues that our lat/lon features being top-3 is the spatial-proximity mechanism already doing the work that attribute regression is failing to do.
claims.effectSize: Attribute regression ≈ single median global parameter set (difference described as 'very close'; no separation reported). Effectively zero between-catchment skill gain from attribute regression at n=913.

claims.text: THE DONOR-DENSITY SCALING RESULT — the single most decision-relevant number found. Oudin et al. (2008) degraded the French gauging network to test how the proximity-vs-similarity ranking depends on donor density. Parajka et al. (2013, p. 1788) report: 'Oudin et al. (2008), for example, reported that spatial proximity slightly outperformed the similarity method in regions with a dense stream gauge network. They reported that the predictive performance of these two approaches becomes similar when the density of stream gauges decreases to less than 60 gauges per 100 000 km2.' DERIVED FOR IOWA (145,746 km2): our 85 sensor sites = 58 sites per 100,000 km2, and our 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES = 13 per 100,000 km2. Both are at or far below Oudin's 60/100,000 km2 threshold. FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION: at our donor density, spatial proximity should have NO reliable advantage over attribute similarity — the two should be statistically indistinguishable — and neither should be expected to reach the skill Oudin obtained at full French density. This directly predicts that swapping our lat/lon proximity signal for an attribute-similarity donor scheme will be a wash, not a win.
claims.nBasins: 913 French catchments (Oudin), progressively thinned to lower densities; threshold stated at <60 gauges per 100,000 km2
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (pseudo-ungauged leave-one-out) under progressively thinned donor networks
claims.effectSize: Proximity advantage over similarity shrinks to zero below ~60 gauges/100,000 km2. Iowa equivalents: 58 per 100,000 km2 at 85 sites; 13 per 100,000 km2 at 19 independent families.

claims.text: THE PUB CEILING, STATED BY THE AUTHORS: Oudin et al. (2008) abstract, verbatim: 'However, the results obtained with these three methods lag far behind those obtained by full model calibration... there is still considerable room for progress in the field of ungaged catchment modeling.' The best regionalization (proximity, NSE ~0.71-0.74) is substantially below what the same models achieve when calibrated on the target catchment's own observations. The authors also report that 'some improvement could be made by combining spatial proximity and physical similarity' — the ONLY positive lever they identify, and it is described as an improvement, not a fix. IMPLICATION FOR US: the gap we observe between within_r2 0.42 (temporal, site-informed) and between_r2 0.21 (transfer to unseen basin) is the canonical, expected, 25-year-unsolved PUB signature, not a defect specific to our feature set. Our project's 'good timer, mediocre site-ranker' diagnosis is the field's standard result restated.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (pseudo-ungauged) compared against same-site full calibration — the two protocols are explicitly contrasted, which is the correct comparison to make and is exactly our within vs between decomposition
claims.effectSize: All three regionalization families 'lag far behind' full calibration (magnitude not quotable from abstract alone — the paywalled Tables would be needed). Combining proximity + similarity gives an unquantified improvement.

claims.text: HOW SKILL SCALES WITH NUMBER OF DONOR CATCHMENTS — an actual curve, from Parajka et al. (2013) Figs. 4 and 5, Level 1 meta-analysis of 34 studies / 75 results / 3874 catchments. Findings, verbatim and paraphrased: (a) 'the 21 studies with less than 20 catchments have the largest scatter in the performance because of the smallest sample size'; (b) 'As the number of catchments increases the performance tends to decrease'; (c) 'For 12 studies with more than 250 catchments the performance however tends to increase.' The authors attribute the small-n advantage to selection bias, not method quality: 'in some of the studies with few catchments, these catchments were hand picked in terms of suitability for regionalisation and this happens less frequently in the studies with more catchments.' CRITICALLY for us: 'The maximum performance exceeds 0.8 for the similarity, regression and model averaging methods, but this performance is documented only for the small datasets. Interestingly, the performance of similarity-based regionalisation is clearly lower for assessments with large datasets.' Result counts by method: 33 spatial proximity, 9 similarity, 12 model averaging, 17 parameter regression, 4 regional calibration. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION AT OUR n=19: we sit in the highest-variance, most selection-biased stratum of the entire PUB literature. Any single-number regionalization gain we measure on 19 families carries scatter comparable to the full 0.3-0.9 NSE spread of that stratum, so a reported improvement of less than roughly 0.05 in our transfer metrics is not distinguishable from donor-set luck. This is an argument for repeated/nested CV over families and for reporting confidence intervals, NOT for abandoning regionalization.
claims.nBasins: 34 studies, 75 results, 3874 catchments (Level 1); 9 studies, 1832 catchments (Level 2, of which 1479 humid and 353 arid)
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout throughout — Level 2 performance 'estimated by a leave-one-out strategy, where each gauged catchment was in turn considered as ungauged and estimated runoff was compared with the observed runoff hydrographs'; Level 1 aggregates study-reported ungauged-mode results
claims.effectSize: Strata used: <20, 20-200, >200 catchments. Median NSE band across strata roughly 0.5-0.75 with the <20 stratum spanning ~0.3-0.9. Max NSE >0.8 for similarity/regression/model-averaging occurs ONLY in small datasets. Level 2 ranking over 1832 catchments: highest = similarity and spatial proximity (tied at top); lowest = model averaging. In humid catchments specifically: spatial proximity and similarity highest, model average lowest.

claims.text: THE ABSENCE FINDING ON WATER-QUALITY PUB — reported plainly because the absence is itself the result. The IAHS PUB Decade's own flagship comparative assessment (Parajka et al. 2013, Part 1, with companion Parts by Salinas et al. 2013 and Viglione et al. 2013) surveys 34 studies and 3874 catchments and is ENTIRELY streamflow. A full-text search of the paper for 'water quality', 'nitrate', 'nutrient', and 'concentration' returns exactly ONE hit, and it is motivational rather than a study: environmental-change interest in 'the runoff hydrographs and water quality for which accurate runoff predictions are needed'. Not a single one of the 34 assessed studies predicts a concentration or an exceedance signal. Likewise Oudin et al. (2008), the largest-n regionalization comparison in the literature at 913 catchments, regionalizes rainfall-runoff MODEL PARAMETERS, not a water-quality state. CONSEQUENCE: there is no published water-quality PUB benchmark against which our LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 can be compared, and every effect size quoted in this source transfers to us only by ANALOGY — streamflow regionalization skill is not evidence about nitrate concentration regionalization skill. Any claim that a regionalization technique 'works for water quality' on the strength of this literature is unsupported.
claims.nBasins: 3874 catchments across 34 studies, of which zero are water-quality studies
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — this is a claim about the absence of studies, not a performance number
claims.effectSize: 0 of 34 PUB studies / 0 of 3874 catchments address a concentration or exceedance target. 1 of 1 textual mentions of 'water quality' is motivational.
