claims.text: Gorski et al. (2024) built deep-learning (LSTM-family) hindcasts of 7-day backward-looking average stream nitrate concentration at 46 predominantly agricultural sites in the midwestern and eastern US. SINGLE-SITE models -- trained AND tested at the same location, i.e. using that site's own nitrate history -- achieved a median Kling-Gupta Efficiency of 0.66. This is the paper's headline skill number and it is an INTERPOLATION result, not a transfer result: it is not comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC / R2 0.328, and it describes a setting our deployment target (arbitrary ungauged map pin, no local nitrate history) categorically does not have. VERIFIED FROM ABSTRACT ONLY -- Wiley full text returned HTTP 402/403 on all routes.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (within-site: 'trained and tested at a single location'; exact partition not verifiable from abstract)
claims.effectSize: median KGE = 0.66 across 46 sites, single-site models

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON GLOBAL POOLING FOR WATER QUALITY: in Gorski et al. (2024), 'developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model' (n=46 sites). This directly contradicts the streamflow-PUB/CAMELS finding that one large multi-basin model beats per-basin models. Falsifiable prediction for our project: naively pooling all 85 Iowa sites into one global model will degrade skill at the most hydrologically distinct basin families rather than improve them, and any gain must come from similarity-based grouping, not from adding rows. Per-site or per-group effect sizes are in the paywalled full text; only the directional claim is verified.

claims.effectSize: direction only -- 'reduced performance at several locations'; magnitude not verifiable from abstract

claims.text: ATTRIBUTE-SIMILARITY GROUPING BEAT BOTH EXTREMES: Gorski et al. (2024) report that 'accuracy at poorly performing sites could be improved by grouping sites with similar characteristics' (n=46). This ranks the regionalization families as: partial pooling by attribute similarity > single-site models (at weak sites) > full pooling across all sites (at distinct sites). This is the one piece of positive regionalization evidence in the paper and it is the family most compatible with our n=19-independent-basin-families constraint, since it requires only that families be clusterable, not that hundreds of donors exist. Consequence for our project: any recommendation whose evidence is streamflow regionalization at 300+ basins must be flagged as unvalidated for concentration/exceedance targets, independent of the separate n=19 sample-size objection.

claims.text: DISCHARGE IS THE DOMINANT PREDICTOR, AND IT IS UNAVAILABLE AT OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: Gorski et al. (2024) report that 'across all sites, discharge and watershed soil and physiographic attributes showed a strong influence on model performance', with daily observed discharge used as a model INPUT at all 46 sites. Every skill number in this paper therefore presupposes a co-located streamflow gauge. Our shipped product has no discharge at an arbitrary map pin, and on-disk discharge exists at only 22 of 85 sites (zero of 61 IWQIS sites), so this paper's performance is not attainable by our architecture. The actionable residual is the SECOND-ranked driver group -- watershed soil and physiographic attributes -- which is static, map-derivable everywhere in Iowa, and is precisely the between-site information our model currently lacks (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42).

claims.text: Baggio & Muzy (2026, arXiv:2605.31079) directly test regression/distributional-then-threshold against direct binary classification for environmental threshold exceedance, and find the full-distribution approach (M2: model the complete conditional law of the target, then integrate its tail above the threshold) consistently outperforms direct binary classification (M1) for RARE events, while the two are essentially EQUIVALENT at moderate exceedance probabilities. Reported ratio PSS_1/PSS_2 approaches 1.0 at exceedance probability p=0.2 and falls to roughly 0.65 at p=0.002 for 1-hour-ahead wind speed. Direct implication for this project: our violation base rate is 0.263, which is ABOVE the p=0.2 regime where the paper finds no advantage for the distributional route — so this paper does NOT support switching our primary CLF target from direct binary classification to regression-then-threshold. It would only argue for the switch if we moved to a much rarer threshold (e.g. a 20-30 mg/L alarm, or a rare-percentile site-specific exceedance).
claims.effectSize: PSS_1/PSS_2 ~1.0 at p=0.2; ~0.65 at p=0.002. Brier Skill Score: BSS_2 stays positive as p decreases while BSS_1 degrades sharply. Thresholds tested, wind: p in {0.2, 0.1, 0.08, 0.05, 0.03, 0.01, 0.005, 0.002}; rainfall: p in {0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025}. Results reported graphically (Figs 4-5); no exact numeric tables recoverable, so the 0.65 figure is read off a figure and should be treated as approximate.
claims.nBasins: 278 ground stations (wind), 268 stations (rainfall), southeastern France, MeteoNet 2016-2018; ~3.5e6 training samples
claims.splitProtocol: random-split (random partition of CALENDAR DAYS into 85% train / 10% val / 5% test, with all samples from a day kept together to block within-day autocorrelation leakage). This is a random temporal split, NOT a spatial holdout. Numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC.

claims.text: The paper gives a sample-size argument for why direct binary classification degrades on rare events: the direct classifier's EFFECTIVE sample size is approximately pN (only the exceedance-positive cases carry information about the threshold), whereas the distributional model uses all N observations, since moderate-intensity events still inform the conditional mean and variance. The stated error ratio is E_2/E_1 = O(p). Applied to this project: at base rate 0.263 with 160,074 site-days, effective positive count is ~42,000 events, so the direct classifier is NOT in the data-starved regime this argument describes. The binding constraint here is n=19 independent basin families, which is a between-site degrees-of-freedom problem this paper's theory does not address at all — its efficiency argument is about event rarity within a pooled sample, not about spatial transfer.
claims.effectSize: Effective sample size pN for direct classification vs N for distributional; error ratio E_2/E_1 = O(p) (Eqs. 24-25). No explicit minimum event count stated.

claims.text: Baggio & Muzy EXPLICITLY REJECT extreme value theory / peaks-over-threshold for this problem. They use no Generalized Pareto Distribution and no POT threshold selection, citing EVT's 'notoriously difficult bias-variance trade-off' in threshold selection, and instead fit full-support parametric conditional distributions: a three-parameter multifractal-Rice (M-Rice) law with parameters (nu, sigma^2, lambda^2) for wind speed, and a zero-inflated mixed lognormal (p_wet, mu, sigma^2) for hourly rainfall. This is a directly relevant negative signal for the research angle: a 2026 paper whose entire subject is threshold exceedance forecasting deliberately declined to use POT/EVT, on the grounds that fitting the bulk and integrating the tail is more stable than fitting the tail directly.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative methodological choice; no EVT baseline was run, so the paper provides no head-to-head EVT-vs-distributional number.

claims.text: The paper reports that the specific PARAMETRIC SHAPE of the assumed conditional distribution 'plays a secondary role' compared with accurately capturing shifts in the bulk properties (conditional mean and variance) of the distribution. Differences among alternative parametric families are described as 'limited' though not negligible, with a full sensitivity analysis deferred to future work. Implication for this project: if we ever do move to a distributional target for nitrate, the payoff would come from getting the conditional MEAN and VARIANCE right per site-day, not from choosing a fancy heavy-tailed family. That maps directly onto our known deficit — between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42 means we are failing on the conditional MEAN LEVEL of an unseen basin, which is exactly the quantity the paper says dominates exceedance skill. A distributional reformulation would not fix that; it would inherit the same between-site error.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative; sensitivity analysis across parametric families explicitly deferred, so the 'secondary role' claim is asserted rather than fully quantified in this paper.

claims.text: CRITICAL LIMITATION for our use case: Baggio & Muzy train a SINGLE POOLED model across all 278 stations with station metadata (latitude, longitude, altitude) as contextual features — architecturally the same trick as our lat/lon/static-geography features — but they NEVER evaluate transfer to unseen stations. Their split partitions calendar days, not stations, so every test-set station was also in training. The paper therefore provides ZERO evidence about the ungauged/unmonitored-location deployment target, which is precisely our product's setting (arbitrary map pin, no local history). Its conclusions about M2 > M1 are established only under station-interpolation conditions and must not be transferred to our LOFO regime without independent validation.
claims.effectSize: Generalization to unseen locations is unexplored; the authors' own framing is 'at a specific location', i.e. locations with training history.
claims.splitProtocol: random-split by calendar day; explicitly NOT a spatial/station holdout

claims.text: For evaluation of environmental exceedance forecasts, Baggio & Muzy use a two-tier metric set that is standard in the meteorological verification literature: PROPER SCORING RULES on the probabilistic output (Brier score and logarithmic score, reported as skill scores against climatology, i.e. BSS) plus DETERMINISTIC categorical skill scores after thresholding the probability (Peirce Skill Score, Critical Success Index, Heidke Skill Score). Notably they do NOT report ROC-AUC or PR-AUC as headline metrics. Implication for this project: our current reporting (AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634, 2.41x lift, Brier 0.137) is missing the climatology-referenced skill scores that this literature treats as the comparison standard. Converting our Brier 0.137 to a Brier Skill Score against the base-rate-0.263 climatological forecast (whose Brier is 0.263*0.737 = 0.1938) gives BSS = 1 - 0.137/0.1938 = 0.293, and adding PSS/CSI/HSS at our operating points would make our numbers directly comparable to the meteorological exceedance-forecasting literature instead of incomparable.
claims.effectSize: Metric set: Brier score, logarithmic score, BSS, Peirce Skill Score, CSI, HSS. The BSS = 0.293 figure is our own arithmetic from our Brier 0.137 and base rate 0.263, not a number from the paper.
claims.splitProtocol: random-split by calendar day (their numbers); our derived BSS 0.293 is spatial-holdout (LOFO) and the two must not be compared

result.sourceQuality: Primary source, fully accessible. arXiv:2605.31079 (Baggio & Muzy, submitted 29 May 2026, 24 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables) was read via the arXiv HTML full text (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.31079v1) after the PDF failed to decode. Abstract and metadata confirmed from the arXiv abstract page. CAVEATS: (1) This is a very recent arXiv preprint with no evidence of peer review; no DOI beyond the arXiv identifier. (2) Numerical results in the paper are presented GRAPHICALLY (Figures 4-5) rather than in extractable tables, so the specific values quoted (PSS_1/PSS_2 ~0.65 at p=0.002, ~1.0 at p=0.2) are figure reads relayed through an extraction model and should be verified against the figures before being cited as exact. Treat them as approximate directions-and-magnitudes, not precise measurements. (3) The conclusion section was returned in paraphrase, not verbatim quote. (4) DOMAIN MISMATCH: this is atmospheric science (wind speed, hourly rainfall), not water quality. It answers research question (a) on exceedance methodology only. It contains NOTHING on the nitrate MCL, its averaging period, TMDL or stream-monitoring practice, sensor-derived daily statistics, sampling-frequency bias, or virtual-sensor benchmarks — research question (b) and most of the 'what we need' list are entirely unaddressed by this source and must be sought elsewhere. (5) MOST IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL CAVEAT: the study is pooled-across-278-stations with a random calendar-day split and no held-out-station evaluation, so it speaks to the temporal-forecasting question and is silent on spatial transfer to ungauged locations — our actual deployment problem. Its n=278 stations also vastly exceeds our n=19 independent basin families, though the paper's core claim is a within-sample rarity argument rather than a between-site one, so the n=19 constraint bears on it less than on transfer-learning papers.

claims.text: Zero-shot spatial transfer of an exceedance classifier collapsed to near-chance. Random Forest models trained on one city's beaches and applied to another city's beaches with NO target-site data scored AUC 0.567 (Chicago source -> San Diego target) and AUC 0.482 (San Diego -> Chicago), versus AUC 0.733 and 0.607 for same-region models. The authors describe the San Diego -> Chicago generalization as 'no better than chance alone' (AUC 0.482). DIRECT RELEVANCE: this is the closest published analogue to our deployment target (arbitrary ungauged pin, no local history), and it says between-site/between-region absolute-level transfer is exactly where these models break — consistent with our within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21. Our LOFO AUC 0.820 is ABOVE every cross-region number in this paper, though the comparison is imperfect (different analyte, and their spatial units are two whole metro regions rather than 19 basin families).
claims.nBasins: 33 beaches total (19 Chicago freshwater, 2016-2019; 14 San Diego marine, 2014-2021); 15,033 beach-days. But transfer was evaluated at the REGION level, so n=2 effective independent transfer units — an even more severe version of our n=19-families constraint, and the authors' own headline finding is that they could not tell which source beaches transfer well.
claims.effectSize: AUC 0.733 (SD local) / 0.607 (Chicago local) vs 0.567 and 0.482 zero-shot cross-region; sensitivity dropped 0.742 -> 0.463 (Chicago->SD) and 0.256 -> 0.208 (SD->Chicago)

claims.text: The paper's headline improvement — '28.3% increase in WF1 scores and 5.4% in AUC' — comes from SUPERVISED transfer learning that REQUIRES LABELED OBSERVATIONS AT THE TARGET SITE. The paper states: 'The assumption in supervised TL is that a few samples of labeled target data are provided (in this study, the label is the ENT threshold exceedance).' The two methods that produced the gains (Feature Augmentation FA, Boosting for Weighted Transfer BWT) are supervised; the regularization parameter gamma controls 'the importance attributed to labeled target data.' The number of labeled target samples required is NOT stated. VERDICT AGAINST OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: this technique DOES NOT WORK for an arbitrary map pin with no nitrate history. It would only work for adding a NEW MONITORED site after it has accumulated some observations. This must be stated prominently if TL is proposed.
claims.effectSize: Chicago->SD TL-FA: AUC 0.713, sens 0.729, spec 0.701, WF1 0.680 (vs zero-shot 0.567/0.463/0.620/0.535). SD->Chicago TL-FA: AUC 0.610, sens 0.291, spec 0.825, WF1 0.642 (vs zero-shot 0.482/0.208/0.807/0.408). TL essentially RECOVERED local-model performance (0.713 vs 0.733 local) but did not exceed it.

claims.text: On methodology question (a): this paper provides NO evidence for regression-then-threshold vs direct classification, because it only ever built DIRECT BINARY CLASSIFIERS (Logistic Regression and Random Forest) of threshold exceedance. It did not fit a continuous FIB regression and threshold the prediction, and it used no extreme-value / peaks-over-threshold machinery. This is the field norm for beach nowcasting exceedance work rather than a tested choice. Do not cite this paper as support for our binary CLF target being superior to REG-then-threshold; it is only evidence that direct classification is the ESTABLISHED default in the FIB exceedance literature. Random Forest generally outperformed Logistic Regression across transfer scenarios.
claims.effectSize: no head-to-head regression-vs-classification numbers reported

claims.text: PRECEDENT FOR MOVING OUR THRESHOLD: the authors deliberately set the exceedance threshold at 50% OF THE REGULATORY VALUE — 320 CCE/100 mL for Chicago (vs the EPA Beach Action Value of 640, qPCR) and 30 CFU/100 mL for San Diego (vs BAV 60, culture) — justified as 'a more health-protective (conservative) level,' referencing the 2012 EPA Recreational Water Quality Criteria. Their stated reason includes that 'neither Chicago nor San Diego beaches typically approach their respective BAVs,' i.e. the full regulatory threshold produced too few positives to model. The outcome was defined on SINGLE DAILY MEASUREMENTS (Chicago samples collected once daily at 06:00-08:00), with no averaging period. This is a peer-reviewed, ES&T-published precedent for (i) using a sub-regulatory threshold to obtain a workable positive class and (ii) defining exceedance on a single daily grab value rather than an average — both of which support the legitimacy of our 'daily max >= 10 mg/L' construction, while also showing that shifting the threshold is a normal and defensible modeling choice rather than a corruption of the target.
claims.effectSize: threshold set at 0.5x BAV; resulting exceedance base rates 26.9% (Chicago) and 33.6% (San Diego) — strikingly close to our violation base rate of 0.263

claims.text: EXTERNAL BENCHMARK for what 'good' exceedance sensitivity looks like in published environmental-threshold models: the paper's literature summary reports model sensitivity of 27-65% at Great Lakes sites and 28-30% at California beaches, with specificity typically 85-99%; the authors also note 'model sensitivity was generally better in models of FIB at rivers ... than at coastal waters.' In their own results, 'only four of the 12 models had sensitivity above 0.70.' CALIBRATION FOR OUR NUMBERS: our LOFO recall of 0.524 at a 10% false-alarm rate (i.e. specificity 0.90) sits INSIDE the upper half of that published band, and our AUC 0.820 exceeds every AUC in this paper (max 0.733, achieved with same-region training). The high-recall deployment setting (beta=2, recall 0.864, 59% false alarms) trades specificity far below the 0.85-0.99 the FIB literature holds; that is a defensible public-health choice but is out of line with published practice and should be presented as an explicit cost-sensitive decision, not as a performance claim.
claims.nBasins: unknown for the summarized prior studies (aggregated from a literature table spanning Great Lakes and California beach studies); the paper's own results are from 33 beaches
claims.effectSize: prior-literature sensitivity 27-65% (Great Lakes), 28-30% (California beaches), specificity 85-99%; this paper's own max AUC 0.733

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULTS worth heeding before we spend effort: (i) CORAL (correlation-alignment, an UNSUPERVISED domain-adaptation method needing only unlabeled target features — the one family that WOULD be legal for our deployment target) 'never improved performance' over plain zero-shot generalization in any transfer direction; (ii) class-imbalance oversampling via SMOTE and ADASYN showed 'significant underperformance.' Implication for us: the deployment-legal adaptation methods were exactly the ones that failed, and the methods that worked were the deployment-illegal supervised ones. Also note their feature set (12 features) INCLUDED 3-day and 7-day cumulative precipitation and binary any-rain flags, which were useful there — but that is a coastal FIB system with hours-scale response, not a tile-drained agricultural nitrate system, so it is not evidence against our own rolling-precipitation failure (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003). The authors' stated limitation is that they did not incorporate physical site characteristics (beach slope, pollutant sources, bathymetry) that might explain WHICH source sites transfer — the direct analogue of our missing tile-drainage-density and static between-site information.
claims.effectSize: CORAL: zero improvement over baseline generalization in all directions; SMOTE/ADASYN: 'significant underperformance'

result.sourceQuality: HIGH, with one caveat. Peer-reviewed research article in Environmental Science & Technology 59(42):22386-22396, published 15 Oct 2025, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, PMID 41091646, PMC12573789. The publisher page (pubs.acs.org) returned HTTP 403, but the FULL OPEN-ACCESS TEXT was successfully retrieved and read via PubMed Central (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12573789/), so these are not abstract-only claims — methods, results tables, and limitations were all read. Metadata cross-verified against Crossref, Europe PMC, and Semantic Scholar. Numbers are quoted as reported in the retrieved full text; verbatim phrases are in quotation marks. One caveat: exact per-model table values were extracted through a page-summarization step rather than by reading the rendered PDF table directly, so if any specific figure becomes load-bearing for a decision, re-verify it against the PMC PDF. RELEVANCE CAVEAT: this is FECAL INDICATOR BACTERIA at recreational beaches, not stream nitrate. Its methodological findings on spatial transfer, threshold choice, and metric benchmarks transfer well; its feature-level findings (precipitation, tide, wave height) do not. WEB SEARCH BUDGET for this session was exhausted (200/200) before any search ran, so no supplementary sources were consulted.

claims.text: Two identical-model in situ UV-Vis spectrophotometers (s::can spectro::lyser) installed side-by-side in the same stream disagreed substantially on sub-daily NITRATE structure: Pearson r between the two sensors' deviations-from-background was only 0.429 (NF site), 0.454 (SHA) and 0.813 (TTP) while in parallel position, whereas for dissolved organic carbon the same paired sensors agreed at r > 0.98 (p < 0.001) at all three sites. Implication for a daily-max nitrate target: the WITHIN-DAY component of a UV-Vis nitrate record is only weakly reproducible between instruments, so a daily maximum inherits instrument-specific noise that a daily mean or median would average out. Study: 4 tropical headwater/mixed catchments in Kenya (27-36 km2 sub-catchments plus a 1021 km2 outlet), 5-year record (Nov 2014-Oct 2019), 10-minute sampling.
claims.nBasins: 4 catchments (3 nested sub-catchments 27-36 km2 + 1021 km2 outlet), Kenya; mobile-sensor comparison at 3 of the 4 sites
claims.effectSize: nitrate inter-sensor r = 0.43-0.81 vs DOC r > 0.98 in parallel position; during shading treatment nitrate r = 0.657 (NF), 0.505 (SHA), 0.236 (TTP) vs DOC r > 0.8 at all sites

claims.text: Physically moving or shading one of two co-located UV-Vis sensors changed the measured diurnal nitrate pattern, but NOT in a consistent direction: shading reduced the nitrate amplitude at NF, produced lower minima at SHA and TTP, increasing sensor depth reduced amplitude at TTP but had no visible effect at SHA, and changing orientation at NF reduced amplitude of both nitrate and DOC while at TTP it left nitrate essentially unchanged. The authors conclude the observed diurnal patterns 'are not (solely) caused by natural processes' and that incident solar radiation reaching the measurement window is a likely but unproven interferent. This is a falsifiable statement that sub-daily UV-Vis nitrate structure is partly a deployment-geometry artefact rather than a biogeochemical signal.
claims.nBasins: 3 sites instrumented with a paired mobile sensor (NF, TTP, SHA); each treatment >= 3 days, parallel phase >= 2 weeks
claims.effectSize: no consistent sign of effect across sites; qualitative amplitude and phase shifts (a ~6 h phase shift appeared at SHA after 18 Nov 2017 and persisted through depth change and shading)

claims.text: The manufacturer-stated accuracy of the s::can spectro::lyser nitrate measurement at 5 mm optical path length is '±2% + 0.2 mg N L−1' over a 0-60 mg N L−1 range, and the authors explicitly warn against interpreting diurnal patterns 'when the diurnal variations are of the same order of magnitude as sensor accuracy or resolution.' This sets a quantitative decision rule for whether a daily-maximum target is defensible: it is defensible only when within-day amplitude materially exceeds ~0.2 mg N/L plus 2% of the reading (i.e. ~0.4 mg N/L at 10 mg N/L). At the 10 mg/L nitrate MCL, ±2%+0.2 implies roughly ±0.4 mg N/L instrument uncertainty on any single reading, meaning site-days whose daily max falls within ~0.4 mg/L of the 10 mg/L threshold have effectively coin-flip label assignment.
claims.effectSize: ±2% + 0.2 mg N/L nitrate accuracy; 220-720 nm, 2.5 nm resolution, 5 mm path length, 10-min measurement interval

claims.text: Published diurnal nitrate amplitudes compiled by this paper span three orders of magnitude across streams: 0.01-0.15 mg N L−1 in temperate and subtropical rivers in the US, Spain and the UK; 0.4-0.6 mg N L−1 in other UK rivers; and 1.5 mg N L−1 in a Mediterranean headwater stream; the Kenyan study's own amplitudes were up to 0.25 mg N L−1 (sensor B, low flow) and < 0.02 mg N L−1 during high flow. This quantifies the maximum possible divergence between a daily-MAXIMUM and a daily-MEAN nitrate target: in the typical temperate agricultural case the gap is roughly 0.005-0.3 mg N/L, i.e. small relative to a 10 mg/L threshold, but in the worst documented case (1.5 mg N/L amplitude) daily-max could exceed daily-mean by ~0.75 mg N/L, which is enough to flip exceedance labels near the threshold.
claims.nBasins: literature compilation across ~6 cited studies plus the 4 Kenyan catchments; individual study n not stated in this paper
claims.effectSize: diurnal nitrate amplitude 0.01-0.15 mg N/L (US/Spain/UK), 0.4-0.6 mg N/L (UK rivers), 1.5 mg N/L (Mediterranean headwater), <=0.25 mg N/L (this study, low flow), <0.02 mg N/L (this study, high flow)

claims.text: Diurnal amplitude in nitrate decreased monotonically with discharge class at all four Kenyan sites, becoming 'barely discernible' with mean deviations from background < 0.02 mg N L−1 during high flow (Qd > Q30), while background nitrate concentration INCREASED with discharge at SHA (0.52 -> 0.89 -> 1.30 mg N/L), TTP (1.17 -> 1.74 -> 2.21) and OUT (0.65 -> 0.84 -> 0.99) across low/medium/high flow. For an exceedance-prediction target this means the daily-max-minus-daily-mean gap is SMALLEST exactly on the high-flow days when concentrations (and therefore exceedance risk in a transport-limited agricultural system) are highest — so choosing daily max over daily mean should have least effect on the positive class and most effect on low-flow negatives.
claims.nBasins: 4 catchments, Kenya; flow classes defined by Q70 and Q30 exceedance percentiles of mean daily discharge
claims.effectSize: high-flow diurnal deviation < 0.02 mg N/L vs up to 0.25 mg N/L at low flow; background nitrate rises 0.52 -> 1.30 mg N/L (SHA) and 1.17 -> 2.21 mg N/L (TTP) from low to high flow

claims.text: The paper reports that multiple prior studies establish turbidity thresholds above which UV-Vis sensors cannot provide valid nitrate measurements — cited as > 80 FTU, > 300-450 FTU, and > 1000 NTU depending on the study — and notes this is 'especially problematic' where rainfall events cause short sharp turbidity spikes. Because high-turbidity storm periods coincide with the runoff events that drive nitrate exceedance, this predicts a systematic, non-random measurement gap or bias in sensor-derived daily maxima precisely on the highest-risk days. Testable on the Iowa dataset directly: co-located turbidity exists at 61 of 85 sites, so one can check whether nitrate observations are preferentially missing, flagged, or biased on days exceeding these turbidity levels, and whether the daily-max label is disproportionately unreliable on those days.
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (threshold values cited from Huebsch et al. 2015 HESS, Kamari et al. 2018 J. Hydrol., Lee et al. 2015 Biogeosciences)
claims.effectSize: turbidity invalidity thresholds for UV-Vis nitrate: >80 FTU, >300-450 FTU, >1000 NTU across three cited studies

result.sourceQuality: Full open-access text obtained (CC BY) via Europe PMC XML (PMC7039225) after the MDPI HTML page returned HTTP 403 and doi.org redirected cross-host; abstract independently confirmed via OpenAlex and Europe PMC REST. Peer-reviewed, Sensors 20(3):859, doi:10.3390/s20030859, PMID 32041157. Underlying data are public at Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.3593769. CAVEAT ON RELEVANCE: this source addresses only part (b) of the research question — whether the TARGET STATISTIC (daily maximum from a high-frequency UV-Vis sensor) is trustworthy. It contains ZERO material on the other requested topics: no regression-then-threshold vs direct classification comparison, no peaks-over-threshold or extreme-value analysis, no regulatory MCL/TMDL averaging-period discussion, no machine-learning metrics, no spatial holdout, no AUC/PR-AUC numbers. No claim here carries a split protocol or a comparable virtual-sensor benchmark. FURTHER CAVEATS: (1) the study is in 4 TROPICAL Kenyan headwater catchments with background nitrate of 0.36-2.21 mg N/L — one to two orders of magnitude below the Iowa 10 mg/L threshold — so the authors' own explanation that inconsistency arises from measuring 'close to the detection limit' at 'low solute concentrations' may not transfer to Iowa's high-nitrate agricultural streams, where amplitudes would be a far smaller fraction of the reading; the paper explicitly notes 'patterns are more reproducible when the background concentration is higher.' (2) Iowa IWQIS sites use nitrate sensors of the same optical-absorbance family (s::can / Hach Nitratax class), so the accuracy-floor and turbidity-interference claims are plausibly transferable, but the paper does not test any US or agricultural site. (3) n=19 basin-family constraint is not engaged by this source at all; nothing here is a modelling method. NET ASSESSMENT for the project: this is weak-to-moderate evidence that daily MEDIAN or daily MEAN would be a more instrumentally stable target than daily MAXIMUM, but the effect sizes it documents (<=0.25 mg N/L typical diurnal amplitude, ±2%+0.2 mg N/L accuracy) are small relative to a 10 mg/L threshold, so switching targets is unlikely to move LOFO AUC 0.820 materially except for site-days sitting within ~0.4 mg/L of the threshold. The genuinely actionable, cheap test it suggests is the turbidity-interference check against the 61 Iowa sites with co-located turbidity.

claims.text: The 10 mg/L nitrate threshold used as the project's violation target is, in federal regulation, a drinking-water Maximum Contaminant Level expressed AS NITROGEN: the 40 CFR 141.62(b) table reads '(7) Nitrate | 10 (as Nitrogen)', '(8) Nitrite | 1 (as Nitrogen)', '(9) Total Nitrate and Nitrite | 10 (as Nitrogen)'. A sensor reporting nitrate as NO3 ion rather than NO3-N differs by a factor of 4.43, so the label definition is falsifiable by checking IWQIS/USGS parameter units against the CFR basis.
claims.effectSize: MCL = 10 mg/L as N; 4.43x conversion risk if units are NO3 ion

claims.text: Nitrate is one of the few Safe Drinking Water Act contaminants whose compliance is determined on a SINGLE sample rather than a running annual average: 40 CFR 141.23(i)(3) states 'Compliance with the maximum contaminant levels for nitrate and nitrate is determined based on one sample if the levels of these contaminants are below the MCLs.' This is regulatory support for an event-level (daily) binary framing rather than a smoothed or annual-average target, and is consistent with the project's finding that 3-day/7-day rolling smoothed targets performed worse.
claims.effectSize: n=1 sample compliance basis for nitrate, versus annual-average basis used for other inorganic contaminants in 141.23(i)(1)-(2)

claims.text: The operative regulatory exceedance statistic for nitrate is the MEAN OF TWO samples, not a single reading: 40 CFR 141.23(f)(2) requires that 'Where nitrate or nitrite sampling results indicate an exceedance of the maximum contaminant level, the system shall take a confirmation sample within 24 hours', and 141.23(i)(3) continues 'If the levels of nitrate and/or nitrite exceed the MCLs in the initial sample, a confirmation sample is required ... and compliance shall be determined based on the average of the initial and confirmation samples.' The regulatory analogue of the project's target is therefore closer to a 24-hour mean conditional on an initial exceedance than to a daily maximum, implying the current daily-max label is systematically MORE permissive of positives than the regulatory statistic.
claims.effectSize: averaging window = 24 hours, 2 samples; daily-max label is an upper bound on the regulatory 2-sample mean

claims.text: A second regulatory decision threshold exists at 50 percent of the MCL (5 mg/L as N), which triggers increased monitoring frequency: 40 CFR 141.23(d)(3) provides that a surface water system may reduce sampling 'to annually if all analytical results from four consecutive quarters are <50 percent of the MCL. A surface water system shall return to quarterly monitoring if any one sample is >=50 percent of the MCL', and 141.23(d)(2) imposes quarterly monitoring on groundwater systems 'for at least one year following any one sample in which the concentration is >=50 percent of the MCL.' This means a 5 mg/L classification target is a genuine, citable regulatory decision boundary and not an arbitrary alternative threshold, and it would have a substantially higher base rate than the current 0.263, plausibly improving the between-site signal-to-noise the project is short of.
claims.effectSize: regulatory trigger at 5 mg/L as N = 50% of MCL; drives quarterly vs annual monitoring

claims.text: The federal nitrate MCL applies to TREATED water at the entry point to the distribution system, not to ambient raw stream water: 40 CFR 141.23(a)(2) requires that 'Surface water systems shall take a minimum of one sample at every entry point to the distribution system after any application of treatment or in the distribution system at a point which is representative of each source after treatment.' Applying the 10 mg/L MCL to raw in-stream nitrate at an arbitrary map pin is therefore an analogy to a drinking-water standard, not a regulatory exceedance in the CFR sense, and any product framing must say so; the ambient-stream regulatory instruments (state water quality standards, 303(d) listing, TMDLs) are not defined in 40 CFR 141.
claims.effectSize: compliance point = post-treatment entry point; zero CFR 141 provisions apply to ambient streams

claims.text: 40 CFR 141.23 establishes a QUARTERLY (surface water) or ANNUAL (groundwater) nitrate sampling regime -- '(d)(1) Community and non-transient, non-community water systems served by groundwater systems shall monitor annually beginning January 1, 1993; systems served by surface water shall monitor quarterly beginning January 1, 1993' -- and contains NO provision addressing continuous, high-frequency, or daily sensor measurements. This is direct evidence of the sampling-frequency bias problem: the regulatory record against which any 'violation' rate would historically be judged is built from 4 grab samples per year, whereas the project's label is built from ~365 daily sensor maxima per year, so the project's 0.263 base rate is not comparable to any published regulatory exceedance rate.
claims.effectSize: 4 samples/year (surface water) or 1/year (groundwater) regulatory frequency vs ~365 daily maxima in the project label; ~90x frequency mismatch

result.sourceQuality: Authoritative primary regulatory source, fetched successfully and in full (Cornell LII mirror of 40 CFR 141.23, plus 40 CFR 141.62 for the MCL table). All quoted text verified verbatim against the fetched page. IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMITATION: this source answers ONLY the regulatory-definition half of the research question. It contains ZERO evidence on (a) regression-then-threshold vs direct binary classification, (b) peaks-over-threshold / extreme value theory for water quality, (c) cost-sensitive or calibrated classification, (d) evaluation metrics for spatially-held-out exceedance prediction, or (e) any published virtual-sensor AUC/PR-AUC numbers against which the project's LOFO 0.820 / 2.41x lift could be benchmarked. It also says nothing about TMDL or 303(d) stream practice -- 40 CFR 141 is the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations and governs treated water at public water systems only; ambient-stream exceedance methodology lives in 40 CFR 130/131 and state water quality standards, which must be sourced separately. No performance claims are present in this source, hence splitProtocol and nBasins are 'not-applicable' throughout rather than 'unknown'.

result.correction:
The claim stands as written; four precision fixes and three usage caveats.

PRECISION FIXES
(a) The server does NOT honor HTTP Range. There is no accept-ranges header, and a request with `-r 400000000-400002000` returned HTTP 200 with content-length 493183556 and the file from byte 0 (I got the header back, not the middle). Header verification works only because curl truncates a streamed full GET. Practical consequence: you cannot cheaply sample the middle of these files — plan on streaming and filtering (`curl ... | awk`) or a full 493 MB download.
(b) "1 row per NHDPlusV2 COMID" is right but not exactly — the file also carries a small number of negative synthetic reach ids (e.g. -92000151, -91074001) that are not NHDPlusV2 COMIDs. 18 of the first 167,893 rows. Filter comid > 0 before joining.
(c) The record lists 8 files, not 7: the seven data files plus an FGDC XML metadata file (listed with size 0 in JSON but fetchable). The XML is where the units live and should be read before deriving anything.
(d) Item-level `rights` is null. USGS data releases are public domain / CC0 by agency policy, but the release itself does not state a license string.

USAGE CAVEATS FOR THIS PROJECT
(1) The concentration derivation is NOT unit-safe as stated. al_tn is a long-term mean annual load and wbm_meanq is a mean flow whose units (kg/yr and ft3/s, most likely) are defined only in the FGDC XML — do not compute al_tn/(annual volume) until you have read the XML. Get the units right or the derived "concentration" will be off by a constant factor per reach, which is harmless for a tree split but not for interpretation.
(2) CIRCULARITY RISK, and it is the real one. SPARROW is a calibrated model, not an observation. Robertson & Saad (2019, SIR 2019-5114) calibrated the Midwest TN model against monitored load estimates at stream sites — and Iowa's monitoring network is exactly where this project's ~85 sites live. If any of the 85 sites (or their reaches) were SPARROW calibration sites, then al_tn/il_tn at those reaches encodes the observed nitrate level at the site, and a LOFO fold that holds out a basin family will still see a feature that was fit to that family's own loads. That is leakage that LOFO does not catch, because the leak is baked into the covariate rather than into the split. Before using this, pull the calibration-site list from SIR 2019-5114 and check overlap with the 85 sites; if there is overlap, report both "with SPARROW" and "with SPARROW, calibration-overlapping families dropped".
(3) It is a static 2012 base-year mean-annual product, so it can only move the between-site term. That is the correct place to aim — the project's own diagnostic (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24, seven failed temporal ablations, wins only from static geography) says the deficit is between-site static information. il_tn/IncAreaKm2 (incremental TN yield), the fert/man/nfix source shares, and DEL_FRAC are per-reach static scalars that describe exactly the "how loaded is this basin" quantity the model is missing, and they can be aggregated over an arbitrary NLDI-delineated basin at prediction time with no local history and no gauge — so it IS compatible with the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target. But note that with n=19 independent basin families you are adding correlated static columns to a between-site regression with ~19 effective units; expect the honest test to be whether between_rate_r2 moves at all under LOFO, and expect wide error bars on any gain. Add a small number of SPARROW-derived columns (yield, dominant source share, DEL_FRAC), not all 40.

claims.text: Iowa's 10 mg/L nitrate-nitrogen criterion is a DESIGNATED-USE-SPECIFIC criterion applying ONLY to Class C waters ('source of a water supply'); Iowa has NO nitrate criterion for any aquatic-life class. The Table 6 criteria matrix lists 'nitrate-nitrogen (mg/L)' as 'none' for Class A1/A2/A3 (swimmable), BWW1, BWW2 & BWW3, BCW1, BCW2, BLW and Class HH, with the single value '10' under 'Class C: source of a water supply'. Narrative: 'The Iowa Water Quality Standards identify this 10 mg/L MCL as the water quality criterion to protect surface waters used as a source of a municipal water supply. At concentrations seen in surface waters, nitrate is not believed to be toxic to aquatic life; thus, there are no water quality criteria in the Iowa Water Quality Standards that apply to aquatic life uses.' IMPLICATION FOR THE ARBITRARY-MAP-PIN PRODUCT: a 'violation' prediction at an arbitrary Iowa pin has NO regulatory meaning unless that segment is Class C designated; elsewhere the label is merely a physically-defined threshold exceedance, and the product must say so rather than implying a regulatory exceedance.
claims.effectSize: 10 mg/L as N; applies to exactly 1 of 9 designated-use classes in Table 6; nitrate criterion = 'none' for all 6 aquatic-life classes

claims.text: The regulatory unit of nitrate exceedance in Iowa is NOT a single day and NOT a single sample — it is the FRACTION of samples exceeding 10 mg/L over a THREE-YEAR assessment period, tested for significance against a 10% rule at >90% confidence. Verbatim: 'Data for inorganics (i.e., nitrate) in the raw water source: If, over the three-year assessment period, significantly more than 10% of the samples violate Iowa's Class C criterion for nitrate for drinking water use (i.e., the maximum contaminant level (MCL)), impairment of the Class C uses will be identified. The methodology of Lin et al. (2000) (Table 11) will be used to determine whether significantly more than 10% of the samples exceed the MCL.' Contrast the co-located atrazine rule, which DOES use an averaging period: 'moving annual average values for the three-year assessment period will be compared to the respective Class C criterion' — Iowa deliberately uses frequency-of-exceedance for nitrate and a moving annual average for atrazine. DIRECT RELEVANCE TO THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the regulatorily meaningful quantity is a site's long-run exceedance RATE, precisely the between-site term the project predicts worst (between_rate_r2 0.24 vs macro_auc 0.90). A model that is 'a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker' is optimized for the wrong functional of the distribution relative to how the regulator defines the problem.
claims.effectSize: 3-year assessment window; 10%-of-samples threshold; >90% confidence level; nitrate uses frequency-of-exceedance while atrazine uses a moving annual average

claims.text: Iowa's nitrate assessment outcome is THREE-CLASS, not binary. Table 10, for 'Waterbodies designated for use as a source of potable water (=raw water source)' with 'Nitrate, chloride, fluoride data', defines: FULLY SUPPORTED = '<10% of the samples violate the nitrate, chloride, and fluoride maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) (90% CL)'; PARTIALLY SUPPORTED = '>10% to <25% of the samples violate the MCL(s) (90% CL)'; NOT SUPPORTED = '>25% of the samples exceed the MCL(s)'. Minimum sample sizes apply: Table 10 requires 'A minimum of 10 samples is needed' for conventional-parameter assessments and 'A minimum of 10 samples is needed for Fully Supported' for toxic parameters. IMPLICATION: the decision-relevant output is a site-level exceedance-RATE estimate binned at the 10% and 25% cut points. This suggests evaluating the model on whether it places an unseen basin in the correct <10% / 10-25% / >25% bin — a regulator-aligned test of the between-site term that is feasible at n=19 independent basin families, because it needs 19 rate estimates rather than 160k row-level predictions.
claims.effectSize: cut points at 10% and 25% of samples exceeding; minimum n=10 samples for an assessment

claims.text: Iowa DNR's binomial small-sample correction (Lin et al. 2000, as tabulated by NDEQ 2006 in Table 11) specifies exact exceedance counts required to declare impairment at >90% confidence: n=10 requires 3 exceedances (CL 0.930); n=11 requires 3 (0.910); n=12 requires 4 (0.974); n=19 requires 5 (0.965); n=25 requires 5 (0.902); n=40 requires 7 (0.900); n=50 requires 9 (0.942); n=75 requires 12 (0.931); n=100 requires 15 (0.927). The required exceedance FRACTION is far above 10% at small n (3/10 = 30%, 5/25 = 20%) and converges toward 15% only at n=100. OPERATIONAL VALUE: an agency-sanctioned uncertainty rule that can be applied directly to the project's per-site sensor records and to model-predicted exceedance rates. It quantifies how many observations a site needs before its exceedance rate is even estimable — relevant because the project's sites vary greatly in record length, and short-record sites carry rate estimates the regulator itself would refuse to act on.

claims.text: Iowa DNR has an EXPLICIT precedent for reducing continuous (sub-daily) sensor data to a DAILY BINARY violation flag and then applying the 10% rule over days — but only for dissolved oxygen, and with replication requirements the project's nitrate target does not impose. TWO IMPLICATIONS: (1) the project's 'daily statistic -> binary day flag' construction matches the agency's own reduction of continuous sensor data, supporting the target's construction; (2) the agency requires the >10%-of-days condition to recur in TWO DIFFERENT YEARS within five years before listing, explicitly guarding against single-year weather anomalies — a robustness criterion the per-day label does not encode, and one reinforced by the document's rationale for three-year windows, which 'helps address the problem of weather-related year-to-year fluctuations in water quality.'

CITATION: "Spatially Referenced Models of Streamflow and Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Suspended-Sediment Loads in Streams of the Midwestern United States," By Dale M. Robertson and David A. Saad, USGS SIR 2019-5114. Author/report/DOI attribution in the claim is exact.

TABLE 5 (caption: "Summary of calibration results for the 2012 Midwest SPARROW total nitrogen model") — every quoted number matches verbatim:
- Conditioned RMSE, natural log units: 0.487
- Conditioned RMSE, percentage in real space: 51.8
- Unconditioned RMSE, natural log units: 0.555
- Unconditioned RMSE, percentage in real space: 60.0
- Mean exponentiated weighted error: 1.129
- R2: 0.950
- Yield R2: 0.913
- Number of sites: 1,334
Body text (p. 29) corroborates: "The model explained 95 percent of the variance in TN loads and 91 percent of the variances in yields... conditioned RMSE was 0.487 and... unconditioned RMSE was 0.555 (both in natural logarithmic units). These values equate to an RMSE of 51.8 percent for conditioned predictions and an RMSE of 60.0 percent for unconditioned predictions in real (kilograms per year) space."

TARGET VARIABLE: confirmed "long-term mean-annual TN loads," detrended to the 2012 base year; water-quality record within 3 years of 2012, min 3 yr record, >=24 samples, >=3 samples per season, paired streamgage within 40 km.

SPLIT PROTOCOL — the load-bearing part of the claim, CONFIRMED: grep of the full text for "cross-valid", "holdout", "hold-out", "independent test", "validation dataset", "withheld", "jackknife", "leave-one", "split sample", "out-of-sample" returns ZERO hits. The only "bootstrap" hit (p.~11) is parametric bootstrap for load-estimation uncertainty at the calibration sites, not model validation. All reported fit statistics are in-sample calibration fit on the same 1,334 sites used to estimate the 17 coefficients. There is no spatial holdout of any kind.

DEFINITIONS confirming the conditioned/unconditioned distinction the claim relies on (Table 5 footnotes b and d): conditioned RMSE resets predicted accumulated loads to MEASURED loads at upstream calibration sites; unconditioned does not. So the claim is right that unconditioned (0.555 / 60.0%) is the closer analogue to true prediction, and right that even that is still in-sample. Footnote c gives the real-space conversion: 100 x (exp[RMSE^2]-1)^0.5 — i.e. 60.0% is a coefficient of variation, not a percent bias.

ADDITIONAL EVIDENCE STRENGTHENING THE CLAIM (report's own limitations, p. 29): "the model did not predict the loads and yields as well for sites with relatively small loads. The unconditioned RMSE was 0.65 for TN loads less than 14 logarithmic units compared to 0.39 for loads greater than 14 logarithmic units." Also: residuals have significant regional structure (Moran's I = 0.199, p = 0.0005) with systematic over/underprediction in the western study area — i.e. the model has exactly the between-site level bias that is our project's central problem, even in-sample.

TWO FACTUAL ERRORS IN THE CLAIM (detail only, do not change the conclusion):
1. Site-count provenance is garbled. Table 1 gives, for TN: 1,344 sites CONSIDERED and 1,335 used in the final SPARROW model, out of 93,994 original water-quality sites. The 1,346 figure in the claim is the TOTAL PHOSPHORUS "considered" count, not TN. (The report is itself internally inconsistent by one site: Table 1 says 1,335 final TN sites, Table 5 and p. 28 text say 1,334.)
2. "Factor-of-1.6 typical error" is a loose reading. 60.0% is a real-space CV derived from exp(RMSE^2); the one-sigma multiplicative error implied by 0.555 log units is exp(0.555) = 1.74x, not 1.6x.

ONE FRAMING OVERSTATEMENT: the claim says R2 0.950 "is on accumulated load, a quantity dominated by drainage area." True and standard, but the report also publishes Yield R2 = 0.913, which is area-normalized and still high, so area dominance alone does not explain the number away. The decisive objection is the absence of any holdout, not the area effect.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET — the claim's non-comparability conclusion holds for a reason stronger than it states: SPARROW's target is a LONG-TERM MEAN-ANNUAL LOAD (kg/yr) at a reach, a single number per site. Our target is a DAILY binary exceedance of 10 mg/L concentration. These differ in temporal resolution (decadal mean vs daily), in units (mass flux vs concentration), and in the discharge dependence (SPARROW load requires a modeled streamflow; our product has no gauge). No mapping exists between AUC 0.820 / R2 0.328 on daily site-days and R2 0.950 on log mean-annual load, under ANY split protocol. Note however that SPARROW is a genuinely ungauged-capable paradigm — it predicts on every NHDPlus reach in the network, so it is architecturally the right shape for an arbitrary map pin; it is only the reported statistics that are in-sample.

HIGHLY ACTIONABLE SIDE FINDING for the parent agent: the Midwest 2012 SPARROW TN model includes "Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)" as a calibrated land-to-water delivery variable, coefficient 0.101 (90% CI 0.064-0.139), SE 0.023, p<0.0001, t=4.5, VIF 2.3, over 1,334 Midwest sites. This is exactly the tile-drainage covariate our project lists as missing with "NO data source identified," it is significant across the Midwest including all of Iowa, and the underlying tile-drainage layer is a public USGS/SPARROW model input. This is a concrete lead worth a separate acquisition task. Other calibrated delivery terms: ln(runoff) 0.673 (t=18.5, the strongest), detrended air temperature -0.048, ln(soil clay %) 0.292, CRP/farm-acre ratio -4.758, ln(% no-till) 0.124.

N-CONSTRAINT NOTE: n=1,334 calibration sites vs our 19 independent basin families. SPARROW's coefficient estimates are a ~70x larger spatial sample, so its per-coefficient standard errors are not achievable by refitting anything comparable on our data. The usable transfer is to INGEST SPARROW's already-fitted covariates and, potentially, its per-reach predicted TN yield as a static between-site feature — not to reproduce its calibration.

The two numbers are not on the same axis in any sense — target, units, and time scale all differ — so no rescaling of SPARROW's RMSE makes it a benchmark for LOFO AUC 0.820. result.correction:
The claim is directionally right and its primary-source quotations are accurate, but three things need correcting before it is acted on.

(a) NUMBER: it is 1,335 TN sites in the final model (1,344 considered), not 1,334. Report Table 1, p.13.

(b) MECHANISM IS OVERSTATED. "SPARROW output at that reach partly encodes that site's own observed level" is not how the released product works. Load-substitution ("conditioning") is applied during calibration and to the calibration-RMSE, not to the distributed reach predictions; the public data release ships "simulated" = unconditioned loads. The actual leakage pathway is therefore diffuse: one Iowa site is one of 1,335 calibration targets influencing a ~10-20 parameter nonlinear regression fit over the whole Mississippi/Great Lakes/Red River domain, and it is further downweighted by the nested-share weighting scheme the report describes (p.9). That is closer to 1/1335 leverage on global coefficients than to memorization of a reach's level. Additional criteria the claim omits also shrink the contaminated set: the paired gauge must include 2012 with no gaps, be within 40 km, have a watershed-area ratio 0.75-1.33, and be on the same stream if the WQ basin exceeds 260 km2.

(c) TARGET MISMATCH. SPARROW TN is long-term (2000-14) MEAN-ANNUAL TOTAL NITROGEN LOAD, detrended to a 2012 base year. Our target is daily-max NITRATE CONCENTRATION exceedance of 10 mg/L. Even a fully contaminated reach leaks only a slow, basin-average level signal, not the daily label. That said, the between-site absolute-level term is precisely this project's stated deficit, so the leak, if present, would land exactly where it would most flatter a LOFO number.

NET RECOMMENDATION, revised: keep the audit, drop the alarm level. Before reporting any LOFO gain from a SPARROW-derived feature, join our ~85 sites (and the 19 families) against the SIR 2019-5069 / P93QMXC9 calibration-site table by NHDPlus comid or lat/lon, and report how many FAMILIES (not sites) contain at least one TN calibration site. At n=19 folds, even 3-4 contaminated families is worth a caveat, which is why the check is worth doing despite the diffuse mechanism. Report the gain with and without those families. The claim's inference that IWQIS sensors are cleaner is sound in its logic — a post-2015-only record cannot satisfy "period of record within 3 years of 2012" plus 24 samples — but note IA DNR is a listed provider and many IWQIS sensors sit at USGS gauges, so this must be checked per site rather than assumed by network.

The claim is correct as stated. Six operational caveats that must accompany its use, none of which refute it:

(a) ATTRIBUTION OF THE COEFFICIENT. The coefficient 0.101 and its statistics are NOT in the cited ScienceBase item (5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3); they are in Table 5 of the companion report, Robertson & Saad 2019, USGS SIR 2019-5114, doi:10.3133/sir20195114. The ScienceBase item correctly holds the data file with the tile columns. Cite both.

(b) USE THE RAW COLUMN, NOT THE LOG COLUMN. In the file, ltiles13_perc2 = ln(tiles13_perc2) but zeros are mapped to 0.0, which collides with ln(1%) = 0. Verified: the only ltiles value where tiles==0 is exactly 0.0. Ingest tiles13_perc2 and do your own transform.

(c) THE VALUES ARE INCREMENTAL-CATCHMENT, NOT BASIN-ACCUMULATED. tiles13_perc2 is percent of the local NHDPlusV2 catchment. To get a basin-level predictor for an NLDI-delineated pin you must area-weight over all upstream comids yourself. This is a plus for this project — it means the tile layer can be aggregated into the existing distance-bucket feature scheme exactly like CDL, at 2.7 km2 resolution.

(d) THE TILE LAYER IS MODELED, NOT INVENTORIED. Nakagaki & Wieczorek (2016) is a geospatial ESTIMATE of likely-tiled extent from land cover, soils and slope, not a tile inventory; ND/SD are permit polygons, a different and non-comparable construction. Errors are spatially structured, which for a between-site predictor is the worst kind. Treat it as a strong proxy, not ground truth.

(e) THE CITED EFFECT SIZE DOES NOT PREDICT YOUR GAIN, AND IS NOT COMPARABLE TO YOUR LOFO 0.820. It is an in-sample calibration coefficient from a mass-balance NLLS model of LONG-TERM MEAN-ANNUAL TN LOAD (kg/yr) at 1,334 gauged sites, with a runoff term (coefficient 0.673, t=18.5) carrying most of the delivery signal. Your target is daily-max nitrate CONCENTRATION exceedance at ungauged pins. t=4.5 with VIF 2.3 establishes that tile percentage carries independent between-catchment information about nitrogen delivery in exactly this region; it establishes nothing about incremental PR-AUC in an XGBoost daily classifier. Also note the same variable enters the companion TP model with a NEGATIVE coefficient (-0.091, 90% CI [-0.156,-0.026], p=0.0221, t=-2.3), which shows the term is doing pathway-partitioning work, not acting as a universal "more tile = more nutrient" flag.

(f) n=19 CONSTRAINT — this one actually survives it, better than most. The evidence base is 1,334 basins, vastly more than 19, so by the project's own rule it would normally be flagged as infeasible. But the flag does not bite here, because what is being imported is a DATASET COLUMN, not a fitted method. You are not estimating a tile coefficient from 1,334 basins and hoping it transfers; you are adding one static per-basin covariate and letting your own 19-family LOFO CV decide whether it earns its place. One additional static feature against 19 effective independent units is the cheapest possible test of the between-site hypothesis. Expect it to help the between-site term (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24) or not at all; it can supply no temporal signal, exactly as the claim concedes.

=== WHAT VERIFIED EXACTLY (primary source read in full) ===
Source confirmed: Robertson, D.M., and Saad, D.A., 2019, "Spatially Referenced Models of Streamflow and Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Suspended-Sediment Loads in Streams of the Midwestern United States," USGS SIR 2019-5114, doi:10.3133/sir20195114. Site-selection criteria — VERBATIM: water-quality site needed "a minimum record length of 3 years, have at least 24 samples, and have at least 3 samples in each of the four 3-month seasons"; "The water-quality period of record also had to be within 3 years of the 2012 base year"; streamgage needed "a minimum record length of 10 years of daily mean values (with no data gaps)" and the record "had to include 2012."

4. Window 1999-10-01 to 2014-09-30 — CONFIRMED twice: report text ("from October 1, 1999, to September 30, 2014") and the data release metadata (Start Date 1999-10-01, End Date 2014-09-30).

5. n=1,334 TN calibration sites — EXACT. Table 5: "Number of sites 1,334"; text: "the model was calibrated with TN loads from 1,334 monitoring sites." (Table 1 separately reports 1,346 TN sites *considered*; the claim correctly used the final figure.)

=== WHY THE CONCLUSION IS REFUTED ===
A. The distributed output is UNCONDITIONED, and the report defines the distinction itself. SIR 2019-5114 p.9: "the model-simulated load at each upstream calibration site is replaced with its measured load... The resulting downstream load that is simulated using the upstream measured load is referred to as the 'conditioned' predicted load used in model calibration, whereas the load exclusively predicted by the model is referred to as the 'unconditioned' predicted load or simply the 'simulated load.'" Conditioning exists ONLY inside calibration.

B. I checked what is actually published. Data release: Saad & Robertson, 2020, doi:10.5066/P93QMXC9 (ScienceBase item 5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3), titled "...and SIMULATED streamflow, nutrient and suspended-sediment loads." Eight files; I range-fetched the header of mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt (493 MB). Full column set: comid, IncAreaKm2, CumAreaKm2, wbm_meanq, al_tn + 7 source-specific al_tn_* (accumulated load), alse_* (standard errors), il_tn + il_tn_* (incremental load), DEL_FRAC, SE_DEL_FRAC, res_decay, se_res_decay. There is NO station ID, NO observed/measured load, NO residual, and NO conditioned prediction anywhere in the file. Every reach value is a deterministic function of that catchment's attributes and the ~20 GLOBAL coefficients — computed identically at calibrated and uncalibrated reaches. There is no site-specific anchor to leak.

C. Magnitude. A single Iowa site's own observations influence the shipped number at its own reach only via its ~1/1,334 share of a globally shared coefficient vector, spread across the entire Mississippi/Great Lakes/Red River domain. That is not "SPARROW output at that reach partly encodes that site's own observed level" in any sense that biases a LOFO evaluation.

D. Target mismatch further attenuates it. SPARROW TN is long-term MEAN-ANNUAL TOTAL NITROGEN LOAD in kg/yr, detrended to 2012 — not daily nitrate concentration. The information path (site's 2009-2014 TN grab samples -> 1/1334 of a global coefficient -> mean-annual TN load at a comid -> our XGBoost's estimate of that site's violation rate) is far too attenuated to produce the optimistic bias asserted.

E. The claim's prescribed remedy is also not executable as written. It says to check overlap "site-by-site against the SPARROW calibration site list" — that list is NOT in the P93QMXC9 data release (no station field in any of the 8 files). Site-level loads and station lists live in the companion Saad, D.A., Schwarz, G.E., Argue, D.M., Anning, D.W., Ator, S.W., Hoos, A.B., Preston, S.D., Robertson, D.M., and Wise, D., 2019, SIR 2019-5069, doi:10.3133/sir20195069.

=== RULE-1 PROTOCOL FLAG (matters more than the leakage worry) ===
SPARROW TN reports R2 0.950 and Yield R2 0.913 — these are IN-SAMPLE calibration fits over 1,334 sites, NOT spatially held out. They are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and must never be quoted as evidence of ungauged-reach skill. The honest transfer-relevant number the report gives is unconditioned RMSE = 0.555 natural-log units = 60.0 percent in real space for TN (vs conditioned 0.487 / 51.8 percent) — and even that is computed at calibration sites, so it is still not a true held-out figure. The report explicitly states unconditioned RMSE "provides the best representation of the predictive skill of a calibrated SPARROW model."

=== TRANSFERABILITY / DEPLOYMENT ASSESSMENT ===
SPARROW TN is a legitimate and well-targeted candidate static between-site feature, and this claim would wrongly discourage it. It is keyed by NHDPlusV2 comid (the project already stores comid per basin), covers the whole Mississippi/Great Lakes/Red River domain including every multi-state portion of Iowa basins, requires no local history and no gauge at the target, and supplies exactly the absolute-level between-site information the project's diagnosis says it lacks (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). It is free, no authentication, public domain, bulk HTTP download. Caveat under the n=19-families constraint: it adds 1-2 static columns, not a method needing hundreds of basins to fit, so n=19 is not a barrier — but with only 19 independent units, a single strong static covariate can also be overfit at the fold level, so it should be added as one or two features (e.g. delivered TN yield = al_tn/CumAreaKm2) and evaluated under the existing LOFO, not as a large block.

=== HIGH-VALUE SIDE FINDING (directly answers an open project gap) ===
The project states tile drainage density is "the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet." SIR 2019-5114 uses it as a SIGNIFICANT land-to-water delivery variable in the TN model: "Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)", coefficient 0.101 (90% CI 0.064-0.139), p<0.0001, t=4.5, variable name LTILES13_PERC2. Source, fully operational: Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, "Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012," USGS data release, doi:10.5066/F7W37TDP (ScienceBase 55f6e42ae4b0477df11bff10). 30-meter raster; single time slice (2012, from the 2012 Census of Agriculture + NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland + STATSGO2 drainage class); per-cell value = estimated tile-drained area in square meters; covers SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY — which encompasses ALL upstream multi-state portions of Iowa basins; free bulk download, no authentication, USGS public domain. Note the metadata's Iowa-specific caveat: reported tile-drained area exceeded cropland on poorly drained soils, so the excess was assigned to cropland on moderately drained soils — Iowa is the one state given special treatment, so the product is smoothed from state-level totals and carries no within-state independent signal beyond the crop/soil mask. That is a real limitation: it may correlate strongly with CDL crop fractions already in the feature set. A catchment-attributed version already joined to NHDPlusV2 comid exists via Wieczorek and others, 2019 (USGS Select Attributes for NHDPlus v2.1 Reach Catchments, doi:10.5066/F7765D7V), which would avoid re-doing the raster aggregation.

=== WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY ===
I did not enumerate how many of the project's ~85 Iowa sites appear on the TN calibration list (would require pulling SIR 2019-5069's site tables). Given finding B, that check is no longer necessary to justify using SPARROW as a feature. Web search budget for this session was exhausted, so I could not survey independent literature on SPARROW-as-covariate; all findings above come from the primary source and the published data files themselves, which is the stronger evidence for this particular question.

result.correction:
The claim is correct as stated. Four refinements, none fatal, plus one interpretive overreach to guard against.

(a) VINTAGE IS 2012, NOT 2013. The claim says "circa-2013 snapshot." The underlying Nakagaki & Wieczorek layer is the 2012 vintage, built from the 2012 Census of Agriculture state-level tile acreage + NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland + STATSGO2 drainage class. The "13" in TILES13_PERC2 is not the data year. ND/SD permit polygons are 2016 (ND) and 2012 (SD). Say "circa-2012."

(b) THE BOUNDING BOX IS NOT EVIDENCE OF TILE COVERAGE. The -114.85/-72.51, 27.66/50.15 box and the 30 place tags describe the SPARROW model domain, not the tile layer's footprint. The tile layer covers 12 states only: SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY (plus ND/SD permit polygons). The operative conclusion still holds — all of Iowa and every upstream state Iowa basins reach are inside those 12 — but the claim reaches the right answer via the wrong evidence.

(c) THE FIELD IS INCREMENTAL, NOT ACCUMULATED. Appendix 2 defines it as "percent of catchment" — the local NHDPlusV2 catchment (mean 2.7 km2), not upstream-accumulated. To get a basin-level tile fraction the project must area-weight tiles13_perc2 across all catchments in the delineated basin itself. Do NOT feed ltiles13_perc2 (a log of a 2.7 km2 local value) directly as a basin feature. Also note the access route is clumsy: extracting 2 columns requires streaming a 740 MB text file. The Wieczorek et al. (2019) "Select Attributes for NHDPlus Version 2.1 Reach Catchments" series publishes NHDPlus attributes in CAT/ACC/TOT form (pre-accumulated upstream), which would be the better route if a tile-drainage member of that series exists — I could not confirm one within budget (my ScienceBase keyword search returned 0 hits, likely a query-syntax issue, not proof of absence). Worth 10 minutes to check before committing to the 740 MB parse.

(d) EFFECT SIZE IS MODEST — AND CONTRADICTS THE PROJECT'S PRIOR. In a ln-ln land-to-water term, coefficient 0.101 means doubling tile percentage raises TN delivery by only 7.3% (2^0.101 = 1.0725); a 10x increase gives +26%. Compare the other land-to-water terms in the same Table 5: Ln(runoff) 0.673, Ln(soil clay) 0.292, Ln(no-till) 0.124, tile 0.101. Tile drains are the WEAKEST significant land-to-water delivery term in SPARROW's own TN fit. The project's stated prior that "tile drainage density is the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa" is NOT supported by this model — runoff dominates by ~7x in log-space elasticity. Expect a real but small between-site contribution, not a fix for the between_r2 0.21 problem. (Note also Table 7: the TP model gives tile drains a NEGATIVE coefficient, -0.091, 90% CI [-0.156, -0.026] — hydrologically sensible, tiles bypass overland P transport. Sign is nutrient-specific; only the TN sign is relevant here.)

(e) n=19 CONSTRAINT. SPARROW's 0.101 rests on 1,334 calibration sites; that is 70x this project's 19 independent basin families. The coefficient's significance says nothing about whether XGBoost can learn a tile effect from 19 effective units. Worse, tile drainage in Iowa is strongly spatially structured (Des Moines Lobe vs driftless/loess regions), so it will correlate with lat/lon — already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features. Marginal gain over existing geography may be near zero even though the underlying physics is real. Test it as a single scalar basin-mean tile fraction under LOFO, and pre-register that a <0.01 PR-AUC gain is a null. Do not add both linear and log forms and all three distance buckets — that is 6 spatially-smooth columns against 19 units.

(f) ADJACENT LEAKAGE HAZARD NOT IN THE CLAIM. Using the tile INPUT layer is clean. Using the SPARROW OUTPUT files (mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt predicted loads) as features would NOT be — SPARROW was calibrated on 1,334 monitoring sites that plausibly include this project's Iowa sensor sites, so predicted TN load at a target comid is partly a function of observed nitrate at that same location. That would leak under LOFO and inflate the between-site term specifically. Take the input column; leave the output files alone.

(g) DOMAIN MISMATCH TO STATE PLAINLY. SPARROW models long-term MEAN-ANNUAL TN LOAD in log space; this project predicts DAILY-MAX CONCENTRATION exceedance of 10 mg/L. The 0.101 coefficient is in-sample with no holdout, and the R2 0.950 is on loads (dominated by basin area and flow) and is not comparable to anything in this project. The coefficient is legitimate evidence that tile extent carries between-catchment TN information; it is not evidence about daily exceedance skill at an ungauged pin.

The claim is substantively correct and unusually well-verified; I am not refuting it. Five corrections/additions, one of which is a serious hazard the claim omits.

1. LEAKAGE HAZARD — the most important omission. The claim says "~85 input columns per COMID" and frames the file as "directly ingestible by an ML model." The actual 89 columns are NOT all landscape drivers. The file also contains flux_530_final, flux_154_final, flux_600_final, flux_665_final, can_tn_load, can_tp_load, can_ssc_load, can_q_load, mean_dflow_predpd, wbm_rhload, iresload, and four *_inv_resid2_hat weighting columns. The flux_*_final columns are monitoring-derived calibration load estimates (USGS parameter codes: 600 = total nitrogen, 665 = total phosphorus, 530 = suspended sediment), and SPARROW was calibrated on Midwest monitoring stations that plausibly coincide with this project's own sensor sites. Ingesting "all ~85 columns" would leak observed nitrogen load into the features and inflate LOFO scores. Use an explicit whitelist of source/landscape columns only — precisely the subset the claim enumerates. The claim's own column list is safe; the "~85 columns" framing is not.

2. Column count is 89, not ~85. And `huc12` is lowercase (`HUC8` and `STATE` are uppercase as claimed) — a literal HUC12 lookup will KeyError.

3. "Substituted or supplemented" for the 2017-ending N surplus overstates the substitution half. These are 2012 single-year static snapshots with zero temporal dimension. They cannot replace a time-varying surplus; they can only inform the between-site term. This matters because the project already has a directly analogous negative result: broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time scored -0.166. Recommend ADD as static between-site features, never SUBSTITUTE into the existing time-varying slot, or that failure is likely to reproduce.

4. n=19 CONSTRAINT — unaddressed by the claim and binding here. The project's diagnosis is that essentially all headroom is in the between-site term, which has ~19 effective independent units. Adding ~20 new static per-basin predictors to a 19-unit between-site regression is a p>n overfitting setup; LOFO will not reliably distinguish real transfer from noise. Recommend a hand-picked subset of 3-5 area-weighted aggregates (e.g. tiles13_perc2, ManN2012+fert_sw_N_kg combined, ldrainden, CAT_STCLAY) rather than the full block, with the count fixed a priori rather than selected on LOFO score.

5. The claim UNDERSELLS on tile drainage. It says "beyond tile drains," but tiles13_perc2 / ltiles13_perc2 are in this very file at 0.00% missing — directly addressing the project's stated gap that tile drainage density is the dominant Iowa hydrologic control with "NO data source identified yet." Caveat: in Iowa 58.7% of catchments are zero with median 0 and p90 60.9%, a strongly bimodal pattern consistent with real tiling concentrated in the Des Moines Lobe rather than with missingness. It needs area-weighted aggregation to basin scale to be informative; per-catchment it looks sparse.

6. Minor: the same SIR passage the claim quotes describes the catchments as "about 2 km2" while the abstract says a 2.7 km2 mean — a small internal inconsistency in the source, not in the claim.

result.correction:
Claim is substantially correct; four detail corrections plus two omissions.

(a) COLUMN COUNT: 89 columns, not "~85". Key column casing is `ComID`, not `COMID`; HUC12 is lowercase `huc12` and is BLANK for some rows (18 of first 85), so it is not complete.

(b) LEAKAGE TRAP THE CLAIM OMITS -- the most important correction. The input file also contains SPARROW CALIBRATION OBSERVATIONS, not just drivers: flux_600_final (TN load; only 522 nonzero of 484,592 rows), flux_665_final (529), flux_530_final (388), flux_154_final (65), can_tn_load (10), mean_dflow_predpd (793). These are measured loads at monitoring stations. They are structurally absent at an arbitrary ungauged map pin, and present only at the gauged subset. Ingesting all 89 columns naively would leak observed nitrogen load into training and produce an inflated LOFO number. Whitelist the driver columns explicitly.

(c) `aridity` IS USELESS IN IOWA: zero for 26,805 of 26,885 Iowa rows (populated only in the arid western part of the model domain). The claim lists it as a usable feature; drop it.

(d) LOG COLUMNS CARRY SENTINEL FLOORS: ldrainden = -11.51292546 = log(1e-5) where the underlying value is zero. Same pattern for other l-prefixed columns. A tree model will read these as extreme real values unless remapped. Use the untransformed column plus an explicit is-zero indicator.

(e) SIR CAVEAT IS TRUNCATED. The claim quotes the county-average caveat but omits the following sentence, which matters as much for this project: "most of the sites used to calibrate the SPARROW models were located on medium to large streams and may not represent the smallest streams in the Midwest." Iowa sensor basins skew small.

(f) n=19 CONSTRAINT NOT ADDRESSED BY THE CLAIM. These are per-catchment values, but once aggregated to basin means over a delineated NLDI basin they collapse to ~19 effective independent units under the leak-safe CV. Adding ~20 new static columns against 19 independent units is near-saturated and is a serious overfitting risk -- use aggressive selection (3-5 columns max: tiles13_perc2, ManN2012+fert_sw_N_kg summed, CAT_STCLAY, ldrainden) rather than dumping the block. Note also this is a 2012 STATIC snapshot, the same broadcast-a-fixed-year pattern that already failed here (2017 N-surplus, lofo -0.166). The distinction that may rescue it is that a genuinely time-invariant covariate introduces no spurious temporal step and loads purely on the between-site term where the headroom is -- but that is an untested hypothesis, not an established result. Treat expected gain as unproven.

(g) FRAMING: the claim's "Beyond tile drains" undersells the file. tiles13_perc2/ltiles13_perc2 ARE in it and ARE populated for Iowa, directly addressing a gap the project lists as having no identified data source. That is arguably the single most valuable column here.
