result.correction:
The claim is substantively accurate and quotes the primary source almost verbatim; keep it, with five precise fixes.

1. ATTRIBUTION FIX (the only real error). The sentence "The uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model" is NOT in SIR 2019-5114 — the word "uncertainty" appears exactly once in the report, inside a reference title. Do not attribute it to the report. Replace it with the report's actual wording: "it is difficult to know how well the model predicted loads in drainages smaller than this... caution should be taken when interpreting the finest scale model results (for example, predictions for the individual incremental drainages of the reaches)." The quoted sentence appears to be USGS data-release/DSS boilerplate; I could not retrieve the FGDC XML for data release https://doi.org/10.5066/P93QMXC9 to confirm, so cite it as unverified or drop it.

2. THE 5 PERCENT / 31 km2 FIGURE IS TP-ONLY, AND OUR TARGET IS NITRATE. The report gives this calibration-size statistic only for the TP model. It gives no equivalent number for the TN model, whose calibration n (1,334) is close to TP's, so a similar small-basin gap is plausible but is NOT documented. Since our target is nitrate, state that the TN-model small-basin coverage is unquantified in the source rather than importing the TP number.

3. SITE-COUNT LABEL. "1,334 TN ... sites considered" is wrong; 1,334 is the TN model's final calibration n (report text and TN summary table; Table 1 says 1,335 — an internal inconsistency in the report). "Sites considered" were 1,346 TN / 1,344 TP / 1,262 SS / 2,057 streamflow; "used in final models" were 1,335 TN / 1,273 TP / 1,082 suspended solids + 107 suspended sediment / 2,012 streamflow.

4. THE SMALL-BASIN CAVEAT IS ABOUT ACCURACY, NOT AVAILABILITY — which strengthens the operational case rather than killing it. The Midwest SPARROW network has a mean catchment size of 2.7 km2 (vs 480 km2 in the 2002 models), and output is keyed to NHDPlusV2 comid, which this project already stores per basin. So a SPARROW-derived level term IS obtainable for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated map pin with no local history — it is a legitimate deployment-compatible static feature. The correct framing is: cheap to attach, but expect the feature to be least trustworthy exactly where NLDI pins land on small headwater catchments, which is likely a large share of arbitrary map pins in Iowa.

5. POINT (3) OVERREACHES SLIGHTLY. "Systematic regional bias that would propagate into any feature built from SPARROW output" is stronger than the source supports for Iowa. The report locates the large residuals in the "western part of the study area" (elsewhere identified with the Missouri and Arkansas River Basins); it does not document bias in Iowa specifically. Also, a smooth regional bias in a SPARROW feature is partly absorbable by an XGBoost model that already has lat/lon as its 2nd and 3rd most important features — so residual regional bias is a reason to expect diminished marginal value, not a reason to expect harm.

FLAGGING THE n=19 CONSTRAINT (the claim does not do this and should). Adding SPARROW yield as a static per-basin covariate is a between-site term, and between-site signal is precisely what our 19 independent basin families have to estimate. One or two extra static columns is a modest, low-risk ask at n=19 — far safer than any method whose evidence base is 300+ catchments — but LOFO over 19 folds will give a very noisy estimate of its benefit; a gain smaller than roughly 0.03-0.05 PR-AUC will not be distinguishable from fold noise. Pre-register the ablation and report per-fold spread, not just the mean. Note also that SPARROW's own calibration is on 1,334 sites with nested/clustered geometry and in-sample fit statistics; its published R2 0.950 is not evidence of transfer and must not be cited alongside our LOFO 0.820.

result.correction:
The claim is substantively correct on every checkable point — source, columns, coverage, completeness, and both quoted numbers. Six corrections/qualifications, none fatal:

1. COLUMN COUNT AND CASE. 89 columns, not "~85". Join key is `ComID` (mixed case) and the HUC12 field is lowercase `huc12`; `HUC8`/`STATE`/`HUC2` are uppercase. ~29,004 rows (2.1%) have IncAreaKm2 = 0 and many carry negative synthetic ComIDs (e.g. -92000151) that are not real NHDPlusV2 catchments — filter these before joining.

2. "DIRECTLY INGESTIBLE" IS DANGEROUS IF TAKEN OVER ALL 89 COLUMNS — LEAKAGE RISK. The file also contains the model's own calibration/monitoring quantities: flux_530_final, flux_154_final, flux_600_final, flux_665_final (monitored/detrended load estimates at calibration sites), mean_dflow_predpd, and the weighting terms TNAllSN_inv_resid2_hat, TPAllN_inv_resid2_hat, sedN_inv_resid2_hat, flowDN_inv_resid2_hat. Ingesting these would inject observed nitrogen load into the feature set at exactly the monitored locations, and they are unavailable in the ungauged-pin sense. The claim's named subset is safe; a blanket "ingest the file" is not.

3. VALUES ARE INCREMENTAL PER CATCHMENT, NOT BASIN-CUMULATIVE. ManN2012, fert_sw_N_kg, cmaq_TN_12_kg, sum_ptsrc_kgn_wwtp are per-catchment kilogram totals paired with IncAreaKm2. For an arbitrary map pin you must sum over the NLDI-returned upstream COMID set and then divide by CumAreaKm2 to get kg/km2 — raw sums would largely re-encode basin area, which the model already has as log_basin_area. This is mechanically compatible with the existing NLDI delineation step, so it works for the deployment target, but it is an extra accumulation stage, not a lookup.

4. TWO OF THE LISTED COLUMNS ARE NEARLY DEGENERATE IN IOWA. Measured on the downloaded file: `aridity` is exactly 0 for 99.71% of Iowa catchments (it is a western-region delivery term) and `sum_ptsrc_kgn_wwtp` is 0 for 99.10% (nonzero only where a WWTP exists — meaningful only after upstream accumulation). Also `tiles13_perc2`/`ltiles13_perc2` are 0 for 58.68% of Iowa catchments, so this tile variable is far coarser and sparser than the Iowa tile-drainage literature would imply; do not treat it as a resolved tile-drainage layer.

5. THE N-SURPLUS SUBSTITUTION IS PARTIAL, NOT EQUIVALENT. ManN2012/fert_sw_N_kg/cmaq_TN_12_kg/nfix_km2 are a single static 2012 snapshot. They cannot restore the time-varying dimension the gTREND surplus product had before 2017; they replace a 68%-NaN time series with a complete constant. That is a genuine fix for the missingness and for the between-site term, but it must not be described as recovering temporal N-input variation — it removes it.

6. THE n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARDEST HERE, AND THE SIR's OWN CAVEAT AMPLIFIES IT. These are static per-site features: under LOFO they take at most 19 distinct effective values, so adding ~20 of them is a ~20-parameter regression on 19 independent units. Combined with the report's county-apportionment caveat (fertilizer, manure, no-till, CRP all derive from county averages downscaled by land use), the realized between-site resolution is county-scale, which within a single Iowa basin family is close to constant. (b) Their n (~95 sensor sites nationally, unverified) is the same order as our 85 sites but almost certainly exceeds our 19 independent basin families; the n=19 constraint remains more severe for us and this paper does not relieve it. (c) The paper's most actionable content for us is not the KGE drop but the Shapley result naming tile drainage, roadway density, and wetland cover as the dominant controls on MEAN (between-site) nitrate concentration — direct external confirmation that our between-site deficit is a missing-static-attribute problem, with tile drainage first on the list.

Paper identity verified: Pandit A, Golden HE, Christensen JR, Lane CR, Husic A. "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin." Water Resources Research 61(8), e2024WR039207, published 2025-08-09. DOI 10.1029/2024WR039207. PMID 40948694, PMCID PMC12425153. CC-BY-NC. Affiliations: Univ. of Kansas; US EPA Office of Research & Development (Cincinnati); Virginia Tech. Citation in the claim matches on every field.

The abstract, retrieved identically from Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1029/2024WR039207), PubMed efetch (PMID 40948694), and Semantic Scholar, states verbatim:
"We developed a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate concentrations, achieving strong temporal validation performance (median KGE = 0.60). Spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins—yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18). Nonetheless, spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34)."

So: LSTM — confirmed. Daily nitrate concentration — confirmed. Conterminous US — confirmed. Median KGE 0.60 temporal — exact. Median KGE 0.18 spatial — exact. "Prediction at basins NOT in training" — the paper's own gloss is "prediction in unmonitored basins," so the claim's characterization of the spatial protocol is the authors' own wording, not an interpolation. Drop of 0.42 — arithmetic correct. No misattribution, no exaggeration of the quoted figures.

WHAT COULD NOT BE VERIFIED (and why this does not reach refutation): the "95 sites used for training/validation drawn from 148 total monitoring locations, 1980-2022" detail appears nowhere in any accessible abstract or metadata record. The 1980-2022 span is confirmed by the abstract but refers to the MRB *application* period, not necessarily the sensor training record. I could not reach the methods section: Wiley (agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com) returns HTTP 402 to WebFetch and a Cloudflare bot challenge to curl on /doi/, /doi/full/, and /doi/epdf/; a reader-proxy attempt hit the same challenge; the PMC deposit (PMC12425153) is embargoed with the notice "This article will be available in PMC on August 09, 2026" (today is 2026-07-20, one day short); Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no repository PDF; ESS Open Archive is also Cloudflare-gated; the WebSearch budget for this session was fully consumed (200/200) before this task began. The site counts are therefore unsubstantiated but also uncontradicted, and they are not load-bearing for the claim's conclusion.

METHODOLOGY LENS.

(a) The metric is not commensurable with ours. KGE is a continuous-series skill score on concentration; our headline is a binary exceedance AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634. There is no mapping from KGE 0.18 to an AUC. This paper cannot be used to argue our numbers are good, bad, or comparable — only to argue that spatial transfer of daily nitrate degrades sharply, which is a directional statement.

(b) KGE is a composite of correlation, bias ratio, and variability ratio. Our diagnosed failure is specifically the *level/bias* term (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). A spatial-validation KGE collapse is consistent with a level-transfer failure, but the abstract does not decompose KGE, so the paper cannot be cited as confirming our specific diagnosis without the full text. Do not claim it does.

(c) "Median" across held-out sites conceals the tail. A median of 0.18 is compatible with a large fraction of held-out basins at negative KGE (worse than predicting the mean). The claim does not overstate this, but any downstream use should not treat 0.18 as a typical-site guarantee.

(d) Unresolved and materially important: whether streamflow/discharge was an LSTM input. If the model consumed observed Q, its "unmonitored basin" spatial validation is less ungauged than our deployment target and its 0.18 is an optimistic bound; if it consumed simulated Q (NHM/NWM), the input is reproducible at an arbitrary map pin and the result transfers cleanly. Unverifiable here; flag as an open question.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR SETTING.

Strongly relevant, and if anything the claim understates the relevance in one direction while overstating the effect size in another.

Relevance: this is a daily nitrate *concentration* model, spatially held out, explicitly evaluated for "prediction in unmonitored basins," covering Iowa. The abstract also reports that Shapley analysis identified "tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover" as the key spatial drivers of mean nitrate concentration — tile drainage is exactly the dominant control our feature set is missing with no data source identified. That is an independent corroboration of our own gap analysis and is arguably the most actionable line in the abstract, though the claim does not mention it.

n=19 CONSTRAINT — cuts in our favor here, not against. However many CONUS high-frequency nitrate sensor sites the paper used (the unverified figure is 95 for training/validation), it is roughly an order of magnitude more independent units than our 19 basin families. A deep LSTM trained on far more sites still lost most of its skill on spatial holdout. That makes 0.18 (or 0.34) an OPTIMISTIC upper bound on what an LSTM could achieve at n=19 basin families, so the claim's use of the paper — as evidence that switching to an LSTM will not solve our between-site problem — is directionally sound and conservative.

The paper is not, however, evidence that our XGBoost is at a ceiling. Different metric, different target (continuous concentration vs binary exceedance), different domain extent (CONUS vs Iowa). It bounds the LSTM-architecture argument only.

result.evidence:
VERDICT: The claim survives adversarial verification essentially intact. Every quoted number is exact, and the report's own text explicitly endorses the claim's central caveat. One minor numeric detail is wrong (see correction).

PRIMARY SOURCE OBTAINED. doi.org/10.3133/sir20195114 redirects to pubs.usgs.gov/publication/sir20195114; both that page and the PDF return HTTP 403 to the fetcher, so I pulled the PDF directly via curl with a browser user-agent (45,829,732 bytes, 200 OK) and converted with pdftotext. Local copy: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/e3f1f490-6fb8-475d-be0e-c0cebf530519/scratchpad/sir20195114.pdf and sir.txt. Robertson, D.M., and Saad, D.A., 2019, "Spatially Referenced Streamflow, Nutrient, and Suspended-Sediment Models of Midwestern Streams," USGS SIR 2019-5114, 60 p.

1. NUMBERS — ALL EXACT. Table 5 (TN model, "Model summary statistic value" column) reads verbatim: Conditioned RMSE, natural log units = 0.487; Conditioned RMSE, percentage real space = 51.8; Unconditioned RMSE, natural log units = 0.555; Unconditioned RMSE, percentage real space = 60.0; Mean exponentiated weighted error = 1.129; R2 = 0.950; Yield R2 = 0.913; Number of sites = 1,334. Body text confirms: "The model explained 95 percent of the variance in TN loads and 91 percent of the variances in yields... The RMSE obtained during model calibration (conditioned RMSE) was 0.487 and when the model was used for full prediction (unconditioned RMSE) was 0.555 (both in natural logarithmic units). These values equate to an RMSE of 51.8 percent for conditioned predictions and an RMSE of 60.0 percent for unconditioned predictions." No exaggeration, no garbled paraphrase.

2. SITE COUNTS — CORRECT INCLUDING THE INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY. Table 1 columns are "Sites considered for use in SPARROW models" and "Sites used in final SPARROW models": Streamflow 2,057 considered / 2,012 final; Total nitrogen 1,344 / 1,335; Total phosphorus 1,346 / 1,273; Suspended sediment 177 / 107; (also Suspended solids 1,085 / 1,082, which the claim omits but does not misstate). Table 5 and the body both say 1,334 for TN, disagreeing with Table 1's 1,335. The claim correctly flags all three figures (1,344 / 1,335 / 1,334) rather than papering over the report's own 1-site discrepancy. Streamflow 2,012, TP 1,273, sediment 107 all confirmed.

3. THE CRITICAL CAVEAT — NO VALIDATION — CONFIRMED. Case-insensitive grep for "cross-validation"/"cross validation" returns ZERO hits in the 13,723-line extraction. No hits for holdout, hold-out, leave-one-out, jackknife, validation set, independent validation, or split-sample. The only resampling anywhere is a parametric bootstrap (200 iterations) used in the LOAD-ESTIMATION step to put uncertainty on measured loads — not a spatial holdout of the SPARROW model. The reported statistics come from weighted nonlinear least-squares regression fit to the same sites they are scored on. The claim's characterization "in-sample calibration statistics... no cross-validation, no leave-one-basin-out, and no spatial holdout anywhere" is accurate.

4. THE CONDITIONED-RMSE CAVEAT — CONFIRMED VERBATIM, AND THE AUTHORS AGREE. Table 5 footnote b: "Conditioned RMSE is the root mean square error of the difference between the natural logarithm of measured calibration loads and the natural logarithm of predicted accumulated loads that were reset to the measured loads at the calibration sites upstream in the basin." Footnote d confirms unconditioned is the same "except the predicted accumulated loads were not reset." This is exactly the gauged-upstream-neighbor protocol the claim describes. The report's Methods section goes further and makes the claim's argument for it: "This replacement can result in an underestimation of the model error compared to when the model is used to simulate loads throughout the basin, using the unconditioned predictions (Qian and others, 2005; Wellen and others, 2014). Therefore, an unconditioned RMSE also is reported... The unconditioned RMSE provides the best representation of the predictive skill of a calibrated SPARROW model." The claim's insistence that only 0.555 / 60.0% is relevant to us is the authors' own stated position, not an adversarial reinterpretation.

5. INDEPENDENT SUPPORT THAT UNSEEN-BASIN PERFORMANCE WOULD BE WORSE. The report's spatial diagnostics — the closest thing to a transferability check, and they are residual diagnostics rather than holdout — FAIL for TN: loose-cluster Moran's I = 0.199, p = 0.0005 (n=1,334), and nested-share weighting coefficient 0.204, p = 3.3e-6. The report interprets significant Moran's I as meaning "the model might be improved by adding additional explanatory variables (beyond those tested in our study)... where the model consistently overpredicts or underpredicts." Body text admits "patterns of overpredictions and underpredictions in the western parts of the watershed" and that "the model did not predict the loads and yields as well for sites with relatively small loads," with unconditioned RMSE degrading to 0.65 for smaller loads. Spatially clustered residuals are precisely the condition under which in-sample cross-sectional R2 overstates performance at a spatially held-out basin. This strengthens the claim.

6. TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR SETTING — the claim's non-comparability argument holds, and there are two further reasons it under-states the gap. (a) TARGET MISMATCH: SPARROW's response is mean-annual TN LOAD (kg/yr) aggregated over 2012 conditions — a long-term cross-sectional average with the entire temporal axis integrated out. Our between_r2 = 0.21 is a between-site term for DAILY-MAX CONCENTRATION (mg/L) exceedance. R2 on log mean-annual load is inflated by several orders of magnitude of basin-area variation across 1,334 sites; load scales almost mechanically with area and runoff. Yield R2 = 0.913 is the area-normalized version and is the fairer of the two, but it is still an in-sample fit to a long-term mean, not daily concentration. These are different quantities and no rescaling makes 0.913 and 0.21 commensurable — a point the claim makes but could make more forcefully. (b) n=19 CONSTRAINT: SPARROW estimates ~14 coefficients from 1,334 sites (~95 sites per parameter). At our 19 independent basin families, fitting even SPARROW's structure is infeasible — a 14-parameter cross-sectional regression on 19 units is not estimable in any trustworthy way. SPARROW is not a method we can port; it is at best a source of PRIOR STRUCTURE (which source and land-to-water terms matter) or of PREDICTIONS-AS-FEATURES.

7. WHAT IS ACTUALLY USABLE, judged against the arbitrary-map-pin target. SPARROW predictions are published on the NHDPlusV2 catchment network, and the project already stores an NHDPlus comid per basin, so pre-computed SPARROW incremental TN yield for a target catchment is a static between-site covariate obtainable with NO local nitrate history and NO gauged upstream neighbor. That is deployment-legal, and it attacks exactly the between-site term where all our headroom is. Caveats: it is a 2012 static snapshot (no temporal variation — consistent with our finding that only static geography has helped); and its inputs partly overlap features we already have (fertilizer, manure, runoff, land use), so it may be redundant rather than additive. Worth an ablation, not a guaranteed win.

8. BONUS FINDING, DIRECTLY ON A STATED PROJECT GAP. The brief says tile drainage density is "the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet." The SPARROW TN model uses exactly this variable and it is highly significant: "Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)," coefficient 0.101, 90% CI 0.064-0.139, SE 0.023, p<0.0001, t=4.5, VIF 2.3 — a land-to-water delivery term. In the TP model the same variable is significant with the opposite sign (-0.091, p=0.0221). Source, per the report's reference list: Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, "Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012," USGS data release, http://dx.doi.org/10.5066/F7W37TDP — 12 Midwest states (so it covers Iowa AND the multi-state portions of our largest basins, which is where our inner-join under-counting is worst), 2012 snapshot, extrapolated to NHDPlusV2 catchments following Wieczorek and others (2019); supplemented for ND/SD from Finocchiaro (2014, 2016) tile-permit polygons. USGS data releases are free, public, no authentication, public-domain. I verified this citation as printed in the report but did NOT fetch the data release itself, so resolution/format/exact access mechanism are unconfirmed — treat coverage-years and delivery details as needing one confirmation fetch. Note the same 2012-static-snapshot risk that killed the 2017 N-surplus broadcast (-0.166): use it as a TIME-INVARIANT basin attribute, never broadcast as a time-varying feature.

WHAT I COULD NOT CHECK: WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before I started, so I could not survey independent post-hoc validations of Midwest SPARROW against held-out basins. Absence of such evidence here is not evidence it does not exist; the claim's assertion is scoped to "in the entire 60-page report," and that scoping I did verify directly.
result.correction: The claim is correct in every material respect; only one incidental number is wrong. It describes the TN model as "a 16-parameter regression." The claim is directionally correct and its two quoted numbers are exact, but it should be restated as follows before use.

Pandit et al. (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," WRR 61(8), e2024WR039207, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207 (CC-BY-NC), trained an LSTM on high-frequency nitrate sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate CONCENTRATION. Use the 0.34 figure, not 0.18, when reasoning about Iowa: Iowa is in the MRB and is named explicitly in the paper's abstract. The region-matched degradation is 0.60 -> 0.34 (drop 0.26), not 0.60 -> 0.18 (drop 0.42). Citing 0.18 for an Iowa-facing argument overstates the collapse by roughly 60%.

The claim's core inference survives all of this and in fact strengthens: an LSTM does NOT solve ungauged-basin nitrate concentration, and it fails in the same way we do — timing preserved, absolute level lost. Given that the study likely had 5-8x more independent spatial units than our 19 basin families, an LSTM at our sample size should be expected to underperform the current XGBoost, not rescue it. The paper's more useful contribution to this project is not the pessimistic benchmark but its Shapley finding that tile drainage is the leading spatial control on mean nitrate concentration, which independently confirms the project's own between-site diagnosis and points at the missing feature.

The claim states the gain came from "restricting the TRAINING POOL" to hydroclimatically similar basins, and concludes this supports "a regionally-specialized model over a continental one." The abstract describes no such experiment. There is ONE model, trained on CONUS-wide sensor data. The 0.18 -> 0.34 difference is an EVALUATION-SUBSET effect: the same continental model's held-out-basin scores are stratified, and the MRB subset of held-out basins scores higher. The paper's own framing is the opposite of the claim's conclusion — spatial validation "guid[ed] the model's targeted application to the MRB," i.e. they retained the CONUS-trained model and applied it to a region where it validated well. This is evidence FOR training continentally and deploying regionally, not for shrinking the training pool. No retrained MRB-only model is reported in the abstract, and I could not access the full text to check whether one exists in a supplementary ablation.

CONFOUNDS THE CLAIM IGNORES, even taking 0.18 -> 0.34 at face value: (1) Training-data density, not hydroclimatic similarity, is the more parsimonious explanation — high-frequency nitrate sensors in the US are overwhelmingly concentrated in the Corn Belt/MRB, so MRB held-out basins have far more near-neighbor training basins than, say, arid-West or coastal-Southeast holdouts. That is a coverage effect. (2) KGE is variance- and bias-sensitive; MRB basins have large-amplitude, strongly seasonal nitrate signals, which mechanically inflates KGE relative to low-concentration, low-variance basins elsewhere. Both confounds are consistent with the observed gap without any "regional specialization" mechanism.

n NOT VERIFIABLE. The claim itself concedes n is unknown. The abstract gives no site count, and I could not reach the full text (Wiley 402; PMC embargo lifts 2026-08-09, ~3 weeks from now). The claim's "95 training sites" figure is unsourced in anything I could retrieve. Per rule 5, an unverifiable n is grounds for not relying on the effect size.

Our model is Iowa-only, i.e. we already sit at the maximally regionally-specialized end of the axis the claim recommends moving along. The claim therefore offers no headroom for us; it recommends a move we have already made by construction.

If a CONUS-trained LSTM reaches median spatial KGE 0.34 on MRB ungauged basins, the operative lever is a LARGER training pool of monitored basins spanning the MRB, which is precisely the escape hatch from our n=19-independent-families constraint. The claim quotes: "developed interpretable random forest models that explain the spatial variation in long-term streamflow, nitrate concentration, and nitrate yield at 95 sites used for model training." n=95 IS UNSUBSTANTIATED. No site count appears in the abstract. The claim reports "n basins: 95" as if sourced; I could not verify it from any accessible text.

THE STATED SPLIT PROTOCOL IS WRONG, AND THIS IS THE CLAIM'S WORST ERROR. The claim records "split protocol: not-applicable." The paper in fact runs an explicit ungauged-basin (PUB) protocol and reports it in the abstract with hard numbers: temporal validation median KGE = 0.60; "Spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins—yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18)"; and within the MRB specifically, spatial validation median KGE = 0.34. By declaring the protocol not-applicable, the claim discards the single most decision-relevant fact this paper offers our project.

WHAT SURVIVES. The claim's bottom-line advice — do not cite this paper as evidence that LSTM beats gradient-boosted trees for ungauged-basin nitrate — is correct, but for a different reason than the claim gives. It is not that RF was repurposed as an interpretability tool; it is that no RF/XGBoost/gradient-boosting baseline of any kind appears in the accessible text. There is no deep-vs-tree comparison to cite, under any protocol.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR SETTING. (a) The KGE = 0.18 CONUS spatial-validation figure is the genuinely citable result here and it independently corroborates our central problem: a well-resourced CONUS-scale LSTM with static attributes transfers poorly to unmonitored basins for nitrate concentration. It is evidence that between-site nitrate transfer is hard in general, not evidence that we should switch architectures. (b) Not comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC / 0.634 PR-AUC: KGE is a continuous hydrograph-similarity metric on daily concentration, wrong for our binary daily-exceedance target, and it is computed per-site then medianed. Do not place KGE 0.18 next to our between_r2 0.21 as if they measure the same thing. (c) Data overlap, not independent replication: their training data are high-frequency nitrate sensors across the CONUS, which necessarily include the USGS and Iowa (IWQIS) sensors our 85 sites are drawn from. This is largely the same signal, so it cannot serve as external validation of our numbers. (d) n=19 constraint: their spatial-validation site pool is of the same order of magnitude as ours (tens of sensor sites, not CAMELS-scale 531-671 basins), so this paper does NOT demonstrate a method that needs hundreds of catchments — but it also does not demonstrate one that works at small n, since its ungauged-basin performance was weak. (e) Genuinely actionable side-finding: SHAP identified TILE DRAINAGE as a top spatial driver of mean nitrate concentration, with non-linear thresholds. That is exactly the dominant control our feature set is missing, and it implies Pandit et al. sourced a CONUS or MRB-wide tile-drainage layer. Chasing that layer (likely via the paper's data-availability statement once the embargo lifts 2026-04-16, or by emailing husic@vt.edu) is a higher-value follow-up than anything about LSTM-vs-trees.

result.correction:
The claim is correct on substance and on every quoted number; two refinements, neither of which changes its conclusion.

(1) "Reported split protocol: not-applicable" is the one imprecise field. The paper does have an explicit and consequential protocol: temporal holdout at the SAME basins the model was trained on. Main setup: "time periods for training (1 October 1999 through 30 September 2008), validation (1 October 1980 through 30 September 1989), and testing (1 October 1989 through 30 September 1999)." The Fig. 6 sample-size experiment uses "k-fold cross-validation so that all models were tested on the same basin(s) where they were trained (during different time periods)." So it is a GAUGED-basin, temporally-split protocol — the weakest possible protocol relative to our LOFO. Under rule 1 none of its NSE numbers are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, and this fact makes the claim's conclusion stronger, not weaker: the paper does not even measure spatial transfer, which is exactly the axis our project is stuck on. (Minor internal inconsistency worth noting: the Fig. 6 passage says training period "1999-2000" and test period "1980-1989", swapping the roles of the validation and test windows given in the main setup. Looks like an editing slip in the paper; immaterial here.)

(2) The paper contains one section that DOES bear on our situation, and it cuts against using this paper to justify anything at n=19 — worth surfacing rather than discarding. Section 4 "How many basins are necessary?" finds median NSE still rising monotonically at 531 basins: "even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough to train optimal LSTM models for streamflow." Section 5 additionally trains on basins grouped by USGS HUC — "There are 18 HUCs represented in the CAMELS data set, with between 2 and 79 basins per HUC" — i.e. groupings of roughly the size of our 19 independent basin families, and the conclusion is that restricting to such groups is WORSE than pooling everything: "even if enough basins exist to divide your training data into hydrologically informed training sets, one is likely to be better off simply training a single model with all available data." So the paper's own evidence says an LSTM at our effective sample size sits far down the left tail of its learning curve. Anyone citing Kratzert et al. 2024 as support for switching this project from XGBoost to an LSTM is citing a paper that (a) never tested a GBDT, (b) never touched water quality, (c) never held out a basin spatially, and (d) whose sample-size analysis implies our n is well below where regional LSTMs start to pay off.

result.correction: Claim is accurate and should be accepted, with four precisions. (1) QUOTE INEXACT: the phrase "does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation" is presented as an author quote but conflates two distinct caveats. The paper's temporal caveat reads "a static representation of U.S. tile drainage for the year 2017"; the spatial caveat is separate and different - "each 30-m grid identified as tile drained is entirely tile drained", i.e. presence/absence only, no sub-pixel drainage density. The operational conclusion (static basin attribute only, no time-varying tile signal) is nonetheless correct. (2) MODELED, NOT OBSERVED: AgTile-US is derived from SSURGO soil drainage class + SRTM slope threshold + CDL cropland mask, calibrated to county-level USDA Census tile acreage. The near-match of the 22,340,442 ha total to the 22,418,966 ha Census figure is therefore close to tautological at national scale and is NOT independent validation; the independent evidence is the 16,000-point photo-interpretation (86.03% pixel accuracy). Basin-aggregated fractions should be more accurate than 86% since independent pixel errors partly cancel - this favors the intended use. (3) COLLINEARITY RISK, the main reason to temper expectations: because the product is a deterministic function of soil drainage class, slope and cropland, and because Iowa tile drainage is spatially concentrated in the Des Moines Lobe, a per-basin tile fraction will partly duplicate information that lat/lon (already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features) encode. The feature should be benchmarked explicitly against a lat/lon-only baseline, not just against the current model. (4) n=19 FLAG: this adds a single static column evaluated against ~19 effective independent basin families. That is the mildest form of the sample-size constraint - one degree of freedom, not a 300-basin architecture - but a single spurious alignment across 19 units can still masquerade as a win, so any LOFO gain should be checked for stability under leave-one-family-out perturbation. Also note AgTile-US fixes the multi-state under-count for the tile variable only; the CDL and N-surplus joins remain Iowa-truncated.

- Resolution: 30 m. CONFIRMED.

- Binary 0/1. CONFIRMED.
- CONUS tile-drained area 22,340,442 ha. CONFIRMED exact.
- Iowa 5,706,831 ha, largest of any state. CONFIRMED exact.
- Static, no temporal dynamics. CONFIRMED in substance: "The data deliver a static representation of U.S. tile drainage for the year 2017."
- Access: Figshare, DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, CC-BY 4.0, no authentication. Code at github.com/NCAR/AgTile-US. Satisfies the free/public acquisition constraint.
- Validation: 86.03% overall accuracy against 16,000 manually photo-interpreted points across ten states; 82.7-93.6% in heavily drained Midwest. Midwest (i.e. our region) is the best-validated part of the product.

TWO DETAIL ERRORS, both minor, neither load-bearing:

(1) MISQUOTATION. The claim presents "does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation" as an explicit authors' quote. I could not locate that string verbatim in the paper. The paper's actual language is "The data deliver a static representation of U.S. tile drainage for the year 2017." The proposition is correct; the quotation marks are not earned.

(2) CLASS DEFINITION. The claim says 0 = undrained cropland / 1 = tile-drained cropland. The paper's classes are defined over an NLCD-2016 agricultural-land mask, not a CDL cropland mask, and the paper flags 18.15% under-representation of CONUS croplands in NLCD-2016. Operationally this matters: AgTile-US's denominator is NOT the same cropland footprint as our CDL-derived crop-class features, so a basin tile fraction computed as (tile cells / CDL crop cells) mixes two incompatible masks. Compute tile fraction against basin AREA, or against AgTile-US's own 0+1 domain, not against CDL.

METHODOLOGY CAVEAT NOT IN THE CLAIM, and this is the one that should temper expectations. AgTile-US is not an independent observation of tile. It is a top-down disaggregation: county-level USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture drained-acreage totals are allocated within each county by a decision tree over SSURGO drainage class (D=1-7) and SRTM slope (0-20%), poorly-drained/low-slope cells taken first, until the county total is matched. Consequences:
- Within a county, the layer is a deterministic function of soils + slope. A basin-aggregated tile fraction is therefore close to a smooth reparameterization of "fraction of basin that is poorly-drained, low-slope agricultural land," modulated only by the county-total scaling. It is NOT information orthogonal to soils/topography; if you also add SSURGO drainage class or basin slope as features you will be adding a near-collinear copy.
- Its true independent resolution is the COUNTY, not 30 m. Iowa has 99 counties; an Iowa basin of typical size spans a handful of them. So the effective independent variation available to distinguish our 19 basin families is on the order of tens of county values, not millions of pixels. The 30 m number is a rendering resolution, not an information resolution.
- Inherited error: the paper states USDA census dependence carries approximately +/-19.8% average error.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: passes cleanly, and this is the claim's strongest point. It is a static raster lookup. An arbitrary map pin, once NLDI returns the upstream basin polygon, yields a tile fraction with no nitrate history, no discharge gauge, and no monitored neighbor required. Train-time and deploy-time feature construction are identical, so there is no gauged-site dependence and no leakage pathway. CONUS coverage does resolve the stated multi-state under-count problem for the large basins (Iowa basins extending into MN/SD/NE/MO), unlike the Iowa-only joins.

n=19 CONSTRAINT: flagged, and it is the binding limit. This adds ONE static scalar per basin against ~19 independent units. It is the correct KIND of information given the diagnosis (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21; headroom is between-site), and it is cheap and low-risk because static geography is the only feature class that has previously won on this project. But do not expect a large gain: with 19 units, a single covariate must correlate strongly with basin mean nitrate to survive LOFO, and the Des Moines Lobe vs southern-Iowa tile gradient may already be partially encoded by lat/lon, which are currently the #2 and #3 features by permutation importance. Test explicitly whether tile fraction adds anything CONDITIONAL on lat/lon; if lat/lon are already proxying the Des Moines Lobe, the marginal gain could be near zero. That specific ablation, not raw addition, is the experiment worth running.

Note also the project premise "NO data source has been identified yet" for tile drainage is false as stated - AgTile-US exists, is free, CC-BY, CONUS-wide, and best-validated in the Midwest.

result.correction:
The claim is substantively correct and operationally usable; three corrections and one caution.

(1) MISQUOTE. The sentence attributed verbatim to the authors ("does not represent spatial or temporal changes in drainage installation") is not in the paper. Replace with the actual text: "The data deliver a static representation of U.S. tile drainage for the year 2017." The claim's conclusion - static snapshot, cannot supply any time-varying tile signal - is nonetheless correct.

(2) IT IS A MODELED PRODUCT, NOT AN OBSERVATION, AND THIS IS THE MAIN THREAT TO THE CLAIM'S CENTRAL ARGUMENT. AgTile-US is a deterministic decision tree over SSURGO soil drainage category and SRTM slope, thresholded until accumulated area matches USDA COUNTY-level census tile acreage. The per-basin tile fraction is therefore a smooth function of soil drainage class and slope, constrained only at county granularity. The claim asserts this is "exactly the between-site static information the LOFO gap needs." At n=19 independent basin families in Iowa, that new attribute may be substantially collinear with lat/lon - already the #2 and #3 features by permutation importance - and with the CDL crop fractions. It is not guaranteed to be independent information. Before assuming lift, compute the correlation of basin tile-fraction against lat, lon, log_basin_area and the CDL bucket features; if R^2 against existing statics is high, expected gain is small.

(3) DENOMINATOR AMBIGUITY - the claim says "one number per basin" but there are two distinct features. Non-agricultural land is MASKED OUT, not coded 0, so (a) tile cells / total basin cells and (b) tile cells / agricultural cells are different quantities. (b) is drainage intensity, the physically meaningful control; (a) conflates drainage with crop cover already captured by the 8 CDL classes x 3 buckets. Build both; they are not interchangeable. Also note the mask is NLCD-2016 cropland, a different land-cover product from the CDL currently used, so cell-level agreement with existing crop features is imperfect.

(4) CAUTION, NOT A BLOCKER, ON THE 2017 DATE. This is superficially the same 2017 endpoint as the N-surplus product whose forward-broadcast failed badly (-0.166). The failure modes differ: that was a TIME-VARYING feature held constant, whereas this is used as a static basin attribute where no temporal claim is made. Tile installation is also far more inertial than annual nitrogen application, so a 2017 snapshot is a defensible constant across 2008-2026. Do not treat the prior negative result as predicting failure here, but do enter it as a static attribute only - never as a per-day feature.

result.evidence:
PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED — the numbers are NOT fabricated. Source is Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data 7:257, PMC7406500. Confirmed verbatim: "an overall accuracy of 86.03% for the CONUS with an omission error of 13.97%"; 16,000 points from ESRI multi-resolution aerial imagery (acquisition 2012-10-02 to 2017-04-23); Iowa 91.1% on 5,253 points; Midwest range 82.7-93.6%; 30 m resolution, CONUS, year 2017. So the claim is not misattributed or garbled at the level of quoted statistics.

WHAT IS REFUTED IS THE OPERATIVE INFERENCE — "roughly 9% pixel-level misclassification ... a per-basin aggregate would average much of that out, making basin-level tile fraction a low-noise attribute." Four independent defects, each sufficient:

(1) POSITIVES-ONLY GROUND TRUTH — 91.1% IS RECALL, NOT ACCURACY. The authors "manually identified 16000 tile drainage ground-truth points," i.e. all 16,000 are known-drained locations. Commission error / false-positive rate is reported NOWHERE. Note 100 − 86.03 = 13.97 exactly: the paper's "omission error" is just the complement of its "accuracy," which is arithmetically what you get when the sample contains no negatives. A basin tile FRACTION is (drained pixels)/(basin pixels) and its error depends on commission at least as much as omission. The paper places no bound whatsoever on commission, so "9% pixel-level misclassification" is not a misclassification rate of the raster.

(2) THE SAMPLE IS NON-RANDOM AND SELECTED FOR DETECTABILITY. Authors' own limitation: "we limited the tile drainage ground-truth identification mostly to fallow croplands where the tile drainage signature is easily detectable." 91.1% is an optimistic upper bound on recall within the easiest-to-see subset, not an unbiased pixel accuracy over Iowa cropland.

(3) CALIBRATION/VALIDATION CIRCULARITY. The same 16,000 points were used "to validate the AgTile-US and to set the upper limit of slope in the geospatial model" (the 20% slope cap). Validation data parameterized the model — the accuracy figure is partly in-sample and inflated. The claim's stated protocol ("not-applicable, image-interpretation ground truth, not a train/test split") is therefore wrong: there IS a train/test issue, and it is a leak.

(4) DECISIVE FOR OUR USE — ERRORS ARE COUNTY-LEVEL SYSTEMATIC AND DO NOT AVERAGE OUT. AgTile-US is not a per-pixel classifier with independent errors; it is a deterministic greedy fill. It ranks NLCD-2016 cropland pixels by SSURGO drainage class (starting at D=7, very poorly drained, slope S=0), then relaxes slope in 1% steps to 20%, then steps down drainage class, "until the estimated tile drainage area exceeded the USDA census tile drainage area" for the county. Every pixel in a county is therefore tied to one shared constraint — the county Census of Agriculture tile acreage — and to SSURGO polygon geometry. The claim's averaging argument requires error independence; the dominant error term here is a per-county bias shared by all pixels, so a basin overlapping a handful of counties inherits that bias wholesale with no cancellation. The authors quantify it: "The average error in tile drainage estimates based on the Census of Agriculture 2017 is 19.8%," with state-level errors reaching −79.06% (New Mexico) and −42.38% (West Virginia). The relevant noise floor for a basin-mean aggregate is that ~19.8% systematic census error, not 9%. Authors also flag "underestimation ... mainly due to underrepresentation of croplands in NLCD land cover 2016" and that "any uncertainty in these datasets will lead to inaccuracies."

UNVERIFIED SUB-CLAIM: "highest per-state validation density in the paper." Iowa's 5,253/16,000 (33%) is plausibly the largest raw COUNT, but I could not recover per-state point counts for the other nine states, and "density" (points per unit area or per cropland area) was never established. Treat as unsupported.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET — mixed, and better than the refutation implies. Positives: AgTile-US is genuinely operational for an arbitrary Iowa map pin (CONUS coverage, so multi-state basin portions are covered; 30 m static raster, single 2017 epoch; free public download; no auth; no local history needed) and it is a STATIC BETWEEN-SITE attribute, which is exactly the deficit our diagnostics point to (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42) and exactly the class of feature that has historically won on this project while every temporal feature failed. It also embeds a real observed quantity — county USDA census tile acreage — which is authentic between-site information not currently in the 68 features. Negatives to state plainly: (a) because it is a deterministic function of SSURGO drainage class + slope + NLCD cropland + county total, basin-mean tile fraction is substantially a re-encoding of basin soil/topography plus a county indicator, so it will be partly collinear with lat/lon (already the #2 and #3 features) — some of its apparent gain may be the model re-learning geography it already has; (b) the single 2017 epoch means no temporal variation, so it cannot help the timing task at all, only the level task; (c) THE n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARD — one new static covariate is being asked to explain between-family variation across 19 independent units, and because the error is county-correlated rather than independent, the effective information content is closer to the number of distinct county-groups spanned by those 19 families, likely well under 19. This is a one-degree-of-freedom-ish addition evaluated at n=19; expect a noisy LOFO estimate and treat any single-split improvement under ~0.02 PR-AUC as indistinguishable from zero.

BOTTOM LINE: use the feature if you like — the underlying reasoning for wanting a tile-drainage attribute is sound and this is the best free CONUS product available — but do NOT justify it with "91.1% Iowa accuracy so ~9% noise that averages out." That premise is wrong in three ways (positives-only recall, detectability-biased sample, self-calibrated threshold) and the averaging step is invalid because the errors are county-systematic. Budget for a ~20% systematic bias in basin tile fraction that survives aggregation, and validate the feature empirically under LOFO rather than assuming it is low-noise.

I did not obtain the exact download URL, license, or the full per-state table.

Two corrections, both to interpretation rather than to the quoted facts.

(1) THE CENTRAL MECHANISTIC ERROR. AgTile-US is NOT a deterministic function of SSURGO drainage class + slope + cropland alone, so the strong-collinearity prediction is overstated. The construction is a downscaling; the product is nonetheless independently validated as skillful at the pixel level.

PRACTICAL GUIDANCE THAT SURVIVES: the operational advice is still sound — prefer basin-mean AgTile fraction as a SINGLE feature over adding AgTile + SSURGO drainage class + mean slope as three, because at ~19 independent basin families the correlated-static budget is tiny. But add one caveat the claim does not raise: because thresholds are solved per county, AgTile-US has DISCONTINUITIES AT COUNTY LINES. Basin-aggregated values inherit a county-mosaic step artifact, worst for basins spanning many counties and for the multi-state basins. Sanity-check basin AgTile fraction against county boundaries before trusting between-site rank ordering derived from it.

This is precisely sustag's within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21 pathology reproduced independently with a different model class, a different metric, and a continental training set. It is direct evidence that (a) the between-site deficit is a property of the ungauged-nitrate problem, not of XGBoost or of sustag's feature set, and (b) switching to an LSTM is very unlikely to fix it. Note the metric is not comparable to sustag's AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 — KGE on daily continuous concentration vs classification of a 10 mg/L exceedance are different quantities and must not be placed on the same scale.

n=19 CONSTRAINT: not directly threatened by this paper, because the paper is being cited as a negative/corroborating result rather than as a method to adopt. PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED. The cited source is Valayamkunnath et al., "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach", Scientific Data 7:257 (2020), PMC7406500, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x. Every mechanical element of the claim checks out against the paper:

INPUTS — confirmed exactly as stated. USDA Census of Agriculture 2017 county-level tile-drainage acreage as the constraining target; gridded SSURGO (gSSURGO) v2.0, native 10-m resampled to 30-m, with SEVEN drainage classes indexed D=1 (excessively drained) through D=7 (very poorly drained); NLCD 2016 "cultivated cropland" category as the 30-m cropland mask; SRTM-derived 30-m slope with a 20% upper threshold.

ALGORITHM — confirmed as a deterministic decision-tree/threshold search, not a learned or observational product. Paper's stated sequence: start at D=7 with slope S=0; increment S by 1% while accumulated area is below the county census target; on reaching S=20%, reset S=0 and decrement to D=6; repeat until accumulated area exceeds the census target; then fine-tune with 0.1% slope increments to minimize error. The claim's "iterated D=7 down to D=1" is the correct direction (the loop terminates when the county target is met, so D=1 is the floor, not necessarily reached in every county — a trivial imprecision).

AGGREGATE NUMBER — QUOTED NUMBERS ARE EXACT. AgTile-US total 22,340,442 ha vs USDA census 22,418,966 ha = -0.35%. The claim's "22.34 vs 22.42 Mha" and "-0.35%" are faithful. And the claim's "by construction" characterization is correct: the algorithm's termination condition IS matching the county census total, so aggregate agreement is tautological and carries no validation weight. This is the claim's strongest and most important point.

THE CORE FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE HOLDS. AgTile-US is, mathematically, a deterministic function of exactly four inputs: county census total, gSSURGO drainage class, NLCD 2016 cropland, SRTM slope. No independent tile-location observation (permit records, field surveys, LiDAR/imagery tile-line detection) enters the pixel allocation. Therefore a basin-aggregated AgTile fraction cannot be statistically independent of basin-aggregated drainage class, mean slope, and cropland fraction. Feeding AgTile fraction AND SSURGO drainage class/HSG AND mean slope as three separate features would be near-collinear, and attributing a measured gain to "three independent attributes" would be wrong. The claim's prescription — attribute any gain to the composite — is correct.

METHODOLOGY LENS, additional finding the claim did not raise: the paper's 20% slope threshold was CALIBRATED on the same 16,000 manually-interpreted aerial-imagery ground-truth points later used to report 86.03% overall accuracy. Paper text: "To validate the AgTile-US and to set the upper limit of slope in the geospatial model, we have manually identified 16000 ground-truth points... Using the extracted slope values, we have identified the upper limit of slope (=20%)." There is no stated held-out split. The headline accuracy is therefore partly in-sample and should be treated as an upper bound. The paper also performs no comparison against any independently produced tile-drainage map or field-verified permit dataset.

SPLIT PROTOCOL: not-applicable is the correct designation — this is a static geospatial product, not a predictive model with a train/test split. No basin-level protocol exists to compare against our LOFO 0.820.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT: favorable on access, mixed on information content. AgTile-US is a static 30-m CONUS raster covering ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of large basins — it does not require the target site's own observations or a gauged upstream neighbor, so it is compatible with the arbitrary-ungauged-map-pin deployment target, and it is a STATIC BETWEEN-SITE attribute, which is precisely the class of feature that has worked on this project while every temporal feature failed. Distributed free via ORNL DAAC / the paper's Zenodo-linked repository, no authentication, open license. At n=19 independent basin families, though, it is one more static covariate competing for a very small effective sample; and because it is heavily collinear with soil and slope, the marginal information it adds over an SSURGO drainage-class basin summary is limited to the county-census scaling term.
result.correction:
The claim is directionally correct and its quoted numbers are exact, but it overstates redundancy in two specific ways that change what you should do with it.

(1) "NOT AN INDEPENDENT OBSERVATION" IS TOO ABSOLUTE. The pixel ALLOCATION is pure downscaling, as claimed. But one genuinely exogenous observation does enter: the USDA county-level tile acreage itself is farmer-reported survey data, not derived from soil or terrain. AgTile encodes, per county, WHERE ON THE (drainage-class, slope) ORDERING THE CUTOFF FALLS — and that cutoff is set by real reported acreage that cannot be recovered from gSSURGO + NLCD + SRTM alone. So AgTile fraction is not a deterministic function of the other three candidate features; it is those three features PLUS a county-resolution intensity signal. Practical consequence for this project: WITHIN a county, AgTile variation is pure soil+slope and is fully redundant. BETWEEN counties, AgTile carries real information. Since Iowa basins typically span many counties, the between-county component is where any genuine gain would come from — and that is exactly the between-site term where the project's headroom lies. Do not dismiss the feature; dismiss the triple-counting.

(2) The paper DID conduct an accuracy assessment against non-census data — 16,000 manually interpreted aerial-imagery points, 86.03% overall CONUS accuracy, 13.97% omission error — which the claim omits entirely. However, this assessment is compromised rather than absent: the same points calibrated the 20% slope threshold, and no held-out split is described, so treat 86.03% as an optimistic in-sample figure. State-level breakdowns (an Iowa-specific figure near 91% on roughly 5,000 points) came back inconsistent across two extraction passes and should be read directly from the paper's tables before being cited.

(3) Minor precision fixes: the soil input is GRIDDED SSURGO (gSSURGO) v2.0, native 10-m resampled to 30-m, not vector SSURGO; and the D-loop terminates when the county census target is exceeded, so D=1 is the floor of the search rather than a step every county reaches.

RECOMMENDED ACTION: add AgTile-US basin fraction as a single static feature; do NOT simultaneously add SSURGO drainage-class and mean-slope basin summaries as if they were independent attributes. If you want to test whether AgTile adds anything beyond terrain and soil, the clean ablation is AgTile-fraction versus (drainage-class + slope + cropland-fraction) as competing feature sets under the same LOFO protocol, not both together — and expect the discriminating signal to be between-county, so check whether it survives at n=19 families before believing it.

result.correction:
The claim is factually exact on inputs, algorithm, and the -0.35% / 22.34 vs 22.42 Mha figures, and its collinearity warning is operationally sound. Two corrections:

(1) "Not an independent observation of tile drainage" is too strong on both ends. The county input IS an observation — USDA Census of Agriculture farmer-reported tile acreage — and the paper reports genuine INDEPENDENT validation the claim omits entirely: 16,000 tile-drainage ground-truth points manually identified from ESRI multi-resolution aerial imagery (15 m / 1 m / 0.6 m / 0.3 m) across ten states, giving 86.03% overall accuracy for CONUS (13.97% omission), 82.7-93.6% across the tile-drained Midwest, and 91.1% for IOWA specifically on 5,253 ground-truth points, with >98% accuracy in poorly drained soils and errors concentrated in marginal drainage categories 3-5. For this project's Iowa-basin use case that is the number that matters, and it is good. AgTile-US should be described as a census-constrained downscaling that has been independently validated at 91.1% in Iowa, not as an unvalidated composite.

(2) The redundancy is exact WITHIN a county but not ACROSS counties. Because the county census acreage enters as a per-county calibration constant, two counties with identical SSURGO drainage-class and slope distributions and identical cropland fraction receive DIFFERENT tile fractions whenever their census acreages differ. So basin-aggregated AgTile fraction carries county-scale information that is not recoverable from SSURGO + slope + NLCD alone; it is not a pure function of them. Practical consequence, which strengthens rather than weakens the claim's advice: add AgTile fraction as a single static per-bucket feature and do NOT also add the SSURGO drainage-class histogram or mean slope as separate features — they are the ingredients, not independent evidence. Also note the product is BINARY extent (drained yes/no, "does not distinguish drainage intensity/spacing"), so it proxies drained AREA, not the drainage DENSITY the project brief names as the dominant Iowa hydrologic control.

These are AgTile-US tile-area vs USDA census tile-area differences (the downstream consequence), not the cropland-mask deficit (the cause). The actual state-level CROPLAND deficits reported are WV -92.00% and NM -27.45%. The numbers are exact and the direction is right; the label on them is wrong.

So the claim's conclusion that bias "should be modest for the core Iowa basins" is CORRECT and in fact conservative: the residual bias in the tile-belt is sub-percent at state aggregate, with the highest-quality validation of any region.

The paper supports higher false negatives in SSURGO categories 3-5, but says nothing about basin-level aggregate bias as a function of basin-mean drainage class, and nothing about how that would interact with a ranking model. Iowa's tile is overwhelmingly on categories 6-7 (poorly/very poorly drained Des Moines Lobe soils), the classes AgTile-US captures BEST. The "discriminating middle" framing is speculation.

result.correction:
The claim is directionally correct and its core technical assertions are verbatim-accurate, with one labeling error and two unsupported extrapolations.

The source is stronger than that - Iowa validation accuracy is 91.1% on 5,253 ground-truth points (the densest validation of any state), and the north-central tile belt as a whole shows tile-area difference vs USDA census of less than -0.25%. Iowa tile sits predominantly on categories 6-7, which AgTile-US captures best, so the practical exposure in our study region is small. (b) "larger for multi-state basin tails" has no support for OUR geography - none of the five flagged states (NM, WV, MS, OK, TX) is adjacent to or upstream of Iowa; Iowa's out-of-state tails run into MN, SD, NE, MO, IL, WI, and MN/IL/IN/OH are inside the <-0.25% good group.

It mainly reveals whether the NLCD cropland mask left enough area to place the mandated acreage - which is why mask-starved states blow up and Iowa does not. Treat it as a consistency check, not independent validation. The independent evidence is the 16,000-point ground-truth accuracy, and those points are spatially clustered (a third are in Iowa), not a random CONUS sample.

NET RECOMMENDATION UNCHANGED: this refutation attempt fails to disqualify AgTile-US for our use. It remains a free, static, 30 m, CONUS-wide, no-local-history-required between-site covariate - the exact profile of feature that has worked on this project - and its known weaknesses land outside the Iowa tile belt. Test it as a single basin-mean tile-fraction (optionally per distance bucket) feature under LOFO only, and pre-register that with 19 independent families the confidence interval on any between-site gain will be wide.

PROTOCOL: not applicable in the ML sense — this is a validation-against-ground-truth-points exercise (n~16,000 points, 5,253 in Iowa), not a train/test split. No leakage concern, but also no held-out-basin evidence.

The corresponding NLCD CROPLAND deficits for those two states are WV -92.00% and NM -27.45%, i.e. the claim has the two quantities swapped in magnitude and mislabeled. The reported effect-size line is therefore internally mixed.

The algorithm allocates cells iteratively "until the estimated tile drainage area exceeded the USDA census," then backs off in 0.1% slope increments. County totals are therefore approximately CONSERVED by construction wherever the mask is large enough to absorb them. In Iowa — 91.1% accuracy, no listed shortfall — the dominant error is spatial PLACEMENT of tile within a county, not county-aggregate under-allocation. New Mexico, West Virginia, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Texas are geographically irrelevant to any Iowa drainage basin. The paper also notes the problem states' "total tile drained area of these states is less than 0.11 Mha" — trivial. So "bias larger for multi-state basin tails" has no support.
(d) "WORST IN INTERMEDIATE DRAINAGE CLASS" IS UNQUANTIFIED. The paper says most omissions fall in categories 3-5 but reports NO category-stratified error rate. There is no number to propagate into a bias model. Iowa tile is concentrated on poorly/very-poorly drained soils (Des Moines Lobe, categories 1-2), so the cat 3-5 penalty applies to a minority of Iowa tile — and the 91.1% Iowa figure already includes it.
(e) UNMENTIONED, LARGER CAVEAT. The paper states "The average error in tile drainage estimates based on the Census of Agriculture 2017 is 19.8%." This census-input error applies to Iowa too and likely dominates the mask-induced bias for our basins. The claim omits it.

AgTile-US is 30 m, CONUS-wide, covers every state an Iowa basin reaches, and validates at 91.1% in Iowa — the best-validated state in the product. Deployment target is fine: it is a static raster, requires no local nitrate history and no gauge, so it works at an arbitrary map pin. There IS a soft circularity worth noting: the ground-truth points informed the slope threshold, so 86.03% is partly in-sample. Sample size is ample; the metric (point accuracy) is appropriate for a classification map.

DECISIVE METHODOLOGICAL FACT THE CLAIM OMITS: the model is AREA-CONSTRAINED to USDA county-level census tile totals. Cells are added in priority order of drainage class and slope "until the estimated tile drainage area exceeded the USDA census tile drainage area." CONUS-wide AgTile-US is −0.35% versus census — essentially unbiased by construction. It is calibrated, not systematically low. The five listed states underestimate only because the NLCD cropland mask exhausts available candidate cells before the county census total is reached; that is a corner case, not the general behavior.

(b) "Bias worst in basins with intermediate soil drainage class = precisely the discriminating middle for site ranking" is an unsupported inference, and it runs backwards for Iowa. The 13.97% miss rate is POINT-level false negatives, but the county area constraint means a missed cell is reallocated, not deleted — the failure mode is spatial MISALLOCATION within a county, not a low area total. And Iowa tile is concentrated in SSURGO classes 6–7 (poorly/very poorly drained: Des Moines Lobe, Clarion-Nicollet-Webster), which is where AgTile-US is most accurate, hence the 91.1%. The weak classes 3–5 are the drained/undrained margin at continental scale, not Iowa's discriminating range.
(c) The 20% slope cap is near-vacuous for Iowa cropland, which is almost entirely well below 20% slope, and the cap was derived empirically as the upper envelope of observed tile ground truth rather than imposed a priori.

AgTile-US is a static 30 m raster for 2017 covering all CONUS, so it is computable for an arbitrary ungauged map pin's NLDI-delineated basin with no local history and no gauge — exactly the static between-site geography class of feature that is the only thing that has worked on this project. It is immune to the n=19-families constraint on the feature-construction side (it is a covariate, not a fitted model). The n=19 constraint still binds on whether one new static feature can be shown to improve between-site ranking under LOFO — a single covariate against 19 effective units is a real but ordinary power problem, not a reason to skip it. result.correction:
The claim is accurate on every identifier and should be acted on, but four corrections matter, one of them material.

1. MATERIAL — the "no authentication / free for commercial use / shippable" chain is valid for Figshare and INVALID for the GEE path. The claim correctly establishes CC-BY 4.0 on the data, then attaches that to the Earth Engine delivery mechanism. Earth Engine is a separate licensing regime from the dataset: it requires a Google account and a registered Google Cloud project (authentication, contradicting "NO authentication" for that path), and Google's Earth Engine FAQ states it "is free for noncommercial use" while directing "commercial or operational applications" to paid Cloud pricing. A deployed public-facing product is an operational application. So AgTile-US-via-GEE is NOT free-and-unauthenticated for the shipped product; AgTile-US-via-Figshare is.

2. The GEE asset is an ee.Image (the catalog loads it as a single Image), not an ImageCollection — the claim's hedge resolves to Image. It is also a community mirror maintained under samapriya's sat-io project, not an official NCAR or Google-curated asset, so its persistence is not guaranteed by the data producer.

3. The "no local raster storage" framing is backwards for this deployment target. The CONUS GeoTIFF is 126 MB zipped — trivial to vendor. Local storage is strictly superior here: no auth, no EE quota, no per-request latency, no third-party runtime dependency, and it dodges correction (1) entirely. A 30 m reduceRegion over a large multi-state NLDI basin is a seconds-to-minutes call subject to EE timeouts, on the critical path of every map-pin request. RECOMMENDATION: bulk-download the GeoTIFF from Figshare and compute basin tile fraction locally with the existing basin-cell machinery. Reserve GEE for prototyping only.

4. Fitness for this project (the claim does not overstate, but the ceiling should be stated). Genuine strengths: it is CONUS-wide, so unlike the Iowa-truncated CDL/N-surplus inner join it correctly covers the multi-state portions of the largest basins — it fixes that known under-counting bug for this one variable. It is binary at 30 m, so "mean over basin cells" is a clean, well-defined tile fraction. And it is a purely STATIC between-site covariate, which is precisely the class that has worked on this project (geometry + static geography) rather than the temporal class that has failed seven times. Iowa validation accuracy is 91.1%.

Caveats to carry: (a) n=19 FAMILIES — this variable moves only between sites, so it is evaluated against ~19 effective independent units. Add ONE basin-wide tile fraction first, not three distance-bucketed copies; the bucketed version spends three degrees of freedom on a between-site term that has ~19 points, and the riparian-bucket result (CLF +0.039 PR-AUC, REG worse) shows bucketing static geography is not reliably free. (b) It is a MODELED product that downscales county-level Ag Census totals using NLCD cropland + slope + SSURGO drainage class, not observed tile locations. It is therefore a soils-plus-cropland-plus-census composite and may be partly collinear with existing CDL crop-fraction features — expect a smaller incremental gain than "the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa" suggests. (c) It is single-year 2017 held constant across 2008-2026. This superficially resembles the known failure "broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward (-0.166)", but differs in kind: N surplus is a genuinely time-varying flux, whereas tile infrastructure is near-static on decadal timescales, so a constant value is defensible. That prior failure is still a reason to test rather than assume.

The claim is correct in substance and verdict but wrong in three details, none of which reverse it.

The ablation should (a) report per-distance-bucket tile fraction as well as basin-total, (b) report LOFO fold-level spread rather than a point estimate, and (c) check variance inflation against lat/lon before interpreting.

The claim's core assertion stands: this paper cannot be cited for any effect size linking tile fraction to between-site nitrate variance. That evidence must come from separate Corn Belt water-quality literature, which this source does not supply.

result.correction:
Six corrections. None overturn the core claim; two matter operationally.

1. COLUMN NAMES ARE WRONG. Actual header of TILES92_CONUS.txt: COMID,CAT_TILES92,CAT_NODATA,ACC_TILES92,ACC_NODATA,TOT_TILES92,TOT_NODATA. The claim's "CAT_TILES_Early90s" / "ACC_TILES_Early90s" / "TOT_TILES_Early90s" do not exist. Any ingest code written from the claim will KeyError. (TILES_Early90s is the SPARROW-model naming, not this release's.)

2. THE -9999 SENTINEL NEVER OCCURS IN THIS TABLE, AND NODATA IS INFORMATIONALLY EMPTY. grep -c -- "-9999" over all 2.7M rows returns 0. Computed column ranges: CAT_TILES92 [0.0, 100.0], ACC_TILES92 [0.0, 100.0], TOT_TILES92 [0.0, 100.0], and CAT_NODATA / ACC_NODATA / TOT_NODATA are all identically 0.0000 (min = max = 0.0, zero rows with NODATA > 0). This directly undercuts the claim's headline transferability argument. The claim says the NODATA column "directly addresses the project's known inner-join undercount for out-of-state basin area, because the NODATA column reports coverage explicitly instead of silently dropping cells." For the tile table that is vacuous — NODATA is a constant zero and carries no coverage diagnostic. The source raster was evidently zero-filled outside its footprint, so a catchment with no NRI drainage data and a catchment with genuinely 0% tile drainage are indistinguishable. The argument may hold for other tables in the release; it must be re-checked per table before being relied on.

3. FILE SIZES AND FORMAT. Zip is 12,107,588 bytes (11.5 MiB), not "13 MB". Uncompressed is 139,700,008 bytes (133 MiB), not "154 MB". The member file is TILES92_CONUS.txt (comma-delimited, .txt extension), not a .csv.

4. "EVERY TABLE SUPPLIES THREE SPATIAL AGGREGATIONS" IS FALSE AS A UNIVERSAL. The parent summary states FOUR spatial components, not three: reach catchments, riparian buffer zones, network-accumulated catchments, network-accumulated riparian buffers. Several child items ship only one aggregation: the ClimGRID water-balance items are split into separate items per routing type ("per Flowline Catchment" / "Using Divergence Routing" / "Using Total Upstream Routing"), and riparian items (e.g. "NLCD 2001 Percent Imperviousness in 100 Meter Riparian Buffer") are buffer-only. Others split CAT/ACC/TOT into separate zips within one item — e.g. "Select Topographic Attributes: Select Basin Attributes" ships BASIN_CHAR_CAT_CONUS.zip (50.4 MB), BASIN_CHAR_ACC_CONUS.zip (55.0 MB), BASIN_CHAR_TOT_CONUS.zip (57.2 MB) as three separate downloads. Budget for per-item schema discovery; do not assume one zip = one 7-column table.

5. CC0 IS NOT STATED ON THE RECORD. The ScienceBase JSON `rights` field is null for both the parent and the tile item; no occurrence of "CC0", "Creative Commons", "public domain", or "license" anywhere in either JSON or in the FGDC XML. The XML carries only a liability disclaimer and "Use of this data is considered acceptance of the limitations of this data." The data are almost certainly free to use (USGS-authored, 17 U.S.C. 105), but "License: CC0 1.0 Universal" is an inference the cited source does not support. Cite it as a USGS public-domain data release, not CC0.

6. "ALL ATTRIBUTES ARE STATIC SINGLE-EPOCH SNAPSHOTS" IS FALSE — and the truth is better for this project. Many child items are multi-epoch: NLCD 2019 version supplies 2001/2004/2006/2008/2011/2013/2016/2019; housing density 1940-2010; block-level population density 1990/2000/2010; CDL as separate 2012/2013/2014 items; monthly PRISM and ClimGRID series. That means some of these can be used as slowly-varying covariates, not only as static ones.

ADDITIONAL FINDINGS THE CLAIM OMITS, ALL MATERIAL TO THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET:

A. THE PIN LOOKUP IS SIMPLER THAN THE CLAIM SAYS. The claim hedges "provided the pin's basin can be decomposed into NHDPlusV2 COMIDs." Not needed. TOT_ and ACC_ are already the accumulated upstream value at that reach, so the deployment path is: NLDI resolves the pin to one outlet COMID (this repo already does exactly that — /Users/isaac/dev/sustag/deploy/build_virtual_basin.py and /Users/isaac/dev/sustag/src/build/_make_basins.py both already call NLDI for the enclosing COMID), then one hash lookup into the table. No basin decomposition, no zonal statistics, no local history. This is a genuinely deployment-compatible static feature source — the strongest part of the claim.

B. THE TILE LAYER IS 1992 AND COARSE — a serious caveat the claim does not mention. FGDC process step: source is "Downloaded the source data from http://water.usgs.gov/GIS/metadata/usgswrd/XML/nri92_cp606.xml", i.e. Wieczorek (2004) "Estimated area of artificial drainage for the year 1992", derived from the 1992 National Resources Inventory Conservation Practice 606 — an expanded statistical sample, not a mapped drainage network. The abstract's own hierarchy of results makes the dependence explicit — the copula wins under "perfect information", wins at "partially gaged sites with several years of available data", and degrades to "competitive albeit nondominating" for truly ungaged sites once realistic FDC/correlation estimation error is introduced. That final case is our case, and it is the one where the method is admitted not to dominate.
