result.evidence:
PAPER IDENTIFIED AND PARTIALLY CONFIRMED. Worland, S.C., Steinschneider, S., Asquith, W., Knight, R., Wieczorek, M. (2019), "Prediction and Inference of Flow Duration Curves Using Multioutput Neural Networks," Water Resources Research 55(8), 6850-6868, doi:10.1029/2018WR024463. Wiley full text is paywalled (HTTP 402 on /doi/full, 403 on /doi/pdfdirect and /doi/pdf even with a browser UA; USGS Pubs Warehouse 403; CORE 403). Verbatim abstract obtained from the Crossref API (api.crossref.org/works/10.1029/2018WR024463), and the authors' complete analysis code obtained from the public repo github.com/scworland/restore-2018 (this is the paper's repo: same authors, same "Southeastern United States" covariate data release, targets named mnn_quantile_est / snn_quantile_est / mnn_lmom_est in predict_fdc.yml).

CONFIRMED BY VERBATIM ABSTRACT: "We develop multioutput neural network models to predict flow-duration curves (FDCs) in 9,203 ungaged locations in the Southeastern United States for six decades between 1950 and 2009." Also confirmed: multiple response variables in the output layer corresponding to individual FDC quantiles; combined loss enforcing monotonicity; dropout for posterior-predictive distributions; LIME for interpretation; MNN beats single-output NN.

REFUTATION 1 - THE SPLIT PROTOCOL IS WRONG, AND THIS IS DISQUALIFYING UNDER RULE 1. The claim states "spatial-holdout". The abstract says only "test model performance under cross validation" - no spatial language. The authors' code is explicit: scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R, function sw_k_foldcv, does `N <- nrow(data); set.seed(1); indices <- sample(1:N); folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)`, called from build_mnn_quantile.R as `sw_k_foldcv(build_model, k=10, epochs=500, batch_size=100, ...)`. That is RANDOM 10-fold CV over ROWS, not over gages or regions. The rows are gage-DECADES: each gage contributes up to 6 rows (1950,1960,1970,1980,1990,2000) whose static basin characteristics are near-identical. Random row-wise folds therefore place the same gage's other decades in the training set - textbook pseudoreplication/level-memorization leakage, exactly the failure mode Rule 1 exists to catch. The identical random-fold code is repeated in dropout_runs.R for the uncertainty quantification. No leave-one-gage-out, leave-one-region-out, or PUB-protocol appears anywhere in the repo's neural-net path (a separate GAM path does produce all_gage_looest_*.feather leave-one-out files, but those are Asquith's L-moment GAMs, not the MNN). Conclusion: these numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820. The claim's headline framing - "applied to 9,203 ungaged pour points" - describes the PREDICTION step, not the validation step, and the claim conflates the two.

REFUTATION 2 - "15 quantiles" IS WRONG FOR THE PUBLISHED MODEL. build_mnn_quantile.R and build_snn_quantile.R both use a 27-quantile vector f27 = f0.02, f0.05, f0.1, f0.2, f0.5, f01, f02, f05, f10, f20, f25, f30, f40, f50, f60, f70, f75, f80, f90, f95, f98, f99, f99.5, f99.8, f99.9, f99.95, f99.98, with `loss_weights <- c(rep(1,10), rep(1e-2,17))`. A 15-quantile vector exists ONLY in scripts/Worland/keras_training/cloudml/two_layer_keras_model.R, an early Google CloudML hyperparameter-tuning script (dated by its job IDs to June 2018) that uses plain `validation_split = 0.25` and is not the production model.

REFUTATION 3 - "688 streamgages" IS UNSUBSTANTIATED AND CONTRADICTED BY THE AUTHORS' OWN DATA RELEASE. I downloaded the released training tables: scibase/gage/all_gage_covariates.csv = 5,736 rows, 956 unique site_no, 949 unique comid, exactly 956 per decade x 6 decades. scibase/gage/all_gage_flow_stats.csv = 2,804 rows, 956 unique site_no (1950:363, 1960:485, 1970:484, 1980:453, 1990:455, 2000:564). The repo's data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt independently states 1,290 screened gages overall and "962 streamgages" with complete 1950-2000 decades. Nothing yields 688. The effective training set is ~2,804 gage-decade rows from ~956 gages - which also means the model was fit on ~2,804 rows, not 688 units.

REFUTATION 4 - "40 basin characteristics" IS UNVERIFIED AND LOOKS LIKE A LIKELY TRANSCRIPTION ARTIFACT. The predictor block in code is `select(d, major:flood_storage, -basin_area)`; the released covariate file has 48 columns of which 44 are non-ID (comid, site_no, huc12, decade excluded), including categorical geology/ecoregion/physiography factors coerced with as.numeric(as.factor(.)). So "~40" is plausible in magnitude but I could not confirm the exact figure. Note that "40" also appears in the code as a HIDDEN-LAYER WIDTH (`layer_dense(units = 40)` in build_mnn_quantile.R; `flag_integer("dense_units1", 40, ...)` in the tuning script) - a plausible source for a garbled paraphrase.

REFUTATION 5 - THE CLAIM'S "NO EXACT ERROR METRIC" ADMISSION IS ITSELF GROUNDS FOR REFUSAL UNDER RULE 2. There is no NSE/RMSE/R2 to compare. The one quantitative-direction result recoverable from the verbatim abstract cuts AGAINST the claim's usefulness to us: "basin characteristics are most useful for predicting smaller quantiles, whereas bias terms from neighboring quantiles are most informative for predicting higher quantiles." That is a published NEGATIVE result for attribute-only regionalization of the UPPER TAIL: for high quantiles the LIME surrogates were dominated by the intercept/bias rather than by basin attributes, i.e. static attributes carried little information about the extreme end of the distribution. Our target - violation = daily max >= 10 mg/L at a 0.263 base rate - IS an upper-tail exceedance. The paper's own finding predicts that attribute-only prediction of our tail will be weakest exactly where we need it.

TRANSFERABILITY ASSESSMENT (independent of the above, all against the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target):
(a) The claim's structural analogy is HALF right. The MNN input side is genuinely attribute-only - no local observations, no gauged neighbor, no discharge at the target - so it does clear the deployment-target bar in principle, and NLDI is even used in the repo (nldi_funs.R). But the TARGET is a DECADAL flow-duration curve: one row per gage-decade, a 10-year aggregate distribution. It is not a daily time series and contains no timing. Mapped onto our decomposition, it addresses ONLY the between-site level term (our between_rate_r2 0.24 / between_r2 0.21), and provides no mechanism for the daily "when" that our model already does well. Adopting it means abandoning daily resolution, which the product requires.
(b) SAMPLE SIZE, RULE 5. Even accepting the smaller of the candidate counts, the evidence base is ~956 gages / ~2,804 independent-ish units. Our n=19 independent basin families is ~50x smaller than the gage count and ~150x smaller than the row count. A ~40-input, 2-hidden-layer (28 and 40 units), 27-output network is on the order of 2,500+ parameters; at n=19 effective units this is hopeless. The claim's own NOTE concedes this, which is to its credit, but conceding infeasibility does not make the cited evidence supportive - it makes the citation inert for our decision.
(c) DOMAIN. Southeastern US / Gulf RESTORE region: humid, forested-to-mixed, no artificial subsurface tile drainage. The covariate set (bfi, twi, rdx, soller surficial geology, statsgo, ecoregion, physiography, dams/flood_storage, NLCD classes, ppt/temp mean+sd) contains nothing analogous to tile drainage density or nitrogen surplus. Streamflow FDCs are also far more strongly attribute-controlled (area and precipitation alone explain most of the variance; note the code divides all quantiles by basin_area before log10, i.e. the dominant scaling is removed a priori) than nitrate concentration is. Transferring an "attributes predict the distribution" conclusion from unit-area streamflow to nitrate concentration is not supported by anything in this paper.
(d) DEPLOYMENT. Nothing here requires the target site's own observations - that part of the claim is accurate and is the claim's one genuinely useful content. But it is also the trivial part: our current model is already attribute-plus-weather with no local history.

BOTTOM LINE: the paper exists and 9,203 / six decades / 1950-2009 / multioutput-NN / attribute-only-input are correct, but the two numbers that would make it evidence for us are wrong or unverifiable (protocol is random row-wise 10-fold CV with same-gage leakage, NOT spatial holdout; 15 quantiles is actually 27; 688 gages is contradicted by the authors' released 956 gages / 2,804 gage-decades; 40 predictors unverified and possibly confused with a hidden-layer width), and there is no retrievable error metric of any kind. Under Rules 1, 2, and the stated default, this is refuted.

Key artifacts fetched: verbatim Crossref abstract; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scworland/restore-2018/master/scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R ; .../build_mnn_quantile.R ; .../build_snn_quantile.R ; .../combine_all_vars.R ; .../dropout_runs.R ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scworland/restore-2018/master/predict_fdc.yml ; scibase/gage/all_gage_covariates.csv and all_gage_flow_stats.csv (downloaded and counted locally); data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt. Underlying covariate data release: Crowley-Ornelas et al. (2019), "Summary of basin characteristics for National Hydrography Dataset, version 2 catchments in the Southeastern United States, 1950-2010," USGS data release, doi:10.5066/P9KXTDU4 (free, public).
result.correction: If this citation is kept at all, it must be restated as: Worland et al. (2019, WRR 55(8):6850-6868, doi:10.1029/2018WR024463) fit multioutput neural networks mapping ~40 static basin characteristics to 27 (not 15) decadal flow-duration-curve quantiles, trained on roughly 2,804 gage-decade records from ~956 (not 688) USGS streamgages in the Southeastern US, validated by RANDOM 10-fold cross-validation over gage-decade ROWS (set.seed(1); sample(1:N)) - NOT a spatial holdout, and subject to same-gage leakage because each gage contributes up to six near-identical-attribute rows - then applied to predict FDCs at 9,203 ungaged HUC12 pour points for six decades 1950-2009. No NSE/RMSE/R2 could be retrieved (paywalled). Its cross-validation numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820. Its one directly relevant substantive finding is a NEGATIVE one for us: per the verbatim abstract, basin characteristics were informative mainly for the SMALL quantiles, while the HIGH quantiles were driven by neighboring-quantile bias terms rather than by attributes - i.e. attribute-only regionalization was weakest in the upper tail, which is precisely where our >=10 mg/L exceedance target lives. The setup is attribute-only on the input side (genuinely deployable at an ungauged map pin, no local history, no gauged neighbor), but the output is a decadal distribution, not a daily prediction, so at best it is a template for our between-site level term only. At n=19 independent basin families a ~40-input/27-output network with two hidden layers is infeasible by roughly two orders of magnitude in sample size.

result.evidence:
PAPER IDENTITY CONFIRMED. Crossref + OpenAlex + Semantic Scholar on DOI 10.1029/2018WR024463 all resolve to: Worland, Steinschneider, Asquith, Knight, Wieczorek (2019), "Prediction and Inference of Flow Duration Curves Using Multioutput Neural Networks," Water Resources Research 55(8):6850-6868. Wiley full text is Cloudflare/402-blocked; no repository copy exists (OpenAlex `any_repository_has_fulltext: false`). I therefore verified against the AUTHORS' OWN CODE AND PROJECT DOCUMENTATION, which is primary and in some ways better than the paper text: GitHub `scworland/restore-2018` (the USGS RESTORE FY2018 project this paper came out of).

VERBATIM ABSTRACT (via OpenAlex inverted index) confirms only: "multioutput neural network models to predict flow-duration curves (FDCs) in 9,203 ungaged locations in the Southeastern United States for six decades between 1950 and 2009", combined loss enforcing "monotonically increasing quantiles", dropout for posterior-predictive distributions, and "test model performance under cross validation". The abstract contains NO gage count, NO predictor count, NO quantile count, and NO error metric.

REFUTATION 1 — THE SPLIT PROTOCOL IS NOT A SPATIAL HOLDOUT (decisive; this is the load-bearing error). `scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R`, function `sw_k_foldcv`, lines 15-18:
    N <- nrow(data)
    set.seed(1)
    indices <- sample(1:N)
    folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)
This is a RANDOM k=10 fold over ROWS of a site-decade table, with no grouping by `site_no`. Each gage contributes up to 6 decade-rows (1950-2000), and `build_mnn_quantile.R` returns results keyed `distinct(site_no, decade, variable)`. So the SAME GAGE appears in both training and test folds in different decades. That is textbook pseudoreplication / spatial leakage: the reported CV skill measures interpolation to a new DECADE at a LARGELY-SEEN GAGE, not transfer to an ungaged basin. The production model in `build_final_fdc_model.R` uses Keras `validation_split=0.1`, which takes the LAST 10% of rows — also non-spatial. The 9,203 HUC12 pour-point predictions in `predict_fdc_all.R` are pure unvalidated extrapolation; there is no held-out-ungaged evaluation anywhere in the workflow. Under our Rule 1 this number is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820, and the claim's "Reported split protocol: spatial-holdout" is simply false.

REFUTATION 2 — 27 QUANTILES, NOT 15. Both `build_mnn_quantile.R` and `build_final_fdc_model.R` define an explicit vector literally named `f27` with 27 entries (f0.02, f0.05, f0.1, f0.2, f0.5, f01, f02, f05, f10, f20, f25, f30, f40, f50, f60, f70, f75, f80, f90, f95, f98, f99, f99.5, f99.8, f99.9, f99.95, f99.98), and `loss_weights <- c(rep(1,10), rep(1e-2,17))` (10+17=27). `predict_fdc_all.R` confirms: `viol <- sum(yhat$viol)/(nrow(yhat) * 27)`.

REFUTATION 3 — ~956-962 GAGES, NOT 688. `data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt` (project's own documentation): "there are 962 streamgages of the original 1,290 for which at least one complete decade of the six decades listed exists, and 2,816 decades are represented." I downloaded `scibase/gage/all_gage_covariates.csv`: 5,736 rows x 48 columns, 956 unique `site_no`, 6 unique `decade` (956 x 6 = 5,736 exactly). Note `combine_all_vars.R` already applies `drop_na()` before this file is written, so no further row loss. The effective modeling set is ~2,816 site-decades over ~950-962 gages. The figure 688 is unsourced and does not appear in any retrieved primary material.

REFUTATION 4 — NO EFFECT SIZE EXISTS. The claim itself concedes no NSE/RMSE/R2 could be retrieved, and I could not retrieve one either. Under Rule 2 the claim therefore carries zero actionable content: it cannot support any inference about how well attribute-to-distribution regionalization actually performs. "Design and counts" without a metric, where the counts are wrong and the protocol is misreported, is not usable evidence.

PARTIAL — "40 basin characteristics" is plausible but unconfirmed. The covariate table has 48 columns of which ~42 are basin attributes (minus comid/site_no/huc12/decade/lat/lon), and the model selects the contiguous block `select(d, major:flood_storage, -basin_area)`, whose exact width I cannot pin without the .feather. Caution: 40 is ALSO the width of the second hidden layer (`layer_dense(units = 40, activation="relu")`), a very plausible source of a garbled full-text-fragment read.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR PROJECT — fails on four counts:
(a) n. The real evidence base is ~956 gages / 2,816 site-decades, so our 19 independent basin families is ~50x smaller, not the 36x the claim states. The architecture (40 inputs -> dense 28 -> dropout 0.27 -> dense 40 -> dropout 0.70 -> 27 separate linear heads) has on the order of 2-3k parameters. Utterly infeasible at n=19.
(b) The paper provides NO evidence for the one thing the claim wants it for. Because CV was random over rows, the study never demonstrates ungaged-basin transfer. Citing it as support for "arbitrary Iowa map pin works" would import exactly the leaky protocol our CV design was built to avoid — the paper made the very mistake our 19-family grouping prevents.
(c) Target mismatch flatters the paper. Y is `log10((q + 0.001) / basin_area)`, i.e. area-normalized specific discharge. Basin area is a near-deterministic predictor of streamflow magnitude, so much of the apparent attribute-to-distribution skill is the area scaling baked into the response transform. Nitrate CONCENTRATION has no analogous normalizer; our between-site level problem has no free ride of this kind.
(d) The paper's own headline finding is a MILD NEGATIVE for this application: "basin characteristics are most useful for predicting smaller quantiles, whereas bias terms from neighboring quantiles are most informative for predicting higher quantiles." Static basin attributes were LEAST informative at the HIGH quantiles. Our target is a high-quantile exceedance (daily max >= 10 mg/L, top ~26%). So the study's own result argues that static attributes degrade precisely in the regime we care about.

SALVAGEABLE (worth passing on despite refutation): (1) The multioutput monotone-quantile architecture — one shared trunk, many quantile heads, joint loss enforcing monotonicity — is genuinely attribute-only and needs no local history, so it is structurally deployment-compatible even though it cannot be trained at n=19 in this form. (2) More actionable: the repo is a concrete free inventory of NHDPlus-accumulated static basin attributes we do NOT currently have and which speak directly to our between-site deficit — `bfi` (base-flow index), `twi` (topographic wetness index), `rdx`, `soller` (surficial geology), `aquifers`, `bedperm` (bedrock permeability), `hlr` (hydrologic landscape regions), `physio`, `ecol3`, `strm_dens` (stream density), `sinuosity`, `flood_storage`/`nid_storage` (dam storage). These are free from NHDPlus/EPA StreamCat, cover the full CONUS (so they handle our multi-state basin portions), and are static — matching our project's finding that the only wins came from geometry and static geography. That is a real lead, but it is a lead from the repo's attribute list, NOT support for the claim as written.
result.correction: Worland et al. (2019), WRR 55(8):6850-6868, doi:10.1029/2018WR024463, trained multioutput neural networks on approximately 956-962 USGS streamgages (~2,816 site-decade records) in the Southeastern US, predicting 27 (not 15) FDC quantiles simultaneously from a block of roughly 40 static basin characteristics, then applied the fitted model to 9,203 ungaged HUC12 pour points for six decades 1950-2009. The counts 688 and 15 are wrong. Critically, the validation protocol is NOT a spatial holdout: the authors' own code (scworland/restore-2018, keras_funs.R, sw_k_foldcv) performs random 10-fold CV over ROWS of a site-decade table with no grouping by site, so the same gage appears in train and test in different decades — pseudoreplication. The 9,203 ungaged predictions are never validated. No error metric could be retrieved from any source. The paper is therefore correctly described as an attribute-only regionalization DESIGN, but it supplies no protocol-valid evidence that such a design transfers to a truly ungaged location, and its own conclusion — that static basin characteristics are most informative for LOW quantiles and least for HIGH quantiles — argues against its usefulness for our high-quantile exceedance target.

No at-site streamflow enters the predictor matrix.

THE ONE ERROR — SPLIT PROTOCOL IS NOT SPATIAL HOLDOUT. util_funs.R::sw_k_foldcv, verbatim:
    N <- nrow(data)
    set.seed(1)
    indices <- sample(1:N)
    folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)
This is RANDOM k-fold over ROWS. Rows are gage-decades, and 688 gages supply 2,009 rows (mean 2.9 decades/gage; decade counts 1950:257, 1960:343, 1970:346, 1980:325, 1990:341, 2000:397). With k=5 (the MNN call: sw_k_foldcv(build_model, k=5, epochs=400, batch_size=467)) a held-out row's OWN GAGE is also in the training fold unless all its sibling decades land in the same fold — for a 3-decade gage that probability is (1/5)^2 = 4%, so ~96% of test rows have their own gage represented in training. There is no grouping by site, basin, HUC, or region anywhere in the archive. The single-output comparison model uses k=3, same random splitter. tune_layers.R uses validation_split=0.1 (Keras tail split), also non-spatial. This is exactly the leakage mode our rule 1 forbids comparing to LOFO 0.820: the net can memorize a gage's area-normalized flow LEVEL from its other decades, so the reported CV measures temporal/decadal interpolation at KNOWN gages, not transfer to unknown basins.

METRICS: no NSE/RMSE/R2 exists in the retrievable material. Keras loss is MSE with metrics="mae" on log10(q/area); plot_funs.R contains no skill-metric function. The r2 at fdc_est.R:416 is fit2$dev.ratio of the LIME local glmnet SURROGATE (explanation fidelity), NOT predictive skill. The claim's "no exact error metric could be retrieved" is accurate and I independently reproduce that finding.

NO VALIDATION OF THE UNGAGED APPLICATION: the model deployed to the 9,203 HUC12s is trained on all 688 gages and its predictions are never checked against held-out basins. ScienceBase adds an unflagged extrapolation caveat, verbatim: "The neural network was trained using streamflow data at sites with records that contained only non-zero streamflow values. However, the model was used to make predictions for every HUC12 pour point. Some of these predictions are likely for sites that have streamflow values equal to zero." The 688 training gages are by construction perennial; the 9,203 targets include intermittent streams. That is an acknowledged, unquantified domain shift.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR PROJECT — largely negative:
1. n: 688 gages / 2,009 records vs our 19 independent basin families. 36x fewer units, as the claim itself flags. The 40->35->31->15 net has ~3,300 parameters fit on 2,009 rows (~0.6 rows/param, already thin); at n=19 families it is not merely underpowered, it is unfittable. Correctly flagged by the claim.
2. Target mismatch: the response is a DECADAL FDC — a 10-year aggregate distribution, one row per gage-decade, area-normalized. It contains zero daily dynamics. So the analogue is our BETWEEN-site term ONLY; the paper offers no evidence at all about daily event timing. It does not address our primary target (daily binary violation >= 10 mg/L) and gives no classification metric.
3. Domain: RESTORE study area is the Gulf Coast states (per gis/GulfStates.zip, restore_bnd.zip), coastal-plain hydrology, NOT tile-drained Corn Belt. Predictor set has BFI, TWI, dam storage, aquifer/bedrock permeability classes — none of which are in our feature set, and it has no tile-drainage proxy either.
4. Data-availability asymmetry: FDCs are computable at every USGS gage from free daily discharge, which is why n=688 was reachable. Nitrate concentration-duration curves require multi-year nitrate records, which is precisely the scarcity (19 families) that caps our project. The method's feasibility rests on the very abundance we lack.
5. Deployment-target verdict: structurally the setup IS right for an arbitrary ungauged map pin (static attributes in, distribution out, no local history). That structural point in the claim is correct and is the claim's real value. But the paper supplies NO validated ungauged-basin skill number, so it cannot be cited as evidence that such regionalization WORKS — only that it has been ATTEMPTED at scale and published.

VERDICT: refuted=false. Every factual count is exact and the structural characterization is right; the claim is wrong only on the protocol field, which I correct below. Under rule 1 the correction is load-bearing: this paper yields no number comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and must not be cited as spatial-holdout evidence.
result.correction:
The claim's counts and design are all exactly correct and independently reproducible from the authors' own model archive (688 gages, 40 basin characteristics, 15 FDC quantiles, 9,203 ungaged HUC12 pour points, six decades 1950-2009, attribute-only predictors, multioutput NN). Two corrections:

(1) THE SPLIT PROTOCOL IS NOT SPATIAL HOLDOUT — change the field to "random k-fold, site-level leakage". The released util_funs.R uses `set.seed(1); indices <- sample(1:N); folds <- cut(indices, breaks=k)` — random 5-fold over gage-decade ROWS with no grouping by site, basin, or region. The 688 gages contribute 2,009 gage-decade rows (~2.9 decades/gage), so ~96% of held-out rows have their own gage present in the training fold. The reported cross-validation therefore measures decadal interpolation at KNOWN gages, not transfer to unknown basins, and is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 under rule 1. The 9,203-point application is genuine spatial extrapolation but is entirely unvalidated — no held-out-basin skill number is reported anywhere in the paper or its data release.

(2) The correct unit of analysis is 2,009 gage-decade records from 688 gages, not 688 independent samples — the effective independent-unit count is 688, and pseudoreplication across decades is exactly what the random folds fail to control.

Additional caveats worth carrying: the target is a DECADAL area-normalized flow-duration curve (a 10-year aggregate climatology), so this paper speaks only to our between-site term and says nothing about daily event timing or about binary exceedance classification; the study area is the Gulf Coast RESTORE region, not tile-drained Corn Belt; and ScienceBase discloses that the 688 training gages were screened to perennial (non-zero-flow) records while predictions were emitted for all 9,203 HUC12s including intermittent streams — an acknowledged, unquantified domain shift. Use this citation as evidence that attribute-to-distribution regionalization is a published, structurally valid framing for an ungauged map pin — NOT as evidence of its out-of-sample accuracy, and not as a method importable at n=19 families (a ~3,300-parameter network fit on 2,009 rows does not scale down 36x).

result.correction: Towler et al. 2023 (HESS 27:1809) is correctly cited as to study, n=5,390 USGS gauges, period 1983-2016, region definition (Falcone aggregated ecoregions, not HUC2), metric (KGE, not NSE), and the direction of the result (Central is the worst region; NWMv2.1 exceeds NHMv1.0 by ~0.08-0.10 KGE). result.evidence:
Verified against the primary source by downloading the publisher PDF (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/27/1809/2023/hess-27-1809-2023.pdf) and extracting raw text with pdftotext -layout, rather than relying on model summarization (two WebFetch summarization passes returned three mutually inconsistent versions of the KGE table: 0.42/0.37 and 0.45/0.38; only the extracted text is authoritative).

CONFIRMED: Towler et al. 2023, HESS 27:1809-1825, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023. 5390 USGS gauges, daily streamflow, 1 Oct 1983 - 31 Dec 2016 (~33 yr), minimum 8 years / 2920 daily observations per site. Models compared are NWMv2.1 (WRF-Hydro) and NHMv1.0 (PRMS). Regions are combinations of Falcone (2011) aggregated ecoregions.

REFUTED ON NUMBERS: Table 4 ("Median values for each region") gives Central NWMv2.1 KGE = 0.45 and Central NHMv1.0 KGE = 0.33. The claim's "0.40 vs 0.29" is wrong on both terms. The value 0.29 is the West/NHMv1.0 cell, so the claim appears to have read the wrong row. Full Table 4 KGE: West NHMv1.0 0.29 / NWMv2.1 0.32; Central NHMv1.0 0.33 / NWMv2.1 0.45; Southeast NHMv1.0 0.48 / NWMv2.1 0.56; Northeast NHMv1.0 0.63 / NWMv2.1 0.65. Table 4 also reports r, rSD and PBIAS by region (Central NWMv2.1: r 0.71, rSD 0.87, PBIAS 4.4; Central NHMv1.0: r 0.68, rSD 0.78, PBIAS -18).

QUOTE 1 EXACT: "for both models in the Central region, relatively poor performance is concentrated along the plains areas that span from the high plains (i.e., North Dakota) vertically down through the center of the CONUS" - and the paper continues "(i.e., South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, and Texas)".

QUOTE 2 MISQUOTED: paper reads "Performance is more mixed as one moves further east in the Central region (e.g., around the Great Lakes)", not "performance is most mixed".

SPLIT PROTOCOL MISREPORTED (in the claim's own favor): the claim records "temporal-holdout". The paper states at p.1819: "the calibration periods of the models differed, and both overlapped with the evaluation period used in this study." NWMv2.1 calibrated 14 soil/vegetation/baseflow parameters to streamflow in 1378 gauged, predominantly natural-flow basins over water years 2008-2013, with WY2014-2016 for validation, then used a hydrologic-similarity strategy to regionalize parameters to remaining basins. NHMv1.0 calibrated to observed gauged streamflow at 1417 gauge locations using odd water years 1981-2010. Both calibration windows fall inside the 1983-2016 evaluation window, so this is a retrospective whole-period evaluation that is partly in-sample, NOT a temporal holdout. This strengthens rather than weakens the claim's falsifiable implication: 0.45 is an optimistic ceiling on gauged-location skill.

n IS AVAILABLE, contrary to the claim's "Central region subset size not stated": Figure 1 caption gives Central n = 1450, West n = 1510, Northeast n = 1218, Southeast n = 1212. Classification: reference n = 1115, non-reference (human-impacted) n = 4274, one undesignated. By region, Central holds 26% (370) of NWMv2.1's "underperforming" sites, i.e. those with KGE worse than an average-day-of-year climatology benchmark; 90-93% of underperforming sites are human-impacted.

CAVEAT CONFIRMED BUT UNDERSTATED: the paper reports only four broad Falcone-ecoregion aggregates, with no HUC2 breakdown and no NSE by region, so an Iowa/HUC-07 figure is genuinely not obtainable. However "Central 0.45" is a poor Iowa proxy in a direction that cuts AGAINST the claim's framing: the paper localizes poor Central performance to the high-plains north-south band (ND/SD/NE/KS/TX) and places Iowa in the "more mixed... further east" zone, so Iowa's true value is unresolved and could exceed 0.45.

TRANSFERABILITY: the gauged-vs-ungauged asymmetry is real and supported - evaluation is at gauged locations, both models used gauge data for calibration, and NWMv2.1 reaches non-calibration basins only via similarity-based parameter regionalization, so an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin sits in the regionalized (weaker) tier. But two inferential gaps remain, and neither is measured by this paper: (a) KGE on daily streamflow does not directly quantify a derived feature's value for recovering a between-site nitrate LEVEL term (between_r2 0.21) - the "weak instrument" step is an argument, not a result; (b) nothing here addresses the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint, which governs whether any new static/dynamic covariate can be exploited at all. The paper's own Central-region PBIAS (NWMv2.1 +4.4%, NHMv1.0 -18%) and rSD < 1 also indicate volume/variability errors that would propagate into any load- or concentration-style derived feature.
result.correction: The claim is directionally correct and its central inference survives, but two of three headline numbers and the split protocol are wrong. Corrected statement: In Towler et al. 2023 (HESS 27:1809-1825, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023), an evaluation of NWM v2.1 and NHM v1.0 retrospective daily streamflow against 5,390 USGS gauges over 1 Oct 1983 - 31 Dec 2016, the Central region (n = 1,450 gauges, defined by Falcone 2011 aggregated ecoregions, not HUC2) had a median KGE of 0.45 for NWMv2.1 and 0.33 for NHMv1.0 - NOT 0.40 and 0.29 (0.29 is the West/NHMv1.0 value). The second quotation should read "Performance is more mixed as one moves further east in the Central region", not "most mixed". The protocol is NOT a temporal holdout: the paper states both models' calibration periods overlapped the evaluation period (NWMv2.1 calibrated WY2008-2013 at 1,378 gauged natural-flow basins with parameters regionalized elsewhere by hydrologic similarity; NHMv1.0 calibrated on odd water years 1981-2010 at 1,417 gauges), making 0.45 a partly in-sample, optimistic estimate of gauged-location skill. This correction preserves and slightly strengthens the falsifiable implication: median KGE ~0.45 is an upper bound obtained where gauge information was available, so skill at an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin - reachable only through parameter regionalization - is expected to be lower, and a covariate of that fidelity is a weak instrument for the between-site level term. Two additional qualifiers should be attached when using this claim. First, "Central 0.45" is a poor Iowa proxy in a direction that cuts against the argument: the paper concentrates poor Central performance in the high-plains band (ND/SD/NE/KS/TX) and places Iowa in the "more mixed" eastern zone, so Iowa's true value is unresolved and may be better than 0.45; no HUC-07 or NSE-by-region figure exists in the paper. Second, the step from streamflow KGE to nitrate between-site level skill is an inference the paper does not test, and the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint is untouched by this evidence.

METHODOLOGY — THE PREVIOUSLY "UNKNOWN" FIELDS, NOW RECOVERED:
- Model version: NWM V2.0 (explicitly, Sec. 2.3). NOT v2.1 or v3.0.
- Domain: Upper Mississippi River Basin + Ohio River Basin (two HUC2 regional domains); Iowa is inside the domain, and the South Fork Iowa River watershed (USDA-ARS) supplies 6 flux and 12 soil-moisture sites for ET/SM validation. Directly relevant geography.
- n: 188 USGS hourly gauges in the observation pool; 49 calibration basins (subset of the 1,469 official NWM V2.0 calibration basins, area 10–20,000 km², filtered to tile-drainage fraction ≥10% and <20% missing data); regional streamflow evaluation at 139 USGS gauges; parameters regionalized to 939 HUC10 basins by Gower's-distance donor matching. So n is large, not unknown.
- Split protocol: TEMPORAL, not spatial. Calibration 1 Oct 2007 – 1 Oct 2013 (DDS, 300 iterations, objective NSE+NSE_LOG, 14 NWM parameters + tile spacing); evaluation 1 Oct 2013 – 1 Oct 2019. The regional 139-gauge evaluation uses regionalized parameters (a genuine spatial-transfer element via donor basins), but the paper does not state that the 139 evaluation gauges exclude the 49 calibration basins — so partial calibration/evaluation gauge overlap is possible and unquantified. This is the one real leakage caveat; it inflates Calib and CalibTD equally and does not affect the Default-vs-DefaultTD contrast.
- Experiments: Default, DefaultTD, Calib, CalibTD; tile extent from AgTile-US 30 m binary map (Valayamkunnath, Barlage et al. 2020) regridded to 1 km; forcing AORC 1 km.

THE CLAIM AS STATED ABOUT THE PAPER IS FULLY SUBSTANTIATED. The refutable part is the "falsifiable implication," which the source does not support and in two places contradicts (see correction).
result.correction:
Keep the source-level claim; discard or heavily qualify the derived implication. Four corrections, in order of importance to this project:

1. THE BIAS DIRECTION IS WRONG. The implication asserts NWM carries a "structural, spatially systematic LOW bias" in tile-drained Iowa. The paper's own bias statistics say the opposite for the operational (calibrated) configuration: median event PEAK-FLOW BIAS in Calib is +5% (over-prediction), reduced to +0.57% in CalibTD; the median low-flow bias in Calib is TWICE that of Default, and even CalibTD "still overestimated low flows by 50%." The paper attributes low-flow over-prediction to excessive groundwater recharge and the one-way NWM groundwater scheme (citing Jachens et al. 2021; Karki et al. 2021). Operational NWM in tile country reads as biased HIGH at low flow and mildly high at peaks, not low.

2. THE +14%/+2.3%/+11% ARE MODEL-MINUS-MODEL SENSITIVITIES, NOT MEASURED BIASES AGAINST OBSERVATIONS. They come from "comparing 'No tile drainage' with 'With tile drainage'" simulations (Sec. 3.4), i.e. CalibTD vs Calib. Critically, when TD is added WITHOUT recalibration the level does not move: "There are no considerable differences in the estimated Bias between Default and DefaultTD" and "There is no considerable difference between Default and DefaultTD in the estimated peak flow bias." What TD buys is DYNAMICS and TIMING — COR +0.15, NSE +0.16, KGE +0.22 for high flows (DefaultTD vs Default); event hit rate 44%→~65% (Default→DefaultTD), 78% in CalibTD vs 71% in Calib; false-alarm rate 22.5%→17.5%; peak timing error −3/0/4/2 h. The 20–50% figure is likewise an improvement in NSE/KGE-type skill (e.g. spring median NSE 0.22→0.33 for DefaultTD vs 0.22→0.55 for Calib), not a bias correction.

3. THE PAPER NEVER TESTS ERROR-VS-TILE-DENSITY SCALING, AND ITS DESIGN CANNOT. Both gauge sets are pre-screened to tile fraction ≥10% (49 calibration basins and the 188-gauge pool), truncating the range of the exact covariate the implication needs. No regression or stratification of NWM error against tile fraction appears anywhere in the paper. The paper's actual closing mechanism runs the other way for level: "the operational NWM parameters are over-calibrated to accommodate the absence of the TD process in the model during winter and spring" — i.e. operational calibration has already absorbed much of the missing-TD water-balance effect into parameter values, which makes residual level error idiosyncratic-per-donor-basin rather than a clean monotone function of tile density. That is a weaker and messier error structure than the claim asserts, but it is still bad for a between-site feature — just for a different reason (regionalization-donor artifacts, not tile-scaled low bias).

4. VERSION AND MAGNITUDE SCOPE. The study is NWM V2.0; it says nothing about v2.1 or v3.0 retrospective, so "v2.1/v3.0 carries this bias" is an extrapolation, not a finding (that these versions still lack a tile scheme is plausible but must be verified separately against NWM release documentation, not this DOI). And the alarming −43% to −50% figure is GROUNDWATER RECHARGE, an internal flux absent from the streamflow product; the streamflow-volume effect is 2.3% annually (seasonal 17% winter / 13% spring / 13% fall / 2.8% summer). The risk to a modeled-Q feature is real at event/peak scale, small at annual-volume scale.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT (deployment target: arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin). Do not use this paper to rule out NWM retrospective Q as a feature; it does not establish the tile-scaled low bias the argument needs. But also do not expect NWM Q to fix the between-site deficit: everything the paper demonstrates TD improves — timing, hit rate, event dynamics — is the axis on which this model is already strong ("a good timer"), and the paper shows the LEVEL effect gets absorbed by calibration. Prior expectation for NWM Q as a between-site level feature should therefore be LOW, on the paper's own evidence.

CHEAP DIRECT TEST THAT DOMINATES FURTHER LITERATURE SEARCH: the project already has observed discharge at 22 USGS sites. Pull NWM v3.0 retrospective Q (CONUS, hourly, 1979–2023, NHDPlusV2 comid-indexed — comids are already stored per basin; free, no auth, Zarr/NetCDF on the NOAA Open Data Dissemination AWS bucket noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds, s3://noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds, public domain) and regress NWM-vs-observed percent bias on AgTile-US tile fraction across those 22. That measures the error structure directly in Iowa instead of inferring it, and it needs no new data acquisition. AgTile-US itself (30 m binary tile-drained cropland, CONUS, one epoch ~2017, Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis, Franz 2020, Scientific Data, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x, free download) is separately the most concrete answer to the project's flagged "no tile-drainage data source identified" gap — note its CONUS extent covers the multi-state portions of the large basins, which is exactly where the current Iowa-only crop/N-surplus inner join under-counts.

n=19 CAVEAT: this source's n (49 calibration basins, 139 evaluation gauges, 939 HUC10s) is not a constraint on using its FINDING, since the finding is about a physical model's structure, not a learned mapping. The n=19 constraint bites only on the downstream test above, where 22 gauged sites give weak power to detect a bias-vs-tile-density slope — expect to be able to rule out only large effects.

result.correction:
The claim itself is accurate and should stand. Two corrections to how it is being used, plus one actionable finding.

1. The FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION overstates what the paper supports. The paper's own headline result — the TD scheme "enhanced the UNCALIBRATED NWM performance by about 20-50% of the fully calibrated NWM" — means calibration alone already recovers roughly half to four-fifths of what the missing tile-drainage process costs. The operational NWM v2.1/v3.0 retrospectives are calibrated products with regionalized parameters, i.e. the Calib/CalibTD arm of the paper, not the Uncalib arm. The paper shows CalibTD beats Calib, so residual structural error exists, but its magnitude in the calibrated configuration is not the 14%/11%/2.3% numbers — those are TD-on-vs-TD-off simulation deltas, and the volume delta is only 2.3%. Correct statement: "Calibrated NWM in tile-drained regions absorbs the missing tile-drainage process into distorted parameter values rather than leaving a clean unmitigated low bias; a residual, plausibly tile-density-correlated error remains, of unquantified magnitude in the calibrated retrospective."

2. The sign is not established as a uniform "low bias." Adding TD increased peaks and baseflow but DECREASED surface runoff (−7 to −29%) and recharge (−43 to −50%); the redistribution is between flow pathways, with net volume changing only 2.3%. The no-TD NWM is therefore mis-partitioned rather than simply low. Since nitrate delivery in Iowa is dominated by the tile pathway specifically, a mis-partitioned NWM Q is arguably a worse feature than a uniformly biased one — the caution in the claim is directionally right, but the mechanism should be stated as pathway mis-partitioning, not low bias.

3. ACTIONABLE, AND MORE VALUABLE THAN THE CLAIM ITSELF: the same first author published the tile-drainage dataset this project lists as an unfilled gap ("NO data source has been identified yet"). Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis, Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x, open access CC BY. Dataset AgTile-US: 30 m binary raster (1 = tile-drained cropland, 0 = undrained), CONUS-wide (so it covers the multi-state portions of the large basins, not just Iowa), static representation for base year 2017 (built from USDA NASS 2017 Census of Agriculture county tile acreage + SSURGO drainage class + SRTM slope + NLCD 2016 crop mask). Overall accuracy 86.03% against 16,000 ground-truth points; IOWA SPECIFICALLY 91.1% accuracy on 5,253 ground-truth points; heavily tile-drained Midwest states 82.7-93.6%. Access: figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, no login, no authentication — verified via the figshare v2 API, license CC BY 4.0, files AgTile-US-TIFF.zip (125.8 MB), AgTile-US-NetCDF.zip (128.9 MB), AgTile-US.zip (185.2 MB), plus a metadata txt. Direct download e.g. https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/23079140.

Fit to the deployment target: this is a STATIC RASTER, so tile-drained fraction can be computed for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated basin at a map pin with zero local history and zero gauge — it satisfies the deployment constraint completely, unlike modeled NWM discharge. It is exactly the class of feature that has historically worked on this project (static geography and geometry) and not the class that has failed seven times (temporal/hydrologic). Caveats to flag: (a) n=19 families still applies — tile fraction per basin is one number per site, so it adds at most a couple of degrees of freedom to the between-site term and cannot be validated as a "win" on 19 units without wide error bars; (b) it is static for 2017, so it carries no time variation and cannot be broadcast as a time-varying feature (recall the 2017 N-surplus broadcast failure — use it as a static basin attribute only, never expanded per-day as a pseudo-temporal variable); (c) it is a modeled product constrained to county census totals, so within-county spatial detail is a decision-tree allocation, not observation, and its errors are spatially structured by county boundary; (d) the crop mask is NLCD 2016, which the authors report has 18% less cropland than the USDA census, so tile area is under-allocated in some counties.

Bottom line on the original claim's practical advice: the caution against using NWM modeled discharge as a between-site feature is reasonable but rests on an over-strong reading of the abstract. The far stronger move implied by the same author's work is to skip modeled Q entirely and ingest AgTile-US tile fraction per distance bucket as a static basin attribute.

result.evidence:
PRIMARY-SOURCE CHECK — the quoted sentences are genuine and near-verbatim.

Paper confirmed: Marinos, R., Van Meter, K. J., & Basu, N. B. (2020). "Is the River a Chemostat?: Scale Versus Land Use Controls on Nitrate Concentration-Discharge Dynamics in the Upper Mississippi River Basin." Geophysical Research Letters. DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051. Retrieved via Semantic Scholar Graph API (paperId 252ca9192fcd9eefc16382599e3ab833d8e1853a, CorpusId 216193772, 39 citations as of retrieval).

Abstract text (verbatim, relevant clauses): "...we show, using high-resolution nitrate concentration data, that tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior. We further find that concentration variability increases, relative to discharge variability, with increasing basin size across six orders of magnitude, and this pattern is attributed to different spatial correlation structures for C and Q."

The claim's first quoted clause is an exact match, word for word. The second is an accurate paraphrase. So there is NO misattribution, no exaggeration, no garbling of the cited sentences. On the primary-source lens the claim survives.

WHAT COULD NOT BE VERIFIED (and why this matters):
- Publisher full text: HTTP 402 at agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2020GL087051.
- Unpaywall (api.unpaywall.org, 10.1029/2020gl087051): "oa_status": "closed", "is_oa": false, "best_oa_location": null, "oa_locations": [], "has_repository_copy": false. There is no green/preprint copy anywhere in the Unpaywall index.
- Semantic Scholar has no openAccessPdf. Citation contexts from 4 citing papers (2025-2026) reference it only for generic C-Q framing ("linear, break-point, and power-law relationships"; "piecewise power law ... with threshold discharge as fitted parameter"; "temporal variability of NO3- ... depending on catchment characteristics and spatial scale") and quote none of its numbers.
- Therefore: number of sites, drainage-area range, power-law b values, and actual CVc/CVq magnitudes are STILL unknown. Web search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200), so no further hunt was possible.

Consequence: the project cannot cite a threshold from this paper, only a direction. Any statement of the form "Marinos et al. found median CVc/CVq = X" would be fabrication. Note also one citing paper (Ma et al. 2023 lineage, "Coupled Hydrologic and Biogeochemical Responses of Nitrate Export in a Tile-Drained Agricultural Watershed", 2025) attributes to Marinos a PIECEWISE power law with a fitted discharge threshold — i.e., the paper apparently did not fit a single global b, which further undercuts reading a single "chemostatic/non-chemostatic" label off it.

METHODOLOGY / INDEPENDENCE CAVEAT: "high-resolution nitrate concentration data" in the UMRB in 2020 almost certainly means the IIHR/IWQIS and USGS super-gauge sensor networks — plausibly overlapping the very 85 sites this project trains on. If so this is not independent external evidence about our data; it is a prior analysis OF our data. Unverified but should be assumed until the full text is obtained.

THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION IS THE PART THAT FAILS — four defects:

1. SELF-CONTRADICTORY USE OF THE TWO FINDINGS. The abstract's second finding says CVc/CVq INCREASES with basin size over six orders of magnitude — i.e., larger basins are LESS chemostatic. The project's inference assumes "Iowa nitrate is largely chemostatic" as a blanket property. The paper explicitly denies scale-invariance; its title is a question, and its answer is "it depends on scale and on tile density." You cannot license a blanket chemostasis premise from a paper whose headline result is that chemostasis erodes with scale.

2. THE 22-GAUGED-SITE TEST IS BIASED IN EXACTLY THE WRONG DIRECTION. All 22 discharge-bearing sites are USGS, which skews to larger drainage areas. Per the paper's own scaling result, that is the regime with the HIGHEST CVc/CVq. So a median computed on those 22 sites is an upper bound, not a representative value, and it says nothing about the small headwater basins an arbitrary map pin will frequently delineate. The test as designed would systematically fail to detect chemostasis where chemostasis is actually strongest. Additionally CVc is sensitive to record length and to 15-min vs daily aggregation, and CVc/CVq requires the site's own C and Q — a within-site, gauged-site statistic that is structurally uninformative about ungauged transfer, the deployment target.

3. "CHEMOSTATIC ⇒ Q CARRIES LITTLE INFORMATION ABOUT C" IS A NON-SEQUITUR. Chemostasis (Godsey/Thompson) bounds a VARIANCE RATIO, not a CORRELATION. A predictor with small amplitude can still be decisive, and here the target is a THRESHOLD, not a level: base rate 0.263 at 10 mg/L means many site-days sit near the boundary. For a site with mean C near 9-11 mg/L, even a low-amplitude, highly-correlated Q signal flips exceedance. Chemostasis therefore predicts Q adds little to R2 on concentration while remaining potentially useful for the binary violation target — close to the opposite of the stated implication. The implication also conflates b≈0 with zero residual structure; hysteresis and spring-flush seasonality persist under b≈0.

4. IT POINTS AT THE WRONG TERM AND MISREADS WHICH FINDING IS ACTIONABLE. Chemostasis means C ≈ a, a site-level near-constant. That is precisely the project's diagnosed deficit (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). So the paper's first finding is not a reason to drop the discharge angle; it is direct evidence that TILE DRAINAGE DENSITY is a first-order control on the site-level regime — the one static attribute the project has already identified as missing with no data source found. Read correctly, this paper is an argument for prioritizing tile-drainage density as a STATIC between-site feature (which survives the n=19-families constraint far better than any temporal method, since it adds one static covariate rather than a learned per-site level), not an argument about Q.

n=19 CONSTRAINT: the paper's scale finding is a cross-basin regression whose effective n is unknown but, spanning six orders of magnitude of area, is likely well above 19 and certainly not restricted to independent basin families. Fitting a CVc/CVq-vs-area relation on this project's 22 gauged sites collapsing to a handful of independent families would be badly underpowered; do not expect to reproduce the scaling result locally, and do not treat failure to reproduce it as refutation.

DEPLOYMENT VERDICT: nothing in this paper requires or endorses target-site observations, so it is compatible with the ungauged-pin product — but the CVc/CVq diagnostic the project proposes is a gauged-site-only statistic and cannot be computed at the deployment target.
result.correction:
The citation is accurate — the quoted clause "tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior" is verbatim from the abstract of Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020), GRL, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051. Two details to fix: (a) the paper says "six orders of magnitude" of basin size, not "multiple orders"; (b) the paper reports a piecewise/threshold power law (per a 2025 citing paper), not a single global slope b, and no b, CVc/CVq, or site-count values are retrievable — the article is closed access (Unpaywall: oa_status "closed", zero OA locations, no repository copy), so no numeric threshold may be attributed to it.

The FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION, however, does not follow and should be rewritten. Three corrections:

1. The paper does NOT support a blanket "Iowa nitrate is largely chemostatic" premise. Its second finding is that CVc/CVq RISES with basin size, so chemostasis is a property of small, tile-dense headwaters and erodes toward the large multi-state basins. The project's proposed test on 22 USGS-gauged sites samples the large-basin end preferentially — the least chemostatic end — so its median CVc/CVq is an upper bound and is not generalizable to the small ungauged basins a map pin will often produce. Stratify any such test by drainage area rather than reporting a single median.

2. "Chemostatic ⇒ Q is uninformative about concentration" is a non-sequitur. CVc/CVq << 1 constrains a variance ratio, not a correlation, and the operative target is a 10 mg/L threshold with a 0.263 base rate — a low-amplitude but well-correlated Q signal can still flip exceedance for sites whose level sits near the threshold. The defensible prediction is narrower: chemostasis predicts Q will add little to concentration R2 while possibly still helping the binary violation target near the threshold, and predicts that load (C x Q) is close to a linear function of Q and therefore adds little independent information beyond Q itself.

3. The actionable content of this paper for this project is the OPPOSITE of "drop the fluid-dynamics angle." Chemostasis means C ≈ a site-level constant, which is exactly the between-site term the model fails (between_r2 0.21). The paper identifies TILE DRAINAGE DENSITY as a dominant control on that regime — i.e., it is external, geographically on-target (Upper Mississippi Basin) evidence that the project's single known missing static feature is first-order. As a static per-basin covariate it costs one degree of freedom and is compatible with the n=19-families constraint and with ungauged deployment, unlike per-site level learning. Caveat: the paper's "high-resolution nitrate" data may be the same IIHR/IWQIS + USGS sensor network this project trains on, in which case it is a prior analysis of our own data rather than independent corroboration; obtain the full text to check before citing it as external validation.

Downloaded the PDF (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/27/1809/2023/hess-27-1809-2023.pdf) and extracted text with pdftotext -layout rather than trusting a summarizer. WHAT THE PAPER ACTUALLY SAYS (Towler, Foks, Dugger, Dickinson, Essaid, Gochis, Viger, Zhang 2023, HESS 27:1809-1825, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023):

CONFIRMED EXACTLY:
- "The evaluation is performed on daily streamflow for 5390 streamflow gages from 1983 to 2016 (~33 years)"; precisely "1 October 1983 to 31 December 2016, or just over 33 years (~12 100 d)". Claim's n and period are exact.
- Models: National Water Model v2.1 (WRF-Hydro) vs National Hydrologic Model v1.0 (PRMS). Correct.
- Central is among the two worst regions; NWMv2.1 > NHMv1.0 there. Correct.
- Quote 1 is verbatim: "for both models in the Central region, relatively poor performance is concentrated along the plains areas that span from the high plains (i.e., North Dakota) vertically down through the center of the CONUS (i.e., South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, and Texas)."
- Regions are ecoregion aggregations from Falcone (2011), not HUC2. Claim correctly notes this, and the caveat that an Iowa/HUC-07-specific figure is NOT obtainable is honest and correct.

FOUR ERRORS IN THE CLAIM:
1. NUMBERS WRONG. Table 4 ("Median values for each region") prints, for Central: NHMv1.0 KGE 0.33, NWMv2.1 KGE 0.45. Not 0.40 and 0.29. Both understated (~0.05 and ~0.04). Full Table 4 KGE, NHM/NWM: West 0.29/0.32; Central 0.33/0.45; Southeast 0.48/0.56; Northeast 0.63/0.65. Also printed for Central NWMv2.1: r 0.71, rSD 0.87, PBIAS +4.4%.
2. QUOTE 2 MISQUOTED. Paper says "Performance is MORE mixed as one moves further east in the Central region (e.g., around the Great Lakes)." Claim says "most mixed".
3. "Central region subset size not stated" IS FALSE. The paper states it explicitly in the Fig. 3 caption: Central n = 1450 (Central Plains + Western Plains + Mixed Wood Shield). Other regions: West 1510, Northeast 1218, Southeast 1212.
4. SPLIT PROTOCOL MISLABELED. The claim reports "temporal-holdout". It is NOT. The authors' own limitation: "the calibration periods of the models differed, and both overlapped with the evaluation period used in this study. While this overlap can introduce biases into the evaluation process, it allowed us to evaluate long-term performance for the same sites and time periods for both models." NWMv2.1 calibrated on WY2008-2013 (validated 2014-2016); NHMv1.0 calibrated on odd water years 1981-2010. Both sit inside the 1983-2016 evaluation window. This is a calibration-overlapping evaluation, which makes 0.45 OPTIMISTIC — which strengthens rather than weakens the claim's conclusion.

ONE SUBSTANTIVE CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM'S REASONING (matters for the project): the claim argues 0.40 "is the performance at GAUGED locations where NWM parameters were regionalized with gauge information available" and that ungauged performance "is bounded above by this." That framing is loose. NWMv2.1 calibrated 14 soil/vegetation/baseflow parameters at only 1,378 predominantly-natural gaged basins, then used a hydrologic-similarity strategy to REGIONALIZE parameters to the remaining basins. So roughly 74% of the 5,390 evaluation gauges (~4,000) never had their own observations fit — they received transferred parameters, which IS the ungauged-transfer case. The 0.45 median is therefore already largely a regionalized-parameter number, not a strict upper bound reachable only at calibrated sites. The calibration-period overlap still inflates it somewhat. Net: the practical conclusion survives intact, and arguably on firmer ground than the claim's own argument.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT (the lens I was assigned):
- The plains quote does NOT describe Iowa. The named poor-performance corridor is North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, Texas. Iowa sits in the EASTERN part of Central, exactly where the paper says performance is "more mixed" and gives the Great Lakes as the example. Using the plains sentence to characterize expected NWM fidelity in Iowa is a stretch; the honest statement is that the paper supports "Central regional median KGE 0.45, no Iowa-specific number obtainable, Iowa is in the better-performing eastern portion of that region."
- Metric mismatch is real and under-stated: this is KGE on DAILY STREAMFLOW. The project needs a between-site LEVEL term for nitrate exceedance. KGE rewards correlation, variability ratio, and bias jointly; a KGE of 0.45 is compatible with decent timing and poor absolute volume. Note Central NWMv2.1 PBIAS is only +4.4% (median), so volume bias is actually modest in Central — the KGE penalty there comes mostly from r 0.71 and rSD 0.87. That is a timing/variability deficit, and this project already has a timing-adequate model (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90). So NWM's strongest axis in Central is the axis the project needs LEAST.
- n=19 FAMILIES CONSTRAINT: this paper is a benchmark of a physically-based model, not an ML method with a learned-from-basins parameter budget, so the n=19 objection does not bite in the usual way — NWM output is a pre-computed covariate, available at any NHDPlus reach regardless of how many training basins exist. Adding 1-2 NWM-derived features costs ~1-2 degrees of freedom against 19 independent units, which is affordable. That is a genuine point in favor of trying it, independent of whether this specific claim's numbers were right.
- TILE DRAINAGE: NWM/WRF-Hydro has no explicit tile-drainage representation, which the project itself identifies as the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa. This is a strong a priori reason to expect NWM discharge to mis-rank Iowa basins specifically, but it is NOT supported by this paper — the paper never mentions tile drainage. Anyone citing Towler for that point is over-reading it.
- DEPLOYMENT TARGET: NWM retrospective output is keyed to NHDPlus comid, which the project already stores per basin, and requires no local nitrate history or local gauge. So it IS compatible with the arbitrary-map-pin product, unlike most gauge-dependent methods. That compatibility is the main reason to care.
- The project's own prior negative results are the stronger caution: seven hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL features have already failed, and NWM discharge is another temporal hydrologic covariate. A long-term-mean or flow-regime-summary NWM statistic (a static between-site descriptor) is far better aligned with the diagnosed deficit than a daily NWM discharge series would be.

BOTTOM LINE: directionally correct, materially wrong in four specifics. Corrected numbers still support the claim's falsifiable implication — NWM Central fidelity is mediocre and is a weak instrument for a between-site level term — but the argument should be made with 0.45/0.33, with the calibration-overlap caveat, and WITHOUT implying the plains sentence describes Iowa.

The second quotation is misquoted: the paper says performance is "more mixed" (not "most mixed") as one moves further east in the Central region. The Central subset size IS stated (n = 1,450); the claim wrongly says it was not.

The claim's inference that 0.45 is an upper bound only achievable where gauge information was available is loose: NWMv2.1 calibrated parameters at just 1,378 predominantly-natural gaged basins and regionalized to the rest by hydrologic similarity, so roughly 74% of the 5,390 evaluation gauges are already effectively ungauged-transfer cases. The practical conclusion nonetheless holds.

Critically for Iowa: the "plains" sentence names North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, and Texas. Iowa lies in the eastern portion of the Central region, which the paper describes as "more mixed," not as the poor-performing plains corridor. No Iowa/HUC-07-specific figure is obtainable from this paper — that caveat in the original claim is correct and should be retained. Also note the Central KGE shortfall is driven mainly by correlation (r 0.71) and variability ratio (rSD 0.87) rather than volume bias (PBIAS +4.4%), i.e. a timing/variability deficit — the axis on which this project's model is already adequate, not the between-site level term where the headroom lies.

So there is NO misattribution, exaggeration, or garbling of the cited text.

METHODOLOGY — the claim's "n unknown / protocol unknown" caveats are now RESOLVED, and they matter.
- Model: NWM **V2.0** (not v2.1/v3.0), WRF-Hydro/Noah-MP, 1 km land grid, NHDPlusV2 routing. Hooghoudt tile-drainage equation added; tile-drained grids defined from AgTile-US 30 m regridded to 1 km.

WHERE THE CLAIM'S "FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION" BREAKS (this is the part that does not survive).
1. WRONG COMPARISON. The +14%/+2.3%/+11% figures are NOT Calib vs CalibTD. §3.4 states explicitly they come from "No tile drainage" vs "With tile drainage", where "No tile drainage" is CalibTD's own parameter set with the TD module switched off — "which is not equal to Calib". They are a process-attribution sensitivity, not a measured bias of any operational NWM configuration.
2. THE OPERATIONAL NWM IS CALIBRATED, AND CALIBRATION ABSORBS THE MISSING PROCESS. The paper's own mechanism: "In Calib (without tile drains), DKSAT is an effective hydraulic conductivity for the combined subsurface material and tile drain system", and §3.2 concludes "the Calib parameters are over-calibrated to accommodate the absence of TD in the model during winter and spring." The missing-process error is largely re-expressed as compensated parameters, not left as raw streamflow bias.
3. THE SIGN IS WRONG. The claim asserts a systematic LOW bias. Measured against 139 gauges: median event peak-flow bias in Calib is **+5%** (high), reduced to +0.57% in CalibTD. 4. THE KEY REGRESSION IS NEVER RUN. The paper nowhere reports bias (or NSE/KGE) as a function of basin tile-drainage percentage. Percent TD appears only as one of 13 Gower similarity attributes. The specific quantity the implication needs — "error magnitude scales with tile density" — is untested in this source. There is no per-gauge NSE/KGE table in the accessible text, so it cannot be recovered post hoc either.
5. VERSION MISMATCH. The study is V2.0. The claim is asserted about v2.1/v3.0 retrospective. V2.1/v3.0 use different calibrated parameter sets and (v3.0) revised Noah-MP; nothing in this paper licenses a quantitative statement about them. ATTRIBUTION: VERIFIED EXACT. Paper is Marinos, R. E., Van Meter, K. J., & Basu, N. B. (2020), "Is the River a Chemostat?: Scale Versus Land Use Controls on Nitrate Concentration-Discharge Dynamics in the Upper Mississippi River Basin," Geophysical Research Letters, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051 (Crossref pub date 13 Aug 2020; Unpaywall: is_oa=false, oa_status=closed, oa_locations=[], has_repository_copy=false — the 402 paywall is real and there is no legal free copy; scholar.archive.org returns 0 hits).

The quoted sentence is verbatim from the abstract (retrieved independently from Crossref and Semantic Scholar, identical text): "Here, we show, using high-resolution nitrate concentration data, that tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior. We further find that concentration variability increases, relative to discharge variability, with increasing basin size across six orders of magnitude, and this pattern is attributed to different spatial correlation structures for C and Q." So: not misattributed, not exaggerated, not garbled. Correction of one detail: the abstract says SIX orders of magnitude, not "multiple."

METHODS RECOVERED FROM CITING LITERATURE (full text unavailable, so these are second-hand but from three independent citing papers): n = 33 watersheds. "This range of threshold discharge is consistent with a previous study based on 33 watersheds of various sizes in this region (Marinos et al., 2020)" (Coupled Hydrologic and Biogeochemical Responses of Nitrate Export in a Tile-Drained Agricultural Watershed); "for nitrate at 33 sites in the Mississippi River Basin (Marinos et al., 2020)" (Solute export patterns across the contiguous USA). Data basis: ">1 year of daily mean sensor data (Marinos et al., 2020; Speir et al., 2021)" and "Discrete CVC/CVQ ratio, >1 year of 5-15 min frequency sensor data (Marinos et al., 2020; Wymore et al., 2021)" (Catchment concentration-discharge relationships across temporal scales: A review). Scale finding independently confirmed: "Marinos et al. (2020) found an increase in CVC/CVQ with catchment area" (Persistent chemostatic behaviour of stream solutes in a northern hardwood forest).

METHODOLOGY: This is a descriptive/correlative study — C-Q metrics per site regressed against catchment attributes. There is NO predictive split protocol of any kind (not random, not spatial); it is not a predictive-skill study and cannot be cited as evidence about whether a feature improves out-of-sample ML skill. n=33 sites is comparable to our n≈19 families, so it is NOT one of the 500-basin CAMELS-class results that fails to transfer downward — but it also means its regressions of CVc/CVq on area/tile density rest on ~33 points. Nestedness/pseudoreplication is a live concern: spanning six orders of magnitude in the UMRB necessarily means many sites are nested inside others (the exact structure our 19-family CV was built to neutralize), and whether Marinos controlled for it is NOT determinable from the abstract.

CRITICAL: THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION IS NOT SUPPORTED BY THE PAPER, AND PARTLY INVERTS IT.
(1) The paper's headline scale result is that nitrate becomes MORE chemodynamic (CVc/CVq rises) as basin size increases. Iowa's monitored network is dominated by mid-to-large basins, i.e. the end of the gradient where the paper predicts LESS chemostasis. The claim cites the paper to argue Iowa nitrate is "largely chemostatic," which is the opposite of the paper's own scale finding.
(2) Marinos et al. did not fit chemostatic (b≈0) power laws — citing papers state they used a PIECEWISE power law with a fitted threshold discharge Qt: "Following previous studies in this region (Ma et al., 2023; Marinos et al., 2020), we used a piecewise power law relationship... where a, b1, b2, and the threshold discharge Qt are fitted parameters." A threshold-mobilization model is a chemoDYNAMIC description; the paper is repeatedly cited as a source for nonlinearity/breakpoints in C-Q, not for flat C-Q.
(3) An independent UMRB study explicitly reads Marinos the opposite way: "Nitrate exhibited consistently chemodynamic behavior across events, as seen in previous studies of long-term C-Q behavior in the basin (Crawford et al., 2019; Marinos et al., 2020; Zimmer et al., 2019)" (River Geomorphology Affects Biogeochemical Responses to Hydrologic Events in a Large River Ecosystem).
(4) The "more chemostatic" statement is RELATIVE and comparative (high-tile vs low-tile), not an absolute claim that b=0 anywhere. No CVc/CVq value, no b value, and no median CVc/CVq is retrievable from any accessible source. The claim's proposed decision rule ("if the median is well below 1") has no numeric anchor in the cited paper.
(5) Logical error independent of the paper: chemostasis is a WITHIN-SITE statement about C-Q slope over the flow range. Our project's deficit is explicitly BETWEEN-SITE (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). Even perfect chemostasis would not imply Q is uninformative — under chemostasis a site's mean C is set by its static source strength, so chemostasis STRENGTHENS the case for the paper's OTHER finding (tile drainage density as a dominant between-site control), which is precisely the static between-site covariate this project is missing and matches its own empirical pattern that geometry/static features win and temporal features fail.
result.correction:
The quoted sentence is verbatim-accurate from the abstract of Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020) GRL 10.1029/2020GL087051 ("Is the River a Chemostat?..."), so the citation itself stands. Three corrections to how it is being used:

1. SCALE FINDING IS BEING READ BACKWARDS. The paper says CVc/CVq INCREASES with basin size across SIX orders of magnitude — i.e. larger basins are MORE chemodynamic. Iowa's ~85 monitored sites sit at the larger end of that gradient, so the paper predicts nitrate at our sites is chemoDYNAMIC, not chemostatic. The "more chemostatic" phrase is a relative, comparative statement about high-tile-density vs low-tile-density catchments, not an absolute b≈0 claim, and no CVc/CVq or b value is retrievable from any accessible source (paper is closed-access, Unpaywall oa_locations empty, no repository copy, no preprint). The claim's threshold rule ("median well below 1") is invented, not sourced.

2. THE PAPER FIT THRESHOLD C-Q MODELS, NOT FLAT ONES. Citing papers state Marinos et al. used a piecewise power law with fitted breakpoint Qt (b1, b2, Qt), and the paper is routinely cited as a canonical source for BREAKPOINTS and nonlinearity in nitrate C-Q. A separate UMRB study cites it as evidence that "nitrate exhibited consistently chemodynamic behavior." So the paper cannot be used to predict that discharge carries little information about concentration; if anything it implies a threshold/mobilization response that a monotone linear Q feature would miss but a tree model like XGBoost is well suited to capture.

3. THE INFERENCE "CHEMOSTASIS => Q USELESS FOR CONCENTRATION" IS A CATEGORY ERROR FOR THIS PROJECT. Chemostasis is a within-site C-Q slope statement; our headroom is between-site (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). Under chemostasis a site's absolute concentration level is set by static source strength — which makes the paper's FIRST finding (tile drainage density is a dominant control) the actionable one: it is a static, between-site, ungauged-transferable covariate, exactly the class of feature that has worked on this project (lat/lon/geometry) while every temporal-hydrology feature has failed. Marinos et al. is therefore evidence FOR prioritizing a tile-drainage-density layer over NWM discharge ingestion, but NOT evidence that discharge will fail.

METHODOLOGICAL LIMITS TO STATE WHENEVER THIS IS CITED: n=33 watersheds (per citing papers; not verifiable in the closed full text), UMRB, >1 year of high-frequency (5-15 min to daily-mean) nitrate sensor data. Purely descriptive/correlative — NO split protocol, no held-out prediction, so it is not comparable to and says nothing directly about our LOFO 0.820. n=33 is in the same order as our 19 families, so it is not a 500-basin result that cannot transfer; but its site set spans six orders of magnitude in area within one basin, so nested-catchment pseudoreplication in the CVc/CVq-vs-area regression is plausible and undetermined. Every C-Q metric it reports requires the site's OWN nitrate AND discharge record, so nothing in this paper is directly computable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin — its only deployable output for us is the qualitative ranking of tile density as a between-site control.

The proposed diagnostic (compute CVc/CVq on the 22 USGS-gauged sites before any NWM ingestion) is still worth running — it is cheap and it is the right descriptive statistic — but the decision rule attached to it is wrong on two counts: (a) the paper predicts CVc/CVq > 1 (chemodynamic) at our basin sizes, so a low median would CONTRADICT rather than confirm the paper; and (b) whatever CVc/CVq comes out, it is a within-site statistic and cannot adjudicate the between-site deficit that holds essentially all remaining headroom. Do not use it to kill the discharge feature; use it to decide whether Q enters as a threshold/percentile-of-local-flow-regime feature rather than a raw magnitude.

The cited finding is quoted VERBATIM and correctly attributed — do not treat Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020) as misused. Both abstract sentences appear word-for-word in the claim, and I independently REPLICATED the scale finding on this project's own data (Spearman(drainage area, CVc/CVq) = +0.688 across 18 gauged sites spanning 17–12,483 km²).

What IS wrong is the FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION, and it is wrong at its logical core, not in detail. Three corrections:

1. THE PROPOSED TEST WAS RUN AND ITS DECISION RULE FAILS. Median CVc/CVq = 0.443 on the 20 usable gauged sites — "well below 1", which by the claim's own stated criterion predicts "the fluid-dynamics angle will fail". Yet at those same sites, log Q explains a MEDIAN 50.9% of the variance in log nitrate concentration (per-site R² range 0.21–0.87), with median power-law slope b = +0.61. A slope of +0.61 is strongly MOBILIZING/enriching, not chemostatic (chemostasis is b ≈ 0). CVc/CVq is low here because CVq is large (median 1.4), not because C is insensitive to Q. CVc/CVq is a variance-ratio, not a mutual-information measure; it conflates "C is buffered" with "Q is wild". The test as specified cannot license the conclusion drawn from it.

2. "IOWA NITRATE IS LARGELY CHEMOSTATIC" IS NOT WHAT THE PAPER SAYS. The abstract asserts a GRADIENT ("increasing drainage density contributing to MORE chemostatic behavior") — a comparative statement — plus the finding that chemostasis WEAKENS with basin size. Iowa's monitored network is dominated by mid-to-large basins, exactly the regime the paper says is LEAST chemostatic. The claim's premise therefore inverts the paper's own scale result when applied to this network.

3. THE 10 mg/L TARGET IS WHERE Q IS MOST INFORMATIVE, NOT LEAST. At the highest-exceedance gauged sites the C-Q coupling is strongest: USGS-05481000 (55.2% violation-days) b=0.75, R²=0.63; USGS-05482500 (37.1%) b=0.73, R²=0.50; USGS-05451210 (33.0%) b=0.90, R²=0.87. The prediction that Q would help load but not exceedance is contradicted at precisely the sites that carry the exceedance signal.

CAVEATS THAT STILL FAVOR CAUTION ON Q — but for reasons unrelated to chemostasis, and these must be stated instead of the chemostasis argument: (a) the 50.9% R² is a WITHIN-SITE, non-spatially-held-out diagnostic; it speaks to the within_r2=0.42 timing term the model ALREADY handles, not the between-site absolute-level term where all the headroom is; (b) it requires OBSERVED Q at the site, which the deployment target (arbitrary ungauged map pin) does not have — modelled Q (NWM) is largely a deterministic function of the same weather + basin geometry already in the feature set, so its marginal information may be far below 50%; (c) only USGS sites have Q, so all 61 IWQIS sites — smaller, higher tile-drainage density, i.e. the MOST chemostatic per the paper — are untested here, and the true statewide median CVc/CVq is likely lower than 0.443; (d) 20 sites collapse to ≈19 independent basin families, so the per-site medians rest on very few effective units.

UNVERIFIABLE: the paper's site count, drainage-area range, b values, and CVc/CVq magnitudes remain unretrievable. Unpaywall, OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar all report is_oa=false with zero OA locations; agupubs returns HTTP 402. The claim's own SOURCE CAVEAT is accurate and should be carried into the report verbatim. "Six orders of magnitude" is the only quantitative figure that can be sourced.
