result.correction:
Claim is accurate as written; adopt it, but state these five caveats explicitly when using the layer.

(a) "86.03% accuracy" is RECALL ON POSITIVES ONLY — there is no false-positive assessment. All 16,000 points were manually digitized from ESRI aerial imagery at locations "when a tile drainage signature is detected," i.e. all are tile-present positives. The paper's own arithmetic confirms this: 86.03% accuracy + "13.97% omission error" = 100%. There is no confusion matrix, no true negatives, no commission error, no kappa. A map that over-painted tile everywhere would score ~100% under this validation. This matters directly for us: we intend a basin-MEAN fraction, and mean fraction is biased precisely by commission error, which is the one error mode never measured. Do not describe this as "86% classification accuracy" in project docs; describe it as "86.03% of known tile-drained ground-truth points correctly captured (omission error only; commission error unquantified)."

(b) Validation is not fully independent of model fitting. The paper extracts the slope thresholds that constrain the decision tree from the same ground-truth point set later used for validation. Treat 86.03%/91.1% as optimistic in-sample-flavored numbers.

(c) The map is CENSUS-CONSTRAINED BY COUNTY by construction — cells are accumulated until the county total matches the 2017 USDA census. So county aggregates reproduce the census almost exactly, and the map's genuine added value is sub-county ALLOCATION. For a basin spanning several counties, basin-mean tile fraction is close to an area-weighted county-census average. Effective independent information is ~county-scale (99 counties in Iowa), not 30 m. Still fine at n=19 families, but do not claim 30 m of real signal.

(d) Known systematic low bias, stated by the authors: NLCD-2016 underrepresents cropland by "18.15% underrepresentation for the CONUS," and average USDA census error is "19.8%." Tile fraction is therefore biased low, unevenly.

(e) Denominator ambiguity — a practical implementation note. Because non-cropland cells are 0, a naive basin-mean conflates "not tiled" with "not cropland." Compute BOTH tile_area/basin_area and tile_area/cropland_area per distance bucket; the latter is the actual management-intensity signal and the former is the loading-relevant one.

Finally, one risk to the falsifiable prediction that the claim should have flagged: tile-drained fraction is spatially very smooth across Iowa (Des Moines Lobe vs. Loess Hills / driftless SE), and lon and lat are already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features. There is a real chance XGBoost has already absorbed most of this signal through lat/lon and the new columns add little. That does not argue against trying it — it is cheap, static, and of the exact class that has produced this project's only wins — but the ablation should be run against a lat/lon-included baseline (not a stripped one), and a null result should be interpreted as "already captured by coordinates," not as "tile drainage does not matter."

VERIFIED: DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605 = Thompson, S.E., Basu, N.B., Lascurain, J., Aubeneau, A., Rao, P.S.C. (2011), "Relative dominance of hydrologic versus biogeochemical factors on solute export across impact gradients," Water Resources Research 47(10). Crossref abstract confirms the paper analyzes concentration variability "using the ratio of coefficients of variation (CV_C/CV_Q)" and that the ratio "generally decreases as exported loads increase."

The claim's homogeneous->chemostatic / heterogeneous->chemodynamic framing is a faithful paraphrase.

VERIFIED (legacy store): Basu et al. 2010, DOI 10.1029/2010GL045168, GRL, "Nutrient loads exported from managed catchments reveal emergent biogeochemical stationarity." Abstract: "inter-annual variations in loads for total-N and total-P, exported from a catchment are dominantly controlled by discharge," yielding stable annual flow-weighted concentrations "attributed to accumulated nutrient legacies."

NOT VERIFIED: that Basu 2010 specifically used the r-squared of an annual-load vs annual-discharge linear regression as the chemostasis metric. The annual load-Q linearity framing is consistent with the abstract, but the r-squared detail could not be confirmed (paper not openly accessible).

REFUTED IN DETAIL: the "0.3" threshold. No source uses it. egusphere-2025-1588 (Copernicus preprint, open access), section 2.3.3, lines 353-362 verbatim: "Solutes with CVC/CVQ > 0.5 were classified as chemodynamic (high concentration variability relative to discharge variability), whereas CVC/CVQ <= 0.5 indicated chemostatic behaviour. The threshold of 0.5 for distinguishing chemostatic (CVC/CVQ <= 0.5) from chemodynamic behaviour (CVC/CVQ > 0.5) was chosen following Thompson et al. (2011)... Although alternative thresholds (e.g. 1) exist in the literature (Musolff et al. 2015), 0.5 was deemed most appropriate for our data structure and applied here as a classification tool." HyGCS classification suite documentation also uses 1. The two conventions in circulation are 0.5 and 1; 0.3 appears fabricated. Note the 0.5 users' own hedge: chosen because it "provides a clear separation of solute groups in our dataset" -- a dataset-tuned convention, not a physical constant.

ATTRIBUTION CONTESTED: Speir, Rose et al. (2023) WIREs Water review, line 201: "The ratio of the coefficients of variation for C and Q (CVC/CVQ) can aid in distinguishing chemostatic from chemodynamic behavior (Figure 1c; Musolff et al., 2015)" -- crediting Musolff et al. 2015 (Advances in Water Resources 86), not Thompson 2011. The egusphere preprint credits Thompson 2011 ("as proposed by Thompson et al. (2011)"). Both attributions appear in the literature.

TRANSFERABILITY -- SCALE DEPENDENCE (the serious problem, a negative result the claim omits): Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020), "Is the river a chemostat? Scale versus land use controls on nitrate concentration-discharge," GRL, found "concentration variability increases, relative to discharge variability, with increasing basin size across six orders of magnitude," attributed to "different spatial correlation structures for C and Q." CVc/CVq is therefore a function of basin area. Applying a fixed cutoff across the project's 22 gauged sites (which span a wide area range) will partly sort sites by size rather than by biogeochemical regime, and risks being a laundered proxy for the existing log_basin_area feature. Exact n for Marinos 2020 could not be retrieved.

TRANSFERABILITY -- DEPLOYMENT TARGET: CVc/CVq requires discharge AND concentration at the site. Confirmed on disk: /Users/isaac/dev/sustag/data_inventory.md line 31 documents discharge only for USGS-prefixed sites (22 of 85; zero of 61 IWQIS sites). At an arbitrary ungauged map pin there is neither Q nor C, so this quantity can never enter the shipped feature vector. It is a diagnostic on 26% of sites, not a deployable feature. The claim's phrase "concrete, cheap decision rule computable on the project's own 22 gauged sites" is accurate as far as it goes but must be stated as diagnostic-only.

TRANSFERABILITY -- LOGICAL GAP IN THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: CVc/CVq is a within-site temporal variance ratio. It constrains how concentration varies through time at one site; it is mathematically silent on how site-mean concentration varies across sites. The claim asserts chemostasis "predicts the sign of the between-site relation" -- it does not. Basu's legacy-store narrative motivates that expectation, but the metric does not test it. This conflates exactly the within_r2 (0.42) vs between_r2 (0.21) distinction that is the project's central problem. Confirming chemostasis would corroborate a story already inferred from feature importances without supplying new between-site signal.

n=19 CONSTRAINT: does not bite for computing the per-site descriptive statistic (no model is fitted). It does bite for the downstream step the claim implies -- regressing site-mean C on source terms across sites returns to n~19 independent units, and with basin area confounding CVc/CVq per Marinos 2020, that regression is underpowered to separate source effects from scale effects.

SPLIT PROTOCOL: not applicable, correctly reported. CVc/CVq is a descriptive statistic, not a predictive model, so no LOFO-comparable number exists and none should be inferred.

n BASINS in Thompson 2011: could not be determined from available metadata (paywalled). Reported as unknown, correctly.
result.correction:
The claim is substantively correct on attribution and mechanism but wrong on its one load-bearing number, and overstates what the metric delivers. Precise corrections:

(1) THRESHOLD: replace "CVc/CVq < 0.3" with the two thresholds actually used in the literature: CVc/CVq <= 0.5 (chemostatic) vs > 0.5 (chemodynamic), cited to Thompson et al. 2011 by users such as egusphere-2025-1588; OR CVc/CVq < 1, cited to Musolff et al. 2015 (Advances in Water Resources 86, DOI 10.1016/j.advwatres.2015.09.026). No published source uses 0.3. Both thresholds are conventions tuned to particular datasets, not physical constants -- one paper states plainly it chose 0.5 because it "provides a clear separation of solute groups in our dataset."

(2) ATTRIBUTION: attribution of CVc/CVq to Thompson et al. 2011 is defensible but not uniquely correct; the Speir/Rose 2023 WIREs Water review credits Musolff et al. 2015. Cite both.

(3) BASU 2010 DETAIL: the annual load vs annual discharge linearity framing is consistent with the abstract, but the specific claim that they used the r-squared of that regression as the chemostasis measure is UNVERIFIED. Do not quote it as established.

(4) SCALE CONFOUND (must be added): CVc/CVq rises systematically with basin area across six orders of magnitude (Marinos, Van Meter & Basu 2020, GRL, "Is the river a chemostat?"). A fixed cutoff applied across the project's 22 gauged sites will partly sort them by size, not regime. Any use of CVc/CVq here must control for log_basin_area or it risks reproducing a feature already in the model.

(5) SCOPE (must be added): CVc/CVq requires both C and Q at the site. It is computable on only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS; zero IWQIS, confirmed in data_inventory.md) and is NEVER computable at the deployment target -- an arbitrary ungauged map pin. It is a hypothesis diagnostic, not a candidate feature.

(6) THE BETWEEN-SITE INFERENCE IS NOT ENTAILED: CVc/CVq is a within-site temporal statistic and does not predict the sign or strength of the between-site relation between mean concentration and N-source terms. The legacy-store narrative motivates that expectation; the metric does not test it. Confirming low CVc/CVq on the gauged subset would be consistent with the project's observed pattern (static geography wins, temporal hydrology fails) but would add no new between-site information and would not close the between_r2 = 0.21 gap. Testing the actual between-site hypothesis requires regressing site-mean concentration on source terms across sites -- n~19 independent families, underpowered, and confounded by basin area.

Claim is accurate in every checkable detail; two refinements. (1) METRIC: "86.03% accuracy" is NOT balanced/confusion-matrix accuracy — it is one-sided positive-class recall. The paper states "overall accuracy of 86.03% for the CONUS with an omission error of 13.97%" (sums to exactly 100%), because all 16,000 ground-truth points are known-DRAINED locations, manually identified from tile signatures visible on fallow cropland in ESRI 15m/1m/0.6m/0.3m imagery. No false-positive/commission rate is established anywhere in the paper; its limitations section concedes "uncertainty in croplands without tile drainage." So the layer's over-prediction rate is unquantified. (2) IOWA IS BETTER THAN CLAIMED: the claim quotes only the generic 82.7-93.6% Midwest band, but the paper reports Iowa specifically as the most tile-drained state (5.7 Mha) with 5,253 ground-truth points and 91.1% accuracy, and county-total bias of only +/-0.04% (Illinois +0.07%). Accuracy exceeds 98% on very-poorly/poorly-drained soils with slope <=1% — i.e. Des Moines Lobe conditions. Also note the paper's own Data Availability cites figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.12668234, but that item contains only a metadata record (data.json, 275-byte CSV); the claim's URL (figshare 11825742) is the correct data item and is the one to use. Finally, the layer is not orthogonal information: within-county allocation is driven ONLY by gSSURGO drainage class + slope under a county census total, so basin-mean tile fraction is a smooth deterministic function of soil+slope+cropland. It is genuinely new relative to this project's current 68 features (which contain no soil drainage class, no slope, no county tile totals), but it should be expected to correlate with, not add to, any future soils feature.

result.evidence:
PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED. DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605 resolves to Thompson, S. E., N. B. Basu, J. Lascurain Jr., A. Aubeneau, and P. S. C. Rao (2011), Water Resources Research 47, W00J05. Full text obtained from the author's copy at https://www.ce.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/assets/users/thompson/WRRThompson2011Biogeochem.pdf (Wiley pdfdirect and DOI landing page both 402/403 to automated fetch; OpenAlex/Unpaywall confirm bronze OA). Note the exact title is "...on solute export across impact GRADIENTS", not "across impacted watersheds" as the claim renders it. There is also a formal Correction (Thompson et al. 2012, doi:10.1029/2012WR012754) — it is only a missing data-use acknowledgment for the Little Vermillion River data, no scientific content changed.

Point-by-point against the paper text:

(1) METRIC PROPOSED BY THOMPSON ET AL. 2011 — TRUE, verbatim. Para [19]: "An alternative, nonparametric, measure of chemostatic response can be defined as the ratio of the coefficients of variation of concentration and discharge... The proposed metric is the ratio CVC/CVQ = (sigma_Q/mu_Q)(sigma_C/mu_C)^-1" (Eq. 1).

(2) CVc/CVq << 1 AS CHEMOSTATIC — TRUE, verbatim. Para [20]: "Godsey et al. [2009] proposed a simple null hypothesis that in-stream concentrations should reflect dilution of a fixed mass available for export (i.e., C = aQ^-1). A propagation of variance analysis... implies that for this null hypothesis, CVC/CVQ = 1. Chemostatic behavior could then be considered a case where the variability in concentration was highly buffered compared to this null hypothesis, i.e., CVC/CVQ << 1. Note that if C = aQ^0 (the Godsey et al. [2009] criterion), then CVC/CVQ = 0."

(3) THE 0.3 THRESHOLD — TRUE and exact, but "conventionally taken" is an overstatement. Para [28]: "For the geogenic species... the mean CVC/CVQ was 0.17 (range 0.15–0.19) with standard deviation 0.06 (range 0.04–0.07), i.e., uniformly well below 1... We define a chemostatic CV ratio as being within two standard deviations of the mean geogenic CVC/CVQ, that is ~0.3." So 0.3 = 0.17 + 2(0.06), an internal empirical calibration to the geogenic reference solutes measured at THIS paper's own 31 subwatersheds. It is not a community convention and the paper does not present it as one.

(4) "CHEMODYNAMIC" TERMINOLOGY — the word "chemodynamic" appears ZERO times in the paper (grep count 0). CVc/CVq = 1 is the DILUTION null hypothesis (C proportional to 1/Q), not "chemodynamic". Numerically harmless, terminologically drifted.

(5) BASU ET AL. 2010 ANNUAL LOAD–Q r-squared — TRUE, verbatim. Para [19]: "Basu et al. [2010a] argued that chemostatic behavior implied near linearity in the annual load (LT)–discharge (QT) relationship (LT = Cf QT), as measured by the correlation coefficient (r^2)." Basu et al. 2010a = GRL 37, L23404, doi:10.1029/2010GL045168, "Nutrient loads exported from managed catchments reveal emergent biogeochemical stationarity" (MARB + Baltic Sea Drainage Basin, TN and TP, annual aggregates). Thompson himself flags a circularity the claim omits: "the definition of load as LT = Cf QT complicates the interpretation of the LT-QT r^2 value as a measure of linearity, due to the construction of LT as a linear function of QT."

(6) LEGACY-STORE BUFFERING — TRUE, abstract verbatim: "These 'chemostatic' responses are hypothesized to arise when a large mass store, the parent material for geogenics or chemically recalcitrant legacies of fertilization in agricultural catchments, buffers concentration variability."

(7) HOMOGENEOUS vs HETEROGENEOUS SOURCES — PARTIALLY TRUE, and materially garbled. Abstract: "the decline in CVC/CVQ arises if the internal mass store is distributed homogeneously in space AND there is sufficient time for mass transfer to reach steady state between runoff events." The claim drops the second, co-necessary timescale condition. Further, the "homogeneity" is a parameter xi in a single-reactor model denoting UNIFORM VERTICAL mass distribution in the soil profile: para [26] region, "repeating the analysis with xi != 0 (not shown) showed that chemostatic behavior couldn't be recovered unless xi ~ 0, recapitulating the Seibert et al. [2009] requirement of spatial homogeneity." This is a modeled inference, never an empirical test of landscape source heterogeneity across catchments.

METHODOLOGY / SAMPLE SIZE. Para [12]-[13]: "data from 31 small intensively studied watersheds (0.1–22 km2)" drawn from only NINE experimental watersheds (LTERs/experimental forests) — i.e. 31 nested subwatersheds within 9 independent sites, the exact pseudoreplication structure this project already corrected for with its 85 sites -> 19 families. Sites were deliberately chosen small "thus minimizing the effects of spatial averaging on the hydrochemistry" — the opposite regime from Iowa's large, partly multi-state basins. Only TWO of the nine are agricultural (Little Vermillion River, IL — tile-drained; McDonogh, MD). Sampling: daily flow, "daily to monthly sampling of nitrate over at least a 3 year period"; CVs computed on the full record, no spatial holdout of any kind (protocol: not applicable, this is a descriptive synthesis, not a predictive study). Para [23] documents that CV is unstable when the mean is low or near detection limit.

THE NITRATE RESULT IS THE WEAKEST PART OF THE PAPER, AND IT IS THE PART THE CLAIM LEANS ON. Abstract: "Nitrate showed a suggestive pattern in CVC/CVQ with export, but further data are needed to confirm its generality." Para [30]: nitrate CVc/CVq had "mean 0.70, standard deviation 0.49" across sites, decreasing with export "albeit less abruptly than in the case of the exogenous salts"; "The lowest values of CVC/CVQ for NO3- were in the range of 0.2–0.4, comparable to the geogenic species. Although suggestive, the data at high export levels remain scarce." So on the paper's own ~0.3 criterion, MOST of its nitrate sites are NOT chemostatic; only the sparse high-export tail approaches it. Same paragraph warns the metrics disagree for N specifically: "Numerous sites displayed b ~ 0, but nonetheless exhibited a wide range of variability as measured by CVC/CVQ."

AUTHOR'S OWN CAVEAT AGAINST THE CLAIM'S USE, para [20]: "Describing a condition of low CVC/CVQ as chemostatic behavior, however, should not be overinterpreted. This use of the term chemostatic does not imply that concentrations are truly invariant, or uncorrelated with variations in flow."
result.correction:
The citation checks out and the numbers are exact — keep it — but three things must be fixed before this is used to justify anything.

1. PROVENANCE OF THE 0.3. It is not a "conventional" threshold. It is 0.17 + 2 x 0.06, two SDs above the mean CVc/CVq of GEOGENIC solutes measured at Thompson's own 31 subwatersheds (nested in 9 experimental sites, 0.1-22 km2). It is a relative reference calibrated on that dataset, in a paper with only 2 agricultural catchments. Do not cite it as a community standard, and do not treat crossing 0.3 as a physical fact about an Iowa basin. Also fix the title ("across impact gradients") and drop "chemodynamic" — the word never appears; CVc/CVq = 1 is Godsey et al. 2009's pure-DILUTION null (C ~ 1/Q), not a chemodynamic label.

2. THE PAPER DOES NOT ESTABLISH THAT AGRICULTURAL NITRATE IS CHEMOSTATIC. Its nitrate result is mean CVc/CVq = 0.70 (SD 0.49) — above the 0.3 line for most sites — with only the sparse high-export tail reaching 0.2-0.4, and the abstract explicitly says "further data are needed to confirm its generality." The agricultural-legacy-N story rests on Basu et al. 2010 GRL (doi:10.1029/2010GL045168), which is ANNUAL total-N load vs ANNUAL discharge over MARB and Baltic basins, not daily concentration. Cite Basu for the legacy-N mechanism, not Thompson.

3. THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION AS STATED IS NOT WHAT CHEMOSTASIS PREDICTS. Chemostasis constrains WITHIN-site variance of C relative to Q. It does not say the between-site mean concentration tracks the source term alone. Under Basu's own formulation the invariant quantity is the flow-weighted concentration Cf = LT/QT — a RATIO. So chemostasis predicts site-mean concentration ~ (delivered N load per unit area) / (mean annual runoff depth), which means the hydrologic term does not drop out, it moves into the DENOMINATOR as a long-term water-yield normalizer. That is a genuinely different and more useful engineering prescription than "use surplus and row-crop fraction": build a static per-basin feature of the form (N surplus or row-crop fraction) / (long-term mean annual runoff or precipitation), i.e. a normalized source-loading intensity, rather than the raw source terms currently in the model. This is a static, climatological feature computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from PRISM/Daymet normals plus a runoff-coefficient raster — it does not need the target's discharge. That is the actionable, deployment-compatible reading, and it is not what the claim states.

Two further constraints to attach. (a) DIAGNOSTIC ONLY, NEVER A FEATURE: CVc/CVq needs paired C and Q at the site. That exists at 22 of 85 sites (26%, all USGS, zero IWQIS) and at ZERO arbitrary map pins. It can characterize the training sites; it can never be an input at deployment. (b) THE n CONSTRAINT BITES TWICE: those 22 gauged sites collapse to well under 19 independent basin families, so any regression of site-mean level on chemostasis-derived predictors has single-digit effective units — smaller than Thompson's own 9 independent sites, and with the same nesting problem. Additionally the timescale is wrong for the product: CVc/CVq is a whole-distribution variance statistic computed on daily-to-monthly grab samples (Basu's on annual aggregates), while the target is DAILY-MAX nitrate crossing 10 mg/L. A basin can be perfectly chemostatic at CVc/CVq = 0.3 and still swing across 10 mg/L constantly if its mean sits near 8. Chemostasis says nothing about the upper tail, which is the entire classification problem.

Finally, "consistent with our observed pattern that static geography wins and temporal features fail" is post-hoc, not diagnostic. A chemodynamic system with uninformative same-day weather features would produce the identical symptom, and the failed features were precipitation and fuel moisture, not discharge — the C-Q relation was never actually tested here. If you want a real test, compute CVc/CVq on the 22 gauged sites (checking, as Thompson does in para [23], that the flow range during concentration sampling spans the full flow-duration curve, and noting the 0.66-0.97 discharge density gaps), and separately regress site-mean nitrate on surplus/runoff. The CV ratio itself decides nothing about the model.

It is producer's accuracy/recall on visually-identified tile-drained points. No commission error, no class balance, no kappa, no precision are reported. False-positive rate of the layer is UNQUANTIFIED. "86.03% classification accuracy" reads as balanced two-class accuracy and is not.
2. VALIDATION-POINT SELECTION BIAS, stated by the authors: points were "limited mostly to fallow croplands where the tile drainage signature is easily detectable," and "Unavailability of tile drainage ground truth points over vegetated croplands and uncertainty in croplands without tile drainage constitutes the primary limitations of the validation approach we adopted." Accuracy is measured where tiles are most visible — optimistic.
3. The 16,000 points are drawn from TEN STATES, not distributed CONUS-wide, and ~33% (5,253) sit in Iowa alone. The claim's metadata field "16,000 ground-truth validation points, CONUS-wide" overstates spatial spread. Points are also spatially clustered — pseudoreplication means effective n is far below 16,000.
4. COUNTY TOTALS ARE MATCHED BY CONSTRUCTION. The model ranks pixels by gSSURGO drainage category (starting D=7) and zero slope, accumulates area, and iteratively relaxes the slope threshold "until estimated tile drainage area exceeded USDA census." That distinction is sound: N-surplus is an inherently time-varying quantity frozen at its last value, whereas tile presence is a genuinely slow-varying stock. Residual caveat the claim does not make: the paper's own abstract says tile drainage "has greatly expanded since the late 1990s," so a 2017 snapshot applied across 2008-2026 carries real epoch mismatch in absolute drained area; only the between-site RANK is likely stable.

It contains no independent observation of tiles. Two consequences at n=19. First, its incremental value over simply aggregating gSSURGO drainage class and slope per distance bucket is unknown and could be near zero; the project should test both arms rather than assuming the census-allocation step adds signal. Second, the allocation is constrained to county sums, so the layer has step discontinuities at COUNTY LINES — a political artifact, not hydrology. Since lon and lat are already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features, a county-blocky covariate risks being partly collinear with spatial structure the model already exploits.
- n=19 FRAMING NEEDS TIGHTENING. The claim calls 1-3 static columns on ~19 units "a defensible ratio," which is true as far as column count goes, but the binding constraint is EVALUATION POWER, not parameter count. With 19 LOFO folds, PR-AUC deltas below roughly 0.03-0.05 are indistinguishable from fold noise. The feature is cheap and worth testing, but a single positive LOFO delta at n=19 should be reported with a fold-level confidence interval and not treated as established. Note also that AgTile-US's evidence base is a mapping-accuracy study, not an n-basins hydrology benchmark, so rule 5's "hundreds of catchments" concern does not apply — there is no transfer-from-large-n inference being made here.

(1) n IS recoverable and the paper IS readable. 49 calibration basins (subset of the 1,469 NWM v2.0 CONUS calibration basins with TD >= 10% of area), regionalized to 939 HUC10 basins over the Upper Mississippi + Ohio HUC2s. The Gower's-distance regionalization to 939 HUC10s is never scored against held-out gauges. So the "20-50%" figure is an out-of-time, in-sample-basin gain and is not an ungauged-basin result. Do not present it as evidence about transfer.

(3) THE INFERENCE OVERREACHES ON BIAS. The claim argues NWM-Q error "is likely correlated WITH tile density... so it can bias rather than merely add noise," implying a between-site LEVEL offset — the exact axis where our model has headroom. The paper's own numbers point the other way: "There are no considerable differences in the estimated Bias between Default and DefaultTD," and adding TD changes volume by only +2.3% while changing peaks +14% and baseflow +11%, with gains concentrated in NSE/KGE/COR/RMSE. The signature of the missing TD process is therefore predominantly TIMING, PEAK SHAPE and FLASHINESS — a within-site temporal distortion, which is the axis where our model already performs adequately (within_r2 0.42) — not a systematic between-site mean-flow bias. Additionally, the operational NWM is calibrated, and the CalibTD-noTile ablation shows calibration partially compensates for the missing physics; that compensation holds at gauged calibration basins and degrades at ungauged reaches only as far as donor-basin matching degrades. Net: the "structurally mis-specified" verdict is correct, but the specific escalation to "biases the between-site gradient" is unsupported by this source and should be downgraded to an untested hypothesis. Practical implication: NWM retrospective Q is still worth testing as a feature, but expect it to help WITHIN-site timing (already our strength) rather than fix between-site level, so its expected marginal value against our actual deficit is LOW.

(4) Minor: 2.7 million reaches is the v2.0 figure; SCN 23-76 states v3.0 covers "over 3.2 million river reaches." Use 2.7M only when describing the paper.

HIGH-VALUE COLLATERAL FIND — this paper directly closes the project's open "no tile-drainage data source identified" gap. It uses AgTile-US: a 30-m binary tile-drained-cropland map covering the CONUS (so it covers all of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of the multi-state basins, unlike the Iowa-clipped CDL/N-surplus layers that currently under-count). Download: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742 (figshare, free bulk download, no authentication; figshare datasets are CC-licensed — confirm the CC-BY/CC0 tag on the record page before redistribution). Static in time (a single snapshot, no year dimension — so no repeat of the "N-surplus broadcast forward" failure mode, since it is never presented as time-varying). It is a STATIC, GEOMETRIC, BETWEEN-SITE covariate — the exact class of feature that produced this project's only wins (lat, lon, log_basin_area) while every temporal feature failed. n=19-families caution: add it as ONE basin-mean tile fraction first, not as 3 distance-bucket copies; 3 new columns against 19 effective independent units is a real overfitting risk and the bucketed version should only be tried if the single-scalar version wins under LOFO.

1. VERBATIM QUOTE — EXACT. The published abstract reads: "The National Water Model (NWM) is a distributed 1-km resolution hydrological model designed to provide accurate streamflow forecasts at 2.7 million reaches across the US. The current NWM lacks TD representation which adds considerable uncertainty to streamflow forecasts in heavily tile-drained areas." Word-for-word match with the claim (published text uses a non-breaking hyphen in "tile‐drained"). No exaggeration, no garbling.

2. "AS OF v2.0" — CONFIRMED FROM METHODS. The paper repeatedly names the base model: "NWM V2.0 and used 30-m resolution AgTile-US to identify tile-drained…", "NWM V2.0 without parameter calibration", "NWM V2.0 with calibrated parameters, mimicking the operational NWM", "a subset of 49 basins from V2.0 calibration basins". Base physics is Noah-MP (Niu et al. 2011) inside WRF-Hydro, 1-km LSM grid disaggregated to a 250-m routing grid, Muskingum-Cunge channel routing on NHDPlusV2 flowlines. The claim's "1-km land-surface resolution routed to 2.7 million NHDPlus reaches" is accurate; "NHDPlus" is the claimant's own addition but is correct (NHDPlusV2 is listed in the Data Availability Statement).

I checked the operational code lineage directly: NCAR/wrf_hydro_nwm_public release v5.4.0 (2025-03-14) states in its release notes "consistent with the NOAA National Water Model (NWM) v3.1 code in operations." A GitHub code search of that repo for tile drainage returns only three hits, all false positives — computational "tiles" (its,ite,jts,jte), a GW-basin "tile mapping index", and the Noah-MP `slope` "Soil Drainage Parameter." `TILE_DRAIN`/`TDRAIN` return zero hits, and docs/userguide/model-physics.rest contains no mention of tile or subsurface agricultural drainage. CONCLUSION: no tile-drainage scheme exists in the public NWM/WRF-Hydro code through NWM v3.1. The omission the paper describes for v2.0 persists in the v2.1 and v3.0 retrospectives the project would actually pull.

4. n IS RECOVERABLE — the claim's "unknown, not recoverable" is wrong. Screening: 188 USGS hourly streamflow gauges over the upper Midwest, filtered to <20% missing data AND >10% catchment TD fraction. Calibration: 49 basins (subset of the NWM V2.0 calibration basin set with TD >= 10% of basin area), DDS algorithm, regionalized to HUC10s by donor basin. Regional evaluation: 139 USGS gauge locations across UMRB + ORB, water years 2013-2019 (run 2012-2019, WY2012 discarded as spin-up). Process validation: South Fork Iowa River watershed, Iowa (USDA-ARS soil moisture + flux) plus SMAP/Sentinel-1.

5. METHODOLOGY OF THE UNDERLYING STUDY — the split is TEMPORAL, NOT SPATIAL. Figure 3 is "NWM performance evaluation over 49 calibration basins for the calibration and validation periods" — same basins, different years. There is no leave-one-basin-out / ungauged-basin protocol anywhere in the paper. This does NOT undermine the claim being verified, because that claim is a statement about model source-code structure, not about a learned model's generalization, and the claim itself correctly reports protocol as "not-applicable." But it does mean the paper's headline improvement numbers (+14% peaks, +2.3% volume, +11% baseflow, hit-rate gains) are gauged, temporally-split numbers and must not be quoted as transfer performance.

6. IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION THE CLAIM OMITS — CALIBRATION PARTIALLY ABSORBS THE MISSING TD PHYSICS. From the abstract: "Employing a TD enhanced uncalibrated performance by about 20-50% of fully calibrated (Calib)." That is, adding TD physics to the uncalibrated model recovers only a fifth to a half of what plain parameter calibration already recovers without any TD representation — Calib (no TD) beats DefaultTD. The NWM v2.1 and v3.0 retrospectives are calibrated/regionalized products, so a large fraction of the structural deficit is already compensated by tuned parameters. "Structurally mis-specified estimate of Q" is therefore too strong as stated for calibrated retrospective output.

7. BUT THE CLAIM'S CORE INFERENCE SURVIVES FOR THIS PROJECT'S DEPLOYMENT TARGET. The compensation in (6) is achieved by fitting parameters at gauged basins and transferring them to ungauged HUC10s via donor basins. The deployment target here is an ARBITRARY UNGAUGED MAP PIN — precisely a reach receiving donor-basin parameters rather than its own fit. Where the donor's tile fraction differs from the pin's, the residual bias re-emerges and is by construction organized by tile-drainage fraction. The paper's water-budget numbers show the direction and rough scale of what is being mis-partitioned when TD is absent: surface runoff -7% to -29%, groundwater recharge -43% to -50%, ET -13%, soil moisture -2% to -3%, profile lateral flow +27.7%. Those are large, systematic, and monotone in TD fraction, so "error correlated with tile density, hence with the between-site gradient" is a defensible inference — though it is the claimant's inference, not a sentence in the paper, and the paper offers no quantification of residual bias-vs-TD-fraction in the calibrated configuration.

8. TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR SETTING. The study domain includes the Upper Mississippi River Basin, where ~50% of all US tile-drained cropland sits and TD covers 48% of UMRB cropland; the process-validation site is literally in Iowa (South Fork Iowa River). Geographic transfer is as good as it gets. The n=19-independent-basin-families constraint is NOT a threat here: this is a physics-model structural fact, not a learned relationship requiring basins to estimate, so no sample-size flag applies. The claim also does not require the target site's own observations.

The project brief says "Tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet." This paper's own input dataset fills that gap: AgTile-US, a 30-m binary tile-drainage map for the CONUS (Valayamkunnath, Barlage, et al. 2020), free, no authentication, at https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742/. It is binary per 30-m cell (1 = tile-drained), so basin tile-drained AREA FRACTION per distance bucket is computable by the same zonal machinery already used for CDL — a STATIC, BETWEEN-SITE feature, which is exactly the class of feature that has historically worked on this project (geometry and static geography) rather than the temporal class that has failed seven times. Caveat to check before use: verify CONUS-wide coverage of the multi-state portions of the largest basins, and note it is derived from NASS Census + land cover, so it is a presence map, not a drain-spacing/intensity map.

(d) The v3.0 hedge can now be discharged, in the claim's favor: I verified against the operational code lineage (NCAR/wrf_hydro_nwm_public v5.4.0, release notes state consistency with operational NWM v3.1) that no tile-drainage module or namelist option exists — zero hits for TILE_DRAIN/TDRAIN, no mention in docs/userguide/model-physics.rest, and the only "tile"/"drainage" string matches are computational tiles and the Noah-MP soil-drainage slope parameter. result.evidence:
CITATION IS REAL AND CORRECTLY ATTRIBUTED. Thompson, S. E., Basu, N. B., Lascurain, J., Aubeneau, A., Rao, P. S. C. (2011), "Relative dominance of hydrologic versus biogeochemical factors on solute export across impact gradients," Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605, 334 citations (OpenAlex). Its abstract does concern the concentration/discharge variability ratio and does attribute chemostasis to spatially homogeneous mass stores. So the qualitative core is sound and the DOI is right.

THE NUMBER 0.3 IS WRONG. I found no source using 0.3. The two conventions actually in the literature are 0.5 and 1.0. Frietsch & Schuetz (2026), Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 30, 2059-2077, DOI 10.5194/hess-30-2059-2026 (gold OA, read in full), Section 2.3.3: "Solutes with CVC/CVQ > 0.5 were classified as chemodynamic ... whereas CVC/CVQ <= 0.5 indicated chemostatic behaviour. The threshold of 0.5 ... was chosen following Thompson et al. (2011), who showed that conservative tracers typically yielded values around this level. This benchmark has been adopted in subsequent studies (Ebeling et al., 2021; Musolff et al., 2017) ... Although alternative thresholds (e.g. 1) exist in the literature (Musolff et al., 2015), 0.5 was deemed most appropriate." Independently, the HyGCS toolbox documentation (hygcs.readthedocs.io) uses "CVc/CVq > 1 = chemodynamic, < 1 = chemostatic," citing Musolff et al. 2015, Adv. Water Resour. 86, 133-146. The Speir/Rose et al. 2023 WIREs Water C-Q review (read in full) gives NO numeric threshold at all and attributes the classification scheme to Musolff et al. 2015, citing Thompson et al. 2011 only for the concept. Note also that per Frietsch & Schuetz, Thompson et al. 2011 did not set a hard cutoff; 0.5 is a value later readers inferred from Thompson's conservative-tracer results. So "0.3 conventionally taken as the chemostatic threshold" is unsupported and off by a factor of ~1.7-3.3 from the real conventions.

BASU ET AL. 2010 IS CHARACTERIZED CORRECTLY, BUT ITS OWN TEXT DESTROYS THE PROJECT-LEVEL INFERENCE. Basu et al. (2010), GRL, DOI 10.1029/2010GL045168 (author copy read in full). Sample: 21 MARB catchments (10^4-10^6 km2) + 14 Baltic Sea Drainage Basin catchments (10^2-10^5 km2) + Hubbard Brook/Loch Vale forested reference sites + 3 Lake Okeechobee + 2 Swan River, 10-30 yr records. They do use zero-intercept linear regression of annual load LT on annual discharge QT with R2 as the criterion ("consistent linear relationships (R2 = 0.7 +/- 0.2) between annual exported nutrient loads, LT, and annual discharge, QT"), and a separate model-adequacy criterion "linear fits to the LT-QT relationship are judged adequate (R2 > 0.8) for a range of b values (-0.4 < b < 1.4)". So that part of the claim checks out. BUT the same paper states verbatim: "non-chemostatic responses are typical of nutrient (TN and TP) export from managed catchments in the MARB and BSDB (Figures S1 and S2). Notwithstanding non-chemostatic response at the daily or monthly time scales, we find consistent linear relationships ... between annual exported nutrient loads and annual discharge." Basu's chemostasis is an ANNUAL-scale, flow-weighted-concentration claim about basins of 10^4-10^6 km2. This project predicts DAILY MAX nitrate and daily 10 mg/L exceedance in Iowa, which is inside the MARB. The cited source explicitly says N is NOT chemostatic at that timescale in that region. Basu et al. also pre-empt a statistical objection that applies directly to the proposed decision rule: the LT-QT correlation is partly "spurious ... since discharge is a component of load calculation."

THE METRIC IS SCALE-DEPENDENT IN EXACTLY THIS REGION. Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020), "Is the River a Chemostat?: Scale Versus Land Use Controls on Nitrate Concentration-Discharge Dynamics in the Upper Mississippi River Basin," GRL, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051 (abstract via OpenAlex; paper is closed access): "tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior. We further find that concentration variability increases, relative to discharge variability, with increasing basin size across six orders of magnitude." So CVc/CVq in the UMRB is a strong function of basin area and tile density, not a stable solute property. Computing it across the project's 22 gauged sites (which span a wide area range) would mostly recover basin area — a feature the model already has as log_basin_area.

BROADER NEGATIVE EVIDENCE ON THE LINEARITY IMPLICATION. Moatar et al. (2017), WRR, DOI 10.1002/2016WR019635, 293 French monitoring stations, 40 years: "84% of all catchment-element combinations were chemodynamic for at least half of hydrograph" and "60% showed nonlinear C-Q curves." Diamond & Cohen (2017), DOI 10.1002/hyp.11424, 44 Florida rivers, found significant C-Q slope breaks near median flow and concluded "generic power-law characterization" is inadequate. Universal chemostasis + load-Q linearity is not a safe default.

METHODOLOGICAL WARNING AGAINST THE PROPOSED USE, FROM THE FIELD'S OWN REVIEW. Speir/Rose et al. (2023), WIREs Water: "C-Q metrics are interrelated and may not be independent of each other ... the range of concentration variability is inherently linked to the quantitative estimation of both b and CVC/CVQ (Jawitz & Mitchell, 2011; Musolff et al., 2015; Thompson et al., 2011) ... caution and correction procedures should be applied when conducting statistical analyses on derived metrics (e.g., regressing metrics against each other) because this can involve testing multiple hypotheses on the same dataset and thereby inflating Type I error." The proposed decision rule is precisely "regress a derived C-Q metric against catchment attributes." The same review's methods table lists CVC/CVQ as needing ">1 year of 5-15 min frequency sensor data," so grab-sample sites and sensor sites are not comparable on this metric.

THE LOAD-BEARING INFERENCE IS A NON-SEQUITUR AND IS PARTLY BACKWARDS. The claim asserts chemostasis "predicts ... the site-mean concentration should track the N-source term ... rather than the hydrologic term." Neither source says this, and it does not follow. Basu's own definition is Cf = LT/QT: under chemostasis the site-mean concentration IS mass flux divided by water flux, so long-term mean runoff sits in the denominator and is a first-order BETWEEN-site control, not an eliminated one. Chemostasis implies that SAME-DAY discharge is uninformative about concentration while LONG-TERM CLIMATOLOGICAL water yield is highly informative. The project's seven failed ablations were all short-window/event-scale temporal features; none of them tested a static long-term runoff or precipitation climatology term. So the theory, read correctly, does not "explain" the failures and does not endorse dropping hydrology — if anything it argues for adding a static climatological water-yield normalizer that the current 68-feature set lacks.

DEPLOYMENT-TARGET AND SAMPLE-SIZE VERDICT. CVc/CVq requires paired C and Q at the site. Discharge exists at 22 of 85 sites and zero of 61 IWQIS sites; the shipped product is an arbitrary map pin with no gauge at all, so this can never be a feature at prediction time. As a diagnostic it is computable, but on 22 sites that collapse to well under the project's 19 independent basin families, and any between-site regression of the resulting metric on N surplus / row-crop fraction / tile density would have effective n around 10, with the metric itself confounded by basin area (Marinos et al. 2020) and by sampling frequency. That is not a "cheap decision rule"; it is an underpowered correlation on derived quantities that the field's own review warns against computing this way.

Water Resour. 86, 133-146). (2) The threshold is NOT 0.3. Use 0.5 (the value Frietsch & Schuetz 2026, Musolff et al. 2017 and Ebeling et al. 2021 adopt following Thompson et al. 2011) or 1.0 (Musolff et al. 2015), and state which. Thompson et al. 2011 did not itself publish a hard cutoff. (3) Basu et al. 2010 (GRL, DOI 10.1029/2010GL045168) is correctly described as using zero-intercept linear annual-load-vs-annual-discharge regression, R2 = 0.7 +/- 0.2, on 21 MARB + 14 BSDB large catchments — but it explicitly reports that TN and TP in the MARB are NON-chemostatic at daily and monthly timescales, which is this project's timescale and region. Chemostasis here is an annual, 10^4-10^6 km2 statement and must not be imported to daily 10 mg/L exceedance. (4) The homogeneous-source-to-chemostasis link is real but incomplete: Thompson et al. require BOTH spatial uniformity of the mass store AND sufficient inter-event time for mass-transfer equilibrium; Musolff et al. 2017 (DOI 10.1002/2017GL072630) adds heterogeneity in travel times as a co-driver. The project currently has same-day weather scalars only and no static climatological water-yield term; adding a 30-year mean annual runoff/precipitation basin average as a STATIC feature is the recommendation this theory actually supports, and unlike CVc/CVq it is computable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin (e.g. from PRISM 30-yr normals or a gridded runoff climatology). (6) Treat CVc/CVq itself as a within-site diagnostic on the 22 gauged sites only, report it stratified by basin area because Marinos et al. 2020 (GRL, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051) show it rises systematically with basin size across six orders of magnitude in the Upper Mississippi and falls with tile drainage density, and do not use it as a model feature, since the deployment target has no discharge record.

result.correction:
The claim is correct in substance and its central quote is exact. Four corrections, one of them materially changing the recommendation:

1. MAGNITUDE IS OVERSTATED -- the claim omits the calibration nuance, which is in the same abstract. Verbatim: "Employing a TD scheme enhanced the uncalibrated NWM performance by about 20-50% of the fully calibrated NWM (Calib)." That is, adding TD to the UNCALIBRATED model recovers only 20-50% of what calibration alone already achieves. The NWM retrospective is the CALIBRATED configuration, so calibration absorbs a large share of the missing-TD signal and the residual bias is smaller than "structurally mis-specified" implies. The direction of the claim survives, because CalibTD still beat Calib (higher event hit rates, lower false alarm rates, better high-flow estimation) -- so a residual deficit remains even after calibration. And crucially for this project, NWM calibration is performed at gauged basins and regionalized to ungauged reaches, so the compensation is weakest at exactly the arbitrary ungauged map pins the product targets. Net: caution justified, magnitude should be stated as "residual after calibration," not "raw structural omission."

2. "as of v2.0" IS NOT ESTABLISHED BY THIS SOURCE. The abstract says "the current NWM" with no version. Full text is unreachable (402/403 everywhere). Restate as "as of the paper's 2022 writing." The stronger and verifiable form: no NWM configuration through WRF-Hydro v5.4.0 (March 2025), which ships NWM v2.0/v2.1/v3.0 parameter tables, contains any tile-drainage scheme -- verified by source inspection, no OPT_TDRN, only generic QDRAIN bottom drainage. So v3.0 has NOT added TD, and the claim's open question is now closed in the claim's favor.

3. THE "ERROR CORRELATED WITH TILE DENSITY, SO IT BIASES RATHER THAN ADDS NOISE" STEP IS THE CLAIMANT'S INFERENCE, NOT THE PAPER'S FINDING. The paper reports no analysis of NWM error versus tile-drained fraction. The inference is plausible and directionally supported by the signs and magnitudes reported (peaks +14%, baseflow +11%, recharge -43 to -50%, all scaling with tile-drained fraction), but it must be labeled as inference, not as a published result. Practical implication: if NWM Q is used as a feature, include tile-drained fraction ALONGSIDE it so the model can learn and absorb the bias rather than inherit it.

4. Minor: the abstract says "2.7 million reaches," not "2.7 million NHDPlus reaches." NWM does route on NHDPlus v2.1, so the gloss is correct, but it is an addition to the source.

SEPARATE HIGH-VALUE FINDING -- THE PROJECT BRIEF CONTAINS A FACTUAL ERROR. The brief states tile drainage density is "NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet." A data source exists, published by the SAME first author two years earlier, and it is free, CONUS-wide, and static -- i.e. precisely the between-site, static-geography kind of feature that is the only category that has ever worked on this project, encoding the control the brief itself calls dominant in Iowa:

AgTile-US. Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis, Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x (open access, verified via Europe PMC PMC7406500).
- Resolution 30 m; binary raster (0 = undrained agricultural land, 1 = tile-drained).
- Coverage: entire CONUS, 65 deg 20' 46.49" W to 127 deg 53' 13.65" W, 22 deg 51' 41.18" N to 51 deg 36' 16.74" N. This covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of the large basins -- it does not have the Iowa-boundary truncation problem that corrupts the current CDL/N-surplus inner join.
- Temporal: static, derived from USDA NASS 2017 Census of Agriculture county tile-drainage estimates, constrained by SSURGO soil drainage class and topographic slope via a per-county-calibrated decision tree. No time dimension, so it cannot go stale mid-record the way the 2017-terminating N-surplus does.
- Accuracy: validated against 16,000 ground-truth points, 86.03% CONUS-wide; 82.7-93.6% across the heavily tile-drained Midwest.
- Access: figshare, DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, landing page https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742 (record verified live via figshare API v2; title "AgTile-US", type dataset, posted 2020-07-13). GeoTIFF and NetCDF. Unrestricted public repository, no authentication, bulk download.
- License: CC BY 4.0; article is a US government work not under US copyright.
- Alternative/cross-check source noted in the same paper: Nakagaki et al. (USGS), 30-m gridded tile-drainage FRACTION (continuous, not binary) for the CONUS, updated with the 2012 USDA-NASS census for 12 Midwestern states.

Fit to this project: aggregate tile-drained fraction over basin cells in the existing 3 distance buckets, exactly like the CDL classes, giving 3 new static features. This is a static between-site variable, which is the only feature family that has produced gains here (geometry and static geography), and it targets the between_r2 0.21 / between_rate_r2 0.24 deficit that the brief identifies as holding essentially all remaining headroom. It requires no local nitrate history and no gauged neighbor, so it is fully compatible with the arbitrary-ungauged-map-pin deployment target. The n=19-independent-families constraint still applies and caps how much a handful of new static predictors can be expected to deliver -- 3 extra static columns fit against ~19 effective units risks overfitting the between-site term, so evaluate under LOFO and consider collapsing to a single basin-mean tile fraction before adding all three buckets.

result.correction:
The claim is accurate as stated and needs no factual correction. Five additions matter for how the parent uses it:

1. INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE PAPER, NOT THE CLAIM. The abstract and Section 2.3.1 say 19 regionalization approaches (19+4=23 total), but the Table 2 caption reads "Description of the 18 Regionalization and 4 Benchmark Approaches Tested in This Study" (=22). The claim follows the abstract and main text, which is the defensible reading. Cite as "19 (Table 2 caption says 18; the paper is internally inconsistent)."

2. NO TEMPORAL HOLDOUT - THE SPATIAL HOLDOUT IS REAL BUT THE UPPER BENCHMARK IS OPTIMISTIC. Donors were calibrated on Oct 1989-Sep 1999 and every approach was also evaluated on that same decade (2 preceding years as warm-up only). The receiver catchment's own data are never used to predict it, so the spatial holdout is genuine and the claim's protocol label is right. But the upper benchmark UB is a local calibration scored in-sample, so the relative-performance metric R* is measured against an optimistically biased ceiling. Do not read R* values as out-of-sample skill ratios.

3. EFFECTIVE n IS BELOW 671 FOR SOME APPROACHES. For Climate class, WB class, and Sign class, "Ungauged catchments that did not belong to any class were excluded from the evaluation." The 671 figure is exact for the dataset and for flexible-donor approaches, not uniformly for all 23 methods.

4. TRANSFERABILITY - THE BEST-PERFORMING APPROACHES ARE UNUSABLE AT OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET. This is the most important caveat and the claim does not mention it. The winning categories all require target-site observations. The paper says of its category D/E methods that they "require either estimates of hydrological signatures or a small number of local point observations," and category D is premised on being able "to directly conduct a number of discharge measurements." Volume information was the single best similarity indicator (0.80). Our product is an arbitrary map pin with no nitrate history, no discharge gauge, and no guaranteed gauged upstream neighbor, so Vol, RMSE, Sign, Dist & Vol, Dist & Sign, Dist & RMSE, Attr & Sign and Qobs transfer are all off the table. The deployable subset is Dist (0.79), Attr (0.78), and fixed classifications (0.76), against a random-donor floor of 0.70. So the honest headroom for a no-local-data regionalization scheme in this study is roughly 0.06-0.09 RNP over random donor selection, not the 0.82 headline.

5. TRANSFERABILITY - THREE STRUCTURAL MISMATCHES WITH OUR SETTING.
   (a) n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARD. Every flexible approach selects the 3 most similar donors from a pool of 670. Lesson (b), "almost perfect donors exist for most catchments," is a property of a large diverse donor pool - with 670 candidates you can almost always find 3 close analogs. At 19 independent basin families, "3 nearest of 18" samples the similarity space far more coarsely and there is no basis to assume near-perfect donors exist. This paper's evidence base is ~35x our effective n and its central optimistic finding is the one most dependent on pool size. Flag it as likely infeasible at our scale.
   (b) CAMELS EXPLICITLY EXCLUDES OUR CATCHMENT TYPE. The 671 basins are selected for "minimal human influence" (Newman et al. 2015). Iowa row-crop, tile-drained, fertilized basins are precisely the heavily managed catchments screened out of CAMELS. The donor pool contains essentially no hydrologic analog to our target population, so the reported transferability of donor-selection rules is not demonstrated for tile-drained agricultural systems.
   (c) WRONG TARGET AND WRONG MODEL CLASS. This is streamflow hydrograph regionalization - transferring conceptual rainfall-runoff PARAMETERS of a bucket model - evaluated with KGE-family metrics. It contains no water-quality content whatsoever, and nothing about concentration, exceedance, or classification metrics such as AUC/PR-AUC. Our XGBoost is not a donor-transfer scheme; it already pools all sites globally. The paper's value here is conceptual (donor selection and similarity-based regionalization, plus the discipline of upper/lower/regionalization benchmarks and multi-criteria evaluation), not a method that can be lifted into our pipeline. Its most directly usable idea for us is lesson (c) plus the benchmarking framework: define an explicit lower benchmark (random/base-rate) and an upper benchmark (a site-calibrated model) and report performance relative to that spread - which is a reporting discipline, not a between-site accuracy gain.

result.correction:
The claim is accurate in every number, the source attribution, the protocol label, and n. Two corrections of framing, the first of which is decisive for our deployment target.

(1) THE THREE "SINGLE-INFORMATION FAMILIES" ARE NOT AN EQUAL-COST CHOICE SET — VOLUME REQUIRES THE TARGET'S OWN OBSERVATIONS. The claim implies picking among proximity, attributes, and volume/signature is a free choice that is "nearly a wash." It is a wash in score, but not in data requirements. Table 2 defines Vol verbatim as "The three catchments with the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment are used as donors" — i.e. the volume error is computed against the receiver's measured discharge. Section 2.3.1 category D states these methods assume "it is possible to estimate hydrological signatures for the ungauged catchment... or to directly conduct a number of discharge measurements," and category E (Dist & Vol) states outright: "These approaches also require either estimates of hydrological signatures or a small number of local point observations." So Vol (0.80) and the Dist&Vol category (0.82) are partial-oracle methods, and Best (0.87) is a full oracle (three best donors "defined by RNP," which needs the receiver's full observed hydrograph).

For OUR deployment target — an arbitrary map pin with zero local observations — the realizable menu is only: spatial proximity 0.79, catchment attributes 0.78, fixed classification 0.76, against random 0.69. The zero-observation spread over random is therefore ~0.10 R_NP, not 0.13, and the spread between the two usable single-information families (Dist 0.79 vs Attr 0.78) is 0.01, not 0.02. The claim's headline conclusion actually gets STRONGER for us: among methods we can actually deploy, proximity and attribute similarity are within 0.01 of each other and both are worth ~0.10 over random. The "0.82 best realizable" figure should not be quoted in our context without the local-observation caveat.

(2) TRANSFERABILITY TO SUSTAG IS WEAK ON FOUR AXES, AND THE n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARD AND ASYMMETRICALLY.
- Donor-pool size is the mechanism, and we do not have it. The paper's central Lesson (b) is that "almost perfect donors exist for most catchments" — that is a direct function of choosing the 3 best from a pool of 670. Our pool is ~18 other independent basin families. Both the oracle ceiling (0.87) and the realizable gain over random shrink monotonically with pool size, and the paper offers no evidence at small n. This is a 671-basin result and must be flagged as likely infeasible at n=19: with 18 candidate donors, the nearest neighbor in attribute space is often not near at all. The paper's own Random baseline (3 of 670) is also a much stronger baseline than 3-of-18 would be, so even the direction of the gap is not safely portable.
- Wrong physical system. CAMELS is explicitly screened for minimally-impacted, near-natural catchments. Iowa row-crop basins are artificially drained; the attribute vector Pool et al. use for similarity (area, aridity, precipitation seasonality, snowfall fraction, wetland fraction, clay fraction, forest fraction) contains nothing resembling tile-drainage density, the control our own notes flag as dominant.
- Wrong target. This is calibrated-parameter transfer for streamflow — a mass-conserving water-balance quantity — evaluated by NSE-type efficiency. It is not evidence about transferring the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of a nitrate exceedance rate, which is our actual between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). Nothing in this paper speaks to concentration or exceedance regionalization.
- Wrong model class. The finding concerns donor selection for parameter transfer in a conceptual bucket model (HBV). It does not translate into a feature for a gradient-boosted classifier. The legitimate reading for us is narrow and methodological: it is evidence that ATTRIBUTE-SIMILARITY-BASED transfer is not meaningfully worse than SPATIAL-PROXIMITY-BASED transfer, which mildly discourages spending effort on elaborate similarity metrics and mildly supports the observation that our lat/lon features already capture much of what attribute similarity would. It is NOT evidence that improving static between-site descriptors (e.g. acquiring tile-drainage data) is futile — Pool et al. hold the attribute set fixed and vary only the donor-selection rule, so the study says nothing about the value of a BETTER attribute, only about the value of a better rule for using a fixed attribute set.

The claim is accurate in every quoted number and in its protocol description; no refutation is warranted. Three additions are needed before it is used as support for anything.

(a) PROTOCOL, precise form: the split is spatially held out at the catchment level but has NO temporal holdout - donor parameters were calibrated on 1 Oct 1989 - 30 Sep 1999 and the regionalized predictions were evaluated on that same window. The claim's "spatial-holdout" label is correct but should be stated as "spatial holdout only, calibration and evaluation periods identical."

(b) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE PAPER (not an error in the claim): the abstract and Section 2.3.1 body text say 19 regionalization approaches and "a total of 23 methods," but the Table 2 caption reads "Description of the 18 Regionalization and 4 Benchmark Approaches Tested in This Study" (=22). The claim follows the abstract/body, which is the defensible reading, but anyone quoting "19+4=23" should know Table 2 says 18+4.

(c) MATERIAL OMISSION FOR OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: a large share of the 19 approaches CANNOT be applied at an ungauged map pin. Categories D and E (Vol, RMSE, Sign, Attr & Sign, Dist & Vol, Dist & Sign, Dist & Attr & Sign, Dist & RMSE) are described by the authors as requiring "either estimates of hydrological signatures ... or a small number of local point observations" at the supposedly ungauged catchment, and Qobs transfer requires observed hydrographs from neighbors. The paper's headline winner - distance-plus-volume, median R_NP 0.82 - is in that group. The methods genuinely available with no local observations are the distance-only and attribute-only families at median R_NP 0.79 and 0.78, versus 0.70 for random donors. The usable no-local-data margin over random is therefore roughly 0.08-0.09 R_NP, not the 0.12 implied by the top-ranked method.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT (flagging the n=19 constraint): the evidence base is 671 donor catchments, ~35x our 19 independent basin families. The mechanism transferred is a calibrated conceptual-model parameter vector, which has no analogue in a feature-based XGBoost classifier - so this paper does not supply a method we can implement, only a protocol design and a set of donor-selection heuristics. The flexible region-of-influence approaches select the 3 most similar donors from 670; at n=19 families a 3-donor region of influence draws from 18, so the donor pool is thin enough that the paper's central comparison (flexible RoI beating fixed classification) is untestable here. Target variable also differs fundamentally: daily streamflow evaluated with KGE variants, median catchment area 341 km2, versus our binary daily nitrate exceedance in tile-drained Iowa agricultural basins. Cite this paper for PUB protocol design and for the negative-ish result that attribute-based donor selection lands mid-rank (0.78) and barely beats spatial proximity (0.79), which is consistent with our own finding that static geography carries the between-site signal. Do not cite it as evidence that any regionalization method will deliver gains at n=19.

The claim is accurate as stated; only two refinements and a set of usage caveats are needed.

REFINEMENT 1 (internal inconsistency in the source, not in the claim): the paper's running text and abstract say 19 regionalization approaches and state "a total of 23 methods," but the caption of Table 2 reads "Description of the 18 Regionalization and 4 Benchmark Approaches Tested in This Study" (18+4=22).
