REFINEMENT 2 (protocol, important for our rules): the holdout is SPATIAL ONLY. Donor parameter sets were calibrated on the same window they were evaluated on — "Calibration and evaluation were conducted during the simulation period from October 1, 1989 to September 30, 1999." There is no temporal holdout, and no nesting or region blocking, so this protocol is WEAKER than our leave-one-basin-family-out. Numbers from this study must not be treated as an upper bound comparable to LOFO transfer, and none of its metrics (R_NP/R_KG on daily hydrographs) are comparable to our AUC/PR-AUC on a binary exceedance target in any case.

USAGE CAVEATS FOR OUR PROJECT (the claim is true but should not be used to motivate donor-based regionalization here):

(a) The n=19-families constraint is fatal for the method family this paper evaluates, and the paper's own Figure 1 analysis quantifies why. With 670 candidate donors: "for a relative performance value of 0.7, half of the hypothetically ungauged catchments have at most 23 suitable donor catchments" — i.e. the median catchment has roughly 3.4% of the pool as usable donors. Scaled to our 18 available donor families, the expected number of suitable donors is well under one. The paper also reports that for the median catchment MOST donors are worse than random parameter sets ("For the other 60% of the donor catchments, one would be better off using random parameter sets"). Donor-transfer regionalization derives essentially all its power from a large, hydroclimatically diverse donor pool; at n=19 the pool is too small for the selection step to find anything.

(b) The two best-performing approach families are unavailable at our deployment target. The paper's own conclusion is that approaches combining spatial proximity with VOLUME information (streamflow-derived signatures) rank highest — and it concedes "volume information is per definition missing in ungauged catchments," recoverable only "from a small number of field measurements" or regionalized signatures. Our product pin has no discharge, and only 22 of 85 training sites have streamflow at all (zero of the 61 IWQIS sites), so we cannot even build the donor-side signature library statewide.

(c) Two of the four benchmarks are oracles, not deployable methods. UB requires calibrating on the target's own observations; Best requires knowing the target's observed hydrograph to rank donors by R_NP. The impressive "median 0.87, close to local calibration" number is an oracle ceiling, not an achievable ungauged result. The achievable numbers are the 0.76 (classification-based) to ~0.8x range against a 0.69–0.70 random-donor floor.

(d) Domain mismatch is large: HBV rainfall-runoff parameter transfer for daily streamflow in largely undisturbed CAMELS reference catchments, versus nitrate exceedance classification in tile-drained Iowa row-crop basins. CAMELS gauges are selected for minimal human disturbance, which excludes precisely the artificially drained, fertilized agricultural systems we model; tile drainage is not represented in HBV at all. The transferable insight is conceptual, not numerical: it corroborates our own finding that the hard part is the between-site absolute level, and that similarity must be defined on the right attributes — but it offers no evidence that donor-based transfer will work at n=19 with no volume information.

result.evidence:
PRIMARY SOURCE OBTAINED AND VERIFIED. Pool, S., Vis, M., & Seibert, J. (2021), "Regionalization for Ungauged Catchments — Lessons Learned From a Comparative Large-Sample Study," Water Resources Research 57(10), doi:10.1029/2021WR030437 (published 2021-09-28, CC-BY-NC). Wiley and the ZORA PDF are both bot-walled; I obtained the full published PDF via the ZORA DSpace REST bitstream endpoint and extracted text (local copy: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/e3f1f490-6fb8-475d-be0e-c0cebf530519/scratchpad/pool.txt, 26 pp).

EVERY QUOTED NUMBER IS EXACT — verbatim from Sections 3.1.1 and 3.2.1:
- "The best possible simulation performance was obtained by a local calibration (UB) with a median RNP of 0.89 over all catchments." (UB 0.89 ✓)
- "median RNP values were inferior (RNP of 0.69) to this local calibration" for Random (0.69 ✓)
- "The median performance of these best donors (RNP of 0.87) was identical to the performance of the best regionalization approach found for a given catchment." (Best 0.87 ✓)
- "approaches combine information on spatial distance and volume ... (median RNP of 0.82 and median RKG of 0.67)" (Dist&Vol 0.82/0.67 ✓)
- "Volume seemed to be the best similarity indicator (median RNP of 0.80 and median RKG of 0.66), followed by spatial proximity (median RNP of 0.79 and median RKG of 0.64) and catchment attributes (median RNP of 0.78 and median RKG of 0.62)." (0.80/0.66, 0.79/0.64, 0.78/0.62 ✓)
- "a fixed catchment classification ... typically resulted in lower performances (median RNP of 0.76 and median RKG of 0.58)" (0.76/0.58 ✓)
- "still considerably better than the lower benchmarks or a random selection of donors (median RNP of 0.7 and median RKG of 0.49)" (the 0.69/0.70 discrepancy the claim flags is real and internal to the paper: 0.69 in §3.1.1, 0.7 in §3.2.1; RKG 0.49 ✓)

Derived spreads are arithmetically correct: 0.82 − 0.69 = 0.13; 0.80 − 0.78 = 0.02.

STUDY DESIGN VERIFIED: 671 CAMELS catchments (Addor et al. 2017; Newman et al. 2015), contiguous US, "minimal human influence," HBV bucket model, calibration/simulation 1 Oct 1989 – 30 Sep 1999, 10 calibrated parameter sets per donor, 23 methods (18 regionalization + 4 benchmarks + Qobs transfer). Protocol is leave-one-out cross-validation: "each catchment was treated as ungauged at a time, and its streamflow was simulated with the information of the donor catchments" — so the claim's "spatial-holdout" label is correct for parameter transfer.

METHODOLOGICAL FINDINGS THAT QUALIFY (but do not refute) THE CLAIM:
1. Metric mislabeled. RNP is the NON-PARAMETRIC VARIANT OF THE KLING-GUPTA EFFICIENCY (Pool, Vis & Seibert 2018), not "a Nash-Sutcliffe-type relative efficiency," and it is an ABSOLUTE efficiency. The paper's relative metric is a different quantity, R*NP: "percent improvement from a regionalization with random donors bounded by the local calibration" (Fig. 2 caption). RKG is the standard KGE (Gupta et al. 2009); RNP is the analogue of RKG, not the other way round.
2. "Best realizable" is overstated. The top two methods in the claim's ranking use the target catchment's OWN OBSERVED DISCHARGE. Table 2: "Vol — The three catchments with the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment are used as donors." "Sign" uses the target's observed runoff ratio, mean annual discharge, Q05, Q95, half-flow date, recession slope. Category D is introduced as "it is assumed that it is possible to estimate hydrological signatures for the ungauged catchment ... or to directly conduct a number of discharge measurements." Dist&Vol (0.82) and Vol (0.80) therefore require local observations at the target. The genuinely no-local-data methods are Dist (0.79), Attr (0.78), Dist&Attr, and the classifications (0.76).
3. Medians hide catastrophic tails. §3.2.1: "the regionalization approaches differ considerably in their poorest performance values leading to clear differences in the suitability of the approaches for prediction in ungauged basins." Fig. 2b: under random donors 44 of 671 catchments had RNP between −0.2 and −11.6. A 0.02 median gap is not evidence of tail equivalence.
4. The paper's own Lesson 3 warns against exactly the kind of single-metric ranking the claim leans on: "The ranking of regionalization approaches depends more on how the predicted hydrographs are evaluated than on how the donor catchments are calibrated." Under RKG the three single-information families spread 0.66/0.64/0.62 = 0.04, double the RNP spread. §3.2.3: per-catchment, Dist&Vol was best for 22%, Dist&Sign 12%, Vol/Sign 9%, while continentally poor approaches (Sign class, RMSE, Attr) were best for 2–4% of catchments each; Qobs transfer was best for 12–52% depending on metric.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT (all unfavorable, none of it refuting the claim as stated):
- 670 available donors per target vs OUR 18 (n=19 families minus the held-out one). The paper attributes distance-based methods' edge explicitly to donor density: "This could be linked to the relatively high gauging station density in many humid regions of the United States (Lebecherel et al., 2016; Neri et al., 2020)," and notes that classification pools degrade because "with an increasing number of catchments, the dissimilarity among catchments likely increases" (Arsenault & Brissette 2014; Neri et al. 2020; Oudin et al. 2008). At n=18 donors the entire Dist-vs-Attr comparison is untestable — nearest-neighbor donor selection is meaningless when the pool is 18 basins covering one state.
- Target variable is DAILY STREAMFLOW from a 15-parameter conceptual rainfall-runoff model, not nitrate concentration or a binary exceedance. No water-quality evidence whatsoever.
- CAMELS is explicitly a "minimal human influence" set — the opposite of tile-drained, fertilized Iowa row-crop basins; CAMELS contains very few Corn Belt catchments.
- The mechanism is DONOR PARAMETER TRANSFER (copy a calibrated HBV parameter set), not feature engineering for a gradient-boosted classifier. The 0.02 median gap between similarity families says nothing directly about whether adding static basin attributes to XGBoost features improves between-site ranking.
- Note the direction the claim's own numbers actually point, which cuts AGAINST using it to dismiss static attributes: Attr alone (0.78) beats Random (0.69) by +0.09, i.e. about 70% of the total realizable-without-local-data gain (Dist 0.79 − Random 0.69 = 0.10). Physical catchment attributes carry nearly all of the obtainable no-local-data signal in this study; they are just not separable from spatial proximity at the median.
result.correction:
The claim is numerically exact — every median (UB 0.89, Best 0.87, Dist&Vol 0.82/RKG 0.67, Vol 0.80/0.66, Dist 0.79/0.64, Attr 0.78/0.62, classification 0.76/0.58, Random 0.69–0.70/0.49) is verbatim from Pool, Vis & Seibert (2021), WRR 57(10), doi:10.1029/2021WR030437, 671 CAMELS catchments, HBV, leave-one-out cross-validation. Four corrections of detail:

(1) METRIC. R_NP is the non-parametric variant of the KLING-GUPTA efficiency (Pool, Vis & Seibert 2018), not a "Nash-Sutcliffe-type" metric, and it is an ABSOLUTE efficiency. The paper's relative efficiency is a separate metric, R*_NP, defined as percent improvement over random donors bounded by local calibration. R_KG is the standard KGE; R_NP is the non-parametric analogue OF R_KG, reversing the claim's framing.

(2) "BEST REALIZABLE" IS WRONG FOR AN UNGAUGED PIN. Both Dist&Vol (0.82) and Vol (0.80) are defined using the TARGET CATCHMENT'S OWN OBSERVED DISCHARGE — Table 2: "the three catchments with the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment." Sign likewise uses the target's observed signatures. For a target with NO local observations — this project's deployment case — the best method in the study is Dist at 0.79, so the realizable spread over random is ~0.09–0.10 R_NP, not 0.13. The 0.13 figure is only achievable if you can measure flow at the "ungauged" site.

(3) THE "NEARLY A WASH" GLOSS IS A MEDIAN-ONLY STATEMENT AND THE PAPER EXPLICITLY WARNS AGAINST IT. §3.2.1: approaches "differ considerably in their poorest performance values leading to clear differences in the suitability of the approaches"; under random donors 44/671 catchments fell to R_NP between −0.2 and −11.6. Lesson 3 states the ranking "depends more on how the predicted hydrographs are evaluated than on how the donor catchments are calibrated" — under R_KG the same three families spread 0.04, double the R_NP spread. Per-catchment the best method varies widely (Dist&Vol 22%, Dist&Sign 12%, Vol/Sign 9%, marginal approaches 2–4% each).

(4) SAMPLE-SIZE / TRANSFER CAVEAT THAT MUST ACCOMPANY ANY USE OF THIS RESULT. Each target had 670 candidate donors; this project has 18. The paper attributes distance-based methods' advantage directly to high US gauge density (citing Lebecherel et al. 2016; Neri et al. 2020) and attributes classification-pool degradation to donor-pool heterogeneity — both mechanisms predict that donor-selection comparisons collapse at n=19 basin families. The study also concerns daily streamflow from a conceptual rainfall-runoff model in "minimal human influence" CAMELS catchments, not nitrate exceedance in tile-drained agricultural basins, and concerns transferring calibrated model parameters, not features for a gradient-boosted classifier. Finally, if this result is being used to argue that static catchment attributes are not worth pursuing, it argues the opposite: Attr alone gains +0.09 R_NP over random, roughly 70% of the entire no-local-data realizable gain.

claims.text: In a leave-one-catchment-out pseudo-ungauged experiment over 148 catchments in northeast North America (HYSETS, 1979-2018, drainage area >500 km2, >=30 years of record each), a single LSTM trained across all other catchments achieved median NSE 0.78 at held-out ungauged catchments, versus median NSE 0.58-0.63 for 18 combinations of three conceptual hydrological models (GR4JCN, HMETS, HSAMI) crossed with six regionalization schemes. The LSTM beat every one of the 18 model-regionalization combinations in at least 93% of catchments. This is a streamflow result, not a concentration or exceedance result.
claims.effectSize: median NSE 0.78 (LSTM) vs 0.58-0.63 (18 HM-regionalization combos); LSTM superior in >=93% of basins

claims.text: An oracle-style upper bound on classical regionalization was computed: BEST-HM, which selects for each catchment the best-performing of all hydrological-model/regionalization combinations after the fact (information unavailable at a truly ungauged site), reached median NSE 0.66 - still below the LSTM's 0.78. This implies that no choice among the classical regionalization families (spatial proximity, physical similarity, multi-donor averaging, inverse distance weighting, donor filtering) closes the gap to a cross-catchment learned model, even with hindsight donor selection.
claims.effectSize: BEST-HM oracle median NSE 0.66 vs LSTM 0.78 (+0.12 NSE)

claims.text: The LSTM applied in fully ungauged mode outperformed hydrological models that had been CALIBRATED ON THE TARGET CATCHMENT'S OWN OBSERVED FLOW in 73-78% of catchments (75% vs GR4JCN, 78% vs HMETS, 73% vs HSAMI). That is, cross-catchment learning with static attributes beat local calibration with local data for roughly three-quarters of sites - direct evidence that between-site information can be carried by attributes rather than by local history.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (LSTM) compared against locally-calibrated in-sample hydrological models
claims.effectSize: LSTM >= locally-calibrated HM in 75% / 78% / 73% of basins

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT contradicting prior regionalization guidance: filtering out poorly-calibrated donor catchments (removing donors with calibration NSE < 0.7) did NOT increase regionalization skill. The authors state explicitly 'Removing poorly calibrated catchments did not increase overall regionalization skill, contrary to Oudin et al. (2008).' Similarly, regularization of the LSTM 'failed to improve results' in this study. The paper also reports that the choice of hydrological model mattered only marginally compared to the choice of regionalization method.
claims.effectSize: donor-quality filtering: no measurable gain; median NSE across all 18 HM configs stayed within the narrow 0.58-0.63 band

claims.text: The paper provides NO scaling curve or sensitivity experiment on the number of donor/training catchments - a direct gap against the question of what skill is attainable with few donors. Every LSTM run used ~118 training catchments (80% of the 147 non-held-out basins) with 29 held for validation, and multi-donor hydrological regionalization used a fixed N=5 donors. The only quantitative data-volume guidance offered is temporal, citing Kratzert et al. (2018) that '15 years is a lower bound for the training' per catchment, and the authors required >=30 years of record per catchment. Therefore this paper CANNOT be used to argue the LSTM/cross-catchment advantage survives at n=19 independent basin families; its evidence base is ~118 training catchments with >=30 years each.
claims.nBasins: 148 total; ~118 training per fold; 5 donors for HM regionalization
claims.effectSize: no donor-count scaling experiment reported

claims.text: The regionalization signal was carried by 25 static basin-averaged descriptors supplied as LSTM inputs alongside meteorological forcings: mean elevation, mean slope, mean aspect, latitude, longitude, land-cover fractions (forest, shrub, grass, crop, urban, barren, water, snow/ice, wetland; from NALCMS 2010), mean annual precipitation, temperature, snowfall and rain, and an aridity index (precipitation over estimated PET); elevation from EarthENV 90 m DEM. The authors attribute the LSTM's edge to it being able to 'automatically parse and adjust the weights of catchment descriptors' rather than relying on a hand-specified donor-similarity metric. A stated architectural constraint is that 'the size of the inputs must remain the same throughout the training and regionalization process for all catchments' - i.e. no attribute may be missing for any basin, which is a hard blocker for attributes with partial coverage.
claims.effectSize: 25 static descriptors; lat/lon included among them alongside physical attributes

claims.text: SCOPE LIMITATION relevant to the water-quality PUB question: this paper addresses streamflow only. It contains no water-quality, concentration, or exceedance-threshold prediction, and reports no separate numerical breakdown of spatial proximity (SP) versus physical similarity (PS) median NSE - Figure 4 shows box plots for both but the text makes no explicit claim that either family beats the other, stating only that 'the selection of the regionalization method plays a more significant role' than the choice of hydrological model. So this source does not settle whether attribute similarity beats plain spatial proximity in homogeneous terrain.
claims.effectSize: SP vs PS difference not quantified in text; no water-quality results present

result.sourceQuality: Primary peer-reviewed open-access source (HESS, Copernicus, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-139-2023), full text fetched successfully - not paywalled. High confidence in quoted headline numbers (median NSE 0.78 vs 0.58-0.63, BEST-HM 0.66, 93%, 73-78%, 148 catchments, 118/29 train/val split, 25 descriptors), which appear verbatim in abstract and results text. LOWER confidence on the SP-vs-PS breakdown and on IDW/SEL incremental gains: those are presented only as box plots in Figure 4 and could not be resolved to numbers from the HTML text, so they are recorded as not-quantified rather than guessed. The exact contents of Table 1 (full 25-attribute list) were partially reconstructed from surrounding text and should be verified against the PDF before being relied on item-by-item. Caveat for this project: this is a STREAMFLOW PUB paper with ~118 training catchments and >=30 years per catchment; it is direct evidence that cross-basin learning with static attributes can beat local calibration, but it offers zero evidence at the n=19-families scale and zero evidence for concentration or exceedance targets.

claims.text: The survey's own headline gap-finding, stated verbatim in the abstract: "most prior efforts have been focused on deep learning frameworks built on MANY SITES for predictions at daily time scales in the United States, but that comparisons between different classes of machine learning methods are few and inadequate." FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR US: the published PUB evidence base is built on large-n site pools (CAMELS 531, CONUS stream-temperature networks, 305 lakes); the survey identifies NO body of work establishing skill at n<100 donor units, and identifies NO head-to-head ranked comparison of regionalization families. Our n=19 independent basin families sits outside the regime this literature evidences. The survey also does NOT report any curve or table of skill vs number of donor catchments — we searched the full text specifically for this and it is absent, which is itself the finding: the scaling relationship the research question asks for is not established in the field's own 2025 survey.
claims.nBasins: not-applicable — survey-level claim about the literature
claims.effectSize: No quantitative skill-vs-n-donors curve exists in the survey; comparisons between ML method classes described by the authors as "few and inadequate"

claims.text: WATER QUALITY PUB IS NEARLY ABSENT AS A QUANTITATIVE LITERATURE. Despite the abstract promising review of "streamflow, water quality, and other water resources prediction," the survey's concrete unmonitored-site results are overwhelmingly streamflow, stream temperature and lake temperature. The only broad-scale water-quality-at-unmonitored-sites application named is "dissolved oxygen in streams," cited WITHOUT any performance metric, without a site count, and without a stated split protocol. No nitrate/nitrogen concentration PUB study with numbers appears. DIRECT ANSWER TO OUR RESEARCH QUESTION: the requested "2-3 papers doing water quality PUB rather than streamflow PUB" do not exist in quantified form in the field's most recent survey. Our LOFO CLF AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 for nitrate exceedance therefore has NO published water-quality-PUB benchmark to be compared against, and any transfer of streamflow-PUB expectations (e.g. "LSTM matches calibrated models in ungauged basins") to a concentration/exceedance target is unevidenced.
claims.nBasins: unknown — no water quality PUB study with a reported site count is given
claims.effectSize: Zero quantified water-quality PUB results reported in the survey

claims.text: REGIONAL POOLING BEAT LOCAL/REGIONAL SPECIALIZATION IN THE LARGEST STREAM-TEMPERATURE COMPARISON REPORTED: "regional LSTM models of stream temperature in the United States perform worse than the LSTM model built on all sites in the CONUS for 15 out of 17 regions" (Willard 2023). Companion negative result on the same theme: Wang et al. (2022) "show that localizing an LSTM predicting continental-scale snowpack dynamics to individual regions across the United States had insignificant benefits over the continental-scale LSTM." IMPLICATION AND CAVEAT FOR US: this is evidence AGAINST spending effort on region-specific or cluster-specific models, and FOR one pooled model over all sites — which is what we already do. But it is NOT evidence that pooling rescues between-site level prediction, and both results come from national-scale pools of hundreds-to-thousands of sites. At n=19 families confined to a single flat agricultural state, we have no "other regions" to pool with, so the mechanism that produced these gains (heterogeneous multi-region data) is structurally unavailable to us unless we expand the site pool beyond Iowa.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown — the 15-of-17 comparison's held-out design is not specified in the survey text; likely includes held-out sites but cannot be confirmed
claims.nBasins: unknown site count; 17 CONUS regions for stream temperature; snowpack study is CONUS-scale
claims.effectSize: Pooled CONUS model beat region-specific models in 15/17 regions; regional localization of snowpack LSTM gave "insignificant benefits"

claims.text: THE SURVEY EXPLICITLY REJECTS THE FUNCTIONAL-SIMILARITY / DONOR-CATCHMENT PREMISE that underlies classical regionalization: entity-aware models that simply concatenate static site characteristics to dynamic inputs "challenge a longstanding hydrological perspective that transferring models and knowledge from one basin to another requires that they must be functionally similar," and the authors state "site characteristics can contain sufficient information to differentiate between site-specific dynamic behaviors for a variety of prediction tasks." FALSIFIABLE FOR US: the survey's position is that the winning strategy is NOT donor-catchment selection or similarity-index transfer but attribute concatenation inside one pooled model. Our architecture already does exactly this (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean/max_dist_to_sensor concatenated to dynamic weather). The survey therefore predicts that our remaining between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21) is an ATTRIBUTE-COVERAGE problem — we lack the static descriptors that distinguish basins (tile drainage density being the obvious missing one) — not an architecture or transfer-method problem. This is a testable prediction: adding discriminative static attributes should move between_r2; switching to donor-transfer or similarity-weighted regionalization should not.
claims.nBasins: claim generalized by authors from CAMELS-scale work (531 catchments) and 305-lake studies
claims.effectSize: Qualitative/directional; no head-to-head effect size given between attribute-concatenation and donor-transfer

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON TRANSFER FROM DATA-RICH TO DATA-POOR REGIONS: "Le et al. (2022) transfer ML streamflow models built on North America to data-poor South Africa and Central Asian regions and find that the LOCAL models trained on MINIMAL DATA OUTPERFORM the models from data-rich regions." Second relevant negative from the survey: for hybrid modeling, "the output from the NWM actually impairs the model and prevents it from learning generalizable hydrological relationships." IMPLICATION FOR US: cross-region transfer learning (e.g. pre-training on CAMELS or a national nitrate corpus and fine-tuning on Iowa) has a documented failure mode where the small local dataset wins — this directly contradicts the naive "borrow strength from 531 basins" recommendation and is the single most relevant published caution for an n=19 project considering importing an external large-sample model. It does NOT say local wins always; it says the direction is not guaranteed and must be measured, so any transfer-learning proposal here needs a local-only baseline run under the same LOFO protocol.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown — cross-region transfer evaluation; held-out geography by construction (target regions unseen in training), but the internal split is not specified
claims.nBasins: unknown — North America source pool and South Africa / Central Asia target regions; counts not given in the survey
claims.effectSize: Local minimal-data models outperformed transferred data-rich-region models (direction reported; magnitude not given in survey)

claims.text: THE FIELD'S STANDARD PUB EVALUATION PROTOCOL, as defined by the survey: models "are often tested on PSEUDO UNMONITORED SITES, where data is withheld until the testing stage to mimic model building for real unmonitored sites." This is exactly our LOFO design and confirms our protocol is the field-standard one, so our 0.820 AUC is a protocol-legitimate number. IMPORTANT ABSENCE, hunted for explicitly: the survey does NOT warn about spatial autocorrelation leakage between nested or adjacent held-out sites, and does NOT prescribe grouping hydrologically nested basins into families. Our stricter leave-one-basin-FAMILY-out grouping is therefore MORE conservative than the published norm — which means (a) our numbers are likely pessimistic relative to papers reporting plain leave-one-site-out, and (b) published pseudo-unmonitored results from studies that held out individual nested sites may be optimistically biased and are not strictly comparable to our 0.820. Also note the survey reports no consensus benchmark metric or threshold for "acceptable" unmonitored-site skill.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (pseudo-unmonitored sites; site-level withholding, nesting/grouping not specified as standard)
claims.nBasins: varies by study; CAMELS 531 catchments is the dominant benchmark, 305 lakes for lake temperature
claims.effectSize: Protocol definition, not a performance number; no consensus acceptability threshold reported

result.sourceQuality: HIGH for provenance, MODERATE for extractable effect sizes. Peer-reviewed survey, Environmental Data Science vol 4 art e7 (2025), DOI 10.1017/eds.2024.14, authors Willard (LBNL), Varadharajan (LBNL), Jia (Pittsburgh), Kumar (Minnesota); arXiv preprint 2308.09766 (v2/v3) is openly available and was used for full text since the Cambridge page is partially gated. CAVEAT: as a narrative survey it reports directional findings and citations far more than paired numbers — most claims here lack a stated nBasins or split protocol IN THE SURVEY ITSELF, so several are marked unknown and would need the primary papers (Kratzert et al. 2019c/d, Willard 2023, Le et al. 2022, Wang et al. 2022) fetched to recover exact NSE/RMSE values and held-out designs. The survey provides NO skill-vs-number-of-donor-catchments curve, NO ranked comparison of regionalization families with effect sizes, and NO quantified water-quality PUB result — three of the four things the research question asked for. Those absences are reported as findings rather than filled by guessing. Do NOT treat any number here as comparable to our LOFO 0.820 without first confirming the primary study's split protocol.

claims.text: Pandit et al. (2025) trained an LSTM on high-frequency nitrate sensor data across the conterminous US to predict DAILY NITRATE CONCENTRATION, and report a median KGE of 0.60 under temporal validation but a median KGE of only 0.18 under spatial validation (prediction in unmonitored basins). The ~0.42 KGE drop is a direct, same-paper, same-model measurement of the ungauged-basin penalty for a nitrate CONCENTRATION signal — the exact quantity our LOFO protocol measures. This is verified from the published abstract.
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 (temporal validation) vs 0.18 (spatial validation / unmonitored basins); drop of ~0.42 KGE. KGE=0.18 is barely above the mean-flow benchmark and would be considered unusable for absolute-level prediction.
claims.nBasins: unknown — the abstract says only 'high-frequency sensor data across the conterminous US'. One search snippet asserted 95 CONUS nitrate sensor sites, but this could NOT be verified against the paywalled full text. Treat 95 as unconfirmed. Order of magnitude is tens-to-low-hundreds of sites, i.e. the SAME regime as our 85 sites / 19 families, not the CAMELS 531-671 regime.
claims.splitProtocol: both — the paper reports temporal-holdout AND spatial-holdout numbers separately and explicitly labels them

claims.text: In the same paper, restricting the model's application domain from all of CONUS to the Mississippi River Basin raised spatial-validation (unmonitored-basin) median KGE for nitrate concentration from 0.18 to 0.34 — roughly a doubling — without changing the model. The authors attribute this to the MRB subset having catchment attributes more similar to the training sites. This is evidence that ATTRIBUTE-SPACE / DOMAIN RESTRICTION, not more donors, is what buys ungauged-basin skill, and it directly supports our Iowa-only, agriculturally homogeneous scope being an advantage rather than a limitation.
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.18 (CONUS-wide spatial validation) -> 0.34 (MRB-restricted spatial validation); +0.16 KGE, ~89% relative improvement, from domain restriction alone
claims.nBasins: unknown for the MRB subset; the paper notes the MRB contains 818 HUC-8s but that only a subset share attributes with the training sites. Number of held-out basins behind the 0.34 median is not determinable from available material.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (prediction in unmonitored basins, model applied to basins not in training)

claims.text: Shapley-value interpretation of the spatially-validated nitrate model identified TILE DRAINAGE density, ROADWAY density, and WETLAND COVER as the key spatial drivers of MEAN nitrate concentration (i.e. the between-site level, not the temporal signal), with quantitative non-linear thresholds — the paper illustrates counterfactuals such as reducing tile drain density from 60% to 0% and doubling wetland cover from 5% to 10%. This is a peer-reviewed, continental-scale confirmation that tile drainage is a first-order BETWEEN-SITE control and that its absence from our 68-feature set is a plausible primary cause of our between_r2 = 0.21 deficit. Note their tile-drainage layer is a CONUS-wide gridded product (source not identifiable from the paywalled text) — identifying it is a concrete follow-up, since we have no tile-drainage source.
claims.effectSize: no scalar effect size available from abstract/snippets; the claim is a RANKING (tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover as top spatial drivers of mean concentration) plus the existence of non-linear thresholds. Exact Shapley magnitudes are in the paywalled figures.
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (interpretation of a fitted model, though the model interpreted was the spatially-validated one)

claims.text: The paper's temporal-validation protocol was 5-fold cross-validation in which 80% of each site's time series was used for training and a DIFFERENT 20% window of the SAME site's time series was held out for testing — the site's own history is in the training set. Its spatial protocol held out entire basins. Because the identical architecture scored KGE 0.60 under the first and 0.18 under the second, this paper is a clean, citable demonstration that within-site temporal holdout and spatial holdout are NOT interchangeable protocols for nitrate, and that any literature number reported without a stated protocol must be assumed to be the optimistic (temporal/random) one.
claims.effectSize: same model, same hyperparameters, two protocols: KGE 0.60 vs 0.18. Protocol choice alone accounts for a 3.3x difference in reported skill.

TWO IMPORTANT GAPS THE PARENT SHOULD KNOW ABOUT:

1. WATER-QUALITY PUB IS ABSENT FROM EVERYTHING I COULD REACH. The assignment asked for 2-3 papers doing WATER QUALITY PUB rather than streamflow PUB, and instructed me to say so plainly if none exist. I found NONE in this source set. Every regionalization study I could read — Oudin (913 FR), Patil & Stieglitz (756 US), Kuana (126 BR), plus everything in Patil's reference list (Merz & Blöschl 2004, Parajka 2005, Seibert 1999, Skøien & Blöschl 2007 on 376 Austrian catchments, Zhang & Chiew 2009, Archfield & Vogel 2010, Young 2006) — predicts STREAMFLOW, not concentration or exceedance. Targeted searching for nitrate/water-quality regionalization returned only GROUNDWATER nitrate mapping (a spatial-interpolation problem, not a PUB time-series problem) and one watershed-health-index paper. THE ABSENCE IS ITSELF THE FINDING: the 25-year PUB literature's effect sizes are for streamflow, and transferring its conclusions to a nitrate exceedance target is an untested extrapolation that should be stated as such in any synthesis. One promising unexplored lead: arXiv:2308.09766, "Time Series Predictions in Unmonitored Sites: A Survey of Machine Learning Techniques in Water Resources" — I could not parse its PDF (binary), but its title targets exactly this question and it should be assigned to another agent.

2. A DEPLOYMENT-TARGET CAVEAT THAT APPLIES TO THE WHOLE PUB LITERATURE. Every regionalization method in these papers — including the donor-transfer methods that perform best — REQUIRES GAUGED NEIGHBORS at prediction time. Patil & Stieglitz literally interpolate observed streamflow from 5 nearby gauges. Per the project's non-negotiable rule 8, this DOES NOT WORK for an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no guaranteed monitored neighbor. The claims are still decision-relevant because they bound what between-site skill is attainable and show which attribute families are worthless, but no method described here is directly shippable. The one partial exception is our existing rest_of_state_nitrate_lag features, which are a crude state-wide analogue of donor transfer — and notably, that feature is already our #1 by permutation importance, which is consistent with Claim 2's finding that donor transfer is the strongest regionalization family.

CROSS-PROTOCOL WARNING: all numbers in Claims 2-6 are Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency on daily STREAMFLOW under spatial holdout. They are NOT numerically comparable to our LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 / between_r2 0.21. They are comparable only STRUCTURALLY — as evidence about the shape of the donor-count curve, about which attribute families carry transfer signal, and about the ceiling in flat terrain.

claims.text: The AgTile-US spatial pattern is NOT independently observed — it is a downscaling of county Census totals. The algorithm iterates within each county: start with the most poorly drained SSURGO class (D=7) at 0% slope, increase slope in 1% steps until accumulated area reaches the county Census target, and on hitting a 20% slope ceiling drop to the next drainage class (D=6) and reset slope to 0%, then fine-tune in 0.1% increments to minimize absolute error against the county total. Consequence for this project: a basin-aggregated tile fraction from AgTile-US is essentially a deterministic function of (county Census tile acreage, SSURGO drainage class, slope) and is therefore substantially COLLINEAR with any separately added SSURGO hydrologic-soil-group or slope feature. claims.text: In a cross-sectional analysis of 153 monitored watersheds in the Mississippi River Basin (1997-2006 data), a regression model of winter-spring nitrate-N yield explained 83% of the total spatial variation, decomposed as: the interaction term river runoff x fertilizer N input = 76% of variation, tile drainage extent = 17%, and sewage effluent = 7%. Source: PubMed abstract for David, Drinkwater & McIsaac (2010) J. Environ. Qual. 39:1657-1667, DOI 10.2134/jeq2010.0115, plus the University of Illinois press release. This is an IN-SAMPLE multiple regression with no spatial hold-out, so the 83% is NOT comparable to a LOFO/ungauged-basin number and should be treated as an upper bound.
claims.effectSize: 83% of spatial variation explained overall; runoff x fertilizer N = 76%, tile drainage = 17%, sewage effluent = 7%

claims.text: Tile drainage extent is an independently significant STATIC basin attribute for cross-site nitrate yield, accounting for 17% of the spatial variation in winter-spring nitrate-N yield across 153 Mississippi Basin watersheds AFTER the runoff x fertilizer-N term (76%) was already in the model. This is direct evidence that a tile-drainage-fraction covariate carries between-site information not present in weather + crop-area features, which is precisely the between-site deficit in the current model (between_r2 0.21).
claims.effectSize: 17% of spatial variation, incremental to a 76% runoff x fertilizer term

claims.text: The paper's headline negative result: conventional net nitrogen input (NNI) / N-balance calculations were NOT a reliable predictor of riverine nitrate yields across the 153 watersheds. The predictive term that worked was fertilizer N input MULTIPLIED BY river runoff, not an N surplus/balance quantity on its own. This directly bears on the project's gTREND N-surplus features: it predicts that a raw surplus covariate entered additively will underperform, and that surplus (or fertilizer N) should be entered as an INTERACTION with a hydrologic transport term.
claims.effectSize: NNI reported as not a reliable predictor; runoff x fertilizer N explained 76% of variation instead

claims.text: The fraction of annual net N input exported as riverine nitrate-N varies by roughly 30-fold across subbasins purely as a function of hydrology/drainage: 0.05 for the lower Mississippi subbasin, 0.3 for the upper Mississippi River basin, and 1.4 (rising to 4.2 in a wet year) for the Embarras River watershed, a mostly tile-drained Illinois basin. Because the export fraction exceeds 1.0 in tile-drained basins, N inputs alone cannot rank basins; a drainage-intensity attribute is required to convert input to export.
claims.effectSize: export fraction 0.05 (lower MS) vs 0.3 (upper MS) vs 1.4-4.2 (tile-drained Embarras River)

claims.text: The spatial maximum of nitrate-N yield in the Mississippi Basin coincides with the tile-drained cornbelt running from southwest Minnesota across Iowa, Illinois, Indiana and Ohio, characterized by extensive fertilized corn-soybean row cropping, flat topography with tile drainage, and channelized ditches. Implication for this project: essentially ALL ~85 Iowa sensor sites sit inside this single high-yield regime, so the between-site variance the model must explain is WITHIN-regime variation in drainage intensity and N input, a harder and lower-signal problem than the CONUS-scale contrast this paper resolves.
claims.effectSize: qualitative spatial maximum; no per-attribute coefficient recoverable from open sources

It therefore provides no evidence that these attributes discriminate among 19 Iowa basin families at DAILY resolution, and the paper does not supply a coefficient or standard error for tile drainage that could be ported as a prior. The specific tile-drainage data source used (whether Census of Agriculture drained-acreage, Sugg 2007, or another product) could NOT be determined from the openly available abstract and press materials; the Wiley full text returned HTTP 403 and Semantic Scholar has the abstract elided.

claims.text: Oudin et al. (2010) tested directly whether physically similar catchments are hydrologically similar, using 893 French + 10 English catchments (903 total). Verbatim from the abstract: "The results show that the overlap between the two pools is significant for only 60% of the catchments." I.e. for ~40% of catchments, the pool of catchments selected as most physically similar (via physiographic descriptors) has NO significant overlap with the pool that is empirically hydrologically similar (defined by which donors' model parameters actually transfer successfully). This is the canonical falsification of the core assumption behind attribute-based regionalization. RELEVANCE TO US: our per-basin static attributes (crop fractions, N-surplus, area, mean/max distance) are exactly this kind of physiographic descriptor set, and this result predicts they will identify the right hydrologic analogue for only ~60% of unseen basins.
claims.nBasins: 903 (893 French + 10 English); the 893 figure is confirmed in the open-access HESS 2011 review, which states Oudin et al. (2010) used "893 French and 10 English catchments"
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — behavioral similarity is defined by transferring calibrated model parameter sets between catchment pairs, i.e. each catchment is treated as hypothetically ungauged and scored on donors' parameters. Note this is a pool-overlap analysis, not a single held-out skill score; no NSE table could be retrieved because the paper is paywalled.
claims.effectSize: Overlap between apparent-similarity and behavioral-similarity pools significant for only 60% of catchments (40% failure rate).

claims.text: Oudin et al. (2010) identify a SPECIFIC cause of the attribute-similarity failure, verbatim from the abstract: the non-overlapping catchments failed because "(1) these catchments often have a quite specific hydrological behavior and (2) the role of the underground properties of the catchment on its hydrological behavior was not found to be accurately described by the available physical descriptors, meaning that more relevant catchment descriptors should be sought to better describe the geological and lithological context in hydrological terms." DIRECT IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: the diagnosed missing information is SUBSURFACE, not surface land use or weather. In an Iowa nitrate context the analogous missing subsurface control is tile drainage density / subsurface hydraulic connectivity — which this project has already flagged as the dominant Iowa control and absent from the feature set. This is independent literature support for prioritizing a subsurface-drainage covariate over any further weather feature engineering.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative diagnosis, no number attached; explains the 40% non-overlap in the claim above.

claims.text: The companion study Oudin et al. (2008), 913 French catchments, ranks regionalization families head-to-head. Verbatim from the abstract: "in France, where a dense network of gauging stations is available, spatial proximity provides the best regionalization solution. The regression approach is the least satisfactory, with results very close to those obtained using one median parameter set for the whole country. The physical similarity approach is intermediary. However, the results obtained with these three methods lag far behind those obtained by full model calibration. Our results also show that some improvement could be made by combining spatial proximity and physical similarity." RANKING: spatial proximity > physical similarity > regression-on-attributes ~= a single national constant. RELEVANCE: this is direct evidence that lat/lon (spatial proximity) already being top-3 in our feature importance is the EXPECTED outcome, not an anomaly, and that adding more catchment-attribute regressors is the family with the WEAKEST published payoff. Caveat: the abstract explicitly conditions the proximity win on a DENSE gauge network; no per-method NSE values could be extracted because the paper is paywalled.
claims.nBasins: 913 French catchments, two lumped rainfall-runoff models (daily)
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — ungauged-basin protocol, each catchment treated as ungauged and predicted from other catchments' parameters
claims.effectSize: Ordinal ranking only from the abstract (proximity > similarity > regression ≈ national median parameter set); all three 'lag far behind' full local calibration. Exact NSE values not retrievable.

claims.text: Pool et al. (2021), 671 CAMELS catchments (contiguous US), leave-one-out cross-validation, HBV-light, 23 regionalization methods — the largest homogenized comparison available. Median RNP (Nash-type relative performance): local calibration (upper benchmark) 0.89; best-available-donor 0.87; distance+volume combined 0.82; volume/signature-based 0.80; spatial proximity alone 0.79; CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES alone 0.78; fixed catchment classification 0.76; RANDOM donor 0.69-0.70. Verbatim: "we found that distance-based approaches tend to outperform attribute-based approaches." NOTE THE EFFECT SIZES: the entire spread from random donor (0.69) to the best method (0.82) is 0.13 RNP, and the spread between spatial proximity (0.79) and attribute similarity (0.78) is 0.01 — i.e. choosing attribute-similarity over proximity buys essentially NOTHING even with 670 donors available. VERDICT ON THE RESEARCH QUESTION: attribute-based similarity does NOT beat plain spatial proximity, and the authors attribute the proximity win partly to high gauge density and partly to "the lack of catchment attributes representing a wide range of catchment responses over large scales (Merz et al., 2020; Oudin et al., 2010)."
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — explicit leave-one-out cross-validation with the receiver catchment treated as ungauged
claims.effectSize: Median RNP: local calib 0.89 / best donor 0.87 / dist+volume 0.82 / volume 0.80 / distance 0.79 / attributes 0.78 / classification 0.76 / random 0.69. Attribute-vs-proximity gap = 0.01 RNP. Full method spread = 0.13 RNP.

claims.text: Pool et al. (2021) quantify DONOR SCARCITY directly, and this is the single most important number against the n=19-families constraint. With all 671 CAMELS catchments calibrated and each of the other 670 tested as a donor: "For a relative performance value of 0.7, half of the hypothetically ungauged catchments have at most 23 suitable donor catchments" — i.e. only ~3.4% of 670 candidate donors are usable at that threshold. Further: "at least three potential donors exist for 85% of the hypothetically ungauged catchments" at that threshold, and at a 0.9 threshold "for 40% of the catchments, only one donor exceeds the performance threshold." Also verbatim: "for 50% of the hypothetically ungauged catchments, more than 40% of the donor catchments perform at least as well as randomly selected parameter sets" — meaning for the other half, MOST donors are worse than random parameters. EXTRAPOLATION TO THIS PROJECT: if only ~3.4% of donors are suitable, a pool of 19 independent basin families yields an EXPECTED 0.65 suitable donors per target basin — under one. Any donor-transfer or nearest-analogue regionalization scheme is therefore very likely infeasible at n=19, and this paper's own numbers are the evidence, not an assertion. It also means the observed between_r2 of 0.21 may be near the structural ceiling for donor-style transfer at this sample size.
claims.nBasins: 671 (each tested against the other 670 as donors)
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — every catchment treated as hypothetically ungauged, exhaustive all-pairs donor evaluation
claims.effectSize: At relative performance 0.7: median catchment has ≤23 suitable donors out of 670 (3.4%). At 0.9: 40% of catchments have exactly one suitable donor. For 50% of catchments, >60% of donors are worse than random parameter sets.

claims.text: Spatial-proximity regionalization has a GAUGE-DENSITY CLIFF, which bounds how far proximity can carry this project. Lebecherel, Andréassian & Perrin (2016, J. Hydrol. 539:196) deliberately degraded the French hydrometric network using a 'hydrometrical desert' protocol (progressively deleting the CLOSEST gauged stations to the target, which they argue is more realistic than random deletion). Reported result: performance of spatial-proximity output-averaging methods deteriorates strongly once station density falls below roughly 0.6 gauges per 1000 km2. ARITHMETIC FOR IOWA: 85 sensor sites over ~145,746 km2 = 0.58 gauges per 1000 km2 — AT the reported cliff. Using the leak-safe count of 19 independent basin families instead gives 0.13 per 1000 km2, roughly 4.5x BELOW the cliff. This predicts that lat/lon proximity, already top-3 in our permutation importance, is operating near or past the density at which proximity-based transfer degrades, and that further squeezing the proximity family has limited headroom. CAVEAT: the 0.6 threshold was obtained from a secondary summary of the paper, not from the full text, which is paywalled at Elsevier; treat the exact threshold value as unverified, though the qualitative density dependence is corroborated by Oudin et al. (2008)'s own conditioning of its proximity result on 'a dense network of gauging stations.'
claims.nBasins: French national dataset (same family as the 913-catchment Oudin set); exact retained count not verified from full text
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — ungauged-basin protocol with deliberate network degradation ('hydrometrical desert', deleting nearest gauges)
claims.effectSize: Spatial-proximity performance 'strongly deteriorates' below ~0.6 gauging stations per 1000 km2 (threshold value unverified from primary text). Iowa equivalent: 0.58/1000 km2 at 85 sites; 0.13/1000 km2 at 19 independent families.

claims.text: In Jones et al. (2019, Ambio 48:1143-1153, doi:10.1007/s13280-019-01150-9), across 9 western-Iowa watersheds (areas 1,049 km2 Soldier River to 8,350 km2 Little Sioux River) using 2017 flow-weighted-average (FWA) NO3-N as the cross-site response, FWA nitrate correlated significantly (p < 0.01) with surplus N, with commercial+manure+fixation N, with commercial+manure N, and with generated manure N, but DID NOT correlate with commercial fertilizer N alone (verbatim: 'The FWA concentrations did not correlate with commercial N (p > 0.10)'). This is direct evidence that the MANURE component, not total or commercial N, carries the cross-site signal in a Corn Belt setting — relevant because the project's current N-surplus features do not separate manure from commercial N. Caveat: pure Pearson correlation, no predictive model, no holdout, and n=9 watersheds means only ~7 df, so individual p-values are fragile.

claims.text: In the same 9-watershed Iowa dataset, the paper reports verbatim: 'The surplus N relates much more strongly to generated manure N (R2 = 0.83) than commercial N inputs (R2 = 0.14) among the nine watersheds.' Note carefully what this R2 describes: it is the regression of the SURPLUS-N basin attribute on its manure and commercial components, NOT the regression of stream nitrate on those components. The paper does not numerically report an R2 for FWA nitrate versus any predictor in the main text (Figure 4 shows the scatter/regression lines for FWA vs six N predictors but the caption and text give no R2 values). So this source establishes DIRECTION and SIGNIFICANCE of manure as a cross-site nitrate control but does NOT supply a usable partial effect size for cross-site mean-nitrate variance explained.

The two highest-nitrate basins were also the two highest-density: Rock River (5.00 AU/ha, FWA 11.5 mg/L) and Floyd River (3.53 AU/ha, FWA 16.2 mg/L), versus the other seven watersheds averaging 0.84 AU/ha. N yields were 30.5 kg/ha (Floyd) and 24.7 kg/ha (Rock) versus 20.0 kg/ha average for the other seven. This is a >3x range in mean concentration spanned by ~11x range in a STATIC, basin-aggregatable attribute — precisely the between-site term this project's model fails on (between_r2 0.21). Actionable: livestock/manure density is a first-tier candidate static attribute.

claims.text: Land use alone was the WEAKEST of the significant predictors in this study: 'area portion in corn and soybean' correlated with FWA nitrate only at p < 0.05, versus p < 0.01 for manure N and the N-input sums. This is a targeted negative result for the project's current feature design, which encodes land use (8 CDL crop classes x 3 distance buckets = 24 features) but encodes NO livestock/manure attribute at all. It suggests that adding more crop-class resolution has low expected yield, while a manure/animal-density attribute is untested and is the variable that outperformed crop area in the only Iowa study examined here.

Fitness for this project: county resolution is coarse relative to 3 distance buckets, so it is best used as a single basin-level area-weighted static attribute, not a per-bucket feature. claims.text: TWO IMPORTANT ABSENCES/NEGATIVES from this source. (a) The 2017 N-surplus cliff is NOT resolved by the USGS lineage: Falcone (2021) also terminates at 2017 because it is keyed to USDA Census of Agriculture years (1950...2012, 2017); the next Census year is 2022, so any post-2017 continuation must be built from NASS 2022 Census county tables directly, not from an existing USGS product. Jones et al.'s own workaround was to use the Iowa DNR Animal Feeding Operations database (2018 snapshot) for animal counts, but they explicitly caution it undercounts: 'The IDNR's database is mostly limited to regulated facilities; therefore, numbers obtained from this source are likely to represent less than the actual number of animals raised.' (b) This paper performs NO analysis of tile drainage, soil drainage class, hydrologic soil group, baseflow index, depth to water table, riparian/wetland fraction, or drainage density — it does not mention tile drainage as an analyzed control at all. So it provides ZERO evidence on the tile-drainage attribute the assignment asked to resolve; Valayamkunnath et al. 2020, Nakagaki/Wieczorek, and Sugg 2007 must be sourced elsewhere. Separately, the paper's design supports treating N inputs as a STATIC basin RANK attribute: the cross-site correlations are computed on a single-year (2017) snapshot of inputs against a single-year FWA concentration, i.e. exactly the static-rank usage, which the project's failed forward-broadcast time-series experiment does not rule out.
