All extracted figures come from the OpenAlex reconstructed abstract plus USGS/ProQuest metadata mirrors, which agree with each other on every number (n=15 and n=10 watersheds, area ranges, row-crop ranges, nitrate ranges, slope 0.11, p<0.0003). Those figures are therefore high-confidence. The r-squared values, the intercepts, any multivariate model, and any discussion/limitations content are NOT recoverable and are marked unknown. Split protocol is 'not-applicable' throughout: this is a 2000-era cross-sectional OLS fit on 25 watersheds with no holdout of any kind, so its numbers are in-sample and are NOT comparable to the project's LOFO 0.820 AUC. Sample size is small (n=15 and n=10), which is however the SAME order as the project's 19 independent basin families - unlike CAMELS-scale evidence, this study's design is directly feasible at n=19.

claims.text: The assigned source (Nakagaki, N., Wieczorek, M.E., and Qi, S.L., 2016, 'Estimates of Subsurface Tile Drainage Extent for the Conterminous United States, early 1990s', USGS data release, DOI 10.5066/F7RB72QS) is a 30-meter raster covering the full conterminous US (so it covers all of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of multi-state basins), with raster cell values expressed in square meters of estimated tile drainage. It was built from county-level acres of subsurface tile drains for the EARLY 1990s taken from Sugg (2007), cultivated cropland from NLCD 2011, poorly drained soils from STATSGO2, federally-owned land extent, and county boundaries. License is CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain), free bulk download via the DOI landing page / ScienceBase. FALSIFIABLE WEAKNESS FOR THIS PROJECT: the drainage census underlying it is ~1990s while the nitrate record is 2008-2026, and the disaggregation is driven by county totals plus a soil/cropland mask, so within-county spatial variation is a modeled artifact rather than an observation. NOTE: www.sciencebase.gov returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; specs recovered from the USGS data-catalog mirror at usgs.gov/data and from search-index metadata, so field-level details (exact file list, projection) are unverified at the source record.
claims.effectSize: 30 m resolution; CONUS extent; early-1990s vintage; CC0; DOI 10.5066/F7RB72QS

claims.text: A newer companion USGS release, Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, 'Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012' (DOI 10.5066/F7W37TDP), is also 30 m but is derived from STATE-level (not county-level) 'land drained by tiles' acreages from the 2012 Census of Agriculture, plus NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland and STATSGO2 poorly-AND-moderately drained soils. It covers SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: because it disaggregates from state totals rather than county totals, it carries LESS spatial information than the 1990s CONUS product for distinguishing basins within Iowa, despite being 20 years more recent. It also does not cover the whole CONUS, so basins extending outside these 12 states would be truncated.
claims.effectSize: 30 m; 12 states; 2012 Ag Census, state-level disaggregation

claims.text: AgTile-US (Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz 2020, Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x) supersedes the Nakagaki products for this project's purpose: 30 m binary raster (0 = undrained agricultural land, 1 = tile-drained agricultural land) over the full CONUS, built from USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture COUNTY-level tile drainage, NLCD-2016 cropland, SSURGO soil drainage category, and SRTM slope (<=20% threshold). Validation against ~16,000 independent ground-truth points gave 86.03% overall CONUS accuracy, 82.7%-93.6% across the heavily tile-drained Midwest, and 91.1% in IOWA specifically (5,253 Iowa ground-truth points). Iowa is the most tile-drained state at 5.71 million hectares (vs Illinois 3.83, Minnesota 3.27, Indiana 2.57, Ohio 2.18, Michigan 1.22 Mha; CONUS total 22.34 Mha). GeoTIFF and NetCDF, CC-BY-4.0, free unauthenticated download from Figshare (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742); also mirrored as a Google Earth Engine community dataset. This directly closes the project's stated 'no tile drainage data source identified' gap: basin tile-drained fraction is computable as a per-distance-bucket mean of a 30 m binary layer using the existing cell-aggregation pipeline, and it is a STATIC attribute so it is immune to the temporal-feature failure pattern.
claims.effectSize: 86.03% CONUS accuracy, 91.1% Iowa accuracy, n=16,000 ground-truth points (5,253 in Iowa); Iowa 5.71 Mha tile-drained

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT / KNOWN LIMITATION of AgTile-US, stated by its own authors: the product UNDERESTIMATES tile drainage by -18.15% CONUS-wide relative to the census totals, has a 13.97% omission error, and 'performs weakly in marginal drainage categories' (soils that are neither clearly well-drained nor clearly poorly-drained). The underestimation is attributed primarily to NLCD cropland underrepresentation and is worst OUTSIDE the Midwest. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: the bias is spatially structured, not random, so basin-mean tile fraction will be systematically compressed for basins with ambiguous soil drainage classes; and because the error is smallest in the Midwest core, Iowa-interior basins will be measured more accurately than basins extending into non-Midwest states - the same directional bias already noted for the existing crop/N-surplus inner-join undercount on multi-state basins. Any observed tile-fraction effect should be tested for robustness against this.
claims.effectSize: -18.15% area underestimation CONUS-wide; 13.97% omission error

claims.text: The strongest published cross-site (between-basin) effect size for Iowa stream nitrate comes from Schilling, K.E., and Libra, R.D., 2000, 'The Relationship of Nitrate Concentrations in Streams to Row Crop Land Use in Iowa', Journal of Environmental Quality 29(6):1846-1851, DOI 10.2134/jeq2000.00472425002900060016x. Across 15 large Iowa watersheds (1,002-2,774 km2) and 10 small ones (47-775 km2) for 1996-1998, row-crop percentage ranged 24->87% and MEAN ANNUAL NO3-N ranged 0.5-10.8 mg/L (large) and 3.0-10.5 mg/L (small). Nitrate was directly related to row-crop percentage at p<0.0003, with essentially the SAME regression slope of 0.11 in both size classes - i.e. mean annual stream nitrate (mg/L) is approximated by watershed row-crop percentage x 0.1 (1.1 mg/L per 10% row crop). This is a static-attribute, purely cross-sectional result with n=25 watersheds - the same order as this project's n=19 independent basin families - so it is one of the few Corn Belt between-site findings whose evidence base is NOT dependent on hundreds of catchments. CAVEAT: the search snippet also indicates more recent work reports a substantially weaker slope of just under 0.4 mg/L per 10% row crop, so the 0.11 slope should be treated as an upper bound and re-estimated on this project's own 19 families rather than assumed.
claims.nBasins: 25 Iowa watersheds (15 large 1,002-2,774 km2 + 10 small 47-775 km2)
claims.effectSize: slope 0.11 mg/L NO3-N per 1% row crop (= 1.1 mg/L per 10%), p<0.0003; more recent work reportedly ~0.4 mg/L per 10%

claims.text: THE N-SURPLUS 2017 CLIFF IS NOT FIXABLE BY SWITCHING PRODUCTS - every authoritative county-level N-input product also terminates at 2017. (a) Falcone, J.A., 2021, USGS Open-File Report 2020-1153, 'Estimates of county-level nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer and manure from 1950 through 2017 in the conterminous United States' (ScienceBase item 5ebad56382ce25b51361806a) gives county-level kg of N and P from commercial fertilizer and from livestock manure separately - which DOES supply the manure-vs-commercial N split the research angle asks for - but only at ~5-year Ag-Census intervals ENDING IN 2017; the 2017 fertilizer values are themselves a new model fit from 11 predictors including county fertilizer expenditures and acres fertilized, i.e. not measurements. (b) The related USGS release 'Nitrogen and phosphorus inputs from fertilizer and manure in the Continental United States, 2002-2017' (ScienceBase 65787037d34e952b22746538) likewise stops at 2017. (c) The gTREND-Nitrogen data paper published in Scientific Data is titled 'Long-term nitrogen mass balance data for the contiguous United States (1930-2017)' - the product this project already uses - confirming no post-2017 continuation exists as of this search. FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE: since no vendor extends past 2017, the only defensible use of N surplus is as a STATIC per-basin attribute (e.g. the 2012 or 2017 snapshot, or a multi-decade basin mean/rank), which is a DIFFERENT hypothesis from the already-failed experiment of broadcasting the 2017 surplus field forward as a time-varying feature (that ablation scored -0.166) and is not ruled out by it. All three products are free, unauthenticated, public-domain/USGS-open, and cover the full CONUS including the multi-state portions of Iowa basins.
claims.effectSize: all products terminate 2017; Falcone at ~5-year Ag-Census intervals 1950-2017, county resolution, separate fertilizer and manure N

result.sourceQuality: MIXED - the assigned URL (ScienceBase catalog item 56e86a60e4b0f59b85d71ff9) returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to automated fetching on both the HTML and the ?format=json endpoints, as did the /catalog/item/get/ variant; the record was recovered instead from the authoritative USGS data-catalog mirror at usgs.gov/data plus search-index metadata, so dataset specs (30 m, CONUS, early-1990s, Sugg 2007 + NLCD 2011 + STATSGO2 inputs, DOI 10.5066/F7RB72QS, CC0) are confirmed by an agency source but the full FGDC metadata (file list, projection, exact field definitions) was NOT read. The assigned source itself is a metadata record, not a study, and contains NO effect sizes and NO model-performance numbers - so no splitProtocol or nBasins can attach to it; claims 1-2 are dataset-specification claims only. Effect-size evidence and the tile-drainage resolution therefore come from stronger peer-reviewed sources fetched in full: Valayamkunnath et al. 2020 Scientific Data (full text read via PMC, high quality, includes the authors' own negative results) and Schilling & Libra 2000 J. Environ. Qual. (abstract-level only, via search index - the 0.11 slope and n=25 are from the abstract, NOT verified against the full text, and the contrasting ~0.4 mg/L-per-10% figure is from an unattributed search summary and should be independently confirmed before use). The N-surplus continuation finding is a NEGATIVE existence result assembled from three agency/journal titles and abstracts; it is strong evidence that no post-2017 product was found, but absence of evidence - a newer unindexed release could exist. HEADLINE ACTIONABLE ITEM: AgTile-US (30 m, 2017 census, 91.1% Iowa accuracy, CC-BY-4.0, free Figshare download) concretely closes the project's stated tile-drainage data gap and is a STATIC between-site attribute, the one feature class that has historically won on this project.

claims.text: Basu et al. (2010) fitted daily water-quality monitoring data from the Mississippi-Atchafalaya River Basin (MARB) catchments to the C-Q power function C=AQ^b and found the exponent b had a mean of -0.02 with standard deviation 0.25, which they interpret as "an overall chemostatic response for these constituents." Splitting by constituent type, geogenic (Type I) constituents had mu_b = -0.1, sigma_b = 0.2 and anthropogenic (Type II, includes nitrate/TN and TP) had mu_b = -0.09, sigma_b = 0.3, with the two distributions statistically different (Kruskal-Wallis p = 4.36 x 10^-13). DIRECT CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: b near zero is the definition of chemostasis and means concentration is nearly INDEPENDENT of discharge at a given site. If Iowa agricultural nitrate is chemostatic in this sense, then adding a discharge feature (modeled NWM Q or otherwise) is predicted to add little or nothing to CONCENTRATION or threshold-exceedance prediction, even though it would strongly predict LOAD. This is the central falsifiable test of the research question, and this paper's own numbers argue AGAINST the discharge-as-savior hypothesis for a concentration target.
claims.effectSize: C-Q power-law exponent b: all MARB constituents mu_b=-0.02, sigma_b=0.25; Type I geogenic mu_b=-0.1, sigma_b=0.2; Type II anthropogenic mu_b=-0.09, sigma_b=0.3; Kruskal-Wallis p=4.36e-13
claims.nBasins: 21 MARB catchments (10^4 to 10^6 km2) for the primary b-value distribution; supplemented by 31 forested catchments (10^1-10^3 km2) in continental US and Puerto Rico, 3 Lake Okeechobee (FL) catchments, and 2 Swan River Basin (W. Australia) catchments
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — descriptive in-sample power-law fits to observed C-Q pairs, no predictive train/test split of any kind

claims.text: The paper's headline quantitative result is that ANNUAL exported nutrient load L_T is a linear function of ANNUAL discharge Q_T with "consistent linear relationships (R2=0.7±0.2) between annual exported nutrient loads, L_T, and annual discharge, Q_T" for total-N and total-P. CRITICAL SCOPE LIMITS that must be stated when citing this number: (a) it is an INTER-ANNUAL, WITHIN-CATCHMENT regression — each catchment gets its own fit and its own slope — NOT a between-catchment regression, so it is NOT evidence that discharge predicts the absolute level of an unseen basin; (b) the target is LOAD, not concentration, and load contains Q on both sides of the equation, a spurious-correlation problem the authors explicitly acknowledge ("it is a spurious correlation since discharge is a component of load calculation"); (c) the timescale is ANNUAL, roughly 10-30 annual points per catchment, not daily. It provides no support for daily-resolution concentration or exceedance prediction.
claims.effectSize: Annual load vs annual discharge linear fit R2 = 0.7 +/- 0.2 for TN and TP
claims.nBasins: 21 MARB catchments (10^4-10^6 km2) plus 14 Baltic Sea Drainage Basin catchments (10^2-10^5 km2); record length 10 to 30 years per catchment
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — in-sample ordinary least squares fits per catchment on annual aggregates; no held-out spatial, temporal, or random split

claims.text: The paper reports that annual flow-weighted concentration (Cf = L_T/Q_T) is TEMPORALLY INVARIANT within a catchment "even with significant (~1.5 times) increase in nutrient inputs over the last three decades in the MARB," and that in the Baltic Sea Drainage Basin "concerted efforts to decrease nutrient inputs towards a target level of ~50% have failed to show positive results." Supporting trend evidence: nitrate concentrations in the MARB were stable after 1975 in contrast to increasing trends over the previous 25 years (1950-1975). FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT'S FEATURES: contemporary annual nitrogen input/surplus is decoupled from stream nitrate concentration on decadal timescales, because legacy subsurface N stores buffer it. This independently explains the project's observed negative result that broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time HURT performance (-0.166) — the temporal dimension of an N-surplus feature carries little signal even in principle. It also predicts, conversely, that a TIME-INVARIANT per-basin N-legacy or long-term-mean-surplus static feature is the better parameterization than a time-varying one.
claims.effectSize: Nutrient inputs rose ~1.5x over three decades in MARB with no corresponding change in annual flow-weighted concentration; BSDB ~50% input-reduction target produced no detected improvement; MARB nitrate concentrations stable post-1975 vs rising 1950-1975
claims.nBasins: 21 MARB catchments plus 14 BSDB catchments (35 total)
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — long-term observational trend description, not a predictive model

claims.text: Basu et al. propose that each catchment "may be characterized with a constant, mean annual, flow-weighted concentration (slope of the linear fit in Figure 1), Cf, as a useful index for 'effective biogeochemical stationarity'," and state that "annual nutrient loads can be robustly estimated as L_T = Q_T * Cf, where the hydro-climatic controls (e.g., precipitation, evapotranspiration) are manifested in Q_T, and the anthropogenic drivers (e.g., land-use; nutrient inputs) are reflected in Cf." IMPORTANT NEGATIVE FINDING FOR THE RESEARCH QUESTION: although this framing implies exactly the between-site relation the project is looking for (a per-basin concentration constant set by land use and N inputs), THE PAPER NEVER FITS OR REPORTS IT. There is no regression of Cf on N input, N surplus, specific discharge, or any land-use covariate, and NO between-catchment R2 is reported anywhere in the paper. Cf is obtained empirically as a per-catchment fitted slope from that catchment's OWN observed loads — which requires local nitrate observations and therefore is NOT available at an arbitrary ungauged, unmonitored map pin. Cited as support for a predictive between-site C ~ input/discharge relation, this paper is a decomposition framework, not evidence.
claims.effectSize: Zero — no between-catchment regression of Cf on nutrient inputs or specific discharge is reported; no cross-site R2 appears in the paper
claims.nBasins: n/a — the between-site analysis was not performed
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — the between-site predictive relation implied by the framework was never estimated or validated

claims.text: The paper's own counter-example establishes that chemostatic/linear L-Q behavior for nitrate is CONDITIONAL on accumulated anthropogenic legacy, not universal: "Our analysis of data from the Hubbard Brook (US) catchment showed that, under conditions of minimal anthropogenic influence, and resulting low nitrate concentrations, the L_T-Q_T relationship lacked any significant correlation. At the same site, however, the geogenic constituent sodium, exhibited significant linear correlation." Pesticides behave the same supply-limited way because short half-lives ("1 to 100 days") preclude legacy buildup. The authors conclude nutrient export from managed catchments is "transport- rather than supply-limited, such that contemporary distributed and point sources have lesser influence on inter-annual fluctuations in stream nutrient concentrations." IMPLICATION: the discharge-as-predictor logic applies only where legacy N is large. Iowa row-crop basins plausibly qualify, but the strength of any Q-based feature should be expected to VARY BETWEEN BASINS as a function of legacy N accumulation — meaning a single global discharge coefficient may underperform, and the between-site term the project needs is legacy-N magnitude, which discharge itself does not carry.
claims.effectSize: Hubbard Brook nitrate annual L-Q: no significant correlation (qualitative, no R2 given); sodium at the same site: significant linear correlation; pesticide half-lives 1-100 days cited as reason legacy cannot accumulate
claims.nBasins: 1 (Hubbard Brook) for the nitrate counter-example; 31 forested US/Puerto Rico catchments in the broader supplementary compilation
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — descriptive correlation analysis on observed annual data

claims.text: SCALE AND RESOLUTION MISMATCH — the strongest caveat on transferring this paper to the Iowa virtual-sensor problem. The catchments analyzed are 10^4 to 10^6 km2 (MARB, i.e. whole-Mississippi-scale) and 10^2 to 10^5 km2 (Baltic), and every headline result is at the ANNUAL aggregation scale. The paper states plainly that at finer resolution the opposite behavior holds: "non-chemostatic responses are typical of nutrient (TN and TP) export from managed catchments in the MARB and BSDB" at the DAILY or MONTHLY time scales. The linear-L-Q criterion is also loose: linear fits are "judged adequate (R2>0.8) for a range of b values (-0.4<b<1.4)," a band wide enough to include strong dilution AND strong mobilization, so an R2>0.8 annual load fit does NOT establish that concentration is flat. Since this project predicts DAILY-MAX concentration and daily threshold exceedance on basins far smaller than 10^4 km2, the paper's chemostatic conclusion is outside its demonstrated domain, and its daily-scale statement actively predicts that daily nitrate is NOT chemostatic — which is the regime where a discharge feature could still help.
claims.effectSize: Catchment areas 10^4-10^6 km2 (MARB) and 10^2-10^5 km2 (BSDB); chemostasis claimed only at annual scale; explicit statement of non-chemostatic daily/monthly nutrient response; linear L-Q judged adequate (R2>0.8) across b in (-0.4, 1.4)
claims.nBasins: 21 MARB + 14 BSDB = 35 catchments in the primary analysis
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — no predictive validation performed at any timescale

result.sourceQuality: Full text obtained (accepted-manuscript PDF of the published GRL paper), not just abstract. The publisher page at agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com returned HTTP 403 (paywalled), so I retrieved the author-hosted full manuscript at https://ce.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/assets/users/thompson/9.%20Basu%20et%20al%20GRL%202010.pdf and read all 18 pages directly; bibliographic metadata cross-confirmed via Crossref. All quoted figures are verbatim from the main text. LIMITATION: the supplementary material (Table S1 catchment list, Table S2 b-value compilation, Figures S1-S4, Sections S1-S4) is NOT in this PDF, so per-catchment b values, individual catchment names/areas, and the derivation details could not be verified. SOURCE TYPE: peer-reviewed, Geophysical Research Letters 2010, vol 37, L23404, doi:10.1029/2010GL045168; highly cited foundational C-Q paper. RELEVANCE VERDICT FOR THE RESEARCH QUESTION: this source is a THEORETICAL/CONCEPTUAL foundation, not an evidence base for the specific question asked. It contains ZERO evaluation of the NOAA National Water Model, SPARROW, GAGES-II, or any modeled-discharge product (NWM did not exist in 2010), ZERO between-site predictive R2, ZERO machine learning, ZERO spatial-holdout validation, and ZERO daily-resolution prediction. It does NOT answer whether modeled Q converts into between-site skill. Its main contribution is a strong PRIOR AGAINST that hypothesis for a concentration target: chemostasis (b ~ -0.02 to -0.09) means Q predicts LOAD well and CONCENTRATION poorly, so a discharge feature is most likely to help only if the project switches the target to load, or if Iowa daily-scale behavior departs from chemostasis (which the paper itself says daily/monthly behavior does). Separately it supplies a mechanistic explanation for this project's already-observed N-surplus-broadcast failure. The NWM bias assessment in tile-drained low-relief basins, the SPARROW/GAGES-II comparison, and the load-vs-concentration target evaluation MUST be sourced elsewhere — this paper cannot speak to them. Also flag against the n=19-independent-families constraint: this paper's evidence rests on 35 catchments analyzed descriptively with no held-out validation, so it offers no guidance on whether any of this is learnable at n=19.

claims.text: OPERATIONAL TILE-DRAINAGE DATA SOURCE EXISTS AND IS PUBLIC — DIRECTLY FILLS THE PROJECT'S KNOWN #1 DATA GAP. Gorski & Zimmer (2021, HESS 25:1333, doi:10.5194/hess-25-1333-2021) state in Sect. 2.2: 'Data for landforms, drainage infrastructure, and stream network were downloaded from the Iowa Department of Natural Resources.' They compute 'drainage infrastructure density' in units of km of built drainage per km^2 of watershed (a line-density of mapped tile drains, ditches, and canals), reporting 1.11 km km^-2 for the heavily drained Upstream Sac City watershed and 0.37 km km^-2 for the least-drained Middle Redfield watershed. Figure 1 maps 'built drainage infrastructure' as gray line features across the entire 8,870 km^2 Raccoon River basin. FALSIFIABLE: a mapped built-drainage line layer for Iowa is obtainable free from the Iowa DNR NRGIS library (https://www.iowadnr.gov/ , NRGIS geodata portal), and basin-level line-density (km/km^2) can be computed per delineated basin. CAVEATS THE PAPER FORCES: (a) the paper gives no URL, no layer name, no vintage, and no statement of statewide completeness — the layer must be independently verified before any claim of Iowa-wide coverage; (b) it is explicitly an IOWA agency product, so it will NOT cover the multi-state portions of the project's largest basins, exactly reproducing the existing crop/N-surplus under-counting bias for out-of-state area; (c) it is a static attribute with no time dimension, which is what the project wants — every temporal feature has failed, and this is a purely between-site static geographic variable of the type that has been the project's only source of wins.
claims.effectSize: Drainage infrastructure density ranged 0.37 to 1.11 km km^-2 across the 5 study watersheds; units km per km^2
claims.nBasins: 5 nested watersheds (Raccoon River, central Iowa); layer coverage is statewide Iowa but unverified in this paper

claims.text: TILE-DRAINAGE DENSITY EXPLAINS BETWEEN-SITE DIFFERENCES IN ANNUAL NITRATE LOAD AT R^2 = 0.71-0.88 — THE EXACT BETWEEN-SITE TERM THIS PROJECT IS MISSING. Gorski & Zimmer (2021) Fig. 7 regresses cumulative annual NO3 load (kg N km^-2 yr^-1) against drainage infrastructure density across their five watersheds and report 'Stormflow – R^2 = 0.71' and 'Baseflow – R^2 = 0.75'. Restricted to spring (April-June), 'both baseflow and stormflow NO3 loads are strongly correlated with drainage infrastructure density (R^2 = 0.88 and 0.88, respectively; p < 0.05)'. Concentrations order the same way: median NO3 was 9.23 +/- 3.09 mg L^-1 at the most heavily tile-drained site (USC, 1.11 km km^-2) versus 6.96 +/- 2.51 mg L^-1 at the least-drained site (MRF, 0.37 km km^-2), with the basin outlet DVM intermediate at 7.38 +/- 3.07 mg L^-1. Text: 'There is a systematic trend toward higher-NO3 load in watersheds with a higher density of built drainage infrastructure.' FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION FOR THIS PROJECT: adding basin-mean drainage-infrastructure density as a static feature should raise between_r2 / between_rate_r2 (currently 0.21 / 0.24) more than any temporal feature tried so far, because the ~2.3 mg L^-1 spread in median concentration it explains is a between-SITE level offset, not a within-site timing signal. HARD CAVEAT ON SAMPLE SIZE: every R^2 quoted here is fitted to FIVE points (3 degrees of freedom), IN-SAMPLE, with no held-out validation of any kind; an R^2 of 0.88 on n=5 is not distinguishable from noise at conventional power. Worse, the five watersheds are NESTED (MJF contains USC; MRF contains UPN; DVM contains all), so the effective independent sample is smaller than 5 — this is the same nesting problem that collapses this project's 85 sites to 19 families. Treat these R^2 values as a hypothesis-generating direction, NOT as an expected effect size.
claims.effectSize: Annual load vs drainage density: R^2 = 0.71 (stormflow), 0.75 (baseflow); spring-only R^2 = 0.88 and 0.88, p < 0.05. Median NO3 spread 6.96 to 9.23 mg L^-1 across the drainage-density gradient. Annual export ranged 4216 +/- 768 kg N km^-2 yr^-1 (USC) to 2222 +/- 371 kg N km^-2 yr^-1 (MRF)

claims.text: STORMFLOW NITRATE IS CHEMOSTATIC — THIS IS A DIRECT ARGUMENT THAT MODELED DISCHARGE WILL NOT BUY CONCENTRATION SKILL IN THE HIGH-CONCENTRATION REGIME THAT DRIVES VIOLATIONS. Gorski & Zimmer (2021) partitioned 4 years of daily data (2016-2019) into stormflow and baseflow and fitted log-log c-Q slopes (chemostatic defined as |slope| <= 0.2, enrichment > 0.2, dilution < -0.2). They report: 'Stormflow showed consistent chemostatic patterns across all seasons' and, for individually fitted storm events, 'event-averaged c-Q slopes form a narrow distribution around zero across all seasons' (Fig. 5a histogram, ~15 events per watershed per year x 5 watersheds x 4 years). Also: 'Although tile-drained watersheds show higher stormflow NO3 concentrations (Fig. 3b), there does not appear to be a systematic effect on stormflow c-Q slopes (Fig. 4b). This indicates that the nitrate sources activated during stormflow are transport limited across all watersheds.' Mechanistically: 'landscapes with such agricultural intensity are a saturated solute source for which delivery is flow limited' (citing Thompson et al., 2011). IMPLICATION AGAINST THE RESEARCH ANGLE: a c-Q slope of ~0 means concentration is approximately INVARIANT to discharge during storms. Knowing Q at an ungauged site — however obtained, NWM retrospective or otherwise — therefore carries near-zero marginal information about C during exactly the periods when maximum daily nitrate (and hence the >= 10 mg L^-1 violation flag) is highest. This predicts that a modeled-Q feature will fail the same way the seven prior hydrologic temporal features failed. The information that DOES separate sites is the chemostatic PLATEAU LEVEL (the intercept a in C = aQ^b), which this paper attributes to static landscape attributes — drainage density and cropped area — not to Q.
claims.effectSize: Stormflow event-averaged c-Q slopes distributed narrowly around 0 across all seasons and all 5 watersheds; spring export regimes chemostatic with average c-Q slope 0.15 (stormflow) and 0.18 (baseflow); ~15 storm events per watershed per year over 4 years

claims.text: BASEFLOW C-Q IS SEASONALLY NON-STATIONARY AND ITS SLOPE IS NEGATIVELY CORRELATED WITH TILE DRAINAGE (SPRING R^2 = 0.85) — MEANING ANY SINGLE C-Q PARAMETER PER SITE IS THE WRONG ABSTRACTION. Gorski & Zimmer (2021): all five watersheds showed enriching baseflow behavior annually, with slopes from 0.21 (USC, most tile-drained) to 0.79 (UPN, least drained). Seasonally, summer baseflow was strongly chemodynamic (average c-Q slope 0.73 across all watersheds; DVM summer = 0.75) while spring baseflow was chemostatic (DVM spring = 0.08). The tile-drainage control: 'There is a negative correlation between seasonal baseflow c-Q slope and drainage infrastructure density, which is strongest during the spring months (R^2 = 0.85; p < 0.05).' Mechanism: heavy built drainage 'serves to homogenize baseflow sources', eliminating the low-flow / low-NO3 periods that create enrichment slopes; the end-members are MRF (0.37 km km^-2) which was chemodynamic in every season (0.34 winter to 0.75 summer) versus USC (1.11 km km^-2) which was chemostatic in every season except summer (0.29). CONSEQUENCE FOR FEATURE DESIGN: the sign and magnitude of any Q-to-C relationship flips by season AND by tile-drainage density, so a global Q feature is mis-specified; if Q is used at all it must be interacted with season and with drainage density. Note this also predicts a QUALITATIVE interaction the project could test cheaply with its existing 22 gauged sites before ever touching NWM. n=5 caveat applies to the R^2 = 0.85 (five nested points, in-sample, no held-out validation).
claims.effectSize: Baseflow c-Q slope vs drainage density: R^2 = 0.85, p < 0.05 (spring). Annual baseflow slopes 0.21-0.79. Summer baseflow slope average 0.73; spring baseflow chemostatic (DVM 0.08 vs 0.75 summer)

claims.text: EXPLICIT NEGATIVE RESULT: C-Q SLOPES ARE UNSTABLE TO A HANDFUL OF DAYS AND DO NOT CORRELATE WITH WATERSHED AREA — THE AUTHORS WARN AGAINST SINGLE-PARAMETER C-Q CHARACTERIZATION. Gorski & Zimmer (2021) Sect. 3.5 document that in UPN, two anomalous low-flow low-NO3 events in October 2017 (mean 1.34 and 0.46 mg L^-1) shifted the fall bulk stormflow c-Q slope from 0.09 to 0.71 despite representing '<1 % of annual flow and NO3 load'. In MJF, an anomalous low-flow period (mean 96 cfs, <0.1 flow percentile) from 26 July to 19 October 2017 changed the annual baseflow c-Q slope from 0.42 to 1.42 — a factor of 3.4 from one ~3-month low-flow window. The authors conclude: 'The ability of a single anomalous period (whether real or due to sensor artifacts) to influence the overall characterization of a hydrologic system highlights the difficulty in representing nutrient export behavior based on a single parameter fit across several seasons and flow regimes.' Separately: 'Seasonal and annual c-Q slopes across all hydrologic regimes show only weak correlations with watershed area' — i.e. the one static attribute the project ALREADY has (log_basin_area) does not predict c-Q behavior. They also state their records 'do not cover a sufficient length of time to thoroughly examine interannual variability, and it remains an open question as to how stable the c-Q patterns presented in this study are over time.' FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION: fitting a per-site c-Q slope as an engineered feature on this project's 22 gauged sites will produce estimates whose leave-one-out variance exceeds their between-site spread, and it will not transfer to the 63 ungauged sites at all — c-Q slope is not derivable without Q AND C at the target, which the deployment target has neither of.
claims.effectSize: Single anomalous period changed annual baseflow c-Q slope from 0.42 to 1.42 (3.4x); two events comprising <1% of annual flow changed seasonal stormflow slope from 0.09 to 0.71 (7.9x). c-Q slope vs watershed area: 'only weak correlations' (no R^2 given)

claims.text: RIPARIAN CROPPED AREA WITHIN 100 m OF THE STREAM EXPLAINS SUMMER BASEFLOW NITRATE LOAD AT R^2 = 0.94 — A MUCH TIGHTER BUFFER THAN THE 0-2 km RIPARIAN BUCKET THIS PROJECT ALREADY TESTED. Gorski & Zimmer (2021): 'The baseflow NO3 load during the summer is most strongly correlated with the percentage of cropped area within 100 m of the stream (R^2 = 0.94; p < 0.01)', concluding 'land use near the stream has a large impact on NO3 loadings, indicating that buffer strips or other near-stream management practices may be effective management practices for reducing loads during these periods' and 'land use in riparian areas exhibits strong influence on baseflow nitrate loads'. Land use was NLCD 2016 at 30 m x 30 m (Dewitz, 2019), binned to four classes (water/wetlands, developed, forested, barren/shrubs, crops-including-pasture); the stream network came from the Iowa DNR. ACTIONABLE FOR THIS PROJECT: the existing riparian test used a 0-2 km bucket and yielded CLF +0.039 PR-AUC with REG worse. This paper's signal is at 100 m — a 20x tighter band that a 2 km bucket would dilute by roughly its area ratio. Recomputing crop fraction in a 100 m (or 100-500 m) stream buffer, using the same 30 m CDL/NLCD grid already in the pipeline plus an NHDPlus flowline layer the project already has via COMID, is a cheap, purely-static, between-site feature requiring no new data acquisition and no gauge. CAVEATS: R^2 = 0.94 is fitted on FIVE nested watersheds in-sample with no validation split, so it is a direction not an expected effect size; the relation was established for SUMMER BASEFLOW LOAD specifically, which is the LOW-concentration, low-load regime (baseflow was <= 15% of annual load in every watershed), not the spring stormflow regime that carried 37.5 +/- 11.5% of annual load and produced the maximum concentrations that drive violation flags.
claims.effectSize: Summer baseflow NO3 load vs % cropped area within 100 m of stream: R^2 = 0.94, p < 0.01. Drainage structures vs number of cropped areas: R^2 = 0.95, p < 0.01. Baseflow was <=15% of annual load; spring stormflow 37.5 +/- 11.5% of annual load

result.sourceQuality:
HIGH SOURCE QUALITY, LOW STATISTICAL POWER. Gorski, G. and Zimmer, M. A. (2021), "Hydrologic regimes drive nitrate export behavior in human-impacted watersheds", Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 25:1333-1345, doi:10.5194/hess-25-1333-2021. Peer-reviewed (edited by Genevieve Ali; reviewed by Douglas Burns and one anonymous referee), open access CC-BY. FULL TEXT RETRIEVED AND READ DIRECTLY (all 13 pages of the publisher PDF) — no paywall, nothing inferred from abstract mirrors, all quoted figures verbatim from the text, Tables 1 and 4, and Figures 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

EXCEPTIONAL DOMAIN MATCH: this is the SAME STUDY SYSTEM as the project. Central Iowa, Raccoon River (8,870 km2, HUC 07100006/07100007), the SAME two sensor networks the project draws on — USGS gauges 05482300, 05483600, 05482500, 05484500 plus IIHR site WQS0032 — the SAME Hach Nitratax plus sc probes at 15 min resolution aggregated to daily, and an overlapping period (Jan 2016 - Dec 2019). The authors thank IIHR for providing data. Findings should transfer to this project's setting more directly than any CAMELS- or CONUS-scale study.

CRITICAL LIMITATION — n=5 AND NESTED: every quantitative relation in this paper is a Pearson correlation fitted to FIVE watersheds, in-sample, with NO cross-validation, NO spatial holdout, and NO out-of-sample test of any kind. splitProtocol is therefore "not-applicable" for all reported R^2 values; none of them are comparable to this project's LOFO AUC 0.820 and none should be read as an expected predictive effect size. Worse, the five watersheds are NESTED (MJF contains USC; MRF contains UPN; DVM contains all five), which is precisely the dependency structure that collapses this project's 85 sites to 19 independent basin families — so the effective independent sample here is well below 5, and an R^2 of 0.94 on 3 nominal degrees of freedom is weak evidence. The authors themselves flag temporal instability, noting the 4-year record is too short to assess interannual stability of c-Q patterns.

BEARING ON THE RESEARCH QUESTION (does modeled Q buy between-site skill?): this source is EVIDENCE AGAINST the discharge angle and EVIDENCE FOR the static-landscape angle. Stormflow nitrate is chemostatic (c-Q slope ~0), so discharge carries little marginal information about concentration in the high-concentration regime that generates violations; the between-site signal lives in the chemostatic plateau LEVEL, which the paper ties to tile-drainage density and near-stream cropped area — both static, both obtainable without a gauge, both compatible with the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target. The paper contains NOTHING on the NOAA National Water Model, SPARROW, GAGES-II, or streamflow regionalization, and does NOT test concentration ~ N-input-yield / specific-discharge as a between-site relation; those parts of the research question must be answered from other sources.

MOST VALUABLE SINGLE ITEM: the paper identifies a concrete public source for the project's acknowledged #1 missing control — Iowa Department of Natural Resources built-drainage-infrastructure line data, used as km km^-2 basin density. The paper gives no URL, no layer name, and no vintage, so this requires independent verification at the Iowa DNR NRGIS portal, and it will not cover out-of-state basin area.

HIGH-VALUE FOLLOW-UP CITATIONS VISIBLE IN THE REFERENCE LIST (larger n, better suited to the between-site question): Marinos, R. E., Van Meter, K. J. and Basu, N. B. (2020), "Is the River a Chemostat?: Scale Versus Land Use Controls on Nitrate Concentration-Discharge Dynamics in the Upper Mississippi River Basin", GRL 47, e2020GL087051, doi:10.1029/2020GL087051 — cited in-text as a study of 33 AGRICULTURAL MIDWEST WATERSHEDS reaching the same conclusion, i.e. ~6.6x this paper's sample in the same region; this is the single best next source for the C-Q angle. Also: Basu et al. (2010) GRL 37 (biogeochemical stationarity), doi:10.1029/2010GL045168; Thompson et al. (2011) WRR 47, doi:10.1029/2010WR009605; Godsey/Kirchner (2009) Hydrol. Process. 23:1844, doi:10.1002/hyp.7315; Musolff et al. (2015) Adv. Water Resour. 86:133; Moatar et al. (2017) WRR 53:1270; Van Meter, Chowdhury, Byrnes and Basu (2020) Limnol. Oceanogr. 65:848 (seasonal concentration regimes, Great Lakes Basin); Schilling, Jindal, Basu and Helmers (2012) Hydrol. Process. 26:3092 on artificial subsurface drainage in an Iowa watershed; and Wherry, Tesoriero and Terziotti (2021) ES&T 55:902, "Factors affecting nitrate concentrations in stream base flow", doi:10.1021/acs.est.0c02495.

DATA AVAILABILITY: the authors' storm/baseflow-partitioned Raccoon River records are archived and citable at https://doi.org/10.4211/hs.173cff98da3c4263a110cba8c6d62406 (Gorski and Zimmer, 2020, HydroShare) — a free, directly reusable labeled hydrograph-partition dataset for five Iowa basins that overlap this project's own sites and study period.

claims.text: The NOAA National Water Model CONUS Retrospective v3.0 provides hourly simulated streamflow for 2,776,734 river reaches spanning 1979-02-01 through Jan 2023 (385,704 hourly timesteps), in units of m3 s-1, as a cloud-optimized Zarr store at s3://noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds/CONUS/zarr/chrtout.zarr. Access is anonymous (no AWS account, `--no-sign-request`, or plain HTTPS GET), license is 'Open Data. There are no restrictions on the use of this data.' Sibling stores exist for gwout, lakeout, ldasout, and forcing. VERIFIED DIRECTLY: I fetched the .zmetadata from the live bucket rather than relying on the registry page; the registry page itself does not document reach identifiers or Zarr paths. This satisfies the project's operational-dataset bar (name, resolution, years, coverage, URL, access mechanism, no auth, permissive license) and covers the ENTIRE CONUS, so it covers the multi-state portions of Iowa basins that the current Iowa-only crop/N-surplus inner join silently under-counts.
claims.effectSize: 44 years hourly; 385,704 x 2,776,734 grid; anonymous access confirmed HTTP 200

claims.text: The NWM v3.0 chrtout Zarr reach identifier is `feature_id`, whose own metadata states verbatim: 'NHDPlusv2 ComIDs within CONUS, arbitrary Reach IDs outside of CONUS' (cf_role: timeseries_id, long_name: 'Reach ID'). The store also ships per-reach `gage_id` (S15), `latitude`, `longitude`, `elevation`, and Strahler `order` as coordinate arrays. FALSIFIABLE AND DIRECTLY ACTIONABLE FOR THIS PROJECT: the project already stores an NHDPlus comid per delineated basin, so joining modeled discharge to any basin outlet is a single integer key lookup with NO fuzzy spatial matching — and critically it works at an ARBITRARY UNGAUGED MAP PIN, since NLDI delineation already returns a comid. The `gage_id` array additionally allows the 22 USGS-gauged sites to be used as a held-out validation set for NWM discharge error WITHOUT contaminating the LOFO folds.
claims.effectSize: exact integer COMID join; 2,776,734 reaches carry lat/lon/elevation/stream-order/gage_id

claims.text: THE DECISIVE NEGATIVE FOR THIS PROJECT: Valayamkunnath, Gochis, Chen, Barlage & Franz (2022), 'Modeling the Hydrologic Influence of Subsurface Tile Drainage Using the National Water Model', Water Resources Research 58(4), DOI 10.1029/2021WR031242, states that the NWM — a 1-km distributed model forecasting 2.7 million U.S. reaches — 'currently lacks tile drainage representation, creating considerable uncertainty in areas with extensive drainage systems.' Adding a tile-drainage scheme produced 20-50% accuracy improvements, and increased simulated streamflow peaks by 14%, volume by 2.3%, and baseflow by 11%. This is EXACTLY the failure mode that matters here: the project already identifies tile drainage as 'the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa' and absent from its features. NWM retrospective discharge in Iowa is therefore biased by the SAME missing process the project is trying to proxy, and the bias is SPATIALLY STRUCTURED by drainage density — i.e. it is a between-site error, precisely the term where all remaining headroom lies. Modeled-Q error could swamp the signal. Note the abstract was obtained via OpenAlex; the Wiley full text returned HTTP 403.
claims.nBasins: unknown (regional Midwest tile-drained domain; per-basin count not determinable from abstract — full text paywalled/403)
claims.effectSize: 20-50% accuracy improvement from adding tile drainage; peaks +14%, volume +2.3%, baseflow +11%

claims.text: The authoritative CONUS benchmark of the NWM v2.1 retrospective (HESS 27:1809-1834, 2023, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023) evaluated 5,390 USGS gages ('cobalt gages', GAGES-II derived) on daily streamflow over 1 Oct 1983 - 31 Dec 2016 (~33 yr) and reports median KGE 0.53 overall, 0.65 at reference (near-natural) sites, and 0.49 at non-reference (human-impacted) sites; PBIAS -4.0% at reference sites vs +5.3% at non-reference sites; and 90-93% of underperforming sites are human-impacted non-reference gauges. Regionally, performance was BEST in the Northeast and POOREST in the 'Central' region plains and arid Southwest. CAVEAT I COULD NOT RESOLVE: the paper does not explicitly single out Corn Belt or tile-drained basins, and I could NOT determine how many of the 5,390 gages overlap the gauges NWM v2.1 was itself calibrated against — so median KGE 0.53 is plausibly partly IN-SAMPLE and is an optimistic ceiling for a truly ungauged Iowa pin. Iowa sites are agricultural and overwhelmingly non-reference, placing them in the KGE~0.49 / Central-region-poorest stratum.
claims.splitProtocol: unknown (model-vs-gauge evaluation, not an ML split; overlap with NWM calibration gauges not determinable — possibly partly in-sample)
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.53 overall / 0.65 reference / 0.49 non-reference; PBIAS -4.0% ref vs +5.3% non-ref; 90-93% of poor sites human-impacted

claims.text: OPERATIONAL COST WARNING, measured directly: the NWM v3.0 chrtout Zarr arrays are chunked [672 time, 30000 feature_id], and a single compressed streamflow chunk is 3,938,919 bytes (3.94 MB, verified by HTTP HEAD on .../streamflow/0.0). Retrieving the full 44-year hourly record requires 573 time-chunks per feature-chunk. Because the ~85 project sites' COMIDs are scattered across the feature_id axis, extraction cost is roughly 573 x (number of distinct feature-chunks touched) x 3.94 MB: best case ~2 GB if all sites fall in one 30,000-reach chunk, worst case ~190 GB if all 85 land in separate chunks. FALSIFIABLE AND CHEAP TO TEST BEFORE COMMITTING: compute the project's 85 COMIDs' indices in the 2,776,734-long feature_id array (a single 22 MB coordinate-array download) and count distinct floor(index/30000) values. This decides in minutes whether NWM extraction is a coffee-break job or a multi-day transfer, and should be run BEFORE any modeling work.
claims.effectSize: 3.94 MB per [672 x 30000] chunk; 573 time-chunks for full record; 2 GB best case to ~190 GB worst case for 85 sites

claims.text: ON THE C-Q REGIME QUESTION (LOWER-CONFIDENCE — from search-result summaries, not primary full-text fetches; treat as leads to verify, not as established figures): the nitrate C-Q literature uses the ratio of coefficients of variation CVc/CVq as the chemostasis metric, with Thompson et al. (2011, WRR, DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605) proposing CVc/CVq < 0.3 as the chemostatic threshold, and Basu et al. reporting that 'chemostatic behavior and constant CVc/CVq values below 0.5 are typical for agriculturally influenced catchments', arising 'when a large mass store buffers concentration variability' (i.e. legacy N). STRATEGIC IMPLICATION IF TRUE, AND IT CUTS AGAINST THE DISCHARGE ANGLE: chemostasis means nitrate CONCENTRATION is approximately INVARIANT to discharge in exactly this catchment class, so knowing Q at an ungauged Iowa site would add little direct information about concentration — the between-site level would instead be set by the N mass store (legacy N, tile density), NOT by Q. This is CONSISTENT with the project's own seven failed temporal/hydrologic ablations and with the finding that gains came only from static geography. It also argues the reverse of the LOAD-target proposal: under chemostasis L = C x Q is dominated by Q, so modeling load then back-dividing by a BIASED modeled Q would inject NWM's tile-drainage bias directly into the recovered concentration. I could NOT verify the primary Basu et al. (2010) and Thompson et al. (2011) numbers, sample sizes, or catchment counts within this fetch.
claims.nBasins: unknown (catchment counts for Basu et al. 2010 and Thompson et al. 2011 not determinable from secondary summaries)
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (descriptive C-Q regime classification, no predictive split)
claims.effectSize: CVc/CVq < 0.3 = chemostatic threshold (Thompson 2011); CVc/CVq < 0.5 typical of agricultural catchments (Basu)

result.sourceQuality: MIXED, with a clear tiering the parent agent must respect. TIER 1 (highest confidence, primary and independently verified): the NWM v3.0 operational specs, the feature_id=NHDPlusv2 COMID join key, and the chunk-cost measurement were NOT taken on trust from the AWS registry page — I fetched the live .zmetadata JSON and ran an HTTP HEAD against a real chunk. These are as authoritative as it gets and are directly reproducible. Note that the assigned registry page was reachable but THIN: it does not document reach identifiers, Zarr store names, or variable lists, so on its own it would not have answered the question. TIER 2 (strong, peer-reviewed, fetched): the HESS 2023 CONUS benchmark (DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023, 5,390 gages) — but with an unresolved and material caveat that I could not establish how much of it is in-sample relative to NWM's own calibration gauges, so median KGE 0.53 should be read as an optimistic ceiling. TIER 3 (peer-reviewed but abstract-only): Valayamkunnath et al. 2022 WRR (DOI 10.1029/2021WR031242) — the Wiley full text returned HTTP 403, so the 20-50%/14%/2.3%/11% figures come from the OpenAlex abstract and the per-basin sample size is unknown. This is the single most important source for the research question and warrants a full-text retrieval. TIER 4 (weakest, flagged in-claim): the C-Q chemostasis material came from search-engine summaries rather than primary fetches; the Basu et al. 2010 and Thompson et al. 2011 catchment counts and R2 values remain unverified and should not be cited as fact. IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMIT: this source assignment covered the NWM access page only, so I could NOT evaluate the requested alternatives — SPARROW predicted mean-annual flow and N yield per reach, GAGES-II, or regionalizing Q from the project's own 22 gauged sites. Those need separate sources. On the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint: nothing here is affected by it, because NWM is a physics-based model requiring NO training on the project's sites — it is one of the few candidate inputs that is genuinely immune to the small-sample problem. That said, VALIDATING whether NWM discharge helps still runs through the same 19-family LOFO bottleneck, and the honest prior from Tier 3 plus Tier 4 is pessimistic: NWM omits the very tile-drainage process that dominates Iowa hydrology, and chemostasis predicts Q carries little concentration signal in agricultural catchments anyway. I would recommend the cheap COMID-chunk-count test and a 22-gauge NWM-vs-observed error audit BEFORE any modeling investment.

claims.text: Falcone (2021), USGS OFR 2020-1153 / data release DOI 10.5066/P9VSQN3C, provides county-level kilograms of N and P for all 3,066 conterminous-US counties for the 15 USDA Census of Agriculture years 1950, 1954, 1959, 1964, 1969, 1974, 1978, 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997, 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017. Two Excel workbooks: fertilizer (sheets 'total' with tot-fertN/P-kg-YYYY for 1950-1982, 'farm' with farmfertN/P-kg-YYYY for 1987-2017, 'nonfarm' with nonffertN/P-kg-YYYY for 1987-2017) and manure (one sheet per year, fields Cattle_N_kg-YYYY, Hogs_N_kg-YYYY, Poultry_N_kg-YYYY, Other_N_kg-YYYY, Total_N_kg-YYYY plus P equivalents and raw head counts bcows/mcows/cows/othercows/hogs/chickens/broilers/turkeys/sheep/horses). Keyed on STCOFIPS. License CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain), bulk download, no authentication. Because coverage is CONUS county-complete, it does NOT suffer the Iowa-boundary truncation that the project's current gTREND grid inner-join causes for multi-state basins. VERIFICATION: these exact files are already on disk in this repo at experiments/erin/data/N-P_from_fertilizer_1950-2017-july23-2020.xlsx and N-P_from_manure_1950-2017-july23-2020.xlsx.
claims.effectSize: 3,066 counties x 15 years; N and P; fertilizer farm/nonfarm split from 1987; manure split into Cattle/Hogs/Poultry/Other
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (county units, 3066 CONUS counties, 99 in Iowa)

claims.text: COMPUTED DIRECTLY FROM THE FALCONE FILES IN THIS REPO: across Iowa's 99 counties, county-level N inputs are highly rank-stable over two decades. Spearman rank correlation of farm fertilizer N against its 2017 value is 0.946 (1997), 0.910 (2002), 0.921 (2007), 0.969 (2012). For total manure N against 2017 it is 0.803 (1997), 0.887 (2002), 0.932 (2007), 0.963 (2012). This is direct quantitative support for using N input as a TIME-INVARIANT STATIC basin attribute (a basin's rank among basins barely moves), which is a different and untested use from the project's failed experiment of broadcasting the 2017 gTREND surplus value forward as a time-varying feature (loso_r2 -0.166). The failed broadcast result does not falsify the static-rank use. Falsifiable: recompute the Spearman values from the two workbooks; the claim fails if any drops below ~0.80.
claims.effectSize: Spearman rho 0.910-0.969 (fertilizer N, 1997-2012 vs 2017); 0.803-0.963 (manure N). n = 99 Iowa counties
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (99 Iowa counties; no basin-level model fit performed)

claims.text: COMPUTED DIRECTLY FROM THE FALCONE FILES: in Iowa in 2017, manure N totals 4.633e8 kg versus farm-fertilizer N 1.123e9 kg (manure/fertilizer ratio 0.41), and manure N is far more spatially discriminating between counties than fertilizer N — cross-county coefficient of variation 1.029 for manure N versus 0.404 for fertilizer N (2.5x more between-unit spread). The two are only partially redundant: Spearman correlation between county farm-fertilizer N and county manure N in Iowa 2017 is 0.611, so they should enter a model as SEPARATE features, not a single 'total N input'. Iowa 2017 manure N composition is hogs 54.0%, cattle 39.7%, poultry 5.5%, other 0.8%, so a hog-manure-specific feature carries most of the manure signal. Nonfarm (urban) fertilizer N in Iowa 2017 is only 0.56% of farm fertilizer N, so the nonfarm sheet can be dropped for this application. RELEVANCE TO THE n=19 CONSTRAINT: because the between-site term is where all remaining headroom is and only ~19 independent families exist, a feature with 2.5x higher between-unit variance (manure N) is a better candidate than fertilizer N for the small number of degrees of freedom available.
claims.effectSize: cross-county CV: manure N 1.029 vs fertilizer N 0.404; rank corr between them 0.611; hogs = 54.0% of Iowa manure N; nonfarm = 0.56% of farm N

claims.text: The 2017 farm-fertilizer values in Falcone (2021) are MODEL OUTPUT, not measurements, and this matters for treating 2017 differently from 1950-2012. AAPFCO state-level fertilizer tonnage for 2017 was never completed (report cites J. Slater, University of Missouri, written commun., May 4, 2020: the AAPFCO 2017 data 'have not been completed', and 'no other State-level summaries of fertilizer use by weight' were available), so Falcone substituted a random-forest regression with 11 predictors (percent county area in corn, pasture, N-fixing, small-grain, misc crops; fertilizer dollars divided by fertilizer-price index; manure N or P kg; annual ET; annual precipitation; fertilized acres; population density), trained on 9,198 records (3,066 counties x years 2002, 2007, 2012) with published county masses from Brakebill & Gronberg (2017) as the target, 1,000 trees. Reported out-of-bag proportion of variance explained: r2 = 0.948 for the nitrogen model and r2 = 0.921 for the phosphorus model. Dominant predictor by a wide margin: county fertilizer expenditure in dollars (%IncMSE 73.3 for N, 67.7 for P), next fertilized acres (34.9 / 28.3), then pasture percent (24.7 / 26.7), population density (22.4 / 20.4), ET and PPT (22.1 / 20.8 each), corn percent (23.0 / 22.5), N-fixing percent (20.7 / 27.6), misc crops (19.3 / 18.7), small grain (15.4 / 13.3), manure kg (15.9 / 13.9). CAUTION: the r2 = 0.948 is an OOB estimate over a random-ish resample of county-years, NOT a spatially held-out estimate, so it is not directly comparable to any leave-one-basin-out number and likely overstates transfer to unseen counties.
claims.effectSize: RF OOB variance explained r2 = 0.948 (N), 0.921 (P); n_train = 9,198 county-years; 11 predictors; 1,000 trees; top predictor %IncMSE 73.3
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (3,066 counties x 3 years = 9,198 county-year records; no basins)

claims.text: The Falcone manure series can be extended past the 2017 cliff without any new data product, because the manure method needs only (a) county livestock inventories from USDA NASS QuickStats and (b) published fixed coefficients. Falcone's stated procedure: multiply county head counts (beef cows, milk cows, other cattle, hogs, broilers, layers, turkeys, sheep, horses) by the nutrient-production formulas of Gronberg & Arnold (2017), then by a livestock-weight coefficient equal to average federally-inspected live slaughter weight in the target year divided by that in the 1992 base year. The published 2017 coefficients are cattle 1.152, hogs 1.117, sheep 1.078, broilers 1.374, chickens 1.295, turkeys 1.425 (horses held static because USDA reports no weight). Since the 2022 Census of Agriculture is published and this repo already contains experiments/erin/data/NASSAgCensusDownload2022.xlsx and experiments/erin/create_county_data_2022.ipynb, a 2022 manure-N county layer is reproducible with existing assets. FALSIFIABLE AND FAILURE MODE: USDA withholds county values for disclosure. Falcone reports that withheld hog counties grew from 26 (1974) to 212 (1992) to 576 (2012), and for 2017 he backfilled 515 withheld hog counties from the most recent prior year (up to 6 census periods / 30 years back), leaving only 14 unfillable. So a 2022 extension inherits a growing imputation burden concentrated exactly in counties with one very large confinement operation - i.e. the high-manure counties that matter most for Iowa nitrate.
claims.effectSize: 2017 weight coefficients: cattle 1.152, hogs 1.117, broilers 1.374, chickens 1.295, turkeys 1.425, sheep 1.078. Withheld hog counties: 26 (1974) -> 212 (1992) -> 576 (2012) -> 515 backfilled in 2017, 14 left blank

claims.text: A CATCHMENT-LEVEL (not county-level) successor product exists and is a better fit for this project's pipeline than Falcone's county tables: Sekellick, A.J., and Sherr, C.E., 2024, 'Nitrogen and phosphorus inputs from fertilizer and manure in the Continental United States, 2002-2017', USGS data release DOI 10.5066/P9WDBIXC, published 26 September 2024. It downscales the county-level estimates to NHDPlus Version 2.1 catchments keyed by COMID using NLCD land-cover classes, for the years 2002, 2007, 2012, and 2017. Eight CSV tables covering total N and total P from four source categories: agricultural fertilizer, confined animal manure, unconfined animal manure, and developed-land fertilizer. CONUS coverage (so multi-state basins are complete). Format CSV plus XML metadata; license CC0 1.0 Universal; bulk download, no authentication. OPERATIONAL RELEVANCE: this project already stores an NHDPlus COMID per basin and delineates arbitrary map pins via USGS NLDI (which returns COMIDs), so these tables join by COMID with NO county-to-basin areal reapportionment step and NO dependence on any observation at the target site - it satisfies the ungauged-arbitrary-pin deployment constraint. The confined-vs-unconfined manure split is additional information that neither the county Falcone tables nor the gTREND surplus product provides. CAVEAT: it still ends at 2017; it does not solve the post-2017 cliff, only the spatial-aggregation and multi-state-truncation problems.
claims.effectSize: NHDPlusV2.1 catchment resolution (COMID-keyed); 4 years (2002, 2007, 2012, 2017); 8 tables; 4 source categories x N and P; CONUS
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (CONUS NHDPlusV2 catchments, ~2.6 million nationally; no model performance reported)

result.sourceQuality: High — primary source read in full. The USGS HTML landing pages returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, but the authoritative 20-page PDF (https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2020/1153/ofr20201153.pdf) was retrieved by curl and text-extracted, so all method, coefficient, variable-importance, and limitation figures are quoted from the report itself rather than from an abstract mirror. The USGS data-release page for DOI 10.5066/P9VSQN3C and the USGS data page for the Sekellick & Sherr catchment product (DOI 10.5066/P9WDBIXC) were fetched successfully; the ScienceBase item page 403'd, so per-file names and byte sizes for the catchment CSVs are NOT verified and should be confirmed at download time.
