claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2019, 10.1029/2019WR026065) report that an LSTM predicting in basins that supplied ZERO training data ('PUB LSTM', 10-member ensemble, inputs = 5 NLDAS daily meteorological forcings + 27 static CAMELS catchment attributes, 256 cell states, dropout 0.4) achieved median NSE 0.69 over 531 CAMELS catchments in water years 1996-2010, versus 0.64 for SAC-SMA calibrated SEPARATELY IN EACH BASIN on 15 years of that basin's own data and 0.58 for the NOAA National Water Model reanalysis. The PUB LSTM beat SAC-SMA in 307 of 531 catchments (58%) and the NWM in 347 of 531 (66%). This is the headline evidence that a spatially-transferred deep model can beat locally-calibrated process models — but note the target is STREAMFLOW, not any water-quality or concentration variable, and no gradient-boosted-tree, random-forest, or any other ML baseline appears anywhere in the paper.
claims.nBasins: 531 CAMELS catchments (subset of 671; 4-2000 km2), ~30 years daily data each; train 1981-1995, test 1996-2010
claims.effectSize: PUB LSTM median NSE 0.69 vs calibrated SAC-SMA 0.64 (+0.05) vs NWM 0.58 (+0.11); win rate 307/531 and 347/531

claims.text: The spatial holdout in Kratzert et al. (2019) is k-fold with k=12 where the 531 basins were split RANDOMLY into 12 groups of approximately equal size (~44 held out, ~487 used for training each fold) — the paper states this explicitly ('splits the 531 basins randomly into k = 12 groups'). Groups were NOT formed by region, watershed nesting, hydrologic unit, or any spatial-blocking rule, so every held-out basin almost certainly had geographically and climatically adjacent basins in its own training set. The paper contains NO leave-one-region-out experiment and no analysis of whether the 0.69 median NSE degrades as the held-out basin's distance or dissimilarity from the nearest training basin increases. Therefore this number is NOT directly comparable to a leave-one-basin-FAMILY-out protocol that removes nested/overlapping neighbors, and it should be treated as an upper bound on what random-basin-holdout can show about true regional transfer.
claims.nBasins: 531 total; k=12 random folds, ~44 test / ~487 train per fold
claims.effectSize: n/a — protocol characterization; no region-blocked variant reported

claims.text: In Kratzert et al. (2019), STATIC CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES — not temporal dynamics — are what makes cross-basin transfer work. Two LSTMs trained on all 531 basins with identical meteorological forcings differ only in whether the 27 static attributes are appended at each timestep: median NSE 0.74 WITH statics vs 0.63 WITHOUT (+0.11 NSE; the authors state the NSE difference was statistically significant at p < 1e-9). Correspondingly, the fully out-of-sample PUB LSTM (0.69) gave up only 0.05 median NSE relative to the in-sample Global LSTM with statics (0.74), i.e. most of the achievable skill survives never having seen the basin — the transferable information lives in the static descriptors. The 27 attributes span climate indices (aridity, precip seasonality, snow fraction, high/low precip frequency and duration), topography (elevation, slope, area), vegetation (forest fraction, LAI max, LAI difference, GVF max/difference), SOIL (depth to bedrock, soil depth, porosity, saturated hydraulic conductivity, max water content, sand/silt/clay fractions) and GEOLOGY (carbonate rock fraction, log10 surface permeability).
claims.nBasins: 531 (both global LSTM variants trained on all basins, in-sample); PUB LSTM 531 under k=12 holdout
claims.effectSize: statics vs no-statics: median NSE 0.74 vs 0.63 (+0.11), p<1e-9; in-sample-to-PUB penalty only 0.74->0.69 (-0.05)

claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2019) report a heavy left tail for the ungauged LSTM that the median conceals: PUB LSTM mean NSE 0.54 versus median 0.69, with minimum NSE -13.02 (Table 2, 531 catchments). The authors state 'SAC-SMA tended to out-perform the PUB LSTM in catchments with low NSE values' — i.e. the locally-calibrated conceptual model was MORE robust exactly where the transferred deep model failed. They also report a negative result on static attributes: adding catchment attributes HURT the model in some catchments, and 'there is generally no correlation between the values of individual catchment attributes and whether the Global LSTM with vs. without statics performs better' (their Figure 5), so they could not diagnose which attribute or which catchment type causes the degradation; their tentative explanation is error/uncertainty in the attribute data itself. Comparable spread for other models: SAC-SMA median 0.64 / mean 0.51 / min -12.28; Global LSTM without statics median 0.63 / mean 0.45 / min -31.72; NWM median 0.58 / mean 0.31 / min -20.28.
claims.effectSize: PUB LSTM mean 0.54 vs median 0.69, min -13.02; SAC-SMA wins in the low-NSE tail (SAC-SMA better in 224/531 = 42% of catchments)

claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2019) found that a large fraction of ungauged-LSTM failure is RANDOM SEED, not model structure, and that single-model results are therefore untrustworthy: across the 10-member PUB LSTM ensemble, 103 of 531 basins had at least one ensemble member with NSE below zero, yet only 9 of those 103 had all 10 members below zero, and 55 of the 103 had at least one member with NSE > 0.5. In one named basin (USGS 01142500), 9 of 10 members scored NSE < 0 while one member scored NSE > 0.7. All reported LSTM metrics are computed from the mean of the 10-member ensemble (chosen to match the 10 SCE random restarts used to calibrate SAC-SMA). Practical implication for any small-n deep-learning attempt: a single training run's held-out score can be off by more than the entire claimed advantage over the benchmark, so seed-ensembling is mandatory and a one-seed LSTM-vs-XGBoost comparison would be uninterpretable.
claims.effectSize: 103/531 basins have >=1 of 10 seeds with NSE<0; only 9/531 have all 10 seeds NSE<0; 55/103 have >=1 seed NSE>0.5

claims.text: The Kratzert 2019 PUB result rests on a training set roughly four orders of magnitude larger in INDEPENDENT SPATIAL UNITS than a 19-basin-family problem: ~487 training basins per fold x ~15 years of daily data (approximately 2.7 million basin-days per fold, ~5.8 million basin-days across the full 30-year record). The paper offers no experiment at reduced basin count. The follow-up literature that does test this reports the scaling is still climbing at CAMELS scale: Gauch, Klotz, Nearing, Kratzert et al., 'HESS Opinions: Never train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network on a single basin' (HESS 28:4187, 2024, doi 10.5194/hess-28-4187-2024) trains LSTMs on random groups of approximately 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, and 50 basins plus the full 531 and reports median NSE rising monotonically with training-set size, 'continuing up to the maximum size of the CAMELS data set (531 basins)' with no plateau — exact per-group NSE values are shown only in their Figure 6, not tabulated in text. Their companion conclusion is that for LSTMs, regional models beat single-basin models while for conceptual/process models the reverse holds. At 19 independent basin families this places any LSTM/EA-LSTM proposal at the extreme low end of a curve that had not yet flattened at 531 basins; neither paper compares LSTM against XGBoost, random forest, or any gradient-boosted baseline at ANY basin count, so there is no published evidence in this line of work that a deep sequence model beats a booster in the small-n regime.
claims.nBasins: Kratzert 2019: ~487 train / ~44 test per fold of 531. Gauch et al. 2024 ablation: ~2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 531 basins
claims.effectSize: median NSE increases monotonically with training basin count through 531 with no observed plateau; exact values figure-only

result.sourceQuality: HIGH for the primary source, with one access caveat. The requested Wiley URL (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2019WR026065) returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch. I recovered the COMPLETE author preprint PDF from eartharXiv (https://eartharxiv.org/repository/object/713/download/1565/) and read all 11 pages directly, including Table 2 (full benchmark statistics: median/mean/min/max NSE, fractional bias, standard deviation ratio, 95th-percentile difference for all five models), Table 1 (complete input list), the k-fold description, and the full Discussion. All quoted figures are from that primary text, not from an abstract mirror or summary. The neuralhydrology.github.io author blog post independently corroborates 0.69 / 0.64 / 0.58 and the 531-basin count. Two important scope limits on this source for the current project: (1) the target is STREAMFLOW only — the paper contains nothing on nitrate, nutrients, or any concentration variable, so its transfer results do not directly license a water-quality claim; (2) the paper contains NO gradient-boosted-tree, random-forest, or other ML comparator — every benchmark is a process/conceptual hydrologic model (SAC-SMA, NWM), so it cannot answer 'does LSTM beat XGBoost' at any n. The basin-count-scaling claim (claim 6) is SECONDARY: Gauch et al. 2024 HESS Opinions was fetched and summarized but its per-group NSE values exist only in a figure and could not be read numerically, so that effect size is directional (monotonic increase, no plateau) rather than exact — flagged as such in the claim text. My targeted search for LSTM-vs-RF/XGBoost on nitrate CONCENTRATION under spatial holdout returned no study meeting the bar (results were groundwater nitrate spatial-interpolation studies, single-basin time-series studies, or watershed-health-index regressions with unclear/random splits); that gap should be treated as 'not found', not as 'no such study exists'.

claims.text: The evaluated product is NWM **version 2.1 retrospective**, an hourly simulation covering **February 1979 – December 2020 (42 years)** for **2.7 million NHDPlusV2 river reaches** across CONUS, forced by NLDAS, with **no streamflow data assimilation in the retrospective** (nudging DA is used only in forecast cycles). Outputs are available in NetCDF and, notably, in **Zarr on AWS**, and the authors state they "downloaded [data] based on the NWM forecast point reference number" (feature_id / NHDPlusV2 COMID) and processed locally. This confirms the exact access mechanism our project would use: cloud Zarr on S3, joined per-reach by COMID, which we already store per basin. CAVEAT: this is v2.1, NOT v3.0; the retrospective ends 2020 while our nitrate record runs to 2026, so NWM v2.1 alone cannot cover 2021-2026 (v3.0 extends to ~2023 and would need separate verification).
claims.nBasins: 2.7 million modeled reaches; 3260 USGS gauges used for evaluation
claims.effectSize: 1979-02 to 2020-12, hourly, NetCDF + Zarr on AWS, joined by NWM feature_id/COMID

claims.text: Across **3260 USGS gauges (548 natural-flow, 2712 regulated-flow)**, only **57% of natural-flow points had KGE > 0.5** and only **43% of regulated-flow points had KGE > 0.5** for hourly NWM v2.1 retrospective streamflow. On percent bias, **only 50% of natural-flow points and 36% of regulated-flow points fell within ±10% PBIAS**. The authors conclude "bias correction is crucial for utilizing the NWM retrospective streamflow dataset." DIRECT IMPLICATION FOR OUR PROJECT: at a randomly chosen ungauged Iowa pin there is roughly a coin-flip chance that NWM Q is off by more than 10% in the mean, and roughly a 43-57% chance KGE ≤ 0.5. Since our proposed use is a BETWEEN-SITE dilution/specific-discharge denominator, a per-site multiplicative bias of this magnitude propagates directly into the between-site concentration term — the exact term where our headroom lies. Bias correction is not available at an ungauged pin (it requires local observed Q), so we would have to accept the raw biased Q.
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable — physically-based model evaluated against gauges; the paper does NOT state whether evaluation gauges were excluded from NWM v2.1 calibration, so it is unknown whether these are held-out sites (if not, the numbers are optimistic for a truly ungauged pin)
claims.effectSize: KGE>0.5 at 57% (natural) / 43% (regulated) of gauges; |PBIAS|<10% at 50% / 36%

claims.text: Iowa is split between two River Forecast Centers, and the paper gives per-RFC median percent bias by basin size. For **North Central RFC (NCRFC, humid, 55 natural-flow + 362 regulated-flow gauges, median NF drainage area 916.8 km2)**, natural-flow median PBIAS was **−10.15% (Q1 −20.21, Q3 +2.19) for sub-watersheds (10,000–50,000 ha = 100–500 km2)** and **−3.08% (Q1 −9.09, Q3 +6.62) for watersheds (>50,000 ha)** — i.e., systematic UNDER-estimation of flow, worst at the smaller basin sizes that dominate our 85 sites. For **Missouri Basin RFC (MBRFC, semi-arid, covers western Iowa, 58 NF + 269 RF gauges)**, natural-flow median PBIAS was **+4.46% (milli-watersheds), +5.93% (sub-watersheds), +11.02% (watersheds)** — systematic OVER-estimation. This is a falsifiable, directly usable prediction: NWM Q in Iowa should be biased low in the Mississippi-draining east and biased high in the Missouri-draining west, with a swing of order 15-20 percentage points across the state. That is a spatially structured error that would inject a spurious east-west gradient into any C = Load/Q or dilution feature — and our model's top features already include lon and lat, so a west-east artifact is the worst possible failure mode here.
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (gauge-based model evaluation; held-out status vs NWM calibration unknown)
claims.effectSize: NCRFC natural-flow median PBIAS −10.15% (sub-watershed) / −3.08% (watershed); MBRFC natural-flow median PBIAS +4.46% / +5.93% / +11.02% by increasing basin size

claims.text: Regulated-flow performance in NCRFC is far worse than natural-flow at small basin sizes: median PBIAS **+47.14% (Q1 +15.08, Q3 +78.24) for milli-watersheds (1,000–10,000 ha = 10–100 km2)**, versus **+0.99% for sub-watersheds** and **+2.21% for watersheds**. The authors attribute regulated-flow failure to "natural and anthropogenic alterations in the drainage basin environment that may not be accurately captured by the model due to **static inputs such as land use/cover and catchment topography**." RELEVANCE: many Iowa stream reaches are hydrologically altered (channelization, tile drainage, impoundments) and would be classified as regulated or at least non-natural; small headwater basins are exactly where an arbitrary map pin is most likely to land. A ~47% median flow bias at 10–100 km2 basins would make a modeled-Q dilution denominator worse than useless at the small end of the deployment range.
claims.effectSize: NCRFC regulated median PBIAS +47.14% at 10–100 km2 basins vs +0.99% at 100–500 km2

claims.text: NEGATIVE-RESULT / SCOPE GAP: the paper's 25 pages of error attribution discuss forcing-data bias, model structure, parameters, snowpack, aridity, regulation, and static land-cover inputs — but contain **NO assessment whatsoever of artificial subsurface (tile) drainage**, and no evaluation stratified by drainage-class, soil, or low-relief agricultural terrain. The paper's only relevant structural statement is that regulated-flow error arises because "static inputs such as land use/cover and catchment topography" do not capture basin alterations. Therefore the specific bias we most need to know about — NWM v2.1 skill in tile-drained, low-relief Iowa catchments where subsurface drainage rather than surface runoff dominates the hydrograph — **is not answered by this source and must be sourced elsewhere** (candidates: the HESS benchmarking paper Johnson et al. 2023, hess.copernicus.org/articles/27/1809/2023, and the USGS ScienceBase NWM v2.1 daily benchmark dataset at sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/62336af9d34ec9f19eeb48fd, which publishes per-gauge NSE/KGE and would let us compute the Iowa-specific distribution ourselves at our 22 gauged sites). Do NOT treat this paper's CONUS-level 'humid regions perform best' finding as evidence that NWM works in tile-drained Iowa; NWM's WRF-Hydro/Noah-MP core has no tile-drainage parameterization at all.
claims.effectSize: absent — no tile-drainage, soil-drainage-class, or relief-stratified evaluation reported

claims.text: Seasonality of NWM bias is large and misaligned with the Iowa nitrate season. In **humid regions** (which includes NCRFC/eastern Iowa) NWM natural-flow median PBIAS is closest to zero in **winter** — described as "the model's best performance" — while "the model tends to **underestimate streamflow during the spring season**, which could be attributed to the model's limitations in snowmelt-dominated regions." In arid regions the median PBIAS ran **+7.85% (fall), +18.80% (winter), +19.54% (spring), +11.89% (summer)**. CRITICAL FOR US: Iowa nitrate violations concentrate in the **spring–early summer flush (roughly April–June)**, precisely the season the paper flags as NWM's weakest in humid/snow-influenced regions. A dilution feature C ∝ Load/Q built on NWM Q would therefore be least trustworthy exactly during the event window our classifier is supposed to call. This yields a concrete, cheap falsification test we can run before investing: at our **22 gauged sites (0.66–0.97 density, up to 18 years)**, pull NWM v2.1 retrospective Q by COMID and compute per-site KGE and monthly PBIAS against observed Q; if spring PBIAS is large and site-varying, modeled Q cannot supply between-site skill and the whole C-Q avenue should be abandoned or restricted to the 22 gauged sites only.
claims.nBasins: 548 natural-flow gauges stratified by climate class and season
claims.effectSize: humid: best in winter, systematic spring underestimation; arid median PBIAS +7.85/+18.80/+19.54/+11.89% for fall/winter/spring/summer

result.sourceQuality: Full text obtained and read directly (MDPI blocked WebFetch with HTTP 403; the PDF was retrieved from mdpi-res.com and text-extracted locally with pdftotext, so all figures below are quoted from the primary source, not an abstract mirror). Peer-reviewed, open access CC BY, Water 2023, 15(13):2319, doi:10.3390/w15132319, Abdelkader, Temimi & Ouarda (Stevens Institute of Technology / INRS-ETE). HIGH quality for what it covers: n=3260 gauges, per-RFC and per-basin-size tables of percent bias, explicit natural vs regulated stratification. IMPORTANT LIMITATIONS FOR OUR QUESTION: (1) it evaluates NWM v2.1, not v3.0, and only through Dec 2020 — our nitrate record extends to 2026; (2) all skill is measured AT GAUGES, so it says nothing directly about accuracy at an ungauged map pin, which is our deployment target — and the paper never states whether its evaluation gauges were excluded from NWM's own calibration, so the reported skill may be optimistic relative to a truly ungauged reach; (3) headline metrics are reported as PERCENTAGES OF GAUGES EXCEEDING THRESHOLDS (e.g. '57% have KGE>0.5') rather than median KGE values, so no single summary KGE can be quoted; (4) the paper contains ZERO content on concentration-discharge behavior, nitrate, water quality, load, or tile drainage — it is purely a streamflow-error assessment. The C-Q literature portion of the research question (Godsey/Kirchner power laws, Basu chemostasis, Van Meter & Basu legacy N, Damkohler framing) is NOT addressed by this source at all and must come from other sources.

claims.text: Kratzert et al. (2019, HESS 23:5089) did NOT perform any ungauged-basin / spatially held-out experiment. Training and evaluation used the SAME 531 CAMELS basins, separated only in time (calibration/training 1 Oct 1999 - 30 Sep 2008; evaluation 1 Oct 1989 - 30 Sep 1999). The paper explicitly states 'we never ask our model to predict in a basin where it did not see training data.' Therefore NONE of this paper's headline NSE numbers are comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC, and this paper is NOT evidence that EA-LSTM transfers to an unseen basin.
claims.nBasins: 531 basins trained; 447 basins used for the benchmark comparison (CAMELS, CONUS)
claims.effectSize: not applicable - protocol claim

claims.text: Under that temporal-holdout protocol, an 8-member EA-LSTM ensemble reached median NSE ~0.74 (single EA-LSTM models: mean NSE 0.67 +/- 0.006, median ~0.71), exceeding process-based models calibrated INDIVIDUALLY per basin (mHM basin-calibrated median NSE ~0.68; HBV upper-bound, 100 calibration trials, median ~0.68). Caveat: exact Table 3 figures were extracted via an HTML render, not the PDF (PDF fetch returned unparseable binary), so individual model rows should be verified against the published Table 3 before citation.
claims.effectSize: EA-LSTM ensemble median NSE ~0.74 vs ~0.68 for the best basin-calibrated conceptual models (delta ~ +0.06 NSE)

claims.text: The paper contains NO comparison to random forests, gradient-boosted trees, or any tree ensemble. Every baseline is either a process-based hydrologic model (SAC-SMA+Snow-17, VIC, mHM, HBV, FUSE) or another LSTM variant. This paper therefore provides ZERO evidence that LSTM/EA-LSTM outperforms XGBoost, and it cannot be cited to justify replacing a gradient-boosted model.
claims.effectSize: zero tree-ensemble baselines present

claims.text: The paper contains NO ablation on the number of training basins. Performance is reported only for the single configuration trained on all 531 basins simultaneously; there is no curve or table of accuracy versus training-basin count. Consequently this paper gives NO evidence that EA-LSTM's regional-embedding advantage survives at n=19 independent basin families, and its entire evidence base is 28x larger than our effective sample.
claims.effectSize: no scaling analysis exists

claims.text: Process-based models calibrated REGIONALLY (i.e. one parameter set transferred across basins, the closest analogue to our between-site problem) collapse relative to per-basin calibration: VIC regional mean NSE 0.17 / median 0.31 versus basin-calibrated performance in the ~0.6-0.68 range; mHM regional mean 0.44 / median 0.53. This independently corroborates that the between-site / absolute-level term is the hard part of the problem, and that it is hard for physically-based models too, not just for our booster.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (regional vs basin-specific calibration, all basins seen in training)
claims.effectSize: VIC median NSE 0.31 (regional) vs ~0.68 (basin-calibrated): loss of ~0.37 NSE. mHM 0.53 vs ~0.68.

claims.text: The EA-LSTM's mechanism is a static-attribute embedding: 27 CAMELS catchment attributes (climate indices, vegetation indices, soil and topographic properties, chosen as the subset derivable from remote sensing or CONUS-wide products) are mapped through a learned input gate into an R^256 embedding, and k-means clustering of that embedding reproduces hydrologically coherent basin groups. The highest-ranked attributes were mean elevation, catchment area, mean precipitation, aridity (PET/P), duration of high-precipitation events, fraction of precipitation as snow, and forest fraction; soil properties ranked lower. This is a direct argument that BETWEEN-SITE static geography carries the transferable signal - consistent with our own finding that only geometry/static-geography features have produced wins - but it is a learned 256-d embedding fit on 531 basins and is very unlikely to be identifiable from 19 families.
claims.effectSize: 27 static attributes -> R^256 embedding

claims.text: The ACTUAL spatially-held-out evidence is in the companion paper, Kratzert, Klotz, Herrnegger, Sampson, Hochreiter & Nearing (2019), 'Toward Improved Predictions in Ungauged Basins: Exploiting the Power of Machine Learning', Water Resources Research 55(12):11344-11354, DOI 10.1029/2019WR026065. Using k-fold (k=12) SPATIAL cross-validation over 531 CAMELS basins so that predictions are made in basins supplying no training data, the out-of-sample LSTM achieved median NSE 0.69, versus 0.64 for SAC-SMA calibrated AT the target gauge and 0.58 for the National Water Model. Note the training set per fold is still ~487 basins; the folds are random basin splits, NOT leave-one-region-out, so spatial-proximity leakage across folds is not excluded. This paper (not the HESS one) is the correct citation for PUB claims, and it also contains no tree-ensemble baseline and no training-basin-count ablation.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (k=12-fold basin-wise cross-validation; random basin folds, not region-wise)
claims.nBasins: 531 CAMELS basins; ~487 training basins per fold
claims.effectSize: out-of-sample LSTM median NSE 0.69 vs locally-calibrated SAC-SMA 0.64 vs National Water Model 0.58

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed, open-access (Copernicus HESS), highly cited (~680+ citations). Full HTML text was fetched successfully; the 6.2 MB PDF fetch returned unparseable binary, so the Table 3 per-model NSE rows (SAC-SMA, VIC, FUSE variants specifically) come from an HTML-render extraction and carry moderate transcription risk - the EA-LSTM headline numbers (mean 0.67, ensemble median 0.74) and the protocol/date-range quotes are high confidence. The companion WRR PUB numbers (median NSE 0.69 / 0.64 / 0.58, k=12, 531 basins) come from search-result abstract text plus the authors' own project page, not from a full-text fetch of the WRR article; they are consistently reported across sources but should be verified in the article before publication. Two critical negatives are high confidence and directly relevant: this paper has NO ungauged-basin experiment, NO tree-ensemble baseline, and NO training-basin-count ablation.

claims.text: Gorski et al. (2024, WRR, doi:10.1029/2023WR036591) modeled the backward-looking 7-day-average nitrate CONCENTRATION at 46 predominantly agricultural stream sites in the midwestern and eastern US using LSTMs whose DAILY INPUTS INCLUDE OBSERVED DISCHARGE plus meteorological time series, alongside static watershed attributes (anthropogenic hydrologic modification, N application, climate, groundwater, land use/land cover, watershed physical attributes, soils). Because observed daily Q is a required dynamic input and every one of the four modeling schemes trained on data FROM the sites being predicted, this design is NOT a prediction-in-ungauged-basins design and is not directly transferable to an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no gauge and no nitrate history; adopting its architecture would require substituting a MODELED Q (e.g. NWM retrospective) whose error at that site is unquantified by this paper. FALSIFIABLE: the paper contains no experiment in which a site is entirely withheld from training.

claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (no spatial holdout; all sites appear in training in all four schemes). Exact temporal train/val/test years could not be retrieved.

claims.text: With observed discharge available as an input, per-site LSTMs reached a MEDIAN Kling-Gupta Efficiency of 0.66 across the 46 sites. This is the performance ceiling reported for the gauged, intensively-monitored case; it is a WITHIN-SITE temporal metric and is NOT comparable to a between-site/spatial-holdout metric such as our LOFO AUC 0.820 or between_r2 0.21. Anyone citing '0.66 KGE' as evidence that nitrate is predictable at ungauged pins is misreading the protocol.
claims.effectSize: median KGE = 0.66 (single-site models, 46 separate models)
claims.splitProtocol: unknown (temporal holdout at gauged sites presumed; exact split not retrievable — Wiley full text returned HTTP 403)

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO OUR n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT: pooling all 46 sites into one 'global' LSTM did NOT beat site-specific or grouped models — median KGE 0.63 (global) vs 0.66 (single-site) vs 0.66 (5 clustered models grouped by basin attributes) vs 0.65 with RMSE 1.03 mg/L (8 models grouped by glacial hydrogeologic terrane). The authors conclude there is 'a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model,' explicitly contrasting water-quality modeling with the streamflow-LSTM literature where global training wins. IMPLICATION: the CAMELS-style 'more basins always help' result does not carry over to nitrate, which both weakens the argument that our n=19 families is fatal AND weakens the argument that acquiring more sites would fix the between-site deficit.
claims.effectSize: global 0.63 vs single-site 0.66 vs clustered 0.66 vs hydro-terrane 0.65 (median KGE); hydro-terrane RMSE 1.03 mg/L
claims.nBasins: 46 (grouped into 5 attribute clusters and 8 glacial hydro terranes)
claims.splitProtocol: unknown (no spatial holdout in any scheme)

claims.text: The paper's headline finding is that DISCHARGE together with WATERSHED SOIL AND PHYSIOGRAPHIC (physical) attributes exert 'a particularly strong influence on model performance' across all 46 sites — ranked above nitrogen-application, land-use/land-cover, and climate attributes. This is a direct challenge to our current feature set, in which (a) discharge is absent, (b) soil attributes are absent entirely, and (c) N-surplus and CDL crop fractions carry the static-geography load. FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION FOR OUR PROJECT: adding basin-aggregated soil/physiographic attributes (e.g. gSSURGO/POLARIS hydraulic conductivity, drainage class, depth to water table, slope, relief) should move our between-site term more than any further temporal feature engineering — consistent with our own pattern that only geometry and static geography have produced wins.
claims.effectSize: qualitative ranking from permutation feature importance + expected gradients; exact importance magnitudes not retrievable

claims.text: Drivers of short-term nitrate variation were found to vary REGIONALLY in a way tied to 'controlling processes such as groundwater contributions,' and site grouping by GLACIAL HYDROGEOLOGIC TERRANE (8 groups) performed on par with attribute-based clustering (median KGE 0.65 vs 0.66). This supports a concrete, low-cost test for our project: replace or augment the raw lat/lon features (currently #2 and #3 by permutation importance, i.e. the model is already using coordinates as a proxy for an unmeasured regional variable) with an explicit categorical/continuous hydrogeologic-terrane or glacial-landform encoding for each basin. If terrane encoding beats lat/lon, the between-site deficit is a missing-geology problem; if it does not, lat/lon is capturing something else.
claims.effectSize: hydro-terrane grouping: median KGE 0.65, RMSE 1.03 mg/L, 8 models; attribute clustering: median KGE 0.66, 5 models

claims.text: SOURCE-ACCESS AND REPRODUCIBILITY CLAIM: the Wiley full text (agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2023WR036591) returns HTTP 403 to automated fetching despite being flagged HYBRID open access under a CC BY license in OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar; ScienceBase also 403s. However, the complete data AND model code are released by USGS at doi:10.5066/P1N6P2QL (ScienceBase item 661436d1d34e633466530330, also on catalog.data.gov), free, public-domain, no authentication. This release is the authoritative route to the exact train/validation/test split, the attribute list, and the per-site metrics that could not be extracted here — and it supplies a ready-made list of static watershed attributes (soils, physiography, hydrologic modification incl. tile/artificial drainage proxies) already assembled for 46 US agricultural basins, several of which are in Iowa.
claims.effectSize: n/a — data/code release, doi:10.5066/P1N6P2QL

result.sourceQuality: MIXED / DEGRADED. The target paper is peer-reviewed (Water Resources Research, AGU, 2024; USGS-authored; CC BY hybrid OA) and is a high-quality, directly on-topic source. HOWEVER the full text could NOT be retrieved: Wiley returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch on both the /doi/full and /doi/pdfdirect routes, ScienceBase returned 403, and a text-proxy attempt hit a CAPTCHA. All claims above are therefore built from (a) the abstract as mirrored by USGS publications and Semantic Scholar, and (b) verbatim sentence fragments returned in search-engine snippets of the full text. Quantities I am confident in because they appeared as direct quotations: 46 sites; median KGE 0.66 (single-site), 0.66 (5 clustered), 0.65 with RMSE 1.03 mg/L (8 hydro-terrane), 0.63 (global); target = backward-looking 7-day-average nitrate concentration; inputs = daily discharge + meteorology + static attributes; interpretability via permutation feature importance and expected gradients; "threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model." NOT VERIFIED and marked unknown throughout: the exact train/validation/test temporal split, sequence length, and any per-attribute importance magnitudes. IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON THE RESEARCH ANGLE: this paper does NOT appear to address concentration-discharge (C-Q) slope regimes, chemostatic vs dilution behavior, Damkohler framing, NWM retrospective bias in tile-drained basins, SPARROW, or load-vs-concentration target choice — none of those seeds surfaced in any retrieved text. It is evidence that DISCHARGE + SOILS + PHYSIOGRAPHY dominate nitrate skill at GAUGED sites, and evidence against naive global pooling for water quality; it is NOT evidence that modeled discharge converts into between-site skill at ungauged pins. That specific question remains open and should be routed to the NWM-evaluation and C-Q literature separately.

claims.text: LSTM streamflow skill increases MONOTONICALLY with the number of training basins across groupings of [2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, ..., 531] basins, with NO observed plateau: 'The blue line in Fig. 6 shows performance (median NSE) increasing as the size of the training data set increases. This effect continues up to the maximum size of the CAMELS data set (531 basins). In other words, it is better to have more basins in the training set, and even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough to train optimal LSTM models for streamflow.' FALSIFIABLE AND DIRECTLY ADVERSE TO OUR PROJECT: our 19 independent basin families sit at the far-left, worst-performing end of this curve. The paper identifies no minimum viable n but explicitly demands 'at least hundreds of basins.' If the curve has not asymptoted by 531, an LSTM trained on 19 families is deep in the regime the authors characterize as an 'improperly trained model.' NOTE: this is a STREAMFLOW result, not water quality, and the curve is measured under temporal holdout, not spatial holdout.
claims.nBasins: 531 (CAMELS-US), partitioned into k-fold groups of size ~2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 107, ..., up to 531; 10-member ensemble at each grouping size
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (train 1999-2008; test 1989-1999; 'All models were tested on the same basins where they were trained (during different time periods)') - explicitly NOT spatial holdout
claims.effectSize: Direction and monotonicity stated in text and shown in Fig. 6; the paper reports NO numeric median NSE values anywhere in text or captions - only CDF/curve graphics. Effect magnitude is therefore NOT extractable from the HTML.

claims.text: THIS PAPER CONTAINS NO UNGAUGED-BASIN / PUB / SPATIAL-HOLDOUT EXPERIMENT. Every reported result trains and tests on the same basins in different time windows. The paper cites Kratzert et al. (2019) ungauged-basin work but quotes NO numbers from it (no LSTM-vs-calibrated-SAC-SMA NSE comparison is reproduced). Consequently, this source provides ZERO evidence bearing on our deployment target (arbitrary ungauged map pin) and none of its numbers may be compared to our LOFO AUC 0.820. Anyone citing this paper as evidence that LSTMs transfer to unseen basins is misreading it.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout throughout; no spatial holdout exists in the paper
claims.effectSize: not-applicable

claims.text: Training on a HYDROLOGICALLY HOMOGENEOUS subset is worse than training on a heterogeneous full sample: 'models trained on any subset of the 531 CAMELS basins performed worse, on average, than models trained on all 531 CAMELS basins.' This was tested two ways - (a) grouping by USGS Hydrologic Unit Code, 18 HUCs with 2-79 basins each, and (b) k-means clustering on 25 basin attributes, 6 clusters with 59-195 basins each. Both underperformed the all-531 model. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR US: restricting a model to Iowa-like basins, or clustering our 19 families into hydrologic sub-groups before fitting, is predicted to HURT, not help. It also implies the fix for our between-site deficit is to ENLARGE the basin sample (e.g. by pulling in out-of-state nitrate monitoring sites), not to specialize the model to Iowa.
claims.nBasins: 531 total; HUC groups 2-79 basins; attribute clusters 59-195 basins
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (tested on same basins as trained, different period)
claims.effectSize: Direction stated ('performed worse, on average'); no numeric median NSE deltas given in text or Fig. 6 caption

claims.text: Regional (multi-basin) training reverses the sign of the single-basin-vs-regional comparison relative to process-based models. For conceptual/process models (VIC and mHM, 489 CAMELS basins), single-basin calibration BEATS regional calibration; for LSTMs (531 basins) the opposite holds - 'In Fig. 3a, single-basin models perform better than regional models, and in Fig. 3b, this is reversed.' The paper states that process models performing worse under regional calibration 'is, to our knowledge, a consistent finding.' FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: the 'pool all sites into one model' strategy we already use is the correct one for a learned model, and per-site models are the wrong direction - but this says nothing about whether a per-site EMBEDDING or random effect helps, which the paper does not test.
claims.effectSize: Sign reversal reported via cumulative density functions (Fig. 3a vs 3b); no numeric NSE values stated

claims.text: Single-basin-trained LSTMs catastrophically fail at extrapolating beyond the range seen in their own training record: across 531 single-basin models, 'there are more than 6346 flow values above the theoretical maximums of their respective single-basin models,' versus only 10 such values for the single regional model trained on all 531 basins. This is a ~635x reduction in out-of-range failures from pooling. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR OUR CLASSIFIER: a model with few effective training units cannot predict magnitudes it has never observed - which is precisely our between-site failure mode (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). It supports the diagnosis that our absolute-level deficit is a SAMPLE-COVERAGE problem (19 families spanning too narrow a range of basin types), not an architecture problem.
claims.effectSize: >6346 out-of-range flow values (531 single-basin models) vs 10 (one 531-basin regional model)

claims.text: The authors report a systematic NEGATIVE result on hybrid/physics-informed deep models: 'so far, to our knowledge, all attempts to add physics to (properly trained) streamflow LSTM models in hydrology have produced lower-performing models.' They further argue that apparent gains from architectural or physics-based adaptations in the literature are artifacts of weak baselines - 'it is trivial (but most likely uninteresting) to beat improperly trained models' - noting that of the top 50 hydrology-ML papers per year for 2021-2023 (150 papers surveyed), 122 trained on individual catchments and only 28 on multiple catchments. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: published claims that hybrid/differentiable hydrologic models beat baselines should be checked for whether the baseline was single-basin-trained; and our project should NOT expect a physics-informed deep architecture to recover the between-site term. CAVEAT: this is an opinion-paper assertion supported by citation, not by a new controlled experiment in this paper, and it concerns streamflow only.
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (literature survey of 150 papers; 122 single-catchment, 28 multi-catchment, 4 of the 28 co-authored by these authors)
claims.effectSize: Qualitative claim ('all attempts...have produced lower-performing models'); survey counts 122/150 vs 28/150

result.sourceQuality:
HIGH for what it covers, but NARROW and only PARTIALLY RELEVANT to our research question. Peer-reviewed, open-access HESS opinion paper (DOI 10.5194/hess-28-4187-2024), fully readable HTML, no paywall, all sections and appendices accessible. Authors (Kratzert, Gauch, Klotz, Nearing - Google Research) are the primary originators of the CAMELS LSTM literature, so this is an authoritative primary source on LSTM training practice.

FOUR MAJOR LIMITATIONS FOR OUR PURPOSES, all confirmed by direct reading:
(1) SPLIT PROTOCOL: every experiment is TEMPORAL holdout on in-sample basins. There is no PUB, no leave-one-basin-out, no leave-one-region-out result in this paper. None of its numbers are comparable to our LOFO 0.820. It cites the Kratzert et al. 2019 ungauged-basin papers but reproduces no numbers from them - those must be fetched separately to answer the actual research question.
(2) NO GBDT COMPARISON: the paper never benchmarks against random forest, XGBoost, or any tree ensemble. Its only non-LSTM comparators are process-based models (VIC, mHM). It therefore provides NO evidence on 'do LSTMs beat gradient-boosted trees.'
(3) NO WATER QUALITY: explicitly rainfall-runoff / streamflow only. Zero mention of nitrate, nutrients, or constituent concentration. Any transfer of its conclusions to a nitrate-violation classifier is an extrapolation we are making, not a claim the paper supports.
(4) NO NUMERIC METRICS PUBLISHED IN TEXT: the paper reports results exclusively through CDF plots and curves (Figs. 3, 4, 6, 7). Median NSE values are not stated numerically anywhere in the main text or figure captions. Effect SIZES are therefore not extractable without digitizing figures or pulling the linked Zenodo/code repository. Directions and sign are reliable; magnitudes are not.

ALSO ABSENT (checked explicitly, all negative): no entity-aware LSTM discussion, no analysis of static catchment attributes as network INPUTS (attributes are used only for k-means clustering in Sec. 5), no multi-task/shared-embedding architecture, no site-embedding or random-effects treatment, and no recommendation about layering per-site effects on a non-neural model. The 'cheaper middle ground' part of our research brief is NOT addressed by this source.

NET VALUE TO THE PROJECT: this source is best used as strong, authoritative evidence on ONE axis - that deep sequence models need hundreds of basins and degrade monotonically as basin count falls, with no plateau even at 531. Against our n=19-independent-families constraint that is a direct argument for NOT pursuing an LSTM, and a direct argument that the productive move is enlarging the basin sample (out-of-state monitoring sites) rather than changing model class. It should NOT be cited for ungauged-basin performance, for LSTM-vs-XGBoost, or for water quality.

claims.text: Pandit et al. (2025) trained an LSTM on daily nitrate CONCENTRATION at 148 sites across the conterminous US (grab samples + high-frequency sensors, 1980-2022), and report a large collapse from temporal to spatial validation: median KGE = 0.60 under temporal (hold-out-time-at-known-sites) validation versus median KGE = 0.18 under spatial validation for unmonitored basins. This is a ~70% loss of skill purely from moving to ungauged sites, and it is the single most decisive number for our question: a continental-scale deep model with 148 training basins still performs near-worthless (KGE 0.18; KGE=0 is roughly the skill of predicting the mean) at ungauged locations for nitrate concentration.
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 temporal vs 0.18 spatial (ungauged); ~0.42 KGE degradation
claims.splitProtocol: BOTH reported separately and explicitly distinguished by the authors: temporal-holdout (KGE 0.60) and spatial-holdout / ungauged-basin (KGE 0.18). The exact spatial fold construction (k-fold leave-basins-out vs leave-region-out, and whether nested/overlapping basins were grouped as our LOFO does) could NOT be determined from accessible metadata — treat the spatial number as 'spatial-holdout, fold construction unknown'.

claims.text: Restricting the spatially-validated LSTM to the Mississippi River Basin raised median spatial-holdout KGE only from 0.18 to 0.34 — i.e. even after narrowing to the hydroclimatic region where training data are densest and most relevant (the ag Midwest), ungauged nitrate concentration prediction remained weak. The authors frame spatial validation as a tool for 'quantifying the impact of current data gaps' and use it to RESTRICT where the model is allowed to be applied, rather than claiming ungauged deployment works. This is a direct precedent for scoping/gating our own deployment map rather than serving predictions at any arbitrary Iowa pin.
claims.effectSize: median KGE 0.18 (CONUS) -> 0.34 (MRB subset); still far below the 0.60 temporal benchmark
claims.nBasins: 148 trained; MRB-applicable subset count not determinable from accessible sources
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (ungauged-basin), evaluated on the MRB subset

claims.text: NEGATIVE / ABSENCE RESULT for the research angle: no head-to-head comparison of the LSTM against random forest, XGBoost, or any gradient-boosted tree could be found in this paper's abstract, the EPA Science Inventory record for the companion CONUS model, or indexed snippets. The EPA record markets it as 'the first continental-scale LSTM model of nitrate' and, per that record, 'does not reference benchmark comparisons against other machine learning or traditional hydrologic models.' Therefore this paper provides NO evidence that LSTM beats GBDT for ungauged water-quality prediction. It should not be cited to justify replacing our XGBoost with an LSTM. (Caveat: full text was paywalled; a supplementary benchmark table cannot be ruled out.)
claims.effectSize: no LSTM-vs-GBDT effect size reported

claims.text: Shapley-value interpretation of the CONUS nitrate LSTM identified TILE DRAINAGE, ROADWAY DENSITY, and WETLAND COVER as the dominant SPATIAL (static, between-site) drivers of mean nitrate concentration, and reported threshold behavior — points beyond which these features exert considerable influence on river chemistry. Catchment attributes were drawn from CAMELS and GAGES-II. This independently corroborates our project's diagnosis that the residual deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE STATIC information: the top three drivers of the site-level mean are all static landscape attributes, and all three (tile drainage, road density, wetland cover) are ABSENT from our current 68-feature set. Falsifiable prediction for us: adding basin-mean tile-drainage fraction, wetland fraction, and road density should improve between_r2 / between_rate_r2 specifically, not within_r2.
claims.effectSize: qualitative ranking (top spatial drivers) plus unreported threshold values; no per-feature effect size recoverable from accessible sources
claims.splitProtocol: unknown (interpretation run on the fitted model; not a performance number)

claims.text: OPERATIONAL DATASET, directly closing our known tile-drainage gap: AgTile-US is a 30-m binary raster of modeled tile-drained cropland covering the ENTIRE conterminous US (so it covers all of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of our largest multi-state basins, which is exactly where our current inner-join under-counting is worst). Built from the USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture county tile-drainage statistics, NLCD 2016 cropland, SSURGO soil drainage class, and SRTM slope. Validated against 16,000 ground-truth points at 86.03% CONUS accuracy, and 82.7-93.6% accuracy over the heavily tile-drained Midwest. Static (single epoch, ~2017), GeoTIFF and NetCDF, free public download from Figshare, no authentication. Aggregating this to our existing distance buckets is a small, cheap change and is the only identified source for the control our project flagged as dominant-but-missing.
claims.effectSize: 86.03% classification accuracy CONUS-wide; 82.7-93.6% in the Midwest, vs 16,000 ground-truth points

claims.text: Over 1980-2022 the MRB exported only 19 +/- 4% of nitrogen surplus as riverine nitrate, but Iowa showed extreme wet/dry-year contrast: wet-year export fraction 42 +/- 24% versus dry-year 6 +/- 6% — a ~7x swing attributed to hydrologic connectivity and legacy nitrogen remobilization. Implication for us: the mapping from N-surplus (a static-ish input we already carry, though ours dies in 2017) to realized in-stream nitrate is strongly WETNESS-REGIME DEPENDENT at ANNUAL scale, not daily scale. Our seven failed temporal ablations were all daily/short-window (same-day, lagged, 3D/7D rolling, travel-time-routed). The untested alternative this supports is an ANNUAL or seasonal basin wetness aggregate (e.g. water-year cumulative precipitation percentile) interacted with N-surplus, which is a per-site-year term rather than a daily one — and, crucially, is computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from weather alone. The very large error bars (+/-24 and +/-6) mean this is a noisy relationship and the claim is that direction of effect is real, not that it is precisely estimable.
claims.effectSize: MRB export 19 +/- 4% of surplus; Iowa wet-year 42 +/- 24% vs dry-year 6 +/- 6% (~7x)
claims.nBasins: MRB-wide aggregate; contributing basin count not determinable from accessible sources
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (descriptive mass-balance result from model application, not a held-out performance number)

result.sourceQuality:
MIXED — strong source, degraded access. The paper itself is peer-reviewed and authoritative: Water Resources Research 61(8), 2025, DOI 10.1029/2024WR039207, Pandit (Univ. Kansas), Golden / Christensen / Lane (US EPA ORD), Husic (Virginia Tech); OpenAlex reports top-10% normalized citation percentile, 8 citations. It is also unusually well-matched to this project: same target (daily nitrate CONCENTRATION, not load), same region (explicitly reports Iowa), and it reports a spatial-holdout number, which most water-quality ML papers do not.

ACCESS CAVEAT — read every claim above with this in mind: the Wiley full text returned HTTP 403 and the ResearchGate mirror returned HTTP 403. No open-access PDF exists (Semantic Scholar's openAccessPdf field just points back to the paywalled DOI). All claims were reconstructed from (a) the Crossref abstract, (b) the OpenAlex record, (c) Semantic Scholar metadata, (d) the US EPA Science Inventory record for the companion CONUS LSTM (cfpub.epa.gov, dirEntryId=360394) which supplied the n=148 site count and the CAMELS/GAGES-II attribute sourcing, and (e) indexed snippets of the full text surfaced via search. Headline numbers (KGE 0.60 / 0.18 / 0.34, 19±4%, 42±24%, 6±6%, n=148) appear verbatim and consistently across two or more independent mirrors and are high-confidence. What could NOT be verified and should be treated as open: (1) the exact construction of the spatial-validation folds — whether it was random k-fold leave-basins-out, leave-one-region-out, or anything analogous to our leak-safe family grouping of nested/temporally-overlapping basins; if their spatial folds did NOT group nested basins, their KGE 0.18 is OPTIMISTIC and the true ungauged number is worse. (2) Whether any supplementary table benchmarks the LSTM against RF/XGBoost. (3) Any ablation of performance versus NUMBER of training basins — none was found, so this source does NOT answer the 'at what n does the deep-model advantage appear' half of the research question.

SEPARATE SOURCE, INDEPENDENTLY STRONG: the AgTile-US claim does not depend on the paywalled paper. It rests on Valayamkunnath et al., 'Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach,' Scientific Data 7, 257 (2020), DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x — open access, PMC7406500, with the dataset itself freely downloadable from Figshare with no authentication.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE RESEARCH ANGLE: this source is evidence AGAINST switching to an LSTM, not for it. A deep model with 148 training basins — roughly 8x our 19 independent basin families — still degraded to median KGE 0.18 on ungauged nitrate concentration, and the authors responded by geographically restricting where they would apply the model. Nothing here supports an LSTM-over-XGBoost move at n=19. The transferable value of this paper to us is its Shapley finding, which points at static landscape attributes we do not yet have (tile drainage, wetland cover, road density) and thus corroborates the between-site-static hypothesis over further temporal feature engineering.

claims.text: Discharge alone is a weak predictor of nitrate concentration WITHIN a site: across the 275 German catchments with paired C and Q data, the log-log power-law C-Q regression for NO3-N had a mean R2 of only 0.27 ± 0.24 (Ebeling et al. 2021, Section 3.1). I independently downloaded the paper's own CC-BY dataset (WQQDB, HydroShare doi:10.4211/hs.9b4deeca259b4f7398ce72121b4e2979, CQ_metrics.csv) and recomputed over the 274 independent catchments with a valid nitrate slope: median C-Q R2 = 0.223, quartiles 0.044 / 0.223 / 0.458, and only 39.4% of catchments exceed R2 = 0.30. DIRECT IMPLICATION FOR THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: even a PERFECT, error-free discharge time series at an ungauged pin would explain a median of ~22% of log-nitrate variance at that site; a modeled Q (NWM retrospective) carrying its own error can only do worse. This bounds the upside of the whole modeled-discharge angle and says it cannot be the fix for the between-site level problem.
claims.nBasins: 275 (274 independent) German catchments with paired C-Q; 2000-2015
claims.effectSize: mean C-Q power-law R2 = 0.27 ± 0.24; median 0.223 (IQR 0.044-0.458); 39.4% of catchments > 0.30

claims.text: Nitrate in these catchments shows ENRICHMENT (mobilization), not dilution: mean C-Q log-log slope b = 0.26 ± 0.35 (median ± IQR 0.16 ± 0.36) for NO3-N, versus b = -0.22 ± 0.27 for phosphate. 69% of catchments (n=188) were classified as enrichment patterns and 74% (n=200) as a chemostatic regime (CVc/CVq = 0.47 ± 0.43, median 0.33). My recomputation on the 274 independent catchments: 82.1% have b > 0; only 5.8% (16 catchments) have b <= -0.1, i.e. genuine dilution; 36.1% fall in |b| < 0.1 and 58.0% in b > 0.1; 90.1% have CVc/CVq < 1. FALSIFIES the dilution-mass-balance framing for the fluid-dynamics angle: a C = Load/Q model (C decreasing with Q) is the WRONG sign for agricultural nitrate in ~82% of catchments. It also means concentration varies far less than discharge, so the site's absolute LEVEL is set by source strength, not by flow — consistent with this project's finding that the deficit is between-site static information.
claims.effectSize: NO3-N b = 0.26 ± 0.35 (median 0.16); 82.1% b>0, only 5.8% b<=-0.1; CVc/CVq median 0.33, 90.1% <1; 74% chemostatic regime, 69% enrichment

claims.text: MEAN nitrate concentration is highly predictable BETWEEN unmonitored catchments from static attributes alone, with no discharge and no local nitrate history: random forest reached R2_crossval = 0.69 (R2_OOB = 0.68) and PLS regression R2_crossval = 0.64 (R2_train = 0.66) for mean NO3-N over n = 759 catchments. Protocol: 3-times-repeated 10-fold cross-validation where each unit is a whole catchment, so every test catchment's concentrations are entirely unseen (the ungauged-basin analogue) — BUT folds are random rather than spatially blocked, so a held-out catchment can have a geographic neighbour in training; this makes 0.69 an optimistic upper bound relative to a leave-one-region-out protocol. Top RF importances: f_forest 20.3, mean annual precipitation P_mm 17.4, precipitation seasonality P_SIsw 16.2, fraction sedimentary aquifer f_sedim 15.8, vertical concentration heterogeneity het_v 14.4, f_agric 13.9. SAMPLE-SIZE FLAG: n=759 catchments versus this project's 19 independent basin families — a 40x difference. A 40-predictor RF fit on 19 units cannot reproduce this; the transferable lesson is WHICH variable classes carry the between-site signal (land-cover fractions, precipitation climatology, aquifer/subsurface type), not the R2 value.
claims.effectSize: RF R2_crossval = 0.69 (OOB 0.68); PLSR R2_crossval = 0.64 (train 0.66)

claims.text: NITROGEN SURPLUS WAS A WEAKER BETWEEN-SITE PREDICTOR OF MEAN NITRATE THAN PLAIN LAND-COVER FRACTION. Forest fraction alone explained 32% and agricultural fraction alone 29% of the between-catchment variance in mean NO3-N in simple linear regression (n=759), while the correlation of mean NO3-N with N surplus was only r = 0.39 for N_surp_80 (1980-2015 legacy-inclusive surplus), i.e. r2 ~ 0.15 — despite N surplus being strongly correlated with agricultural land (r = 0.71). The authors attribute the gap to 'a few catchments that have exceptionally high N surplus but moderate mean NO3-N concentrations', and note the agriculture-to-nitrate relationship is 'highly heteroscedastic', with deviations explained by soil and aquifer properties (denitrification buffering; f_sedim ranked high). N surplus does NOT appear in the top six predictors of mean NO3-N in either the PLSR or the RF model. FALSIFIES the proposed between-site relation 'concentration ~ N-input-yield / specific-discharge' as a strong predictor, and independently corroborates this project's negative result on broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward: the surplus product may be the wrong variable, not merely the wrong vintage. Practical read: crop/land-cover fractions plus subsurface attributes beat an N-budget product.
claims.effectSize: f_forest alone R2 = 0.32; f_agric alone R2 = 0.29; N_surp_80 correlation r = 0.39 (r2 ~ 0.15); all descriptors together 0.64-0.70

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON DISCHARGE-DERIVED FEATURES FOR NITRATE SPECIFICALLY: the study computed a full suite of hydrological descriptors (mean discharge, mean SPECIFIC discharge, runoff coefficient, seasonal ratio, base-flow index, flashiness index) and ran a supplementary analysis adding them. These descriptors 'substantially increased the variance explained ... between 11% and 37%' for TOC on a subset of n = 184 catchments (raising RF slope-b from R2_crossval = 0.28 to 0.44, and PLSR CVc/CVq to 0.58). For NITRATE, no such improvement is reported anywhere in the paper, and not a single hydrological descriptor appears in the top six of ANY of the four NO3-N models (mean concentration, slope b, CVc/CVq — PLSR and RF); the NO3-N models are instead topped by land cover, precipitation climatology, subsurface/aquifer type, topographic slope and TWI. DIRECT ANSWER TO THE RESEARCH QUESTION: in the largest study of its kind, adding real (gauged, not modeled) discharge statistics measurably helped organic carbon but did NOT surface as a control on nitrate level or nitrate C-Q behaviour. This argues that acquiring modeled Q (NWM v3 retrospective) for the ungauged pin is unlikely to convert into between-site nitrate skill, and should be ranked below static subsurface/land-cover attributes. Caveat: absence of reporting for NO3 is weaker evidence than an explicit stated null, and these are OBSERVED gauge discharges, so this does not separately test modeled-Q bias in tile-drained basins — a question this German-catchment paper does not address at all (tile-drainage density is not among its predictors; 'drain_dens' is stream drainage density, not artificial subsurface drainage).
claims.nBasins: 184 catchments in the hydrological-descriptor subset; 274-759 in the main models
claims.effectSize: hydro descriptors: +11% to +37% explained variance for TOC (RF slope-b 0.28 -> 0.44); no reported gain for NO3-N, and zero hydrological descriptors in the top-6 of any of the four NO3-N models

claims.text: THE CHEMOSTASIS HYPOTHESIS FOR AGRICULTURAL CATCHMENTS (Basu et al. 2010; Thompson et al. 2011) IS EXPLICITLY CONTRADICTED AT SCALE. Among agriculturally dominated catchments (f_agric >= 0.5), 34% exhibited CHEMODYNAMIC export regimes — of which 89% were combined with enrichment patterns — compared with only 17% chemodynamic among less-agricultural catchments (f_agric < 0.5). Higher agricultural fraction was associated with HIGHER slope b and HIGHER CVc/CVq, the opposite of the homogenization/chemostasis expectation. The authors state directly: 'Our study therefore does not support the generality of the hypothesis that highly managed, agricultural catchments are necessarily subject to homogenization of sources and thus to chemostatic export regimes (Basu et al., 2010; Thompson et al., 2011).' They attribute the chemodynamic behaviour to vertical concentration heterogeneity (het_v) from subsurface denitrification producing a depth decline in nitrate — high flow taps shallow, N-rich water. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: (a) do not assume a fixed chemostatic C-Q form for Iowa row-crop basins as a modeling prior; (b) the abstract also states that mean NO3 concentrations AND THEIR VARIANCE AMONG SITES both increase with agricultural land use — heteroscedasticity means the highest-agriculture Iowa basins are precisely the hardest to place on an absolute level, which is exactly the failure mode reported here (between_r2 0.21); (c) the mechanism identified (vertical redox/denitrification contrast between shallow seepage and groundwater) is a STATIC subsurface attribute, obtainable without any local sensor, and is the single most important predictor of nitrate C-Q dynamics (het_v ranked first in 3 of 4 dynamics models) — a candidate feature class this project has not tried.
claims.nBasins: 274-759 German catchments (agricultural subset f_agric >= 0.5 within these)
claims.effectSize: 34% of f_agric>=0.5 catchments chemodynamic (89% of those with enrichment) vs 17% for f_agric<0.5

result.sourceQuality: HIGH — peer-reviewed, Water Resources Research 57(4) e2020WR028134, 67-100 citations, from the UFZ water-quality group (Musolff/Kumar), the leading group on large-sample C-Q analysis. The publisher HTML/PDF is bot-blocked (HTTP 403 at Wiley, ResearchGate, ESSOAr/Authorea, and the geo-leo PDF endpoint), but I retrieved the COMPLETE extracted full text via the geo-leo DSpace REST API text bundle (https://e-docs.geo-leo.de/server/api/core/bitstreams/9575cd4a-cfeb-490b-b4ff-0e6a0e6acdd4/content, 135 KB, includes Abstract, Methods, Table 2, Table 3 with all model R2 and variable importances, Discussion). All quoted figures are from that full text, not from an abstract or a secondary summary. Distributional statistics on nitrate C-Q slope b, C-Q R2 and CVc/CVq were INDEPENDENTLY RECOMPUTED by me from the paper's own published CC-BY-4.0 dataset (WQQDB, CUAHSI HydroShare, doi:10.4211/hs.9b4deeca259b4f7398ce72121b4e2979, file CQ_metrics.csv, 1386 stations of which 787 flagged independent, sampling from 2000; free anonymous bulk download via https://www.hydroshare.org/hsapi/resource/9b4deeca259b4f7398ce72121b4e2979/ — no authentication) and agree with the paper's reported means. CAVEATS ON TRANSFER: (1) German catchments, 2000-2015, not Iowa; German agricultural catchments are generally not artificially tile-drained at Iowa's density, and artificial subsurface drainage is NOT among the paper's predictors, so this source says nothing about the tile-drainage control or about NWM bias in tile-drained low-relief basins. (2) Supporting-information tables (S3-S11), which hold the full variable-importance rankings and the hydrological-descriptor subset results, are behind the same Wiley block and I could not read them — my claim that hydrological descriptors did not help the NITRATE models rests on their absence from the main-text Table 3 top-six and from the Results/Discussion narrative, i.e. it is an inference from silence rather than an explicitly stated null. (3) All model R2 values come from 3x-repeated 10-fold CV with random (not spatially blocked) folds over catchments; test catchments are fully unseen, which makes them broadly comparable in kind to a leave-one-basin-out protocol, but the lack of spatial blocking makes them optimistic relative to this project's LOFO. (4) n=759 catchments vs this project's 19 independent basin families — the R2 values are NOT achievable targets here; only the variable-class rankings transfer. (5) This source does not evaluate NWM, SPARROW, GAGES-II, or load-vs-concentration as a target; those parts of the research question must be answered from other sources.

claims.text: Zhi et al. (2021) trained an LSTM to predict daily river dissolved oxygen from hydrometeorology alone using CAMELS-chem, and on a 'core evaluation group of 84 sites' reported mean (median) NSE, RMSE, and Pearson correlation of 0.51 (0.57), 1.2 (1.1) mg/L, and 0.78 (0.82), with NSE >= 0.4 at 74% of sites. The split protocol behind these numbers is NOT stated in the abstract or the authors' README and the full text is paywalled, so these numbers are NOT comparable to a spatially held-out LOFO benchmark without further verification.
claims.effectSize: mean NSE 0.51, median NSE 0.57; RMSE mean 1.2 / median 1.1 mg/L; Pcorr mean 0.78 / median 0.82; 74% of sites NSE >= 0.4
claims.nBasins: 236 watersheds in the dataset; 84 sites in the core evaluation group

claims.text: NEGATIVE / HIGH-RELEVANCE RESULT: the paper's abstract states plainly 'Surprisingly, the model does not perform better where more data are available.' The authors quantify this as essentially zero relationship between per-site model skill and the number of observations at that site (R2 = 0.03), versus a strong relationship between skill and the site's DO standard deviation (R2 = 0.52). Per-site skill is therefore governed by the character of the site, not by how much training data that site contributes — directly analogous to the sustag finding that headroom is in the between-site term rather than in more site-days.
claims.effectSize: skill vs number of data points R2 = 0.03; skill vs DO standard deviation R2 = 0.52

claims.text: The paper claims LSTM skill is predicted by static/hydroclimatic basin character, specifically that the model 'performs better in basins with low variations of streamflow and DO, high runoff-ratio (>0.45), and winter precipitation peaks.' This is a falsifiable, transferable prediction: a deep model trained on hydrometeorology will systematically underperform in flashy, high-variance, summer-precipitation-dominated agricultural catchments — which describes tile-drained Iowa nitrate basins. It implies the deep-learning advantage reported here would NOT be expected to reproduce in the sustag setting.
claims.effectSize: qualitative stratification; runoff-ratio threshold quoted as >0.45

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON THE TARGET MECHANISM: the abstract states 'The model however misses some DO peaks and troughs when in-stream biogeochemical processes become important.' A hydrometeorology-only deep model captured the physically-forced component (DO solubility vs water temperature) but failed on the biogeochemically-forced extremes. Since the sustag primary target is a threshold-exceedance (violation >= 10 mg/L nitrate), i.e. explicitly an extreme/peak-detection problem under biogeochemical control, this is evidence that switching architecture from XGBoost to LSTM would not address the failure mode that matters here.
claims.effectSize: qualitative; no quantified peak/trough error reported in accessible material

claims.text: This paper does NOT contain a head-to-head comparison of LSTM against random forest, gradient-boosted trees, or XGBoost. No tree-ensemble baseline appears in the abstract, the authors' repository README, or the citing review's description. It therefore provides ZERO evidence for the research question 'do deep models beat GBDTs for ungauged water-quality prediction' — it establishes only that an LSTM reaches a given absolute skill level, not that it exceeds a boosted-tree alternative.
claims.effectSize: no baseline comparison identified in any accessible source

claims.text: SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT FLAG: every number in this study rests on 236 watersheds (drawn from a 493-catchment CAMELS-chem pool spanning 1980-2014), and a citing review (Nature npj/PMC11151732) describes a related Zhi et al. ungauged-DO experiment trained on 480 rivers to predict 100 'chemically ungauged basins' — attribution of the 480/100 figure to this specific 2021 paper versus a later Zhi et al. paper could NOT be confirmed. Either way, the evidence base is 236-480 training basins versus sustag's 19 independent basin families, a 12-25x gap. The paper's own finding that skill does not scale with per-site data volume means the deep model's leverage comes from the BREADTH of the basin sample, exactly the resource sustag lacks; an LSTM at n=19 families should not be expected to reproduce these results.
claims.effectSize: 236 basins (this paper) vs 19 independent basin families in sustag = ~12x; 480 basins in the possibly-related PUB experiment = ~25x
claims.nBasins: 236 (this paper); 493 in the parent CAMELS-chem dataset; 480 train / 100 held-out in a related-but-unconfirmed experiment

result.sourceQuality: PAYWALLED - full text NOT obtained. pubs.acs.org returned HTTP 403. Claims are reconstructed from three secondary-but-authoritative sources: (1) the complete verbatim abstract via the Semantic Scholar Graph API (DOI:10.1021/acs.est.0c06783, PMID 33533608, 249 citations); (2) the AUTHORS' OWN GitHub repository README (WeiZhiWater/From-Hydrometeorology-to-River-Water-Quality...), which reproduces the paper's headline results sentence including the 84-site metrics and the R2=0.03 / R2=0.52 figures - this is first-party and high confidence for the numbers themselves; (3) a citing review (PMC11151732, 'Deep learning for water quality') for the ungauged-basin framing. CRITICAL GAP: the Methods section was never accessible, so the TRAIN/TEST SPLIT PROTOCOL for the headline 84-site metrics is genuinely UNKNOWN - it may be temporal holdout at gauged sites rather than spatial holdout, which would make the 0.51 NSE non-comparable to LOFO numbers. Do not treat the 84-site metrics as ungauged-basin performance without obtaining the full text. Also unverified: whether the 480-train/100-heldout PUB configuration belongs to this 2021 paper or to a later Zhi et al. publication. No hyperparameters, no learning-curve-vs-number-of-basins ablation, and no tree-ensemble baseline were found in any accessible source. Peer-reviewed ES&T journal article, so source authority is high; only the retrieval is degraded.

claims.text: In the upper Delaware River Basin (70 stream segments), all deep-learning stream-temperature models degraded ~2.2x when moved from gaged to ungaged locations: 1-day-ahead mean RMSE was 1.45-1.52 degC at gaged sites vs 3.18-3.27 degC at ungaged (spatially held-out) sites. Quote: 'All DL models performed substantially better at gaged locations compared to ungaged locations as mean RMSE ranged from 1.45 to 1.52°C for gaged sites and 3.18 to 3.27°C for ungaged sites.' This is direct evidence that the gaged-vs-ungaged transfer penalty is the dominant error term, matching the sustag project's within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21 gap.
claims.nBasins: 70 river segments in one basin; 5-fold spatial CV, 6 test segments held out per fold (2 mainstem, 2 headwater, 2 reservoir-impacted) plus 3-4 validation segments
claims.effectSize: 2.2x RMSE increase at ungaged sites (1.45-1.52 -> 3.18-3.27 degC, 1-day lead); at 7-day lead 1.89-1.99 degC gaged vs 3.26-3.39 degC ungaged

claims.text: The spread across ALL four deep-learning architectures (LSTM, LSTM-DA, RGCN, RGCN-DA) at spatially held-out ungaged sites was only 0.09 degC (3.18-3.27 degC RMSE, 1-day lead) - i.e. the choice of architecture, INCLUDING whether river-network graph structure was used at all, mattered ~25x less than the gaged/ungaged distinction (1.7 degC). This is a strong negative result for the premise that a graph architecture is what unlocks unmonitored-node prediction.
claims.effectSize: Architecture spread 0.09 degC vs gaged/ungaged gap ~1.73 degC

claims.text: The graph model did NOT win overall: 'Of the DL models, the LSTM model was generally the best performing model when considering all temperature observations' - the plain LSTM, which uses no river-network topology whatsoever, had the lowest RMSE across both gaged and ungaged locations at 1- and 7-day lead times in the validation period. RGCN/RGCN-DA only won on the >18 degC subset. Therefore the headline 'RGCN-DA is best for ungaged locations' applies to a CONDITIONAL SUBSET (high temperatures), not to overall accuracy.
claims.effectSize: LSTM best overall; RGCN/RGCN-DA best only on the >18 degC observation subset

claims.text: Uncertainty estimates collapsed at unmonitored sites: 90% confidence intervals contained the observation only ~60% of the time at ungaged locations vs ~90% at gaged locations. Models trained on monitored sites are systematically OVERCONFIDENT when applied to unmonitored ones. Directly relevant to the sustag deployment target (arbitrary map pin, beta=2 alarm threshold, 59% false alarms): any calibrated probability produced under LOFO should be assumed miscalibrated at a truly novel pin unless separately validated.
claims.effectSize: 90% CI empirical coverage ~60% ungaged vs ~90% gaged

claims.text: The data-assimilation component of this paper requires observations at or near the target site to update model states via an Ensemble Kalman Filter, and the paper's own mechanism for ungaged benefit is that DA lets the network 'borrow information from nearby monitored sites.' This mechanism is UNAVAILABLE at the sustag deployment target, which has no nitrate history at the pin and no guaranteed monitored upstream neighbor. The RGCN-DA ungaged gain is therefore conditional on a dense, hydrologically connected monitored neighborhood (70 segments in a single basin), not on topology features alone.
claims.nBasins: 70 river segments in one contiguous basin (upper Delaware)
claims.effectSize: Not separately quantified; paper does not report the isolated RMSE reduction attributable to DA at ungaged sites

claims.text: The RGCN's graph advantage was network-topology-specific and could be NEGATIVE where topology is complicated: 'RGCN-DA forecasts were worse for locations directly downstream from reservoirs' at gaged locations. The graph adjacency encodes advective connectivity, and where a physical structure breaks that assumption the graph prior hurts. Iowa analogue: tile drainage and impoundments would similarly break a pure NHDPlus flow-topology adjacency, and tile drainage density is already flagged as the dominant unmodeled Iowa control.
claims.nBasins: 70 river segments; 2 of 6 held-out test segments per fold were reservoir-impacted
claims.effectSize: Qualitative — direction stated (worse), magnitude not quantified in accessible text

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed, open access (Frontiers in Water, published 2023-06-23, DOI 10.3389/frwa.2023.1184992), authored by USGS scientists (Zwart et al.) with companion source code on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/6516512). Full text was retrievable via WebFetch — no paywall. CAVEAT: numbers were extracted via WebFetch summarization of the HTML full text rather than from the PDF tables; the RMSE ranges (1.45-1.52 / 3.18-3.27 degC) are quoted verbatim from the paper's text and are high-confidence, but per-architecture point estimates within those ranges, and the isolated effect size of data assimilation at ungaged sites, could NOT be recovered and are recorded as unquantified. The count of 70 segments is quoted verbatim; the split between segments WITH and WITHOUT training observations is NOT stated in the accessible text and remains unknown — this matters, because monitored-node density is exactly the variable that determines whether a graph approach is feasible. RELEVANCE TO ANGLE: this is the strongest available evidence AGAINST investing in a GNN architecture for sustag. A 70-node single-basin network with dense monitoring and 38 years of data produced only a 0.09 degC architecture spread at held-out nodes; sustag's 85 sites / 19 independent families / ~40 known edges (28 upstream_uid, 40 downstream_uid) is a sparser, more fragmented graph with far less signal to support a learned message-passing scheme. The paper supports the "use topology as static FEATURES" fallback by elimination, but does NOT itself test that fallback — a separate source is needed for evidence on drainage area / Strahler order / network position as plain XGBoost features.

claims.text: In the study's ungauged-basin (PUB) experiment, a single top-down LSTM trained on all 782 monitored sites ("LSTM conus") beat both regionally-grouped LSTMs and a bottom-up transfer-learning approach at 580 site-disjoint held-out sites: median per-site RMSE 1.43C (+/-0.98) for LSTM conus vs 1.98C (+/-1.78) for LSTM regional (grouped by the 18 HUC-2 regions), 2.02C (+/-1.66) for LSTM cluster (grouped by catchment-attribute similarity), and 2.00C (+/-1.07) for the MTL bottom-up donor-transfer method. Sites achieving RMSE < 2C: 406/580 (LSTM conus) vs 293 / 287 / 290. LSTM conus had the lowest median RMSE in 14 of 17 regions and 14 of 15 attribute clusters. CAVEAT ON PROTOCOL: the train/test split was made by RECORD LENGTH, not geography — the 782 sites with >=5 years of data trained, the 580 sites with 1-5 years tested. It is genuinely site-disjoint (no test site's own observations are seen), but test sites are geographically INTERSPERSED with training sites and there is no region-level separation and no control for nested/overlapping basins. This is therefore a WEAKER spatial holdout than the project's leave-one-basin-family-out LOFO, and 1.43C is NOT directly comparable to our LOFO numbers.
claims.nBasins: 1362 total sites (782 train / 580 test); Experiment 2 extended set 2999 sites (1346 train)
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (site-disjoint held-out sites, but split assigned by record length, not by region or basin nesting)
claims.effectSize: median per-site RMSE 1.43C vs 1.98C / 2.02C / 2.00C; 406 vs 293/287/290 sites under 2C RMSE

claims.text: DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT — this paper contains an explicit demonstration that deep models trained on small numbers of basins collapse at ungauged sites. The authors state: "the grouped models do quite poorly in all regions with less than 15 training sites" and "When only a few sites are available for training... the models are not seeing sufficient data and site diversity in these cases to be able to extrapolate to unseen locations." Worst cases: Lower Colorado (HUC 15) with only 2 training sites — regional LSTM median RMSE 6.38C vs 2.10C for the CONUS model trained on all 782 sites (3.0x worse); Souris-Red-Rainy (HUC 09) — regional LSTM 9.09C and cluster LSTM 8.70C, versus a CONUS-model worst-region value of 2.34C (California, HUC 18). Region sizes where grouped models worked were much larger (e.g. Pacific Northwest, 142 training sites, regional LSTM 1.27C vs CONUS 1.22C). IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: our 19 independent basin families sits well below the ~15-site threshold at which this paper observed catastrophic grouped-model failure, and far below the 142-site region where a regional deep model was competitive. The LSTM advantage documented here is an effect of LARGE-SAMPLE SITE DIVERSITY (782-1346 basins), not of the architecture per se, and there is no evidence in this paper that it survives at n~19.
claims.nBasins: regional models trained on per-HUC subsets of 782 sites; failing regions had 2-15 training sites, succeeding regions had 47-183
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (site-disjoint; regional models trained on a region's sites and tested on other held-out sites within that same region)
