claims.effectSize: Lower Colorado (2 train sites): regional LSTM 6.38C vs CONUS 2.10C. Souris-Red-Rainy: regional 9.09C, cluster 8.70C. Pacific Northwest (142 train sites): regional 1.27C vs CONUS 1.22C

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON TRAINING-SET SIZE — the paper's explicit data-volume ablation found performance SATURATES: expanding the training set from ~3.82 million observations across 782 sites to ~6.13 million observations across 1346 sites produced NO improvement for the meteorology-only and meteorology+lat/long/altitude models, and only marginal improvement for the models that included discharge (median per-site RMSE 1.57C -> 1.50C) or GAGES-II catchment attributes (1.47C -> 1.43C). The authors conclude: "while increasing data volumes can partially offset the absence of certain input types, its effects may be limited beyond a certain training dataset size." This is a two-edged claim for this project: it means the marginal value of adding basins is strongly diminishing ABOVE ~800 basins, but it says nothing about the region below 100 basins, where the grouped-model failures above show the curve is extremely steep. The paper reports no ablation sweeping training-basin count downward, so it CANNOT be used to estimate what performance is achievable at n=19.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (site-disjoint held-out sites, split by record length)
claims.effectSize: no RMSE improvement for meteo-only and meteo+location models; discharge model 1.57C->1.50C; GAGES-II attributes model 1.47C->1.43C

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON THE 'CHEAPER MIDDLE GROUND' OF REGIONAL FINE-TUNING — the authors tested fine-tuning the large top-down model on data from each target region (the standard remedy for small regional sample sizes, citing Oruche et al. 2021 and Zhu & Zhou 2024) and report that the technique "yielded performance that mirrored the top-down model very closely when applied to both the grouped modeling and bottom-up approaches." That is, region-specific adaptation added essentially nothing over the global model and did not recover the deficit of the small-sample regional models. No numeric table is given for this fine-tuning experiment in the main text, so the effect size is unquantified. This is evidence against expecting gains from region- or site-specific adaptation layers on top of a global model when the local sample is small — relevant to any proposal to layer per-site random effects or site embeddings on top of the existing booster, though it tests fine-tuning specifically, not embeddings or random effects, which this paper does not evaluate at all.
claims.effectSize: unquantified in main text — described only as performance that "mirrored the top-down model very closely"

claims.text: STATIC CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES MATTERED MORE THAN DYNAMIC DISCHARGE, AND A SMALL CURATED STATIC SET WAS AS GOOD AS 274 ATTRIBUTES. Starting from a meteorology-only model (median per-site RMSE 1.78C), adding the 274 GAGES-II static catchment attributes dropped RMSE to 1.47C, while adding river discharge instead dropped it only to 1.57C; the full model with both reached 1.43C. Adding location (lat/long/elevation) to meteorology "did not meaningfully improve performance." Combined permutation importance was 3.97C for the three air-temperature inputs, 1.12C for all 274 GAGES-II attributes combined, and only 0.36C for all discharge features combined. In Experiment 3, replacing the 274 attributes with just 21 EXPERT-SELECTED attributes gave statistically equivalent accuracy (median RMSE 1.46C vs 1.43C) and was actually BETTER on the warmest 10% of observations (1.64C vs 1.70C), and was the best of the three attribute sets at 218/580 test sites vs 186/580 for the full 274-attribute default; a 25-attribute aggregated-z-score set gave 1.47C. Most important individual expert-selected attributes: percent slope (PCT_SLOPE, 0.10C) and drainage area (DRAIN_SQKM, 0.08C); in the z-score model the top category was "Major Dams" (0.16C). RELEVANCE: this supports the project's own finding that static between-site geography, not temporal dynamics, carries the transferable signal — and shows ~20 well-chosen static attributes suffice, which is tractable at n=19 in a way that 274 attributes is not.
claims.effectSize: meteo-only 1.78C; +discharge 1.57C; +GAGES-II attributes 1.47C; both 1.43C. 21 expert attributes 1.46C vs 274 attributes 1.43C (warmest-10%: 1.64C vs 1.70C). Permutation importance: air temp 3.97C, attributes 1.12C, discharge 0.36C

claims.text: THIS PAPER DOES NOT PROVIDE A HEAD-TO-HEAD LSTM-vs-GRADIENT-BOOSTED-TREE COMPARISON ON THE PREDICTION TASK, AND CONTAINS NO NITRATE OR NUTRIENT-CONCENTRATION RESULT AT ALL. XGBoost appears only as a META-model inside the bottom-up MTL pipeline — it predicts the expected RMSE of transferring a single-site LSTM to a target site (152 estimators, learning rate 0.183, 234 features after RFECV), and is used to select the 10 best donor sites; it never predicts stream temperature directly. The only XGBoost-vs-LSTM accuracy figures in the paper are a CROSS-PAPER, CROSS-PROTOCOL comparison the authors themselves flag as non-equivalent: Weierbach et al. (2022) reported MONTHLY stream-temperature RMSE of 0.61C for XGBoost, 0.89C for support vector regression and 1.2C for multilinear regression in the Pacific Northwest (n=54 total sites) and mid-Atlantic (n=24 total sites) using a random-subsampling 100-member ensemble, versus LSTM conus DAILY median RMSE of 1.22C (Pacific Northwest, 208 total / 70 test sites) and 1.27C (mid-Atlantic, 212 total / 121 test sites). These numbers CANNOT be compared — different temporal aggregation (monthly vs daily) and different split protocol (random subsampling vs record-length site holdout). Conclusion for the research angle: this source supplies NO evidence that LSTMs beat XGBoost for ungauged-basin water-quality prediction; its contribution is evidence that TRAINING-SET BREADTH (number and diversity of basins), not architecture, is what drives ungauged-basin skill.
claims.nBasins: Weierbach 2022: n=54 (Pacific Northwest) and n=24 (mid-Atlantic) total sites. This paper's corresponding regions: 208 total/70 test and 212 total/121 test
claims.splitProtocol: mixed and non-comparable — Weierbach 2022 used random subsampling over a 100-member ensemble; this paper used record-length site-disjoint holdout
claims.effectSize: XGBoost 0.61C monthly RMSE (Weierbach 2022) vs LSTM conus 1.22C/1.27C daily RMSE — explicitly non-comparable per the authors

result.sourceQuality:
STRONG SOURCE, FULLY RETRIEVED, BUT ONLY PARTIALLY ON-TARGET. The arXiv landing page gave only the abstract; the PDF returned as binary via WebFetch but was cached to disk and successfully extracted with pdftotext (6,024 lines of full text including all main-text tables), so all figures below are quoted from the full manuscript, not from metadata. Full text at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/408994b9-8d9b-485d-9731-ba0bfa7507ce/scratchpad/willard.txt; cached PDF at /Users/isaac/.claude/projects/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/408994b9-8d9b-485d-9731-ba0bfa7507ce/tool-results/webfetch-1784616609607-wvj6et.pdf. Manuscript is marked "submitted to Water Resources Research" (peer review status at time of the arXiv v1 posting, Oct 2024, not confirmed; no journal DOI found — arXiv:2410.19865). Authors are LBNL / USGS-affiliated (Willard was previously at USGS on the stream-temperature ML program), a credible group.

FOUR IMPORTANT LIMITATIONS ON USING THIS SOURCE FOR THE STATED RESEARCH QUESTION:
(1) TARGET MISMATCH — the target is daily STREAM TEMPERATURE, not nitrate or any nutrient concentration. Stream temperature is far more predictable from meteorology (air temperature alone carries permutation importance 3.97C of a ~1.4C RMSE signal) than nitrate is; conclusions about deep-model transfer should NOT be assumed to carry to a nitrate violation classifier.
(2) NO GBDT HEAD-TO-HEAD — XGBoost is used only as a donor-selection metamodel, never as a competing predictor. The research angle "do LSTMs beat GBDTs for ungauged basins" is NOT answered by this paper.
(3) NO KRATZERT PUB METRICS — the paper cites Kratzert et al. (2018, 2019a, 2024) and Fang et al. (2022a) but reports none of their basin counts or NSE figures; the specific Kratzert CAMELS PUB numbers requested must be obtained from those papers directly.
(4) SPLIT PROTOCOL IS WEAKER THAN OUR LOFO — the site holdout is assigned by record length, not geography. Test sites are interspersed among training sites with no regional separation and no control for nested or hydrologically-connected basins, which is precisely the leakage our basin-family grouping was designed to remove. Every RMSE in this paper is therefore an optimistic bound relative to a LOFO-equivalent protocol, and none of them should be placed on the same axis as our AUC 0.820 / R2 0.328.

WHAT IT IS GENUINELY GOOD FOR: it is one of the cleanest published demonstrations that ungauged-basin skill in deep hydrologic models is driven by the NUMBER AND DIVERSITY OF TRAINING BASINS rather than by architecture, and it contains an explicit, quantified small-sample failure threshold ("regions with less than 15 training sites") that bears directly on the n=19-families constraint. It also independently corroborates this project's own pattern that static catchment geography, not dynamic inputs, carries the transferable between-site signal — and that ~21 well-chosen static attributes match 274.

claims.text: The survey identifies only THREE studies using GNNs for water-resources time-series prediction at unmonitored sites (Sun et al. 2021a; Jia et al. 2021b; Bao et al. 2021), opening the paragraph with 'A few studies use GNNs for prediction in unmonitored sites for water resources applications.' None of the three is a water-quality/nutrient application - two are stream temperature, one is streamflow. The survey reports NO quantitative held-out-node error metrics (no RMSE/NSE numbers) for any of them, only directional statements. FALSIFIABLE: there is no published GNN result in this survey demonstrating a quantified gain for nutrient/nitrate prediction at a held-out node.
claims.nBasins: 3 GNN studies total; 530 basins (Sun et al. 2021a), 42 river segments (Bao et al. 2021, Delaware River Basin), unstated for Jia et al. 2021b
claims.effectSize: no quantitative metrics reported in the survey for any of the three GNN studies

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT, the strongest in the source: in Sun et al. (2021a) on FIVE HUNDRED AND THIRTY CAMELS basins (daily streamflow), two of the three GNN architectures tested were WORSE than a plain LSTM. Survey text: 'They found that for the transductive case, both ChebNet-LSTMs and GCN-LSTM performed worse in terms of median performance across basins than the standard LSTM and GraphWaveNet was the only one that performed better.' GraphWaveNet (the only inductive-capable model) also beat LSTM in the inductive case. Elsewhere the survey characterizes the GNN advantage as marginal: the graph approach 'can SLIGHTLY outperform the concatenated input approach (Sun et al., 2021a).' At n=530 basins the median GNN gain was slight and 2 of 3 architectures lost outright.
claims.effectSize: 2 of 3 GNN architectures BELOW standard LSTM in median performance across basins; the one winner described as only 'slightly' outperforming direct-concatenation baseline; no numeric NSE/RMSE given in survey

claims.text: The Sun et al. (2021a) graph was NOT river-network topology: 'In all cases, the graph is initially constructed as an adjacency matrix containing the pairwise Euclidean distance between stream sites using site characteristics.' The survey then makes an explicit design criticism of exactly this construction: 'Relying solely on the characteristics or location for graph construction in the non-interacting case more easily allows for broad-scale modeling because it can model spatially disconnected entities, however, it INTRODUCES NO NEW INFORMATION (e.g., physical connectivity) BEYOND WHAT' is already in the characteristics. The survey states that graphs built from real physical connections 'has so far only been seen in stream modeling using stream network graphs (Bindas et al., 2020; Jia et al., 2021b; Moshe et al., 2020; Sit et al., 2021).' IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: a similarity-graph GNN over 85 sites is provably redundant with static site features already concatenated into XGBoost; only a true upstream-downstream connectivity graph would add information, and our topology covers only 28 upstream_uid / 40 downstream_uid links.
claims.effectSize: qualitative design claim; no numbers

claims.text: The true river-network-topology GNN work is at a network size COMPARABLE TO OURS, not at hundreds of nodes: the survey's Table 1 lists the PDE-driven/knowledge-guided recurrent graph network study (Bao et al. 2021, Delaware River Basin, stream temperature) as covering 'FORTY-TWO RIVER SEGMENTS IN THE DELAWARE RIVER BASIN.' This is the same order of magnitude as our 85 sites / ~40 topology edges, which undercuts the assumption that river-network GNNs require CAMELS-scale samples. HOWEVER the survey reports no node-level error numbers, does not state how many of the 42 segments were monitored, and does not state whether evaluation held out NODES or TIME PERIODS.
claims.effectSize: survey states only that the approach improves 'beyond existing process-based and ML approaches'; no RMSE, no monitored-node count, no split design given

claims.text: CRITICAL AMBIGUITY THE SURVEY LEAVES UNRESOLVED FOR THE CENTRAL QUESTION 'unmonitored node vs missing time period': the survey describes Jia et al. (2021b) as taking 'a spatiotemporal GNN approach for stream temperature TEMPORAL PREDICTIONS' - i.e. worded as prediction in time, not at held-out nodes - and reports its result only as: pre-training on PRMS-SNTemp process-model simulations 'outperformed both a non-pre-trained GNN and a baseline LSTM model,' with no metric values. More broadly the survey warns that ALL models in its scope are validated on proxies: 'for evaluation purposes, these models are often tested on PSEUDO-UNMONITORED SITES, where data is withheld until the testing stage to mimic model building for real unmonitored sites.' FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE: this survey does not establish that any river-network GNN gain has been demonstrated at genuinely unmonitored nodes with a quantified effect size.
claims.effectSize: no numeric result reported; gain stated only as 'outperformed' a non-pre-trained GNN and an LSTM

claims.text: DEPLOYMENT BLOCKER stated explicitly: transductive GNNs (ChebNet-LSTM, GCN-LSTM) require that 'both training and testing entities must be present in the graph' at training time, and 'introducing new test nodes in the graph can affect how information is diffused' prior to re-training; only INDUCTIVE GNNs 'are able to continuously predict on new test data without the need for re-training.' In Sun et al. (2021a) the only architecture that beat LSTM (GraphWaveNet) is also the only inductive-capable one. For an arbitrary Iowa map pin - a node absent from the training graph - every transductive GNN in this survey is architecturally disqualified, and the survey's own evidence is that transductive GNNs were the ones that LOST to a plain LSTM at n=530.
claims.effectSize: architectural constraint; transductive variants both below LSTM median, inductive-capable variant above

claims.text: DIRECT EVIDENCE AGAINST TRAINING ON A SMALL HOMOGENEOUS SET (our n=19 families): 'in Willard (2023), regional LSTM models of stream temperature in the United States perform worse than the LSTM model built on all sites in the CONUS FOR 15 OUT OF 17 REGIONS, and single-site trained models transferred to the testing sites generally performed worse except when pre-trained on the global model.' The survey also cites 'A recent opinion piece Kratzert et al. (2024) also make an argument against building deep learning models, specifically LSTM models, on streamflow data from SMALL HOMOGENEOUS SETS OF WATERSHEDS, ESPECIALLY FOR PREDICTING UNMONITORED AREAS AND FOR EXTREME EVENTS.' A 19-family Iowa-only training set is precisely the small homogeneous regional set these results warn about; the implied remedy is to pool with out-of-state sites (e.g. multi-state Upper Mississippi nitrate networks) rather than to add architecture.
claims.nBasins: 17 CONUS regions vs 1 CONUS-wide pooled model (Willard 2023, stream temperature)
claims.effectSize: regional models worse than pooled CONUS model in 15/17 regions (88%); no RMSE values given in survey

claims.text: THE MASS-BALANCE / SPARROW HALF OF THE RESEARCH QUESTION IS ABSENT FROM THIS SOURCE. Searching the full text for 'SPARROW', 'mass balance', 'incremental area', and 'load estimation' returns nothing on routed nutrient mass balance; the only routing citation is Bindas et al. (2020), 'Routing flood waves through the river network utilizing physics-guided machine learning.' Mass conservation appears only abstractly, as a candidate knowledge-guided LOSS TERM: 'knowledge-guided loss function terms can impose structure on the solution search space in the absence of labeled target data by forcing model output to conform to physical laws (e.g., conservation of energy or MASS),' with cited successes in lake temperature (Read et al. 2019), lake phosphorus via a power-scaling law (Hanson et al. 2020), and subsurface transport (He et al. 2020) - none at unmonitored river nodes. Also note the water-quality literature for unmonitored sites is thin in this survey: of 40 tabulated studies, the water-quality entries are Kalin et al. (2010) (8 river WQ variables), Noori et al. (2020) (3 nutrient loads, MONTHLY, SWAT output fed to an ANN), and Zhi et al. (2021) (daily dissolved oxygen, 236 CAMELS watersheds); nine of the 40 use CAMELS (671 catchments), and 27 of 40 are US-based.
claims.nBasins: 40 studies tabulated; 9 use CAMELS (671 catchments); Zhi et al. 2021 uses 236 CAMELS watersheds
claims.effectSize: absence of coverage; no SPARROW or incremental-area mass-balance literature reviewed

result.sourceQuality: HIGH provenance, LOW numeric density. Peer-reviewed survey (Environmental Data Science 4:e7, Cambridge, publ. 22 Jan 2025; DOI 10.1017/eds.2024.14), authors are the principals of this literature (Jia and Kumar are themselves the Delaware-River-Basin river-graph authors, so their framing of that work is authoritative). Cambridge page is paywalled and redirected; I obtained the identical accepted manuscript from arXiv:2308.09766v3 (HTML) and the NSF-PAR PDF (par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10592409), extracted to text and read the GNN section (Sec 2.1.3), Table 1, and the open-questions discussion verbatim - so quotes are exact, not from an abstract mirror. MAJOR CAVEAT FOR THIS ANGLE: the survey is descriptive, not quantitative - it reports essentially NO effect sizes, RMSE/NSE values, monitored-node fractions, or split designs for the GNN studies. It is therefore reliable for (a) which papers exist, (b) node counts where tabulated (42 Delaware segments; 530 CAMELS basins), (c) architectural constraints (transductive vs inductive), and (d) negative results, but the primary papers (Sun et al. 2021a; Jia et al. 2021b, SDM 2021 'Physics-guided recurrent graph model for predicting flow and temperature in river networks'; Bao et al. 2021 ICDM; Moshe et al. 2020 HydroNets; Chen, Zwart & Jia 2022 physics-guided graph meta-learning) MUST be fetched separately to obtain held-out-node metrics and monitored-node counts. Note Moshe et al. HydroNets is cited but never described or given numbers anywhere in this survey. Nothing here supports or refutes the 'topology as cheap FEATURES' option - the survey does not evaluate drainage area / Strahler order / network position as static features at all, which is itself a gap worth reporting: the survey's own repeated finding is that entity-aware DIRECT CONCATENATION of site characteristics is the strong, hard-to-beat baseline, which is the architecture our XGBoost already occupies.

claims.text: The entire study is a subset of the Delaware River Basin with exactly 42 river segments (segment lengths 48-23,120 m, each split to ~1 day water travel time, defined by the National Hydrologic Model geospatial fabric), daily data Oct 1 1980 - Sep 30 2016. Water temperature observations existed for 32 of 42 segments (51,103 observations total, 1 to 9,810 per segment) and streamflow observations for 18 of 42 segments (206,920 observations, 4,877-13,149 per segment). Monitored fraction is therefore 76% of nodes for temperature and 43% for flow - an ENORMOUSLY denser monitoring than an arbitrary Iowa map pin, and node count (42) is the same order as our 85 sites / 19 independent families, so this paper is NOT evidence that GNNs need hundreds of basins. It is, however, evidence that they need most of the graph to be gauged.
claims.nBasins: 42 river segments in 1 basin (Delaware River Basin subset); 32 temp-monitored, 18 flow-monitored
claims.effectSize: n/a - dataset description

claims.text: The paper's headline result ('33%/14% improvement over the state-of-the-art physics-based model and 24%/14% over LSTM ... using very sparse (0.1%) observation data') is measured under a TEMPORAL holdout, not a spatial one: all ML models are global, trained on data from the first 24 years (Oct 1 1980 - Sep 30 2004) and tested on the next 12 years (Oct 1 2004 - Sep 30 2016) AT THE SAME SEGMENTS. The '0.1%' sparsity is a random subsample of labeled site-days within the training period, i.e. sparsity in TIME at already-monitored nodes, not sparsity in SPACE. Exact temperature RMSE at 0.1% labels: PRMS-SNTemp 3.661, ANN 3.706+/-0.114, RNN 3.234+/-0.057, RNNptr 2.818+/-0.059, RGrN 2.849+/-0.049, PGRGrN_ptr 2.556+/-0.045, PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 2.464+/-0.105. At 100% labels the graph advantage nearly vanishes: RNN 1.546+/-0.045 vs PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 1.402+/-0.034 (9%). Streamflow at 100%: RNN 4.406+/-0.064 vs PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 4.076+/-0.059 (7.5%). This headline number is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and must not be cited as ungauged-basin evidence.
claims.effectSize: Temp RMSE degC at 0.1% labels: RNN 3.234 -> PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 2.464 (-23.8%); at 100% labels RNN 1.546 -> 1.402 (-9.3%). Flow RMSE cms at 100%: RNN 4.406 -> 4.076 (-7.5%)

claims.text: The only genuinely spatial-holdout experiment (Section V-C, 'Assessing performance on unobserved segments') covers just FIVE segments (Seg A-E), each held out one at a time by deleting that segment's training-period observations while all other segments keep theirs, then scoring only on that segment during the 2004-2016 test period. Temperature RMSE (degC), With Obs -> Without Obs: Seg A RNN 2.297->3.328, RGrN 2.135->2.749, PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 2.084->2.501; Seg B RNN 1.116->1.384, PGRGrN 1.047->1.205; Seg C RNN 1.082->1.804, PGRGrN 0.989->1.589; Seg D RNN 0.955->1.805, PGRGrN 0.996->1.297; Seg E RNN 1.067->1.646, PGRGrN 1.013->1.345. So the graph+physics model beats the segment-agnostic RNN at the held-out node in 5/5 temperature cases, by 8% to 28% RMSE - a REAL but modest ungauged-node gain, demonstrated on n=5 nodes with no confidence intervals across nodes.
claims.nBasins: 5 held-out segments, one at a time, within a 42-segment network

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT, directly on point for our deployment target: for STREAMFLOW the graph architecture made the held-out (unobserved) segment WORSE than a plain RNN at the one headwater tested. Seg A streamflow RMSE Without Obs: RNN 0.879+/-0.063 vs RGrN 1.271+/-0.035 - the graph model is 45% WORSE. The authors explain: 'Seg A is a head water and has no upstream river segments. Hence, the graph convolution is not helpful for modeling Seg A. Besides, the information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' Only adding physics pre-training plus the contrastive loss (PGRGrN_ptr,ctr, 0.785) recovered and beat the RNN. Also note RGrN alone barely helps at other held-out flow nodes (Seg C 2.151 RNN -> 2.139 RGrN; Seg E 11.828 RNN -> 12.078 RGrN, i.e. worse). Conclusion: the graph term buys nothing at a node with no gauged upstream neighbor, which is precisely the arbitrary-Iowa-map-pin case.
claims.nBasins: 5 held-out segments within 42-segment network; the headwater case is n=1
claims.effectSize: Seg A held-out streamflow RMSE (cms): RNN 0.879 vs RGrN 1.271 (+44.6% worse); PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 0.785 (-10.7% vs RNN). Seg E: RNN 11.828 vs RGrN 12.078 (+2.1% worse)

claims.text: Removing a segment's own observations degrades error at that segment substantially even for the best model, quantifying the irreducible ungauged-node penalty: PGRGrN_ptr,ctr temperature RMSE rises from 2.084 to 2.501 (Seg A, +20%), 0.989 to 1.589 (Seg C, +61%), 0.996 to 1.297 (Seg D, +30%); the plain RNN degrades far more (Seg D 0.955 -> 1.805, +89%; Seg C 1.082 -> 1.804, +67%). The paper states plainly: 'We can observe larger errors produced by all the three models after we remove training data for a segment. This is expected because segment-specific observation data has not been used for refinement of the model.' Also: 'for unobserved river segments, the performance of pre-trained ML models can be no better than physics-based models that can have rather poor performance.' This is independent confirmation of our project's central problem - the between-site absolute level is what is lost when a site's own history is unavailable - and confirms that network topology only PARTIALLY substitutes for it.
claims.effectSize: Best model's own-observation removal penalty on temperature RMSE: +20% to +61% (median ~+30%); RNN penalty +24% to +89%

claims.text: The ungauged-node gain in this paper is NOT attributable to graph topology alone - it depends critically on a calibrated process model providing dense simulated targets everywhere. The method pre-trains on PRMS-SNTemp (Precipitation-Runoff Modeling System + Stream Network Temperature Model, 84 parameters) simulations assumed available 'on every single date from Oct 01 1980 to Sep 20 2016' at every segment, and additionally uses PRMS-SNTemp INTERNAL VARIABLES (shade fraction, solar radiation, potential evapotranspiration) as 6 of the 10 model input features. Removing pre-training (RGrN alone) is what produces the held-out-node failures above. Separately, the authors' own assessment of the other leading river-network GNN, HydroNets (Moshe et al.), is a documented limitation: 'This method focuses on predicting basins that are well monitored and it remains limited in generalizing to different scenarios or learning with less data.' Implication for our project: there is no calibrated, publicly runnable process model for Iowa daily stream NITRATE that could supply the equivalent dense pre-training signal, so the transferable ingredient here is unavailable to us; the residual, cheap, deployable ingredient is topology as STATIC FEATURES (upstream drainage area, stream order, network position, distance to confluence), which NHDPlus supplies at an arbitrary ungauged pin, unlike upstream-sensor-reading features.
claims.nBasins: 42 segments (Delaware River Basin subset); HydroNets comparison basin count not given in this paper
claims.effectSize: Pre-training contribution at 0.1% labels, temperature: RGrN 2.849 -> PGRGrN_ptr 2.556 (-10.3%) -> PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 2.464 (-13.5% vs RGrN). Streamflow: RGrN 6.299 -> PGRGrN_ptr 5.824 (-7.5%)

result.sourceQuality: Primary source, full text obtained. Peer-reviewed: SIAM SDM 2021 (DOI 10.1137/1.9781611976700.69), USGS pub 70247905, arXiv:2009.12575v2. Full PDF text extracted locally via pypdf, including Tables I-IV verbatim - all numbers quoted are exact from the paper, not from abstract mirrors or search snippets. High confidence. Caveats on the evidence itself, not the extraction: (1) the headline 33%/14% claim is a TEMPORAL holdout at monitored segments and is routinely miscited as ungauged-basin evidence - the abstract does not disclose this, only Section V-A does; (2) the genuine spatial-holdout evidence is n=5 segments with no cross-node significance testing, and one of those five (a headwater) is a clear negative result for the graph architecture; (3) exactly ONE segment in the whole dataset was truly never-labeled with sufficient test data, and its result is shown only as a dashed circle in Figure 6(a) with no number reported; (4) the paper does not report AUC/classification metrics or any water-quality constituent - it is temperature and flow only, so transfer to nitrate violation classification is an extrapolation. Node count (42) is favorable to our n=19-families constraint, but monitored fraction (76% temp / 43% flow) is not remotely comparable to an arbitrary ungauged Iowa pin.

claims.text: HydroNets was evaluated ONLY at gauged nodes under a TEMPORAL holdout, never at held-out ungauged nodes. The dataset covers five monsoon periods (Jun-Oct) 2014-2018; the paper states 'We used the first four years for training and the last one for testing.' Every node in the graph is a Central Water Commission gauge with its own water-level record, and each node's model is fit to that node's own labels. There is no leave-node-out, spatial-holdout, or ungauged-basin experiment anywhere in the paper. Therefore HydroNets provides ZERO published evidence that river-network architecture helps at an unmonitored node, which is exactly the deployment target of an arbitrary Iowa map pin.
claims.nBasins: 52 gauged basins total (39 Brahmaputra + 13 Ganga), across 2 regions in India
claims.effectSize: n/a - protocol claim

claims.text: HydroNets requires the target basin's OWN past gauge readings as model input, disqualifying it for prediction at a location with no sensor. The paper states the temporal feature vector 'can include features such as precipitation, temperature, past readings of the gauge itself', and in the experimental setup: 'Every example (i.e., timestamp) in the dataset contains a historical window of length T of the precipitation and past water-levels as the features, and the measurement at t+h as the label.' Additionally, the headline metric R2-persist is defined against a persistence baseline 'that always predicts the future using the present reading of the target label measurement (i.e., y_hat_i^{t+h} = y_i^t)' - a baseline that is undefined at a site with no observations. Both the method and its evaluation metric presuppose a gauged target.
claims.effectSize: n/a - input-requirement claim

claims.text: The per-basin gain of the river-network architecture over a flat (structure-free) linear baseline is small at typical basins and is driven by a handful of outliers. Over all 39 Brahmaputra basins the mean R2-persist improvement is +0.049, but excluding the three largest outliers (Dibrugarh -0.440 -> 0.223 = +0.663; Dholabazar -1.365 -> -1.118 = +0.247; Bhalukpong -0.055 -> 0.163 = +0.218) the mean drops to +0.022. Over all 13 Ganga basins the mean is +0.070, dropping to +0.021 after excluding Kora (-0.542 -> -0.053 = +0.489) and Chillaghat (0.552 -> 0.735 = +0.183). Median improvements are on the order of +0.01 to +0.03 R2-persist. The largest gains occur precisely at basins where the baseline had NEGATIVE skill, i.e. the architecture mainly rescues catastrophic failures rather than improving already-working sites.
claims.effectSize: Brahmaputra mean diff +0.049 (+0.022 excluding 3 outliers); Ganga mean diff +0.070 (+0.021 excluding 2 outliers); median ~+0.01 to +0.03 R2-persist

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT: the river-network architecture made predictions WORSE at 12 of 52 basins (23%). Brahmaputra basins with negative diff: Bihubar (-0.003), Chenimari (-0.019), Chouldhowaghat (-0.001), Margherita (-0.011), Naharkatia (-0.009), Nanglamoraghat (-0.008), Numaligarh (-0.006), Tezpur (-0.056), Tezu (-0.010) - 9 of 39. Ganga basins with negative diff: Hamirpur (-0.002), Shahijina (-0.006), Udi (-0.002) - 3 of 13. The paper's own framing is hedged: 'HydroNets outperforms the flat linear model in a large majority of cases, and provides comparable performance in the rest.' The largest single degradation (Tezpur, -0.056) is larger in magnitude than the median improvement.
claims.effectSize: 12/52 basins degraded; worst -0.056 R2-persist (Tezpur); median improvement only +0.01 to +0.03

claims.text: HydroNets used NO static catchment attributes and only LINEAR sub-models, meaning the paper contains no evidence at all about the between-site / absolute-level problem. The paper states explicitly: 'Note that our implementation of HydroNets (and the baseline) does not include static features' and 'we instantiated HydroNets such that all sub-models are linear.' Adding static basin features is listed only as future work: 'Future work may include non-linear and recurrent sub-models, experimenting in other regions, working with discharge as the label and adding static basin features to the implementation.' The mechanism by which HydroNets gains skill is therefore propagation of upstream GAUGE-DERIVED temporal embeddings downstream - a purely temporal, observation-dependent mechanism, not a static/geographic one. This is directly opposed to the Iowa project's diagnosis that its deficit is in between-site static information rather than temporal dynamics.
claims.effectSize: n/a - architecture/ablation claim

claims.text: The claimed benefit of HydroNets is sample-complexity reduction in a DENSE, FULLY GAUGED tree, not transfer to new locations - and the density requirement is far beyond the Iowa project's 85 nodes / ~40 known edges. The two study regions pack 39 and 13 gauges into single contiguous river trees (every node gauged, in-degree>=1 for most non-leaf nodes), and gains grow as training data shrinks ('HydroNets has a substantial and increasing advantage over the flat linear baseline when the training set becomes smaller', from 4 years down to 1 year of monsoon data). Experiment 1 shows the flat baseline degrades with tree depth while HydroNets 'keeps leveraging information from deeper branches' - a gain that exists only because deeper branches contain MORE GAUGES. The paper's related work confirms the contrasting regime: Kratzert et al. (2019) is described as 'a regional model for hundreds of gauged basins that strongly depends on basin-specific static features', and Shalev et al. (2019) is noted as working 'in the fully gauged setting' with a learned site embedding - a site embedding that cannot be learned for an unseen pin.
claims.nBasins: 39-node and 13-node fully gauged river trees; contrasted with Kratzert et al. 2019 at 'hundreds of gauged basins'
claims.effectSize: Advantage over flat baseline increases monotonically as training years reduced from 4 to 1 (Fig. 5, basins Golaghat, Neamatighat, Chillighat)

result.sourceQuality: Primary source fully retrieved and read. The workshop PDF at the given URL would not parse through WebFetch (returned raw binary), so I downloaded it and extracted the complete text with pdftotext -layout; full text is at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/408994b9-8d9b-485d-9731-ba0bfa7507ce/scratchpad/hydronets.txt. All 8 pages including Appendix C Table 1 (the complete per-basin results table for all 52 basins) were recovered as text, so per-basin numbers are quoted exactly rather than inferred. LIMITATION: Figures 3, 4, 5 and 7 are raster images and did not extract - the depth-ablation curves, the 6-representative-basin bar charts, and the few-samples curves are described only qualitatively in the body text, so no numeric values from those figures could be quoted. This is a 4-page ICLR 2020 workshop paper (non-archival, workshop-track, not a peer-reviewed journal article); it has no DOI. arXiv mirror: arXiv:2007.00595. VERDICT FOR THE RESEARCH ANGLE: this paper does NOT support the GNN-for-ungauged-nodes case. It is a gauged-node, temporal-holdout study whose mechanism is propagation of upstream gauge observations, which is explicitly unavailable at an arbitrary Iowa map pin. It should be cited as evidence AGAINST the architecture route and in favor of the topology-as-static-features route, and its 52-gauge dense-tree setting should be flagged against the Iowa project's 19 independent basin families.

claims.text: HydroNets was evaluated with a TEMPORAL holdout only, never a spatial/ungauged holdout: the dataset covers five monsoon periods (June-October) 2014-2018, with 'the first four years for training and the last one for testing.' Every basin evaluated in the results tables is a gauged basin that was also present during training. The paper contains no leave-one-basin-out, held-out-node, or ungauged-basin experiment of any kind. Therefore its reported gains are gains at GAUGED nodes over held-out time periods, not gains at unmonitored nodes.
claims.nBasins: 52 gauged basins total (39 Brahmaputra + 13 Ganga), all seen in training
claims.effectSize: N/A - this claim is about protocol, not effect size

claims.text: HydroNets' architecture is structurally incapable of predicting at a node absent from the training graph. Each node Hi contains three sub-models, two of which are BASIN-SPECIFIC and have per-node parameters: the combiner FiCMB (which fuses upstream embeddings with static features) and the prediction head FiPRD (which emits the target label). Only the middle 'shared hydrologic model' F_SHA has weights shared across basins. A new ungauged map pin has no trained FiCMB or FiPRD, so the published architecture provides no mechanism to instantiate it. Additionally the paper states 'our implementation of HydroNets (and the baseline) does not include static features' - the only route by which an unseen basin could be parameterised is explicitly absent from the tested model.
claims.effectSize: N/A - architectural claim

claims.text: HydroNets uses the target gauge's own past observations as an input feature, at every node. The paper states the temporal feature vector 'can include features such as precipitation, temperature, past readings of the gauge itself,' and the empirical setup confirms 'Every example (i.e., timestamp) in the dataset contains a historical window of length T of the precipitation and past water-levels as the features, and the measurement at t+h as the label.' The reported metric R2-persist is defined against a persistence baseline that predicts y_hat(t+h) = y(t), i.e. the model is scored on how much it beats simply repeating the site's own current reading. Both the inputs and the evaluation therefore presuppose a live sensor at the prediction location.
claims.effectSize: N/A - input-specification claim

claims.text: Across all 52 basins, HydroNets' gain over a flat linear baseline (which concatenates the same features without using river structure) is small at most sites and concentrated in a few sites where the baseline had catastrophically failed. On the Brahmaputra (39 basins) HydroNets improved R2-persist at 29 basins, tied at 1, and was WORSE at 9; typical improvement was +0.01 to +0.03 (e.g. Dhubri 0.855 -> 0.865, Goalpara 0.851 -> 0.861, Guwahati 0.886 -> 0.911). The headline gains came from basins where the linear model was below zero: Dibrugarh -0.440 -> 0.223 (diff +0.663), Jiabharali -0.014 -> 0.182 (+0.196), Bhalukpong -0.055 -> 0.163 (+0.218), Dholabazar -1.365 -> -1.118 (+0.247). On the Ganga (13 basins) 10 improved, 3 got worse; largest gains Kora -0.542 -> -0.053 (+0.489) and Chillaghat 0.552 -> 0.735 (+0.183); worst regressions Shahijina -0.006, Hamirpur -0.002, Udi -0.002. Results averaged over 10 random initializations.
claims.effectSize: Median diff ~+0.02 R2-persist; 39/52 improved, 12/52 worse, 1 tie; max +0.663 at a site where baseline was -0.440

claims.text: HydroNets demonstrates that river-structure priors can be exploited at SMALL network sizes - 39 and 13 nodes respectively - rather than requiring the hundreds of catchments used by CAMELS-scale LSTM work. The paper explicitly frames this as the mechanism: 'The injection of the river structure prior knowledge reduces sample complexity and allows for scalable and more accurate hydrologic modeling even with only a few years of data,' and Experiment 3 shows 'HydroNets has a substantial and increasing advantage over the flat linear baseline when the training set becomes smaller' when trained on 1, 2, 3 vs 4 years (test set fixed to the fifth year). This is a direct counterexample to the assumption that network-structure methods need 300+ basins - but the sample-complexity reduction is in TEMPORAL samples per gauged node, not in the number of independent spatial units, and every node is gauged.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative from Figure 5 (Golaghat, Neamatighat, Chillighat); gap between HydroNets and flat baseline widens monotonically as training years drop from 4 to 1. Exact numbers only shown as plots.

claims.text: The graph depth over which structure helps is shallow and saturates: in Experiment 1, when predicting at the region drain basin using upstream trees of increasing depth, 'initially both models gain from deepening the tree but while the baseline model starts deteriorating, the HydroNets model keeps leveraging information from deeper branches.' The flat baseline was fixed at depth 2 for all subsequent experiments 'following our previous experiment,' indicating depth 2 was the optimum for the non-structural model. All HydroNets sub-models in this study were LINEAR; the authors list non-linear and recurrent sub-models, static basin features, discharge as the label, and other regions as UNTESTED future work - so no published evidence exists for HydroNets on a water-quality target, with static catchment attributes, or outside these two Indian regions.
claims.nBasins: 2 region drains (one per region), from graphs of 39 and 13 nodes
claims.effectSize: Depth curve reported only as plots (Figure 3, R2-persist; Figure 7, R2); no tabulated numbers

result.sourceQuality: PRIMARY SOURCE, FULL TEXT OBTAINED. The PDF was 2.6MB binary that WebFetch could not parse; extracted locally with pdftotext to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/408994b9-8d9b-485d-9731-ba0bfa7507ce/scratchpad/hydronets.txt (591 lines, complete including all four appendices and the full 52-basin results table). Non-archival 4-page ICLR 2020 AI for Earth Sciences WORKSHOP paper, not a peer-reviewed journal article; no DOI. Authors are Google Research plus Kratzert (JKU Linz, the CAMELS/LSTM author). Caveats for the research angle: (a) all results are R2-persist or R2 against a flat LINEAR baseline, not against an LSTM or any strong learned baseline, so the comparison is weak; (b) key figures (Experiments 1 and 3) are plots with no tabulated values - only Experiment 2's 52-basin table has exact numbers; (c) the target is water LEVEL, not water quality or nitrate; (d) rainfall input is JAXA GSMaP satellite hourly, basins from HydroSHEDS, gauges from the Indian Central Water Commission. VERDICT FOR THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: this paper does NOT support GNN-over-reaches for prediction at an arbitrary ungauged pin. It has zero held-out-node experiments, per-node learnable parameters that cannot be instantiated for an unseen basin, and gauge-observation inputs at every node. Its evidence is that structure improves forecasting AT GAUGES over held-out time. The favourable note is that it worked at n=39 and n=13 nodes, which rebuts the "needs 300+ basins" objection for structure-as-prior generally - but not for the ungauged case.

claims.text: The USGS 2012 SPARROW Midwest models produce simulated mean-daily streamflow plus average-annual total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and suspended-sediment loads on a modified NHDPlusV2 (1:100,000-scale) reach-and-catchment network covering the Great Lakes, Lake Winnipeg, Upper Mississippi, and Ohio River basins — an extent that fully contains Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of Iowa's multi-state basins. The Midwest network contains over 1.36 million catchments with a median catchment size of 1.4 km2 (page states typical watershed size ~2.5 km2). Falsifiable: any Iowa map pin's NLDI-delineated basin should join to SPARROW reaches by NHDPlus COMID, which the project already stores per basin.
claims.nBasins: 1,360,000+ NHDPlus catchments (model network, not calibration sites)
claims.effectSize: median catchment 1.4 km2; 1:100,000 scale NHDPlusV2

claims.text: SPARROW Midwest 2012 outputs are published as BOTH 'incremental' values (generated within the individual catchment only) and 'accumulated' values (total from all upstream sources), plus 'delivery fraction' attenuation factors to downstream targets (Gulf of America, Great Lakes, or the US/Canada border). This means a per-COMID incremental total-nitrogen yield AND an upstream-accumulated TN load are both directly available as candidate static between-site features — exactly the between-site absolute-level information the project's model lacks (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42).
claims.effectSize: n/a — describes available output variables, not a performance gain

claims.text: The SPARROW Midwest 2012 geospatial data (model inputs, model outputs, AND calibration-site information) is released at DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, published 2020-01-07 by the USGS Upper Midwest Water Science Center, marked CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain, no copyright restriction), with direct download from the USGS/ScienceBase data repository and NO authentication required. This satisfies the project's free/public acquisition constraint with no request-to-agency step needed.
claims.effectSize: license CC0 1.0; DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9; release date 2020-01-07

claims.text: The SPARROW Midwest 2012 models represent a SINGLE STATIC 2012 base-year condition, hydrologically normalized to long-term average conditions for 1999-2014 (streamflow simulated for 1999-2014 conditions). They therefore carry NO daily or seasonal temporal signal. Consequence for this project: SPARROW output can only enter as a time-invariant per-site static feature (like lat/lon/log_basin_area), and cannot address WHEN nitrate rises. It is, however, aligned with the project's observed pattern that only geometry and static geography have produced gains while every temporal feature has failed.
claims.effectSize: base year 2012; hydrologic normalization period 1999-2014

claims.text: The SPARROW Midwest page states explicitly that 'the uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model,' and that the smallest calibration sites for the nutrient and sediment models have drainage areas typically in the range of 10-100 km2 (5-50 km2 for the streamflow model). Falsifiable, deployment-relevant test: any Iowa map pin whose NLDI basin is under ~10 km2 falls below the calibration support of the TN model, so a SPARROW-derived feature should be expected to degrade — this predicts a measurable interaction between basin area and any SPARROW-feature gain in LOFO CV.
claims.nBasins: unknown (smallest TN/TP/SS calibration sites 10-100 km2; streamflow 5-50 km2)
claims.effectSize: stated qualitative increase in uncertainty below 10-100 km2; no numeric uncertainty bound given on this page

claims.text: CIRCULARITY RISK IS DIRECTLY TESTABLE, NOT SPECULATIVE: the DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9 data release explicitly includes 'calibration site information' as a published component. Because SPARROW TN calibration loads are derived from ambient stream monitoring sites, some of this project's 85 Iowa nitrate sites (particularly the USGS-operated subset that also supplies the 22 discharge records) are plausibly among them. Falsifiable check before any use: join the released calibration-site table to the 85 site locations by coordinates/COMID; every matched site makes SPARROW output partially label-derived at that site and inflates LOFO estimates, and matched sites' SPARROW features must be treated as leakage under leave-one-basin-family-out CV. NOTE: the primary calibration documentation (Robertson and Saad 2019, SIR 2019-5114, doi:10.3133/sir20195114) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the calibration site count and model R2/RMSE for the Midwest TN model COULD NOT BE VERIFIED from this source and remain unknown.
claims.nBasins: unknown — calibration site count not retrievable (SIR 2019-5114 returned HTTP 403)
claims.effectSize: unknown — no calibration R2 or RMSE obtainable from the accessible pages

result.sourceQuality: Authoritative primary agency source (USGS SPARROW Mapper model-description page) plus its companion USGS data release, both fetched successfully. Sufficient for operational data-acquisition facts: spatial unit, extent, vintage, output types, DOI, license, access mechanism. INSUFFICIENT for performance evidence: the two documents holding calibration statistics — Robertson and Saad 2019 (SIR 2019-5114, doi:10.3133/sir20195114) and Robertson et al. 2021 (JAWRA, doi:10.1111/1752-1688.12905) — both returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to WebFetch, and search-result snippets did not surface calibration site counts, R2, or RMSE. No performance number in this extraction is comparable to the project's LOFO AUC 0.820; none is offered as such. Additionally, a targeted search for published work using SPARROW output as an INPUT FEATURE to a machine-learning nitrate model returned NO such study — that specific combination appears untested in the retrievable literature, so any gain from injecting SPARROW as a feature here is unevidenced and would be a novel experiment, not a replication. The n=19-independent-basin-families constraint does not bear on SPARROW acquisition itself (SPARROW is a pre-calibrated external product, not something this project must fit), but it does bear hard on DETECTING a gain: a between-site improvement must be demonstrated across ~19 effective units, so only a large effect would be distinguishable from noise.

claims.text: The entire study is a single 42-segment river network — a subset of the Delaware River Basin whose segments feed the mainstream Delaware at Wilmington, DE, each segment split to be roughly one day of water travel time. Of those 42 nodes, water temperature observations existed for 32 segments (76% monitored; 51,103 observations total, 1 to 9,810 per segment) and streamflow observations for 18 segments (43% monitored; 206,920 observations, 4,877 to 13,149 per segment), over daily data from Oct 1 1980 to Sep 30 2016 (13,149 dates). This is a SMALLER and DENSER-MONITORED graph than the Iowa problem's ~85 sites / 19 independent families, so the n=19 constraint is not automatically disqualifying here — but note the monitored fraction (43-76%) is far higher than what an arbitrary Iowa map pin implies, and the paper explicitly frames its own graph as tiny relative to real basins.
claims.nBasins: 42 river segments, 1 basin (Delaware River Basin subset); 32 segments with temperature obs, 18 with streamflow obs
claims.effectSize: n/a — dataset description

claims.text: THE HEADLINE NUMBERS ARE A TEMPORAL HOLDOUT, NOT A SPATIAL ONE: all ML models are global and 'trained and applied to all the river segments', training on the first 24 years (Oct 1 1980 – Sep 30 2004) and testing on the next 12 years (Oct 1 2004 – Sep 30 2016). Every test segment therefore appears in training. Temperature RMSE at 100% labels: PRMS-SNTemp 3.661, ANN 1.575±0.035, RNN 1.546±0.045, RNNptr 1.444±0.039, RGrN 1.408±0.068, PGRGrNptr,ctr 1.402±0.034 — i.e. the graph model beats a plain LSTM by only 0.144 degC (9.3%) when data is plentiful. Streamflow RMSE at 100%: PRMS-SNTemp 6.834, RNN 4.406±0.064, RGrN 4.139±0.067, PGRGrNptr,ctr 4.076±0.059 (7.5% over RNN). The abstract's advertised '24%/14% over traditional machine learning' gains are obtained only in the artificially sparse 0.1%-label regime (temperature 3.234 RNN -> 2.464 PGRGrNptr,ctr; streamflow 6.885 -> 5.895), not at full data. These numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820.
claims.effectSize: RGrN vs RNN at 100% labels: temperature RMSE 1.408 vs 1.546 (-8.9%); streamflow 4.139 vs 4.406 (-6.1%). At 0.1% labels PGRGrNptr,ctr vs RNN: 2.464 vs 3.234 temp (-23.8%), 5.895 vs 6.885 flow (-14.4%)

claims.text: The paper's only true unmonitored-node evidence is a leave-ONE-segment-out experiment on just 5 segments (Seg A–E), and it shows the graph helps but that ALL models degrade substantially when a segment's own observations are removed. Temperature RMSE (with own obs -> without own obs): Seg A RNN 2.297->3.328 vs PGRGrNptr,ctr 2.084->2.501; Seg C RNN 1.082->1.804 vs PGRGrN 0.989->1.589; Seg D RNN 0.955->1.805 vs PGRGrN 0.996->1.297; Seg E RNN 1.067->1.646 vs PGRGrN 1.013->1.345. So on held-out nodes the graph+physics model beats the per-segment-agnostic RNN by roughly 0.18–0.51 degC (10–28%), but even the best model loses 20–30% accuracy relative to having the site's own history. Critically, the authors state there was 'only one segment in the data set for which we have no training data but sufficient testing data' — the genuinely-ungauged evidence base is a SINGLE node, and the 5-segment ablation is a simulation of ungauged conditions at sites that are in fact gauged.
claims.nBasins: 5 segments held out one at a time out of 42; only 1 genuinely never-observed segment in the whole dataset
claims.effectSize: Held-out-node temperature RMSE, PGRGrNptr,ctr vs RNN: 2.501 vs 3.328 (Seg A), 1.205 vs 1.384 (B), 1.589 vs 1.804 (C), 1.297 vs 1.805 (D), 1.345 vs 1.646 (E). Mean degradation from removing own obs: RNN +0.69 degC, PGRGrN +0.36 degC

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT — the graph architecture ALONE (RGrN, without physics pre-training) made held-out streamflow prediction WORSE than a plain RNN at some nodes and catastrophically worse under cross-segment distribution shift. On held-out Seg A (a headwater with no upstream segments), streamflow RMSE was RNN 0.879±0.063 but RGrN 1.271±0.035 — the graph model was 45% WORSE, because 'graph convolution is not helpful for modeling Seg A' and 'information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' Worse, in the spatial-transfer experiment where models were trained only on segments with mean flow >3 m3/s and tested on segments with flow <1 m3/s (2005–2016), RGrN scored RMSE 4.073±0.082 versus RNN 3.012±0.432 — the graph model was 35% WORSE than the non-graph baseline, and only recovered (2.099) once physics pre-training plus the contrastive loss were added. This is directly analogous to the Iowa transfer problem: graph message-passing degrades when the held-out node is unlike its training neighbors.
claims.nBasins: 42 segments; held-out low-flow (<1 m3/s) segments trained only on high-flow (>3 m3/s) segments
claims.effectSize: Streamflow RMSE on low-flow held-out segments: RGrN 4.073±0.082 vs RNN 3.012±0.432 (graph 35% WORSE); PGRGrNptr,ctr 2.099±0.088 recovers. Held-out Seg A: RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 (graph 45% worse)

claims.text: The graph gains are inseparable from a calibrated process-based simulator: the best-performing variants (PGRGrNptr, PGRGrNptr,ctr) require PRMS-SNTemp (Precipitation-Runoff Modeling System coupled to Stream Network Temperature Model, 84 parameters) to be run on every date at every segment from 1980–2016 to generate BOTH pre-training targets AND three of the ten input features (shade fraction, solar radiation, potential evapotranspiration), which the authors admit 'are difficult to measure frequently.' Pure RGrN — the architecture-only version obtainable without a simulator — delivered only 1.408 vs RNN 1.546 temperature RMSE at full data and was WORSE than RNN in the two ungauged-transfer settings above. For the Iowa nitrate product, there is no equivalent free, pre-run, per-basin nitrate simulator, so the replicable portion of this paper is the weakest-performing variant.
claims.effectSize: Architecture-only RGrN vs RNN at 100% labels: 1.408 vs 1.546 temp RMSE (-8.9%); with simulator-based pretraining PGRGrNptr,ctr reaches 1.402 (no further gain at full data) but 2.464 vs RGrN 2.849 at 0.1% labels (-13.5%)

claims.text: The paper's topology encoding is a CHEAP DISTANCE-DECAY WEIGHT, NOT learned structure, and longer routing delays monotonically HURT — both of which support using topology as features rather than as an architecture in the Iowa project. Edges are created wherever segment i is anywhere upstream of segment j, and the adjacency is a closed-form affinity A_ij = 1/(1+exp(dist(i,j))) on standardized along-river outlet-to-outlet distance. In the time-delay ablation (Fig. 7c,d), varying how many days prior the upstream information influences a downstream segment from 1 to 5 steps produced 'a general increase of RMSE when we set a larger time delay' for both temperature and streamflow — i.e. multi-day advective routing degraded performance, matching this project's own finding that travel-time-shifted lagged weather HURT (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019). Separately, the authors characterize the main competing river-network GNN, Moshe et al.'s HydroNets, as a method that 'focuses on predicting basins that are well monitored and it remains limited in generalizing to different scenarios or learning with less data' — i.e. HydroNets is NOT evidence for ungauged-node prediction.
claims.effectSize: Time delay 1 -> 5 days: monotone RMSE increase for both targets (figure only, exact values not tabulated). Adjacency requires only NHDPlus-computable along-network distance, no sensor readings

result.sourceQuality: HIGH — full text obtained and read directly from the arXiv PDF (arXiv:2009.12575v2, 8 Dec 2020), the version published at SIAM SDM 2021; USGS-coauthored (USGS pub 70247905), with all six result tables (I–VI) extracted verbatim including standard deviations. No paywall issue. Every number quoted above is read off the paper's own tables rather than the abstract. CAVEAT ON APPLICABILITY, not on source quality: this is a stream TEMPERATURE and STREAMFLOW paper, not a water-chemistry paper; nitrate has a very different (largely land-use and tile-drainage driven, non-conservative) generation process, so transfer of the architecture conclusion to nitrate is an extrapolation the paper does not support. Two further limits for the Iowa deployment target: (1) the paper's graph is DENSELY monitored (43–76% of nodes gauged) whereas an arbitrary Iowa map pin has zero monitored guarantee, and the paper's ungauged evidence rests on 5 simulated-ungauged segments plus exactly 1 truly unobserved segment; (2) every gain requires a per-segment process-model simulation (PRMS-SNTemp) that has no free nitrate equivalent. The paper does NOT report a leave-one-region-out or multi-basin generalization test, so nothing in it is directly comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC.

claims.text: The primary source PDF (Schwarz, Hoos, Alexander & Smith 2006, USGS Techniques and Methods 6-B3, 248 p.) returned HTTP 403 on every attempted fetch (pubs.usgs.gov PDF, pubs.usgs.gov landing page, and the digitalcommons.unl.edu full-text mirror). Only the bibliographic record was retrievable. All SPARROW claims below are therefore sourced from authoritative USGS secondary pages (water.usgs.gov SPARROW FAQ and USGS 'Everything you need to know about SPARROW') and from peer-reviewed SPARROW applications, NOT from direct reading of tm6b3. Treat quoted figures as second-hand and verify against the PDF before citing.
claims.effectSize: source unreachable; 403 Forbidden

claims.text: SPARROW distinguishes CONDITIONED from UNCONDITIONED predictions: conditioned predictions substitute the OBSERVED monitoring-station load for the model-predicted load on reaches that have a station, so downstream reaches inherit an observation-corrected upstream flux; unconditioned (simulated) predictions use only the model. USGS/RSPARROW guidance states conditioned predictions 'provide the most accurate reach predictions... and reduce the downstream propagation of errors,' but 'unconditioned predictions are most representative of the model skill and performance at monitored and unmonitored stream locations.' DECISIVE FOR THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no upstream gauge can only ever receive an UNCONDITIONED prediction. Any published SPARROW or mass-balance accuracy figure that is conditioned on observed upstream loads is not achievable at an ungauged pin and must be discarded as evidence for this product.
claims.effectSize: qualitative but categorical: conditioned > unconditioned accuracy, by construction, and only conditioned requires upstream observations

claims.text: SPARROW's core value proposition is exactly the ungauged-prediction problem: it calibrates a nonlinear regression on a few hundred monitored stations and then predicts flux/concentration/yield on a stream network two to four orders of magnitude larger — ERF1 has ~62,000 reaches (1:500K) and NHDPlus has ~2,600,000 reaches (1:100K). The routing is a mass-balance constraint rather than a learned graph architecture: 'contaminant loads coming from upstream as well as those from intervening stream reaches are balanced against the measured downstream load to estimate the amount of instream loss,' with all sources required to be balanced by attenuation losses. This is an EXPLICIT incremental-area mass balance, i.e. topology used as model STRUCTURE with hand-specified decay terms, not as a message-passing GNN, and it requires no observation at the prediction reach.
claims.nBasins: ~62,000 ERF1 reaches / ~2.6M NHDPlus reaches predicted; hundreds of calibration stations

claims.text: Published SPARROW calibrations use station counts 10x to 40x larger than this project's 19 independent basin families. The multi-agency regional nutrient SPARROW effort compiled 2,739 monitoring sites from 73 agencies across Major River Basins MRB1-MRB7; per-model counts ranged from 178 sites (MRB7, total nitrogen) to 810 sites (MRB3, total phosphorus), against a network of roughly 240,588 watershed reaches. Reported calibration site density ranged from 0.15 sites/1,000 km2 (MRB4, TN) to 1.09 sites/1,000 km2 (MRB1). No minimum-station or degrees-of-freedom threshold is stated; the emphasis is that 'the range of digital stream-reach network sizes is nearly covered by the range of monitored watersheds,' i.e. representativeness of the calibration set matters more than raw count. FLAG: at n=19 effective independent units, this project sits an order of magnitude below the SMALLEST published SPARROW calibration, so any SPARROW-style regression with more than a handful of free source/decay coefficients is likely overparameterized here.
claims.nBasins: 2,739 sites total; 178 (MRB7 TN) to 810 (MRB3 TP) per model; ~240,588 reaches

claims.text: SPARROW's reported goodness-of-fit is high but is measured on LOG MEAN ANNUAL FLUX, a quantity dominated by drainage area and discharge, and is an in-sample calibration fit rather than a spatial holdout: USGS states SPARROW models 'explain about 90% of the spatial variability in the log-transformed values of mean annual flux.' A yield-based comparison (USGS SIR 2013-5103, table 8) reports R2 of yield = 0.908 for the NHD-resolution model vs 0.759 for the coarser RF1 model for total nitrogen, and 0.810 vs 0.712 for total phosphorus — evidence that finer network resolution materially improves the area-normalized (between-site level) term. CAUTION: these are calibration-fit R2 values on long-term mean annual aggregates at monitored stations; they are NOT comparable to this project's LOFO daily numbers, and log-flux R2 in particular is inflated by the area/discharge scaling that is trivially predictable.
claims.effectSize: ~0.90 R2 on log mean annual flux; yield R2 TN 0.908 (NHD) vs 0.759 (RF1); TP 0.810 vs 0.712

claims.text: Two structural limits of SPARROW bound how much of it can transfer to this project. (a) TEMPORAL: SPARROW is a steady-state LONG-TERM MEAN ANNUAL model — 'predictions of nutrient sources and loads reflect long-term mean annual nutrient conditions in streams,' standardized to a base year and de-trended to mean flow conditions. It has no daily dynamics at all, so its routing formulation speaks ONLY to the between-site absolute-level term (this project's weak term, between_r2 0.21) and offers nothing for the daily timing term. (b) ACCURACY AT UNGAUGED REACHES IS COARSE: for the 2012 MARB models, 'the prediction accuracy of the mean annual flux in unmonitored reaches is within 55-76% of the mean (RMSE),' described as ~20% lower error than prior SPARROW models. That is a 55-76% relative RMSE on a long-term annual average — a weak bar, and a realistic ceiling estimate for what pure topology-plus-mass-balance buys at an ungauged location.
claims.nBasins: unknown (Robertson & Saad 2021 MARB; article 403, figures via USGS/search summaries)
claims.effectSize: unmonitored-reach RMSE 55-76% of the mean, mean annual flux

result.sourceQuality: DEGRADED — the assigned primary source could not be read. pubs.usgs.gov/tm/2006/tm6b3/PDF/tm6b3_part1a.pdf, the tm6b3 landing page, and the digitalcommons.unl.edu full-text mirror all returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to WebFetch; only the citation record (Schwarz, G.E., Hoos, A.B., Alexander, R.B., and Smith, R.A., 2006, USGS Techniques and Methods 6-B3, 248 p. and CD-ROM) was retrievable. Substitute sources are authoritative but secondary: the official USGS SPARROW FAQ (water.usgs.gov/nawqa/sparrow/FAQs/faq.html), the USGS 'Everything you need to know about SPARROW' page, the peer-reviewed multi-agency calibration dataset paper (PMC3307626), and search-engine summaries of Robertson & Saad 2021 (10.1111/1752-1688.12905) and USGS SIR 2013-5103 table 8 — the latter two were themselves 403-blocked and their figures come from search snippets, so those specific numbers are the least reliable and should be verified before use. NOTE ON THE RESEARCH ANGLE: this source is the mass-balance/topology half of the question only. It contains NO graph-neural-network content — Jia/Kumar process-guided recurrent GCN (Delaware River Basin stream temperature), Moshe et al. HydroNets, and held-out-NODE water-quality GNN results are absent here and must be sourced separately. The single most transferable idea recovered is the conditioned/unconditioned prediction distinction, which is the exact formal analogue of this project's deployment constraint and should be used as the screening test for every paper in this angle: if the reported gain is conditioned on observed upstream loads, it does not apply to an arbitrary ungauged map pin.

claims.text: The 2012 Midwest SPARROW total-nitrogen model (Robertson & Saad 2019, USGS SIR 2019-5114, DOI 10.3133/sir20195114) was calibrated on long-term mean-annual TN loads at 1,334 monitoring sites and reports R2 = 0.950 for loads and Yield R2 = 0.913, conditioned RMSE 0.487 ln-units (51.8% in real space) and UNCONDITIONED RMSE 0.555 ln-units (60.0% in real space). The distinction is load-bearing for our deployment target: the conditioned number resets predictions to MEASURED loads at upstream calibration sites and is therefore unavailable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin; the unconditioned 0.555 / 60% is the figure that applies to an ungauged reach. These are in-sample calibration statistics on log-space mean-annual loads (which are dominated by basin size); no spatial holdout, no leave-one-basin-out validation is reported, so 0.950 is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC or to any held-out ML number.
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites (of 93,994 original water-quality sites; 1,346 considered). Streamflow model 2,057 of 11,575 gauges; TP 1,344 considered; SS 1,262 considered.
claims.effectSize: TN: R2 0.950 loads, Yield R2 0.913, conditioned RMSE 0.487 ln (51.8%), unconditioned RMSE 0.555 ln (60.0%), mean exponentiated weighted error 1.129. Error is much worse at small loads: unconditioned RMSE 0.65 for TN loads <14 ln-units vs 0.39 for >14 ln-units. Residuals spatially correlated, Moran's I = 0.199 (p=0.0005), with systematic overprediction in the southwestern study area.

claims.text: SPARROW Midwest 2012 outputs are fully public, no-authentication bulk downloads at NHDPlusV2 catchment/reach resolution, via USGS data release Saad & Robertson (2019), DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9 / ScienceBase item 5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3. Files fetched directly over HTTPS (verified 2026-07): mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt (493 MB), _TP.txt (446 MB), _SS.txt (501 MB), _FLOW.txt (270 MB), plus mw_reach.zip (802 MB) and mw_cats.zip (600 MB) geospatial layers and mw_sparrow_model_input.txt (740 MB) containing every catchment-level explanatory attribute used by the model. ScienceBase rightsStatement is null (USGS public domain); item created 2019-04-23. The domain covers ~1.36 million catchments spanning the entire Mississippi River, Great Lakes and Red River of the North basins, i.e. it covers ALL of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of our multi-state basins — which is precisely where our current CDL/N-surplus inner join under-counts. An interactive subsetting alternative (export to CSV/Excel/geospatial by state, HUC, or catchment) exists at https://sparrow.wim.usgs.gov/sparrow-midwest-2012/.
claims.nBasins: ~1.36 million NHDPlusV2 catchments; median catchment 1.4 km2, mean 2.7 km2 (vs 480 km2 mean in the older 2002 SPARROW models)
claims.effectSize: n/a - data availability claim

claims.text: The Midwest SPARROW TN model includes ln(percentage of catchment with tile drains) as a statistically significant (p<0.05) land-to-water delivery variable with a POSITIVE coefficient, derived from Nakagaki & Wieczorek (2016) subsurface tile-drainage extent for 12 Midwest States, extrapolated to NHDPlusV2 catchments by the methods of Wieczorek and others (2019), and supplemented for North/South Dakota with 2016/2012 tile-permit polygons. This directly contradicts our project's assumption that 'NO data source has been identified' for tile drainage: a catchment-level tile-drainage percentage covering all of Iowa is already sitting inside mw_sparrow_model_input.txt in the same public data release, and can be aggregated over an NLDI-delineated basin as a static between-site feature without running SPARROW at all. Note the model's TP counterpart uses the same variable with a NEGATIVE coefficient (tile drains bypass overland flow), so sign expectations differ by nutrient.
claims.nBasins: Tile-drainage source layer covers 12 Midwest states, extrapolated to all ~1.36M NHDPlusV2 catchments
claims.effectSize: Coefficient significant at p<0.05; average coefficient of variation 0.23 across the TN land-to-water delivery variables and 0.22 across source variables. Full TN variable set: sources = atmospheric deposition, wastewater treatment plants, urban+open area, farm fertilizer, manure, fixation, Canada load; delivery = ln(runoff), detrended air temperature, ln(tile drains %), ln(soil clay %), CRP/farm-acre ratio, ln(no-till %); aquatic loss = instream decay for flows <1.4 m3/s, reservoir loss, groundwater-irrigation pumping loss (coefficient fixed at 1.221).

claims.text: SPARROW Midwest 2012 is a STEADY-STATE, long-term mean-annual model and the authors state explicitly that its results 'enable model results to be used to rank areas based on their typical losses of a specific constituent; however, this feature does not allow areas to be ranked during any specific year or season.' Nutrient/sediment models use a 2012 base year with loads detrended to 2012 from the 2000-14 period; the streamflow model uses 2000-14 mean precipitation minus actual evapotranspiration. The report notes dynamic season-to-season SPARROW was still only under development (Smith and others, 2016). Consequence for our project: SPARROW output can ONLY serve as a static per-basin feature (one number per site, constant across all 160,074 site-days) - it can carry no temporal signal and cannot help the within-site timing term. But that is exactly the deficit our diagnostics identify (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42, between_rate_r2 0.24), so it targets the right term; it also means it adds effectively ~1 static column against n=19 independent basin families, so any measured gain will have wide error bars.
claims.effectSize: Temporal resolution: 1 value per catchment for the 2012 base year (nutrients/sediment) and 2000-14 mean (streamflow). Zero temporal variability.

claims.text: CIRCULARITY WARNING, CONFIRMED FOR IOWA: the SPARROW TN calibration loads were assembled from 71 Federal, State, regional, local, Tribal, university and private agencies, and Appendix 3 of SIR 2019-5114 explicitly lists five Iowa contributors - Iowa Department of Natural Resources (IA DNR), Des Moines Water Works (IA DMWW), Iowa Geological Survey Watershed Snapshots (IA GSWSP), Des Moines River Water Quality Network (IA ISUCOE), and Iowa Volunteer Water Monitoring Program (IA VWMP). Some of our 85 Iowa nitrate sensor sites are therefore plausibly among the 1,334 TN calibration targets, meaning SPARROW-predicted TN yield at those reaches is partly fit TO our own observations. Any measured LOFO improvement from injecting SPARROW yield as a feature is optimistically biased at held-out families whose outlets were SPARROW calibration sites. Mitigating detail: the SPARROW site-inclusion screen required >=3 years of record, >=24 samples, >=3 samples in each of four 3-month seasons, a period of record within 3 years of 2012, and a paired streamgage within 40 km with basin-area ratio 0.75-1.33 - criteria that many IWQIS continuous-sensor sites (61 of our 85, no discharge gauge) would fail. The overlap must be measured, not assumed: cross-check our site COMIDs against the calibration-site table in the data release before reporting any gain.
claims.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites drawn from 71 agencies; 5 of the listed agencies are Iowa organizations
claims.effectSize: Unquantified overlap - requires COMID join against the data release to determine how many of our 85 sites are SPARROW calibration targets.

claims.text: The authors caution against using SPARROW at exactly the finest spatial scale: 'most of the sites used to calibrate the SPARROW models were located on medium to large streams and may not represent the smallest streams in the Midwest. For example, for the SPARROW TP model, only 5 percent of the calibration sites were on streams with drainage areas less than about 31 km2 ... caution should be taken when interpreting the finest scale model results (for example, predictions for the individual incremental drainages of the reaches).' They further note that although catchments are ~2 km2, 'much of the source data and landscape data used to describe variability in land-to-water delivery were derived from county-wide averages or totals' apportioned by fine-scale land use - so the apparent 1.4 km2 resolution is partly downscaled county data and does not represent genuine sub-county information. For our arbitrary-map-pin product this means SPARROW-derived features are trustworthy for the accumulated/total-yield value at a reasonably sized delineated basin, but a per-cell incremental SPARROW yield used as a distance-bucket feature would be over-interpreting the product. They also warn against using calibrated SPARROW to predict the effect of adjusting individual land-to-water delivery variables, because correlated delivery variables cause omission and coefficient blending.
claims.nBasins: 1,344 TP sites considered / 1,334 TN sites used; only ~5% of TP calibration sites had drainage area <31 km2
claims.effectSize: 5% of TP calibration sites below ~31 km2 drainage area; unconditioned TN RMSE degrades from 0.39 (loads >14 ln-units) to 0.65 (loads <14 ln-units) ln-units, i.e. small-basin predictions are ~1.7x worse in log-error terms.

result.sourceQuality: Primary source, fully retrieved and read. USGS pubs.usgs.gov and sciencebase.gov both return HTTP 403 to WebFetch; the full 74-page PDF was obtained via curl with a browser User-Agent from https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2019/5114/sir20195114.pdf (45.8 MB) and converted with pdftotext, and the ScienceBase file manifest via the ?format=json endpoint. All figures above are quoted from the primary text (abstract, Methods, Table 1, Table 5, and the 'Model Limitations and Future SPARROW Model Development' section) or from the ScienceBase item record, not from secondary summaries. Authoritative peer-reviewed-equivalent agency report; DOI 10.3133/sir20195114; companion data release DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9. IMPORTANT SCOPE GAP: this source is purely a process-model report and contains NOTHING on the process-guided ML literature (Read/Jia/Karpatne pretrain-then-fine-tune, physics-informed loss terms), nothing on the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy modeling, and nothing on EPIC/APEX/SWAT Iowa applications - those parts of the research question need separate sources. There is also NO experiment anywhere in this report testing SPARROW output as an input feature to an ML model, so this source establishes availability, resolution, vintage, limits and circularity risk, but provides ZERO evidence on whether injecting SPARROW yield improves ungauged-site ML skill. Note also the successor product: Robertson et al. (2021, JAWRA, DOI 10.1111/1752-1688.12905) applies these 2012 models to the Mississippi/Atchafalaya basin, and a newer 2018-base-year Mississippi SPARROW data release exists on data.gov - both worth checking for a more recent vintage than the 2012 models documented here.

claims.text: Topp et al. (2023) compared a recurrent graph convolutional network (RGCN) against Graph WaveNet (a temporal-convolution graph model) for daily stream temperature in the Delaware River Basin. When test data were well represented in training, the two architectures were statistically indistinguishable: test RMSE 1.64 °C (Graph WaveNet) vs 1.65 °C (RGCN). Graph WaveNet outperformed RGCN in 4 of 5 experiments whose test partitions represented unseen environmental conditions (including geographic hold-out scenarios). CRITICAL LIMITATION FOR OUR ANGLE: neither the abstract nor any accessible mirror reports a held-out-UNMONITORED-reach RMSE; the headline 1.64/1.65 °C figures are for monitored reaches under a temporal split, and the paper's contribution is XAI-based explanation of *why* one graph architecture generalizes better, not a demonstration that graph structure enables prediction at unmonitored nodes. Full text is paywalled (Wiley returned HTTP 403), so this claim rests on abstract-level metadata.
claims.nBasins: unknown — Delaware River Basin reach network; the paper's own reach count could not be confirmed from accessible metadata. Associated USGS DRB data releases describe 456 river reaches; the closely related Jia et al. RGCN work used a 42-segment DRB subset.
claims.effectSize: 1.64 °C vs 1.65 °C RMSE (a 0.01 °C / 0.6% difference — i.e. NO architectural advantage under in-distribution testing); Graph WaveNet better in 4/5 out-of-distribution experiments, magnitudes not available from abstract.

claims.text: Jia et al. (2021, Physics-Guided Recurrent Graph Networks, IEEE ICDM/arXiv 2009.12575) ran an EXPLICIT held-out-node ablation: they deleted all training observations for one segment at a time (Segs A–E) and evaluated only on that segment during the held-out test period (Oct 2004–Sep 2016). Stream temperature RMSE degraded for every model when the node's own observations were removed, e.g. Seg A: RNN 2.297 -> 3.328 °C, RGCN (RGrN) 2.135 -> 2.749 °C, PGRGrN(ptr,ctr) 2.084 -> 2.501 °C; Seg D: RNN 0.955 -> 1.805, RGrN 0.902 -> 1.597, PGRGrN 0.996 -> 1.297. The graph model's degradation was consistently smaller than the plain RNN's — at Seg D the graph model gave 1.297 °C vs the RNN's 1.805 °C at the unmonitored node, a 28% RMSE reduction.
