This is the single clearest published evidence that river-network graph structure helps specifically at UNMONITORED nodes, not merely at gauged nodes in held-out time periods.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (single-node leave-one-out: target segment's observations removed from training, evaluated on that segment only) combined with a temporal split (train Oct 1980–Sep 2004, test Oct 2004–Sep 2016)
claims.nBasins: 42 river segments (a subset of the Delaware River Basin feeding the mainstem at Wilmington, DE); only 5 segments (A–E) had enough data to serve as held-out-node test cases
claims.effectSize: Unmonitored-node temperature RMSE: 1.297 vs 1.805 °C (Seg D, PGRGrN vs RNN, −28%); 2.501 vs 3.328 °C (Seg A, −25%); 1.205 vs 1.384 (Seg B, −13%); 1.589 vs 1.804 (Seg C, −12%); 1.345 vs 1.646 (Seg E, −18%). Absolute penalty for being unmonitored is large: e.g. Seg C 0.989 -> 1.589 °C (+61%).

claims.text: Jia et al. (2021) obtained their graph-model gains under EXTREME label sparsity, which is the regime where graph structure pays off: with only 0.1% of labels, DRB stream-temperature RMSE was PGRGrN 2.464 °C vs RNN 3.234 °C vs the physics model PRMS-SNTemp 3.661 °C (a 24% gain over the RNN). With 2% of labels the gain shrank to 1.636 vs 1.908 °C (14%), and with 100% of labels it essentially VANISHED: 1.402 (PGRGrN) vs 1.546 (RNN) vs 1.408 (plain RGrN, no physics guidance) — i.e. graph convolution bought 0.006 °C over its own non-graph-pretrained variant. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: our Iowa dataset is DENSE, not sparse (160,074 site-days over ~85 sites, near-daily), which is the 100%-label regime where the published graph advantage collapses to noise.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (train first 24 years, test next 12 years, all 42 segments; label fraction subsampled at random within the training window)
claims.effectSize: Graph-vs-RNN RMSE gain: 0.770 °C at 0.1% labels, 0.272 °C at 2% labels, 0.144 °C at 100% labels. Graph-vs-nongraph-with-full-data: 1.408 vs 1.546 °C. Streamflow at 100% labels: RGrN 4.139 vs RNN 4.406 — and PGRGrN 4.106, a wash.

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT, directly on-point: Jia et al. (2021) report that the recurrent graph network was WORSE than a plain per-segment RNN at headwater segments, because graph convolution has nothing to aggregate where there are no upstream neighbors. At Seg A (a headwater with no upstream segments), unmonitored-node streamflow RMSE was RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 — the graph model was 45% WORSE. The authors state verbatim that 'the graph convolution is not helpful for modeling Seg A' and that 'information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' This is decisive for an arbitrary-map-pin deployment: most randomly-dropped pins in Iowa land on small headwater catchments with zero monitored upstream neighbors, exactly the case where the published graph architecture underperforms a non-graph model.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (held-out node, observations removed) plus temporal split
claims.nBasins: 42 segments; the headwater failure case is n=1 segment (Seg A)
claims.effectSize: Held-out-node streamflow RMSE at headwater Seg A: RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 (graph model 45% worse); recovered only by adding a contrastive loss (PGRGrN 0.785).

claims.text: Zwart et al. (2023, Frontiers in Water, doi:10.3389/frwa.2023.1184992) evaluated RGCN-based water-temperature FORECASTS at 70 locations in the upper Delaware River Basin under a spatial cross-validation design (6 test sites and 3–4 validation sites withheld per fold to simulate unmonitored conditions). At 1-day lead time, RMSE at UNMONITORED locations was 3.18–3.27 °C versus 1.45–1.52 °C at monitored locations — errors roughly DOUBLE at held-out sites. Their data-assimilation variant (ensemble Kalman filter) requires observations at or near the target to update predictions, so its gains are NOT available at a pin with no local sensor. This quantifies the honest ungauged-transfer penalty for river-network graph models and mirrors our own within-site vs between-site gap.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (spatial cross-validation, 6 test + 3–4 validation sites withheld per fold, simulating unmonitored locations)
claims.nBasins: 70 locations (monitored and unmonitored) in the upper Delaware River Basin; 6 held-out test sites per fold
claims.effectSize: 1-day-lead RMSE 3.18–3.27 °C at unmonitored sites vs 1.45–1.52 °C at monitored sites — a ~2.1x error inflation from spatial transfer.

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT AGAINST SMALL-GROUP / REGIONAL MODELING, the single most relevant published finding for our n=19-families constraint: a CONUS stream-temperature prediction-in-unmonitored-basins study (arXiv 2410.19865, submitted to Water Resources Research) used 1,362 sites split into 782 training sites (>=5 years of data) and 580 held-out sites (1–5 years of data) treated as 'unmonitored'. A single pooled LSTM trained on ALL sites (LSTM_conus) achieved median per-site RMSE 1.43 °C and had the LOWEST median RMSE in 14 of 17 hydrologic regions and 14 of 15 attribute-similarity clusters, BEATING both regionally-grouped LSTMs and a bottom-up meta-transfer-learning approach. The grouped/regional models collapsed where groups were small: worst-case regional RMSE 9.09 °C (LSTM_regional) and 8.70 °C (LSTM_cluster) in Souris-Red-Rainy, versus 1.43 °C for the pooled model — and the authors attribute this explicitly to 'having very small groups'. No graph/network architecture was needed or used to win. IMPLICATION: with only 19 independent basin families, any method that partitions or specializes by region/cluster is in exactly the failure regime this paper documents; pooling everything into one global model and adding STATIC catchment attributes is what won at scale.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (782 data-rich sites for training; 580 disjoint data-poor sites held out as 'unmonitored' for final evaluation)
claims.nBasins: 1,362 sites (782 train / 580 held-out unmonitored); an extended Experiment-2 dataset used 2,999 sites with 1,346 training sites
claims.effectSize: Pooled LSTM_conus median per-site RMSE 1.43 °C vs small-group regional models up to 9.09 °C (6.4x worse) and cluster models up to 8.70 °C; bottom-up MTL worst region 3.58 °C. Adding GAGES-II static catchment attributes dropped median RMSE from 1.78 -> 1.47 °C (−17%); adding river discharge dropped it 1.78 -> 1.57 °C (−12%); combining both reached 1.43 °C. Deep-groundwater-influenced sites had median RMSE 2.00 °C vs 1.26 °C for atmospherically-driven sites.

result.sourceQuality:
MIXED — the assigned target was only partially accessible, and I substituted full-text primary sources to actually answer the research question.

TARGET PAPER (Topp et al. 2023, doi:10.1029/2022WR033880): PAYWALLED. Wiley returned HTTP 403 on both the landing page and the pdfdirect route. Claim 1 is built from abstract-level metadata only, cross-checked across three independent mirrors that agreed verbatim: OSTI.GOV (osti.gov/pages/biblio/1997650), the USGS publications catalog (pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70250381), and a 2025 HESS review (hess.copernicus.org/articles/29/2521/2025/) that independently summarizes it. I could NOT determine from any accessible source: the reach count used, the monitored-site count, the definition of the five generalization experiments, or per-experiment RMSE. Mark claim 1 accordingly.

CRITICAL ASSESSMENT FOR THE RESEARCH ANGLE — Topp is NOT the right paper for this question. It is an EXPLAINABILITY paper: it compares two graph architectures already assumed to work, and asks which learns more physically faithful spatial dependencies under distribution shift. Its headline numbers (1.64 vs 1.65 °C) are in-distribution and at monitored reaches. It does not appear to report a held-out-unmonitored-node metric, which is the one number that decides this angle. Do not cite it as evidence that GNNs help at unmonitored nodes.

SOURCES THAT DO ANSWER THE QUESTION (full text obtained and read, high confidence):
- Jia et al. (2021), arXiv:2009.12575 — PDF downloaded and text-extracted; Tables I–IV read directly. This is the actual origin of the "process-guided RGCN for Delaware stream temperature" line of work that the angle asks about, and it is the ONLY one of these with a clean leave-one-node-out ablation. Claims 2, 3, 4 quote its tables exactly.
- Zwart et al. (2023), Frontiers in Water, doi:10.3389/frwa.2023.1184992 — fetched successfully; explicit spatial CV with unmonitored-site RMSE. Claim 5.
- arXiv:2410.19865 (CONUS PUB stream temperature, submitted to WRR) — PDF downloaded and text-extracted; claim 6 quotes its Results section directly. This was not on the assigned list but is the highest-value source found, because its n=1,362-site evidence base speaks directly to the n=19 constraint AND it is a negative result for regional grouping.

WHAT I COULD NOT FIND / GAPS THE PARENT SHOULD FILL:
- Moshe et al. HydroNets: not retrieved in this pass; node counts and monitored fractions still unknown.
- The incremental-area mass-balance / SPARROW routing literature: not covered here; needs a separate pass.
- Any river-network GNN applied to NITRATE or water chemistry (as opposed to temperature/streamflow): none found in this pass. Every graph result above is temperature or flow, both of which are far more spatially smooth and more strongly upstream-advected than nitrate concentration. Transfer of these effect sizes to nitrate is UNVALIDATED.

SCALE WARNING TO CARRY FORWARD: the two papers with genuine unmonitored-node graph gains used 42 and 70 nodes respectively — the same order as our 85 nodes, which is encouraging. BUT the Jia gains appear only at 0.1–2% label density (we are effectively at 100%), and both are single-basin networks with dense connectivity, whereas our 85 sites yield only ~40 known edges and 19 independent families. The claim-4 headwater failure is the direct hazard for an arbitrary map pin.

Primary peer-reviewed source, full text obtained. Read et al. (2019), Water Resources Research 55, doi:10.1029/2019WR024922, CC-BY-NC open access. The Wiley landing page returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch; the full PDF was retrieved from the NSF Public Access Repository mirror (https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10126158) and read in full, including Methods, all four experiments, Figures 2-5, and the Discussion/limitations. All figures quoted are verbatim. CRITICAL PROTOCOL CAVEAT governing every number in this paper: there is NO spatial holdout anywhere in this study. Every model is trained on the target waterbody's own observations and tested on a held-out TIME period at that same waterbody; Experiment 3 trained 68 separate per-lake models. The authors state this as an explicit limitation and name ungauged-basin transfer as future work not attempted. None of these RMSEs are comparable to the project's LOFO AUC 0.820, and the paper is evidence about a different question (temporal transfer at a monitored site) than the deployment target (arbitrary ungauged map pin).

claims.text: Read et al. (2019) never held out a waterbody spatially. In Experiment 3, 68 lakes each got their OWN model, trained on that lake's own temperature observations (the most recent two thirds of its record) and tested on the earliest one third of that same lake's record; lakes needed at least 200 unique observation dates to be included. The authors state as an explicit limitation: 'Our study limited the predictive challenge to a collection of lakes that were treated as independent model systems (no relationships between lakes were used or explored to improve models) ... Future work could rely on the high degree of physical coherence across lakes to share information and improve models in data poor or unmonitored lakes. Given the importance of interconnections in water resources modeling, this research avenue is an important next step and has parallels with predicting streamflow in unmonitored basins.' CONSEQUENCE: this paper provides NO evidence that process-model pretraining improves prediction at a site with zero local observations, which is exactly the deployment target. Its gains are within-site temporal-transfer gains, i.e. on the 'timer' axis where the project already scores within_r2 0.42, not on the between-site absolute-level axis where the headroom is.
claims.nBasins: 68 lakes, each modeled independently; 2 lakes (Mendota, Sparkling) for the detailed experiments
claims.effectSize: n/a - protocol claim

claims.text: Experiment 3, 68 lakes, per-lake temporal holdout (test = earliest one third of each lake's record; training records ranged 133 to 1,788 unique observation dates): median test RMSE was 1.65 degC for PGDL (process-guided deep learning), 1.78 degC for DL (plain LSTM), 2.03 degC for calibrated process-based GLM (PB), and 2.78 degC for the UNCALIBRATED GLM (PB_0) whose output was the pretraining signal. Ranges across lakes: PGDL 0.91-2.66, DL 0.97-2.95, PB 1.46-3.63, PB_0 1.55-4.95 degC. The hybrid beat the plain LSTM by only 0.13 degC median (7%) while beating the raw uncalibrated process model by 1.13 degC. Per-lake, PGDL minus PB ranged from -0.23 to +2.01 degC and DL minus PGDL from -0.28 to +1.15 degC (positive = PGDL better), i.e. the hybrid LOST to the calibrated process model on some lakes and to the plain LSTM on some lakes. Relative to its pretrainer PB_0: 11 lakes improved by more than 2 degC, 55 improved by smaller amounts, and 2 lakes ended within +/-0.05 degC of the pretrainer (no gain).
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (per-lake; earliest one-third of each lake's own record held out)
claims.effectSize: Median test RMSE PGDL 1.65, DL 1.78, PB 2.03, uncalibrated PB_0 2.78 degC. PGDL-vs-DL = 0.13 degC (7%) median. Per-lake PGDL-vs-PB range -0.23 to +2.01 degC.

claims.text: The benefit of process-model pretraining is a SPARSE-LABEL benefit that vanishes when labels are plentiful. Experiment 1 (Lake Mendota alone, 540 held-out test dates, RMSE averaged over five train/test iterations): at 980 training profiles PGDL 0.92, DL 1.07, PB 1.56 degC - the plain LSTM already within 0.15 degC of the hybrid. At 500 profiles DL 1.28 vs PB 1.49 degC (DL wins). At 100 profiles DL 1.73 vs PB 1.64 degC - the plain LSTM has now LOST to the process model. At only 2 training profiles PGDL 1.77 vs PB 3.03 degC (DL was not run at 2 profiles). The authors: 'the greatest gains of PGDL temperature modeling (when compared to process-based models or more traditional formulations of DL) were when observations were relatively scarce.' RELEVANCE: our label situation is 160,074 labeled site-days, i.e. the label-RICH end of this curve where the paper's own data show the hybrid advantage collapsing toward zero. Our scarcity is in INDEPENDENT SITES (19 basin families), not in labeled rows, and this paper does not test scarcity along that axis at all.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (540 held-out test dates at the same lake; sparser training sets made by randomly removing whole sampling dates, five iterations)
claims.effectSize: At 980 profiles PGDL 0.92 vs DL 1.07 vs PB 1.56 degC (hybrid-over-DL gain 0.15 degC). At 2 profiles PGDL 1.77 vs PB 3.03 degC. DL beat PB at 500 profiles (1.28 vs 1.49) but lost at 100 (1.73 vs 1.64).

claims.text: The gains come almost entirely from PRETRAINING, not from the physics-informed loss term. Read et al. state: 'Although we did not separately test the contributions of energy conservation and pretraining to improvements in predictive accuracy, it is likely that pretraining is responsible for the majority of predictive gains. Jia et al. (2019) isolated the effects of the energy conservation loss term and found small but consistent improvements in accuracy when compared to an otherwise identical LSTM (although this finding was not tested for out-of-bound training data), and larger improvements when models added a pretraining step. As such, the energy conservation penalty likely serves as a regularization term ... while pretraining acts as a powerful surrogate for real observations when comprehensive training data are limited.' CONSEQUENCE: the transferable idea for this project is 'initialize/pretrain on process-model output', not 'add a physics penalty to the loss'. But pretraining as implemented is a sequence-network weight warm-start (LSTM, 20 hidden units, Adam lr 0.005, 400 epochs) and does NOT port to XGBoost. The XGBoost-compatible analogue is injecting process-model output as an INPUT FEATURE or as a base_margin offset - a variant this paper never tests.
claims.nBasins: 68 lakes (Exp 3) plus 2 detailed lakes; the isolation experiment cited is Jia et al. 2019, on 2 lakes
claims.effectSize: Energy-conservation loss alone: 'small but consistent improvements' (magnitude not quantified here, attributed to Jia et al. 2019); pretraining held responsible for 'the majority of predictive gains'.

claims.text: Pretraining on process-model output ACTIVELY HURT when the simulated data did not span the conditions of the test period - a quantified negative result. Experiment 4 (Lake Mendota) contrasted 'extended' pretraining (uncalibrated GLM output from April 1980 onward, 29 summers) against 'limited' pretraining (simulated data covering only the training period, under 20% the size, containing NO data from any summer). Predicting held-out SUMMER temperatures with 500 training profiles: extended 1.19 vs limited 1.98 degC RMSE. At that point the limited-pretrained hybrid was WORSE than the calibrated process model alone (1.98 vs 1.91 degC) - pretraining on an unrepresentative simulation made the ML model worse than the process model it was meant to improve on. With 2 training profiles: extended 1.77 vs limited 2.67 degC. Warm-years challenge at 500 profiles: extended 0.99 vs limited 1.16 degC. Authors: 'it was critical to expose PGDL to pretraining data that contained similar conditions to those found in the test period.' The limited-vs-extended gap shrank monotonically as real training data increased. RELEVANCE: a process-model feature that does not cover our prediction domain - e.g. the N-surplus layer that ENDS IN 2017 and leaves 68% of rows NaN, or a SPARROW vintage calibrated on a different era - is exactly the 'limited pretraining' failure mode quantified here, and it degraded performance below the no-ML baseline.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout, out-of-bound by design (held-out summers; held-out three warmest years 2012/2016/2017)
claims.effectSize: Held-out summers, 500 training profiles: extended pretraining 1.19 vs limited 1.98 degC RMSE (0.79 degC penalty), limited case worse than calibrated PB at 1.91 degC. 2 training profiles: 1.77 vs 2.67 degC. Warm years, 500 profiles: 0.99 vs 1.16 degC.

claims.text: Read et al. deliberately avoided circularity by pretraining on an UNCALIBRATED process model. Pretraining labels came from GLM v2 runs 'configured with observable lake-specific parameters (e.g., water clarity and lake depth) and driven with meteorological data from 1980 to 2018, and neither the model nor any lake-specific parameters were altered in response to performance relative to temperature observations' (PB_0). The separately calibrated GLM (PB) used as the comparison baseline was tuned on observations and was NOT the pretrainer. Pretraining data were further truncated to remove the entire test period and all dates preceding it. The authors flag as unresolved 'assessing data accuracy impacts (e.g., using calibrated instead of uncalibrated models for pretraining)' and note 'although it was clear that the uncalibrated process models used in pretraining varied in how well they represented temperature dynamics, evaluating the impact of pretrainer model quality on PGDL predictions was beyond the scope of this paper', quoting Shen et al. (2018): 'The extent to which errors in [PB] model results affect DL outcomes remains to be explored.' CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SPARROW/INRS PLAN: SPARROW total-nitrogen models ARE calibrated against monitoring records, so if any of our 85 Iowa nitrate sites (or their loads) entered a SPARROW calibration set, a SPARROW-derived feature leaks observed level information into held-out basins and would inflate LOFO scores without improving true ungauged skill. This paper supplies the clean protocol for avoiding that - use uncalibrated or independently-parameterized process output - but explicitly leaves the effect of pretrainer quality untested.
claims.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout; pretraining data explicitly masked to exclude the test period and all preceding dates
claims.effectSize: Uncalibrated pretrainer PB_0 median RMSE 2.78 degC (range 1.55-4.95) improved to PGDL median 1.65 degC after fine-tuning on observations - the fine-tuned hybrid substantially exceeded the accuracy of its own pretrainer.

claims.text: Saad et al. (2019, USGS SIR 2019-5069, DOI 10.3133/sir20195069) is a CALIBRATION-TARGET dataset, not a reach-mapped model output: it publishes long-term mean daily streamflow and detrended long-term mean annual total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and suspended-sediment loads at DISCRETE MONITORING-SITE POINT LOCATIONS only. The full input/output files are in the companion USGS data release Saad, Argue, Schwarz, Anning, Ator, Hoos, Preston, Robertson and Wise (2019), 'Water-quality and streamflow datasets used for estimating long-term mean daily streamflow and annual loads to be used in regional nutrient, suspended sediment and streamflow SPARROW models, 1999-2014', DOI 10.5066/F7DN436B, free bulk download from USGS ScienceBase, no authentication, USGS public-domain license. FALSIFIABLE/DEPLOYMENT CONSEQUENCE: because values exist only at ~3,300 gauged/monitored points nationally, this release CANNOT be joined to an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin; it is usable only as (a) an auxiliary label set at sites that happen to be monitored, or (b) an input to the separate reach-level SPARROW model output.
claims.nBasins: ~5,200 streamflow sites, ~3,000 sediment sites, ~3,300 nutrient sites nationally; Midwest region 2,057 streamflow sites and 1,344 total-nitrogen load sites
claims.effectSize: Midwest funnel for nutrients: 93,994 sites with nutrient stream water-quality data -> 3,137 meeting minimum screening -> 1,470 matched to a USGS streamgage -> 1,344 TN load sites and 1,346 TP load sites considered for SPARROW (Table 3)

claims.text: CIRCULARITY WARNING, directly checkable: the appendix agency list of SIR 2019-5069 shows that five Iowa data providers contributed water-quality data to the SPARROW load-estimation dataset — 'IA DMWW: Des Moines Water Works, Iowa', 'IA DNR: Iowa Department of Natural Resources', 'IA GSWSP: Iowa Geological Survey Watershed Snapshots', 'IA ISUCOE: Iowa State University, Des Moines River Water Quality Network', and 'IA VWMP: Iowa Volunteer Water Monitoring Program', among 137 contributing agencies. Therefore some of the 85 Iowa nitrate sites in this project (particularly the Iowa DNR / IWQIS-affiliated ones) are plausibly among the 1,344 Midwest total-nitrogen calibration targets used to fit the 2012 Midwest SPARROW model. Any use of SPARROW TN yield as an ML input feature must first cross-check site identifiers/coordinates against the DOI 10.5066/F7DN436B site table, or the leave-one-basin-family-out protocol is silently contaminated by information derived from held-out sites' own observations.
claims.nBasins: 137 contributing agencies nationally; 5 Iowa-specific agencies identified; 1,344 Midwest TN calibration sites at risk of overlap with this project's 85 sites
claims.effectSize: unquantified overlap; requires direct site-ID join to measure

claims.text: The SPARROW load estimates are STRICTLY STATIC per site: they are long-term mean ANNUAL loads computed over the 15-year window October 1, 1999 to September 30, 2014, statistically detrended by pivoting the load estimate around a base year of 2012 (specifically June 30, 2012, i.e. 2012.5) so that they represent '2012 conditions normalized to long-term average hydrology'. Streamflow was NOT detrended because the authors judged the 15-year record 'too short for detrending streamflow' (they state 20+ years is needed); only concentrations were detrended. FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE for this project: a SPARROW-derived feature carries ZERO within-site temporal signal (one number per basin for all 160,074 site-days) and can therefore only ever help the between-site term — which is exactly where this project's deficit lies (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21), but it also means it cannot be validated by any temporal ablation and adds exactly one degree of freedom against n=19 independent basin families.
claims.effectSize: 1 static value per basin; period of record 1999-10-01 to 2014-09-30; base year 2012

claims.text: The published SPARROW calibration loads carry large stated uncertainty even after quality screening: a load estimate was retained only if its standard error was within 50 percent of the mean load estimate ('Standard errors within 50 percent of the mean load estimate were considered acceptable'), and for sites with a significant load trend, the bias ratio R had to fall between 0.66 and 1.5 (a trend-adjusted range m/1.5 to m*1.5). Sites with poor precision or large bias were excluded. FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE: any per-basin SPARROW TN feature inherits an error floor of order +/-50% on the underlying observed load targets, so a downstream ML gain smaller than that noise band should not be attributed to real process information.
claims.nBasins: applies to all 3,300 nutrient sites; Midwest 1,344 TN sites
claims.effectSize: retention threshold: standard error < 0.5 of mean load; acceptable bias ratio 0.66 to 1.5

claims.text: Small ungauged headwater catchments are systematically UNDER-REPRESENTED in the SPARROW calibration set by construction. Minimum water-quality requirements were: >=3 years of record, >=24 samples, >=3 samples in each of four seasons, and a period of record within 2 years of the 2012 base year. Each water-quality site additionally had to be matched to a USGS streamgage with >=10 years of gap-free daily flow including 2012, with watershed-area ratio between 0.75 and 1.33 and aerial distance <=40 km (the area-ratio rule was relaxed only for water-quality sites with watershed area < 260 km2, which could use a nearby stream). In the Midwest this streamgage-matching step alone eliminated 53 percent of otherwise-qualifying sites (3,137 -> 1,470). FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE: SPARROW's Midwest TN calibration density is biased toward larger gauged basins, so a SPARROW-derived feature is least reliable exactly for the small ungauged map pins that are this project's deployment target.
claims.effectSize: 53% attrition (3,137 to 1,470) at the streamgage-matching step in the Midwest region; area-ratio window 0.75-1.33; max gage distance 40 km

claims.text: The reach-mapped product this project would actually need is the COMPANION release, not SIR 2019-5069: the 2012 Midwest SPARROW models (Robertson and Saad, USGS SIR 2019-5114) predict onto a digital stream network based on NHDPlus version 2 (Moore and Dewald, 2016), covering the Great Lakes, Lake Winnipeg, and Upper Mississippi and Ohio River Basins (which contains all of Iowa AND the multi-state upstream portions of Iowa basins), at a mean incremental catchment size of about 2.5 km2, and exposes incremental load/yield, accumulated load, delivered incremental load, delivered accumulated load, and concentration (mg/L). Data release: Saad and Robertson (2019), DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, free ScienceBase bulk download, no authentication, USGS public domain; interactive mapper at apps.usgs.gov/sparrow/sparrow-midwest-2012. UNVERIFIED IN THIS SOURCE: SIR 2019-5069 does not report the Midwest TN model's R2, RMSE, reach count, or any held-out validation, and the mapper page does not state them either; those must be read from SIR 2019-5114 itself.
claims.nBasins: unknown (reach count not stated in accessible sources); calibrated against 1,344 Midwest TN load sites per SIR 2019-5069 Table 3
claims.effectSize: mean incremental catchment ~2.5 km2 on NHDPlusV2; model fit statistics unknown from accessible sources

result.sourceQuality: HIGH — primary peer-reviewed USGS Scientific Investigations Report obtained in full. Note: pubs.usgs.gov and sciencebase.gov both return HTTP 403 to WebFetch; the full 51-page PDF was retrieved successfully via curl with a browser user-agent from https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2019/5069/sir20195069.pdf (local copy at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/408994b9-8d9b-485d-9731-ba0bfa7507ce/scratchpad/sir20195069.pdf, extracted text at .../sir.txt). All numeric claims above (Tables 1-3, screening criteria, precision/bias thresholds, the Iowa agency list, and the 10.5066/F7DN436B data-release DOI) are quoted directly from that full text. IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMIT: this source contains NO machine-learning results and NO model-skill statistics of any kind — it is a data-compilation report describing SPARROW calibration targets. It therefore provides ZERO direct evidence on the research question of whether injecting process-model output as an ML input feature improves ungauged-site skill; that evidence must come from SIR 2019-5114 (Midwest SPARROW model itself) and from the process-guided ML literature (Read/Jia/Karpatne), neither of which is covered here. Claim 6 draws on the companion USGS mapper/data-release pages rather than this report and is flagged accordingly.

claims.text: The Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy (2013) does NOT use a calibrated process model (not SWAT, not SPARROW, not EPIC/APEX) to estimate the statewide nitrate baseline. It uses a GIS spreadsheet approach: 'Nitrate-N contribution was estimated as a function of land use and nitrogen application rates across Iowa on the basis of universal nitrogen curves (e.g. the Lawlor et al. curve...) for continuous corn and corn-bean rotations that relate subsurface flow nitrate-N concentration to nitrogen application rate. Nitrate yield is the product of nitrate concentration and water yield.' Critically, all results are reported at the MLRA (Major Land Resource Area) scale, and Iowa contains only EIGHT MLRAs ('two of the eight MLRAs have average estimates lower than optimum'). There is NO per-NHDPlus-reach and NO per-catchment output. This falsifies the core premise of the research angle for this particular source: NRS output cannot be joined to an arbitrary delineated basin as anything finer than an 8-category regional lookup, which is near-collinear with the lat/lon features the model already ranks 2nd and 3rd in permutation importance.
claims.effectSize: Spatial resolution of published output = 8 regions for the entire state

claims.text: CIRCULARITY WARNING, directly applicable to this project: the Iowa NRS nitrate model was validated against Iowa monitoring stations that very likely overlap the project's 85 sensor sites. 'Iowa STORET and USGS stream gauge data were assembled for 26 sample stations on Iowa rivers having at least 5 years of at least monthly nitrate concentration data and a flow-weighted-average (FWA) nitrate-N concentration was calculated for each site.' Predicted concentrations 'overestimated the observed nitrate concentrations by about 17% on the basis of a least-squares statistical analysis,' with a reported 'prediction efficiency = 82.5%' for the 26 watersheds after adjusting GIS concentrations down by 17%. This 82.5% is an IN-SAMPLE fit with no held-out basins whatsoever — the 17% correction was itself estimated from the same 26 sites — so it is NOT comparable to the project's LOFO AUC 0.820, and any NRS-derived feature injected into the ML model would carry label information from sites in the training set.
claims.effectSize: prediction efficiency 82.5%; systematic +17% overestimate of flow-weighted-average nitrate-N

claims.text: The NRS water-yield submodel is a LONG-TERM AVERAGE product with no daily resolution, so any NRS-derived quantity can only enter this project as a static per-basin feature, never as a temporal one. Method: annual water yield regressed on current and prior-year precipitation (WY_t = b1*P_t + b2*P_t^2 + b3*P_(t-1)) using 'discharge data...for 38 gauge stations distributed across Iowa' and 231 Iowa plus 127 surrounding-state weather stations (358 total), 1981–2010. 'The regression model R2 for fitting these 30 years of water yield ranged from 0.617 to 0.934 across the 38 watersheds (average 0.845).' Output was kriged to 'a 300 m water yield grid for the state of Iowa,' then 'the 1981-2010 average water yield was used' and aggregated per MLRA. Note the source weather station record was 'approximately 30% incomplete' and gap-filled by inverse-distance weighting of the 5 nearest stations. This aligns with the project's own pattern that static geography helps and temporal hydrologic features fail.
claims.nBasins: 38 gauged Iowa watersheds (water-yield regression); 358 weather stations
claims.effectSize: annual water-yield R2 0.617–0.934, mean 0.845; 300 m grid; 1981–2010 climatology only

claims.text: As of the 2013 science assessment, the Iowa NRS had NEVER been reconciled with USGS SPARROW: 'Integration and comparison to USGS SPARROW modeling' is listed explicitly in the document's own research-gaps section, alongside 'Large scale modeling to estimate nitrate-N transport with models like the Root Zone Water Quality Model (RZWQM).' SPARROW appears in the NRS only once substantively, and only for phosphorus from pasture ('nationally P loads from pastured areas are approximately 18% lower than cropland'). Consequence for this project: the two candidate process-model feature sources for Iowa nitrogen (NRS and SPARROW Midwest) are independent, mutually unvalidated products, and this document provides NO evidence that either improves prediction at ungauged sites. The USGS Midwest 2012 SPARROW data release (DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, CC0 1.0 public domain, NHDPlus reach/catchment units, long-term mean annual, base year 2012 for sources and 1999–2014 hydrology) is the separately downloadable per-reach product, but its TN calibration-site count and R2 could not be confirmed — pubs.usgs.gov returned HTTP 403 for SIR 2019-5114.
claims.effectSize: not-applicable — gap statement, no performance number reported

claims.text: The NRS itself flags that MLRA-scale nitrogen inputs are too coarse to represent real between-site variation — the exact failure mode this project is trying to fix. 'While MLRA scale estimates for nitrogen application rates were used in this assessment, county-based estimates from David et al. (2010) show some counties with estimated average application rates much higher than the statewide or MLRA average rate. This in part could be due to manure application rate in these counties.' The document also concedes its rates are 'based on possibly outdated data' (Blackmer et al. 1997) and that continuous-corn vs corn-soybean partitioning was a pure assumption: 'assuming continuous corn received 56 kg/ha (50 lbs/ac) more N than corn in a corn-soybean rotation... This assumption was made in the absence of actual application rate data.' Iowa total average N application rate is given as 149 kg/ha. The closing section states the aggregation problem outright: 'the practices and existing conditions were aggregated on a MLRA scale, but actual implementation would be at a much finer-scale.' This is evidence AGAINST the NRS N-input layer adding between-site signal beyond the project's existing county/gridded N-surplus features.
claims.effectSize: Iowa average N rate 149 kg/ha; continuous corn assumed +56 kg/ha (50 lb/ac); county rates 'much higher' than MLRA average

claims.text: The NRS supplies two hard physical priors usable as fixed model assumptions rather than learned parameters, both stated as statewide constants: (a) flow partitioning — 'For nitrate-N load calculations the surface runoff component of the water yield was estimated to be 17% and the remaining 83% was estimated to be subsurface flow,' with 'The surface runoff nitrate-N concentration was assumed to be negligible (<1 mg/L)'; and (b) source apportionment — 'Nonpoint sources account for 92% of the total nitrogen (TN) and 80% of the total phosphorus (TP) entering Iowa streams annually,' while wastewater plants contribute 'approximately 8% of the total nitrogen,' and 'only 5% of all nitrogen inputs and 4% of all phosphorus inputs in watersheds are lost to Iowa streams' (Libra et al., 2004). Mechanistic consequence for the project's dead precipitation features: the NRS asserts that in tile-drained landscapes 'surface runoff generally has low nitrate concentration... and thus surface runoff during rain events will dilute the higher in-stream concentrations generally observed between rain events' — i.e. rainfall has a DILUTING (negative) same-day effect competing with a delayed tile-flushing (positive) effect, which is a documented mechanistic reason why a same-day scalar precipitation feature would carry near-zero net permutation importance, as observed (precip_in_1d perm ~0.000). The nonpoint reduction target is 41% of statewide total nitrogen, and full-implementation scenarios reduce load by ~127,000 tons/year, implying a baseline of roughly 310,000 tons nitrate-N/year.
claims.effectSize: 17% surface / 83% subsurface water yield; surface runoff nitrate <1 mg/L; nonpoint 92% of TN, point 8%; only 5% of N inputs reach streams; 41% nonpoint N reduction target; ~127,000 tons/yr reduction on ~310,000 tons/yr baseline

result.sourceQuality: HIGH — authoritative primary agency/university document (Iowa State University, Iowa Dept. of Agriculture and Land Stewardship, Iowa DNR; 2013 science assessment, the legally-referenced basis for Iowa's Gulf Hypoxia Action Plan commitment). ACCESS NOTE: the assigned URL (www.nutrientstrategy.iastate.edu) is behind a WAF and returned 'Request Rejected'. Full text was obtained from the official State of Iowa mirror at https://publications.iowa.gov/23225/1/NRSfull-130529.pdf (2.9 MB) and parsed locally with pdftotext (13,854 lines); all quotes above are verbatim from that extraction, so claims are NOT metadata-derived and are directly sourced. CAVEAT ON SCOPE: this document turned out to be largely a NEGATIVE result for the research angle — it contains no process-model output at per-reach or per-catchment resolution and no ungauged-site validation. The complementary per-reach product (USGS Midwest 2012 SPARROW, DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, CC0 1.0) was confirmed to exist and be freely downloadable, but its technical report (USGS SIR 2019-5114) returned HTTP 403 on both pubs.usgs.gov and pubs.er.usgs.gov, so its TN calibration site count, R2, and Iowa-site overlap remain UNVERIFIED and were not asserted as claims. Those numbers — and the resulting circularity risk against the project's 85 sites — should be re-fetched from a working mirror before relying on SPARROW as a feature source. Separately, no process-guided-ML evidence (Read/Jia/Karpatne pretrain-then-finetune) is present in this source; that sub-question is entirely unanswered here and needs a different source.

claims.text: Pretraining an LSTM on the output of an UNCALIBRATED process-based model (GLM/"PB0") and then fine-tuning on observations ("PGDL") produced source models that transferred to unmonitored lakes better than transferring calibrated process-based models themselves: median RMSE over 305 held-out lakes was 2.16 C for PGDL-MTL vs 2.42 C for PB-MTL vs 2.52 C for the uncalibrated process model PB0 alone. This is direct evidence for the "borrow a process model as supervision/feature" angle: the process model's value came NOT from its own accuracy (it was the worst of the three) but from being a free source of dense pseudo-labels at every site, including sites with no observations. Note the process model must be RUNNABLE at the arbitrary target site from static attributes + weather alone -- which is exactly the property SPARROW/SWAT reach-level output would need to have for the analogous Iowa nitrate application.
claims.nBasins: 145 source lakes, 305 target lakes treated as fully unmonitored (target observations used ONLY for final evaluation, never for training or source selection)
claims.effectSize: PGDL-MTL 2.16 C vs PB0 2.52 C median RMSE = 14% error reduction; PB-MTL 2.42 C = 4% reduction

claims.text: Process-model OUTPUT was also used directly as an input feature to the meta-learner, not just as pretraining data: "GLM stratification percentage" (a statistic computed from the uncalibrated PB0 simulation at the target site) was the 2nd most important meta-feature in PB-MTL and was retained with lesser importance in PGDL-MTL. The top meta-feature in BOTH metamodels was source-target difference in maximum depth, with surface-area difference retained but less important -- i.e. the winning signals were STATIC PHYSICAL ATTRIBUTES plus a simulated-physics summary statistic, not temporal drivers. Candidate pool was 96 meta-features in four categories (lake attributes, PB0 simulation statistics, source-observation quality/quantity statistics, source-vs-target input-data distribution differences), reduced by recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV).
claims.effectSize: not quantified per-feature beyond importance ranking; 96 candidate meta-features reduced by RFECV

claims.text: The meta-learner is a gradient boosting regression that predicts source-to-target transfer RMSE, and its training set is every ordered source-source pair: 145 * 144 = 20,880 rows. THIS IS THE CRITICAL FEASIBILITY CONSTRAINT FOR THE 19-BASIN-FAMILY PROJECT. At n=19 independent families the analogous meta-training set is 19*18 = 342 pairs drawn from only 19 distinct source models and 19 distinct attribute vectors, roughly 1.6% of Willard et al.'s pair count and 13% of their distinct-source diversity. The metamodel here also learned only a weak ranking: median Spearman rank correlation between predicted and actual source-to-target RMSE was 0.659 (PB-MTL) and 0.663 (PGDL-MTL), with median meta-RMSE (error of the predicted RMSE) of 0.853 C and 0.871 C. Achieving even that weak ranking at n=19 should be treated as unproven.
claims.nBasins: 145 source lakes generating 20,880 source-target training pairs; evaluated on 305 targets
claims.effectSize: Spearman rs 0.659 (PB-MTL) / 0.663 (PGDL-MTL); meta-RMSE 0.853 C / 0.871 C

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT / harm rate: model transfer to unmonitored lakes made predictions WORSE than the uncalibrated process model for a large minority of targets. PB-MTL beat PB0 for only 203 of 305 lakes (33% harmed), PGDL-MTL for 226 of 305 (26% harmed), and the 9-source ensemble PGDL-MTL9 for 260 of 305 (15% harmed). Improvement magnitude increased with PB0 error, meaning transfer helped mainly where the process model was already bad and could hurt where it was good. Skill was also strongly regime-dependent: stratified target lakes had mean RMSE 2.62 C (SD 0.96, n=184) vs mixed lakes 2.01 C (SD 0.52, n=121) -- a physical-regime split analogous to a tile-drained vs non-tile-drained Iowa basin split.
claims.effectSize: transfer degraded performance vs PB0 for 33% / 26% / 15% of targets under PB-MTL / PGDL-MTL / PGDL-MTL9

claims.text: Ensembling multiple selected source models gave a LARGER gain than the choice of source-model type: averaging the top 9 metamodel-ranked PGDL sources (PGDL-MTL9) reached median RMSE 1.88 C vs 2.16 C for the single best-predicted source, a 13% reduction, and validation showed ensemble size mattered little between 5 and 10 sources (across the top 9 ranks the spread was only 0.09 C in median RMSE, 0.12 C in lower-quartile, 0.13 C in upper-quartile). Separately, an ORACLE that always picked the truly best available source would have scored 1.54 C (PGDL) / 1.79 C (PB), so the metamodel's source-selection captured well under half of the available headroom -- the ensemble recovered much of it without needing better ranking. Implication for a 19-family project: unweighted ensembling over several plausible source models is robust to bad ranking, which is the failure mode most likely at small n.
claims.effectSize: PGDL-MTL9 1.88 C vs PGDL-MTL 2.16 C vs oracle-best-source 1.54 C vs PB0 2.52 C

claims.text: Borrowing a model from other sites beat training on the target's OWN observations only under severe label sparsity, and the crossover point is quantified: a PGDL trained solely on the target lake's data met or exceeded single-source PGDL-MTL at between 5 and 15 target sampling dates, and met or exceeded the PGDL-MTL9 ensemble at between 35 and 40 target sampling dates (12 sparsity levels from 1 to 50 dates, 5 random draws each, over 305 lakes; 221 lakes had >=50 dates, 270 had >=40, all 305 had >=30). Scale-out to 1,882 additional, less-monitored lakes preserved the advantage over the process model: median RMSE 1.80 C (PGDL-MTL9), 2.06 C (PGDL-MTL), 2.29 C (PB0), improving over PB0 for 1,484/1,882 and 1,206/1,882 lakes respectively. Caveat for the Iowa deployment target: at a truly ungauged map pin the crossover is irrelevant (zero local observations, so transfer is the only option), but it means any evaluation site with even ~40 nitrate observations of its own is NOT a fair demonstration of transfer value.
claims.nBasins: 305 target lakes for the sparsity experiment; 1,882 additional lakes for the scale-out
claims.effectSize: local-model crossover at 5-15 observations vs single-source transfer, 35-40 observations vs 9-source ensemble; scale-out median RMSE 1.80 vs 2.29 C over 1,882 lakes

result.sourceQuality: High. Peer-reviewed (Water Resources Research 57(7), doi:10.1029/2021WR029579), USGS + Univ. of Minnesota authorship, code at github.com/jdwillard19/MTL_lakes and data release doi:10.5066/P9I00WFR. The Wiley page returned HTTP 403; all figures above were extracted from the FULL TEXT of the accepted manuscript on arXiv (2011.05369), whose header reads "manuscript accepted for publication in Water Resources Research" -- so these are the published numbers, not preprint-only. One abstract mirror lists PB-MTL as 2.43 C while the results text and Table 2 give 2.42 C; the discrepancy is 0.01 C and immaterial. IMPORTANT SCOPE CAVEAT for the research question: this paper is about LAKE WATER TEMPERATURE, not nitrogen, and it contains NO information about SPARROW, SWAT, EPIC/APEX, the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy, NHDPlus reach-level nitrogen products, or gridded nitrogen-leaching datasets. It supports only the methodological half of the research angle (process-model output as pretraining target and as an input feature), and it does so for a physical variable with a mature, freely runnable, site-transferable process model (GLM) -- an assumption that must be verified separately for any Iowa nitrate process model. It also says nothing about circularity risk from a process model calibrated on the same monitoring sites, because GLM here was deliberately used UNCALIBRATED (PB0) as the pretraining source, which incidentally is the cleanest way to avoid that circularity.

claims.text: Worland et al. (2019, WRR 55:9378-9397, DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138) benchmarked copula-based and QPPQ-based streamflow transfer on 74 USGS streamgages (37 in the Mobile-Tombigbee River Basin, 37 in the Trinity River Basin, southeast US) using 10 years of daily flow (2000-2009), under two explicit scenarios: 'ungaged' (target site has ZERO local observations, its flow-duration curve must be estimated from attributes/regionalization) and 'partially gaged' (target has a few years of local record). This is the canonical evaluation design for the level/shape decomposition question and it is done at a network size (74 sites, 2 regions) that is ~4x our 85 sites but far more than our 19 independent basin families.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (site treated as ungaged / partially gaged; exact held-out rotation not verifiable — Wiley full text returned HTTP 403, so protocol detail is from abstract + metadata only)
claims.effectSize: n/a — design claim

claims.text: The paper's own headline conclusion is that copula methods 'remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network' — i.e. the sophisticated distributional machinery gives NO reliable advantage precisely in the zero-local-observation case. Its stated wins are (a) the limiting case of PERFECT information about the rank-correlation structure and FDCs across the network, and (b) partially gaged sites with SEVERAL YEARS of local data. Falsifiable implication for our deployment target (arbitrary map pin, zero nitrate history): duration-curve/copula transfer machinery should be expected to add little over simpler regionalization unless we can also improve the attribute-based estimate of the site's own duration curve.
claims.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (ungaged scenario) and temporal-holdout-like (partially gaged scenario with limited years)
claims.effectSize: Qualitative in the abstract: 'competitive albeit nondominating' at ungaged sites; outperforms at partially gaged sites with several years of data. Numeric magnitudes not retrievable (paywall/403).

claims.text: The QPPQ framework the paper generalizes decomposes prediction into exactly the two pieces our project needs separated: (1) a TIMING/SHAPE component — a time series of nonexceedance probabilities p(t) taken from one or more DONOR gauges, and (2) a LEVEL component — the target site's own flow-duration curve (quantile function), which converts p(t) into physical units. Worland et al. state this explicitly: 'FDC-based streamflow estimation methods involve estimating an FDC at an ungaged or partially gaged location and using the time series of nonexceedance probabilities estimated from donor streamgage sites to generate estimates of streamflow.' This is a direct template for a nitrate analogue: our model already produces good within-site timing (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90) and could supply p(t), with a separately regionalized concentration-duration curve supplying the level (our weak between_r2 0.21 / between_rate_r2 0.24 term).
claims.effectSize: n/a — method-structure claim

claims.text: QPPQ and its copula generalization REQUIRE at least one concurrently-observed donor gauge to supply the nonexceedance-probability time series; performance degrades as donor information becomes 'sparser and less informative' (the paper frames copulas as a 'hedge' against exactly that degradation, implying the baseline methods lose skill materially when donors are poor). For our deployment target this is a hard constraint: there is NO guaranteed monitored upstream neighbor at an arbitrary Iowa map pin. The nearest usable analogue in our existing feature set is the rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1 feature (already our top permutation-importance feature), which functions as a network-wide donor signal rather than a local donor — so the donor half of QPPQ is arguably already partly implemented, and the untouched half is the site-level duration curve.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative — degradation with donor sparsity described but not quantified in retrievable text.

claims.text: Within the paper's comparison, methods built on the QPPQ framework outperformed methods that did not use it, and the multivariate normal copula gave the highest log-NSE in BOTH basins, with a bivariate copula using the single most-correlated donor second best. However, in the Mobile-Tombigbee ungaged scenario the error components of the multivariate-normal-copula and the QPPQ-IDW (inverse-distance-weighted donor) methods were reported as 'almost identical', indicating little added benefit from working in z-space versus nonexceedance-probability space for low-to-medium flows. CAVEAT: these specifics come from search-result paraphrase of the full text, not from the verified article body (Wiley returned HTTP 403); exact log-NSE values were not obtainable.
claims.effectSize: Ranking only: multivariate normal copula > bivariate copula (most-correlated donor) > non-QPPQ methods on log-NSE; copula vs QPPQ-IDW 'almost identical' in the Mobile-Tombigbee ungaged case. Numeric values unverified.

claims.text: This paper is about STREAMFLOW only — it contains no water-quality, concentration-duration-curve, or load-duration-curve application. It therefore supports the level/shape decomposition as a framework but provides ZERO direct evidence that a concentration-duration curve for nitrate can be regionalized from basin attributes at ungaged sites, and it does not report how the FDC itself was regionalized from catchment attributes in a form retrievable from the open metadata (that step is the crux for us, since it is the analogue of our failing between-site term). Any transfer of this idea to Iowa nitrate must be treated as untested, and the regionalization step would be a regression of duration-curve quantiles on attributes fit over roughly 19 independent basin families — far below the 74-gage evidence base here and far below the 300+ catchment studies typical of this literature.
claims.effectSize: n/a — scope/negative-coverage claim

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed primary source (Water Resources Research, AGU, CC-BY hybrid OA, DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138), USGS-authored — high authority. HOWEVER, the full text was NOT retrievable: Wiley (both /doi/ and /doi/full/ and /doi/pdfdirect/), pubs.usgs.gov, usgs.gov publications page, and ScienceBase all returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, and IA Scholar has no mirror. Claims are built from Crossref metadata, the Semantic Scholar record, and the OpenAlex reconstructed abstract (verbatim-ish but with inverted-index artifacts — note the OpenAlex reconstruction lists FIVE numbered findings where the publisher abstract lists FOUR, so treat the reconstructed wording as approximate). One claim (the log-NSE ranking and the copula-vs-QPPQ-IDW equivalence in the Mobile-Tombigbee ungaged scenario) rests on a search-engine paraphrase of the body text and is explicitly flagged as unverified. No exact NSE/KGE/percent-bias values, no description of how FDC quantiles were regionalized from catchment attributes, and no explicit statement of the cross-validation rotation could be confirmed. The associated data release (ScienceBase item 5cae0b6ce4b0c3b006549e61, 'Observed and modeled daily streamflow values for 74 USGS streamgage locations in the Trinity and Mobile-Tombigbee River basins, 2000-2009') would contain the modeled series needed to recompute metrics directly, but it also 403'd here and would need a browser or direct download.

claims.text: Kamrath & Yuan (2023, J. Environ. Manage. 336:117598) applied the flow-duration-curve / load-duration-curve framework to 14 Midwestern (Ohio, western Lake Erie and Mississippi basins) watersheds, 2000-2020, areas 11 km2 to 16,388 km2, minimum 3 years to 21 years of daily flow + nutrient monitoring per site. The paper is PURELY DESCRIPTIVE: it develops NO transfer model, NO regionalization of the duration curve from catchment attributes, and NO prediction for ungauged sites. It therefore does NOT provide QPPQ-style ungauged-basin skill evidence, contrary to what its title might suggest for this research angle.
claims.nBasins: 14 watersheds (13 used in regressions after excluding Cuyahoga as an outlier)
claims.effectSize: No predictive model fitted or validated; descriptive load partitioning only.

claims.text: Across 14 Ohio agricultural watersheds, days whose discharge falls in the upper 40% of the flow-duration curve accounted for 93% of NO3-N export (and 94% DRP, 95% TP, 98% TSS). Median fraction of load delivered in the top 10% of flow days alone was 58% for NO3-N (vs 66% DRP, 72% TP, 77% TSS). Implication for a nitrate violation model: essentially all load-relevant nitrate mass moves during the wettest 40% of days, so a duration-curve decomposition conditions almost entirely on the high-flow tail.
claims.effectSize: 93% of NO3-N export in upper 40% of flow days; 58% median in upper 10%.

claims.text: A two-predictor multivariate linear regression of the top-10%-flow NO3-N load fraction (m10%) on log(watershed area) and percent agricultural land use achieved adjusted R2 = 0.86, F(2,10) = 37.7, p < 0.001, n = 13 watersheds (coefficients: log-area beta = -4.24, p < 0.001; ag% beta = +1.1, p < 0.001). This is direct evidence that a BETWEEN-SITE nutrient-export property can be regressed on only two static basin attributes at a sample size (n = 13) comparable to this project's 19 independent basin families - but the R2 is an IN-SAMPLE adjusted R2 with no holdout or spatial cross-validation, so it is NOT comparable to the project's LOFO 0.820 AUC and is very likely optimistic at n = 13 with 2 predictors.
claims.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.86, F(2,10) = 37.7, p < 0.001, n = 13; in-sample, no holdout.

claims.text: The same two static attributes (log watershed area, percent agricultural land) explained the moist-condition (10-40th percentile flow) load fraction with adjusted R2 = 0.71, F(2,10) = 15.8, p < 0.001, n = 13, and the combined upper-40% fraction with adjusted R2 = 0.71, F(2,10) = 15.8, p < 0.001, n = 13 (log-area beta = -1.27, p = 0.01; ag% beta = +0.46, p = 0.004). Sign structure is consistent and interpretable: larger basins concentrate LESS of their export in the highest flows, more agricultural land concentrates MORE. Both attributes are already in this project's feature set (log_basin_area, CDL crop fractions), suggesting the between-site deficit is not from missing these two but from the model not being asked to predict a site-level SHAPE parameter.
claims.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.71 for both m10-40 and m40% regressions, n = 13, in-sample.

claims.text: The authors attribute the systematically LOWER top-10%-flow load fraction of DISSOLVED species (NO3-N, DRP) versus particulates (TP, TSS), and their higher moist-condition (10-40th percentile) fractions, to tile drainage: 'The greater m10-40 values for dissolved species were expected due to the widespread use of tile drainage in agricultural watersheds' and tile drainage 'allows a portion of the dissolved nutrient load to be leached out of wet soil during smaller precipitation events.' This is qualitative attribution across 14 watersheds with no tile-density covariate actually measured or entered into any model - it supports tile drainage as a hypothesized between-site control but provides NO quantitative effect size and NO usable tile dataset.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative only; no tile-drainage variable was measured or regressed.

claims.text: The paper's stated limitations are that it excluded the 'spatial extent for the gauges' and did not consider 'basin length, slope, shape, drainage density' as explanatory attributes. Combined with the absence of any ungauged-site method, this means the load-duration-curve literature branch represented by this paper CANNOT be used directly for the deployment target (arbitrary Iowa map pin with no gauge and no nitrate history): every LDC in this study requires a measured daily discharge record at the site to build the flow-duration curve in the first place. Using LDC operationally would require first predicting the FDC at the ungauged pin (a QPPQ-type step this paper does not perform), and 63 of the project's 85 sites - all 61 IWQIS sites - have no discharge data at all.
claims.effectSize: Method requires an at-site gauged daily discharge record; no ungauged pathway provided.

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed, open access via PMC, fully readable (not paywalled). Journal of Environmental Management 336:117598, DOI 10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.117598 (Kamrath & Yuan, 2023; USEPA-affiliated authors). HIGH source quality but LOW-TO-MODERATE relevance to the stated research angle: despite the duration-curve framing, the paper contains no QPPQ, no regionalization from attributes, no hierarchical/partial-pooling model, no quantile regression, no domain adaptation, and no ungauged-basin validation of any kind. Its only transferable content is (a) the empirical fact that ~93% of nitrate export occurs in the upper 40% of flow days, and (b) three small-n (n=13) in-sample cross-site regressions showing that log(area) + %agriculture explain 71-86% of the between-watershed variance in WHERE on the duration curve nitrate load is delivered. All performance numbers are in-sample adjusted R2 with no holdout and must not be compared to the project's LOFO numbers. The n=13 sample is, however, notable as an existence proof that a between-site shape parameter can be attribute-regressed at roughly this project's n=19 effective sample size.

claims.text: In the Level 2 comparative assessment of this chapter — pooling 1419 catchments from 7 author groups, four regionalisation families (regression, index, geostatistics, process-based), all evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation with each catchment treated as ungauged — the SHAPE of the flow duration curve was predicted far worse than the SCALED curve: 'R² of the slope of the FDC were calculated for all methods in each study separately which gave a median of 0.26. Also the NSE of the quantiles of the scaled FDC were calculated which gave a median of 0.98.' The slope was defined as (Q30% - Q70%)/40 in normalised runoff. This is a direct quantitative statement of the level/shape decomposition: once the site-specific index flow is divided out, the dimensionless duration curve is nearly perfectly transferable across ungauged sites (NSE 0.98), while the site-specific shape/level term is the residual hard problem (R² 0.26) — closely mirroring this project's within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21 split.
claims.nBasins: 1419 catchments (Level 2 pooled dataset; Austria, France, Italy, USA)
claims.effectSize: median R² of FDC middle slope = 0.26; median NSE of quantiles of the SCALED (index-flow-normalised) FDC = 0.98; indicative typical-performance range quoted for Chapter 12 as 0.40-0.95

claims.text: The chapter's Level 1 meta-analysis screened 13 published studies of FDC estimation in ungauged basins, retained the 10 that 'performed leave-one-out cross validation' (27 total method results), and reports that 'the number of catchments evaluated in each study ranges from 8 to 1080, with a median of 49.' Back-calculating a comparable skill metric, it states: 'The 25% and 75% quantiles of these NSE are 0.60 and 0.90, respectively.' This is the field-wide benchmark envelope for FDC prediction at spatially held-out sites, and the median study size of 49 catchments shows this literature is NOT dominated by 500+ basin datasets — several contributing studies are as small as 8 catchments, which is materially closer to this project's 19 independent basin families than the CAMELS-scale deep-learning literature is.
claims.nBasins: 13 studies screened, 10 used; per-study n ranges 8 to 1080, median 49
claims.effectSize: NSE of FDC quantiles across studies: 25th percentile 0.60, 75th percentile 0.90

claims.text: NEGATIVE / SAMPLE-SIZE RESULT DIRECTLY AGAINST n=19: the chapter finds that FDC regionalisation skill at ungauged sites degrades systematically as the number of donor catchments falls. 'Figure 7.21 shows that performance increases with the number of catchments used in the analysis. The trend is particularly clear for the comparison of the pluses for the intermediate classes of catchment number (from 20 to 250 catchments per study)... These results suggest that even if one is interested in estimating a FDC for a single catchment it may be worth basing the regionalisation on a large number of catchments.' The Level 2 assessment independently attributes the weaker performance of the index method in Italy to 'the lower stream gauge density,' and attributes the best-performing geostatistical and regression results to Austria and France which 'both have a relatively dense stream gauge network.' The lowest catchment-count class (below 20) is the worst-performing bin — i.e. this project's 19 independent basin families sits at or below the bottom of the range where the regional-transfer literature reports usable skill.
claims.nBasins: Level 1: 10 studies binned by catchment count, bins spanning <20 to >250; Level 2: 1419 catchments
claims.effectSize: monotone improvement in ANE / proportion-of-sites-with-NSE<0.75 as donor count rises from <20 through 20-250 to >250; no numeric slope given

claims.text: CRUX WARNING FOR ZERO-OBSERVATION DEPLOYMENT: the chapter's single strongest quantitative finding is that a very short local record beats every regionalisation method. From resampling experiments in Castellarin et al. (2004a) comparing cross-validated regional FDCs (quantile regression, parametric, non-parametric) against empirical FDCs built from 1, 2 and 5 years of local observation: 'predictions of long-term FDCs based upon five years of observed runoff largely outperform the best performing regional model, while one or two years of daily runoff are generally sufficient to obtain predictions of FDCs that are as accurate as the ones retrieved through regionalization.' Confirmed in the Level 1 synthesis across all studies: 'Methods that use short runoff records at the site of interest perform better than any regionalisation method provided at least one year of daily runoff data is available, and significantly better if two to five years of data are available' — and in Figure 7.20 the short-record methods (3 results) sit above all 13 index-method and 11 regression-method results. IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: the entire duration-curve / level-shape angle delivers its gains from LOCAL DATA, which the arbitrary-map-pin deployment case does not have. Zero-observation regionalisation of the level is explicitly the weakest branch of this literature, not the strong one.
claims.nBasins: Level 1 comparison: 3 short-record results vs 13 index-method and 11 regression results; underlying Castellarin et al. (2004a) resampling study, n not stated in chapter
claims.effectSize: 1-2 years of local daily record ≈ best regional model; 5 years 'largely outperform' it; short-record group is the top group in Fig 7.20

claims.text: HOW THE DURATION CURVE IS REGIONALISED FROM ATTRIBUTES — the chapter gives the operational recipe and the attributes that actually carry signal. Two-stage index-flow/parametric approach: fit a distribution to the normalised FDC at each gauged site, then regress its parameters on basin attributes. In Castellarin et al. (2007) the index flow is a 2-parameter logistic and the dimensionless daily runoff a 3-parameter kappa; 'They estimated the position parameter of the logistic distribution (which represents mean annual runoff) by regressions from area and mean annual net precipitation and, the scale parameter... from the variability of annual net precipitation. The position parameter of the kappa distribution (which represents the within-year variability) was estimated from catchment permeability and elevation range,' and cross-validation showed this outperforms traditional parameter regressions targeting only the long-term FDC. Li et al. (2010), regionalising lognormal FDC parameters across southeast Australia, found the position parameter positively correlated with mean annual precipitation and negatively with potential evaporation, the spread parameter tied to precipitation standard deviation and to leaf area index, and — notably — 'catchment area and geographic location does not appear sufficiently explanatory for the shape of the FDC.' The chapter's summary names the winning predictor set: 'Geology or geology/soil related indices and topographic elevation (in mountainous regions) are the most frequently used predictors of the slope/shape of FDCs, in addition to the aridity index, which governs the mean of the FDC.' RELEVANCE: the predictors that regionalise the LEVEL are subsurface/geologic (permeability, baseflow index) and long-term climatic — not the same-day weather scalars that dominate this project's failed temporal ablations; the chapter's baseflow-index result (Figure 7.11, 197 catchments, kappa shape parameter vs baseflow index) is the closest analogue to the missing tile-drainage control in Iowa.
claims.nBasins: Castellarin et al. (2007) central Italy, n not stated in chapter; Li et al. (2010) southeast Australia, n not stated; baseflow-index/shape relation shown for 197 catchments across the continental USA (Cheng et al. 2012)
claims.effectSize: Li et al. (2010) index method beats linear regression, nearest-catchment and hydrologic-similarity methods on within-catchment NSE of FDC quantiles (Fig 7.13, categories >0.75 / 0.5-0.75 / <0.5); no single scalar reported in the chapter

claims.text: NEGATIVE RESULT ON THE WATER-QUALITY ANGLE: this chapter — the authoritative IAHS/PUB synthesis on predicting duration curves in ungauged basins — contains NO treatment of concentration-duration curves, load-duration curves, TMDL practice, or any water-quality constituent. The only water-quality touchpoint in the entire chapter is a single citation, Bonta & Cleland (2003), 'Incorporating Natural Variability, Uncertainty, and Risk Into Water Quality Evaluations Using Duration Curves,' JAWRA 39(6):1481-1496, doi:10.1111/j.1752-1688.2003.tb04433.x, cited only in passing alongside Vogel & Fennessey (1995) for the generic technique of combining an FDC with a rating curve to build a derived duration curve (the worked examples given are habitat-duration and power-duration curves, not concentration or load). SEPARATELY, the chapter never uses the term 'QPPQ'; Archfield (2009) and Archfield & Vogel (2010) are cited only for recursive regression to prevent quantile-crossing and for map-correlation reference-gauge selection, not as a named QPPQ method. CONCLUSION: the load-duration-curve literature is genuinely underused as claimed, but it is NOT covered by this canonical source and must be sourced separately (Bonta & Cleland 2003 is the entry point); and the chapter also reports zero hierarchical/Bayesian mixed-model or random-intercept regionalisation, and zero quantile-regression-forest / distributional-GBDT work — the regionalisation toolkit reviewed is entirely regression, index-flow, geostatistical (Topkriging / PSBI) and process-based.
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (absence-of-coverage claim, verified over the full extracted text of the chapter)
claims.effectSize: 1 water-quality citation in ~90 references; 0 occurrences of 'QPPQ', 'load duration', 'TMDL', 'concentration duration', 'hierarchical Bayes', 'random effect', 'quantile regression forest'

result.sourceQuality: HIGH — authoritative peer-reviewed source, fully retrieved. This is Chapter 7 of Bloschl, Sivapalan, Wagener, Viglione & Savenije (eds), "Runoff Prediction in Ungauged Basins: Synthesis Across Processes, Places and Scales", Cambridge University Press 2013 (book doi:10.1017/CBO9781139235761), the capstone synthesis of the IAHS Decade on Predictions in Ungauged Basins. The file retrieved is the authors' accepted manuscript dated "July 29, 2012" hosted on Tufts (R.M. Vogel is a co-author), so page/figure numbering and minor wording may differ from the published chapter; all figures cited (7.13, 7.18-7.24) and Tables A7.1/A7.2 are referenced in text but the extracted text does not include the tables' per-study rows, so per-study catchment counts other than the "8 to 1080, median 49" range could not be recovered. CAVEATS ON USE: (a) WebFetch returned undecodable binary; text was extracted locally with pdftotext -layout, so quoted strings are verbatim from that extraction. (b) Every performance number here is for STREAMFLOW duration curves, not nitrate — transfer of the level/shape decomposition to concentration is an untested analogy, not an established result. (c) The chapter's own comparative assessment uses leave-one-out cross-validation over catchments, which IS a spatial holdout and therefore protocol-comparable in kind to this project's LOFO, but the metrics (ANE of FDC slope, NSE over FDC quantiles, R² of slope) are NOT numerically comparable to a classification AUC/PR-AUC. (d) The chapter is from 2012/2013 and predates the ML-based PUB literature entirely; it contains no machine-learning, deep-learning, or domain-adaptation content.

claims.text: The EPA load-duration-curve (LDC) framework is an explicit level/shape decomposition of exactly the kind this project needs: the 'shape' is the site's flow duration curve (a cumulative distribution of daily average flow, observations ranked high-to-low with exceedance percentile on the x-axis, log flow on the y-axis), and the 'level' is applied separately as Load = Flow (cfs) x target concentration (mg/L) x a unit conversion factor (0.002695 for tons/day). EPA's own worked nutrient example (Figure B-2, Sangamon River) builds a nitrate loading-capacity curve using the drinking-water MCL of 10 mg/L — the identical threshold to this project's `violation` definition — 'derived directly from the MCL (10 mg/L) and the duration curve ... across the range of all daily average flows'. However, the document is agency guidance, not a study: it reports NO predictive skill statistics, no validation, no cross-validation, and no error bars anywhere in its 74 pages.
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (guidance document; illustrative single-site figures only)
claims.effectSize: none reported — zero quantitative skill metrics in the document

claims.text: EPA explicitly acknowledges the ungauged-site problem and names three transfer methods, but supplies NO accuracy figures for any of them: 'Not all waters or watersheds have gaging stations or flow data available. In such cases estimation techniques are needed (USEPA, 2007). For instance, it may be appropriate to use flow data of a similar, representative water body to develop the duration curve, based on regression methods or drainage area ratios. The use of rainfall / runoff models can also be used to develop stream flow estimates for use in a duration curve analysis.' The document further warns that 'dealing with ungaged, headwater streams could present some obstacles in constructing a duration curve, as there is usually less data available on such waters.' This means the standard US TMDL practice for the exact deployment case (arbitrary ungauged pin) is drainage-area-ratio transfer, with no published error characterization in this source — regionalization skill must be sourced elsewhere.
claims.effectSize: no accuracy or transfer-error statistics reported for drainage-area ratio, regression, or rainfall-runoff FDC estimation

claims.text: The Appendix A South Carolina (Pee Dee River Basin, SCDHEC) fecal coliform case study specifies an operational index-gauge regression protocol for estimating flow at unmonitored water-quality stations, with an explicit numerical rejection threshold: all flow data are log-transformed to linearize; linear regressions are built between daily streamflow at the station to be filled/extended and streamflow at 'all gages within 93 miles (150 kilometers) that have at least 300 daily flow measurements on matching dates'; the gauge with the highest r-squared is chosen as the index gauge; and 'Flows will not be estimated based on regressions with r-squared values less than 0.25, even if that is the best regression.' Remaining gaps are filled from successively weaker index gauges. CRITICAL LIMITATION FOR THIS PROJECT: this method requires a donor gauge with concurrent record; where no coincident gauge exists it falls back to a 'watershed area ratio method derived by delineating subwatersheds, and relying on the Natural Resources Conservation Service runoff curve numbers and antecedent rainfall condition' — i.e. it still presumes an upstream or downstream gauge on the same network. Only the drainage-area-ratio / curve-number variant is usable at an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no gauged neighbor.
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (record infilling, not held-out prediction; no held-out evaluation performed)
claims.nBasins: unknown — case study covers 303(d)-listed SCDHEC WQM stations in the Pee Dee River Basin; exact station count not extractable from the text
claims.effectSize: r-squared >= 0.25 is the stated minimum acceptable donor-gauge regression; no out-of-sample error reported

claims.text: The canonical duration-curve binning is five fixed exceedance-percentile zones — high flows 0-10%, moist conditions 10-40%, mid-range 40-60%, dry conditions 60-90%, low flows 90-100% (Table 4-1, attributed to Cleland 2003) — chosen so that 'the midpoints of the moist, mid-range, and dry zones [are] at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles respectively (i.e., the quartiles). The high zone is centered at the 5th percentile, while the low zone is centered at the 95th percentile.' EPA states other schemes can be used depending on local hydrology, citing an arid Southwest stream with zero flow more than half the time where 'two, three, or four zones' may be preferable. This is directly testable as a discretization for a site-conditional model: bin site-days by a regionalized flow (or precipitation-runoff) percentile rather than by raw weather scalars, which is a coarse (5-bin) shape representation that could be transferred with far fewer effective degrees of freedom than 68 features — relevant given the n=19 independent basin families constraint.
claims.effectSize: 5 zones; midpoints at 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th percentiles

claims.text: EPA asserts a falsifiable diagnostic signature: the flow-percentile location of criterion exceedances discriminates pollutant source type. 'Impairments observed in the low flow zone typically indicate the influence of point sources, while those further left [high-flow zone] generally reflect potential nonpoint source contributions.' Table 4-1 formalizes this, rating point sources as High importance only in the low-flow zone and Medium in dry, while 'Storm water: Upland' is High in high/moist/mid-range zones and bank erosion High only at high flow. A supporting hydrograph-separation example (LaPlatte River, Figure 4-1) reports that surface runoff has 'its greatest effect during high flow conditions (median value of 61 percent)' of total streamflow. For Iowa row-crop nitrate — an upland nonpoint, tile-mediated source — this predicts violations should concentrate in the high/moist zones (0-40% exceedance), and the exceedance-vs-flow-percentile signature could serve as an unsupervised, transferable site descriptor. NOTE: EPA presents this as expert heuristic, with no statistics or classification accuracy given.
claims.nBasins: not-applicable (one illustrative gauge, LaPlatte River, for the 61% storm-flow figure)
claims.effectSize: surface runoff = 61% median fraction of total streamflow in the high-flow zone (LaPlatte River)

claims.text: EPA states explicit scope limits that constrain the LDC framework's applicability to nitrate specifically. Section 3a: 'The duration curve alone does not consider specific fate and transport mechanisms, which may vary depending on watershed or pollutant characteristics. Such processes may include sediment attenuation, plant uptake of nutrients, or chemical transformations.' It concludes 'The duration curve is more appropriate in cases where flow is a primary driver in pollutant delivery mechanisms, and other processes are a relatively insignificant part of the total loading', and 'Practitioners should consider using a separate analytical tool ... when factors other than flow significantly affect a water body's loading capacity.' Additionally, the SC case study excludes the tails from TMDL development: 'The extreme high flow conditions (<10th percentile) and low flow conditions (>95 percentile) are not considered in development of these TMDLs.'
