This is a NEGATIVE result of direct relevance: nitrate is subject to plant uptake and denitrification (the named exclusions), so a pure flow-percentile mapping is expected by EPA itself to be an incomplete predictor of nitrate concentration — consistent with this project's finding that a fixed weather-to-nitrate mapping fails to transfer the absolute level across basins. EPA also cautions the approach 'may not work in situations involving lakes or large coastal embayments'.
claims.effectSize: tails excluded: <10th and >95th flow percentiles; no quantitative bound on fate-and-transport error

result.sourceQuality: Authoritative primary agency source, retrieved in full and text-extracted successfully (EPA 841-B-07-006, August 2007, 74 pp; PDF fetched then converted locally with pdftotext because WebFetch could not decode the binary). It is GUIDANCE, not research: it contains zero predictive-skill statistics, no validation study, no cross-validation, no held-out evaluation, and no sample sizes of catchments. Every quantitative figure in it is a procedural threshold (percentile bin edges, r-squared >= 0.25 donor-gauge cutoff, unit conversion factors) or a single illustrative gauge value (61% storm-flow fraction, LaPlatte River). It therefore CANNOT supply any number comparable to this project's LOFO AUC 0.820. Its value to the research angle is threefold and structural rather than empirical: (1) it establishes that load-duration curves are the standard US regulatory formalism for separating hydrologic condition (flow exceedance percentile = the "when") from allowable level (criterion x flow = the "how high"), and that EPA's own nutrient worked example uses the 10 mg/L nitrate MCL — the same threshold as this project's violation target; (2) it documents that standard TMDL practice for ungauged water-quality stations is drainage-area-ratio or index-gauge regression transfer of the flow duration curve, i.e. the QPPQ family, but with NO published accuracy; (3) it supplies EPA's own limitations section flagging that duration curves ignore plant uptake of nutrients and chemical transformations, which is a caveat squarely aimed at nitrate. IMPORTANT GAPS relative to the assignment: this document contains NO concentration-duration curves (it plots instantaneous loads, not concentration quantiles), NO hierarchical/Bayesian or mixed-model content, NO random-effects-from-attributes regionalization, NO quantile regression forests or distributional GBDT, and NO quantile mapping or post-hoc site calibration. Those must be sourced from the peer-reviewed QPPQ / regional FDC literature (e.g. Hughes & Smakhtin 1996; Archfield & Vogel 2010; Smakhtin 2001) and from the hierarchical water-quality modeling literature. Reliability of extraction: high — all quotes verified against the extracted text at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isaac-dev-sustag/408994b9-8d9b-485d-9731-ba0bfa7507ce/scratchpad/ldc.txt (3,065 lines). One extraction limit: the exact count of SCDHEC WQM stations in the Appendix A Pee Dee case study could not be recovered from the linearized text, so nBasins is recorded as unknown for that claim rather than guessed.

claims.text: Kamrath & Yuan (2023, J. Environ. Manage., DOI 10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.117598) is a DESCRIPTIVE load-duration-curve study, NOT a QPPQ / regionalization / ungauged-prediction study. It builds no concentration-duration curves and performs NO ungauged-site validation of any kind; every number in the paper comes from watersheds with both a USGS discharge gauge and a long-term nutrient monitoring record. It therefore provides zero direct evidence that duration-curve transfer works for a site with no observations, and cannot be cited as support for the deployment case (arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin).
claims.nBasins: 14 watersheds (Ohio, western Lake Erie + Mississippi basins), 11–16,388 km^2
claims.effectSize: No predictive validation performed; in-sample descriptive statistics and in-sample multivariate linear regression only.

claims.text: The SHAPE of the nitrate load-duration relationship is strongly predictable from two static basin attributes alone. A multivariate linear regression of the percentage of annual load exported in the top-10% flow interval (m10%) on watershed area and agricultural land fraction achieved adj R2 = 0.86, F(2,10) = 37.7, p < 0.001, with area coefficient beta1 = -4.24 (p < 0.001) and agricultural-land coefficient beta2 = +1.1 (p < 0.001). For the moist-conditions interval (10–40th percentile) adj R2 = 0.71, F(2,10) = 15.8, p < 0.001 (area beta1 = +3.0, p = 0.002; ag land beta2 = -0.61, p = 0.02).
claims.nBasins: 13 (Cuyahoga removed as an outlier) of 14; df denominator = 10
claims.splitProtocol: unknown — reported statistics are in-sample fit (adj R2), no held-out or cross-validated skill reported

claims.text: This is a directly relevant precedent for the n=19-families constraint: the adj R2 = 0.86 attribute-to-load-shape regression was fit on only 13 independent gauged watersheds with 2 predictors. That sample size is the same order as this project's 19 independent basin families, so an attribute-driven regionalization of a site's nitrate DISTRIBUTION SHAPE (as opposed to a per-day time series) is statistically feasible at this project's n — unlike methods whose evidence base is CAMELS-scale (531–671 basins). The caveat is that adj R2 with n=13 and 2 predictors is an in-sample number with wide uncertainty and no out-of-sample confirmation.
claims.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.86 (m10% nitrate), adj R2 = 0.71 (m40%), 2 predictors, n = 13

claims.text: Nitrate export is concentrated in the highest flows but markedly LESS so than particulate constituents, and the between-watershed spread in this concentration is very large. Median m10% (fraction of annual load in the top 10% of flows) was 58% for NO3-N, 66% for dissolved reactive phosphorus, 72% for total phosphorus, and 77% for total suspended solids; NO3-N was significantly lower than TSS (p = 0.027). The upper 40% of flows carried 93% of annual NO3-N load. Individual watershed m10% values ranged from 20% (Cuyahoga, dissolved nutrients) to 96% (Lost Creek).
claims.effectSize: NO3-N median m10% = 58%; m40% = 93%; cross-watershed range 20%–96%

claims.text: The paper's mechanism for why nitrate deviates from particulates is TILE DRAINAGE: 'The tile drainage allows a portion of the dissolved nutrient load to be leached out of wet soil during smaller precipitation events that don't generate high flows,' and small agricultural watersheds with extensive tile drainage are described as more hydrologically reactive. This is an independent, peer-reviewed statement that tile drainage controls the flow-interval distribution of dissolved N export — supporting the project's existing identification of tile-drainage density as the missing dominant between-site control. The paper does NOT quantify tile density or include it as a regression predictor.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative/mechanistic only; tile drainage never enters any model as a numeric covariate.

claims.text: Two hard limitations restrict transfer of this work to the Iowa virtual-sensor problem. First, the entire framework requires a DISCHARGE TIME SERIES at the target site to place each day on the flow-duration curve — the project has streamflow at only 22 of 85 sites and none at an arbitrary deployment pin, so a load-duration-curve approach is not directly deployable without first regionalizing the FDC itself (which this paper does not do). Second, the authors state the study excludes spatial extent and that watershed morphological characteristics (basin length, slope, shape, drainage density) were not considered, and that results are limited to Ohio agricultural watersheds and may not represent other U.S. agricultural regions. Record lengths were also short and uneven: 3–21 years over 2000–2020, with only 4 of 14 sites having 20+ years.
claims.effectSize: Record length 3–21 years, period 2000–2020.

result.sourceQuality: Peer-reviewed research article in Journal of Environmental Management (Elsevier), DOI 10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.117598, open access via PubMed Central (PMC10168011). Authors Brock Kamrath and Yongping Yuan (US EPA-affiliated). Data sources are authoritative: USGS daily discharge plus the National Center for Water Quality Research (NCWQR) Heidelberg Tributary Loading Program, one of the highest-quality long-term nutrient monitoring datasets in the US Midwest. HIGH quality as a source, but LOW relevance to the specific research question as posed: it is a descriptive load-duration-curve/TMDL-practice paper, not a QPPQ or regionalization or ungauged-prediction paper. It contains no hierarchical/mixed model, no quantile mapping, no quantile regression forest, no domain adaptation, and no held-out spatial validation. Its one genuinely transferable contribution is the attribute-to-load-shape regression (adj R2 0.86 from area + ag land at n=13), which demonstrates that regionalizing a DISTRIBUTIONAL SUMMARY from static attributes is tractable at small n — the level/shape decomposition idea — even though the paper never frames it that way or tests it out of sample. Follow-up searching for the actual QPPQ/regional-FDC and hierarchical-Bayesian water-quality literature is required; this source does not cover it.

claims.text: Baggio & Muzy (2026, arXiv:2605.31079) directly test the exact methodological fork this project faces — direct binary classification of threshold exceedance (their model M1, MLP with binary cross-entropy, one model per threshold) versus modeling the full conditional distribution of the continuous target and integrating its tail (their M2, a neural network emitting parameters of a Multifractal-Rice distribution for wind speed and a zero-inflated lognormal for hourly rainfall) — and report that M2 was better or equal everywhere tested: 'metrics associated with model M2 are consistently better than the ones obtained with the classification approach M1', with no reported case where direct classification beat the distributional approach. Data: MeteoNet, southeastern France, 2016-2018, 278 wind stations and 268 rainfall stations, ~4.1e6 samples.
claims.effectSize: Direction only; paper reports results in log-scale figures, not tables. Peirce Skill Score for M2 rises as exceedance becomes rarer while M1's PSS 'sharply deteriorates when p->0'; Brier Skill Score shows 'faster degradation of BSS1 with respect to BSS2'. No exact PSS/BSS/CSI/HSS numbers are tabulated in the paper.
claims.nBasins: 278 wind stations / 268 rainfall stations (meteorological stations, not basins)
claims.splitProtocol: random-split (85/10/5 train/val/test) blocked by calendar day with a 17:00 UTC cutoff to prevent temporal autocorrelation leakage; NOT spatially held out — models are trained and tested on the same stations, so these numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820

claims.text: The mechanism Baggio & Muzy give for the distributional approach's advantage is a sample-size argument that applies directly to our 26.3% base rate and, more sharply, to any rarer threshold we might adopt: for direct binary classification 'the effective amount of information used to calibrate M1 parameters is pN instead of N', where p is the exceedance base rate and N the number of samples, whereas the distributional model 'can effectively learn the parameters of the conditional distribution even from moderate and mild intensity events'. Implication for us: our 160,074 site-days at p=0.263 give the classifier ~42,000 effective informative rows, while a regression/distributional head uses all 160,074 — but the gap the paper documents is largest as p->0 and is small at moderate p, so at p=0.263 the predicted gain is modest.
claims.effectSize: Theoretical asymptotic errors: E1 ~ p^(rho^2/(2+rho^2)) [ln(1/p)]^(-1/(2+rho^2)) versus E2 ~ p^((2+2rho^2)/(2+rho^2)) [ln(1/p)]^((1+rho^2)/(2+rho^2)), where rho^2 is the noise-to-signal ratio; the M2 advantage widens as p->0 and the two are comparable at moderate p
claims.splitProtocol: random-split (day-blocked), same stations in train and test

claims.text: Baggio & Muzy report that the choice of parametric family for the conditional distribution matters far less than getting its first two moments right: 'The specific parametric shape of the chosen distribution plays a secondary role compared to accurately capturing predictable shifts in its bulk properties (i.e., mean and variance).' They interpret this as extreme weather being driven by conditional displacement of the whole distribution rather than by intrinsic tail behaviour. For this project this is a falsifiable, cheap-to-test prediction: a heteroscedastic two-head model (predicted mean AND predicted variance of daily-max nitrate) integrated above 10 mg/L should recover most of the benefit, without needing an exotic tail distribution — and, critically, the between-site deficit we have (between_r2 0.21) is exactly a failure to place the conditional MEAN of an unseen basin, which this framing says is the dominant term.
claims.effectSize: Qualitative claim stated by the authors; no ablation numbers across distribution families are quoted in the text retrieved
claims.splitProtocol: random-split (day-blocked), same stations in train and test

claims.text: Baggio & Muzy explicitly considered and REJECTED extreme value theory for this task: they note that 'Many extreme weather nowcasting approaches integrate Extreme Value Theory (EVT) directly into modeling' and discuss the Peaks-Over-Threshold / Generalized Pareto Distribution route, but decline to use it because threshold selection introduces 'a notoriously difficult bias-variance trade-off', pursuing full-distribution parametric modeling instead. This is a documented negative-leaning judgement against POT/GPD for operational exceedance forecasting at moderate exceedance rates, and it is directly relevant here: at a 26.3% base rate our 10 mg/L violations are NOT in the EVT tail regime at all, so peaks-over-threshold machinery is unlikely to be the right tool for this project's primary target.
claims.effectSize: Not applicable — methodological rejection, no comparative numbers reported

claims.text: MAJOR LIMITATION FOR OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: Baggio & Muzy's evaluation is entirely in-station interpolation, not spatial transfer. Their exceedance thresholds are defined per-station ('thresholds Qp are calculated station-wise', i.e. as station-specific empirical quantiles rather than a single absolute physical threshold), and the paper contains no experiment applying a trained model to a station absent from training. Their protocol therefore measures WHEN exceedance happens at a known site — precisely the 'good timer' capability this project already has (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90) — and provides NO evidence about the between-site absolute-level problem that constitutes essentially all of our remaining headroom (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). Their skill numbers must not be compared to our LOFO 0.820 AUC.
claims.effectSize: No spatially-held-out results reported
claims.nBasins: 278 wind stations / 268 rainfall stations, all seen in training

claims.text: Baggio & Muzy's evaluation-metric set for threshold exceedance is proper scoring rules (Brier score and logarithmic score, reported as skill scores BSS relative to a climatological reference) PLUS threshold-dependent deterministic skill scores (Peirce Skill Score, Critical Success Index, Heidke Skill Score) evaluated as a function of the exceedance probability p — not AUC/PR-AUC. Because PSS, CSI and HSS are computed against a climatological/base-rate reference, they are far more comparable across studies with different base rates than raw AUC is; this project currently reports AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift) and Brier 0.137 but no BSS, PSS, CSI or HSS, which is a concrete reason our numbers cannot be benchmarked against this literature. Adding BSS against a base-rate-0.263 climatology and PSS/CSI/HSS at the operating point would make our LOFO results directly citable against exceedance-forecasting papers.
claims.effectSize: Metric-choice claim, no performance number attached; our Brier 0.137 against a 0.263-base-rate climatological Brier of 0.263*0.737 = 0.1938 implies BSS ~ 0.293 (derived here, not from the paper)
claims.splitProtocol: random-split (day-blocked), same stations in train and test

result.sourceQuality: Primary source, fully retrievable — arXiv abstract page plus complete HTML full text (arxiv.org/html/2605.31079) were both fetched successfully; not paywalled. This is an arXiv preprint (submitted 29 May 2026), so NOT peer-reviewed, and no DOI beyond the arXiv identifier. Authors: Roberta Baggio and Jean-Francois Muzy, Laboratoire Sciences Pour L'Environnement UMR 6134, CNRS / Universite de Corse. RELEVANCE CAVEAT: the paper is atmospheric (wind speed and hourly rainfall), NOT water quality — it contains NOTHING on the research question's second half: no nitrate MCL, no regulatory averaging period, no TMDL or stream-monitoring exceedance practice, no sensor-derived daily-statistic or sampling-frequency bias literature, and no virtual-sensor benchmark numbers. It answers only question (a), the methodology fork. KEY WEAKNESSES: (1) results are presented in log-scale figures with no numeric tables, so no exact PSS/BSS/CSI/HSS values can be quoted; (2) the split is day-blocked random over stations all seen in training, so nothing here is comparable to our LOFO protocol; (3) their thresholds are station-wise quantiles, whereas our 10 mg/L is a fixed absolute physical threshold, which makes the between-site level problem central for us and absent for them; (4) their headline advantage is asymptotic as p->0 and they concede comparability at moderate p, so at our p=0.263 the expected gain from switching to a distributional head is small. The n=19-independent-basin-families constraint does not directly bite here, since the recommended change is a modeling-head swap requiring no new spatial units — but note their evidence base is 278 stations of in-sample data, and their central mechanism (classifier sees only pN effective rows) is about TEMPORAL sample size, which we have in abundance, not about the between-site sample size of 19 where our actual deficit lies.

claims.text: EPA's official load-duration-curve guidance defines a fixed five-zone partition of the flow duration curve that is standard in US TMDL practice: high flows (0-10% exceedance), moist conditions (10-40%), mid-range flows (40-60%), dry conditions (60-90%), and low flows (90-100%), with zone midpoints placed at the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th percentiles respectively (p.2, Figure 1-1). The document explicitly states other schemes may be used depending on local hydrology, giving the example of an arid Southwest stream with no flow more than half the time where two-to-four zones may be preferable. This is a prescriptive framework, not an empirically validated one - no accuracy or skill numbers are attached to the zone scheme anywhere in the 74-page document.
claims.effectSize: no effect size reported; framework definition only

claims.text: The EPA LDC framework uses EXACTLY the same nitrate threshold as this project's violation label: Figure 2-1 and Appendix B Figure B-2 construct a nitrate loading-capacity duration curve using the drinking-water Maximum Contaminant Level of 10 mg/L, applied to the Sangamon River. The load duration curve is built as Load = Flow (cfs) x Concentration (mg/L) x conversion factor, applied across the range of all daily average flows, with the target held CONSTANT across all flow conditions for nitrate (p.4, p.7, p.38). The guidance explicitly lists nitrate alongside chloride and phosphorus as pollutants whose numeric target 'may be constant across all flow conditions'. This makes an exceedance of the LDC mathematically identical to concentration >= 10 mg/L - i.e. the LDC adds no information beyond the concentration threshold when the target is flow-invariant, and its value is purely diagnostic (WHICH flow zone the exceedances fall in), not predictive.
claims.nBasins: 1 (Sangamon River nitrate example); other examples: Portneuf River phosphorus, Mississippi River at Winona flow
claims.effectSize: n/a - definitional identity: LDC exceedance == concentration >= 10 mg/L when target is flow-constant

claims.text: NEGATIVE / GAP FINDING: EPA 841-B-07-006 acknowledges the ungauged problem in only two sentences and provides ZERO quantitative skill for ungauged duration-curve transfer. It states 'Not all waters or watersheds have gaging stations or flow data available. In such cases estimation techniques are needed... it may be appropriate to use flow data of a similar, representative water body to develop the duration curve, based on regression methods or drainage area ratios. The use of rainfall / runoff models can also be used' (p.2). Section 4b separately warns that 'dealing with ungaged, headwater streams could present some obstacles in constructing a duration curve, as there is usually less data available on such waters' (p.14). No RMSE, no Nash-Sutcliffe, no percent-error, no cross-validation, and no number of test basins is given for any of these transfer methods anywhere in the document. Anyone citing this EPA document as evidence that regional duration-curve transfer WORKS for ungauged sites is citing an unvalidated recommendation.
claims.effectSize: none reported - this is the falsifiable point: the document contains no ungauged-transfer error statistics

claims.text: The only concrete regionalization protocol in the document (Appendix A, South Carolina DHEC fecal coliform TMDL, Step 1, p.21) is an INDEX-GAUGE REGRESSION that requires a gauged neighbour and therefore CANNOT serve this project's deployment target (an arbitrary ungauged map pin). The exact rule: (i) use a USGS gauge if it lies within one-half mile upstream or downstream of the water-quality monitoring station; (ii) otherwise log-transform all flows to linearize, fit linear regressions between daily streamflow at the target gauge and streamflow at ALL gauges within 93 miles (150 kilometers) having at least 300 matching-date daily flow measurements, select the index gauge with the highest r-squared, and REJECT any regression with r-squared below 0.25 'even if that is the best regression' (a threshold the document admits 'was selected based on familiarity with using regression analysis in estimating flows', i.e. expert judgement, not derived); (iii) fill remaining gaps from successively weaker index gauges. The 0.25 r-squared floor is the only numeric quality bar stated anywhere in the guidance.
claims.splitProtocol: not-applicable (record infilling at gauged sites, not spatial holdout; no held-out evaluation reported)
claims.nBasins: unknown - number of SCDHEC WQM stations processed not stated in the extracted methodology section
claims.effectSize: r-squared >= 0.25 acceptance floor; 150 km search radius; >= 300 matching daily observations required

claims.text: For stations with no coincident gauge but with a gauge upstream and/or downstream, the EPA case study prescribes a WATERSHED-AREA-RATIO method: delineate subwatersheds for all impaired 303(d)-listed monitoring stations and all USGS flow stations, then scale flow by drainage area 'relying on the Natural Resources Conservation Service runoff curve numbers and antecedent rainfall condition' (p.21). Separately, Section 2e establishes UNIT-AREA NORMALIZATION as the guidance's mechanism for cross-basin comparability: flow expressed as cubic feet per second per square mile, because 'Unit area rates, determined by dividing the drainage area at the gage into the flow, enable a consistent way to compare flows from watersheds of different sizes' (p.9). Note both methods still presuppose a gauged donor basin - area-ratio scaling has no donor for an arbitrary pin, and unit-area normalization is a rescaling, not a level predictor.
claims.effectSize: none reported for area-ratio transfer accuracy

claims.text: The guidance states two conditions that bound when a duration-curve framework is valid, both directly relevant to nitrate in tile-drained Iowa: (1) 'The duration curve alone does not consider specific fate and transport mechanisms... Such processes may include sediment attenuation, plant uptake of nutrients, or chemical transformations' and 'The duration curve is more appropriate in cases where flow is a primary driver in pollutant delivery mechanisms, and other processes are a relatively insignificant part of the total loading' (p.11, Section 3a); (2) on record length, 'While the number of observations required to develop a flow duration curve is not rigorously specified, a flow duration curve is usually based on more than 1 year of observations, and encompasses inter-annual and seasonal variations. Ideally, the drought and flood of record are included' (p.21). In the SC case study, 'The extreme high flow conditions (<10th percentile) and low flow conditions (>95 percentile) are not considered in development of these TMDLs' (p.21), and seasonal variation was addressed by 'using more than 5 years of water quality' data (Section 5.5). Interpretation flag: because nitrate is strongly modulated by plant uptake and denitrification, EPA's own criterion for LDC appropriateness (flow as the dominant driver, other processes insignificant) is the assumption most at risk for this application.
claims.effectSize: >1 year minimum record (not rigorously specified); >5 years water quality data used for seasonality in case study; percentiles <10th and >95th excluded

result.sourceQuality: Authoritative primary agency source, retrieved and read in full (74 pp., EPA 841-B-07-006, August 2007). PDF was fetched successfully but WebFetch could not parse it; text was extracted locally with pdftotext -layout (3,065 lines) and read directly, so all quotes are verbatim from the primary document, not from a mirror or abstract. IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON RELEVANCE TO THE RESEARCH ANGLE: this is a regulatory/procedural guidance document, NOT a validation study. It is the canonical definition of the load-duration-curve method and confirms that LDCs are standard US TMDL practice with nitrate at exactly the 10 mg/L threshold this project uses, but it contains no performance metrics of any kind - no RMSE, no Nash-Sutcliffe, no cross-validation, no number of test basins, and no comparison of methods. It therefore CANNOT support any claim that regional/ungauged duration-curve transfer achieves a given level of skill. It also contains nothing on QPPQ proper (the query-percentile-percentile streamflow transfer method of Fennessey/Hughes-Smakhtin), nothing on quantile mapping, nothing on hierarchical or Bayesian partial-pooling models, nothing on quantile regression forests or distributional GBDT, and nothing on domain adaptation - those must be sourced elsewhere (suggest Farmer 2016 HESS on QPPQ, Archfield & Vogel 2010 WRR on nearest-neighbour FDC transfer, Smakhtin 1999, and the GAGES-II / USGS regional FDC regression literature). The one operationally useful piece for this project's deployment target is negative: every ungauged technique the document names (index-gauge log-linear regression within 150 km with r-squared floor 0.25, drainage-area ratio with NRCS curve numbers, rainfall-runoff modelling) requires a gauged donor basin, which the arbitrary-map-pin product does not have. Its constructive contribution is conceptual rather than predictive: the five-zone FDC partition and unit-area normalization are a defensible way to STRATIFY and REPORT predictions, and the LDC diagnostic (do exceedances cluster in high-flow vs low-flow zones) distinguishes nonpoint-source from point-source signatures, which could be a useful output-side framing - but note that when the water quality target is flow-invariant (as it is for nitrate at 10 mg/L), an LDC exceedance is algebraically identical to a concentration exceedance, so the LDC adds zero predictive information over the existing binary violation label. Given the project's 22-of-85-sites discharge coverage and zero discharge at all 61 IWQIS sites, even the diagnostic use is unavailable at most sites without first solving ungauged flow prediction. Confidence in the extracted claims: high (verbatim quotes with page numbers). Confidence that this angle yields a performance gain: low, based on this source alone.
